Mishnah according to the text of the Kaufmann Manuscript, following the corrector who added the vocalization.
The vocalization <note>the system of dots and dashes used to indicate vowels in Hebrew</note> was corrected according to grammatical rules regarding full and deficient spelling, and according to the sound regarding the *Qamatz* and *Patah*, *Tsere* and *Segol*, which are interchanged in the Kaufmann Manuscript due to Sephardic pronunciation.
Changes in the numbering of the laws have been noted.

# Tractate Berakhot
<note>Tractate 'Berakhot' (Blessings) is the first volume of the Mishnah, focusing on prayers and thanksgivings.</note>

## Chapter 1
### Tractate Berakhot, Chapter 1, Mishnah 1

**A**
**From what time do we recite the *Shema* in the evenings?** <note>The 'Shema' is the central declaration of Jewish faith, traditionally recited twice daily.</note>
**From the time that the priests enter to eat their contribution,** <term>Terumah: a portion of the harvest given to the priests which could only be eaten when the priest was ritually pure at nightfall</term>
**until the end of the first watch.** <note>The night was divided into three 'watches'; the first ended approximately four hours after sunset.</note>
**These are the words of Rabbi Eliezer.**
**But the Sages say:**
**Until midnight.**
**Rabban Gamliel says:**
**Until the break of dawn.**

**B**
**It once happened that his sons came home from a banquet hall;**
**they said to him:**
**"We have not yet recited the *Shema*."**
**He said to them:**
**"If the dawn has not yet broken,**
**you are permitted to recite it."**

**C**
**And not only in this case,**
**but in every instance where the Sages said "until midnight,"**
**the performance of the commandment is actually permitted until the break of dawn.**

**D**
**The burning of sacrificial fats and limbs, [and the eating of the Passover offerings]** <note>original: "ואכילת פסחים" (and the eating of Passover offerings); these words appear in the manuscript but were struck through by the corrector</note>
**the performance of their commandment lasts until the break of dawn;**

**E**
**Everything that is designated to be eaten for one day,**
**the performance of its commandment lasts until the break of dawn.**

<summary>This page introduces the first laws of the Mishnah, debating the time limits for the evening recitation of the Shema and establishing dawn as the functional deadline for various religious obligations.</summary>
<keywords>Shema, Berakhot, evening prayer, Terumah, Rabbi Eliezer, Rabban Gamliel, dawn, midnight, sacrificial law, Kaufmann Manuscript</keywords>

--- Page 2 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the time limits for the evening Shema before transitioning into the laws regarding the morning Shema and the proper physical posture for its recitation. It maintains the numbering system found in the Kaufmann Manuscript.</meta>

If so, why did the Sages say "until midnight"?
Rather, it was to keep a person far from transgression. <note>The Sages set an earlier deadline (midnight) than the actual legal limit (dawn) to ensure that a person does not procrastinate and accidentally miss the window for the commandment.</note>

### Tractate Berakhot, Chapter 1, Mishnah 2

->7<-

**From what time do we recite the *Shema* in the mornings?**
**From the time when one can distinguish between blue and white;** <term>Tekhelet: a specific sky-blue dye used for ritual fringes, which looks like white in low light.</term>
**Rabbi Eliezer says:**
**Between blue and leek-green,** <term>Karti: a shade of green similar to a leek; Rabbi Eliezer requires more light to distinguish these closer colors.</term>
**until sunrise.**
**Rabbi Yehoshua says:**
**Until three hours into the day,**
**for such is the way of princes—to rise at three hours.** <note>The "hours" mentioned here are 'seasonal hours,' calculated by dividing the daylight into twelve equal parts.</note>
**One who recites from then on has not lost out,**
**for he is like a person who reads from the Torah.** <note>Even though the specific time for the morning obligation has passed, the person still receives the merit of studying sacred scripture.</note>

### Tractate Berakhot, Chapter 1, Mishnah 3

->8<-

**The House of Shammai say:** <note>Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel were the two primary schools of legal thought in the 1st century CE.</note>
**In the evening, all people should recline and recite,**
**and in the morning they should stand, as it is said:**
**(Deuteronomy 6:7) "when you lie down and when you rise up."**
**The House of Hillel say:**
**Every person recites in their own way, as it is said:**
**(Deuteronomy 6:7) "and when you walk on the way."**
**If so, why is it said "when you lie down and when you rise up"?**
**Rather, it refers to the time when people usually lie down,**
**and the time when people usually rise up.**

->9<-

**Rabbi Tarfon said:**
**"I was once traveling on the road,**
**and I reclined to recite according to the words of the House of Shammai,**
**and I endangered myself because of bandits."** <note>By stopping and reclining on a dangerous road, he made himself a target for "listim" (robbers/bandits).</note>
**They said to him:**
**"You were deserving of whatever might have happened to you,**
**for you transgressed the words of the House of Hillel."**

### Tractate Berakhot, Chapter 1, Mishnah 4

->10<-

<vocab>Mishnah, Berakhot, Shema, House of Shammai, House of Hillel, Rabbi Tarfon, Recitation of the Shema</vocab>

<summary>This page defines the timeframe for the morning Shema based on daylight and social habits, and records a debate on whether the prayer must be recited in a specific physical posture.</summary>

In the morning, one recites two blessings before it and one after it;
and in the evening, two before it and two after it,
one long and one short.
Where they said to lengthen, one is not permitted to shorten;
to shorten, one is not permitted to lengthen;
to seal, one is not permitted not to seal;
and not to seal, one is not permitted to seal. <note>original: "לַחְתֹּם" (to seal). This refers to the formal closing of a blessing with the formula "Blessed are You, Lord..." Some blessings conclude this way (long), while others do not (short).</note>

# Tractate Berakhot Chapter 1 Mishnah 5

->11<-

One mentions the Exodus from Egypt at nights.
Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah said:
"Behold, I am like a man of seventy years old,
yet I did not merit to understand why the Exodus from Egypt should be mentioned at night,
until Ben Zoma expounded it, as it is said:
> (Deuteronomy 16:3) 'So that you may remember the day of your departure from the land of Egypt **all** the days of your life.'
'The days of your life' refers to the days;
'**all** the days of your life' refers to the nights." <note>The inclusion of the word "all" is seen by the Sages as an expansion of the commandment to include the nighttime recitation of the Shema's third paragraph.</note>
And the Sages say:
"The days of your life" refers to this world;
"**all** the days of your life" is to include the days of the Messiah. <note>The Sages argue that even in the future redemption, the memory of the original Exodus from Egypt will remain central.</note>

# Chapter 2

## Tractate Berakhot Chapter 2 Mishnah 1

->1<-

If one was reading in the Torah and the time for the recitation [of the *Shema*] arrived;
if he focused his heart, he has fulfilled his obligation,
and if not, he has not fulfilled it. <note>This introduces the concept of <term>Kavanah</term> (intentionality). Simply reading the words of the Bible is not enough; one must have the specific intent to fulfill the religious duty of the Shema.</note>
And at the breaks,
one may greet someone out of respect and respond [to a greeting];
and in the middle [of a section],
one may greet someone out of fear and respond;
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
In the middle,
one may greet out of fear and respond out of respect;
and at the breaks,
one may greet out of respect and respond with "Peace" to any person. <note>"Fear" in this context refers to greeting someone of great authority, such as a king or a parent, where silence might be dangerous or deeply offensive. "Respect" refers to social peers or elders.</note>

## Tractate Berakhot Chapter 2 Mishnah 2

These are the [permitted pauses] between the sections:
Between the first blessing and the second;
between the second blessing and the "Shema";
between the "Shema" and "And it shall come to pass if you surely listen"; <note>original: "וְהָיָה אִם שָׁמֹעַ" (Vahaya Im Shamoa). This is the second paragraph of the Shema prayer (Deuteronomy 11:13–21).</note>
between "And it shall come to pass if you surely listen" and "And the Lord spoke"; <note>original: "וַיֹּאמֶר" (Vayomer). This is the third paragraph of the Shema (Numbers 15:37–41), which discusses the ritual fringes (Tzitzit).</note>
and between "And the Lord spoke" and "True and Firm." <note>original: "אֱמֶת וְיַצִּיב" (Emet Veyatziv). This is the blessing recited immediately after the Shema.</note>
Rabbi Yehuda says:
Between "And the Lord spoke" and "True and Firm,"
one may not pause. <note>Rabbi Yehuda believes the connection between the end of the Shema (which mentions God taking the Israelites out of Egypt) and the start of the next blessing (which affirms God's truth) must be seamless.</note>

# 3

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha said:
Why does the "Shema" section precede the "And it shall come to pass if you surely listen" section?
So that one may first accept upon himself the **Kingdom of Heaven**,
and afterwards accept upon himself the **Yoke of the Commandments**. <note>The first paragraph of the Shema is a declaration of God's oneness; the second paragraph is a commitment to perform His laws.</note>
And why does "And it shall come to pass if you surely listen" precede "And the Lord spoke"?
Because "And it shall come to pass if you surely listen" applies both by day and by night,
while "And the Lord spoke" applies only by day. <note>The third paragraph discusses the *Tzitzit* (fringes). Since the Torah says "and you shall see them," the commandment is traditionally linked to the hours of visibility (daylight).</note>

## Tractate Berakhot Chapter 2 Mishnah 3

# 4

One who recites the Shema but does not make it audible to his own ear <note>Whispering so softly that even the speaker cannot hear the words.</note>
has **fulfilled his duty**. <term>Fulfilled his duty (Yatza): To have successfully performed a religious obligation so that it does not need to be repeated.</term>
Rabbi Yose says:
He has **not fulfilled his duty**.
If one recited it but was not precise in its lettering, <note>Failure to clearly enunciate the distinct sounds of the Hebrew letters, which might change the meaning of the words.</note>
Rabbi Yose says:
He has **fulfilled his duty**.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
He has **not fulfilled his duty**.
One who recites it out of order has **not fulfilled his duty**.
If one recited it and made a mistake, he must return to the place where he erred.

## Tractate Berakhot Chapter 2 Mishnah 4

# 5

Craftsmen may recite [the Shema] while at the top of a tree or at the top of a layer of stones, <note>original: "הַנִּדְבָּךְ" (Nidvakh). A row or course of stones in a wall under construction.</note>
which they are not permitted to do regarding the **Prayer**. <note>The "Prayer" (Tefillah) here refers to the *Amidah* (The Standing Prayer). Because the Shema is a biblical obligation with a strict timeframe, the Sages allowed workers to recite it where they stood to avoid danger or loss of work time. The *Amidah*, however, requires deeper focus and a standing posture on the ground.</note>

->6<-

A groom is exempt from the recitation of the *Shema* <note>original: "קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע" (Kriyat Shema). This is the central declaration of faith in Jewish prayer.</note> on the first night of his marriage, and until the conclusion of the Sabbath, if he has not yet consummated the marriage. <note>original: "לֹא עָשָׂה מַעֲשֶׂה" (literally, "did not do the deed"). The exemption exists because the groom is assumed to be too mentally preoccupied with his new marriage to focus with the required intention.</note> It happened with **Rabban Gamliel** that he recited the *Shema* on the night he was married. His students said to him: "Our teacher, did you not teach us that a groom is exempt from the recitation of the *Shema* on the first night?" He said to them: "I will not listen to you to remove from myself the **Kingdom of Heaven** even for a single hour."

->Tractate Berakhot Chapter 2 Mishnah 6<-

->7<-

He also bathed on the first night after his wife died. His students said to him: "Did you not teach us that a mourner is forbidden to bathe?" He said to them: "I am not like all other men; I am <term>sensitive</term>." <note>original: "אִסְטְנִיס" (istinis). Derived from the Greek word for "weak" or "delicate," it refers here to someone whose physical discomfort is so great that it prevents them from functioning or focusing without bathing.</note>

->Tractate Berakhot Chapter 2 Mishnah 7<-

->8<-

And when **Tabi**, his servant, died, he accepted condolences for him. His students said to him: "Did you not teach us that one does not accept condolences for the death of servants?" He said to them: "My servant Tabi was not like all other servants; he was <term>worthy</term>." <note>original: "כָּשֵׁר" (kasher). While today this usually refers to food, here it refers to Tabi’s character, meaning he was "proper," "upright," or "pious."</note>

->Tractate Berakhot Chapter 2 Mishnah 8<-

->9<-

A groom, if he wishes to recite the *Shema* on the first night, may recite it. **Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel** says: "Not everyone who wishes to take the **Name** may take it." <note>This refers to a "reputation for piety." Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel argues that if an ordinary person performs a religious act they are exempt from, it may appear as "spiritual arrogance" or showing off, unless they are already known for exceptional devotion.</note>

### Chapter 3

->Tractate Berakhot Chapter 3 Mishnah 1<-

<summary>This page records several legal precedents set by Rabban Gamliel, who chose to follow stricter personal standards for prayer and mourning than the general law required. It highlights the tension between established exemptions for life events (like marriage or mourning) and the personal desire for constant devotion.</summary>

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the personal anecdotes of Rabban Gamliel in Chapter 2 to the formal legal rulings (Mishnahs) of Chapter 3. The previous page ended abruptly while discussing Rabban Gamliel’s servant, Tabi. This page begins a new chapter focusing on how life’s circumstances—such as mourning, social status, or ritual impurity—affect one's obligation to perform daily prayers.</meta>

#### 1
One whose dead [relative] lies before them [unburied] is **exempt** from the recitation of the *Shema* <note>original: "קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע" (Kriyat Shema). This central prayer requires intense concentration, which a person in immediate grief is assumed to lack.</note> and from the requirement to wear *Tefillin*. <note>original: "תְּפִלִּין" (Tefillin). These are ritual leather boxes containing Torah verses, worn on the arm and head during prayer.</note> Regarding the pallbearers of the bier, their replacements, and the replacements of their replacements: those who are in front of the bier and those who are behind the bier—those whose services are needed for the bier are **exempt**, while those whose services are not needed for the bier are **obligated**. Both groups, however, are **exempt** from the *Amidah* prayer. <note>original: "תְּפִלָּה" (Tefillah). In the Mishnah, this specifically refers to the "Standing Prayer," the core petitionary service.</note>

### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 3 Mishnah 2
#### 2
Once they have buried the dead and returned: if they are able to start and finish [the prayer] before they reach the **line**, <note>original: "שּׁוּרָה" (shurah). This refers to a formal arrangement where the community stands in two rows to comfort the mourners as they pass between them.</note> they should start; but if not, they should not start. Of those standing in the line: those on the inner side <note>Those close enough to see and comfort the mourner.</note> are **exempt**, but those on the outer side are **obligated**.

### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 3 Mishnah 3
#### 3
**Women, slaves, and minors** are **exempt** from the recitation of the *Shema* and from *Tefillin*, but they are **obligated** in the *Amidah* prayer, the *Mezuzah*, <note>original: "מְזוּזָה" (Mezuzah). The parchment scroll containing Torah verses placed on doorposts.</note> and the **Grace After Meals**. <note>original: "בִּרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן" (Birkat Hamazon). The blessings recited after eating a meal containing bread.</note>

### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 3 Mishnah 4
#### 4
One who has had a seminal emission <term>Ba'al Keri</term> <note>original: "בַּעַל קֶרִי" (Ba'al Keri). According to ancient ritual purity laws attributed to Ezra, a man who experienced an emission was restricted from reciting holy words until he immersed in a ritual bath.</note> should meditate on the prayer in his heart but does not recite the blessing—neither the blessings before it nor after it. And regarding food: he recites the blessing after it, but does not recite the blessing before it. **Rabbi Yehuda** says: He recites the blessings both before them and after them.

### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 3 Mishnah 5
#### 5
If he was standing in the *Amidah* prayer and remembered that he is a <term>Ba'al Keri</term>...

He should not interrupt, but rather shorten [his recitation]. He should go down to immerse [in a ritual bath]; if he is able to come up, cover himself, and recite [the *Shema*] before the sun rises, he should come up, cover himself, and recite. But if not, he should cover himself in the water and recite. However, he may not cover himself in "foul water" <note>original: "הַמַּיִם הָרָעִים" (ha-mayim ha-ra'im). Stagnant or smelly water.</note> nor in "soaking water" <note>original: "מֵי הַמִּשְׁרָה" (mei ha-mishrah). Water in which flax has been soaked, which becomes pungent.</note> until he pours [clean] water into them. How far must he distance himself from feces? Four cubits. <note>A cubit, or "ammah," is approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters. This is the standard distance required for maintaining the sanctity of prayer.</note>

### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 3 Mishnah 6
->6<-
A *zav* <note>original: "זָב" (zav). A man experiencing a specific type of genital discharge that renders him ritually impure.</note> who had a seminal emission, a menstruant <note>original: "נִדָּה" (niddah).</note> who discharged semen [after previous intercourse], and a woman who had intercourse and then saw [the onset of] her menstrual flow—all these require immersion <note>Specifically, the "immersion of Ezra," a decree requiring ritual washing before studying Torah or praying after seminal contact.</note>; Rabbi Yehuda **exempts** them.

# Chapter 4
### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 4 Mishnah 1
->1<-
The **Morning Prayer** <note>The *Shacharit* Amidah prayer.</note> may be recited until midday; Rabbi Yehuda says: until four hours [into the day]. <note>In Jewish law, "hours" are calculated by dividing the daylight into 12 equal parts; thus, "four hours" is the end of the first third of the day.</note> The **Afternoon Prayer** <note>The *Mincha* prayer.</note> may be recited until the evening; Rabbi Yehuda says: until the "half-Mincha" <note>original: "פְּלַג הַמִּנְחָה" (plag ha-mincha). This is 1.25 seasonal hours before sunset.</note>. The **Evening Prayer** <note>The *Maariv* prayer.</note> has no fixed [end] time. And the **Additional Prayers** <note>original: "מוּסָפִים" (Musafim). Recited on Sabbaths, New Moons, and Festivals.</note> may be recited all day; Rabbi Yehuda says: until seven hours [into the day].

### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 4 Mishnah 2
->2<-
Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah used to pray a short prayer upon his entry to the House of Study and upon his departure. <note>The Talmud later explains that he prayed for no errors to occur in his rulings upon entering, and gave thanks for his portion in the study of Torah upon leaving.</note>

## Tractate Berakhot Chapter 4 Mishnah 3

### 3

->Rabban Gamliel says:<-
->Every day a person should pray the **Eighteen Blessings**.<- <note>original: "שְׁמוֹנֶה עֶשְׂרֵה" (Shmoneh Esreh). This is the central prayer of the Jewish liturgy, now commonly called the *Amidah* (The Standing Prayer). While it now contains nineteen blessings, it retains its historical name.</note>

->he prays the Eighteen;<-
->and if not,<-
->an abbreviated Eighteen.<-

## Tractate Berakhot Chapter 4 Mishnah 4

### 4

->Rabbi Eliezer says:<-
->One who makes his prayer a **fixed routine**,<- <note>original: "קֶבַע" (keva). This refers to prayer said only out of a sense of burden or rote habit, without personal connection or emotional investment.</note>
->his prayer is not a true **supplication**.<- <note>original: "תַּחֲנוּנִים" (tachanunim). Heartfelt pleas for grace and mercy.</note>
->Rabbi Yehoshua says:<-
->One who travels in a **place of danger**<-
->prays a short prayer, an abbreviation of the Eighteen,<-
->and says:<-
> "Save, O Lord, Your people Israel;
> at every **crossroads** <note>original: "פָּרָשַׁת הָעִבּוּר" (parashat ha'ibur). A difficult phrase that refers to times of transition, crisis, or even when the people are straying. The prayer asks that God remain mindful of their needs even in such moments.</note> may their needs be before You;
> Blessed are You, O Lord, who hears prayer."

### 5

The innermost and most sacred chamber of the Temple in Jerusalem. Even without physical orientation, the worshiper's internal focus must be toward the spiritual center.</note>

## Tractate Berakhot Chapter 4 Mishnah 6

->6<-

->**If one was sitting in a boat, or in a wagon, or on a raft,**<- <note>original: "אַסְדָּא" (asda). A raft or a float made of bound logs.</note>
->**he should direct his heart toward the Holy of Holies.**<- <note>original: "בֵּית קֹדֶשׁ הַקֳּדָשִׁים" (Beit Kodesh HaKodashim). This refers to the innermost chamber of the Temple in Jerusalem. Even when one cannot physically turn toward Jerusalem due to being on a moving vehicle, the mental intention must be directed there.</note>

->(Tractate Berakhot Chapter 4 Mishnah 7)<-

->**Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah says:**<-
->**The Additional Prayer is only said in a communal assembly.**<- <note>original: "תְּפִלַּת הַמּוּסָפִים" (Tefillat HaMusafim). This is an extra prayer service recited on Sabbaths, New Moons, and Festivals. The term "חֶבֶר עִיר" (Chever Ir) refers to a public quorum or a community gathering.</note>
->**And the Sages say:**<-
->**In a communal assembly or not in a communal assembly.**<- <note>The Sages argue that an individual may recite the Musaf prayer even when praying alone.</note>
->**Rabbi Yehuda says in his name:**<- <note>Speaking in the name of Rabbi Eleazar.</note>
->**Anywhere there is a communal assembly,**<-
->**the individual is exempt from the Additional Prayer.**<- <note>Rabbi Yehuda clarifies Rabbi Eleazar's view: if a community is praying Musaf, an individual nearby who is not part of that quorum is exempt because the community fulfills the obligation for everyone.</note>

# Chapter 5
## Tractate Berakhot Chapter 5 Mishnah 1

->1<-

->**One does not stand to pray except with a heavy head.**<- <note>original: "כֹּבֶד רֹאשׁ" (Koved Rosh). A Hebrew idiom for a state of reverence, humility, and serious-mindedness, as opposed to lightheadedness or frivolity.</note>
->**The early pious ones**<- <note>original: "חֲסִידִים הָרִאשׁוֹנִים" (Chasidim HaRishonim). A group in the late Second Temple period known for their meticulous and joyful observance of the commandments.</note>
->**would wait one hour and then pray,**<-
->**so that they might direct their hearts to the Omnipresent.**<- <note>original: "לַמָּקוֹם" (LaMakom). Literally "The Place," a rabbinic name for God, implying that God is the "place" of the world, but the world is not His only place.</note>
->**Even if a king greets him,**<-
->**he should not respond;**<-
->**and even if a snake is coiled around his heel,**<-
->**he should not interrupt.**<- <note>This emphasizes the total absorption required during the Eighteen Blessings, though later Jewish law clarifies that one may interrupt if there is a life-threatening danger.</note>

## Tractate Berakhot Chapter 5 Mishnah 2

->2<-

->**We mention the "Power of Rain" in the [blessing of] the Resurrection of the Dead,**<- <note>original: "גְּבוּרוֹת גְּשָׁמִים" (Gevurot Geshamim). Praise for God's power in providing rain is inserted into the second blessing of the Amidah because rain gives life to the world just as the resurrection gives life to the dead.</note>
->**and we ask for rain in the "Blessing of the Years,"**<- <note>The ninth blessing of the Amidah, which deals with physical sustenance and agriculture.</note>
->**and the Havdalah in "Gracious Giver of Knowledge."**<- <note>original: "הַבְדָּלָה" (Havdalah). The prayer marking the end of the Sabbath and the "separation" between the sacred and the profane. It is inserted into the fourth blessing (Knowledge) because one needs wisdom to distinguish between the holy and the ordinary.</note>
->**Rabbi Akiva says:**<-
->**One says it as a fourth blessing on its own.**<- <note>He believes Havdalah should be its own distinct blessing on Saturday night, rather than being tucked into the existing blessing for knowledge.</note>
->**Rabbi Eliezer says:**<-
->**In the [Blessing of] Thanksgiving.**<- <note>The eighteenth blessing of the Amidah.</note>

## Tractate Berakhot Chapter 5 Mishnah 3

->3<-

->**One who says:**<-
->**"May Your mercy reach even to a bird's nest,"**<- <note>The Mishnah begins to list phrases that lead to a person being silenced during prayer, often because they imply a misunderstanding of God's laws (e.g., suggesting that the commandment to shoo away a mother bird is based solely on "mercy" rather than a divine decree).</note>

### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 6 Mishnah 1

**1**
**How does one bless over fruits?**
Over fruit of the tree, one says:
**"Blessed are You... Who creates the fruit of the tree,"** <note>original: "Borei pri ha-etz." This is the standard blessing for most fruits that grow on perennial trees.</note>
except for wine,
for over wine one says:
**"Blessed are You... Who creates the fruit of the vine."** <note>original: "Borei pri ha-gafen." Because of its importance and its role in sanctifying the Sabbath and festivals, wine receives a specific, more prestigious blessing than other fruit juice.</note>
And over fruits of the earth, one says:
**"Blessed are You... Who creates the fruit of the ground,"** <note>original: "Borei pri ha-adamah." This applies to produce from plants that must be replanted annually or do not have a permanent woody trunk.</note>
except for bread,
for over bread one says:
**"Blessed are You... Who brings forth bread from the earth."** <note>original: "Hamotzi lechem min ha-aretz." Like wine, bread is a dietary staple and thus earns a unique blessing.</note>
And over vegetables, one says:
**"Blessed are You... Who creates the fruit of the ground."**
**Rabbi Yehuda** says:
One says, **"Who creates various kinds of herbs."** <note>original: "Borei minei desha'im." Rabbi Yehuda argues for more specific language when blessing over leafy greens rather than the general "fruit of the ground."</note>

---

### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 6 Mishnah 2

**2**
If one blessed over fruit of the tree [saying], **"Who creates the fruit of the ground,"**
**he has fulfilled his obligation;** <note>This is because, technically, a tree also grows from the ground, making the blessing factually true even if it is not the preferred specific wording.</note>
but over fruits of the earth, [if he said], **"Who creates the fruit of the tree,"**
**he has not fulfilled his obligation.** <note>Because a vegetable or ground-plant is not a tree; therefore, the blessing is factually incorrect.</note>
And for all of them, if one said, **"By whose word everything came to be,"**
**he has fulfilled his obligation.** <note>original: "Shehakol nihyah bidvaro." This is a general, all-encompassing blessing of gratitude for God's creation.</note>

---

### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 6 Mishnah 3

**3**
Over a thing that does not grow from the ground, one says:
**"By whose word everything came to be."** <note>This includes animal products like meat, milk, eggs, and fish, as well as water and salt.</note>
Over vinegar, and over locusts, and over shriveled fruit, one says:
**"By whose word everything came to be."** <note>original: "Govai" (locusts) and "Novlot" (fallen or wind-blasted fruit). These are considered inferior foods or items that have changed for the worse.</note>
**Rabbi Yehuda** says:
**For anything that is a type of curse, one does not recite a blessing over it.** <note>Rabbi Yehuda believes that because locusts are a plague and vinegar is spoiled wine, they represent "curses" or divine punishment, making it inappropriate to bless God for them as one would for a gift.</note>

---

### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 6 Mishnah 4

**4**
If there were many types [of food] before him,
**Rabbi Yehuda** says:
If there is among them one of the **seven species**, <term>Seven Species: The seven agricultural products praised in the Bible as special to the Land of Israel: wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives, and dates.</term>

...over it he blesses. 
And the **Sages** say: 
He may bless over whichever of them he prefers. <note>The debate here concerns a situation where someone has multiple foods of the same blessing category (e.g., two different fruits). ### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 6 Mishnah 5

**5**
If one blessed over the **wine** before the meal, 
he exempts the wine served after the meal. 
If one blessed over the **appetizer** <note>original: "parperet." This refers to side dishes, hors d'oeuvres, or savory snacks eaten to stimulate the appetite.</note> before the meal, 
he exempts the appetizer served after the meal. 
If one blessed over the **bread**, 
he exempts the appetizer; 
but if he blessed over the **appetizer**, 
he does not exempt the bread. 
The **House of Shammai** say: 
[The blessing over bread] does not even exempt **cooked grain dishes**. <note>original: "ma'aseh kederah." This refers to cooked porridges or pasta-like dishes made from the five species of grain. Shammai argues that bread is a distinct category and does not cover these other grain products.</note>

### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 6 Mishnah 6

**6**
If they were **sitting** <note>Meaning they were eating together informally without a designated leader.</note>, 
each and every person blesses for themselves; 
If they **reclined** <note>original: "hesebu." In the Greco-Roman style of formal dining, reclining on couches indicated a communal, organized meal.</note>, 
one person blesses for all of them. 
If **wine** was brought to them during the meal, 
each and every person blesses for themselves; 
If it was brought after the meal, 
one person blesses for all of them, and he also recites the blessing over the **incense** <note>original: "mugmar." It was custom to bring aromatic spices over coals at the end of a meal for fragrance.</note>, 
even though they do not bring the incense 
until after the meal is concluded.

### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 6 Mishnah 7

**7**
If they brought him a **salty food** at the beginning and bread with it, 
he blesses over the salty food and exempts the bread, 
because the bread is **secondary** to it. <note>Usually, bread is the primary food. However, in this specific case, the bread is only being eaten to temper the sharpness of the salt or the salty food (like a cracker with a very strong garnish), making the bread the subordinate element.</note>
**This is the general rule:** 
Wherever there is a **primary** food <note>original: "ikkar."</note> and a **secondary** food <note>original: "tafel."</note> accompanying it, 
one blesses over the primary food and exempts the secondary food.

If one ate **figs, grapes, or pomegranates**,
he recites **three blessings** <note>original: "shalosh berakhot." Rabban Gamliel refers to the full Grace After Meals, which in the Mishnaic period consisted of three blessings (a fourth was added later). Most other authorities rule that only bread requires the full Grace.</note> over them.
These are the words of **Rabban Gamliel**.
But the **Sages** say:
One blessing. <note>original: "berakha achat." This refers to the condensed version of the Grace After Meals, often called "The Threefold Blessing" or *Me'ein Shalosh*.</note>
**Rabbi Akiva** says:
Even if one ate **boiled vegetables** <note>original: "shelek." This usually refers to leafy greens like chard or spinach that have been cooked.</note>, and it serves as his main sustenance,

One who drinks **water** to quench his thirst,

## Chapter 7
### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 7 Mishnah 1

**1**
**Three** who ate together are obligated to **invite** <term>Zimmun|The formal "invitation" to bless God together after a meal. When three or more have shared a meal, one person acts as the leader to invite the others to recite the Grace After Meals collectively.</term>.
If one ate **doubtfully tithed produce** <note>original: "Demai." This refers to produce bought from a common person who may not have properly separated the required tithes for the poor or the Levites.</note>,
or **First Tithe** <note>original: "Ma'aser Rishon."</note> from which its **priestly portion** <note>original: "Terumah."</note> was already taken,
or **Second Tithe** <note>original: "Ma'aser Sheni."</note> and **consecrated property** <note>original: "Hekdesh."</note> that were **redeemed** <note>Food dedicated to the Temple or designated as tithes to be eaten in Jerusalem could be "redeemed" by transferring its sanctity to coins, making the food permissible to eat anywhere.</note>,
the **attendant** <note>original: "shammash." A waiter or servant.</note> who ate at least an **olive's bulk** <note>original: "kazayit." The standard minimum volume for a meal to be legally significant.</note>,
and the **Samaritan** <note>original: "Kuti." During this period, Samaritans were often included in certain Jewish rituals if they were known to observe the relevant laws.</note>,
one may include them in the **invitation**.

**2**
But if one ate **untithed produce** <note>original: "Tebel." Produce from which the required tithes have definitely not been separated; eating it is a religious prohibition.</note>,
or **First Tithe** from which its **priestly portion** was *not* taken,
or **Second Tithe** and **consecrated property** that were *not* redeemed,
the **attendant** who ate less than an **olive's bulk**,
and the **gentile**,
one may *not* include them in the **invitation**.
(Tractate Berakhot Chapter 7 Mishnah 2)
**Women, slaves, and minors**
one does not include them in the **invitation** <note>The Mishnah here records the legal exclusion of these groups from the formal quorum of three for Zimmun, though they are still required to bless for themselves.</note>.
**How much** must they eat to be included in the invitation?
Up to an **olive's bulk**.
**Rabbi Yehuda** says:
Up to an **egg's bulk** <note>original: "ke-beitzah." A larger unit of measure than the olive's bulk.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the laws of the Zimmun—the formal invitation to the Grace After Meals—specifically focusing on how the wording of the invitation changes as the number of participants increases, and the rules for when a large group may split into smaller ones.</meta>

### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 7 Mishnah 3

->4<-

How do they **invite** <term>Zimmun|The call to prayer led by one person after a meal shared by three or more people.</term>?
With **three** participants, the leader says, "**Let us bless.**" <note>original: "nevarekh." By saying "let us," the leader includes himself with the group.</note>
With **three** and he <note>the leader</note> is among them, he says, "**Bless.**" <note>original: "barekhu." This phrasing can imply the leader is addressing the others. The Mishnaic text here reflects early variations in the formula for small groups.</note>
With **ten**, he says, "**Let us bless our God.**" <note>original: "nevarekh l'Eloheinu." The addition of the name "God" (Elohim) is only permitted when a quorum of ten (a Minyan) is present.</note>
With **ten** and he is among them, he says, "**Bless.**"
Whether it is **ten** or **twenty myriads** <note>a "myriad" (ribo) is 10,000; thus, 200,000 people.</note>, the requirement remains the same.

->5<-

With **one hundred**, he says, "**Let us bless the Lord our God.**"
With **one hundred** and he is among them, he says, "**Bless.**"
With **one thousand**, he says, "**Let us bless the Lord our God, the God of Israel.**"
With **one thousand** and he is among them, he says, "**Bless.**"
With **ten thousand** <note>original: "ribo."</note>, he says, "**Let us bless the Lord our God, the God of Israel, the God of Hosts.**"
With **ten thousand** and he is among them, he says, "**Bless.**"
In the same manner that he blesses, so do the others **respond after him**:
"**Blessed is the Lord our God, the God of Israel, the God of Hosts, who dwells among the cherubim, for the food we have eaten.**"
**Rabbi Yose the Galilean** says:
The blessing should correspond to the **size of the gathering**,
as it is said in the Bible: "**In assemblies, bless God, the Lord, from the fountain of Israel.**" <note>original: Psalm 68:27. Rabbi Yose uses this verse to argue that the language of the blessing should change to reflect the size of the "assembly."</note>

->6<-

**Rabbi Akiva** said:
What do we find in the **synagogue**?
Whether there are **many** or whether there are **few**,
the leader says, "**Bless the Lord.**" <note>original: "Barekhu et Adonai." Rabbi Akiva argues that just as the synagogue call to prayer doesn't change based on the crowd size, neither should the Zimmun.</note>
**Rabbi Ishmael** says:
"**Bless the Lord, who is blessed.**" <note>original: "Barekhu et Adonai ha-mevorakh." This addition by Rabbi Ishmael—"who is blessed"—is the version that was eventually adopted into the standard Jewish prayer service today.</note>

## Tractate Berakhot Chapter 7 Mishnah 4

->7<-

**Three** who ate as one
are **not permitted to divide** <note>that is, they cannot split up to pray individually; they are bound by the obligation to perform the Zimmun together.</note>;
and likewise **four**, and likewise **five**.
**Six** may divide <note>into two groups of three, as each group still has the minimum number required for a Zimmun.</note>, until the number reaches **ten**.
But **ten** may not divide <note>because splitting would lose the ability to mention the name of "God" in the blessing, which requires ten.</note> until they reach **twenty**. <note>At twenty, they could split into two groups of ten and both groups could still include "God" in their invitation.</note>

## Tractate Berakhot Chapter 7 Mishnah 5
### 5
If **two groups** were eating in **one house**, as long as some of them can **see one another**, then these groups **join together** for the <term>Zimmun|The formal invitation to lead the Grace After Meals, required when three or more have eaten together.</term>.
If not <note>if they cannot see each other</note>,
these **invite** for themselves and those **invite** for themselves.
One does not recite the **blessing over the wine** <note>specifically the blessing "who creates the fruit of the vine"</note> 
until they **put water into it** <note>Ancient wine was extremely strong and concentrated; it was considered unpalatable and unworthy of a blessing until diluted.</note>—these are the words of **Rabbi Eliezer**.
But the **Sages** say:
One may recite the **blessing** <note>even on undiluted wine</note>.

# Chapter 8
## Tractate Berakhot Chapter 8 Mishnah 1
### 1
These are the matters **between the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel** <note>The two primary schools of Jewish law in the 1st century, often debating the specific order of rituals.</note> regarding the **meal**.
The **House of Shammai** says:
One recites the **blessing over the day** <note>The "Kiddush" prayer that sanctifies the Sabbath or a Festival.</note>, and afterward recites the **blessing over the wine**.
And the **House of Hillel** says:
One recites the **blessing over the wine**, and afterward recites the **blessing over the day**.

---

### 2
The **House of Shammai** says:
They **wash their hands**, and afterward **mix the cup** <note>Adding water to the wine to prepare it for drinking.</note>.
And the **House of Hillel** says:
They **mix the cup**, and afterward **wash their hands**.

### 3

They **sweep the house** <note>Cleaning the floor of leftover crumbs or debris from the meal.</note>, and afterward **wash their hands** <note>Referring to "Mayim Acharonim," the final water used for washing fingers before the Grace After Meals.</note>.
And the **House of Hillel** says:
They **wash their hands**, and afterward **sweep the house**.

### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 8 Mishnah 5
### 5

The **House of Shammai** says:
<note>The following refers to the order of blessings for Havdalah, the ceremony marking the end of the Sabbath.</note>
**Lamp**, then **Food** <note>Grace After Meals</note>, then **Spices**, and then **Separation** <note>The Havdalah blessing itself, which thanks God for separating the sacred from the mundane.</note>.
And the **House of Hillel** says:
**Lamp**, then **Spices**, then **Food**, and then **Separation**.
The **House of Shammai** says:
One should say the blessing, "**Who created** <note>original: *she-bara*, in the past tense</note> **the light of the fire**."
And the **House of Hillel** says:
One should say, "**Who creates** <note>original: *borei*, in the present/continuous tense</note> **the lights** <note>original: *me'orei*, plural</note> **of the fire**."

---

### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 8 Mishnah 6
### 6

One **does not recite a blessing**
neither over the **lamp** nor over the **spices of gentiles** <note>original: *goyim*; because these items were not necessarily used for a purpose requiring a blessing of thanks to God, or might have been used for idolatry.</note>;
nor over the **lamp** or the **spices of the dead** <note>Used to mask the odor at a funeral, rather than for enjoyment.</note>;
nor over the **lamp** or the **spices used before an idol** <term>Avoda Zara|Literally "foreign worship," referring to idolatrous practices.</term>.
One **does not recite a blessing** over the lamp **until they can benefit from its light** <note>One must be close enough to the candle to distinguish between two different coins.</note>.

---

### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 8 Mishnah 7
### 7

One who **ate and forgot and did not recite the blessing** <note>The Grace After Meals.</note>,
the **House of Shammai** says:
He must **return to his original place** and recite the blessing.
And the **House of Hillel** says:
He may **recite the blessing in the place where he remembered**.
**Until when can he recite the blessing?**
Until the **food in his stomach has been digested** <note>The tradition generally defines this as the point when he begins to feel hungry again, usually about 72 minutes.</note>.

---

### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 8 Mishnah 8
### 8

If **wine comes to them after the meal**,
and there is **only that one cup** available,
the **House of Shammai** says:
One **recites the blessing over the wine** first, and **afterward recites the blessing over the food**.
And the **House of Hillel** says:
One **recites the blessing over the food** first, and **afterward recites the blessing over the wine**.

<summary>This page outlines the classic disputes between the Houses of Shammai and Hillel regarding the sequence of blessings for the end of the Sabbath (Havdalah) and the Grace After Meals, as well as rules for when a blessing over light or spices is prohibited.</summary>
<keywords>Havdalah, House of Shammai, House of Hillel, Grace After Meals, Birkat Hamazon, ritual purity, idolatry, digestion, wine blessing</keywords>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page concludes the final laws of the eighth chapter regarding responding to blessings and begins the ninth chapter, which focuses on blessings recited upon witnessing natural phenomena, miracles, or hearing news.</meta>

One **responds "Amen"** after an **Israelite** who recites a blessing, but one **does not respond "Amen"** after a **Samaritan** <note>original: *Kuti*; the Samaritans followed their own version of the Torah and the Rabbis were often uncertain if their blessings were directed toward God or their own cultic site on Mount Gerizim.</note> who recites a blessing, until one **hears the entire blessing** <note>to ensure it was a proper blessing without heretical additions</note>.

# Chapter 9
## Tractate Berakhot Chapter 9 Mishnah 1
### 1

One who **sees a place** where **miracles were performed for Israel** says:
> "**Blessed** [is He] **who performed miracles for our ancestors in this place**."
In a place where **idolatry was uprooted**, one says:
> "**Blessed** [is He] **who uprooted idolatry from our land**."

## Tractate Berakhot Chapter 9 Mishnah 2
### 2

Over **shooting stars** <note>or "comets"</note>, and over **earthquakes**, and over **lightnings**, and over **thunders**, and over the **winds**, one says:
> "**Blessed** [is He] **whose strength and power fill the world**."
Over the **mountains**, and over the **hills**, and over the **seas**, and over the **rivers**, and over the **deserts**, one says:
> "**Blessed is the Maker of Creation**" <note>original: *oseh ma'aseh bereshit*; this blessing acknowledges God as the architect of the natural world.</note>.
**Rabbi Judah** says:
One who **sees the Great Sea** <note>The Mediterranean Sea</note> says:
> "**Blessed** [is He] **who made the Great Sea**,"
provided that he sees it only **at intervals** <note>meaning if thirty days have passed since he last saw it</note>.
Over **rainfall**, and over **good tidings**, one says:
> "**Blessed is the Good, and He who does good**";
and over **bad tidings**, one says:
> "**Blessed is the True Judge**" <note>This is the blessing recited upon hearing of a death or a significant loss, acknowledging God's justice even in times of sorrow.</note>.

## Tractate Berakhot Chapter 9 Mishnah 3
### 3

If one **built a new house**, or **purchased new vessels** <note>items of clothing or household goods</note>, one says:
> "**Blessed** [is He] **who has kept us alive and sustained us and brought us to this season**" <note>This is the *Shehecheyanu* blessing, marking joyful milestones.</note>.
One **recites a blessing over evil** in a manner similar to the **blessing over good**, and over **good** in a manner similar to **evil** <note>This means responding to all life events with a blessing, regardless of whether they appear positive or negative at the time.</note>.
One who **cries out over the past** <note>The text continues on the next page regarding "vain prayers" for things that have already been decided.</note>

<meta>This page continues the ninth chapter of Tractate Berakhot, moving from blessings over natural phenomena to the laws of "vain prayers," the obligation to bless God during hardship, and the protocols for showing reverence to the Temple Mount.</meta>

...this constitutes a **vain prayer** <note>original: *tefillat shav*; a prayer for something that has already been decided or is physically impossible to change.</note>.

### 4

**How so?**
If his **wife was pregnant**, and he said:
> "**May it be Your will that my wife gives birth to a male**,"
this is a **vain prayer** <note>because the biological sex of the child is determined at conception; to pray for it to change later is to ask for a redundant miracle.</note>.
If he was **coming along the road**, and he **heard a sound of crying** in the city, and he said:
> "**May it be Your will that these** [distresses] **are not within my house**,"
this is a **vain prayer**.
(Tractate Berakhot Chapter 9 Mishnah 4)
One who **enters a metropolis** <note>original: *kerakh*; a large, often fortified city which could be a place of both great opportunity and great danger in the Roman period.</note> **prays two prayers**, one upon his **entry** and one upon his **exit**.
**Ben Azzai** <note>A famous second-century scholar known for his diligence in study.</note> says:
He prays **four**; **two upon his entry** and **two upon his exit**.
And he **gives thanks for the past**, and **cries out** [in prayer] **for the future**.

### Tractate Berakhot Chapter 9 Mishnah 5

### 5

One is **obligated to bless** [God] **for the evil** <note>referring to bad news, tragedy, or misfortune.</note>, just as he **blesses for the good**, as it is said: (Deuteronomy 6:5)
> "**And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might.**"
"**With all your heart**" means with **both of your inclinations**: with the **good inclination** <note>original: *yetzer tov*; the drive toward moral and spiritual behavior.</note> and with the **evil inclination** <note>original: *yetzer ra*; the base or physical drives which must also be directed toward the service of God.</note>;
"**With all your soul**" means **even if He takes your soul** <note>meaning even at the cost of one's life.</note>;
"**With all your might**" means with **all your money** <note>or possessions.</note>.
**Another interpretation**:
"**With all your might**" <note>original: *me'odecha*</note> means:
For **every single measure** <note>original: *middah*; there is a play on words here between *me'od* (might) and *middah* (measure).</note> **that He measures out to you**, be **very, very thankful** <note>original: *modeh*; another play on the word *me'od*.</note> to Him.

### 6

A person should **not act light-headedly** <note>meaning to behave with frivolity or a lack of respect.</note> opposite the **Eastern Gate** [of the Temple], for it is **aligned with the Holy of Holies**.
One should **not enter the Temple Mount** with his **staff**, or with his **shoes**, or with his **money belt** <note>original: *apundato*; a hollow belt used for carrying coins.</note>, or with the **dust that is upon his feet**.
And he should **not make it a shortcut** <note>original: *kapanderya*; a loanword from the Latin *compendiaria*, meaning a short path or bypass.</note>,

...and **spitting** [on the Temple Mount is forbidden] by an ***a fortiori* reasoning** <note>original: *kal vachomer*; a logical inference that if a lesser case (wearing shoes) is forbidden, then a more disrespectful case (spitting) is certainly forbidden.</note>.

### 5 (continued)

All the **conclusions of the blessings** that were recited in the **Temple** used to say:
> "**From eternity**" <note>original: *min ha-olam*. The word *olam* can mean both "world" and "eternity."</note>.
From the time that the **heretics** <note>original: *minim*; referring here to groups like the Sadducees who denied the resurrection of the dead or the existence of an afterlife.</note> acted corruptly and said:
> "**There is only one world**" <note>meaning there is no existence after death.</note>,
they ordained that people should say:
> "**From eternity to eternity**" <note>original: *min ha-olam ve-ad ha-olam*; literally "from world to world," emphasizing the existence of both this world and the World to Come.</note>.
And they ordained that a **man should greet his fellow with the Name** [of God],
as it is said: (Ruth 2:4)
> "**And behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem, and he said to the reapers: 'The Lord be with you!' And they answered him: 'May the Lord bless you!'**"
And it says: (Judges 6:12)
> "**The Lord is with you, you mighty man of valor.**"
And it says: (Proverbs 23:22)
> "**And do not despise your mother when she is old.**" <note>This verse is cited to support following the "old" traditions or "mother-like" wisdom of the elders who instituted these greetings.</note>
And it says: (Psalms 119:126) "**It is a time to act for the Lord; they have made void Your Torah.**"
**Rabbi Nathan** says:
[Interpret the verse as:] **They have made void Your Torah** [at a] **time to act for the Lord** <note>Rabbi Nathan suggests that at certain critical times, one may "violate" a minor aspect of the law (like using God's holy name in a common greeting) to achieve a greater spiritual goal—in this case, strengthening faith in God's constant presence.</note>.

# Tractate Peah

## Chapter 1

### Tractate Peah Chapter 1 Mishnah 1

### 1

**These are the things that have no fixed measure** <note>original: *shiur*; the Torah does not specify a maximum amount for these, leaving it to the individual's generosity.</note>:
The **Corner** <note>original: *Peah*; the portion of a field that must be left unharvested for the poor.</note>, and the **First Fruits** <note>original: *Bikkurim*; the first of the seven species brought to the Temple.</note>, and the **Appearance-offering** <note>original: *Re'ayon*; the sacrifice brought when visiting the Temple on the three pilgrimage festivals.</note>,
and **acts of loving-kindness**, and the **study of Torah**.
**These are the things from which a person eats their fruits in this world**,
**while the principal remains for him in the World to Come**:
**Honoring one's father and mother**, and **acts of loving-kindness**,
and **bringing peace between a person and his fellow**;
and the **study of Torah is equivalent to them all**.

### Tractate Peah Chapter 1 Mishnah 2
2
One should not grant less than **one-sixtieth** <note>While the Torah does not specify a minimum, the Sages established this ratio (1.67%) to ensure the poor receive a meaningful amount.</note> for the **corner-portion** <term>Peah; the portion of a field left unharvested for the poor to collect</term>,
And although they said:
There is **no fixed measure** for the *Peah*,
Everything is according to the **size of the field**,
And according to the **multitude of the poor**,
And according to the **humility** <note>original: *anavah*; here referring to the owner’s generosity or the quality of the crop yield relative to the harvest's "blessing."</note>.

### Tractate Peah Chapter 1 Mishnah 3
3
They may give the *Peah* from the **beginning of the field**,
Or from its **middle**.
**Rabbi Shimon** says:
[One may do so] provided that he gives the **required measure at the end**.
**Rabbi Judah** says:
If he left even **one stalk** <note>original: *kelach*</note> [at the end], he may rely on it to designate [what he gave earlier] as *Peah*;
But if not, he gives [the earlier portions] only as **ownerless property** <term>Hefker; property renounced by the owner, which is exempt from certain tithes but lacks the specific sanctity of the Peah gift</term>.

### Tractate Peah Chapter 1 Mishnah 4
4
A **general rule** was stated regarding *Peah*:
Anything that is **food** and is **guarded** <note>meaning it is privately owned and protected, not wild.</note>,
And its **growth is from the earth**,
And its **harvesting is done all at once**,
And one **brings it in for storage**,
Is liable for the *Peah*.
**Grain** and **legumes** <note>original: *kitniyot*; such as beans, lentils, and peas.</note> are included in this general rule.

### Tractate Peah Chapter 1 Mishnah 5
5
And among **trees**:
The **pear**, the **carob**,
The **walnut**, the **almond**,
The **vines**, the **pomegranate**,
The **olive**, and the **date**,
Are liable for the *Peah*.

<meta>This page continues the legal discussions of Tractate Peah, specifically focusing on the "corner-portion" of the harvest that must be left for the poor. ### Tractate Peah Chapter 2 Mishnah 7
7
A field that was **harvested by non-Jews**, or **harvested by bandits**,
or **gnawed by ants**, or **broken by the wind or an animal**,
it is **exempt** <note>Meaning the owner is not required to leave a corner-portion (Peah) for the poor from what remains, as the obligation only applies to a standard human harvest by the owner.</note>.
If he harvested half of it and **bandits harvested [the other] half**,
it is **exempt**, because the obligation of the harvest is in the **standing grain** <note>original: "bakammah"; the law requires Peah to be designated from the grain while it is still attached to the ground during a regular harvest.</note>.

### (Tractate Peah Chapter 2 Mishnah 8)
If **bandits harvested half** and the owner **harvested [the other] half**,
he gives the **corner-portion** from what he harvested.
If he harvested half and **sold half**,
the **buyer gives the corner-portion** for the whole field <note>Because the obligation to leave a portion for the poor falls upon the person who completes the harvest of the standing grain.</note>.
If he harvested half and **sanctified half** <note>original: "hikdish"; dedicated the remaining crop to the Temple treasury</note>,
the one who **redeems it from the hand of the treasurer** is the one who gives the **corner-portion** for the whole field.

# Chapter 3

### Tractate Peah Chapter 3 Mishnah 1
1
Regarding **rectangular patches of grain** that are between **olive trees**:
The **House of Shammai** <note>One of the primary schools of Jewish law in the 1st century</note> say:
A **corner-portion** must be given from **each and every one**.
The **House of Hillel** say:
One portion is given for **all of them**.
But they both agree that if the **heads of the rows** were **joined together** <note>Meaning the grain patches were not isolated rectangles but were connected at their ends</note>,
one gives a single **corner-portion** for all of them.

### Tractate Peah Chapter 3 Mishnah 2
2
One who **leopards** his field <note>original: "hamenamer"; a metaphor for spot-harvesting only the ripe patches, leaving the field looking spotted like a leopard</note> and left **moist stalks** [to ripen later]:
**Rabbi Akiva** says:
He gives a **corner-portion** from **each and every** patch.
But the **Sages** say:
He gives from **one for all of them**.
And the Sages **agree with Rabbi Akiva**
regarding one who sows **dill or mustard** in three separate places,
that he must give a **corner-portion** from **each and every one** <note>Because these spices were typically grown in small, distinct beds rather than large contiguous fields.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the third chapter of Tractate Peah. The previous page introduced the discussion of how separate patches of grain—specifically those interspersed among trees—are treated regarding the "corner-portion" (Peah). This page further explores how the farmer's intent, the timing of the harvest, and the physical arrangement of the crops (like onions and peas) determine whether the field is treated as one unit or several for the purpose of the poor-tax.</meta>

### Tractate Peah Chapter 3 Mishnah 3

3
One who **thins out fresh onions** for the market <note>Harvesting some onions early while they are still moist to sell them immediately.</note> but **designates the dry ones** for the granary <note>Leaving the rest in the ground to dry out for long-term storage.</note>,
he must give the **corner-portion** <term>Peah: the edge of the field left for the poor</term> for these by themselves and for those by themselves.
And the same applies to **peas**, and the same applies to a **vineyard**.
One who **thins out** <note>original: "Hamadel"; removing some plants to provide more space for the remaining ones to grow better.</note> gives the corner-portion from the **remainder** based on what he **left behind**.
But one who **clears a spot** <note>original: "Hamachlik me’achat yad"; harvesting everything in one specific area to clear the ground.</note>,
he gives from the **remainder** for the **entirety** of the crop.

### Tractate Peah Chapter 3 Mishnah 4

4
The **"mother" onions** <note>Onions left in the ground for a second year to produce seeds.</note> are **liable** for the corner-portion;
**Rabbi Yossi exempts** them <note>Rabbi Yossi argues that since they are being grown for seed rather than food, the laws of Peah do not apply.</note>.
Regarding **rectangular beds of onions** that are situated **between other vegetables**,
**Rabbi Yossi says**:
A **corner-portion** must be given from **each and every one** <note>He views the vegetable patches as barriers that divide the onions into many tiny, separate fields.</note>.
But the **Sages say**:
He may give from **one bed for the entirety** of the beds.

(Tractate Peah Chapter 3 Mishnah 5)
**Brothers who divided** an inheritance <note>Splitting a single field left to them by their father.</note>,
they give **two corner-portions** <note>Since the field is now legally two separate properties.</note>;
if they **returned to being partners**,
they give only **one corner-portion**.
**Two people who purchased a single tree** together,
they give **one corner-portion**.
But if one **bought the northern half** and the other **bought the southern half**,
this one gives a **corner-portion for himself**,
and that one gives a **corner-portion for himself**.

5
One who **sells individual stalks** of trees <note>Or perhaps large leafy plants like cabbage or kale.</note> within his field,
the buyer gives a **corner-portion for each and every one**.
**Rabbi Yehuda said**:
**When** does this apply?
In a case where the **owner of the field did not leave any for himself**;
but if the **owner of the field did leave some** for himself,
**he** <note>the owner</note> gives the **corner-portion for everything**.

# Chapter 4

## Tractate Peah Chapter 4 Mishnah 1

1
The **corner-portion** <term>Peah: the portion of a crop left unharvested for the poor</term> is given while it is **attached to the ground**.
Regarding a **hanging vine** <term>Dallit: a vine trained to grow over a trellis or high frame</term> and a **palm tree** <term>Dekel</term>,
the homeowner brings the fruit down and distributes it to the poor. <note>Normally, the poor harvest Peah themselves. However, because climbing vines and palms is dangerous, the owner must assist to ensure safety.</note>
**Rabbi Shimon says**:
This rule also applies to **smooth-shell nuts**.
Even if **ninety-nine** poor people say to distribute the crop <note>i.e., they want the owner to harvest it and hand it out equally</note>,
and only **one** says to **plunder** <note>original: "laboz"; this refers to the standard practice of a "free-for-all" where the poor grab what they can</note>,
we listen to the one who spoke **according to the law** <term>Halakha: the binding religious legal tradition</term>. <note>The law dictates that Peah is a free-for-all; the owner cannot interfere with this right unless there is a physical danger involved.</note>

## Tractate Peah Chapter 4 Mishnah 2

2
But regarding the **hanging vine** and the **palm tree**, it is not so.
Even if **ninety-nine** say to **plunder**,
and only **one** says to **distribute**,
we listen to the one who spoke **according to the law**. <note>In the case of high-climbing plants, the law changes to require distribution by the owner to prevent the poor from injuring themselves or each other while climbing.</note>

## Tractate Peah Chapter 4 Mishnah 3

3
If a person took **a portion of the corner-portion** and threw it over the rest of the crop <note>An attempt to "claim" more of the field than they have actually gathered</note>,
he has no claim to it at all.
If he **fell upon it**, or **spread his cloak over it** to claim it,
they remove it from him. <insert>him</insert> <note>The insertion of the masculine "him" clarifies that the community removes the person himself from the spot, rather than just removing the cloak.</note>
And the same applies to **gleanings** <term>Leket: individual stalks that fall during the harvest</term>, and the same applies to the **forgotten sheaf** <term>Shikh’chah: a bundle accidentally left in the field</term>.

## Tractate Peah Chapter 4 Mishnah 4

4
Regarding the **corner-portion**,
they do not harvest it with **sickles** <term>Magalot</term>,
and they do not uproot it with **axes** <term>Kardummot</term>,
so that they do not **strike one another**. <note>Because the gathering is a "free-for-all," using sharp tools in a crowded field would be a safety hazard.</note>
(Tractate Peah Chapter 4 Mishnah 5)
There are **three "corner-portion" times** in the day:
at **dawn**, at **midday**, and at the **afternoon prayer** <term>Mincha: the time of the daily afternoon offering in the Temple</term>. <note>Fixed times were established so that poor people living far away or busy with other tasks (like nursing mothers) would know exactly when they had a fair chance to gather.</note>

**Rabban Gamliel says**:
They only said [these rules] so that they should not **decrease** [the portion].
**Rabbi Akiva says**:
They only said [these rules] so that they should not **increase** [the portion]. <note>This debate concerns whether the Sages' measurements were meant as a minimum requirement to protect the poor or a maximum limit to protect the owner's property rights.</note>
The members of the **house of Namer** used to harvest along a **rope** <note>original: "al hachevel"; likely a guide rope to ensure they harvested in a straight, orderly fashion</note>,
and they would give **Peah** <term>Peah: the corner-portion of the field left for the poor</term> from each and every **row** <term>Umman: a specific section or row of the harvest worked by a laborer</term>.

### Tractate Peah Chapter 4 Mishnah 6
#### 5

A **gentile** who harvested his field and afterward **converted** <note>original: "nitgyer"; underwent the process of joining the Jewish people</note>,
is **exempt** from the **gleanings** <term>Leket: individual stalks that fall during the harvest</term>, from the **forgotten sheaves** <term>Shikchah: bundles unintentionally left behind</term>, and from the **corner-portion** <term>Peah</term>. <note>The law only applies to a field owned by a Jew at the time of the harvest; since he was not Jewish when the grain was cut, the poor-laws do not apply.</note>
**Rabbi Yehuda obligates** him in the case of **forgotten sheaves**,
because the obligation for **forgotten sheaves** does not occur until the **time of binding the sheaves**. <note>Rabbi Yehuda argues that if the owner converted after cutting the grain but before binding it into bundles, he is liable for anything forgotten during that later stage.</note>

### Tractate Peah Chapter 4 Mishnah 7
#### 6

If one **consecrated** <note>original: "hikdish"; dedicated the crop to the Temple treasury</note> **standing grain** and then **redeemed** it while it was still **standing grain**, he is **obligated** [to give the poor-gifts].
If he consecrated **sheaves** and redeemed them as **sheaves**, he is **obligated**.
However, if he consecrated **standing grain** and redeemed it as **sheaves**, it is **exempt**,
because at the **time of its obligation**, it was **exempt**. <note>The "time of obligation" is the moment the grain is bound into sheaves. If the Temple owned the crop at that precise moment, it is legally free from the requirements of the poor-laws, even if a private individual buys it back later.</note>

### Tractate Peah Chapter 4 Mishnah 8
#### 7

**Similarly**:
One who **consecrates his fruits**
before they have reached the **"season of tithes"** <note>The stage of ripeness at which the obligation to set aside a portion for the Priests and Levites (Ma'asrot) takes effect</note>, and then **redeemed them**,
they are **obligated**.
If he redeemed them **after** they reached the season of tithes,
they are [likewise] **obligated**.
But if he consecrated them before they were **processed** <note>original: "nigmru"; refers to the final smoothing or piling of the harvest that prepares it for sale or storage</note> and the **Temple treasurer** <term>Gizbar: the official in charge of Temple property</term> finished the process,
and afterward the owner redeemed them, they are **exempt**,
because at the **time of their obligation**, they were **exempt**.

### Tractate Peah Chapter 4 Mishnah 9
#### 8

One who **collected** the **corner-portion** <term>Peah</term> and said:
> "Behold, this is for **so-and-so, a poor man**,"
**Rabbi Eliezer says**:
He has **acquired it for him** <note>Rabbi Eliezer views the collector as a legal agent for the poor person</note>.
But the **Sages say**:
He must give it to the **poor person who is found first**. <note>The Sages hold that one cannot act as an agent to favor one poor person over another in the field; the produce remains public property for the poor until a poor person physically claims it for themselves.</note>

It also debates whether a person can act as an agent to collect poor-gifts for a specific individual.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the transition of property ownership and the resulting obligations toward the poor. It concludes the 4th chapter of Tractate Peah, defining the precise physical actions that classify grain as "gleanings," and begins the 5th chapter which deals with grain stacks and the effects of wind on the harvest.</meta>

The **gleanings** <term>Leket: individual stalks that fall during the harvest</term>, the **forgotten sheaves** <term>Shikchah</term>, and the **corner-portion** <term>Peah</term> belonging to a **Gentile** are **liable for tithes** <note>original: "ma'asrot"; the requirement to set aside a tenth of the crop for the Levites or the poor. Usually, these gifts to the poor are exempt from tithes, but here the law differs because of the owner's status.</note>, unless he has declared them **ownerless** <note>original: "hefkir"; property renounced by the owner so that anyone may take it.</note>.

### Tractate Peah Chapter 4 Mishnah 10
->9<-

What is considered **gleanings** <term>Leket</term>?
That which **falls** during the time of the **harvesting**. 
If one was harvesting, 
and he harvested a **handful** or plucked a **fistful**, 
and a **thorn pricked him** and the grain **fell from his hand** to the ground, 
this belongs to the **landowner** <note>The fall must be a natural part of the harvesting process to be considered "gleanings" for the poor; an accidental fall caused by a thorn does not count.</note>.
Grain found **within the hand** or **within the sickle** belongs to the **poor**. 
Grain found **behind the hand** or **behind the sickle** belongs to the **landowner**. 
Regarding grain on the **top of the hand** or the **top of the sickle**:
**Rabbi Ishmael** says:
It belongs to the **poor**.
**Rabbi Akiva** says:
It belongs to the **landowner**.

### Tractate Peah Chapter 4 Mishnah 11
->10<-

**Ant holes** <note>Ants often carry fallen grains into their nests.</note> that are within the **standing grain** 
belong to the **landowner**; 
But those found **after the harvesters** have passed:
the **upper** grains belong to the **poor**, 
and the **lower** grains belong to the **landowner**. 
**Rabbi Meir** says:
**Everything** belongs to the **poor**, 
for **doubtful gleanings** <note>original: "safek leket"; grain where it is uncertain if it fell during harvest or was brought from elsewhere by ants.</note> are treated as **gleanings**.

all stalks that **touch the ground** belong to the **poor**. 
And in the case of a **wind** that **scattered the sheaves**, 
they **estimate** <note>original: "omdin"</note> how much **gleaning** the field was likely to produce, <insert>**they estimate**</insert> <note>original: "omdin" vs "omdin"; the insert provides a linguistic variant of the same root meaning "to assess" or "to stand by an assessment."</note>
and the owner gives that amount to the **poor**.

**Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:**
He gives to the poor an amount equal to a **natural fall** <note>original: "kedei nefilah"; the estimated amount of grain that would typically fall during the harvesting process and be available to the poor as gleanings, which the ants then carried away.</note>.

### Tractate Peah Chapter 5 Mishnah 2

->2<-
A **stalk** that is among the **reaped grain**, but its **head reaches** the **standing grain**:
If it can be **harvested together** with the **standing grain**, then it belongs to the **landowner**.
But if **not**, it belongs to the **poor** <note>This law defines whether a stalk is considered "harvested" (and thus potentially a "forgotten sheaf" if left) or "standing." If it can be cut with the standing crop, it retains the status of the main field.</note>.
A **stalk** of **gleanings** <term>Leket: individual stalks that fall during the harvest and belong to the poor</term> that became **mixed** into the **grain stack**:
One **tithes** <note>The act of setting aside a portion of the crop for religious or charitable purposes.</note> a **single stalk** and **gives it** to him <note>the poor person</note>.
**Rabbi Eliezer said:**
But how can this poor person **exchange** something that has **not yet come into his possession**? <insert>this</insert> <note>Rabbi Eliezer questions the legal mechanism of exchanging a specific lost stalk for a different one if the poor person never physically held the original.</note>
Rather, the landowner **grants ownership** of the **entire stack** to the poor person <note>temporarily, for the purpose of the exchange</note>,
and then **tithes** a **single stalk** and **gives it** to him.

### Tractate Peah Chapter 5 Mishnah 3

->3<-
One may **not roll** [grain] with ***tofah*** <note>original: "tofah"; likely a type of legume or a moistening process used during threshing. This was prohibited because it might hide the gleanings or make them inaccessible to the poor.</note>.
These are the **words of Rabbi Meir**.
But the **Sages permit** it,
because it is **possible** <note>Meaning, it is possible to do so without necessarily depriving the poor of their rights, or because it is a standard farming practice.</note>.

### Tractate Peah Chapter 5 Mishnah 4

->4<-
A **landowner** who was **traveling** from place to place, and he **found himself in need** <note>He has run out of money or supplies while on a journey, despite being wealthy at home.</note>:
He may **take gleanings** <term>Leket</term>, **forgotten sheaves** <term>Shikchah</term>, the **corner-portion** <term>Peah</term>, and the **poor tithe** <term>Ma'asar Ani</term>.
And **when he returns** to his home, he must **repay** the value.
These are the **words of Rabbi Eliezer**.
But the **Sages say**:
He was **poor at that moment** <note>Since he lacked resources at the time he took the grain, he was legally considered "poor" and therefore is not required to repay the community or the poor once he regains access to his wealth.</note>.

### Tractate Peah Chapter 5 Mishnah 5

->5<-
One who **exchanges** with the **poor**:
Regarding his **own** [grain], he is **exempt** [from tithes],
but regarding that which belongs to the **poor**, he is **liable** <note>If a landowner trades his own grain for the poor man's gleanings, the gleanings lose their tax-exempt status because they are now "purchased" produce.</note>.
Two people who **received a field** in **sharecropping** <term>Arisut: a system where workers farm the land in exchange for a percentage of the crop</term>:
This one **gives** to that one his **portion** of the **poor tithe**,
and that one **gives** to this one his **portion** of the **poor tithe** <note>If both sharecroppers are poor, they can give their required poor tithes to one another.</note>.
One who **contracts a field** solely to **reap** it:
He is **forbidden** from taking the **gleanings**, the **forgotten sheaves**, the **corner-portion**, and the **poor tithe**.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of agricultural gifts for the poor. It concludes Chapter 5, Mishnah 5, regarding the status of sharecroppers and laborers, and proceeds through Mishnah 8, which defines the laws of "forgotten sheaves" based on the stage of the harvest.</meta>

Rabbi Yehuda said:
When [does this apply]?
When he received it from him [to work the land] for half, a third, or a fourth [of the yield];
But if the owner said to him:
"A third of what you reap shall be yours,"
He is permitted to take **gleanings** <term>Leket: individual stalks that fall during the harvest</term>, **forgotten sheaves**, and the **corner-portion** <term>Peah: the edge of the field left unharvested for the poor</term>,
but he is forbidden from taking the **Poor Man's Tithe**. <note>Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between a sharecropper, who is like a part-owner, and a laborer paid with a percentage of the crop. # Tractate Peah Chapter 5 Mishnah 6
## 6
One who sells his field:
The seller is permitted [to glean if he is poor] and the buyer is forbidden. <note>Even if the buyer is poor, he cannot glean in the field he just purchased, as it would appear he is simply taking his own crop and depriving others.</note>
A person may not hire a laborer on the condition that his son may glean after him. <note>This prevents the landowner and laborer from making a private deal that effectively uses the "gifts for the poor" to subsidize the laborer's wages.</note>
One who does not allow the poor to glean,
or who allows one poor person but not another,
or who assists one of them [to the exclusion of others],
this person is a robber of the poor.
Concerning this it was said: (Proverbs 22:28)
> "Do not move an ancient boundary." <note>original: "Al taseg gevul olam." While usually referring to property lines, the Mishnah applies this to the "boundaries" or rights established for the poor.</note>

# Tractate Peah Chapter 5 Mishnah 7
## 7
A sheaf that the laborers forgot,
but the homeowner did not forget;
or that the homeowner forgot, but the laborers did not forget;
or if the poor stood in front of it or covered it with straw;
this is not considered a **forgotten sheaf** <term>Shikhah: grain left behind by mistake which belongs to the poor</term>. <note>For a sheaf to legally become "forgotten," it must be overlooked by everyone responsible for the harvest. If anyone still has it in mind, or if the poor try to "claim" it before it is truly forgotten, the law does not apply.</note>

# Tractate Peah Chapter 5 Mishnah 8
## 8
One who binds sheaves for **hat-shapes** <note>original: "kov'ot"; bundles shaped to provide shade for the head</note> or for **small bundles** <note>original: "kumasot"</note>,
or for **dough-cakes** <note>original: "chararah"; grain intended to be used for a specific snack</note> or for **regular small sheaves**,
the law of the **forgotten sheaf** does not apply to them.
From that point toward the **threshing floor**,
the law of the **forgotten sheaf** does apply.
One who binds sheaves for the **stack**,
the law of the **forgotten sheaf** applies.
From the stack toward the threshing floor,
the law of the **forgotten sheaf** does not apply.
This is the general rule:
Anyone who binds sheaves for a place that is the **completion of the work**...

...which your ancestors have set." <note>original: "Al taseg gevul olam asher asu avotecha." The Sages use this verse to warn landowners against encroaching on the portions of the harvest legally designated for the poor.</note>

[In a place where the harvest work is finished], it is subject to the law of the **forgotten sheaf** <term>Shikhcha: produce overlooked during the harvest that must be left for the poor</term>;
