# Chapter 3

## Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 3, Mishnah 1

->1<-

> From what point may one bring manure out to the dung heaps <note>The "dung heap" refers to a designated pile for storage, rather than spreading it across the field</note>?
> From the time that laborers cease their labor.
> These are the words of Rabbi Meir.
> Rabbi Yehudah says:
> From the time that the "sweetness" <note>original: "ha-matok" – referring to the moisture or sap in the ground or the weeds</note> has dried up.
> Rabbi Yose says:
> From the time that it becomes knotted <note>original: "she-yikaser" – when the moisture in the soil forms clumps or the sap in plants thickens</note>.

## (Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 3, Mishnah 2)

> How much manure may be applied?
> Up to three dung heaps
> per *beit se'ah* <term>beit se'ah: a measure of land area, approximately 800 square meters</term>, with each heap consisting of ten baskets <note>original: "mashpelot" – large wicker baskets used for transport</note>,
> and for a *letek* <term>letek: a dry measure equal to fifteen se'ahs, or half a kor</term>, [the basket size is] a *letek*.
> One may increase the number of baskets in each heap,
> but one may not increase the number of heaps.
> Rabbi Yehudah says:
> One may even increase the number of heaps.

> But the Sages forbid it,

### Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 3, Mishnah 10

->10<-

One who builds a wall between [his property] and public property <term>Reshut HaRabim: the public domain, such as a street or plaza</term>
is permitted to dig down to the bedrock <note>to create a firm foundation for the wall</note>.
What shall he do with the excavated soil?
He heaps it up in the public domain and then "repairs" the road with it <note>by using the dirt to fill in cracks or level the street</note>.
These are the words of Rabbi Joshua.
Rabbi Akiba says:
Just as one may not damage public property,
so too one may not "repair" it <note>Rabbi Akiba's view is that even "improving" the road is forbidden if it involves placing an obstacle (the dirt heap) in the public path in the meantime</note>.
What shall he do with the soil?
He heaps it within his own field in the manner of those who heap manure <note>referring to the heaps discussed in the previous chapter, which must be arranged specifically so they do not look like the field is being prepared for planting</note>.
And the same rule applies to one who digs a pit, a trench, or a cave.

## Chapter 4

### Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 4, Mishnah 1

->1<-

Originally they used to say:
A person may gather wood and grasses from within his own field,
in the same manner that he gathers from the field of his neighbor—
taking only the large pieces <note>original: "et ha-gas ha-gas." Taking only large pieces shows one is looking for fuel or fodder, rather than clearing the land for farming</note>.
But when transgressors increased <note>referring to people who would pretend to gather wood but were actually clearing their land for cultivation</note>, they ordained
that this person should gather from that person's field and that person from this person's, without [expecting] a favor <note>by gathering from each other's fields, it is clear they are just looking for materials and not "working" their own land</note>;
and it goes without saying that one should not provide them with food <note>the owner should not feed the person gathering, as this would make the gatherer look like a hired laborer</note>.

### Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 4, Mishnah 2

->2<-

A field that was cleared [of stones during the Sabbatical year as a penalty] <note>original: "she-nitkantza." This refers to a field where the owner illicitly gathered stones to improve the soil</note>,
may be sown at the conclusion of the Sabbatical year;
[but] if it was improved <note>original: "she-nitayva" — through illegal plowing or other soil preparation</note> or if cattle were penned in it [to provide manure],
it may not be sown at the conclusion of the Sabbatical year.
A field that was improved: the House of Shammai say:
One may not eat its fruits [that grow] during the Sabbatical year;
<note>The House of Shammai imposes a stricter penalty: not only is the field banned after the Sabbatical year, but its current "wild" growth is also forbidden because the soil was illegally prepared.</note>

They agree in the case of one who clears trees <term>Ha-mahlik: cutting down a series of consecutive trees to clear a space</term>, that he should cut them at the surface.
And what constitutes "thinning"?
[Removing] one or two [trees].
And "clearing"?
[Removing] three trees side by side.
Under what circumstances do these rules apply?
When removing them from within his own [field],
but from within his neighbor’s [field],
even one who clears trees may uproot them <note>because he is clearly doing it as a service to the neighbor, not to illegally improve his own land during the Sabbatical year</note>.

### Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 5, Mishnah 6
->6<-

**These are the tools that a craftsman is not permitted to sell during the Sabbatical year:**
A plow and all its accessories,
The yoke, the winnowing fork, and the mattock. <note>These tools are used exclusively for prohibited agricultural activities like tilling or preparing the soil</note>
However, he may sell a hand-sickle,
A harvest-sickle, a wagon and all its accessories. <note>These items are permitted because they can be used for activities that are allowed during the Sabbatical year, such as gathering ownerless produce for food</note>
This is the general rule:
Any tool whose primary function is for a transgression <note>i.e., forbidden farm work</note> is forbidden to sell;
But if it is used for both forbidden and permitted acts, it is permitted to sell.

### Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 5, Mishnah 7
->7<-

A potter may sell five oil jars,
And fifteen wine jars,
Because it is the custom to bring this amount from the ownerless produce. <note>Produce in the seventh year is "hefker" (ownerless), and individuals are allowed to gather small amounts for personal use. Selling a standard amount of jars suggests the buyer is acting legally</note>
If the buyer brings more than this amount, it is still permitted.
And he may sell to non-Jews within the Land [of Israel],
And to Israelites outside the Land. <note>The laws of the Sabbatical year do not apply to land owned by non-Jews or to land outside the traditional borders of Israel, so there is no concern that the tools/jars will be used for a transgression</note>

### Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 5, Mishnah 8
->8<-

**The School of Shammai say:**
One may not sell a plowing cow to someone during the Sabbatical year. <note>Lest the buyer use it to plow the field illegally</note>
**The School of Hillel permit it,**
Because the buyer might be purchasing it to slaughter it for meat. <note>Hillel's school follows a more lenient principle: if there is a legitimate, non-sinful use for an item, we may assume that is the intent</note>
One may sell produce even during the sowing season.
One may lend a *seah*-measure <term>Seah: A dry volume measure; see previous page</term>,
Even if the lender knows the borrower has a threshing floor. <note>He might be using the measure for permitted food, not for forbidden harvesting</note>
One may change money for him,
Even if he knows the person has laborers to pay. <note>The money might be for something else; the lender is not responsible for the borrower's potential misuse of the funds</note>
But all of these actions are forbidden if the person explicitly states they are for a forbidden purpose.

# Chapter 6

### Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 6, Mishnah 1
->1<-

There are **three regions** regarding the laws of the Sabbatical year: 
In all areas that were settled by those who returned from Babylon, 
from the Land of Israel unto Kziv <note>A coastal town north of Acre, marking the border of the territory re-established during the Second Temple period</note>, 
produce may **neither be eaten** <note>after the time of 'removal' (biur), when that species is no longer in the fields</note> **nor may the land be worked**; 
In all areas settled by those who came out of Egypt <note>the wider borders from the first settlement under Joshua</note>, 
from Kziv until the river and until Amanah <note>The Amanus Mountains in modern-day Turkey/Syria</note>, 
produce may be **eaten but the land may not be worked**; 
From the river and from Amanah and further inward, 
produce may be **eaten and the land may be worked**.

### Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 6, Mishnah 2
->2<-

One may perform labor on **detached produce** in Syria, 
but not on **attached produce**. 
One may thresh, winnow, tread [grapes], and bind sheaves, 
but one may not reap, nor harvest grapes, nor gather olives. 
Rabbi Akiva stated a general rule: 
Any labor that is similar to what is permitted in the Land [of Israel], 
may be performed in Syria.

## Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 7, Mishnah 7

New carobs that one pickled in old wine, or old [carobs] in new [wine], they are liable to the removal requirement.
This is the general rule:
Any [mixture] where [the Sabbatical item] imparts flavor, one is liable to remove [the whole mixture] when the species are different;
but when it is a species mixed with its own kind <note>e.g., Sabbatical wine mixed with non-Sabbatical wine</note>, any amount [of Sabbatical produce] makes it liable.
Sabbatical produce prohibits [the whole mixture] with any amount of its own kind; but with a different kind, [it prohibits] only if it imparts flavor.

# Chapter 8
## Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 8, Mishnah 1
### 1
They stated a great general rule regarding the Sabbatical year:
Anything specifically designated for human food, one may not make a poultice <term>poultice: *malogma*, a medicated paste or bandage applied to the body</term> for a human from it, and it goes without saying [not] for an animal <note>because Sabbatical produce is meant "for eating," using edible food for medicine is considered a form of "waste" or "misuse" of its sanctity</note>;
And anything that is not specifically designated for human food, one may make a poultice for a human from it, but not for an animal;
And anything that is not specifically designated either for human food or for animal food, [if] one intended it for human food or animal food, they apply to it the stringencies of human [food] and the stringencies of animal [food].

## Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 8, Mishnah 2

## Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 8, Mishnah 3
### 3

One may not sell Sabbatical fruits
By measure, nor by weight, nor by count;
Not figs by count,
And not vegetables by weight.
Beit Shammai <note>The "House of Shammai," a school of legal thought known for its strict interpretations</note> say:
Even not in bundles.
But Beit Hillel <note>The "House of Hillel," known for more lenient or communal-focused rulings</note> say:
That which is usually bundled in the home
May be bundled in the market,
Such as leeks and star-of-Bethlehem <term>star-of-Bethlehem: *netz he-halav*, a plant with edible bulbs or flowers</term>.

## Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 8, Mishnah 4
### 4

One who says to a worker:
"Here is this *issar* <term>issar: a small Roman copper coin</term>, and gather vegetables for me today,"
His wages are permitted <note>because the coin is framed as a general payment for labor, not a purchase price for the food</note>;
[But if he says:] "Gather vegetables for me today in exchange for it [this coin],"
His wages are forbidden <note>because this looks like a commercial sale of Sabbatical produce, which is prohibited</note>.
[If] he took a loaf from a baker for a *pundiyon* <term>pundiyon: a copper coin worth two *issars*</term> [and said]:
"When I gather wild greens from the field, I will bring them to you [as payment],"
It is permitted;
[But if] he took from him without specification,
He may not pay him with Sabbatical funds <note>money that has acquired Sabbatical sanctity through the sale of produce</note>,
For one may not pay a debt with Sabbatical funds.

### Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 8, Mishnah 5
->5<-
->One may not give [Sabbatical produce]<-
->neither to a well-digger, nor to a bathhouse attendant,<-
->nor to a barber, nor to a sailor;<-
->but he may give to the well-digger [water or produce] to drink.<-
->And to all of them, he may give [the produce] as a free gift.<-
<note>Sabbatical produce cannot be used to pay off a debt or as wages for labor, as this is considered commercial use. However, providing food or drink as hospitality or as a genuine gift is permitted.</note>

### Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 8, Mishnah 6
->6<-
->Figs of the Sabbatical year,<-
->they should not be cut in the [usual] drying area,<-
->but one may cut them in a [designated] desolate spot.<-
->One may not tread grapes in the [large] winepress,<-
->but one may tread them in a [small] tub.<-
->And one may not process olives in the [large] beam-press or with the press-beam,<-
->but one may crush them and place them in a small olive-press <term>small olive-press: *bodidah*, a smaller, more domestic tool for extracting oil</term>.<-
->Rabbi Shimon says:<-
->One may even grind them in the [large] oil-press and [then] place them in the small olive-press.<-
<note>The law requires a person to change their usual agricultural methods (changing from large-scale commercial equipment to small, private tools) to demonstrate that the produce is ownerless and that the year is sacred.</note>

### Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 8, Mishnah 7
->7<-
->One may not cook Sabbatical vegetables in oil of heave-offering <term>heave-offering: *terumah*, the portion of the crop given to the Priests, which must be kept ritually pure</term>,<-
->so that he does not bring it to a state of invalidity <note>If the *terumah* oil becomes ritually impure, it must be burned. If Sabbatical vegetables are cooked in it, they would also have to be destroyed, but the law requires Sabbatical produce to be eaten, not wasted.</note>.<-
->Rabbi Shimon permits [this].<-
->And [regarding the transfer of sanctity], the very last [item exchanged] is seized by the [laws of the] Sabbatical year,<-
->but the fruit itself [always] remains forbidden.<-
<note>When Sabbatical produce is traded, the money or item received takes on the same "holy" status as the fruit. If that money is spent on something else, the sanctity moves to the next item—but the original fruit never loses its Sabbatical status.</note>

### Tractate Shevi'it, Chapter 8, Mishnah 8
->8<-
->One may not purchase slaves, or lands, or an impure animal <note>original: "בהמה טמאה" — *behemah teme'ah*; referring here to non-kosher animals like donkeys or camels which are not for eating</note><-
->with Sabbatical year funds;<-
->and if he did purchase [them], he must eat [other food] of equal value [under the laws of Sabbatical sanctity].<-
->One may not bring the bird-offerings of men with flux, women with flux <term>flux: *zavim* and *zavot*, individuals requiring specific purification offerings</term>, or women after childbirth<-
->from Sabbatical year funds;<-
->and if he did bring [them], he must eat [other food] of equal value.<-
->One may not grease vessels with oil of the Sabbatical year;<-
->and if he did grease [them], he must eat [other food] of equal value.<-
<note>Sabbatical funds must be spent only on food, drink, or anointing for people. If spent on long-term assets, ritual sacrifices, or maintenance of tools, the owner must "redeem" the sanctity by buying food of the same value and treating it as Sabbatical produce.</note>

# Tractate Terumot

--- Page 110 ---
<meta>This page marks the transition from Tractate Shevi'it (the Sabbatical Year) to Tractate Terumot (Heave-Offerings). While the previous page concluded by discussing the ethics of returning debts to the heirs of converts, this page begins a new legal focus: the laws of Terumah, the sacred gift given from the harvest to the Priests. ### Tractate Terumot Chapter 1 Mishnah 1
# 1

->Five may not separate <term>Terumah: The "heave-offering" or "gift" given from the harvest to the Kohanim (Priests). It is sacred and may only be eaten by Priests and their households in a state of ritual purity.</term>,<-
->and if they did separate it, their Terumah is not valid Terumah:<-
->the deaf-mute, the insane, and the minor;<-
->and one who separates that which is not his own;<-
->and a non-Jew who separated the Terumah of an Israelite, even with permission,<-
->his Terumah is not valid Terumah.<-

---

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 1 Mishnah 2
# 2

->A deaf person who speaks but does not hear should not separate Terumah <note>original: *cheresh ha-medabber ve-eino shome'a*. In Rabbinic law, a person who can speak but not hear has a different legal status than a deaf-mute, though they are still discouraged from performing certain ritual acts where hearing the blessing is required.</note>.<-
->If he did separate it, his Terumah is valid Terumah.<-
->The "deaf person" <note>original: *cheresh*</note> of whom the Sages spoke in every place<-
->is one who neither hears nor speaks.<-

---

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 1 Mishnah 3
# 3

->A minor who has not yet produced two hairs <note>The appearance of two pubic hairs is the traditional physical sign used in Jewish law to determine the onset of puberty and legal adulthood.</note>,<-
->Rabbi Yehuda says:<-
->His Terumah is valid Terumah.<-
->Rabbi Yose says:<-
->If he has not yet reached the age of vows <term>Onat Nedarim: A period of time (typically the year before reaching age 12 or 13) when a child's vows are legally tested to see if they understand the significance of their consecration.</term>,<-
->his Terumah is not valid Terumah;<-
->but if he has reached the age of vows,<-
->his Terumah is valid Terumah.<-

---

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 1 Mishnah 4
# 4

->One may not separate olives as Terumah for oil,<-
->nor grapes as Terumah for wine <note>The law requires Terumah to be "finished" produce. One should not give the raw fruit to exempt the processed liquid, as the value and quantity change during pressing.</note>.<-
->And if he did separate them,<-
->Beit Shammai <note>The "House of Shammai," a school of legal thought known for generally stricter interpretations.</note> say:<-
->Their own Terumah is contained within them <note>Meaning, the olives themselves become Terumah, but they do not exempt the rest of the oil.</note>.<-
->And Beit Hillel <note>The "House of Hillel," a school of legal thought known for more lenient or pragmatic interpretations.</note> say:<-
->Their Terumah is not valid Terumah at all.<-

---

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 1 Mishnah 5
# 5

->One may not separate Terumah from Gleanings <term>Leket: Individual stalks that fall during the harvest, which the Torah mandates must be left for the poor.</term>, from Forgotten Sheaves <term>Shikhchah: Bundles of grain accidentally left in the field, which must also be left for the poor.</term>, or from the Corner of the field <term>Pe'ah: A portion of the field left unharvested for the poor and the stranger.</term>,<-
->nor from ownerless property <term>Hefker: Property that has no owner and is free for anyone to take.</term>,<-

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 1 Mishnah 6
# 6

->Five may not separate Terumah initially,<-
->but if they did separate it, their Terumah is valid:<-
->The mute <note>original: *illem*. In this context, someone who can hear but is unable to speak, meaning they cannot recite the required blessing.</note>, the drunk, the naked,<-
->the blind, and one who has had a seminal emission <note>original: *ba'al keri*. Someone in a state of ritual impurity who is discouraged from speaking sacred words until they have immersed in a ritual bath.</note>,<-
->they may not separate Terumah,<-
->but if they did separate it, their Terumah is valid.<-

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 1 Mishnah 7
# 7

One should not separate Terumah by measure, nor by weight, nor by count <note>The act of giving should be an estimation by eye to avoid making it look like a mundane commercial transaction.</note>,
but one may separate Terumah for produce that has already been measured, weighed, or counted.
One should not separate Terumah using a basket or a crate that are of a known standard volume,
but one may separate Terumah using them if they are only half-full or a third-full.
One may not separate Terumah using a half-seah measure <note>original: *se'ah*. A standard dry measure of volume.</note> even if it is only half-filled,
because even that half-volume is a recognized standard measure.

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 1 Mishnah 8
# 8

One should not separate oil as Terumah for olives that are currently being crushed,
nor wine for grapes that are currently being trodden.
And if one did separate it, it is considered Terumah, but he must go back and separate Terumah a second time <note>The first separation is flawed because the processing is not yet complete.</note>.
The first separation makes a mixture forbidden <note>original: *medamma'at*. If this first offering accidentally falls into common food, it "taints" the whole batch, making it forbidden to non-priests.</note> on its own,
and one who eats it is liable to pay the added fifth <term>Chomesh: An additional 25% penalty (one-fifth of the new total) paid by a non-priest who unintentionally eats sacred Terumah.</term>,
but this does not apply to the second separation.

One may separate oil as Terumah for olives that are being pickled, 
and wine for grapes that are being made into raisins. 
If someone separated oil for olives intended for eating, 
or olives for olives intended for eating, 
or wine for grapes intended for eating, 
or grapes for grapes intended for eating, 
and then changed his mind and decided to press them <note>original: *le-darkan*. To tread on them in a press to extract liquid.</note>, 
he does not need to separate Terumah again.

for produce whose processing is finished,

# Chapter 2

## Tractate Terumot Chapter 2 Mishnah 1
->1<-
One may not separate Terumah from ritually pure produce <note>original: *tahor*.</note> for ritually impure produce <note>original: *tamei*.</note>; 
but if they did separate it, their Terumah is valid. 
In truth <note>original: *be-emet*. This phrase indicates a settled and undisputed halakhic tradition.</note>, regarding a pressed cake of dried figs <note>original: *iggul shel develah*.</note> that became partially impure, 
one may separate from the pure part within it for the impure part within it. 
And the same applies to a bundle of vegetables, and the same applies to a pile [of produce]. 
If there were two separate cakes, two bundles, or two piles—
one impure and one pure—
he may not separate from one for the other. 
Rabbi Eliezer says: 
One may [initially] separate from the pure for the impure.

->2<-

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter 2, Mishnah 1, regarding the validity of separating Terumah (the priestly gift) when the produce involved is in a state of ritual impurity. It explores the legal consequences of actions performed by mistake versus those done intentionally, and extends these principles to the laws of the Sabbath and the Sabbatical year.</meta>

One may not separate <term>Terumah</term> <note>The portion of the harvest designated for the Priests, which must be eaten in a state of ritual purity.</note> from produce that is <term>ritually impure</term> <note>original: *tamei*. Impure items cannot be eaten by Priests and must generally be destroyed or used for fuel.</note> for produce that is <term>ritually pure</term> <note>original: *tahor*.</note>.
And if he did separate it:
If it was done by mistake <note>original: *shogeg*. An act committed through ignorance of the law or a factual error.</note>, his Terumah is valid;
If it was done intentionally <note>original: *mezid*</note>, he has accomplished nothing.
And likewise for a <term>Levite</term> <note>A member of the tribe of Levi who receives the "First Tithe" from the Israelites.</note> who possessed a portion of tithe that was itself still untithed <note>original: *ma'aser tevel*. Produce that is legally "entangled" because the required priestly portion has not yet been removed from it.</note>, 
and he proceeded to separate the priestly portion from it:
If it was done by mistake, what he has done stands;
If it was done intentionally, he has accomplished nothing.
Rabbi Yehudah says:
If he knew about its status from the beginning,
then even if the specific act was a mistake,
he has accomplished nothing.

## Tractate Terumot Chapter 2 Mishnah 3

->3<-
One who immerses vessels <note>To purify them in a ritual bath (mikvah) so they can be used with sacred foods.</note> on the <term>Sabbath</term> <note>original: *Shabbat*. Generally, one may not alter the ritual status of an object on the day of rest.</note>:
If it was by mistake, he may use them;
If it was intentional, he may not use them <note>This serves as a Rabbinic penalty to discourage willful violation of the Sabbath laws.</note>.
One who tithes his produce or cooks on the Sabbath:
If it was by mistake, he may eat the food;
If it was intentional, he may not eat it.
One who plants a tree or seed on the Sabbath:
If it was by mistake, he may keep it;
If it was intentional, he must uproot it.
But during the <term>Sabbatical Year</term> <note>original: *Shvi'it*. The seventh year of the agricultural cycle in which the land of Israel must lie fallow and no planting is permitted.</note>,
whether it was by mistake or intentional, he must uproot it.

## Tractate Terumot Chapter 2 Mishnah 4

->4<-
One may not separate Terumah from one species for a different species.
And if he did separate it, his Terumah is not valid <note>For example, one cannot give wheat to exempt an obligation on barley.</note>.
All types of wheat are considered one species.
All types of figs are considered one species.
The category of figs, including dried figs <note>original: *gerogrot*</note> and pressed fig-cakes <note>original: *develah*</note>, is considered one species,
and one may separate from one of these for the other.
In any place where a <term>Priest</term> <note>original: *Kohen*. The descendant of Aaron to whom the Terumah must be given.</note> is available,
one should separate from the highest quality produce.
In any place where a Priest is not available,
one should separate from the produce that lasts the longest <note>original: *ha-mitkayem*. Literally "that which endures." If a Priest is not nearby to collect the gift immediately, the owner should choose produce that will not spoil before it can be delivered.</note>.
Rabbi Yehudah says:

It also defines the "species" rule, requiring that the priestly gift be taken from the same type of crop it is intended to exempt.</summary>

## Tractate Terumot Chapter 2 Mishnah 5

### 5
One may separate Terumah using a small whole onion,  
but not half of a large onion.  
**Rabbi Yehudah** says:  
No, rather one should use half of a large onion <note>Rabbi Yehudah prioritizes the taste and quality of the large onion over the "completeness" of the small one.</note>.  
And so **Rabbi Yehudah** used to say:  
One may separate Terumah from urban onions for village onions,  
but not from village onions for urban onions,  
because urban onions are the food of <term>refined city-folk</term> <note>original: *politikin*. From the Greek word for "citizens" or "urbanites," referring to those with sophisticated tastes who preferred the milder urban onions.</note>.

## Tractate Terumot Chapter 2 Mishnah 6

### 6
One may separate Terumah from oil-olives for pickling-olives,  
but not from pickling-olives for oil-olives <note>Since oil-olives are considered more valuable for their extract.</note>.  
And one may separate unboiled wine for boiled wine,  
but not boiled for unboiled.  
This is the general rule:  
Any two items that are considered <term>diverse kinds</term> <note>original: *kilayim*. The Torah forbids mixing certain species of seeds or plants; if they cannot be grown together, one cannot serve as the Terumah for the other.</note> in relation to one another,  
one may not separate Terumah from one for the other,  
even from the choice quality for the poor quality.  
But regarding that which is *not* "diverse kinds" in relation to another,  
one may separate from the choice quality for the poor quality,  
but not from the poor quality for the choice quality.  
And if he did separate from the poor for the choice,  
his Terumah is valid,  
except for <term>darnel</term> <note>original: *zunin*. A weed (Lolium temulentum) that resembles wheat but is bitter and potentially toxic.</note> for wheat,  
because darnel is not considered food.  
The cucumber and the melon <note>original: *melafofon*. In the Mishnah, this likely refers to a specific type of sweet melon or a variety of cucumber.</note> are considered one species.  
**Rabbi Yehudah** says:  
They are two distinct species.

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 3 Mishnah 1
### 1

If one separates a cucumber as <term>Terumah</term> <note>The portion of the harvest designated for the Priests, which must be eaten in a state of ritual purity.</note> and it is found to be bitter, or a watermelon and it is found to be rotten: 
It is [considered] Terumah, but he must go back and separate Terumah again <note>This is a "double" status: the first gift is holy enough that it cannot be eaten by a non-priest, but it was not of sufficient quality to fulfill the farmer's obligation.</note>.

If one separates a jar of wine and it is found to be vinegar: 
If it was known that it was vinegar before he separated it, it is not Terumah; 
If it turned into vinegar only after he separated it, it is Terumah; 
If it is a matter of doubt, it is Terumah, but he must go back and separate Terumah again.

The first [separation] does not <term>make it mixed</term> <note>original: *medama'at*. This refers to Terumah falling into ordinary food (*chullin*). Usually, if the ratio is less than 1 part Terumah to 100 parts ordinary food, the whole batch becomes forbidden to non-priests. Here, because the first separation was of poor quality or doubtful, it is treated more leniently.</note> on its own, and one is not liable for the <term>additional fifth</term> <note>original: *chomesh*. A penalty of 20% added to the value if a non-priest accidentally eats Terumah.</note> on its account; and so too with the second.

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 3 Mishnah 2
### 2

If one of them <note>The doubtful or poor-quality gifts mentioned in the previous law.</note> fell into <term>mundane produce</term> <note>original: *chullin*. Ordinary, non-consecrated food.</note>, it does not make the batch mixed. 
If the second one fell into a different place, it does not make that batch mixed. 
If they both fell into the same place, they make it mixed according to the volume of the smaller of the two. <gloss>by the smaller</gloss> <note>original: *biktanah*. This interlinear note clarifies that the calculation for the 1:100 ratio is based on the volume of the smaller portion.</note>

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 3 Mishnah 3
### 3

In the case of partners who separated Terumah one after the other: 
**Rabbi Akiva** says: 
The Terumah of both of them is valid Terumah <note>Meaning both portions are holy, as if both partners intended to give extra.</note>. 
But the **Sages** say: 
The Terumah of the second is not Terumah <note>Because the first partner already fulfilled the obligation for the entire pile of produce.</note>. 
**Rabbi Yose** says: 
If the first partner separated the [full] required amount, the Terumah of the second is not Terumah, 
but if the first did not separate the [full] required amount, the Terumah of the second is Terumah.

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 3 Mishnah 4
### 4

To what circumstances do these words apply? 
In a case where they did not speak [to one another].

But if he granted permission to a member of his household, or to his male slave, or to his female slave to separate <term>Terumah</term> <note>The portion of the harvest given to the Priests.</note>, their separation is valid.

Laborers do not have the authority to separate <term>Terumah</term>, except for those who tread the grapes, for they [the treaders] render the winepress susceptible to ritual impurity immediately <note>Because the grapes are turned into liquid, they become "prepared" to contract ritual impurity. One who says:

> and its <term>Tithes</term> are within it,

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 3 Mishnah 6

6
One who separates <term>Terumah</term> before the <term>First Fruits</term>, 
or the <term>First Tithe</term> before the <term>Terumah</term>, 
or the <term>Second Tithe</term> before the <term>First [Tithe]</term>, 
even though he has violated a negative commandment, 
that which he has done is legally valid, as it is stated: (Exodus 22:28) 
> "You shall not delay the offering from your full harvest and the outflow of your presses." <note>original: *Mele'atcha v'dim'acha lo te'acher*. The Torah establishes a chronological order: First Fruits (fullness), then Terumah (outflow), then Tithes. While "delaying" or swapping this order is forbidden, the resulting gifts are still considered holy.</note>

## Tractate Terumot Chapter 3 Mishnah 7
### 7
And from where do we know that **First Fruits** <term>Bikkurim</term> <note>The very first ripened fruits of the Seven Species brought to the Temple.</note> should take precedence over <term>Terumah</term> <note>The portion given to the Priest.</note>?
For this [First Fruits] is called both "Terumah" and "the first," 
and that [Terumah] is also called "Terumah" and "the first"! <note>original: *reishit*. The Bible uses the same terminology for both, creating a potential for confusion regarding which should be separated first.</note>
Rather, the **First Fruits** take precedence because they are the "first fruits" of everything;
and <term>Terumah</term> takes precedence over the **First Tithe** <term>Ma'aser Rishon</term> because it is called "the first";
and the **First Tithe** takes precedence over the **Second Tithe** <note>A second 10% portion eaten by the owner in Jerusalem.</note> because it [the First Tithe] contains within it "the first" <note>The "Tithe of the Tithe" (*Terumat Ma'aser*) which the Levite gives to the Priest is also called *reishit* (the first/best portion).</note>.

## Tractate Terumot Chapter 3 Mishnah 8
### 8
One who intends to say "<term>Terumah</term>" but [accidentally] says "**Tithe**,"
or intends to say "**Tithe**" but says "<term>Terumah</term>,"
or intends to say a "**Burnt Offering**" <term>Olah</term> but says a "**Peace Offering**" <term>Shelamim</term>,
or a "**Peace Offering**" but says a "**Burnt Offering**,"
or [if he says] "**That I shall not enter this house**" but [accidentally] says "**this one**" [pointing to a different house],
or "**That I shall not derive benefit from this person**" but says "**from this one**"—
he has said nothing at all,
until his mouth and his heart are in agreement <note>In Jewish law, for a declaration of sanctity or a vow to be binding, the spoken words must accurately reflect the person's internal intention. A "slip of the tongue" does not create a holy status.</note>.

## Tractate Terumot Chapter 3 Mishnah 9
### 9
In the case of a **Gentile** <term>Nokhri</term> and a **Samaritan** <term>Kuti</term> <note>The Samaritans followed the Five Books of Moses but were often viewed with legal skepticism regarding their adherence to Rabbinic traditions.</note>:
their <term>Terumah</term> is considered valid <term>Terumah</term>,
their **Tithes** are valid **Tithes**, <insert>and their Tithes</insert>
and their **Consecrated Property** <note>Property donated to the Temple treasury.</note> is considered **Consecrated**.
**Rabbi Yehuda** says:
A **Gentile** does not have the law of a **Fourth-Year Vineyard** <term>Kerem Reva'i</term> <note>The fruit of a vineyard's fourth year of growth, which must be eaten in Jerusalem or redeemed.</note>.
But the **Sages** say:
He does have [this law].
The <term>Terumah</term> separated by a **Gentile** renders a mixture forbidden <term>meduma</term> <note>If his Terumah falls into regular food, it makes the whole batch forbidden to non-priests, just like Jewish Terumah.</note>, and one who eats it [unintentionally] is liable to pay the **additional fifth** <term>chomesh</term> <note>A 25% penalty (one-fifth of the new total) added to the principal value when holy food is eaten by a non-priest.</note>.

--- Page 123 ---
<meta>This page continues the legal debates regarding the "Priest’s Share" (Terumah) and the rules of nullification when it is mixed with common produce. The previous page discussed how to handle mixtures involving ritual impurity and various types of tithes. This page focuses on the specific logic used by the Schools of Hillel and Shammai and the rulings of Rabbi Eliezer versus the majority of scholars.</meta>

The **School of Hillel** said to the **School of Shammai**:
Since the **pure share** is forbidden to **non-priests** <note>original: "zarim," literally "strangers," referring to Israelites who are not from the priestly line of Aaron</note>,
and even the **impure share** is forbidden to the **Priests**,
just as the pure **nullifies the mixture** <note>original: "olah," literally "comes up" or "is raised," referring to the rule where one part of the Priest's Share in 100 parts of common grain is removed, "raising" the status of the rest to be permitted</note>,
so too the impure should **nullify the mixture**!
The **School of Shammai** said to them:
No! If **common produce** <term>chullin: ordinary food with no sacred status</term>, which is considered "light" <note>legally less restrictive</note> because it is permitted to non-priests, can nullify the **pure share**,
should the **Priest’s Share**, which is "grave" <note>legally more restrictive</note> because it is forbidden to non-priests, nullify the **impure share**?
After they reached an agreement <note>scholars debate whether the School of Shammai convinced Hillel or vice-versa, but a consensus was reached</note>,
**Rabbi Eliezer** says:
It must be **set aside and burned** <note>because impure sacred food cannot be eaten and must be destroyed by fire</note>.
But the **Sages** <note>the collective majority of scholars</note> say:
It is **lost in its minority** <note>it is completely nullified because it is the smaller part of the mixture</note>.

->5<-

A **measure** <term>se’ah: a unit of volume, approx. 7.3 liters</term> of the **Priest’s Share** that fell into **one hundred** measures of common produce,

**Rabbi Eliezer** says:
It **creates a mixture** <note>original: "medamma'at," making the new batch forbidden to non-priests</note> as if it were a **certainty** of the Priest’s Share.
But the **Sages** say:
It only **creates a mixture** according to its **proportional calculation** <note>original: "cheshbon," meaning its influence is diluted based on how much common produce it was already mixed with</note>.

if she ate the Priest’s Share before a Priest had **acquired it** <note>meaning the grain was still in the farmer's possession and not yet gifted to a specific priest</note>,

<note>Because she is now the wife of a Priest, she is entitled to consume the holy share herself. Therefore, she effectively "pays" the restitution back into her own household.</note>
if she ate the Priest’s Share after a Priest had **acquired it**,
she pays the **principal to the owners** <note>the specific priest who originally owned the grain</note> and the **fifth to herself**,
because they said:
The one who eats the **Priest’s Share unintentionally**,
pays the **principal to the owners**,
and the **fifth to whomever they wish**.

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 6 Mishnah 3

3
One who **feeds** his **workers** and his **guests** the **Priest’s Share**,
**he** <note>the employer or host</note> pays the **principal**,
and **they** <note>the ones who ate it</note> pay the **fifth**.
These are the words of **Rabbi Meir**.
But the **Sages say**:
**They** <note>the eaters</note> pay both the **principal and the fifth**,
and **he** <note>the host</note> pays **them** the **value of their meal**.
<note>The Sages argue that since the workers were entitled to a meal as part of their wages, and the host gave them forbidden food, he must reimburse them for the value of the food they lost the right to eat.</note>

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 6 Mishnah 4

4
One who **steals** the **Priest’s Share** and did **not eat it**,
pays **double restitution** <note>the "kefel" penalty for theft based on Exodus 22:8</note> based on the **value of the Priest’s Share**.
If he **ate it**,
he pays **two principals and a fifth**:
a **principal and a fifth** from **common produce**,
and a **principal** of the **value of the Priest’s Share**.
<note>He pays the "principal and a fifth" to replace the sacred food he consumed, plus an additional "principal" as the penalty for the theft itself.</note>
If he **stole consecrated Priest’s Share** <insert>the Priest’s Share</insert> and ate it,
he pays **two fifths and a principal**,
<note>This refers to a case where the theft and consumption are both violations of sacred property, leading to a compounding of the "fifth" penalty.</note>

## Tractate Terumot Chapter 7 Mishnah 2
### 2
A **Priest’s daughter** who is **married to an Israelite**,
<note>When a Priest's daughter marries a non-priest (an "Israelite"), she loses her legal right to eat Terumah. If she eats it after this change in status, she is considered a non-priest consuming holy food.</note>

she pays the **principal** but does **not pay the fifth**,
and her **punishment is by burning**.
<note>Because she is a Priest's daughter who committed an act of "profanation" while married, biblical law (Leviticus 21:9) prescribes this specific capital punishment. The financial penalty is reduced because the capital sentence is more severe.</note>
If she was **married** to one of those **disqualified** from the priesthood,

and her **punishment is by strangulation**.
These are the words of **Rabbi Meir**.

In **both cases**, she pays the **principal** but does **not pay the fifth**,
and their **punishment is by burning**.

## Tractate Terumot Chapter 7 Mishnah 4
### 4
**This is the general rule:**
Whoever pays the **principal and the fifth**,
the **restitution** becomes the **Priest’s Share** [holy];
if the **Priest wishes to waive** the debt, he **may not waive it**.
<note>Because the "fifth" is a religious atonement, it belongs to the realm of the Divine; the Priest is merely the recipient and does not have the authority to cancel the obligation.</note>

the **restitution** is **non-sacred** food;
<note>The text concludes that if only the base value is paid, it remains common food (Chullin), and the Priest can treat it like any other civil debt owed to him.</note>

**Let him make them all impure,** <note>Rabbi Eliezer maintains his strict stance: one must not actively hand over a single sacred loaf to be defiled, even if it means the Gentile will then defile every loaf the person is carrying.</note>

<summary>This page explores the halakhic debates between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Joshua regarding the preservation of the Priest's Share (Terumah) when it is at risk of becoming ritually impure. The central conflict is whether one should take an active role in defiling a small portion to save the rest, or remain passive and allow the whole to be lost or defiled naturally.</summary>
<keywords>Mishnah, Terumot, Ritual Purity, Priest's Share, Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Joshua, Halakha, Impurity, Wine Press, Revi'it</keywords>

## Chapter 9

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 9 Mishnah 1

1
**One who sows the Priest's Share,** <note>The Priest's Share, or *Terumah*, refers to the portion of the harvest given to the Priests which must be eaten in a state of ritual purity. Here, the Mishnah discusses what happens if those sacred seeds are planted in a field.</note>
**unintentionally, he must plow it up,** <term>shogeg: an act performed through ignorance or error.</term>
**intentionally, he must let it remain.** <term>mezid: a willful or deliberate act. Counter-intuitively, the penalty for intentional sowing is to let it grow, so the owner does not benefit from the immediate reuse of the land.</term>
**If it has reached a third of its growth,**
**whether unintentionally or intentionally, he must let it remain.**
**But with flax,**
**[if sown] intentionally, he must plow it up.** <note>Flax growth is considered differently because it is particularly taxing on the soil.</note>

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 9 Mishnah 2

2
**And [this crop] is liable for Gleanings, and for Forgotten Sheaves, and for the Corner,** <note>These refer to the three gifts for the poor required by the Torah: *Leket* (fallen stalks), *Shikhchah* (forgotten bundles), and *Pe'ah* (the corner of the field left unharvested).</note>
**and the poor of Israel and the poor of the Priests may glean,**
**and the poor of Israel sell their [share] to the Priests**
**at the price of the Priest's Share, and the money belongs to them.** <note>Since non-priests are forbidden from eating *Terumah*, the poor of Israel cannot consume what they gather. Instead, they sell the produce to a Priest—who is allowed to eat it—and keep the profit.</note>
**Rabbi Tarfon said:**
**Only the poor of the Priests should glean,**
**lest they [the poor of Israel] forget and put [the food] into their mouths.**
**Rabbi Akiva said to him:**
**If so,**
**only those who are ritually pure should glean.** <note>Rabbi Akiva argues that if we were to impose such strict safeguards against accidental misuse, we would eventually exclude almost everyone from the right to glean.</note>

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 9 Mishnah 3

The poor of Israel receive the produce but must sell it to someone permitted to eat it.</note>
**and the money belongs to them.**
**One who beats the grain [with a stick] is praiseworthy.** <note>This manual method avoids the complications of using animals to process sacred produce.</note>
**And the one who threshes with an animal, how should he act?**
**He hangs baskets on the necks of the animal,**
**and places into them [fodder] of that same species.**

**nor does he feed it the Priest's Share.**

## Tractate Terumot Chapter 9 Mishnah 4

4
**The offspring of the Priest's Share is considered the Priest's Share,** <term>Gidulei Terumah: crops grown from sacred seeds. To prevent people from holding onto Terumah seeds to plant them for personal gain, the Sages ruled that the resulting crop retains the sacred status.</term>
**but the offspring of the offspring are common produce.** <term>Chullin: ordinary food that has no sacred restrictions and may be eaten by anyone.</term>
**However, regarding untithed produce,** <term>Tevel: produce from which the required priestly and levitical portions have not yet been removed.</term>
**and the First Tithe,**
**and the aftergrowth of the Seventh Year,** <note>original: "סְפִיחֵי שְׁבִיעִית" — crops that grow on their own during the Sabbatical year when farming is forbidden.</note>
**and the Priest's Share from outside the Land [of Israel],**
**and a mixture of sacred and common food,** <term>Meduma: a case where Terumah was accidentally mixed into common produce.</term>
**and the First Fruits,**
**their offspring are common produce.**
**The offspring of consecrated items and the Second Tithe are common produce,**
**and one redeems them at the time of their sowing.** <note>original: "וּפוֹדֶה אוֹתָם בִּזְמַן זַרְעָן" — the owner pays the value of the seeds to the Temple or brings the equivalent value to Jerusalem to ensure the sanctity is transferred.</note>

## Tractate Terumot Chapter 9 Mishnah 5

5
**If there are one hundred [stalks] in a garden of the Priest's Share and one of common produce,**
**they are all permitted in the case of a thing whose seed decomposes.** <note>When a seed like wheat is planted, the original seed rots away to grow the new plant. In such cases, if the majority of the plants are common produce, the sacred influence is nullified.</note>
**But in the case of a thing whose seed does not decompose,** <note>Such as a bulb (onions or garlic), where the original plant remains part of the new growth.</note>
**even if there are one hundred of common produce and one of the Priest's Share,**
**they are all forbidden.**

## Tractate Terumot Chapter 9 Mishnah 6

**Untithed produce,** <term>Tevel</term>
**its offspring are permitted in the case of a thing whose seed decomposes;**
**but in the case of a thing whose seed does not decompose,**
**even the offspring of the offspring are forbidden.**

**And what is a thing whose seed does not perish?** <note>original: "וְאֵי זֶה הוּא דָבָר שֶׁאֵין זַרְעוֹ כָלֶה?" In Jewish law, if a seed disintegrates, the new plant is a new entity. If the seed/bulb remains, the new plant is seen as a direct continuation of the original sacred seed.</note>

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 9 Mishnah 7

## Chapter 10

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 10 Mishnah 1

1
**An onion that one placed inside lentils:**
**if it is whole, it is permitted;** <note>A whole onion is not thought to impart its flavor to the lentils. If the onion was "Priest's Share" and the lentils were common food, the lentils remain permitted for non-priests.</note>
**and if he cut it, it is judged by the imparting of flavor;** <term>Noten Ta’am: the legal principle that if a forbidden substance gives its taste to permitted food, the entire mixture becomes forbidden.</term>
**and for all other cooked dishes,**
**whether whole or cut,**
**it is judged by the imparting of flavor.**
**Rabbi Yehuda permits its use in fish brine,** <note>original: "בַּצְּחָנָה" (tsachana); a strong, pungent fish sauce.</note>
**because it is only to remove the foul odor.** <note>Since the onion's purpose is to neutralize a bad smell rather than to add a pleasant taste, Rabbi Yehuda argues it does not forbid the mixture.</note>

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 10 Mishnah 2

2
**An apple that one crushed and placed into dough and it leavened it,**
**behold, this is forbidden.** <note>If the apple was the Priest's Share, its ability to act as a leavening agent makes the entire batch of dough sacred and forbidden to non-priests.</note>
**Barley that fell into a cistern of water:**
**even though its water became putrid,**
**its water remains permitted.** <note>Because the barley spoiled the water rather than improving it, the water does not take on the holy status of the Priest's Share.</note>

## Chapter 11

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 11 Mishnah 1

->1<-
One may not put a cake of dried figs or individual dried figs into **fish brine**, <term>Muryas: A brine or sauce made from fish parts, often used as a condiment in the Roman world.</term>

One may not boil wine of the **Priest’s Share**,
because it reduces it [in volume]. <note>Boiling causes evaporation, which was viewed as "wasting" a portion of the sacred wine.</note>
Rabbi Judah permits it,
because it improves it. <note>Rabbi Judah argues that the increase in quality and longevity of boiled wine justifies the loss of volume.</note>

<meta>This page continues the laws concerning the proper use and disposal of the Priest's Share (Terumah). It concludes a discussion on the bran of different grains before moving into practical rulings on how to handle storage containers and animal fodder that have been in contact with sacred produce.</meta>

Bran from new grain is forbidden <note>Original: "Sabbim." This refers to the coarse husks or bran. If the grain is "new" (freshly harvested), the bran still contains a significant amount of flour and is thus considered sacred food that non-priests may not eat.</note>, 
but bran from old grain is permitted. <note>Old grain is drier, and its bran is considered mere waste with no nutritional value for humans.</note>
One may handle the **Priest’s Share** in the same way he handles **common produce**. <term>Chullin: Ordinary, non-sacred food that may be eaten by anyone, unlike the Priest's Share which is restricted to Priests and their households.</term>
One who sifts a *kab* or two *kabs* of fine flour from a *seah* <note>A *seah* is a dry measure containing six *kabs*.</note>, 
should not discard the remainder, 
but rather leave it in a secluded place. <note>The "remainder" still contains the status of the Priest's Share; while it may not be high-quality flour, it must be treated with respect and not discarded like common trash.</note>

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 11 Mishnah 6
### 6

A granary from which one cleared out wheat of the **Priest’s Share**, 
we do not require him to sit and pick up [the grains] one by one; 
rather, he sweeps in his usual manner and then puts **common produce** into it. <note>The law is practical; once the bulk of the sacred wheat is removed, the tiny remaining grains are "nullified" by the large amount of common wheat added later.</note>

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 11 Mishnah 7
### 7

Similarly, an oil jar that was spilled, 
we do not require him to sit and dab [at the residue], 
rather, he treats it in the same way he treats **common produce**.

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 11 Mishnah 8
### 8

One who pours from jar to jar and three drops drip [at the end], 
he may then put **common produce** into [the first jar]. 
If he tilted it and drained it, 
this [liquid] is considered the **Priest’s Share**. 
And how much must there be of the **Priest’s Share of the Tithe** from **doubtfully tithed produce**, <gloss>in the Priest's Share</gloss> <term>Demai: Produce purchased from a common person where it is uncertain if the tithes were properly removed. The "Priest's Share of the Tithe" is the portion a Levite gives to a Priest.</term>
to require him to bring it to the Priest? 
One-eighth of an eighth [of a *log*]. <note>This is a very small volume, approximately 1/64th of a *log* (roughly 7-9 milliliters). If the amount is smaller than this, it is not worth the effort of delivery.</note>

### Tractate Terumot Chapter 11 Mishnah 9
### 9

Bitter vetch of the **Priest’s Share**, <term>Karshinim: A species of legume (Vicia ervilia) used primarily as animal fodder rather than human food.</term>
one may feed them to cattle, wild animals, and poultry. 
An Israelite <note>A non-priest.</note> who rents a cow from a Priest, 
may feed it bitter vetch of the **Priest’s Share**. <note>Since the cow belongs to the Priest, it has the right to eat sacred fodder, even though it is currently in the service of a non-priest.</note>
But a Priest who rents a cow from an Israelite, 
even though he is responsible for its food, 
he may not feed it bitter vetch of the **Priest’s Share**. <note>The animal itself must belong to a Priest to consume the Priest's Share; the identity of the person paying for the food is secondary.</note>
An Israelite who assesses a cow from a Priest <note>A "Shum" arrangement, where the Israelite takes the animal for a period and they split the profits or losses in its value.</note>, 
may not feed it bitter vetch of the **Priest’s Share**.

### Tractate Ma'aserot Chapter 1 Mishnah 1

->1<-

They stated a general rule regarding **tithes**: <term>Ma’aserot: The various portions (First Tithe, Second Tithe, Poor Man's Tithe) that must be set aside from crops grown in Israel before the food is permitted for general consumption.</term>
Anything that is food, and is guarded <note>Meaning the produce is private property and not "hefker" (ownerless or wild).</note>, and grows from the earth,

And they stated another general rule:
Anything that is food at its beginning and food at its end <note>This refers to plants that are edible even in their early, immature stages, like certain herbs or legumes.</note>,
even if one kept it to increase its bulk as food,
is liable [to be tithed] whether it is small or large.
And anything that is not food at its beginning...

But since its end is as food, it is not liable <note>Liability for tithes only begins once the produce is considered "food." For certain items that change use as they grow, the law looks at their final intended state.</note> until it becomes food. <gloss>until it is made [into food]</gloss>

### Tractate Ma’aserot Chapter 1 Mishnah 2
->2<-

From what time are fruits liable for tithes? <note>This "time" refers to the stage of biological development, known as *onah le-ma'aserot* (the season of tithes), after which the fruit can no longer be eaten as a "random snack" in the field without being tithed.</note>
**Figs**: from when they begin to ripen;
**Grapes** and **wild grapes**: from when they produce juice;
**Sumac** and **mulberries**: from when they turn red;
and all **red [fruits]**: from when they turn red.
**Pomegranates**: from when they become soft; <note>Original: *mish-yimmassu*. This refers to the stage where the inner seeds become juicy and pulp-like.</note>
**Dates**: from when they begin to "cast leaven"; <note>Original: *mish-yattilu se’or*. A poetic way of describing the beginning of the fermentation process or the development of sugar that makes the fruit swell.</note>
**Peaches**: from when they develop "veins"; <note>Original: *mish-yattilu gidim*. Referring to the internal fibers or the red streaks that appear near the pit as the fruit matures.</note>
and **walnuts**: from when they form a "chamber." <note>Original: *megurah*. This is the stage when the kernel shrinks away from the shell, creating a hollow space or "room" inside.</note>
**Rabbi Yehuda** says:
**Walnuts** and **almonds**: from when they form a husk. <note>The outer green skin that covers the shell.</note>

### Tractate Ma’aserot Chapter 1 Mishnah 3
->3<-

**Carobs**: from when they become spotted, <gloss>from when they become spotted</gloss> <note>Original: *mish-yinnakedu*. Dark spots appear on the green skin as the carob begins to sweeten and dry.</note>
and all **black [fruits]**: from when they become spotted. <gloss>from when they become spotted</gloss>
**Pears**, and **crustumenian pears**, <note>Original: *krustomilin*. A high-quality variety of pear highly prized in antiquity, likely named after the town of Crustumerium.</note> and **quinces**, and **crab-apples**:
from when they become "bald," <gloss>from when they become "bald"</gloss> <note>Original: *mish-yikrahu*. This refers to the stage when the fruit loses the fine, downy fuzz it had during early growth and becomes smooth.</note>
and all **white [fruits]**: from when they become "bald." <gloss>from when they become "bald"</gloss>
**Fenugreek**: from when it is [mature enough] to sprout;
**Grain** and **olives**: from when they reach a third [of their growth]. <note>This "one-third" rule is a fundamental standard in Jewish law for when grain and olives are considered sufficiently developed to be called a crop.</note>

### Tractate Ma’aserot Chapter 1 Mishnah 4
->4<-

And among **vegetables**:
**Cucumbers**,
and **gourds**,
and **watermelons**,
and **muskmelons**. <note>Original: *melafefonot*. While modern Hebrew uses this for cucumbers, in the Mishnah it refers to a type of melon.</note>
**Apples** and **citrons** <gloss>and citrons</gloss>:
are liable whether they are large or small.
**Rabbi Shimon** exempts **citrons** <gloss>citrons</gloss> when they are small.
That which is liable in **bitter almonds** is exempt in **sweet [almonds]**,
and that which is liable in **sweet [almonds]** is exempt in **bitter [ones]**. <note>Bitter almonds are eaten when they are young and soft (making them liable then), but become inedible/toxic when large. Sweet almonds are the opposite; they are only eaten when large and mature, so they are not liable when small.</note>

# Tractate Tithes Chapter 1 Mishnah 5
## 5
And what is their **threshing floor** <term>original: *goren*; refers to the final stage of processing that renders the produce liable for tithing</term> for tithes?
**Cucumbers** and **gourds**: from when he removes the fuzz; <note>Original: *mish-yefakes*. This refers to rubbing off the fine white down that covers young gourds.</note>
and if he does not remove the fuzz, until he sets them in a pile.
**Watermelon**: from when he scrapes it; <note>Original: *mish-yeshalek*. Scraping the surface to improve its appearance for sale.</note>
if he does not scrape it, until he makes a storage-heap.
**Vegetables that are bundled**: from when he bundles them;
and if he does not bundle them, until he fills the vessel;
and if he does not fill the vessel, until he has gathered all he needs.
A **basket [of fruit]**: until he covers it; <note>It was common to cover baskets with leaves to protect the fruit.</note>
and if he does not cover it, until he fills the vessel;
and if he does not fill the vessel, until he has gathered all he needs.
In what case do these words apply?
To one who is **taking the produce to the market**.
But for one **taking it to his home**, he may eat a **random snack** <term>original: *arai*; an informal, non-fixed meal</term> from them until he reaches his house.

# Tractate Tithes Chapter 1 Mishnah 6
## 6
**Separated kernels**, **raisins**, and **carobs**: from when he sets them in a pile.
**Onions**: from when he peels them; <note>Original: *mish-yepakel*. Specifically, removing the dry outer leaves.</note>
and if he does not peel them, from when he sets them in a pile.
**Grain**: from when he **smooths the pile**; <term>original: *mish-yimrach*; the act of leveling the top of the grain heap with a shovel, marking the end of the harvest work</term>
if he does not smooth it, until he sets it in a pile.
**Legumes**: from when he **sieves** them; <note>Original: *mish-yikbor*. Using a large sieve to separate the beans from the refuse.</note>
and if he does not sieve them, until he smooths the pile.
Even though he has smoothed the pile <insert>the act of smoothing</insert>,
he may still take from the **broken stalks**, from the **sides**,
and from what is inside the **straw**,
and eat. <note>The law is lenient regarding the small amounts left over or stuck in the chaff, allowing one to snack on them even after the main pile is officially "finished."</note>

# Tractate Tithes Chapter 1 Mishnah 7
## 7
**Wine**: from when he **skims** it. <note>Original: *mish-yikpeh*. This is the stage where the foam or "crust" of skins and seeds is removed from the top of the fermenting vat.</note>
Even though he has skimmed it,
he may collect from the **upper press** or from the **pipe**, and drink. <note>Before the wine settles into the lower collecting vat, it is not yet fully "finished" in a way that forbids drinking a small amount.</note>
**Oil**: from when it **descends into the vat**. <note>Original: *ukah*. The collection pit at the bottom of the olive press.</note>

Even though [the oil] has already descended [into the collecting vat], he may still take oil from the **press-beam** <term>original: *ikkal*; the circular rope or beam used in the olive press</term>, from the **crushing-stone** <term>original: *memel*</term>, or from between the **boards** of the press, and put it into a **wafer** <term>original: *hamitah*; a thin pancake</term> or into a **stew-pot** <term>original: *tamhui*; a large serving dish</term>. ## Tractate Tithes Chapter 1 Mishnah 8

### 8

**Dried fig cakes**: [liability begins] from when he smoothes the surface of the cake. One may smooth the cakes with figs or grapes that are **untithed** <term>original: *tevel*; produce that is definitely liable for tithes but has not yet been processed</term>; Rabbi Yehuda forbids this. **Dried figs**: from when he treads them [into the storage jar]; and a **storage-heap**: from when he levels it. # Chapter 2

## Tractate Tithes Chapter 1 Mishnah 1

### 1

If one was passing through the marketplace and [a seller] said:
> "Take figs for yourselves!"
They may eat and are exempt [from tithing]. Therefore, if they eventually brought those figs into their homes, they must tithe them as **certainly untithed** <term>original: *vadai*; produce that has definitely never been tithed</term>. 

[If the seller said:]
> "Take and bring [the figs] into your homes!"
They may not eat a **random snack** from them. Therefore, if they brought them into their homes, they only tithe them as **doubtfully tithed** <term>original: *demai*; produce acquired from a common person where it is uncertain if the tithes were properly taken</term> <note>When the seller says "bring them home," it implies a more formal transfer of ownership that might have already triggered the tithing requirement.</note>.

# Tractate Tithes Chapter 2 Mishnah 2

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the "fixing" of produce for tithing. **Rabbi Yehuda said:**
**A story is told of a rose garden that was in Jerusalem,**
**where figs were sold at three or four for an *issar*,** <term>original: *issar*; a small Roman copper coin of low value</term>
**and never was a priestly offering or tithe separated from it.** <note>The figs were so cheap and sold in such a way that they were always considered a casual snack, which is exempt from tithing.</note>

### Tractate Tithes Chapter 2 Mishnah 6

->6<-

**One who says to his fellow:**
"Here is this *issar* for ten figs that I shall pick for myself," <insert>**for twenty**</insert>
he may pick and eat [one by one, and remain exempt from tithing];
"For a cluster [of grapes] that I shall pick for myself,"
he may pluck individual grapes and eat;
"For a pomegranate that I shall pick for myself,"
he may separate the seeds and eat;
"For a melon that I shall pick for myself,"
he may slice and eat. <note>In these cases, the buyer is selecting the fruit himself from the tree, so it is treated as a casual snack rather than a formal purchase of harvested goods.</note>
But if he said to him:
"For **these** twenty figs,"
"For **these** two clusters,"
"For **these** two pomegranates,"
"For **these** two melons,"
he may eat in his usual way and is exempt [from tithing],
because he purchased them while they were still **attached to the ground**. <note>original: *mchubar l'karka*; because the transaction occurred while the fruit was still growing, the buyer's act of picking them for immediate consumption is still considered a "snack."</note>

### Tractate Tithes Chapter 2 Mishnah 7

->7<-

**One who hires a worker to harvest figs with him,**
**and [the worker] said to him:**
**"On the condition that I may eat figs,"**
he may eat and is exempt [from tithing]; but if he gathered them together <note>i.e., into a basket or vessel to save for later</note>, he is liable.
**"On the condition that I and my son may eat,"**
or "that my son may eat as my wage,"
he [the worker] may eat and is exempt, but his son may eat and is liable. <note>Biblical law allows a worker to eat from the crop he is currently harvesting, but this privilege is personal and does not extend to family members.</note>
**"On the condition that I may eat during the harvest and after the harvest,"**
during the harvest, he eats and is exempt;
after the harvest, he eats and is liable,
since he is not eating **according to the Torah**. <note>The Torah (Deuteronomy 23:25-26) only permits eating while one is actively working in the field.</note>
**This is the general rule:**
**One who eats according to the Torah is exempt,**
and one who does not eat according to the Torah is liable.

### Tractate Tithes Chapter 2 Mishnah 8

**8**

If a worker **was working with *libsin* figs,** <term>original: *libsin*; a lower-quality variety of fig</term>
**he may not eat *bnoth sheva* figs;** <term>original: *bnoth sheva*; a high-quality variety of white figs</term>
and if he was working **with *bnoth sheva* figs,**
**he may not eat *libsin* figs.** <note>According to Jewish Law (based on Deuteronomy 23:25), a worker is entitled to eat from the produce they are currently harvesting, but they cannot "specialize" by eating a different, more expensive variety than the one they are handling.</note>
**But he may restrain himself** from eating
**until he reaches the place of the high-quality figs and then eat.**
**One who exchanges fruit with his fellow—**
**this one to eat and that one to eat,**
**or this one to dry and that one to dry—is obligated** to tithe. <note>original: *liktzot*; referring to the process of laying figs out to dry into cakes. An exchange of goods is considered a formal transaction, which immediately subjects the fruit to tithing, even if the intention is just a snack.</note>
**Rabbi Yehuda says:**
**One who exchanges fruit to eat is obligated,**
**but if it is to dry, he is exempt.**

# Chapter 3

### Tractate Tithes Chapter 3 Mishnah 1

**1**

**One who brings figs through his courtyard to dry,**
**his children and the members of his household may eat and are exempt** from tithing. <note>In this context, the courtyard is not considered a "finished" destination because the figs are just passing through on their way to the drying area.</note>
**The workers who are with him,**
**at a time when he is not responsible for providing their meals,**
**[may eat and are exempt];**
**but if he is responsible for providing their meals,**
**then these workers may not eat** without first tithing. <note>If the employer provides food as part of their contract, any fruit they eat is considered part of their "wages." Since wages are a formal transaction, the fruit must be tithed.</note>

### Tractate Tithes Chapter 3 Mishnah 2

**2**

**One who takes his workers out to the field,**
**at a time when he is not responsible for providing their meals,** <note>The Hebrew word "that there are [meals]" was written by a proofreader over an erased area.</note>
**they may eat and are exempt.**
**If he is responsible for providing their meals,** <note>The Hebrew word "none [no meals]" was written by a proofreader over an erased area.</note>
**they may eat one by one from the fig tree,**
**but they may not eat from the basket, nor from the crate, nor from the drying-place.** <note>Even if the employer provides meals, the workers retain a basic biblical right to snack from the tree itself. However, they cannot eat from gathered containers, as that is considered "finished" produce.</note>

**One who hires a worker to work with olives,**
**and the worker said to him:**
**"On the condition that I may eat olives,"**
**he may eat them one by one and is exempt** from tithing,
**but if he gathered them together, he is obligated.** <note>Eating one by one is considered a "casual snack," but gathering several pieces in one's hand or a basket constitutes a "fixed meal," which triggers the legal requirement to separate tithes.</note>
**To weed among onions,**
**and the worker said to him:**
**"On the condition that I may eat greens,"**
**he may nip off leaf by leaf and eat** and is exempt,
**but if he gathered them together, he is obligated.**

### Tractate Tithes Chapter 3 Mishnah 4
### 4

**If one found dried fig-cakes on the road,** <term>original: *ketzitzot*; figs that have been cut and dried into cakes</term>
**even beside a field of dried figs,** <insert>< a field ></insert> <note>Even if they are found right next to a private field, we assume the owner has given up hope of recovery (despair), making them "ownerless" and thus exempt from tithes.</note>
**and similarly, a fig tree that leans over the road,**
**and he found figs beneath it,**
**they are permitted regarding the laws of theft,**
**and they are exempt from the tithes;**
**but olives and carobs are obligated.** <note>Olives and carobs are distinct because their appearance changes less when they fall, or they are more valuable, so owners do not typically abandon them as easily as figs.</note>
**If he found dried figs,**
**if the majority of people have trodden on them, he is obligated** to tithe;
**and if not, he is exempt.** <note>If they are trodden upon, they are considered "processed" or "finished" by the public's actions, which "fixes" them for tithing once collected.</note>
**If he found slices of a fig-cake, he is obligated,**
**for it is known that they come from a finished product.** <note>Since the figs have already been pressed into a cake, they have reached the final stage of processing (*gmar melacha*), at which point they must be tithed before being eaten as a meal.</note>
**And as for carobs,**
**as long as he has not gathered them to the top of the roof,**
**he may take some down from them for his animal and is exempt** from tithing,
**because he may return the remainder.** <note>Because the carobs can still be returned to the pile to finish drying, they are not yet "fixed" for tithing as long as they are being used for animal feed rather than human consumption.</note>

### Tractate Tithes Chapter 3 Mishnah 5
### 5

**What constitutes a courtyard that is obligated in tithes?** <note>In Jewish law, bringing produce into a "courtyard" (*chatzer*) often acts as the final step that makes the food "fixed" for tithing. The Sages here debate what kind of courtyard has this legal power.</note>
**Rabbi Ishmael says:**
**A Tyrian courtyard, wherein utensils are kept safely.** <note>Tyre was famous for its secure, walled enclosures. Rabbi Ishmael argues that only a secure, private area triggers the tithing requirement.</note>
**Rabbi Akiva says:**
**Any courtyard where one person opens it and another person locks it is exempt.** <note>If a courtyard is shared or semi-public, it lacks the "privacy" needed to finalize the produce for tithing.</note>
**Rabbi Nehemiah says:**
**Any courtyard where a person is not ashamed to eat within it is obligated.** <note>Rabbi Nehemiah focuses on the human element: if a space is private enough that you would eat there without embarrassment, it counts as a "home" environment for tithing purposes.</note>
**Rabbi Yose says:**

## Tractate Tithes Chapter 3 Mishnah 9
### 9
A grapevine that is planted in a courtyard:  
one may take the whole cluster;  
and so too with a pomegranate, and so too with a watermelon.  
These are the words of Rabbi Tarfon.  
Rabbi Akiva says:  
One must pluck individual berries from the cluster, or break off seeds from the pomegranate, or slice pieces of the watermelon. <note>Rabbi Tarfon permits taking the whole fruit for a casual snack in the courtyard, whereas Rabbi Akiva argues that taking a whole "unit"—like a full cluster—looks like a formal harvest and thus triggers the tithe requirement.</note>  
Coriander that is sown in a courtyard:  
one may pluck leaf by leaf and eat,  
but if they are bundled together, he is obligated to tithe. <note>The act of "bundling" or "gathering" is a definitive labor that signals the end of the harvest process.</note>  
Savory, hyssop, and thyme that are in a courtyard:  
if they were being guarded, they are obligated. <note>original: *hasi'ah, ha'ezov, vehakornit*. If the owner protects these herbs, he shows they are a valued crop rather than wild growth, making them subject to the law.</note>

## Tractate Tithes Chapter 3 Mishnah 10
### 10
A fig tree that stands in a courtyard but leans over into a garden:  
one may eat in his usual way and is exempt. <note>Since the tree is rooted in the courtyard, the garden (where he stands to eat) is considered an extension of that casual space.</note>  
If it stands in a garden but leans over into a courtyard:  
one may eat one by one and be exempt,  
but if he gathers them together, he is obligated.  
If it stands in the Land of Israel and leans toward outside the Land,  
or stands outside the Land and leans toward the Land:  
everything follows the root. <note>Laws regarding the Land of Israel, such as tithes, only apply to produce grown within its borders. The root's location determines the legal status.</note>  
And regarding houses in walled cities:  
everything follows the root. <note>Refers to the special laws for selling and redeeming houses in cities that have been walled since the time of Joshua.</note>  
But in Cities of Refuge:  
everything follows the canopy. <note>original: *nof*. If a person fleeing to a City of Refuge reaches the branches that lean out beyond the city limits, he is considered "inside" and protected from the blood avenger.</note>  
And in Jerusalem:  
everything follows the canopy. <note>Regarding the eating of "Second Tithe" or "Holy Things," which must be consumed within the walls of Jerusalem; the space under the branches is treated as being inside the city.</note>

# Chapter 4

## Tractate Tithes Chapter 4 Mishnah 1
### 1
One who pickles, boils, or salts produce in the field: he is obligated. <note>These actions are considered "processing" or "preparing for storage," which completes the harvest and triggers the tithe even before the produce reaches the home.</note>  
One who buries produce in the ground to ripen: he is exempt. <note>original: *hamakmer*; this is seen as a continuation of the natural ripening process rather than a final preparation for a meal.</note>  
One who dips produce in salt or seasoning in the field: he is exempt. <note>This is considered a casual snack; the salt is used to enhance the immediate bite rather than to preserve the whole batch.</note>
