## Tractate Tithes Chapter 4 Mishnah 1
### 1
One who bruises olives so that the sap <note>original: *sharaf*. This refers to the liquid that exudes from the fruit when it is softened.</note> comes out is exempt from tithing.
One who squeezes olives onto his skin <note>to use the oil as an ointment</note> is exempt.
However, if he squeezed the oil and put it into the palm of his hand, he is liable to tithe. <note>Putting the oil into the hand transforms it from a casual application into a "collection" of food, which triggers the law.</note>
One who skims <term>froth</term> <note>original: *hamkapeh*. To remove the film or scum from the top of the oil or wine to prepare it for use.</note> for a dish is exempt;
but if he skims it into a pot, he is liable, because the pot is considered like a small collection vat.

### Tractate Tithes Chapter 4 Mishnah 2
### 2
Children who hid figs on the Sabbath to eat later, 
and forgot to tithe them: 
they may not eat them on Saturday night until they have tithed. <note>The arrival of the Sabbath "fixes" the status of the food; even if it was just a snack, once it has been set aside for the holy day, it must be tithed.</note>
Regarding a basket of fruit designated for the Sabbath:
The School of Shammai exempts it from the requirement,
but the School of Hillel holds it liable. <note>The School of Hillel believes the sanctity of the Sabbath establishes the fruit as a formal "meal," requiring tithes.</note>
Rabbi Yehuda says:
Even one who picks a basket of fruit to send to his friend as a gift
may not eat from it until he tithes.

### Tractate Tithes Chapter 4 Mishnah 3
### 3
One who takes olives from the softening-vat <note>original: *ma'atan*. A place where olives were piled to soften and heat up before being pressed.</note> 
may dip them one by one in salt and eat <note>this is considered a casual snack</note>;
but if he salted them and set them before him, he is liable.
Rabbi Eliezer says:
If he takes them from a ritually pure vat, he is liable;
but if he takes them from an impure vat, he is exempt,
because he returns the leftovers. <note>In an impure vat, the owner is careful not to return contaminated fruit to the pile, but Rabbi Eliezer argues that since one *could* return the leftovers, the act of taking them isn't a final harvest action.</note>

### Tractate Tithes Chapter 4 Mishnah 4
### 4
One may drink wine at the wine-press,
whether it is mixed with hot water or with cold water, and be exempt.
These are the words of Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Eleazar son of Zadok holds him liable to tithe.
But the Sages say:
If he mixes it with hot water, he is liable;
but if he mixes it with cold water, he is exempt. <note>The Sages view the mixing with hot water as a sign of a formal, "finished" drink, whereas cold water is used for a quick, casual refreshment.</note>

### Tractate Tithes Chapter 4 Mishnah 5
### 5

<meta>This page continues the discussion in Tractate Tithes (Ma'aserot) Chapter 4 regarding what actions constitute "processing" food. The previous page established that casual snacking is often exempt, but once a person gathers food into a container or processes it formally, the obligation to give tithes (agricultural taxes to the Priests, Levites, and the poor) begins.</meta>

One who peels barley, peels them one by one and eats <note>without tithing, as this is considered casual snacking</note>. 
But if he peeled them and placed them into his hand, he is liable to tithe <note>because collecting them in the hand signifies the start of a formal meal or processing</note>. 
One who rubs ears of wheat <term>melilot</term> <note>original: *melilot*. The act of rubbing the grain between the fingers to remove the chaff</note>, sifts the grain from one hand to the other and eats. 
But if he sifts it and places it into his lap, he is liable. 
Regarding coriander <note>original: *kasbar*</note> that was sown for its seed: 
its greens are exempt from tithing. 
If it was sown for its greens: 
it must be tithed for both the seed and the greens. 
**Rabbi Eliezer says:** 
Dill <note>original: *shevet*</note> must be tithed for its seed, its greens, and its stalks <note>original: *zirim*</note>. 
**And the Sages say:** 
It is not tithed for both seed and greens, except in the case of garden cress <note>original: *shachalim*</note> and field rocket <note>original: *gargir*</note> only.

## Tractate Tithes Chapter 4 Mishnah 6
### 6

**Rabban Gamliel says:** 
The shoots <note>original: *temarot*. The soft, edible tips of the growing plant</note> of fenugreek <note>original: *tiltan*</note>, of mustard, and of white beans, 
are liable for tithes. 
**Rabbi Eliezer says:** 
The caper-bush <note>original: *hatzalaf*</note> must be tithed for its shoots, its berries <note>original: *aviyonot*</note>, and its flower-buds <note>original: *kafras*</note>. 
**Rabbi Akiva says:** 
It is only tithed for the berries, 
because they alone are the fruit.

## Tractate Tithes Chapter 5 Mishnah 1
### 1

One who uproots seedlings from within his own field, 
and plants them elsewhere within his own property, is exempt <note>as the relocation of a plant is not considered a "harvest" or a "sale" that triggers tithing</note>. 
If he bought produce while it was still attached to the ground, he is exempt. 
If he gathered produce to send to his friend, he is exempt. 
**Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says:** 
If there are similar items being sold in the marketplace, 
then these are liable <note>He believes that once a crop reaches a stage where it is commercially viable, it can no longer be handled casually without tithing</note>.

One who uproots turnips or radishes from within his own [field],

Onions that have taken root in an attic <note>original: *aliyah*. An upper storage room</note> have become pure from becoming impure <note>In Jewish law, harvested food can contract ritual impurity, but a living plant attached to the ground cannot. # Tractate Second Tithe

## Chapter 1

### Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 1 Mishnah 1

->1<-
The **Second Tithe** <note>original: *Ma'aser Sheni*. In certain years of the seven-year agricultural cycle, a second tenth of the produce was set aside. Unlike other tithes given to the Levites or the poor, this was eaten by the owner and his family within the walls of Jerusalem</note>,
one may not sell it,
one may not pawn it <note>original: *memashkenim*. Using the sanctified produce as collateral for a loan</note>,
one may not exchange it,
and one may not use it as a weight against other items <note>original: *shoklin kenegdo*. Using the produce as a counter-weight on a scale for mundane purposes</note>.
And a person should not say to his fellow in Jerusalem:
"Here is wine for you, so give me oil or vinegar" <note>This constitutes a sale or barter, which is forbidden for sanctified food</note>,
and the same applies to all other fruits.
However, they may give these to one another as free gifts.

### Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 1 Mishnah 2

->2<-
The **Animal Tithe** <term>Ma'aser Behemah: the tenth animal of the yearly herd, which was sanctified and sacrificed in the Temple</term>,
one may not sell it while it is unblemished and alive,
nor if it is blemished, whether it is alive or slaughtered,
and one may not betroth a woman with it <note>Since the animal belongs to the "Table of the Most High," the man does not have the legal ownership required to use it as a marriage gift</note>.
The **Firstborn** <term>Bechor: the first male offspring of a cow, sheep, or goat, given to the Priest</term>,
one may sell it while it is unblemished and alive,
and while it is blemished, whether alive or slaughtered,
and one may betroth a woman with it.
One may not redeem Second Tithe [produce] for uncoined metal <note>original: *asimon*. Metal tokens or disks that have not been stamped with an official government image</note>,
nor for currency that is no longer in circulation,
nor for money that is not in one's possession.

### Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 1 Mishnah 3

->3<-
One who purchases an animal for peace-offerings <note>original: *zivchei shelamim*. A type of sacrifice where the meat was eaten by the person bringing it</note>, or a wild animal for "meat of desire" <note>original: *besar ta'avah*. Meat slaughtered for consumption rather than as a sacrifice; tithe money could be used to buy such meat to be eaten in Jerusalem</note>,
the hide becomes common property <term>chullin: non-sacred items that may be used for any secular purpose</term>, even if the hide is worth more than the meat.
Sealed wine jars,
in a place where it is customary to sell them sealed,
the jar becomes common property.
Walnuts and almonds—their shells become common property.

[Purchased] from the money of the **Second Tithe** <term>Ma’aser Sheni: The "Second Tithe," a portion of one’s produce that had to be brought to Jerusalem and eaten there in a state of ritual purity during the first, second, fourth, and fifth years of the seven-year agricultural cycle</term>, [items of] an equivalent value must be eaten [in holiness].

# Chapter 2

## Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 2 Mishnah 1
### 1
**Second Tithe** is designated for eating, drinking, and anointing <note>original: *sikhah*. The practice of rubbing oil on the skin for hygiene or pleasure, which was legally categorized similarly to drinking</note>.
One should eat that which is typically eaten,
and anoint with that which is typically used for anointing.
One may not anoint with wine or vinegar <note>as these are primarily beverages; using them on the skin is considered a wasteful destruction of sanctified food</note>,
but one may anoint with oil.
And one may not spice <note>original: *mefatmin*. To mix with aromatics to create a perfume or ointment</note> oil of the **Second Tithe**,
nor may one purchase spiced oil with **Second Tithe money**;
however, one may spice wine <note>for example, making spiced wine for drinking is permitted as it enhances the consumption</note>.
If honey or spices fell into [tithed produce] and improved it,
the improvement is shared proportionally <term>Ha-shevach le-fi cheshbon: A legal calculation where the increased value of the mixture is divided between the sacred and secular components based on their relative costs</term>.
If fish were cooked with leeks <note>original: *kaplotot*</note> of the **Second Tithe** and they improved [one another],
the improvement is shared proportionally.
But if dough of the **Second Tithe** was baked and improved [by the baking process],
the [entirety of] the improvement belongs to the **Second Tithe** <note>Because the improvement comes from the inherent process of preparing the food, rather than the addition of external ingredients</note>.
This is the general rule:
Wherever the improvement is distinct <note>meaning the added ingredients remain a separate, identifiable part of the value</note>,
the improvement is shared proportionally;
but wherever the improvement is not distinct,
the improvement belongs entirely to the **Second Tithe**.

## Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 2 Mishnah 2
### 2
**Rabbi Simeon** says:
One may not anoint [oneself] with oil of the **Second Tithe** in Jerusalem.
But the **Sages** <note>The majority of the rabbinic scholars</note> permit it.
They said to **Rabbi Simeon**:
If the law was lenient regarding the "strict" **Terumah** <term>Terumah: The "heave-offering" given to the Priests, which has a higher level of sanctity than the Second Tithe</term>,
shall we not be lenient regarding the "light" **Second Tithe**?
He said to them:
In what way was the law lenient regarding the "strict" **Terumah**?
In a place where it was lenient regarding **bitter vetch** <note>original: *karshinim*; used primarily for animal feed</note> and **fenugreek** <note>original: *tiltan*; used for flavor or medicine</note>,
shall we [therefore] be lenient regarding the "light" **Second Tithe**? <note>Rabbi Simeon argues that leniency in one specific area of law—animal feed—does not justify a general leniency for the Second Tithe, which is meant specifically for human joy and consumption</note>

# A Place Where He Did Not Rule Leniently Regarding Vetches and Fenugreek?

## Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 2 Mishnah 3
### 3
->Fenugreek <term>Tiltan: A Mediterranean legume used as a spice, a food, and sometimes as a hair-cleanser</term> of the **Second Tithe** must be eaten as sprouts <note>original: *tzimchonim*. Meaning the plant is consumed while still tender and green, rather than waiting for the seeds to fully ripen</note>;<-
->and regarding that of the **Priestly Gift** <term>Terumah: The portion of the harvest given to the Priests, which must be kept in a state of ritual purity</term>,<-
->the **House of Shammai** say:<-
->all its preparations must be done in ritual purity, except for its shampooing <note>original: *chafifatah*. Scrubbing or rubbing the plant for use as a hair treatment; since this is not "eating," Shammai is lenient</note>.<-
->And the **House of Hillel** say:<-
->all its preparations may be done in ritual impurity, except for its soaking <note>original: *sheriyatah*. Placing the legume in water makes it legally susceptible to ritual impurity; Hillel insists this stage remains pure to protect the sacred food</note>.<-

## Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 2 Mishnah 4
### 4
->Bitter vetches <term>Karshinim: A type of legume (Vicia ervilia) used primarily as animal feed, but occasionally eaten by humans in times of scarcity</term> of the **Second Tithe**<-
->must be eaten as sprouts, and they may be brought into Jerusalem and taken out again <note>Unlike most Second Tithe produce, which must be consumed within the walls of Jerusalem once they enter, these are treated more leniently because they are primarily for animals</note>.<-
->If they became ritually impure,<-
->**Rabbi Tarfon** says:<-
->they should be divided among batches of dough <note>to ensure the amount of impure vetches in any one batch is too small to transmit impurity</note>.<-
->But the **Sages** say:<-
->they must be redeemed <note>the sanctity is transferred to money, and the vetches then become secular fodder</note>.<-
->And regarding those of the **Priestly Gift**:<-
->the **House of Shammai** say:<-
->one must soak and rub them in ritual purity, but they may be fed [to animals] in ritual impurity.<-
->The **House of Hillel** say:<-
->one must soak them in ritual purity, but they may be rubbed and fed in ritual impurity.<-
->**Shammai** <note>the individual Sage, known for his personal stringency</note> says:<-
->they must be eaten dry <note>original: *tzarid*. Perhaps meaning parched or crushed without liquid</note>.<-
->**Rabbi Akiva** says:<-
->all their preparations may be done in ritual impurity <note>Akiva views these strictly as animal feed, exempting them from the purity laws that govern human food</note>.<-

## Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 2 Mishnah 5
### 5
->If secular coins <term>Chullin: Non-sacred, ordinary money or produce</term> and **Second Tithe** coins were scattered and mixed together,<-
->whatever one gathers up, he gathers for the **Second Tithe** until he has completed the full [required] amount,<-
->and the remainder is secular.<-
->If he mixed them together and took a handful, it is [divided] according to the proportion.<-
->This is the general rule:<-
->those gathered one by one are [credited] to the **Second Tithe**,<-
->and those that are mixed together are [divided] according to the proportion.<-

<meta>This page continues the laws of the Second Tithe (Ma’aser Sheni), moving from specific agricultural items like vetches and fenugreek to the financial mechanics of the tithe. Since the Second Tithe must be consumed in Jerusalem, the Torah allows a person to "redeem" the produce for silver coins to make the journey easier. This section deals with how to handle those coins, what to do if they get mixed with ordinary money, and the rules for exchanging silver for gold or copper.</meta>

### Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 2 Mishnah 6
### 6
->If a **Sela** <term>Sela: A large silver coin worth four denarii, roughly equivalent to four days' wages for a laborer</term> of the **Second Tithe** and one of **Ordinary Use** <term>Chullin: Secular or non-sacred items that have no special religious restrictions</term> became mixed together,<-
->one brings a **Sela’s** worth of copper coins and says:<-
->"The **Sela** of the **Second Tithe**, wherever it may be, is hereby **desanctified** <note>original: *mechulelet*. The process of transferring the sacred status from one object (like a coin or fruit) onto another, usually to make transport easier</note> onto these copper coins."<-
->He then selects the finer of the two silver coins and **desanctifies** the copper coins back onto it.<-
->Because the Sages said:<-
->One may **desanctify** silver onto copper only out of necessity <note>original: *mi-duchak*. Typically, holiness is transferred from "lesser" materials to "greater" ones (copper to silver). Doing the reverse is usually avoided but permitted here to resolve the confusion of the mixed coins</note>,<-
->not so that it remains in that state, but rather he must return and **desanctify** them back onto silver.<-

### Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 2 Mishnah 7
### 7
->The **House of Shammai** say:<-
->A person should not convert his silver **Selas** into gold **Denarii** <term>Dinar Zahav: A gold coin worth 25 silver denarii. Gold was more stable and lighter to carry than silver</term>.<-
->But the **House of Hillel** permit it.<-
->**Rabbi Akiva** said:<-
->"I once converted the silver of **Rabban Gamliel** and **Rabbi Joshua** into gold **Denarii**."<-

### Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 2 Mishnah 8
### 8
->Regarding one who exchanges a silver **Sela** from the copper coins of the **Second Tithe** <note>This refers to someone who has accumulated many copper coins from tithe redemption and wants to exchange them for a single silver coin for the journey to Jerusalem</note>:<-
->The **House of Shammai** say:<-
->The entire **Sela** must be exchanged for copper coins.<-
->And the **House of Hillel** say:<-
->He may take a silver **Shekel** <term>Shekel: In the Mishnaic period, this refers to a half-Sela, worth two silver denarii</term> and a **Shekel's** worth of copper coins.<-
->**Rabbi Meir** says:<-
->One may not **desanctify** silver and produce onto other silver <note>Meir argues that if you have some silver and some fruit, you cannot "consolidate" the holiness of both onto a different silver coin; the fruit must be redeemed directly for its own coins</note>.<-
->But the **Sages** permit it.<-

### Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 2 Mishnah 9
### 9
->Regarding one who exchanges a **Sela** of the **Second Tithe** in Jerusalem <note>Having arrived in Jerusalem with a large silver coin, the pilgrim now needs small change (copper) to buy food for his meals</note>:<-

->The entire **Sela** must be exchanged for copper coins.<-

->He takes three silver **Denarii** and one **Denarius** worth of copper coins.<-
->**Rabbi Akiva** says:<-

### Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 2 Mishnah 10
#### 10

One who had some of his children **ritually impure** <term>Tamei: A state of ritual impurity where one is forbidden from eating sacred food like the Second Tithe</term> and some of them **ritually pure** <term>Tahor: A state of ritual purity</term>, 
he sets down the **Sela** coin and says:
"Whatever the pure children drink, this **Sela** is hereby **desanctified** <note>original: *mechulelet*. This transfers the "holiness" of the wine into the coin as it is being consumed</note> upon it."
Thus, it results that both the **impure** and **pure** children may drink from the same jug <note>This legal mechanism allows a family to share a meal. The wine consumed by the pure children is considered the "Sacred Tithe" (offset by the coin), while the wine consumed by the impure children is considered "ordinary," avoiding the prohibition of an impure person consuming sacred food</note>.

## Chapter 3

### Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 3 Mishnah 1
#### 1

A man should not say to his fellow:
> "Take these fruits up to **Jerusalem** for me so that we may divide them!" <note>This is forbidden because it looks like a business transaction or paying a worker with holy Tithe produce</note>
Rather, he says to him:
> "Take them up so that we may eat and drink them together in **Jerusalem**!"
However, they may give one another a **free gift** of the Tithe produce.

### Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 3 Mishnah 2
#### 2

One may not purchase **Terumah** <term>Terumah: The "heave-offering" or portion of the harvest given to the Priests. It is more restrictive than the Second Tithe</term> with **Second Tithe** money,
because he thereby reduces the amount of it that can be eaten <note>Second Tithe can be eaten by any Jewish person in a state of purity, but Terumah can only be eaten by Priests. Buying Terumah with Tithe money "traps" the Tithe in a form that fewer people can enjoy</note>.
**Rabbi Shimon** permits this.
**Rabbi Shimon** said to them:
If the law is lenient regarding **Peace Offerings** <term>Zivchei Shelamim: Sacrifices eaten by the owner in Jerusalem, similar to the Second Tithe</term>,
which a person might bring to a state of **Abomination** <term>Piggul: A sacrifice disqualified by the priest's improper thoughts during the ritual</term>, **Leftover meat** <note>original: *notar*. Holy meat not eaten within the required time</note>, or **Impurity**,
should we not be lenient regarding **Terumah**?
They said to him:
No; just because the law is lenient regarding **Peace Offerings**—seeing as they are permitted to **Laypeople** <term>Zarim: Non-priests</term>—shall we then be lenient with **Terumah**, which is strictly forbidden to **Laypeople**?

### Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 3 Mishnah 3
### 3
One who had **money** <note>Specifically, money that has already been sanctified as Second Tithe</note> in **Jerusalem**, and needed it for personal use,
and his friend has **produce** <note>Ordinary, non-sacred produce</note> in Jerusalem,
he may say to his friend:
"Let this **money** be **desanctified** <note>original: mechullalin. This transfers the sacred status from the coins to the fruit</note> upon your **produce**."
The result is that the friend eats his produce in a state of **purity** <term>Tahora: Ritual purity required for consuming sacred food</term>,
while the first person may use his money for his own needs <note>Since the money is now "secular" and the produce has become the "Second Tithe"</note>.
One should not say this to an **unlearned person** <term>Am Ha'aretz: A common person not scrupulous in the laws of tithes and ritual purity</term> except by paying him the **market value** <note>original: bidmei. This ensures the unlearned person doesn't accidentally misuse the newly-sanctified produce</note>.

### Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 3 Mishnah 4
### 4
If one has **produce** in **Jerusalem** and **money** in the **provinces** <note>The "Medina" refers to any location outside of Jerusalem</note>,
and he says:
"Let this **money** <note>in the provinces</note> be **desanctified** upon that **produce** <note>in Jerusalem</note>," it is valid.
If one has **money** in **Jerusalem** and **produce** in the **provinces**,
he says:
"Let this **produce** be **desanctified** upon that **money**,"
<gloss>Alternative reading: "Let that money be desanctified upon this produce"</gloss>
provided that the **produce** is eventually brought up and eaten in **Jerusalem**.

**Money** may enter **Jerusalem** and then leave <note>It can be taken back out to be exchanged or used to redeem other produce</note>, 
but **produce** that enters may not leave <note>There is a legal principle that once the actual tithe-fruit enters the walls of Jerusalem, it is "captured" by the walls and must be consumed there</note>.
**Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel** says:
Even **produce** may enter and leave.

its **Second Tithe** must return and be eaten in **Jerusalem**.
But if its **processing was not finished**,
such as **baskets of grapes** being taken to the **winepress** or **baskets of figs** to the **drying-place** <term>Muktzeh: A designated area for drying figs</term>, then the following applies:

The **Second Tithe** must return and be eaten in **Jerusalem**.
And the **House of Hillel** say:
It may be **redeemed** <term>Pidyon: The process of transferring holiness from produce to a coin</term> and eaten in any place.

<meta>This page continues the laws regarding the redemption of the Second Tithe—produce that had to be eaten within the walls of Jerusalem. The previous page ended with a discussion on transferring the "holiness" of money to produce or vice versa depending on their location. This page clarifies the boundaries of Jerusalem and the Temple, determining exactly where sacred food may be eaten.</meta>

Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Shimon:
The **House of Shammai** <note>One of the two major schools of Rabbinic thought in the 1st century</note> and the **House of Hillel** did not disagree about **fruit whose processing was not completed** <note>original: she-lo nigmera melachtan. This refers to produce that has not yet reached the final stage of preparation for the market, at which point tithes traditionally become mandatory</note>,
agreeing that its **Second Tithe** <term>Maaser Sheni: The second tenth of a crop, which the owner must bring to Jerusalem and eat there in a state of purity</term> may be **redeemed** <note>Exchanged for money</note> and eaten anywhere.
And regarding what did they disagree?
Regarding **fruit whose processing was completed**,
for the **House of Shammai** say:
The **Second Tithe** of such fruit must return and be eaten in **Jerusalem** <note>Meaning it cannot be exchanged for money once it has entered the city, even if it is later taken out</note>.
But the **House of Hillel** say:
It may be **redeemed** and eaten anywhere.
And **Demai** <term>Demai: Produce purchased from a common person where it is uncertain if the tithes were properly separated</term> may enter [Jerusalem], leave, and be redeemed.

### Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 3 Mishnah 7
->8<-
A tree that stands **inside** <note>Within the walls of Jerusalem</note> and leans **outside**,
or stands **outside** and leans **inside**:
From the point directly above the **wall** and inward, it is treated as being **inside**;
From the point directly above the **wall** and outward, it is treated as being **outside**.
Regarding **olive presses** whose entrances are **inside** but whose interior space is **outside**,
or whose entrances are **outside** but whose interior space is **inside**:
The **House of Shammai** say:
The entire space is treated as being **inside** <note>Likely because the "holiness" of the city extends to any structure connected to it</note>.
And the **House of Hillel** say:
From the point directly above the **wall** and inward, it is treated as being **inside**;
From the point directly above the **wall** and outward, it is treated as being **outside**.

### Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 3 Mishnah 8
->9<-
The **chambers** <note>Lishachot: Side rooms or offices built into the walls of the Temple complex</note> built in the **sacred area** <term>Kodesh: The inner area of the Temple Mount with a higher level of sanctity</term> but open to the **common area** <term>Chol: The non-sanctified area, or the area outside the Temple complex</term>:
Their interior is **common** and their roofs are **sacred**.
If they are built in the **common area** and open to the **sacred area**:
Their interior is **sacred** and their roofs are **common**.
If they are built in both the **sacred** and the **common** areas, and open to both the **sacred** and the **common** areas:
Their interior and their roofs from the point directly above the boundary toward the **sacred area** are **sacred**;
From the point directly above the boundary toward the **common area**, they are **common**.

### Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 3 Mishnah 10

One who purchases [food] with **tithe money** <note>money that was converted from produce and carries sacred status</note> that then becomes defiled, it may be redeemed.

It must be buried <note>because he believes once money is turned back into food, that food cannot be "un-sanctified" again if it spoils</note>.
They said to **Rabbi Yehuda**:
If the **Second Tithe** itself <note>the original fruit from the field</note> which becomes defiled can be redeemed;
is it not logical that food purchased with **tithe money** which becomes defiled should also be redeemed?
He said to them:
No! If you say this regarding the **Second Tithe** itself,
it is because it can even be redeemed while it is **pure** if one is far from the place [Jerusalem], <insert>and pure</insert>
but would you say the same for that which was **purchased with tithe money**,
which cannot be redeemed even when it is pure and one is far from the place?

### Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 3 Mishnah 11

It may be redeemed <note>to recover the value of the money for other food</note>.

it may be redeemed.
**Rabbi Yose** says:
It must be buried.
If he purchased it already slaughtered and it became defiled,
it is treated like **fruit** <note>referring back to the previous rule that defiled produce can be redeemed</note>.

## 2

They redeem Second Tithe at the lowest market rate <note>original: *keshaar hazol*, meaning the price at which goods are most accessible, typically wholesale</note>:
at the price a shopkeeper buys, 
not the price at which he sells; 
at the price a money-changer breaks <note>The rate for exchanging a large coin into smaller change</note>, 
not the price at which he combines <note>The rate for exchanging small change back into a large coin</note>. 
One does not redeem Second Tithe by estimation <note>original: *achsarah*, a rough guess or bulk assessment without precise measurement</note>. 
That which has a known price is redeemed by the word of one [person]; 
that which does not have a known price is redeemed by the word of three [appraisers], 
such as wine that has begun to sour <note>original: *she-kasas*, referring to wine on the verge of turning to vinegar</note>, fruits that have started to rot, 
or coins that have rusted.

### Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 4 Mishnah 3
## 3

If the householder says, "for a **sela**" <note>A silver coin equal to four denarii</note>, 
and another person says, "for a **sela**," 
the householder takes precedence, 
because he adds a **fifth** <note>The Torah requires an owner to add 25% to the value when redeeming his own tithe, whereas a stranger pays only the market value</note>. 
If the householder says, "for a **sela**," 
and another person says, "for a **sela** and an **issar**" <note>A small copper coin</note>, 
 the one who offered a **sela** and an **issar** takes precedence, 
because he increases the principal value. 
One who redeems his own Second Tithe 
adds to it a fifth, 
whether it was his own [from his harvest] or it was given to him as a gift.

### Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 4 Mishnah 4
## 4

One may use a legal artifice <note>original: *maarimim*, a clever way to follow the letter of the law while avoiding a specific penalty or cost</note> regarding Second Tithe. 
How so? 
A man says to his adult son or daughter, 
or to his Hebrew manservant or maidservant: 
"Here are these coins, 
and redeem this tithe for yourself" <note>By giving them the money, they become the "redeemers" instead of the owner. Since they are legally independent but not the original owners, they do not have to pay the extra "fifth" surcharge</note>. 
But he may not say this to his minor son or daughter, 
nor to his Canaanite servants, 
because their "hand is as his hand" <note>In Jewish law, the property of a minor or a non-Hebrew servant is legally considered the property of the head of the household; therefore, the owner would still be liable for the extra fifth</note>.

If he was standing in the threshing floor and had no money in his hand,
he says to his friend:
"Behold, these fruits are given to you as a gift!"

## Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 4 Mishnah 6

6
If one performed a **formal acquisition** <note>original: *mashach*, literally "pulled." In ancient Jewish law, physically moving or "pulling" an object was the standard way to finalize a purchase</note> of Second Tithe from someone for a **sela** <note>A silver coin equal to four denarii</note>,
but did not manage to redeem it before its value rose to two **selas**,
he pays [the seller] one **sela** and profits one **sela**,
for the **sela** of Second Tithe belongs to him.
If he acquired it for two **selas**,
but did not manage to redeem it before its value fell to one **sela**,
he gives one **sela** from his **ordinary funds** <note>original: *chullin*, non-sacred money or property</note>,
and the **sela** of Second Tithe is his.
And if [the seller] was an **unlearned person** <note>original: *am ha'aretz*, a term for someone not strictly observant of tithing or purity laws</note>, they pay from the proceeds.

## Tractate Second Tithe Chapter 5 Mishnah 6

On the eve of the **first festival day of Passover**,

How was the removal performed?
They give the **heave-offering** <note>original: "Terumah"; the portion of the harvest designated for the Priests</note> and the **heave-offering of the tithe** <note>original: "Terumat Ma'aser"; the tenth of the tithe given by the Levite to the Priest</note> to their owners <note>the Priests</note>,
and the **first tithe** <note>original: "Ma'aser Rishon"</note> to its owners <note>the Levites</note>,
and the **poor tithe** <note>original: "Ma'aser Ani"</note> to its owners <note>the poor</note>. <meta>catchword: and tithe</meta>
And the **second tithe** <note>original: "Ma'aser Sheni"</note> and the **first fruits** <note>original: "Bikkurim"</note> are removed in every place <note>they must be destroyed if they have not yet been brought to Jerusalem</note>.
**Rabbi Shimon** says:
The **first fruits** are given to the Priests like the heave-offering <note>suggesting they do not need to be destroyed but can be given to the Priests even at the time of removal</note>.
Regarding a **cooked dish** <note>made from holy fruits</note>,
the **House of Shammai** say:
One must remove it.
The **House of Hillel** say:
It is considered as if already removed.

**Yohanan the High Priest** <note>John Hyrcanus I, the Hasmonean ruler and High Priest (reigned 134–104 BCE).</note> abolished the **Tithe Confession** <note>Likely because the tithes were no longer being given correctly to the Priests, making the declaration "I have done according to all You commanded" untruthful.</note>.

->1<-

Five things are liable for ***Challah*** <note>The "dough offering"—a portion of dough set aside for the Priests as commanded in Numbers 15.</note>:
**Wheat**,
**Barley**,
**Spelt**,
**Oats**,
And **Rye**. <insert>and rye</insert>
Behold, these are liable for ***Challah***,
and they combine with one another <note>To reach the minimum volume of dough (approximately 1.6 kg) required to trigger the obligation of the offering.</note>,
and they are forbidden under the law of the **New Crop** <note>original: "chadash"; the prohibition against eating grain from the new harvest until the Omer offering is brought.</note> before **Passover**,
and it is forbidden to harvest them before the **Omer** <note>The first measure of the barley harvest offered in the Temple on the 16th of Nisan.</note>.
If they took root before the **Omer**,
the **Omer** permits them [for consumption],
but if not, [they remain forbidden until the following year's offering].

->4<-

->One who makes their dough in small batches and they touch one another,<-
->they remain exempt from the **dough offering** until they "bite."<- <note>original: "yishokhu"—this refers to the dough batches sticking together so closely that when pulled apart, some of the dough from one remains attached to the other, effectively making them a single mass</note>
->Rabbi Eliezer says:<-
->Even one who scrapes bread from the oven and places it in a basket,<-
->the basket joins them together for the **dough offering**.<- <note>Rabbi Eliezer's view is that the vessel (the basket) unites the individual loaves into one "batch" for the purpose of the law, even if they aren't physically stuck together</note>

### Tractate Challah Chapter 2 Mishnah 5

->5<-

->One who separates their **dough offering** while it is still flour,<-
->it is not considered Challah, and it is a "theft" in the hand of the priest.<- <note>Because the commandment specifically applies to dough (kneaded flour and water). If a priest takes it before it becomes dough, he has taken something he is not yet entitled to</note>
->The dough itself remains obligated in the **dough offering**;<-
->and the flour [that was set aside], if it contains the required volume,<- <note>five-fourths of a *kav*</note>
->is obligated in the **dough offering**, and is forbidden to **non-priests**.<- <note>original: "zarim"—literally "strangers," meaning anyone who is not a descendant of the priestly line of Aaron</note>
->These are the words of Rabbi Joshua.<-
->They said to him:<-
->An event occurred where an elder "overpowered" this ruling.<- <note>original: "kipecha"—this suggests an elder or scholar argued against or invalidated this practice</note>
->He said to them:<-
->Even so, he harmed himself but set things right for others.<- <note>Meaning the elder may have taken a personal loss or risk by being stringent, but his action clarified the law for the benefit of the community</note>

## Tractate Challah Chapter 2 Mishnah 6
### 6

Five-fourths <note>of a *kav*—a *kav* is an ancient unit of volume approximately equal to 2.2 liters</note> of flour are obligated in the **dough offering**. <note>original: "Challah"—referring to the portion of dough set aside for the priests</note>
Whether it is the flour itself, or the flour along with its **leaven** <note>original: "se’oran"—sourdough starter used for fermentation</note> and its **bran**, <note>original: "mursanan"—the outer husks of the grain</note>
as long as there are five-fourths, they are obligated.
If one removed the bran from within the flour and then returned it,
these are exempt. <note>Once the bran is separated, it is no longer considered "flour" in the legal sense required to reach the minimum volume, even if mixed back in</note>

---

## Tractate Challah Chapter 2 Mishnah 7
### 7

The required amount for the **dough offering** is one-twenty-fourth <note>of the total dough</note>.
One who makes dough for themselves,
or one who makes dough for their son's wedding feast,
gives one-twenty-fourth.
A professional baker who makes dough to sell in the market,
and likewise a woman who makes dough to sell in the market,
give one-forty-eighth. <note>Professional sellers are permitted to give a smaller portion (roughly 2%) compared to private individuals (roughly 4%) to ensure their business remains viable</note>
If her dough became **ritually impure** <note>original: "nitme'at"</note> by accident or by force,
she gives one-forty-eighth.
But if it became impure intentionally,
she must give one-twenty-fourth,
so that a sinner shall not benefit from their wrongdoing. <note>By intentionally making the dough impure, the baker might hope to give the smaller "impure" portion; the Sages penalized this by requiring the higher "private" rate</note>

---

## Tractate Challah Chapter 2 Mishnah 8
### 8

Rabbi Eliezer says:
One may take the offering from the **pure dough** to exempt the **impure dough**.
How so?
If there is a batch of pure dough and a batch of impure dough,
one takes the required amount for the **dough offering** from the batch from which nothing has yet been separated, and places a piece smaller than the size of an egg in the middle <note>According to Jewish law, a piece of food smaller than an egg's volume does not transmit ritual impurity. This acts as a "bridge" to connect the batches without contaminating the pure dough</note>
so that one may take the offering from batches that are **in proximity**. <note>original: "mukkaf"—the law requires the offering to be physically near or "touching" the dough it is intended to exempt</note>
But the Sages forbid this.

## Tractate Challah Chapter 3 Mishnah 2
### 2
If her dough became **mixed with sacred produce** <note>original: "nidme'ah"—the term refers to "Meduma," a mixture where common food and "Terumah" (the priest's share of grain) have become inseparable, making the whole mixture restricted like sacred food</note>: 
if this happened before she rolled the dough, it is exempt, for that which is "Meduma" is exempt from the **dough offering**; 
but once she has rolled it, it is obligated. 
If a **doubt of ritual impurity** <note>original: "sefeq tumah"</note> arose for her: 
if it was before she rolled it, it should be prepared in a state of impurity <note>since the obligation has not yet "captured" the dough, one does not need to maintain the strict levels of purity required for sacred offerings</note>; 
but once she has rolled it, it should be prepared in a state of purity.

## Tractate Challah Chapter 3 Mishnah 3
### 3
If she **consecrated** <note>original: "hikdishah"—formally dedicated to the ownership of the Temple</note> her dough: 
if she consecrated it before she rolled it, and then **redeemed** it <note>paid its value to the Temple to return it to common use</note>, it is obligated. 
If she rolled it and then redeemed it, it is obligated. 
However, if she consecrated it before she rolled it, 
and the **treasurer** <note>original: "gizbar"—the official in charge of Temple property</note> rolled it, and only after that she redeemed it, 
it is exempt, because at the moment it would have become obligated <note>the rolling stage</note>, it was exempt <note>because Temple-owned property is not subject to the dough offering</note>.

## Tractate Challah Chapter 3 Mishnah 4
### 4
Similarly: 
one who **consecrates** their fruits 
before they reached the **season for tithes** <note>the specific stage of growth or processing where the obligation to separate the various agricultural gifts begins</note>, and then redeemed them, they are obligated; 
and once they reached the season for tithes and then he redeemed them, 
they are obligated. 
If he consecrated them before they were **finished** <note>the final processing of the harvest, such as smoothing the grain pile or pressing the grapes</note>, 
and the **treasurer** finished them, and only afterward he redeemed them, 
they are exempt, because at the moment they would have become obligated, they were exempt.

### Tractate Challah Chapter 3 Mishnah 10
->9<-

One who takes **leaven** <note>original: "se'or"—a piece of fermented dough used as a starter</note> from wheat dough and places it into rice dough, <insert>leaven</insert>
if the rice dough now has the **taste of grain** <note>original: "ta'am dagan"—referring to the five specific species of grain: wheat, barley, spelt, rye, and oats</note>, it is liable for the **dough offering** <note>original: "challah"</note>;
but if not, it is exempt.
If so, why did the Sages say:
**Untithed produce** <note>original: "tevel"—crops from which the required tithes and offerings have not yet been separated</note> renders a mixture forbidden in **any amount** <note>original: "kol she-hu"—even a microscopic amount of untithed food can make a whole mixture forbidden to eat until rectified</note>?
This applies when a species is mixed with its **own species**; however, when mixed with a **different species**, it is only forbidden if it **imparts a flavor** <note>original: "be-noten ta'am"—the legal standard where a substance is only considered "present" if its taste can be detected</note>.

## Chapter 4

### Tractate Challah Chapter 4 Mishnah 1
->1<-

Two women who made two **kabs** <note>a "kab" is a measure of volume; two kabs is less than the five-quarters of a kab required to trigger the dough offering obligation</note> of dough, and the pieces of dough touched one another,
even if they are of the same species, they are exempt <note>because they belong to two different people, the batches do not combine to reach the minimum required volume</note>.
In a case where they belong to one woman:
if they are of the **same species**, the dough is liable; but if they are of **different species**, it is exempt.

### Tractate Challah Chapter 4 Mishnah 2
->2<-

What is considered the **same species** <note>regarding the laws of combining doughs</note>?
**Wheat** does not combine with anything
except for **spelt** <note>original: "kusmim"</note>.
**Barley** combines with everything
except for wheat.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says:
The other species <note>spelt, goatgrass, and oats</note> all combine with one another.

### Tractate Challah Chapter 4 Mishnah 3
->3<-

If there are two **kabs** <note>of grain dough</note>, and a kab of **rice** or a kab of **priestly gift** <note>original: "terumah"—sanctified produce given to the priests, which a commoner may not eat</note> is in the middle,
they do **not combine** <note>the non-obligatory rice or the sanctified priest's portion acts as a physical barrier, preventing the two small batches of dough from being viewed as a single large batch</note>. <insert>combine</insert>
However, if a dough from which the **dough offering has already been taken** is in the middle,
they do combine, because that middle dough was already once **obligated** in the dough offering.

### Tractate Challah Chapter 4 Mishnah 8

8
Rabban Gamliel says:
There are **three lands** <note>geographic zones with different legal statuses</note> regarding the dough offering:
From the **Land of Israel** until **Chezib** <note>modern-day Achziv, marking the northern border of the territory settled by those returning from the Babylonian exile</note>, one **dough offering** <note>original: "challah"</note> is taken.
From **Chezib** until the **River** <note>the Euphrates</note> and until **Amanum** <note>Mount Amanus</note>,
**two dough offerings** are taken: one for the **fire** <note>burned because the land is technically outside the borders of holiness and the dough is considered impure</note> and one for the **priest**.
The one for the **fire** has a minimum required **size** <note>one-forty-eighth of the dough</note>, but the one for the **priest** has no minimum **size**.
From the **River** and from **Amanum** and **further inward** <note>referring to the Diaspora/foreign lands</note>,
**two dough offerings** are taken: one for the **fire** and one for the **priest**.
The one for the **fire** has no minimum **size**, but the one for the **priest** has a minimum **size**,
and a **Tevul Yom** <note>term: a person who has immersed in a ritual bath (mikvah) but is waiting for the sun to set to complete their purification</note> may eat it.
Rabbi Yose says:
He does not even need **immersion** <note>Rabbi Yose believes the impurity of foreign lands is not strict enough to forbid eating this specific rabbinic dough offering</note>.

9
And it is **forbidden** to **Zavim** and **Zavot** <note>men and women with specific ritual impurities resulting from bodily discharges</note>, and to **menstruants** and **women after childbirth**.
But it may be **eaten with a non-priest** <note>original: "zar"—literally a "stranger" to the priesthood</note> at the same **table**,
and it may be **given to any priest**.

### Tractate Orlah Chapter 1 Mishnah 5

->5<-
->A tree that was uprooted but has a branch layered into the ground,<- <note>original: "berekha." This refers to "layering," a method of propagation where a branch is bent down and buried in the soil to grow its own roots while still attached to the "mother" tree.</note>
->and the main tree draws life from that layered branch,<-
->the old tree returns to the status of the layered branch.<- <note>If the original "mother" tree is uprooted and dies but is kept alive by the nutrients from the "daughter" branch, the old tree loses its mature status and must start its three-year Orlah count anew, just like the young branch.</note>
->If one layered a branch year after year, and it was eventually severed,<-
->one counts the years from the moment it was severed.<-
->The extending of vines,<- <note>term: "Sippuk," a method of extending vines by layering them across a distance.</note>
->or extending a vine from another extended vine,<-
->even if one layered it into the earth, it is permitted.<- <note>As long as the vine remains connected to its original, mature source, the new growth is not considered a new "planting" subject to Orlah.</note>
->Rabbi Meir says:<-
->In a place where its strength is good, it is permitted,<-
->but in a place where its strength is poor, it is forbidden.<- <note>Rabbi Meir distinguishes based on whether the new branch is strong enough to survive on its own; if it is, it might be considered a new planting.</note>
->A layered branch that was severed while full of fruit,<-
->if the fruit increased in size by one two-hundredth, it is forbidden.<- <note>The <term>Orlah</term> prohibition is "nullified" or neutralized only in a ratio of 1 to 200. If the fruit grew even a tiny amount (1/200th) after becoming a separate entity, that new growth is prohibited and renders the whole fruit forbidden.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Tractate Orlah, Chapter 2. While Chapter 1 focused on identifying which parts of a plant are subject to the prohibition of Orlah (fruit from the first three years), this chapter explores the complex laws of "neutralization" or "nullification." This occurs when a small amount of forbidden produce becomes mixed with a larger quantity of permitted produce, potentially making the entire mixture permitted or forbidden depending on the ratios.</meta>

->...but not to forbid.<-

## Tractate Orlah Chapter 2 Mishnah 2
### 2
->The **heave-offering** <term>terumah: the portion of a crop designated for the Priests, which is holy and forbidden to non-priests</term> lifts up the **Orlah**,<-
->and the **Orlah** lifts up the **heave-offering**.<-
->How so?<-
->A **se'ah** <note>A biblical unit of volume, roughly 7 to 14 liters depending on the historical estimate.</note> of **heave-offering** fell into one hundred [se'ahs of permitted produce],<-
->and afterward, three **kavs** <note>A smaller unit of volume; six kavs equal one se'ah. Three kavs are half a se'ah.</note> of **Orlah** fell in,<-
->or three **kavs** of **mixed seeds in a vineyard**, <term>Kil’ay ha-Kerem: the biblical prohibition against planting grapevines and grain or vegetables together; such produce is forbidden for use.</term><-
->this is a case where the **heave-offering** lifts up the **Orlah**,<-
->and the **Orlah** lifts up the **heave-offering**.<-
<note>In Jewish law, forbidden substances are "nullified" if they are surrounded by enough permitted substance. Terumah requires a 1:100 ratio, while Orlah requires 1:200. This Mishnah teaches that if one forbidden substance is already nullified in the mixture, it can actually "count" as part of the permitted bulk to help nullify a second forbidden substance that falls in later.</note>

## Tractate Orlah Chapter 2 Mishnah 3
### 3
->The **Orlah** lifts up the **mixed seeds**,<-
->and the **mixed seeds** lift up the **Orlah**,<-
->and the **Orlah** [lifts up] the **Orlah**.<-
->How so?<-
->A **se'ah** of **Orlah** fell into two hundred [se'ahs of permitted produce],<-
->and afterward, a **se'ah** and a bit more of **Orlah** fell in,<-
->or a **se'ah** and a bit more of **mixed seeds in a vineyard**,<-
->this is a case where the **Orlah** lifts up the **mixed seeds**,<-
->and the **mixed seeds** [lift up] the **Orlah**,<-
->and the **Orlah** [lifts up] the **Orlah**.<-

## Tractate Orlah Chapter 2 Mishnah 4
### 4
->Anything that causes leavening, or seasons, or creates a holy mixture <insert>creates a holy mixture</insert> <note>original: "medame'a." This technical term refers to the mixing of sacred produce, like Terumah, with common produce, rendering the whole batch restricted.</note><-
->with **heave-offering**, or **Orlah**, or **mixed seeds in a vineyard**,<-
->makes [the mixture] forbidden.<-
<note>Usually, forbidden items are nullified by volume. However, if the forbidden item is a "functional" ingredient—like yeast that makes dough rise or a spice that flavors the whole pot—it cannot be nullified, no matter how small the amount.</note>
->The **House of Shammai** <note>One of the two major schools of early Jewish law, typically known for stricter rulings.</note> say:<-
->It even conveys ritual impurity.<-
->And the **House of Hillel** <note>The school of law that usually argued for more lenient or practical rulings; their view almost always becomes the accepted law.</note> say:<-
->It never conveys ritual impurity,<-
->until there is a quantity the size of an egg.<-
<note>original: "ke-beitzah." An egg-bulk is the standard minimum volume required for food to contract or transmit ritual impurity in Jewish law. The House of Hillel argues that even if a tiny spice forbids a whole pot for eating, it isn't "significant" enough to transmit impurity unless it meets the standard size.</note>

# Chapter 2

## Tractate Bikkurim Chapter 2 Mishnah 1
->1<-
The **Terumah** <term>Terumah: the "heave-offering" or portion of the harvest given to the Priest</term> and the **First Fruits**,
carry the liability of **death** <note>referring to "death by the hands of Heaven," a spiritual penalty for a non-priest who eats these items intentionally</note> and the **Fifth**, <term>Chomesh: a 20% penalty added to the principal value when someone unintentionally eats or uses holy items, which is then paid to the priest</term>
and they are forbidden to **strangers**, <note>original: "zarim"—referring to anyone who is not a Kohen (Priest)</note>
and they are the property of the **Priest**,
and they are neutralized in a mixture of **one hundred and one**, <note>If one part of these holy items accidentally mixes with one hundred parts of ordinary food, the holy status is "dissolved," and the mixture may be eaten by non-priests.</note>
and they require **washing of the hands** and **the setting of the sun**. <note>A priest who was ritually impure must immerse in a ritual bath and wait until sunset before he is permitted to eat these holy offerings.</note>
Behold, these laws apply to Terumah and First Fruits,
which is not the case for the **Tithe**. <term>Ma'aser: the "Second Tithe" (Ma'aser Sheni) which was brought to Jerusalem to be eaten by the owner</term>

## Tractate Bikkurim Chapter 2 Mishnah 2
->2<-
There are rules regarding the **Tithe** and **First Fruits** that do not apply to **Terumah**:
For the Tithe and the First Fruits require **being brought to the Place**, <note>referring to the Temple in Jerusalem</note>
and they require the **Confession**, <note>a formal declaration made at the Temple acknowledging that one has fulfilled all tithing obligations</note> and they are forbidden to a **mourner**; <term>Onen: a person in the intense first day of mourning before their deceased relative has been buried</term>
**Rabbi Shimon** permits a mourner to eat them.
And they are subject to the laws of **removal**. <note>Bi'ur: the requirement to clear all holy produce from one's home every three years</note>
**Rabbi Shimon** exempts them from removal.
And it is forbidden to eat even the smallest amount of them outside of **Jerusalem**,
and their **offshoots** <note>referring to crops grown from the seeds of these holy fruits</note> are forbidden to be eaten in Jerusalem,
even by non-priests or as animal feed.
**Rabbi Shimon** permits these.
Behold, these laws apply to the Tithe and First Fruits,
which is not the case for Terumah.

### Tractate Bikkurim Chapter 2 Mishnah 8
8
The <term>Koy</term> <note>The *Koy* is a creature described by the Sages as having characteristics of both a wild and a domesticated animal. Scholars have debated if it refers to a Mediterranean Muflon, a specific hybrid, or a generic category for any "doubtful" species.</note> has ways in which it is **similar to a wild animal**,
and it has ways in which it is **similar to a domesticated animal**,
and it has ways in which it is **similar to both a wild animal and a domesticated animal**,
and it has ways in which it is **similar to neither a wild animal nor a domesticated animal**.

### Tractate Bikkurim Chapter 2 Mishnah 9
9
How is it **similar to a wild animal**?
Its blood requires **covering** [with earth], like the blood of a wild animal, <note>Leviticus 17:13 requires the blood of hunted wild animals and birds to be covered after slaughter, a rule that does not apply to cattle or sheep.</note>
and one may **not slaughter it on a Festival** [Yom Tov]. <note>Because its status is doubtful, we do not perform the "covering of the blood" on a holiday, as the act of digging or moving earth would be a violation of the holiday's labor laws if the animal is actually a domesticated one.</note>
And if they did slaughter it, they do not cover its blood.
Its **fat** conveys impurity like a carcass, as a wild animal's does, and its impurity status is **doubtful**,
and one may not redeem the **firstborn of a donkey** with it. <note>The firstborn of a donkey must be redeemed with a lamb. Since we are unsure if the *Koy* counts as a "lamb" (domesticated), it cannot be used for this ritual.</note>

### Tractate Bikkurim Chapter 2 Mishnah 10
10
How is it **similar to a domesticated animal**?
Its **fat is forbidden** like the fat of a domesticated animal, <note>Certain fats (chelev) are forbidden in domesticated animals but permitted in wild ones. Due to its status, the *Koy's* fat is treated as forbidden.</note> [but] one is not liable to **excision** for eating it. <note>original: "karet"—a spiritual penalty of being "cut off." Because the status is uncertain, the court cannot impose the highest level of punishment.</note>
And it may not be purchased with **Tithe money** to be eaten in Jerusalem, <note>Second Tithe money was brought to Jerusalem to buy food. One could buy meat, but there were specific rules about whether one could buy wild vs. domesticated meat with these funds.</note>
and it is liable to the [priestly gifts of the] **foreleg, the cheeks, and the stomach**. <note>These three portions must be given to a Priest from every slaughtered domesticated animal.</note>
**Rabbi Eliezer** exempts it [from these gifts],
for "the **burden of proof lies upon the claimant**." <note>original: "ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-re’ayah." A fundamental principle of Jewish civil law: if the Priest wants the meat, he must prove the *Koy* is definitely a domesticated animal. Since it is a doubt, the owner keeps the meat.</note>

### Tractate Bikkurim Chapter 2 Mishnah 11
11
How is it **similar to neither a wild animal nor a domesticated animal**?
It is forbidden under the laws of **diverse kinds** with both a wild animal and a domesticated animal. <note>original: "kilayim." One may not breed the *Koy* with a deer (wild) or a goat (domesticated), nor yoke them together to pull a plow.</note>
One who **writes [a will leaving] his wild animals and domesticated animals** to his son,
has not transferred the **Koy** to him.
If one said:
"I shall be a **Nazirite** [vowing to abstain from wine] if this is a wild animal,"
or "...if it is a domesticated animal,"
he **becomes a Nazirite**. <note>Because it might be either, the vow is considered potentially valid, and the person must observe the restrictions of a Nazirite out of caution.</note>
In all its other ways, it is similar to both a wild animal and a domesticated animal,
and it **requires ritual slaughter** like both this one and that one.

# Chapter 4

## Tractate Bikkurim Chapter 3, Mishnah 1 <note>While the manuscript labels this as Chapter 3, this material is traditionally categorized as Chapter 4. It deals with the "Androgynous"—a person with both male and female physical characteristics—and how they fit into a legal system built on gendered obligations.</note>
### 1
->An androgynous person,<- <note>From the Greek *aner* (man) and *gyne* (woman).</note>
->has ways in which they are equivalent to men;<-
->and has ways in which they are equivalent to women;<-
->and has ways in which they are equivalent to both men and women;<-
->and there are ways in which they are equivalent to neither men nor women.<-

## Tractate Bikkurim Chapter 3, Mishnah 2
### 2
->How are they equivalent to men?<-
->They become ritually impure through "white" discharge like men, <gloss>becomes impure</gloss><- <note>original: "loben." This refers to a discharge that renders a man a *Zav* (a state of ritual impurity requiring a purification process).</note>
->they bind a widow to levirate marriage like men,<- <note>original: "Yibbum." If their brother dies childless, the widow is legally tied to them for marriage or the "removal of the shoe" (halizah) ceremony.</note>
->and they dress and cut their hair like men,<-
->and they take a wife but are not taken as a wife like men,<-
->and they are obligated in all the commandments stated in the Torah like men.<- <note>In Jewish law, men are generally obligated in all positive commandments, including those bound by time, whereas women are exempt from many time-bound commandments.</note>

## Tractate Bikkurim Chapter 3, Mishnah 3
### 3
->How are they equivalent to women?<-
->They become ritually impure through "red" discharge like women, <gloss>becomes impure</gloss><- <note>original: "odem." This refers to menstrual blood.</note>
->and they may not be in seclusion with men like women,<- <note>original: "yichud." The prohibition against a man and a woman being alone in a private space.</note>
->and they do not violate the prohibition against "rounding the corners of the head" nor "destroying the corners of the beard,"<- <note>The Torah prohibits men from shaving the temples or using a razor on the beard; since the androgynous status is uncertain, they are treated with the leniency of women regarding these specific prohibitions.</note>
->nor the prohibition against becoming defiled by the dead like women,<- <note>If they are of the priestly class (Kohanim), they follow the rule for daughters of priests, who are not forbidden from contact with a corpse.</note>
->and they are disqualified from giving testimony like women,<-
->and they are not prohibited from being "entered" in a forbidden act like women,<- <note>This refers to the legal definition of sexual liability; for certain laws of forbidden relations, they are treated as a female partner.</note>
->and they are disqualified from the priesthood like women.<- <note>They cannot perform the service in the Temple or partake in the specific holy portions reserved for male priests.</note>

<meta>The previous page introduced the legal classification of the "androgynous" person—someone possessing both male and female physical characteristics. It began by listing ways in which this individual is legally equivalent to men (such as the obligation to keep all commandments and the prohibition against "marrying" a man). This page continues that legal exploration, comparing them to both genders and then distinguishing them from both, before concluding the entire first "Order" of the Mishnah.</meta>

### Tractate Bikkurim Chapter 3, Mishnah 4
#### 4

How is the androgynous person equivalent to both men and women?
One is liable for striking them or cursing them just as one is for men and women. <note>In Jewish law, causing injury to another or cursing them carries specific legal penalties or religious prohibitions. This ruling ensures the androgynous person's personhood is protected under these laws regardless of their gender ambiguity.</note>
And they "sit" for the blood of purification like both men and women. <note>original: "dam tohar." This refers to the period of ritual purity/impurity following childbirth. According to Leviticus 12, the duration differs for a male or female child; for an androgynous child, the mother must observe the strictest requirements of both.</note>
And they share in the holy offerings of the border like both men and women, <note>original: "kodshei ha-gvul." These are priestly gifts, such as the Great Offering (Terumah), which could be eaten by priests anywhere in the land, including by female members of a priestly family.</note>
and they share in the most holy offerings like both men and women, <note>original: "kodshei kodashim." These are sacrifices that must be eaten within the Temple courtyard; usually, these are restricted to male priests, but the text here discusses the right to a portion of the distribution.</note>
and they inherit all types of inheritances like both men and women.
And if someone said, "I declare myself a Nazirite <note>A Nazirite is someone who takes a vow of abstinence from wine, cutting hair, and contact with the dead.</note> on the condition that this person is both a man and a woman," they become a Nazirite.

### Tractate Bikkurim Chapter 3, Mishnah 5
#### 5

How is the androgynous person equivalent to neither men nor women?
One is not liable for striking them or cursing them like men and women; <note>This reflects a secondary legal opinion or a specific technicality in the wording of the biblical verse that might exclude a "creature" that is not clearly one gender.</note>
and they cannot be "valued" like men or women. <note>original: "ne'erach." This refers to the "Valuations" (Arachin) mentioned in Leviticus 27, where a person vows to give their "worth" to the Temple. The Torah provides a fixed price list based on being "male" or "female"; since the androgynous fits neither category perfectly, the fixed valuation cannot be applied.</note>
And if someone said, "I declare myself a Nazirite on the condition that this person is neither a man nor a woman,"
they do not become a Nazirite.
Rabbi Meir says:
The androgynous person is a unique type of creature unto itself,
and the Sages could not decide whether they are a man or a woman.
But a *tumtum* is not so; <note>original: "tumtum." From a root meaning "hidden" or "blocked." This refers to an individual whose genitalia are covered by a layer of skin, making their biological sex unobservable without medical/surgical intervention.</note>
sometimes they are a man, and sometimes they are a woman. <note>Meaning, a *tumtum* is actually one or the other, just hidden, whereas Rabbi Meir views the androgynous as a fundamentally intermediate or third category.</note>

->The Tractate of Bikkurim is finished<- <note>original: "Bikkurim" (First Fruits).</note>

->The Order of Seeds is finished<- <note>original: "Seder Zeraim." This is the first of the six major sections of the Mishnah, dealing primarily with agricultural laws and prayers.</note>

<meta>The previous page concluded Tractate Bikkurim, which dealt with the laws of first-fruit offerings and the legal status of individuals with ambiguous physical characteristics. This page marks the beginning of a new volume of the Mishnah: Tractate Shabbat. This tractate focuses on the laws of the Sabbath, specifically the types of work that are prohibited on the day of rest.</meta>

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 1, Mishnah 1

**1**
The acts of carrying out on the Sabbath <note>original: "yetsiot ha-shabbat." While the word literally means "goings out," in this legal context it refers to transferring objects between different types of domains, such as from a private home to a public street.</note> are two that are four for one who is inside, and two that are four for one who is outside. 
How so? 
If the poor person stands outside <note>In the public domain.</note> and the homeowner stands inside <note>In the private domain.</note>:
If the poor person reached his hand inside and placed an object into the hand of the homeowner, or if he took an object from the homeowner's hand and brought it out, the poor person is liable <note>original: "hayyav." This means he has violated a Torah prohibition and would traditionally be required to bring a sin-offering if the act was done accidentally.</note> and the homeowner is exempt <note>original: "patur." This means the homeowner is not legally responsible for the violation in this specific case, as he remained passive.</note>.

**2**
If the homeowner reached his hand outside and placed an object into the hand of the poor person, or if he took an object from the poor person's hand and brought it inside, the homeowner is liable and the poor person is exempt.

**3**
If the poor person reached his hand inside and the homeowner took an object from it, or if the homeowner placed an object into the poor person's hand and the poor person then brought it out, both are exempt <note>In these cases, neither person performed the entire act of "lifting" and "placing" the object; the labor was split between two people. Under Sabbath law, to be legally "liable," a single person must usually perform the complete action.</note>.

**4**
If the homeowner reached his hand outside and the poor person took an object from it, or if the poor person placed an object into the homeowner's hand and the homeowner then brought it inside, both are exempt.

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 1, Mishnah 2

**5**
A man should not sit down before a barber near the time of the <term>Mincha</term> <note>The afternoon prayer service.</note> until he has prayed, <note>This is a precautionary law to ensure a person does not become so distracted by his activity that he forgets to pray before the sun sets.</note>
nor should he enter a bathhouse, nor a <term>tannery</term> <note>original: "burski." A place where hides are processed, an intensive and lengthy task.</note>, nor sit to eat a meal, nor begin a court case.
But if they have already begun their activity, they do not need to stop.
One must stop what they are doing for the reading of the <term>Shema</term> <note>The central declaration of Jewish faith ("Hear O Israel..."), which has a specific time requirement.</note>, but one does not need to stop for the <term>Tefillah</term> <note>The "Amidah" or standing prayer; the Sages ruled that if one has already begun a task, they are not required to interrupt it for this prayer if the time has not yet passed.</note>.

<summary>This page introduces the complex laws of carrying objects between private and public domains on the Sabbath, and establishes precautionary rules against starting distracting tasks before afternoon prayers.</summary>
<keywords>Sabbath, Carrying, Domains, Liability, Mincha Prayer, Shema, Religious Law</keywords>

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 1, Mishnah 3

**6**
A tailor should not go out with his needle <note>original: "be-maḥato." A professional tool carried in one's garment might be forgotten and carried into the public domain after the Sabbath begins.</note> close to nightfall on Friday, lest he forget and go out [with it after sunset]; nor should a scribe go out with his pen. 
One should not examine his clothes [for lice] <gloss>search</gloss> <note>original: "yifleh." This refers to searching for vermin in one's clothing by the light of a lamp.</note> and one should not read by the light of the lamp <note>The Sages feared that if the light flickered, the reader might instinctively tilt the oil lamp to improve the flow of oil to the wick, which constitutes the forbidden labor of "kindling" or "extinguishing."</note>.
In truth, they said the attendant <note>original: "hazzan." In this era, the hazzan was not a cantor but a communal official or schoolteacher who oversaw the children's reading.</note> may see where the children are reading, but he himself shall not read.
Similarly:
A man with a discharge <term>Zav: a man in a state of ritual impurity due to a specific physical discharge</term> should not eat with a woman with a discharge <term>Zavah: a woman in a similar state of impurity</term>, because it leads to the habit of transgression <note>original: "hergel averah." This is a social "fence" to prevent physical intimacy while they are ritually forbidden to one another.</note>.

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 1, Mishnah 4

**7**
These are among the laws that were stated in the upper chamber of Hananiah son of Hezekiah son of Garon <gloss>Geron</gloss>, when the Sages went up to visit him. 
They took a vote, and the School of Shammai <note>Beit Shammai, the more stringent school of Jewish law.</note> outnumbered the School of Hillel <note>Beit Hillel, usually the more lenient school.</note>, and they decreed eighteen matters on that day.

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 1, Mishnah 5

**8**
The School of Shammai say:
One may not soak ink, dyes, or vetch <note>A type of legume used for animal fodder.</note> [on Friday] unless there is enough time for them to be fully soaked while it is still day <note>Before the Sabbath begins.</note>.
But the School of Hillel permit it <note>Hillel's school holds that as long as the process is started before the Sabbath, it may continue on its own during the holy day.</note>.

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 1, Mishnah 6

**9**
The School of Shammai say:
One may not place bundles of flax inside an oven unless there is enough time for them to begin steaming; nor may one put wool into a dyer’s vat unless it has enough time to absorb the color <note>original: "yiqlot et ha-ayin," literally "absorb the eye."</note> while it is still day.
But the School of Hillel permit it.

**10**
The School of Shammai say:
One may not spread nets for wild animals, birds, or fish [on Friday] unless there is enough time for them to be caught while it is still day.

# Chapter 2

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 2 Mishnah 1

->1<-

With what may we light [the Sabbath lamp], and with what may we not light?
We may not light with cedar bast <note>The inner bark of the cedar tree.</note>,
nor with uncombed flax,
nor with floss silk,
nor with willow bast,
nor with desert wicks <note>A woolly plant found in the wilderness.</note>,
nor with the green moss that is on the surface of the water.
Not with pitch,
nor with wax,
nor with castor oil,
nor with oil for burning <note>original: "Shemen Sreifa," consecrated oil (Terumah) that became ritually impure and must be destroyed by burning.</note>,
nor with sheep's tail fat,
nor with tallow <note>Solid animal fat.</note>.
Nahum the Mede says:
We may light with cooked tallow.
And the Sages say:
Whether it is cooked or whether it is not cooked,
we may not light with it.

Rabbi Ishmael says:
We may not light with pine resin <note>original: "ittran." A foul-smelling byproduct of tar production.</note>,
out of honor for the Sabbath <note>Because the unpleasant smell might cause the person to leave the room, defeating the purpose of the Sabbath lamp.</note>;
but the Sages permit all oils.

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 2 Mishnah 5

->6<-

->One who extinguishes the lamp because he is afraid of the gentiles <note>This likely refers to historical periods where Zoroastrian officials would go through homes and extinguish lights during their own fire festivals.</note>,<-
->or because of bandits, or because of an "evil spirit" <note>This term was often used to describe severe melancholy or mental distress where darkness was preferred for the patient's comfort.</note>,<-
->or for the sake of a sick person so that they may sleep,<-
->is exempt <note>original: "Patur." In Sabbath law, this usually means the act is forbidden but does not require a sin-offering. However, if a life is in danger, extinguishing the lamp is fully permitted.</note>.<-
->But if he does so to spare the lamp,<-
->or to spare the oil,<- <note>The text here breaks off before concluding that in these cases, where the goal is purely financial, the person is liable for a transgression.</note>

# Tractate Shabbat Chapter 2 Mishnah 6

->7<-
->For three transgressions women die during childbirth:<-

->Light the lamp!"<-
->If it is a time of "doubtful darkness" <note>original: "Ben HaShemashot," the period of twilight when it is unclear if the day has ended and the Sabbath has begun.</note>,<-

->and we do not immerse [purify] vessels in a ritual bath,<-
->and we do not light the lamps;<-
->but we do tithe "doubtful" produce <term>Demai: produce purchased from an unlettered person where it is uncertain if the proper tithes were taken</term>,<-
->and we may prepare the *eruv* and insulate hot food <note>original: "tominin." This refers to wrapping a pot of food to keep it warm for the Sabbath meal.</note>.<-

# Tractate Shabbat Chapter 3 Mishnah 1

->1<-

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 3 Mishnah 3

->2<-
->One may not place an egg beside a water heater <note>original: "mecham." A metal vessel used for heating water.</note> so that it may be "rolled" <note>This refers to light cooking, such as making a soft-boiled egg, using the ambient heat of the vessel.</note>,<-
->and one may not wrap it in hot cloths <note>original: "sudarim." These are cloths that were heated by the sun or another heat source.</note>.<-

->And one may not bury it in sand or in road-dust so that it may be roasted. <note>This is prohibited even though the heat comes from the sun, because it looks too much like the forbidden act of burying food in hot ashes.</note><-

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 3 Mishnah 4

->3<-
->An incident occurred involving the people of Tiberias:<-
->They brought a pipe of cold water through a channel of hot water <note>This refers to the famous hot springs of Tiberias. The people tried to use the natural geothermal heat to warm their running water on the Sabbath.</note>.<-
->The Sages said to them:<-
->If this occurs on the Sabbath,<-
->it is like water that was heated on the Sabbath;<-
->it is forbidden for washing and for drinking.<-
->If this occurs on a Festival,<-
->it is like water that was heated on a Festival;<-
->it is forbidden for washing <note>The Sages prohibited washing the whole body in hot water on a Festival, even if heated legally, to prevent the bathhouses from being operated as usual.</note> but permitted for drinking.<-
->A *miliarum* <term>miliarum: a Roman-style water heater with a central pipe for coals</term> that has been cleared of its coals,<-
->one may drink from it on the Sabbath.<-
->An *antichi* <term>antichi: a double-chambered bronze pot where hot water is kept in an outer jacket</term>, even if it has been cleared of its coals,<-
->one may not drink from it. <note>The Sages are stricter here because the structure of the vessel retains heat so intensely that it is viewed as continued cooking.</note><-
