### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 3 Mishnah 6
->5<-

One may not place a vessel under a lamp to catch the oil <note>original: "shemen."</note>,
but if one placed it there while it was still day <note>meaning, before the Sabbath began at sunset.</note>, it is permitted.
One may not derive benefit from that oil <note>even if it drips into the bowl,</note>
because it is not from the "prepared" <note>original: "mukan." This refers to the concept of Muktzeh—items set aside and not intended for use when the Sabbath began, which are therefore forbidden to handle.</note>.
One may move a new lamp <note>one that has never been lit,</note>
but not an old one <note>which is considered repulsive and thus "set aside" or muktzeh.</note>.
Rabbi Shimon says:
All lamps may be moved, 
except for a lamp that is actually burning on the Sabbath.
One may place a vessel under a lamp to catch sparks.
But one may not put water into it, because he would be extinguishing <note>original: "mechabeh." The water would immediately quench the sparks, which is a form of work forbidden on the Sabbath.</note>.

## Chapter 4

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 4 Mishnah 1
->1<-

With what may we insulate <note>original: "tomnin." This refers to the practice of Hatmanah—wrapping a pot in materials to retain its heat for the Sabbath meal.</note>, and with what may we not insulate?
We may not insulate with olive peat <note>original: "gefet." The residue left after pressing olives.</note>, nor with dung,
nor with salt, nor with lime, nor with sand,
whether they are moist or dry.
We may not insulate with straw, nor with fleeces <note>original: "mochin." Soft materials used for stuffing, like wool or shredded rags.</note>, nor with stalks, nor with herbage,
when they are moist,
but we may insulate with them when they are dry.
We may insulate with clothing, and with fruit,
and with pigeon wings, and with flax tow <note>original: "ne'oret shel pishtan." The coarse fibers left over from processing flax.</note>,
and with a carpenter's sawdust.
Rabbi Yehuda forbids fine [sawdust] but permits coarse [sawdust].

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 4 Mishnah 2
->2<-

We may insulate with hides <note>original: "shelachin."</note>, and we may handle them <note>on the Sabbath, because they are considered useful items.</note>,
[we may insulate] with wool shearings, but we may not handle them <note>because raw wool shearings are not yet "vessels" or tools, they are considered muktzeh.</note>.
How then should one act?
He lifts the lid <note>of the pot,</note> and they fall away on their own.

->And with what may it <note>an animal</note> not go out?<-

->A donkey may not go out with a pack-saddle,<-

A man may not go out with a hobnailed sandal, <note>A sandal reinforced with iron nails. The Rabbis prohibited this because of a historical tragedy where the sound of such sandals caused a panic in a crowded space, leading to many deaths.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the end of Chapter 6 regarding objects carried on the Sabbath and transitions into the fundamental "Great Rule" of Chapter 7, which defines the specific categories of forbidden labor and the laws of liability for unintentional transgressions.</meta>

If a person performed many forbidden labors across many Sabbaths, he is liable for each individual labor. However, one who performs many labors that fall under a single type of labor <note>original: "me'ein melakhah achat." This refers to performing multiple actions that are categorized under the same primary category of work.</note> is only liable for a single sin-offering <note>original: "chatat." A sacrifice brought to the Temple for an unintentional violation of a biblical commandment.</note>.

2

the one who reaps, the one who gathers sheaves, the one who threshes, and the one who winnows;

the one who weaves two threads, and the one who separates two threads;
the one who ties a knot, the one who unties a knot,

# Chapter 10

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 10 Mishnah 1
1
One who stores [something] for seed, for a sample, or for medicine,
and carries it out on the Sabbath, is liable for any amount <note>Since the individual showed the item was important to them by storing it, their personal intent overrides the standard minimum measure.</note>.
But for any other person, they are only liable for the standard measure;
if he changed his mind and brought it back in, he is only liable for the standard measure <note>Once the original intent for storing it is abandoned or the action is reversed, the item reverts to the standard legal measure.</note>.

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 10 Mishnah 2
2
One who carries out food and places it on the threshold,
whether he then went back and carried it out [fully into the street] or someone else carried it out, he is exempt,
because he did not perform his labor in a single continuous action <note>The Sabbath prohibition against carrying requires a complete movement from a private domain to a public one; stopping on the threshold (an intermediate zone) breaks the act into two permitted half-actions.</note>.
A basket that is full of fruit,
and is placed on the outer threshold,
even though most of the fruit is outside [in the public domain], he is exempt,
until he carries out the entire basket.

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 10 Mishnah 3
3
One who carries out [an object] either in his right hand or his left,
in his lap, or on his shoulder, is liable,
for such was the manner of carrying by the sons of Kohath <note>The Kohathites were the family of Levites in the Bible (Numbers 4) charged with carrying the sacred vessels of the Tabernacle on their shoulders; their labor serves as the blueprint for what defines "carrying" on the Sabbath.</note>;
[But if he carries it] on the back of his hand, with his foot, in his mouth, with his elbow,
in his ear, in his hair, in his money-belt <note>original: "afundato," a belt with a pouch used for carrying coins</note> with its opening facing downward,
between his money-belt and his tunic, on the hem of his tunic,
in his shoe, or in his sandal, he is exempt,
because he did not carry it in the manner that people usually carry. <note>Rabbinic law distinguishes between "normal" carrying and carrying in an unusual or awkward way (*ki-le’achar yad*); the latter is Rabbinically forbidden but does not carry the full biblical penalty.</note>

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 10 Mishnah 4

->ד<-

One who intends to carry [an object] in front of him, but it [slipped and] ended up behind him, is exempt <note>Because the person failed to carry the item in the specific manner they intended, and carrying behind one's back is generally considered an inferior or unusual way to carry.</note>; [but if he intended to carry it] behind him and it ended up in front of him, he is liable <note>Since carrying in front is more secure, the person's intent to carry was fulfilled in a superior way.</note>. 

In truth, they said: a woman who girds herself with an apron, whether [the object] is in front of her or behind her, she is liable, for it is prone to turn around <note>Because an apron naturally shifts around the body, any position is considered "normal" and thus constitutes a violation of carrying.</note>. 

Rabbi Yehuda says: This also applies to those who receive notes <note>referring to couriers or tax collectors who might carry documents in a specific fashion on their person.</note>.

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 10 Mishnah 5

->ה<-

One who carries out food items less than the required measure <term>measure: or *shi'ur*, the minimum volume (usually the size of a dried fig) that triggers a biblical violation</term> in a vessel, is exempt even regarding the vessel, because the vessel is secondary to it <note>Since the primary purpose was to carry the food, and the food didn't meet the threshold, the container is ignored by the law.</note>; 

[One who carries] a living person on a bed is exempt even regarding the bed, because the bed is secondary to him <note>The Talmudic principle is that "a living person carries himself," meaning the weight is not fully borne by the carrier.</note>; but [one who carries] a dead person on a bed, he is liable. 

And similarly, [one who carries] an olive-sized piece <note>original: *kezayit*</note> of a corpse, or an olive-sized piece of a carcass <note>original: *nevelah*</note>, or a lentil-sized piece of a "creeping thing" <note>original: *sheretz*, referring to specific small animals that convey ritual impurity</note>, they are liable. 
Rabbi Shimon exempts [in these cases] <note>Rabbi Shimon holds that a "labor not needed for its own sake"—such as removing a carcass only because you don't want it there—is not a biblical violation.</note>.

->ו<-

One who carries out a loaf of bread into the public domain is liable. If two people carried it out together, they are exempt <note>The Sabbath laws require an individual to perform the labor; if two people do what one could have done alone, it is not a biblical violation.</note>. If one person was unable to carry it and two people carried it together, they are liable. Rabbi Shimon exempts.

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 10 Mishnah 6

->ז<-

One who removes his fingernails using another nail or his teeth, and similarly [one who pulls out] his hair, his mustache, or his beard; and similarly a woman who braids [her hair], or paints [her eyes with kohl], or parts [her hair] <note>The Hebrew terms *godelet*, *kochelet*, and *pokeset* refer to various cosmetic acts of grooming and beautification.</note>—Rabbi Eliezer deems him liable for a sin offering <note>original: *chatat*</note>, but the Sages prohibit these actions only as a rabbinic decree <term>rabbinic decree: or *shevut*, a category of actions forbidden by the Sages to protect the sanctity of the Sabbath, though not technically "labors" by biblical definition</term>. 

One who plucks [a plant] from a perforated flowerpot is liable, but if it is not perforated, he is exempt <note>A perforated pot is legally considered connected to the ground, so plucking from it is like harvesting from the earth.</note>. Rabbi Shimon exempts in both cases.

# Chapter 11

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 11 Mishnah 1

1
**One who throws** an object from a private domain <term>private domain: *reshut ha-yachid*, an enclosed area at least four by four handbreadths</term> into a public domain <term>public domain: *reshut ha-rabbim*, an open thoroughfare used by the masses</term>, or from a public domain into a private domain, is liable <note>Meaning they have violated a Torah-level prohibition and would be required to bring a sin offering if the act was accidental.</note>. 

One who throws from a private domain to another private domain, but the object passes through a public domain in the middle:
Rabbi Akiva deems him liable,
but the Sages exempt him <note>The Sages argue that an object merely passing through the airspace of a domain is not the same as it "resting" there, which is required for a violation.</note>.

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 11 Mishnah 2

2
**How so?** <note>Meaning: in what circumstances is one exempt for passing between domains?</note>
If there were two balconies opposite each other across a public domain, 
one who passes an object or throws it from this one to that one is exempt. 
If both balconies were on the same level <note>original: *diyotat*, referring to a single story or side of a street</note>,
one who passes an object is liable, but one who throws it is exempt, 
for such was the labor of the Levites. <note>The laws of Shabbat are derived from the construction of the Tabernacle (Mishkan). The Levites passed the heavy wooden planks from one wagon to another.</note>

3
If there were two wagons one after another in a public domain,
they may pass the planks from this one to that one, 
but they may not throw them. 
The rim of a pit or a rock, 
which are ten [handbreadths] high and four [handbreadths] wide, <insert>Inside: ten, and it was corrected by the proofreader</insert>
one who takes from them or places an object on top of them is liable; 
but if they are less than this size, he is exempt. <note>Objects of this size are considered "private domains" due to their height and width, even if they are located in the middle of a public square.</note>

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 11 Mishnah 3

4
**One who throws** an object four cubits <term>cubit: *amah*, roughly 18 inches or 45-50 cm</term> against a wall:
If he hits the wall above ten handbreadths <term>handbreadth: *tefach*, roughly 3.1-3.9 inches or 8-10 cm</term>, it is as if he threw it into the air <note>The airspace above ten handbreadths in a public domain is considered a "free zone" (*makom patur*) where the usual restrictions on carrying do not apply.</note>; 
If he hits below ten handbreadths, it is as if he threw it onto the ground. 
One who throws an object on the ground for a distance of four cubits in a public domain is liable. 

If he threw an object intended for a spot within four cubits, 
but it rolled outside of the four cubits, he is exempt; 
If he threw it intended for a spot outside of four cubits, 
but it rolled back into the four cubit zone, he is liable. <note>In the law of Shabbat, the status of the act is often determined by where the object first touches or where the person intended it to land.</note>

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 11 Mishnah 4

<summary>This page defines the prohibitions against throwing or passing objects between private and public domains, using the historical Tabernacle construction as a legal precedent. It establishes the specific measurements—such as ten handbreadths in height and four cubits in distance—that determine whether a Sabbath violation has occurred.</summary>

--- Page 229 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Tractate Shabbat, Chapter 11, moving from the laws of throwing between private and public domains to the specific status of the sea, shallow pools, and ships. It concludes Chapter 11 with the fundamental principle of "unintentionality" required for a sin offering and begins Chapter 12.</meta>

5
**One who throws** an object in the sea for a distance of four cubits <term>cubit: *amah*, approximately 18-22 inches, the standard unit of measurement for Sabbath boundaries</term> is exempt <note>The sea is categorized as a *karmelit*, a domain that is neither fully private nor fully public; therefore, carrying within it does not violate Torah law, though it is still Rabbinically prohibited.</note>.

If there was a shallow pool of water and a public thoroughfare passes through it,
one who throws an object within it for a distance of four cubits is liable.
And how shallow must it be to be considered a "shallow pool"?
Less than ten handbreadths <term>handbreadth: *tefach*, roughly 3-4 inches</term> deep. <insert>In the body of the text: "less than five." Corrected in the margin by the proofreader.</insert>
If it is a shallow pool of water and the public thoroughfare passes through it,
one who throws within it for four cubits is liable <note>Because the public continues to walk through the shallow water, it retains its status as a public domain.</note>.

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 11 Mishnah 5

6
**One who throws** from the sea to the dry land, or from the dry land to the sea,
or from the sea to a ship, or from a ship to its fellow ship,
is exempt.
If ships are tied to one another,
one may move objects from one to the other.
If they are not tied, even if they are placed close together,
one may not move objects from one to the other.

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 11 Mishnah 6

7
**One who throws** an object and then remembers <note>Remembers that it is the Sabbath or that throwing is prohibited.</note> before the object leaves his hand,
or if another person caught it, or if a dog caught it, or if it was burned [in mid-air],
he is exempt.
If he threw an object specifically to cause a wound, 
whether to a person or to an animal,
and he remembered before the wound was made,
he is exempt.
**This is the general rule:**
All those who are liable to bring a sin offering <term>sin offering: *chatat*, a sacrifice brought to the Temple to atone for an unintentional violation of a commandment</term>,
are not liable unless the beginning and the end of their action were accidental <note>original: *shigaga*, meaning an act done without the realization that it was prohibited or that it was the Sabbath.</note>.
If the beginning was accidental but the end was intentional <note>original: *zadon*</note>,
or if the beginning was intentional and the end was accidental,
they are exempt,
unless both the beginning and the end of the act were accidental.

# Chapter 12

<meta>This page continues from the end of Chapter 11, which discussed the laws of throwing objects between domains. It marks the beginning of Chapter 12 of Tractate Shabbat, which shifts focus to the minimum measures required for liability in various categories of labor, specifically building, agriculture, and writing.</meta>

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 12 Mishnah 1

**1**
**One who builds**, how much must he build to be liable <term>liable: *chayav*, meaning one has violated a Torah-level prohibition and must bring a sin-offering if the act was unintentional</term>?
One who builds any amount at all, one who carves a stone,
one who strikes with a hammer or an adze <note>tools used for finishing stone or wood</note>,
and one who drills any amount at all, is liable.
This is the general rule:
Whoever performs a labor,
and his labor is of a lasting nature on the Sabbath, is liable.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
Even one who strikes a sledgehammer upon the anvil during the time of work is liable,
because he is like one who improves the labor <note>Professional smiths would often strike the anvil to smooth the hammer's face or maintain a rhythm, which was considered part of the skilled craft</note>.

---

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 12 Mishnah 2

**2**
**One who plows** any amount at all,
one who weeds, one who prunes, and one who thins branches any amount at all, is liable.
**One who gathers wood**,
if it is to improve the land, any amount at all;
if it is for fuel, enough to cook a light egg <note>The time/fuel required to cook a small hen's egg is a standard Rabbinic measurement</note>.
**One who gathers grass**,
if it is to improve the land, any amount at all;
if it is for an animal, a goat's mouthful.

---

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 12 Mishnah 3

**3**
**One who writes**,
whether with his right hand or with his left hand,
whether writing one name <note>original: *shem*</note> or two different names,
whether using two different signs <note>original: *simaniyot*, referring to distinct symbols or marks</note>, in any language, he is liable.
Rabbi Yose said:
They did not make one liable for writing two letters except because of "marking" <note>vocalized in the manuscript as: *roshem*</note>,
for that is how they would mark the planks of the Tabernacle <term>Tabernacle: *Mishkan*, the portable sanctuary used by the Israelites in the desert; its construction serves as the blueprint for the 39 forbidden Sabbath labors</term>,
to know which one was the partner of the other.
Rabbi Yehuda said:
We find a short name that is part of a long name <note>Meaning, one is liable for writing two letters even if they were intended to be part of a longer word, provided those two letters form a valid word on their own</note>,
such as writing "Shem" from the names "Shimon" or "Shmuel,"
or writing "Noach" from "Nachor," or "Dan" from "Daniel." <note>original names: *Shem* (S-M) from *Shimon* (S-M-O-N); *Noach* (N-CH) from *Nachor* (N-CH-R). Rabbi Yehuda argues that since the two letters form a meaningful name, the writer is liable immediately upon completing them</note>

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 12 Mishnah 4

<summary>This page defines the minimum thresholds of activity required to violate Sabbath prohibitions regarding building, agriculture, and writing, grounding these laws in the historical construction of the Tabernacle.</summary>

->4<-

**One who writes two letters in one state of unawareness** <term>state of unawareness: *he'elam*, referring to a period of time during which a person forgets that the day is the Sabbath or that the act is forbidden</term>, **is liable.**
Whether one wrote with **ink, with pigment** <note>original: *sam*, likely a vegetable-based dye</note>, **with red paint, with gum** <note>original: *kumos*, a resin used to make ink adhere</note>, **or with copperas** <note>original: *kalkantos*, vitriol used to blacken ink</note>,
and with any substance that leaves a lasting mark.
Whether writing on **two walls that meet at a corner, or on two leaves of a writing tablet,**
as long as they can be read together.
**One who writes upon their flesh is liable.**
And one who **scratches** <note>tattoos or scars</note> **upon their flesh,**
**Rabbi Eliezer renders them liable** for a sin-offering,
**but Rabbi Joshua exempts them.**

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 12 Mishnah 5

->5<-

If one wrote with **liquids, with fruit juice,**
**in the dust of the roads, in scribal dust,**
**or with anything that does not last, they are exempt.**
If one wrote with the **back of their hand, with their foot, with their mouth, or with their elbow;**
if one wrote **one letter next to existing writing** <insert>to write</insert> <note>the insertion suggests the intention was to complete a word</note>;
if one **wrote over existing writing** <note>re-tracing existing letters</note>;

If one **wrote a single letter as a shorthand** <term>shorthand: *notarikon*, the practice of using a single letter to represent a full word or name</term>,
**Rabbi Joshua ben Betira renders them liable,**
**but the Sages exempt them.**

**But one who destroys in order to improve** <note>such as tearing a cloth to sew it better</note>,

**their minimum measure is a single sit.**

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 13 Mishnah 5
### 5
**Rabbi Yehuda says:**
**Trapping a bird into a cabinet or a deer into a house, one is liable.**
**And the Sages say:**
**A bird into a cabinet,**
**and a deer into a garden, a courtyard, or a corral.** <note>original: *bivarim*, derived from the Latin *vivarium*, an enclosed area for keeping live animals</note>
**Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:**
**Not all corrals are the same.**
**This is the general rule:**
**Anything that still requires further effort to capture** <note>where the animal is still free to move out of reach</note>**, one is exempt,**
**but if it does not require further effort to capture, one is liable.**

6
**A deer that entered a house,**
**if one person locked the door before it, they are liable.** <term>liable: *hayyav*, meaning the person has committed a forbidden labor and must bring a sin-offering</term>
**If two people locked it together, they are exempt.** <term>exempt: *patur*, meaning the act is forbidden, but does not carry the penalty of a sacrifice, as the labor was shared</term>
**If one person was unable to lock it alone,**
**and two locked it, they are both liable.**
**Rabbi Shimon exempts them.** <note>Rabbi Shimon generally maintains that an act performed by two people that could theoretically be done by one (or vice versa) does not meet the legal threshold for "labor" on the Sabbath.</note>

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 13 Mishnah 7

7
**If one person sat at the doorway but did not fill it,** <note>leaving enough space for the animal to escape</note>
**and a second person sat down and filled the gap, the second is liable.**
**If the first person sat at the doorway and filled it,**
**and a second person came and sat beside them,**
**even though the first stood up and went away,**
**the first is liable and the second is exempt.**
**To what is this comparable?**
**To one who locks their house to guard it,**
**and a deer is found to be guarded inside it.** <note>The trapping is a secondary result of a primary, permitted action of securing one's home.</note>

# Chapter 14

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 14 Mishnah 1

1
**The eight creeping creatures mentioned in the Torah** <note>original: *sheratzim*; referring to the weasel, mouse, toad, hedgehog, chameleon, lizard, snail, and mole listed in Leviticus 11:29–30</note>,
**one who traps them or wounds them is liable.**
**But for all other loathsome creatures and creeping things,**
**one who wounds them is exempt.**
**One who traps them for a specific use is liable,**
**but if it is not for a specific use, they are exempt.**
**Regarding a wild animal or a bird in one's possession** <note>already domesticated or previously captured</note>,
**one who traps them is exempt,**
**but one who wounds them is liable.**

**One does not eat wild hyssop on the Sabbath,** <note>original: *ezovyon*; likely a reference to lavender or a specific medicinal hyssop</note>

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 14 Mishnah 4
-> 4 <-

**One who has a toothache**
**may not sip vinegar through them,** <note>Sipping and then spitting it out is a clear act of healing.</note>

**and if he is healed, he is healed.**
**One who has pain in his loins**
**may not rub wine or vinegar on them,**
**but he may rub regular oil, but not rose oil.**
**Princes may rub rose oil on their wounds,**
**since it is their habit to rub it on weekdays.**
**Rabbi Shimon says:**
**All of Israel are considered princes.** <note>Rabbi Shimon believes that since all Jews have high spiritual standing, they should all be permitted to use luxury items like rose oil, making its use "normal" rather than strictly medicinal.</note>

# Chapter 16

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 16 Mishnah 1

1
All Holy Scriptures <note>original: *Kitvei HaKodesh*; referring to the books of the Hebrew Bible (the Tanakh).</note>
may be rescued from a fire [on the Sabbath],
whether they are scrolls that one reads from or those that one does not [regularly] read from. <note>In this context, "not read from" likely refers to the books of the Prophets or Hagiographa (Writings) that were not part of the weekly public liturgy.</note>
Even if they are written in any other language, they require <term>Genizah: A storage area for worn-out or prohibited sacred texts, as they cannot be simply discarded or burned due to the presence of the Divine Name.</term>
Why then do we not [ordinarily] read from [certain scrolls] on the Sabbath?
Because of the "neglect of the Study House." <note>original: *Bittul Beit HaMidrash*; the concern was that if people read these scrolls privately at home, they would fail to attend the communal Torah lectures given by the rabbis on the Sabbath.</note>

2
One may rescue the case of a scroll together with the scroll,
and the case of <term>tefillin: Black leather boxes containing parchment scrolls with Torah verses, worn during weekday morning prayers.</term> together with the tefillin,
even if there is money inside them. <note>Normally, money is *muktzeh* (forbidden to be moved on the Sabbath), but here it is moved incidentally while saving the sacred objects.</note>
And to where may one rescue them?
To an alleyway that is not a thoroughfare. <note>original: *mevoy she-eino mefulash*; an alley closed on three sides, which is considered a private or semi-private domain where carrying is more leniently treated.</note>
Ben Beteira says:
One may rescue them even to a thoroughfare. <note>original: *mefulash*; an alley open on both ends to the public street.</note>

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 16 Mishnah 2

3
One may rescue [from a fire] food enough for three meals: <note>The three meals required by law to be eaten on the Sabbath: Friday night, Sabbath morning, and Sabbath afternoon.</note>
food suitable for humans for humans,
and food suitable for animals for animals.
How so?
If a fire broke out on Friday night,
one may rescue food for three meals.
If it broke out in the morning, one may rescue food for two meals.
If it broke out in the afternoon <note>original: *Mincha*; the time of the late afternoon prayer service.</note>, one may rescue food for one meal.
Rabbi Yose says:
One may always rescue food enough for three meals. <note>Rabbi Yose's view is that the allowance is a fixed amount regardless of when the fire occurs.</note>

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 16 Mishnah 3

4
One may rescue a basket full of loaves,
even if it contains enough for a hundred meals.
One may also rescue a round cake of pressed figs and a barrel of wine.
And one may say to others:

<summary>This page discusses the emergency protocols for a fire on the Sabbath, prioritizing the rescue of Holy Scriptures and the essential three Sabbath meals while navigating the prohibitions of carrying in public domains.</summary>
<keywords>Sabbath laws, fire, Holy Scriptures, Genizah, Study House, food rescue, three meals, tefillin, Ben Beteira, Rabbi Yose</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous discussion on saving holy books from a fire, this page continues detailing the laws for rescuing property and managing a fire on the Sabbath. It explores the tension between the prohibition of carrying items in public and the natural human desire to save one's possessions from destruction.</meta>

"Come and save [property] for yourselves!" <note>original: "Bo-u ve-hatzilu lakhem!" This is an invitation to bystanders to take items for their own ownership, as the owner is legally limited in what they can carry out themselves.</note>
If they were clever, they would settle the account with him after the Sabbath. <note>While a Jew cannot be hired to perform work on the Sabbath, if they "save" the items and later return them, the owner can provide a reward as a gesture of gratitude or a pre-arranged settlement once the Sabbath ends.</note>
And to where may they rescue them?
To a courtyard that is joined by an <term>Eruv: A legal ritual boundary (often a wire or fence) that symbolically transforms a public or shared area into a private domain, allowing residents to carry items on the Sabbath.</term>
Ben Beteira says:
Even to one that is not joined by an Eruv.

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 16 Mishnah 4
->5<-

And to there [the courtyard] he may take out all his usable utensils,
and he may wear all that he is able to wear,
and wrap himself in all that he is able to wrap. <note>By wearing clothes instead of carrying them in a bundle, one avoids the prohibition of "carrying" in a public space.</note>
Rabbi Yosei says:
[He may wear] eighteen garments. <note>This refers to a standard set of ancient garments; any more would look like a burden rather than "wearing" clothes.</note>

and say to others:
"Come and save [items] with me!"

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 16 Mishnah 5
->6<-

Rabbi Shimon ben Nanas says:
One may spread a goatskin
over a chest, a box, or a cupboard that has caught fire,
because it [the skin] only singes. <note>The thick leather of a goatskin is fire-resistant; it will char rather than ignite, creating a protective barrier.</note>
One may make a barrier with any utensils, <gloss>barrier</gloss>
whether they are full or empty,
so that the fire will not spread.
Rabbi Yosei prohibits [using] new clay vessels filled with water,
because they cannot withstand the heat,
and they will burst and extinguish the fire. <note>Rabbi Yosei's concern is "indirect extinguishing" (*grama*). Since the heat causes the jars to break and release water, he views this as too close to actively putting out the fire, which is forbidden on the Sabbath.</note>

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 16 Mishnah 6
->7<-

If a non-Jew comes to extinguish [the fire], one does not say to him:
"Extinguish it!" [nor] "Do not extinguish it!"
because his Sabbath rest is not their responsibility. <note>original: "she-ein shevitato aleihem." A Jew cannot ask a non-Jew to do forbidden work on the Sabbath, but if the non-Jew acts of his own accord, the Jew does not have to stop him.</note>
But a minor who comes to extinguish [the fire], one must not listen to him [one must stop him],
because his Sabbath rest is their responsibility. <note>A Jewish child's education and Sabbath observance are the responsibility of the community or parents; therefore, he must be prevented from performing "work."</note>

a hand-needle to remove a thorn;
and a sack-maker's needle <note>A larger, stouter needle used for coarse fabrics.</note> to open a door.

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 17 Mishnah 3
### 3

A reed used for olives <note>A rod used to stir olives or check their level in a vat.</note>:
if there is a knot at its head, it is susceptible to <term>Ritual Impurity: The status of an object (Tumah) that makes it unfit for use in sacred contexts; only "finished" vessels with a receptacle or specific form can contract impurity.</term>;
and if not, it is not susceptible to ritual impurity.
In either case, it may be handled on the Sabbath. <note>Since it is considered a functional tool, it is not "set aside" (Muktzeh) even if it isn't technically a "vessel" regarding impurity laws.</note>

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 17 Mishnah 4
### 4

All utensils may be handled on the Sabbath,
except for the large saw and the plowshare <note>These are "Muktzeh due to monetary loss." Because they are expensive, delicate, and have a very specific professional use, people are careful not to use them for anything else, so they are "set aside" and forbidden to move.</note>.
All utensils may be handled whether for a specific need <note>Using the tool for its intended purpose or another permitted purpose.</note> or not for a specific need <note>Moving the tool simply because you need the space it occupies.</note>.
**Rabbi Nehemiah says:**
They may only be handled for a specific need.

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 17 Mishnah 5
### 5

All utensils may be handled on the Sabbath, and their shards may be handled, <gloss>The text says "handled" (nitalim), and the proofreader added the letter Heh [to make it "the handled ones"]</gloss>
provided they can perform some semblance of labor:
shards of a trough to cover the mouth of a barrel;
shards of glass to cover the mouth of a vial.
**Rabbi Yehuda says:**
Provided they can perform some semblance of their *original* labor:
shards of a trough to pour thick stew into them,
and shards of glass to pour oil into them. <note>Rabbi Yehuda is stricter; he believes a shard is only a "utensil" if it can still do what the original vessel did, albeit on a smaller scale.</note>

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 17 Mishnah 6
### 6

The stone that is in a hollowed gourd <note>Hollowed-out gourds were used as water buckets. Because they were light and would float, a stone was often placed inside to weigh them down so they would sink and fill with water.</note>:
if they fill [water] with it and it does not fall out, one may fill [water] with it;
and if not, one may not fill [water] with it. <note>If the stone is firmly fixed, it becomes part of the "vessel." If it is loose, handling the gourd would be like handling a plain stone, which is forbidden (Muktzeh) on the Sabbath.</note>
A vine-branch that is tied to a pitcher:
one may fill [water] with it on the Sabbath. <note>The branch acts as a handle. Since it is tied, it is considered part of the vessel.</note>

# Chapter 18

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 18 Mishnah 1
1
One may move even four or five baskets of straw or of grain
on account of [making room for] guests and on account of preventing the cancellation of [study in] the House of Study <note>original: bittul beit ha-midrash; meaning to ensure there is enough space for students to sit and learn.</note>,
but [one may] not [clear out] the entire storehouses.
One may move <term>Pure Heave-offering (Terumah): A portion of the crop given to the Priests (Kohanim) which must be eaten in a state of ritual purity. Since it is edible for a Priest, it is not "set aside" (Muktzeh).</term>,
and <term>Demai: Produce purchased from a commoner who is suspected of not properly separating tithes. It may be handled because it could theoretically be declared poor-man's tithe and eaten.</term>,
and First Tithe whose Heave-offering has [already] been taken,
and Second Tithe and consecrated items that have been redeemed <note>Once redeemed, these items become ordinary food and are no longer restricted to being eaten in Jerusalem or belonging to the Temple.</note>,
and dry lupine <note>A type of legume.</note>,
because it is food for goats;
but [one may] not [move] <term>Untithed Produce (Tevel): Produce from which the required priestly gifts and tithes have not yet been separated. It is forbidden to be eaten, and therefore forbidden to be handled on the Sabbath.</term>,
nor First Tithe whose Heave-offering has not been taken,
nor Second Tithe and consecrated items that have not been redeemed,
nor <term>Arum (Luf): A plant with edible tubers (Arum palaestinum) that requires complex preparation (boiling) to be edible; raw, it is considered useless on the Sabbath.</term>,
nor mustard.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits [moving] Arum,
because it is food for crows <note>He argues that since wealthy people sometimes keep crows as pets, the plant is considered "animal food" and therefore not Muktzeh.</note>.

Bundles of straw, bundles of wood, and bundles of twigs—

Rabbi Yose says:
When [is this permitted]?
At a time when he [the child] lifts one [foot] and places the other [down].
But if he was dragging [his feet],
it is forbidden <note>If the child cannot support any of his own weight, assisting him is seen as carrying him, which is a prohibited labor in a public space.</note>.

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 18 Mishnah 3

->3<-

One may not deliver the young of an animal on a Festival <note>original: Yom Tov; while some labors are permitted on Festivals for food preparation, assisting an animal in birth is more restricted than assisting a human.</note>,
but one may assist it <note>One may support the newborn so it does not fall on the ground or help the mother, but not perform the full delivery.</note>.
One may deliver the young of a woman on the Sabbath,
and one may call a midwife <note>original: chakhamah; literally "a wise woman."</note> from place to place <note>Even from outside the "Sabbath boundary" (the limit one can walk outside a city).</note>,
and one may violate the Sabbath for her [the mother's] sake.
One may tie the umbilical cord.
Rabbi Yose says:
One may even cut [it].
All the needs of circumcision may be performed on the Sabbath.

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 19 Mishnah 2

And Rabbi Eliezer further said:
One may cut wood to make charcoal [in order] to forge iron [tools for the circumcision]. <note>Rabbi Eliezer held the minority view that even the preliminary preparation of tools overrides the Sabbath if they are needed for the commandment.</note>
Rabbi Akiva stated a general rule:
Any labor that could have been performed before the Sabbath
does not override the Sabbath;
but that which could not have been performed before the Sabbath
overrides the Sabbath. <note>Akiva’s rule became the standard: the circumcision itself overrides the Sabbath, but making the knife does not, as it could have been done on Friday.</note>

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 19 Mishnah 3

One may perform all the needs of circumcision [on the Sabbath]:
One circumcises, and performs <term>periah; uncovering the glans by tearing the thin inner membrane</term>, and performs <term>metzitzah; the traditional suctioning of the wound for medical/ritual safety</term>,
and one applies a plaster and cumin to it.
If one did not grind the cumin before the Sabbath,
one may chew it with their teeth and apply it.
If one did not mix wine and oil [for the dressing] before the Sabbath,
one may apply this one by itself and that one by itself.
And one does not make a <term>haluk; a specially shaped "shirt" or bandage</term> for it for the first time [on the Sabbath],
but one may wrap a rag over it.
If one did not prepare [the rag] before the Sabbath,
one may wrap it around their finger and bring it,
even from another courtyard. <note>By wrapping it on a finger like a garment, one avoids the prohibition of "carrying" an object in a public area.</note>

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 19 Mishnah 4

One may wash the infant both before the circumcision and after the circumcision,
and one may sprinkle [water] on him by hand, but not with a vessel.

One may wash the infant on the third day [after the circumcision] even if it falls on the Sabbath,
as it is said: (Genesis 34:25)

A <term>safek; a child of "doubtful" status, such as one born at twilight</term> or an <term>androgynos; an individual possessing both male and female physical characteristics</term>—one does not desecrate the Sabbath for them. <note>Only a certain male child born on the eighth day previously overrides the Sabbath; cases of uncertainty do not.</note>

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 19 Mishnah 5

->6<-

An infant is circumcised on the eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, or twelfth day [of life]; 
no less and no more. 
In the standard way, on the **eighth** day; 
if he was born at twilight <note>original: "בין השמשות" (bein hashmashot). This is the period after sunset but before the stars appear; in Jewish law, it is uncertain whether this time belongs to the day passing or the day beginning.</note>, he is circumcised on the **ninth**; 
if he was born at twilight on the eve of the Sabbath <note>Friday evening</note>, he is circumcised on the **tenth**; 
if a Festival day follows the Sabbath, he is circumcised on the **eleventh**; 
if the two Festival days of Rosh Hashanah [follow the Sabbath], he is circumcised on the **twelfth**. 
An infant who is ill, 
one does not circumcise him until he becomes healthy.

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 19 Mishnah 6

->7<-

These are the <term>tzitzim; shreds of skin</term> that invalidate the circumcision: 
skin that covers the majority of the <term>atarah; the glans or "crown" of the penis</term>, 
and [one with such skin] may not eat <term>terumah; the sanctified produce given to the Priests</term>. 
If the man was fleshy <note>obese</note>, 
one must repair the appearance for the sake of <term>mar'it ayin; avoiding the false impression of being uncircumcised</term>. 
One who circumcises but does not perform <term>periah; the tearing and folding back of the inner membrane</term>, 
it is as if he did not circumcise at all.

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 20 Mishnah 2
->2<-

but one may place them into a sieve or into a basket <note>Allowing the animal to eat from the basket such that the chaff falls away naturally without the person actively sifting.</note>. 
One may not sift straw with a sieve, 
nor may one place it in a high place so that the <term>chaff|The dry scales or husks of grain</term> will fall away as it descends,

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 21 Mishnah 1

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 21 Mishnah 2

If a stone is resting on the mouth of a barrel <note>The stone acts as a temporary lid but remains forbidden to handle directly.</note>, 
one may tilt the barrel on its side and the stone falls off. 
If the barrel was located among other barrels <note>Such that there is no room to tilt it without hitting others.</note>, 
one may lift the barrel, carry it elsewhere, and then tilt it on its side so that the stone falls. 
If coins are on a pillow, one may shake the pillow and they fall off. 
If there was filth <note>Specifically bird droppings or similar waste.</note> on the pillow, one may wipe it with a rag; 
if the filth was on a leather pillow, one may pour water on it until it disappears <note>Cleaning leather with water was not considered "laundering" in the same way as cleaning fabric.</note>.

# Chapter 22

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 22 Mishnah 1
### 1
If a **barrel** broke <note>on the Sabbath, causing its contents to spill</note>, one may rescue from it enough food for three meals <note>The three meals of the Sabbath are the legal limit for what one can "rescue" to prevent financial loss without violating the spirit of the day.</note>.
And one may say to others: "Come and rescue some for yourselves!"
This is permitted provided that he does not use a sponge <note>Lest he come to wring it out.</note>.
One may not squeeze fruits to extract liquids from them; if the liquids flowed out on their own, they are forbidden to use.
**Rabbi Yehuda** says:
If the fruits were intended for eating, the liquid that flows out is permitted; but if they were intended for juicing, the liquid that flows out is forbidden <note>If intended for eating, the juice is considered a mere byproduct; if intended for juicing, the juice is the primary goal, making its appearance on Sabbath a violation of the laws of "extracting."</note>.
Regarding **honeycombs** that one crushed on the eve of the Sabbath: if the honey flowed out on its own, it is forbidden.
**Rabbi Eleazar** permits it.

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 22 Mishnah 2
### 2
Anything that was placed in hot water before the Sabbath <note>meaning it was already cooked</note> may be soaked in hot water on the Sabbath.
And anything that was not placed in hot water before the Sabbath may be rinsed with hot water on the Sabbath <note>Rinsing is a superficial heat, whereas soaking can further the cooking process.</note>,
except for **old salted fish** and the **Spanish mackerel** <note>original: "Kolyas Ha-Ispanan," likely referring to the Spanish tunny or Chub mackerel which was preserved in brine.</note>,
for rinsing them is the completion of their preparation <note>These specific fish are so thin or salt-cured that rinsing them in hot water is equivalent to cooking them entirely, which is a prohibited labor.</note>.

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 22 Mishnah 3
### 3
A person may break a barrel to eat **dried figs** from it,
provided that he does not intend to make it into a functional vessel <note>One may break an enclosure to get to food, but one cannot "create" a permanent opening or a useful container on the Sabbath.</note>.
One may not pierce the stopper of a barrel.

[These are] the words of **Rabbi Yehuda**.
And **Rabbi Yose** says:
He may not pierce it from its side.
If it was [already] pierced, one may not put wax on it, because he would be **smoothing** it <note>original: "memare’ach"—the prohibited labor of spreading or smoothing a pliable substance on the Sabbath</note>.
**Rabbi Yehuda** said:
A case once came before **Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai** in Arav, and he said:
"I fear for him [that he may be liable] for a **sin offering**" <note>original: "chatat"—the sacrifice required for an unintentional but major violation of a Sabbath law</note>.

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 22 Mishnah 4
### 4
One may place a cooked dish into a cistern so that it will be preserved <note>kept cool and protected from spoilage</note>,
and [one may place] fresh water into foul water so that it will cool, <gloss>so that it will be cooled</gloss>
and cold [water] into the hot [water] so that it will be warmed. <note>In the hot [water]: it appears that under the erasure it is written: "in the sun"</note>
One whose clothes fell [into the water] on the road may continue to walk in them and need not worry <note>he does not need to fear being suspected of laundering his clothes on the Sabbath</note>.
Once he reaches the outer courtyard, he may spread them out in the sun, but not in front of the people <note>to avoid giving the impression that he is washing clothes on the Sabbath</note>.

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 22 Mishnah 5
### 5
One who bathes in a cave or in the [hot] springs of **Tiberias** may dry himself even with ten **towels** <note>original: "lenatiyot"—large linen cloths used for drying</note>.
He may not bring them back in his hand <note>because the wet towels are heavy with water and one might wring them out, which is a violation of the labor of laundering</note>;
but ten people may dry themselves with a single towel—their faces, hands, and feet—and they may bring it in their hand. <gloss>bring them</gloss> <note>When shared by many for only their extremities, the towel does not become saturated enough to tempt someone to wring it out.</note>

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 22 Mishnah 6
### 6
One may apply oil and **massage** [the body], <gloss>inner reading: and they may be massaged</gloss>
but one may not perform **vigorous exercise** nor may they be **scraped** <note>original: "mit-amlin" and "mitgardin"—referring to intense physical training or the use of a metal scraper (strigil) to remove sweat and oil, which were considered weekday activities</note>.
One may not go down to a **muddy pond** <note>original: "philoma"—from the Greek 'pelos', meaning mud or clay; likely referring to a therapeutic mud bath</note>,
and one may not induce vomiting <note>original: "aphiktaphizin"—likely from the Greek 'apophthisis', a medicinal treatment to induce vomiting</note> on the Sabbath,
and one may not **straighten** [the limbs of] a newborn child,
nor may one set a **fracture**.
One whose hand or foot was dislocated should not splash them with cold water; <gloss>splash them</gloss>
but he may wash in his usual manner, and if it is healed, it is healed <note>Meaning, if the natural washing results in healing, it is permitted, but one may not perform actions specifically intended for medical healing on the Sabbath unless it is a life-threatening emergency</note>.

<summary>This page details Sabbath restrictions regarding the cooling or heating of food and water, drying oneself after bathing, and physical therapies. It highlights the prohibition against "smoothing" substances like wax and restricts medicinal treatments or vigorous physical activities that resemble weekday labor.</summary>

<header>Chapter 23</header>

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 23 Mishnah 1

### 1
A person may ask a friend for jugs of wine or jugs of oil, provided that he does not say to him: "Lend me!" <note>original: "Halveini"—this specific Hebrew verb refers to a formal, long-term loan which often involves writing a debt contract, an act forbidden on the Sabbath</note>.
And similarly, a woman may ask her friend for loaves of bread.
If he <note>the one giving the items</note> does not trust him,
he may leave his cloak with him <note>as a security deposit</note> and make a formal accounting with him after the Sabbath.
And similarly, if the eve of **Passover** <note>original: "Pesach"</note> in **Jerusalem** falls on a Sabbath,
one may leave his cloak with him <note>the seller</note> and eat his **Passover offering**,
and make a formal accounting with him after the Festival day.

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 23 Mishnah 2

### 2
A person may count his guests and his appetizers <note>original: "parperotav"—side dishes or desserts</note> from memory <note>original: "mi-piu"—literally "from his mouth"</note>,
but not from a written list.
One may cast lots <note>original: "mefis"—a method of distributing portions by chance</note> with his children and the members of his household at the table,
provided that he does not intend to exchange a large portion for a small portion,
because of **gambling** <note>original: "kubiya"—playing with dice or games of chance, which are forbidden because they resemble commercial transactions</note>.
They may cast lots for the **sacrificial portions** <note>original: "kodashim"—the meat from holy offerings shared among priests</note> on a Festival,
but not for the [ordinary] food portions.

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 23 Mishnah 3

### 3
One may not hire workers on the Sabbath, <insert>to him - erased</insert>
nor may a person tell his friend to hire workers for him.
One may not wait at the **Sabbath boundary** <term>techum: the 2,000-cubit limit beyond a city's edge within which a person is permitted to walk on the Sabbath</term> until dark <note>original: "machshichin"—waiting until the Sabbath ends to get a head start on work</note> in order to hire workers or to bring in fruit,
but one may wait until dark at the boundary to guard [his field], and he may bring fruit back in his hand <note>since he is already there for a permitted purpose, like guarding</note>.
**Abba Shaul** stated a general rule:
Anything that I am entitled to speak of [on the Sabbath], <insert>that is not</insert>
I am permitted to wait until dark at the boundary for its sake.

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 23 Mishnah 4

### 4
One may wait at the boundary until dark to attend to the affairs of a **bride**,
or the affairs of the **deceased**, such as bringing a coffin and shrouds for him.
If a non-Jew brought flutes <note>for a funeral procession</note> on the Sabbath,

--- Page 249 ---
<meta>Continuity: This page concludes Chapter 23, which details the laws of mourning and preparing for post-Sabbath needs, and begins Chapter 24, the final chapter of Tractate Shabbat, which addresses miscellaneous laws regarding travel at the onset of the Sabbath and the feeding of animals.</meta>

An **Israelite** <note>original: "Yisrael"—referring to a Jewish person</note> may not be eulogized with them <note>referring to mourning instruments or shrouds prepared by a non-Jew on the Sabbath</note>, unless they were brought from a nearby place. If they made a coffin for him <note>for a non-Jew</note> and dug a grave for him, an **Israelite** may be buried in it; but if it was made specifically for an **Israelite**, he may never be buried in it.

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 23 Mishnah 5
->5<-

One may perform all the necessary needs for the deceased on the **Sabbath**:
One may anoint and wash the body, provided that they do not move any limb.
They may slide the pillow from beneath him and place him on cold sand <note>to keep the body cool and slow the process of decomposition</note> so that he will endure.
They may tie the jaw, not so that it will rise <note>to close it</note>, but so that it will not drop further.
And similarly, if a ceiling beam was broken,
one may support it with a bench or with the side-frames of a bed,
not so that it will rise, but so that it will not sag further.
One may not close the eyes of the dead on the **Sabbath**,
nor on a weekday at the very moment the soul departs.
And anyone who closes the eyes at the moment the soul departs,
behold, such a person is a shedder of blood <note>original: "shofech damim"—a metaphor for murder; the sages believed that touching a dying person in their final moments could hasten their death</note>.

## Chapter 24

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 24 Mishnah 1
->1<-

One for whom it became dark while on the way <note>meaning the Sabbath began while he was still traveling with his belongings</note>, gives his purse to a non-Jew.
And if there is no non-Jew with him, he places it on his donkey.
Once he reaches the outermost courtyard <note>the first safe enclosure of the town</note>,
he removes the vessels that may be handled on the **Sabbath**;
and as for those that may not be handled <note>items categorized as <term>muktzeh</term>: objects set aside or forbidden to be moved on the Sabbath, such as money or tools</note>,
he unties the ropes and the sacks fall of their own accord.

### Tractate Shabbat Chapter 24 Mishnah 2
->2<-

One may untie bundles of fodder <note>original: "amir"</note> before cattle,
and one may spread out small bundles of stalks <note>original: "kefim"</note>,
but one may not spread out the large cedar-grass bundles <note>original: "zirim"—these were considered too much labor to break apart on the Sabbath</note>.
One may not crush young grain <note>original: "shachat"</note>...

<summary>This page concludes the laws of honoring the dead on the Sabbath and begins the final chapter on how to handle money when the Sabbath begins during a journey and the permissible ways to feed livestock.</summary>
<keywords>burial laws, Sabbath, muktzeh, deathbed ethics, animal welfare, carrying on Sabbath</keywords>

--- Page 250 ---
<meta>Continuity: This page continues the final chapter of Tractate Shabbat (Chapter 24), shifting from the feeding and care of various animals to the laws of vows and ritual measurements on the Sabbath.</meta>

...and one may not [place] carobs before an animal, whether small <note>original: "dakkah"—referring to sheep or goats</note> or large <note>original: "gassah"—referring to cattle or camels</note>. **Rabbi Judah** permits carobs for small livestock <note>as their mouths are smaller and they chew carobs more easily, making it a natural way of feeding</note>.

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 24 Mishnah 3
### 3

One may not stuff a camel <note>original: "ovsim"—cramming food into the stomach</note>, nor may one force food down its throat <note>original: "dorsim"</note>, but one may hand-feed <note>original: "mal'itim"—placing food into the mouth to be swallowed voluntarily</note> it. One may not fatten calves <note>original: "ma'amirin"—a process of intensive force-feeding to enlarge the animal</note>, but one may hand-feed them. 

And one may toss food to chickens, and one may put water over bran <note>original: "mursan"—the outer husks of grain</note>, but one may not knead <note>original: "govlim"—the act of mixing a solid and liquid into a paste or dough, which is a forbidden labor on the Sabbath</note> it. 

And one may not put water before bees or before pigeons of a dovecote <note>because these animals are independent and can find their own water</note>, but one may put water before geese, chickens, and "Herodian" pigeons <note>original: "yonei dorsiyot"—domesticated pigeons that live in the house and are dependent on human care</note>.

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 24 Mishnah 4
### 4

One may cut up gourds before an animal, and a carcass before dogs. **Rabbi Judah** says: If it was not already a carcass from the eve of the **Sabbath**, it is forbidden <note>it is considered "muktzah" (set aside) and may not be moved</note>, because it was not among the things that were "prepared" <note>original: "mukan"—provisions ready for use before the holy day began</note>.

## Tractate Shabbat Chapter 24 Mishnah 5
### 5

One may nullify vows <note>original: "mefirim"—a husband or father’s legal right to cancel certain vows</note> on the **Sabbath**, and one may consult a sage <note>original: "nish'alim"—to ask for the release of a vow</note> regarding vows that are necessary for the **Sabbath**. 

One may plug a window <note>original: "maor"—literally a 'light-hole'</note>, and one may measure a piece of cloth or the volume of a ritual bath <note>original: "mikveh"—a pool used for immersion</note>. 

A story occurred in the days of **Rabbi Zadok’s** father and in the days of **Abba Shaul ben Botnit**, who plugged a window with a small jar <note>original: "tefiach"—an earthenware vessel</note> and tied a bowl <note>original: "mekedah"</note> with a reed <note>original: "gemi"</note> to see if there was an opening of a handbreadth <note>original: "tefach"—a standard unit of measurement</note> in the vat or not <note>they were checking to see if ritual impurity would pass from one area to another through an opening</note>. From their words, we learned that one may plug, measure, and tie on the **Sabbath**.

# Tractate Eruvin
<note>Tractate Eruvin ("Communal fusions") deals with the laws of Sabbath boundaries and how to create legal partitions to allow carrying objects between private and semi-public domains.</note>

## Chapter 1

### Tractate Eruvin Chapter 1 Mishnah 1

->1<-

An **alleyway** <note>original: "mavoi"—a street or alley into which several private courtyards open</note> that is higher than **twenty cubits** <note>approximately 30-40 feet; the height refers to the crossbeam placed at the entrance</note>, one must diminish it <note>lower the beam, as it is too high for the eye to notice it as a boundary</note>. 
**Rabbi Judah** says: It is not necessary. 
One that is wider than **ten cubits**, one must diminish it <note>narrow the entrance</note>. 
If it has the **shape of a doorway** <note>original: "tzurat hapetach"—consisting of two vertical side-posts and a horizontal lintel on top</note>, even though it is wider than ten cubits, it is not necessary to diminish it.

### Tractate Eruvin Chapter 1 Mishnah 2

->2<-

The **validation** <note>original: "hechsher"—the symbolic legal modification</note> of an alleyway <note>to permit carrying within it on the Sabbath</note>:
The **School of Shammai** say: It requires a **side-post** <note>original: "lechi"</note> and a **crossbeam** <note>original: "korah"</note>.
And the **School of Hillel** say: A **side-post** or a **crossbeam**.
**Rabbi Eliezer** says: Two **side-posts**.
In the name of **Rabbi Ishmael**, a certain student said before **Rabbi Akiva**: 
The School of Shammai and the School of Hillel did not disagree regarding an alleyway that is less than **four cubits** wide, that it requires [both] a **side-post** and a **crossbeam**; 
On what did they disagree? On [an alleyway] from **four cubits** up to **ten**, 
where the **School of Shammai** say: A **side-post** and a **crossbeam**;

<summary>This page marks the beginning of Tractate Eruvin, outlining the physical requirements for an alleyway's entrance to legally permit carrying objects within it on the Sabbath. It details disputes between the Schools of Hillel and Shammai regarding the necessary symbolic partitions, such as side-posts and crossbeams.</summary>

<keywords>Tractate Eruvin, alleyway, Sabbath carrying, cubits, side-post, crossbeam, School of Hillel, School of Shammai, Rabbi Judah, Rabbi Akiva</keywords>

And the **School of Hillel** say:
Either a **side-post** <note>original: "lechi"—a vertical post at the entrance of an alleyway</note> or a **crossbeam** <note>original: "korah"—a horizontal beam across the top of the entrance</note>.
**Rabbi Akiva** said:
Regarding both this and that they disagreed <note>Akiva clarifies that the dispute between the schools applies to both the width of the alley and the type of markers required</note>.

### Tractate Eruvin Chapter 1 Mishnah 3
### 3

The **crossbeam** which they spoke of
must be wide enough to support a **half-brick** <note>original: "ariach"</note>,
and a half-brick is half of a large brick of **three handbreadths** <note>original: "tefachim"; a handbreadth is a standard Talmudic unit of measure, approximately 3 to 4 inches</note>.
It is sufficient for the crossbeam to be **one handbreadth** wide,
so that it can support the half-brick lengthwise.

---

### Tractate Eruvin Chapter 1 Mishnah 4
### 4

It must be wide enough to support a half-brick,
and **strong** enough to support a half-brick. <insert>And strong</insert> <note>original: "u-virya"; a manuscript insertion emphasizing the requirement of physical stability</note>
**Rabbi Judah** says:
It must be wide enough, even if it is not strong enough <note>Judah argues that since the beam is a symbolic legal marker rather than a functional structural element, it does not actually need to be capable of supporting a heavy brick</note>.

---

### Tractate Eruvin Chapter 1 Mishnah 5
### 5

If the beam was made of **straw** or of **reeds**,
we view it as if it were made of **metal**;
if it was **curved**,
we view it as if it were **straight**;
if it was **round**,
we view it as if it were **square**.
Any round object that has a **circumference** of **three handbreadths**
has a **width** <note>diameter</note> of one handbreadth <note>The Mishnah uses the mathematical approximation that the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter is 3:1</note>.

The **side-posts** which they spoke of
must have a height of **ten handbreadths**,
but their width and thickness may be any amount.
**Rabbi Yose** says:
Their width must be **three handbreadths**.

### 6

One may make side-posts from **anything**...

...even with something that has a **living spirit** <note>original: "ruach chayim"; referring here to using a living animal as a side-post or part of a partition</note>.
**Rabbi Yose** declares it susceptible to ritual impurity as a **tomb cover** <note>original: "golel"; the stone or object used to seal a grave, which can contract impurity</note>,

### Tractate Eruvin Chapter 1 Mishnah 8
7

A **caravan** <note>original: "shayyara"</note> that camped in a **valley** <note>original: "bik'ah"; an open area where carrying would usually be forbidden on the Sabbath</note>,
and they surrounded it with **animal equipment** <note>original: "kelei behemah"; such as saddles, packs, or harnesses to create a perimeter</note>,
they may **carry within it**,
provided that the **partition** <note>original: "gader"</note> is **ten handbreadths** high <note>original: "tefachim"; a handbreadth is approximately 3 to 4 inches, making the required height about 30–40 inches</note>,
and that the **gaps** are not greater than the **built-up** parts.
Any gap that is up to **ten cubits** <note>original: "amot"; a cubit is approximately 18 inches</note>
is **permitted**, because it is considered an **entrance**;
but more than this is **forbidden**.

### Tractate Eruvin Chapter 1 Mishnah 9
8

One may surround the area with **three ropes**,
one above the other, and one above the other,
provided that there is not a space of **three handbreadths** between one rope and another <note>This relies on the legal principle of "lavud," where small gaps are viewed as if they are filled/closed</note>.
The measurement of the **thickness** of the ropes must be more than **one handbreadth** [collectively],
so that the total height is **ten handbreadths**.

### Tractate Eruvin Chapter 1 Mishnah 10
9

One may surround the area with **reeds**,
provided that there is not a space of **three handbreadths** between one reed and another.
"They spoke of these rules [specifically] regarding a **caravan**,"
these are the words of **Rabbi Judah**.
But the **Sages** say:
They did not speak of a caravan except as a **common example** <note>original: "ba-hoveh"; meaning the law applies to any group, but caravans were the most frequent case</note>.
Any partition that does not have both **warp and woof** <note>original: "sheti ve-erev"; weaving terms referring to vertical and horizontal components</note>
is not a valid partition.
These are the words of **Rabbi Yose** son of Rabbi <insert>Judah</insert> <note>original: "Yudah"</note>.
But the **Sages** say:
**One of the two things** is sufficient <note>The Sages argue that a partition needs only vertical OR horizontal elements, not necessarily both</note>.
**Four things** were exempted [from certain restrictions] in a **military camp**:
They may bring **wood** from anywhere <note>Soldiers in a camp were permitted to take wood for their needs without worrying about the laws of theft/property in the same way civilians would be</note>,

It highlights disputes between Rabbi Judah and the Sages over whether these leniencies apply only to traveling caravans or to any group.</summary>

# Chapter 2

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 2 Mishnah 1
**1**
One may construct **enclosures** <note>original: "passim"; literally 'strips' or 'slats' of wood used to create a symbolic partition</note> for **public wells** <note>original: "beirayot"</note> to allow for watering animals on the Sabbath:
**four corner-posts** <note>original: "dyomdin"; L-shaped brackets placed at the four corners of a square area</note> which appear like **eight** <note>since each L-shaped post has two visible faces</note>,
according to the words of **Rabbi Akiva**.
**Rabbi Meir** says:
**Eight** posts are required which appear like **twelve**;
namely, **four corner-posts** and **four flat-posts** <note>original: "peshutin"; single-faced boards placed between the corner posts</note>.
Their height must be **ten handbreadths** <note>original: "tefachim"; approximately 30–40 inches</note>,
their width **six handbreadths**,
and their thickness may be **any amount**;
and the space between them may be as much as the width of **two teams**
of **three oxen** each <note>referring to a team of oxen yoked together for plowing</note>,
according to the words of **Rabbi Meir**.
**Rabbi Judah** says:
Each team may consist of **four oxen**;
they must be **tied together** and not **loose**,
one team **entering** and one **exiting**.

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 2 Mishnah 2
**2**
It is permitted to bring the partition **close to the well**,
provided that when a **cow** drinks, 
its **head and the majority of its body** are within the enclosure.
It is also permitted to **distance** the partition any amount,
provided that one **increases the number of posts** <note>as the distance grows, the gaps become larger, requiring more boards to maintain the legal integrity of the partition</note>.

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 2 Mishnah 3
**3**
**Rabbi Judah** says:
The area may only be up to the size of **two seahs** <note>original: "beit satayim"; an area of approximately 5,000 square cubits, the size of the Tabernacle's courtyard</note>.
They <note>the other Sages</note> said to him:

<meta>Continuity: This page continues from the previous discussion on conditional eruvs—meals placed to establish a Sabbath residence—specifically addressing situations where there is doubt about which day is the true holiday or which direction a person might need to travel.</meta>

->9<-
The Sages say: One establishes an **eruv** <note>original: "eruv"; a meal placed before the Sabbath or a holiday to establish a legal residence, allowing a person to walk an additional 2,000 cubits beyond that point</note> for a single direction, or one does not establish an eruv at all; or one establishes an eruv for two days, or one does not establish an eruv at all. 

How should he act? He takes the meal there on the first day, waits until nightfall <note>at which point the "residence" is legally established for the first day</note>, then takes it and returns home; on the second day, he waits until nightfall, then eats the meal and returns home. Thus, he benefits from his travel <note>his boundary is extended</note> and he benefits from his eruv meal. If the meal was eaten on the first day, it serves as a valid eruv for the first day, but it is not a valid eruv for the second day.

Rabbi Eliezer said to them: Do you not agree with me that these are **two distinct sanctities**? <note>original: "shtei kedushot"; a legal debate over whether two consecutive days of a holiday are treated as one long block of holiness or two separate independent units</note>

# Chapter 4

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 4 Mishnah 1
### 1
One who was taken out <note>beyond the **Sabbath boundary**; the 2,000-cubit limit one is permitted to walk outside their city on the Sabbath</note> by gentiles or by an **evil spirit** <note>original: "ruach ra'ah"; this refers to a state of temporary insanity or being forcibly moved by an external spiritual force</note>, has only **four cubits** <note>original: "arba amot"; approximately 6 to 8 feet, representing a person's immediate personal space</note> in which he may move.
If they returned him, it is as if he never left.
If they took him to another city, or placed him in a **sheepfold** or a **cattle-pen** <note>original: "dir" and "sahar"; enclosed areas for livestock</note>:
**Rabban Gamliel** and **Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah** say: He may walk throughout the entire area <note>because an enclosed space is legally considered as being within one's four cubits</note>.
**Rabbi Yehoshua** and **Rabbi Akiva** say: He has only four cubits.
An incident occurred where they were coming from **Plandrisim** <note>likely a port city, possibly Brindisi</note>, and their ship set sail into the sea.
Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah walked throughout the entire ship;
but Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva did not move beyond four cubits, because they wished to be **stringent** upon themselves.

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 4 Mishnah 2
### 2
On another occasion, they did not enter the **harbor** <note>original: "lamen," from the Greek "limēn"</note> until it had become dark <note>meaning the Sabbath had already begun while they were still at sea</note>.
They said to Rabban Gamliel:
"What is the rule for us to descend?" <note>they were unsure if they had been within the Sabbath boundary of the port when the sun set</note>
He said to them:
"It is permitted, for I was already watching, and we were within the **boundary** <note>original: "techum"; the legal limit</note> before it became dark."

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 4 Mishnah 3
### 3
One who went out **with permission** <note>original: "bi-reshut"; meaning for a legally sanctioned or mandatory reason, such as a medical emergency, to testify about the new moon, or to save a life</note>, and they said to him:
"The deed has already been performed,"
He has **two thousand cubits** in every direction from where he stands.
If he was within the boundary <note>of his home city</note>, it is as if he never left;
for all who go out to **rescue** <note>lives or property from immediate danger</note> are permitted to return to their original place.

# Chapter 5

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 5 Mishnah 1

1
How do we **extend the boundaries** <note>original: "me'abrin"; literally "to make the city pregnant" by adding outskirts to its legal definition</note> of towns?
If a house recedes or a house protrudes; if a ruin recedes or a ruin protrudes;
if there were ruins ten **handbreadths** <note>original: "tefahim"; a standard unit of measure</note> high,
or bridges or monuments that contain a dwelling place—
we extend the measurement relative to them.
One makes the city like a **square tablet**,
so that one may benefit from the **corners**. <note>By squaring the city's boundaries rather than following its irregular shape, the 2,000-cubit limit is measured from the flat edge of the square, granting extra distance in the diagonal directions.</note>

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 5 Mishnah 2

2

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 5 Mishnah 3

### 3

And so it is with **three villages** arranged in a triangle: 
if there is a distance of **one hundred and forty-one and a third [cubits]** <note>original: "me'ah ve-arba'im ve-ahat u-shlish"; this specific number is the calculated diagonal of a square with sides of 100 cubits. ## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 5 Mishnah 4

### 4

They do not measure [the boundary] except with a **rope of fifty cubits**, 
neither shorter nor longer. 
And one should only measure [with the rope held] **at the level of his heart**. 
If he was measuring and reached a **valley** or a **collapsed wall**, 
he "swallows" it <note>original: "mavlivo"; a surveying technique where the rope is stretched horizontally across a gap rather than following the contour of the ground</note> and then returns to his measurement. 
If he reached a **mountain**, he "swallows" it and returns to his measurement, 
provided that he does not go beyond the **Sabbath boundary**. 
If he is unable to "swallow" it <note>because the gap is wider than the 50-cubit rope</note>, 
concerning this **Rabbi Dostai bar Yannai** said in the name of **Rabbi Meir**: 
> "I have heard that they **pierce through mountains**." <note>original: "mekadedim"; a method of measuring a steep incline by using shorter, vertical and horizontal "steps" with a smaller rope to determine the horizontal distance.</note>

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 5 Mishnah 5

### 5

They only measure [the boundary] based on the word of an **expert**. 
If one [expert] increased the distance in one place and another [expert] decreased it in another place, 
we listen to the place where he **increased** it. 
If one increased and another decreased for the same spot, 
we listen to the **larger** measurement. 
Even a **slave**, or even a **maidservant**, are trusted to say: 
> "The **Sabbath boundary** extends until here," 
for the Sages did not speak on this matter to be restrictive, 
but rather to be **lenient**. <note>Because the 2,000-cubit boundary is a Rabbinic law rather than a Torah law, the rules of evidence are relaxed to allow people more freedom of movement.</note>

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 5 Mishnah 6

### 6

A **private town** <note>original: "ir shel yahid"; a town owned by one person or a single entity</note> that became a **public town** <note>populated by many different residents</note>, 
one may create a single **eruv** for all of it. 
But a **public town** that became a **private town**, 
one does not create a single **eruv** for all of it; 
unless one leaves out an area [from the eruv] like a **"New City" in Judea**, 
which contains **fifty residents**. <note>original: "diyurim"; this refers to leaving a section of the town outside the communal merging of domains to serve as a reminder that the town's legal status has changed.</note>

### Tractate Eruvin Chapter 5 Mishnah 7
->ז<-

One who was in the **east** [at the start of the Sabbath], and told his son to establish an **eruv** <note>original: "le'arev"; to place a food deposit that legally shifts one's center of residence for the Sabbath</note> for him in the **west**; or [one who was] in the **west**, and told his son to establish an eruv for him in the **east**;
If there are **two thousand cubits** <note>The maximum distance one is permitted to walk outside a settlement on the Sabbath.</note> from his current location to his **home**, but to his **eruv** it is further than that,
he is **permitted** to return to his **home** but **forbidden** from using his **eruv** <note>Because he could not have physically reached the eruv at the moment the Sabbath began, the eruv is invalid for him.</note>.
If it is **two thousand cubits** to his **eruv**, but to his **home** it is further than that,
he is **permitted** to use his **eruv** but **forbidden** from returning to his **home**.
One who places his eruv in the **outskirts of the city** <note>original: "ibura shel ir"; the 70-cubit extension area added to a city's legal boundary</note> has accomplished **nothing** <note>Because any resident of the city already has the right to walk through the entire city and its outskirts as if they were four cubits; the eruv does not extend his range further than if he had done nothing.</note>.
If he placed it **outside the boundary**, what he **gains** [in one direction] he **loses** [in the other] <note>By moving his 2,000-cubit radius forward, he loses the equivalent distance from the area behind him.</note>.

### Tractate Eruvin Chapter 5 Mishnah 8

The residents of a **large city** may walk through the entirety of a **small city** [if it falls within their boundary],

may walk through the **entirety** of that city and **two thousand cubits** beyond its limits.
**Rabbi Akiva** says:
He only has **two thousand cubits** from the specific **place of his eruv**.

### Tractate Eruvin Chapter 5 Mishnah 9

It turns out that it is more lenient [to have the eruv] **inside it** than **on top of it** <insert>on its back</insert> <note>original: "gavah/gavo"; the roof or upper surface. even if the end of his measurement finishes in the **cave**.
