# Chapter 6

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 6 Mishnah 1
### 1
One who dwells with a **gentile** <note>original: "nochri"; a non-Jew whose presence in a shared courtyard complicates the legal "merging" of domains</note> in a courtyard,
or with one who **does not acknowledge the eruv** <note>original: "mi she-eino modeh ba-eruv"; referring to a Sadducee or someone who rejects the Rabbinic oral law regarding the merging of domains</note>,
this person **prohibits** him <note>The resident is forbidden from carrying objects from his private home into the shared courtyard because the non-participant has not joined the legal merger</note>.
[These are] the words of **Rabbi Meir**.
**Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov** says:
He **never prohibits** [the resident],
until there are **two Israelites** [living there] who prohibit one another <note>Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that a single Jew living with a non-Jew is not restricted; the prohibition only applies if there are at least two Jews who would otherwise need an eruv between themselves</note>.

---

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 6 Mishnah 2
### 2
**Rabban Gamliel** said:
It happened that a **Sadducee** <note>A member of a Jewish sect that followed a literal interpretation of the written Torah and rejected many Rabbinic traditions, including the eruv</note> dwelt with us in an **alleyway** <note>original: "mavoi"; a shared path or alley that connects multiple courtyards to the public street</note> in **Jerusalem**,
and **Father** <note>Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel</note> said to us:
"Hurry and bring out all the **vessels** <note>utensils or portable objects</note> into the **alleyway**,
before he brings [his] out and **prohibits** you" <note>By placing their items in the shared space first, they established their legal possession of the area for the Sabbath before the non-believing neighbor could assert his rights and block them</note>.
**Rabbi Yehuda** says it in a different language:
"Hurry and perform all your **needs** in the **alleyway**,
before he brings [his] out and **prohibits** you."

---

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 6 Mishnah 3
### 3
Residents of a **courtyard** where one of them **forgot** and did **not join the eruv**,
his **house** is **forbidden** for [him] to bring items in or take items out, both for him and for them,
but **their [houses]** are **permitted** both for him and for them <note>Since the other neighbors merged their domains, their homes are considered a single unit, but the neighbor who forgot is excluded and his home remains a separate, private domain</note>.
If they **granted him their rights** <note>original: "natnu lo reshutam"; a legal procedure where residents renounced their share of the shared courtyard to a single individual</note>, he is **permitted** and they are **forbidden**;
If there were **two** [who forgot to join the eruv], they **prohibit one another**,
for **one** person can give rights and take rights,
but **two** people can give rights but cannot take rights <note>A single person can be the sole legal "owner" of the courtyard for the Sabbath, but two people cannot both be the sole owner simultaneously</note>.

---

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 6 Mishnah 4

From what time may they **grant rights**?
**Beit Shammai** <note>The School of Shammai</note> say: While it is still **day** [on Friday].
And **Beit Hillel** <note>The School of Hillel</note> say: From the time it gets **dark** [on the Sabbath].
One who **granted rights** and then **brought [vessels] out**, whether **unintentionally** or **intentionally**...

[If the opening is] **less than four [handbreadths] by four** <note>original: "arba'ah al arba'ah." A handbreadth (tefach) is roughly 3–4 inches. This size is the minimum for a "significant" opening.</note> or **higher than ten** [handbreadths from the ground],

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 7 Mishnah 2

### 2
A **wall between two courtyards** that is **ten [handbreadths] high** and **four [handbreadths] wide**,
they **make two eruvs** and **cannot make one**.
If there were **fruit on top of it**,
**these [residents] may go up** from here and eat,
and **those [residents] may go up** from here and eat,
provided that they **do not bring [the fruit] down**. <insert>from below</insert> <note>original: "mil-matan." If the **wall was breached** up to **ten cubits** <note>A cubit (amah) is approximately 18 inches. A breach of this size is legally considered a "doorway."</note>, they **may make two eruvs**;
if they wish, they **may make one**, because it is **like a doorway**.
**More than this**, they **must make one eruv** and **cannot make two**. <note>A breach larger than ten cubits is considered a complete collapse of the wall, merging the two spaces into one by default.</note>

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 7 Mishnah 3

### 3
A **trench between two courtyards** that is **ten [handbreadths] deep** and **four [handbreadths] wide**,
they **make two eruvs** and **cannot make one**,
even if it is **filled with straw or stubble**; <note>Since straw is intended for animal feed, it is considered temporary and does not "fill" the trench in a legal sense.</note>
[But if it is] **filled with dirt or pebbles**,
they **make one eruv** and **cannot make two**. <note>Earth and stones are permanent; they legally nullify the trench, removing the barrier between the courtyards.</note>

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 7 Mishnah 6

->How do we join in a partnership for an alleyway?<- <note>original: "shittuf," a specific type of legal merger for an alleyway (mavo), distinct from the eruv used for courtyards.</note>
->One places a jar and says:<-
->"Behold, this is for all the residents of the alleyway."<-
->He may transfer ownership to them through his adult son or daughter,<-
->or through his Hebrew male or female servant,<-
->or through his wife.<-
->But he may not transfer ownership through his minor son or daughter,<-
->nor through his Canaanite male or female servant,<-
->because their hand is as his hand.<- <note>In ancient legal tradition, minor children and certain servants were considered legally part of the householder’s domain. To "transfer ownership" to the neighbors, the food must be held by someone legally independent of the donor.</note>

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 7 Mishnah 7

->7<-
->If the food has diminished [below the legal limit],<-
->one adds to it and transfers ownership, and he does not need to inform [the residents].<-
->If new residents were added to the alleyway,<-
->he adds food and transfers ownership, and he must inform them.<- <note>Existing residents are presumed to want the partnership to continue, but new residents must be made aware of the arrangement for it to be legally binding for them.</note>

->How much is its required measure?<-
->When the residents are many,<-
->food for two meals for everyone.<- <note>This serves as the collective minimum for the entire community.</note>
->When they are few,<-
->the size of a dried fig<- <term>grogeret: a dried fig, a standard Talmudic unit of volume equivalent to about one-third of an egg.</term>
->for the purpose of carrying on Shabbat for each and every person.<-

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 7 Mishnah 10

A loaf <note>original: "kikar"</note> of bread is the proper eruv.

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 7 Mishnah 11

A person may give a *ma’ah* <note>A small silver coin.</note> to a shopkeeper or to a baker 
so that the merchant might acquire a share in the eruv on his behalf.
These are the words of **Rabbi Eliezer**.
But the **Sages** say:
His coins did not acquire the share for him. <note>The Sages argue that a simple monetary transaction with a professional provider is insufficient to transfer ownership for the specific religious purpose of an eruv without further formal action.</note>
However, the Sages agree in the case of any other [private] person, that the coins do acquire a share for him, 
for an eruv may only be established for a person with their knowledge and consent.
**Rabbi Judah** said:
To what circumstances does this apply? To the **eruv of boundaries**; <note>original: "eruvei techumim." This eruv allows a person to walk an extra 2,000 cubits in one direction but restricts them in the opposite direction, therefore requiring their explicit consent.</note>
But for the **eruv of courtyards**, <note>original: "eruvei chatzerot." This eruv only provides the benefit of carrying objects on the Sabbath.</note>
one may establish the eruv whether with the person's knowledge or without it; 
because one may act to a person's benefit in their absence, but one may not act to their disadvantage.

# Chapter 8

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 8 Mishnah 1

### 1

How do we join in a partnership for the boundaries? <note>original: "techumim." This refers to the "shittuf," a communal food deposit that extends the distance one can walk outside the city on the Sabbath.</note>
One places a jar [of food] and says:
"Behold, this is for all my fellow townspeople, 
for anyone who needs to go to a house of mourning or a house of feasting." <note>This creates a "reserved" eruv for anyone in the community who might have a religious or communal obligation to travel beyond the standard limits.</note>
Anyone who accepted the arrangement upon themselves while it was still day [before the Sabbath begins] is permitted to use it.
But if they only accepted it after dark, it is forbidden; 
for one may not establish an eruv once the sun has set.

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 8 Mishnah 2

How much is its required measure?
Food for **two meals** for each and every person.

...food enough for a weekday, but not for the Sabbath. <note>The quantity needed for a weekday meal is generally smaller than the more substantial meals eaten on the Sabbath.</note>

Food enough for the Sabbath, but not for a weekday.

**Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka** says:
The amount is calculated from a loaf <note>original: "kikar"</note> worth a *pundiyon* <note>A small Roman copper coin.</note> when four *seahs* <note>A unit of volume, roughly 7 liters.</note> of grain sell for a *sela* <note>A silver coin equal to 48 pundiyons.</note>.

### Tractate Eruvin Chapter 8 Mishnah 3
### 3

Residents of a courtyard who forgot and did not establish an eruv <note>A legal partnership that merges private domains into one shared space for the purpose of carrying objects on the Sabbath.</note>:
Anything higher than ten handbreadths <note>original: "tefachim." A handbreadth is approximately 3 to 4 inches.</note> belongs to the balcony, 
but anything lower than this belongs to the courtyard.
The rim of a pit or a rock
that are ten handbreadths high belong to the balcony,
but if they are lower than this, they belong to the courtyard.
To what circumstances does this apply? To a structure that is nearby.
But if it is distant,
even if it is ten handbreadths high, it belongs to the courtyard.
What is considered "nearby"?
Anything that is not further than four handbreadths.

### Tractate Eruvin Chapter 8 Mishnah 4
### 4

One who places his eruv in a gatehouse, 
a portico, or a balcony—it is not a valid eruv, 
and one who lives there does not restrict the other residents; <note>Because these areas are not considered proper "dwellings," placing the food there doesn't work, but conversely, someone living there doesn't have enough "ownership" to prevent others from carrying if they fail to join the eruv.</note>
But if it is placed in a granary <note>literally "house of straw"</note>, a cattle-shed,
a woodshed, or a storehouse,
then it is a valid eruv, and one who lives there restricts the others. 
**Rabbi Judah** says:
If the homeowner maintains a right of storage there, 
the resident does not restrict the others. <note>Rabbi Judah argues that if the main owner still uses the room for storage, the person living there is considered a guest rather than a permanent resident with legal power to block the eruv.</note>

# Tractate Eruvin Chapter 9 Mishnah 2

### 3
->A large roof [that is] adjacent to a small [roof],<-
->the large one is permitted, and the small one is forbidden.<- <note>This refers to the "rule of the majority": since the large roof "overlooks" the small one, the small one is seen as an extension of the large one's space, creating a legal imbalance.</note>
->A large courtyard that was breached into a small [one],<-
->the large one is permitted, and the small one is forbidden,<-
->because it is like the entrance of the large [one].<- <note>The breach is small relative to the large courtyard (making it look like a doorway), but it is wide relative to the small courtyard (making it look like a missing wall).</note>

### 4
->A courtyard that was breached into the public domain,<-
->one who carries [an object] from within it into a private domain,<-
->or from a private domain into it, is liable.<- <note>Because the breach into the street makes the courtyard legally resemble a public space, carrying into a private home is considered a violation of the Sabbath.</note>
->[These are] the words of Rabbi Meir.<-
->And the Sages say:<-
->[Carrying] from within it to the public domain,<-
->[or] into it, one is exempt,<-
->because it is like a semi-public area.<- <term>semi-public area: "karmelit", a domain that is neither fully private nor fully public; while carrying there is forbidden by Rabbinic law, it does not carry the biblical penalty (liability) of a sin offering.</term>

### Tractate Eruvin Chapter 10 Mishnah 3
->3<-

A tree that spreads over the ground,
if its foliage is not higher than three handbreadths from the ground,
one may carry [objects] beneath it. <term>handbreadth: "tefach," a unit of measurement approx. 3-4 inches. Anything less than three handbreadths is legally considered "attached" to the ground (lavud).</term>
[If] its roots are higher than three handbreadths from the ground,
one may not sit upon them. <note>Sitting on roots that high is considered "using a tree," which is Rabbinically prohibited on the Sabbath to prevent one from accidentally breaking a branch.</note>
A door in a backyard,
or thorns in a breach [in a wall], or a mat—
one may not lock [or close] with them,
unless they are raised from the ground. <note>If they drag on the ground, closing them might look like building or leveling the earth; if they are suspended, they are clearly just "doors."</note>

### Tractate Eruvin Chapter 10 Mishnah 9

->9<-
A person should not stand in a private domain,
and open [a lock] in the public domain,
or [stand] in the public domain, and open [a lock] in the private domain,
unless they have made for him a partition ten handbreadths high.
These are the words of Rabbi Meir. <note>Rabbi Meir is concerned that while turning the key in the lock, the person might accidentally pull the key from one domain into the other.</note>
They said to him:
[There was] an incident in the Market of the Fatteners <note>original: "shook shel ha-pattamim," where livestock were fattened for sale.</note> that was in Jerusalem,
where they would lock [their shops],
and place the key in the window above the doorway. <note>The Sages argue that this was common practice in Jerusalem, proving that such a concern does not prohibit the action.</note>

### Tractate Eruvin Chapter 10 Mishnah 11

A bolt that is laid aside <note>original: "ha-munach" — one that is completely detached and resting on the ground</note> is forbidden both here and there.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
The one laid aside is permitted in the Temple, and the dragging one is permitted in the province.

The upper [hinge is permitted] in the Temple, and the lower [hinge] in the province. <note>Fixing a door hinge normally constitutes "building" or "repairing," which is forbidden on the Sabbath. ## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 10 Mishnah 14

14
A priest who suffered a wound on his finger may wrap it with reed-grass <term>gemi: a type of soft, flexible marsh plant</term> in the Temple,
but not in the province;
If the intent is to extract blood, it is forbidden in both places. <note>Wrapping the wound is permitted in the Temple to allow the priest to continue his service, but doing so in a way that intentionally draws blood would violate the Sabbath labor of "wounding."</note>

## Tractate Eruvin Chapter 10 Mishnah 15

16
If a creeping animal <term>sheretz: one of eight specific small animals whose carcasses convey ritual impurity, such as a mouse or lizard</term> is found in the Temple,
a priest removes it with his belt <term>hemyano: the long, embroidered sash that was part of the priestly vestments</term>,
so as not to allow the impurity to remain [in the holy space].
These are the words of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka.
But Rabbi Yehuda says:
It is removed with wooden tongs,
so as not to increase the impurity. <note>Rabbi Yehuda argues that by using his belt, the priest makes his own clothing impure; using wooden tongs, which are less susceptible to impurity, prevents the spread of ritual "uncleanness."</note>

17
From where exactly do they remove it?
From the Sanctuary <term>Heikhal</term> and from the Entrance Hall <term>Ulam</term>, and from the area between the Entrance Hall and the Altar.
These are the words of Rabbi Shimon ben Nanas.
Rabbi Akiva says:
In any place where the intentional violation [of entering while impure] would incur excision <term>karet: a severe spiritual penalty of being "cut off" from the community</term> and accidental violation requires a sin offering,
from there they must remove it immediately;
but in all other places, they simply cover it with a copper vessel <term>psakter: a large brass pot or basin</term> until the Sabbath ends.
Rabbi Shimon says:
In any place where the Sages have permitted something to you,
they have only given you what was already yours,
for they only permitted things that were restricted by Rabbinic decree <term>shevut: Sabbath rest mandated by the Sages rather than by biblical law</term>.

->Eruvin is completed<-

# Tractate Pesachim

## Chapter 1

### Tractate Pesachim Chapter 1 Mishnah 1
#### 1
On the evening <note>original: "Or" - literally "light," but used idiomatically here to mean the night preceding the day</note> of the fourteenth [of the month of Nisan], 
one searches for the **leaven** <term>chametz: any food product made from grain and water that has fermented and risen, which is forbidden on Passover</term> by the light of a candle. 
Any place into which leaven is not typically brought 
does not require **searching** <term>bedikah: the ritual inspection of the home to ensure no leaven remains</term>. 
And why did [the Sages] say "two rows in the wine cellar"? 
In a place where one might bring leaven <note>referring to a cellar where a waiter might bring bread while fetching wine</note>. 
**The House of Shammai** say: 
[The search must include] two rows across the entire surface of the cellar; 
but **The House of Hillel** say: 
The two outermost rows, which are the uppermost ones.

### Tractate Pesachim Chapter 1 Mishnah 2
#### 2
We do not fear that perhaps a marten <note>original: "chuldah" - a weasel or similar small land animal</note> has dragged [leaven] 
from house to house or from place to place. 
If [we were to worry about] such things, [one would have to fear leaven was carried] from courtyard to courtyard or from city to city, 
and there would be no end to the matter.

### Tractate Pesachim Chapter 1 Mishnah 3
#### 3
**Rabbi Yehuda** says: 
One searches on the evening of the fourteenth, 
and on the fourteenth in the morning, and at the time of **removal** <term>biur: the final destruction or nullification of leaven before the forbidden period begins</term>; 
but **the Sages** say: 
If one did not search on the evening of the fourteenth, 
he should search on the fourteenth [during the day]; 
if he did not search on the fourteenth, 
he should search during the **Festival** <note>the intermediate days of Passover</note>; 
if he did not search during the Festival, 
he should search after the Festival <note>to ensure he does not benefit from leaven that was "owned" during the holiday, which remains forbidden by Rabbinic law</note>. 
And whatever [leaven] he leaves over [for his final meal], he should put in a hidden place,

## **Tractate Pesachim Chapter 1 Mishnah 4**
### **4**
**Rabbi Meir says:**
One may eat [leaven] all five [hours],
and one must burn it at the beginning of the sixth [hour].
<note>The hours mentioned here are "proportional hours," calculated by dividing the daylight into twelve parts. The "sixth hour" refers to midday.</note>
**Rabbi Yehuda says:**
One may eat all four [hours],
one "suspends" <note>original: "tolim" - meaning to keep the leaven in a state of limbo, neither eating it nor destroying it yet</note> during the fifth [hour],

## **Tractate Pesachim Chapter 1 Mishnah 5**
### **5**
**And Rabbi Yehuda further said:**
Two loaves of the **thanksgiving-offering** <term>todah: a sacrifice offered in gratitude to God, which included forty loaves of bread</term> that were disqualified <insert>of the thanksgiving-offering</insert>
were placed on the roof of the colonnade <note>original: "istaba" - a portico or covered walkway in the Temple courtyard</note>.
As long as they were placed there, all the people would eat [their leaven].
When one of them was removed,
they would "suspend"—neither eating nor burning.
When both of them were removed,
all the people began to burn [their leaven].

### **6**
**Rabban Gamliel says:**
**Ordinary food** <term>chullin: non-sacred food for everyday use</term> may be eaten all four [hours],
and **priestly dues** <term>terumah: the portion of the harvest given to the priests, which has a higher level of sanctity</term> may be eaten all five,
and one must burn [everything] at the beginning of the sixth.

## **Tractate Pesachim Chapter 1 Mishnah 6**
### **7**
**Rabbi Hananya, the Deputy High Priest, says:**
In all the days of the priests,
they never refrained from burning meat that had been made impure by a **derivative of impurity** <term>vlad ha-tumah: a secondary level of ritual impurity</term>
together with meat that had been made impure by a **primary source of impurity** <term>av ha-tumah: a "father" or high-level source of ritual impurity</term>,
even though they are adding impurity to its [existing] impurity.
<note>This refers to the general rule that one should not intentionally make something impure. However, since the meat is already disqualified and being burned, the Sages allowed burning different levels of impurity together.</note>

In all the days of the priests,
they never refrained from lighting oil that was disqualified by a **one who immersed that day** <term>tevul yom: a person who has purified themselves in a ritual bath but must wait until sunset for the process to be complete</term>,

### Tractate Pesachim Chapter 2 Mishnah 1
->1<-

Throughout the time that it is permitted to eat [leaven],
one may feed it to domesticated animals, to wild animals, and to birds,

<note> "Benefit" includes any use that provides value, such as selling it or using it for fuel.</note>
Once its time has passed, its benefit is forbidden.
One may not fuel an oven or a stove with it.

There is no [proper] removal of **leaven** <term>chametz: leavened grain products forbidden on Passover</term> except through burning;

### Tractate Pesachim Chapter 2 Mishnah 3 (3)

->A non-Jew who lent money to a Jew against his leaven [as collateral], after Passover,<-

->it is forbidden for benefit.<-
<note>The law distinguishes based on ownership. If a Jew effectively owned the leaven during the holiday, it is forbidden for use or sale forever after.</note>
->Leaven upon which a collapse occurred [and was buried],<-

<note>If a building collapses and buries leaven under three handbreadths (about 9-10 inches) of rubble, it is considered legally non-existent because a dog cannot sniff it out.</note>

## Tractate Pesachim Chapter 2 Mishnah 7
->6<-
One may not soak bran for chickens,
but one may scald it. <note>Scalding with boiling water (chalitah) was thought to cook the grain instantly, preventing it from fermenting into leaven, whereas soaking in cool water triggers the leavening process.</note>
A woman may not soak bran to carry in her hand to the bathhouse, <note>Bran was used as a cosmetic or skin scrub.</note>
but she may rub it on her skin dry.
A person may not chew wheat and place it on his wound,
because they leaven. <note>The moisture from saliva combined with the wheat creates leaven (chametz), which is forbidden to possess or benefit from during the holiday.</note>

## Tractate Pesachim Chapter 2 Mishnah 8
->7<-
One may not put flour into **charoset**
or into mustard. <note>Charoset is the fruit-and-nut paste used at the Seder. Mustard and charoset were often made with acidic liquids like vinegar; adding flour to these was thought to cause rapid fermentation.</note>
If one did put it in, he must eat it immediately;
Rabbi Meir forbids it. <note>Rabbi Meir is more stringent, concerned that fermentation happens too quickly to be safe.</note>
One may not cook the Paschal lamb
in liquids or in fruit juices;
but one may baste it or dip it in them. <note>The Torah (Exodus 12:9) explicitly requires the Paschal lamb to be "roasted over fire" and forbids it being "boiled in water."</note>
The water used by a baker must be poured out,
because it leavens. <note>Water used by a baker to cool his hands or rinse vessels becomes cloudy with flour residue and will ferment quickly.</note>

# Chapter 3

## Tractate Pesachim Chapter 3 Mishnah 1
->1<-
And these [items] cause one to transgress on Passover: <note>Meaning, possessing these items during the holiday violates the prohibition against owning leaven.</note>

**Median beer**, <term>Median beer: a grain-based alcoholic drink from the region of Media</term>
**Edomite vinegar**, <term>Edomite vinegar: vinegar made by adding barley to wine to speed fermentation</term>
**Egyptian zithum**, <term>Egyptian zithum: a medicinal drink or beer made from barley, saffron, and salt</term>
**Dyers’ bran-water**, <note>A fermented mixture used by craftsmen to treat hides or set dyes.</note>
**Cooks' starch**, <note>A flour-based paste used to skim the top of cooking pots.</note>
**and Scribes' paste**. <note>A flour-based glue used for binding or repairing documents.</note>
Rabbi Eliezer says:
Even women’s cosmetics. <note>Referring to grain-based pastes used as hair removers or skin treatments.</note>
This is the general rule:
Anything made from a species of grain causes one to transgress on Passover. <note>The "species of grain" refers to the five primary grains: wheat, barley, spelt, rye, and oats.</note>

### Tractate Pesachim Chapter 3 Mishnah 2
### 2

Dough that is in the cracks of a kneading bowl:
if there is a quantity the size of an olive <note>original: "kazayit". This is the standard legal minimum for many Jewish laws, roughly the size of a modern large olive.</note> in one place, 
one is obligated to remove it; 
if there is less than this, it is nullified by its small quantity. 
And so too regarding the matter of ritual impurity: <term>Tumah: A state of ritual "unfitness" that prevents a person or object from participating in Temple service or touching sanctified food.</term>
if he is fastidious about it, it forms an intervention; <term>Chatzitzah: An "intervention" or barrier. If a person wants the bowl clean, the dough is a foreign object that prevents a ritual bath's water from touching the bowl itself.</term>

it is considered part of the bowl. 
"Deaf dough" <note>original: "batzek hacheiresh". This refers to dough that shows no visible signs of fermentation, such as rising or cracking. It is "deaf" because it does not "respond" to the baker's visual inspection.</note>: 
if there is dough similar to it that has already fermented, 
then this dough is forbidden.

### Tractate Pesachim Chapter 3 Mishnah 3
### 3

How does one separate the impure dough-offering on a Festival? <note>original: "challah teme'ah". Challah is the portion of dough gifted to the Priests. Usually, it is separated and eaten, but if it is ritually impure, it cannot be eaten and must be burned. On a Festival, one cannot burn things that aren't for food, creating a legal dilemma.</note>
**Rabbi Eliezer says:**
One should not designate it by name until it is baked; <note>Once it is baked, it is no longer raw dough that might leaven, and the "challah" portion can be set aside then.</note>
**Ben Beteira says:**
One should place it in cold water. <note>Cold water slows down the fermentation process, preventing the impure dough from becoming leaven (chametz) while it waits to be dealt with after the holiday.</note>
**Rabbi Yehoshua said:**
This is not the kind of leaven for which we are warned 
"it shall not be seen" and "it shall not be found," <note>Quoting Exodus 12:19 and 13:7. These are the biblical prohibitions against possessing leaven on Passover.</note>
rather, she separates it and leaves it until evening, 
and if it leavens, it leavens. <note>Rabbi Yehoshua argues that since she is required by law to set it aside, she is not culpable if it happens to ferment while she waits for the holiday to end to burn it.</note>

### Tractate Pesachim Chapter 3 Mishnah 4
### 4

**Rabban Gamliel says:**
Three women may knead their dough at the same time 
and bake in one oven, one after the other; 
**But the Sages say:**
The three women must be occupied with the dough simultaneously— 
one kneads, one forms the shape, and one bakes. <note>The Sages are more concerned about the dough sitting still; as long as the dough is being worked by hand, it does not begin to ferment. By having them work in a "rotation" (kneading, rolling, baking), no dough is ever left resting.</note>
**Rabbi Akiva says:**
Not all women, not all wood, and not all ovens are equal. <note>Akiva argues that a fixed rule is impossible because some women work faster, some wood burns hotter, and some ovens bake more quickly than others.</note>
This is the general rule:

# Chapter 6

## Tractate Pesachim Chapter 6 Mishnah 1

->1<-

**These are the tasks for the Passover sacrifice that override the Sabbath:**
Its slaughtering, the sprinkling of its blood, the scraping of its innards, and the burning of its fats [on the altar]; however, its roasting and the rinsing of its innards do not override the Sabbath. Carrying the animal [on one's shoulders], bringing it from outside the **Sabbath limit** <note>original: "techum." The boundary of 2,000 cubits around a city beyond which travel is restricted on the Sabbath.</note>, and cutting off its **wart** <note>original: "yabbelet." A physical blemish that must be removed for the animal to be a valid sacrifice.</note> do not override the Sabbath. **Rabbi Eliezer says:** They do override it.

## Tractate Pesachim Chapter 6 Mishnah 2

->2<-

**Rabbi Eliezer said:** 
If slaughtering, which is considered a **primary labor** <note>original: "melacha." One of the 39 categories of work forbidden by the Torah on the Sabbath.</note>, overrides the Sabbath, then shouldn't these other tasks, which are only forbidden as **secondary prohibitions** <note>original: "shevut." Rabbinic safeguards meant to protect the sanctity of the Sabbath.</note>, also override the Sabbath? 
**Rabbi Joshua said to him:** 
The laws of a **Festival** <note>original: "Yom Tov."</note> prove the opposite; for on a Festival, the Law permits **primary labor** [such as cooking food], yet it still forbids **secondary prohibitions**.
**Rabbi Eliezer said to him:** 
What is this comparison, Joshua? How can you bring a proof from a **voluntary act** <note>original: "reshut." Preparing food for personal enjoyment on a Festival.</note> to a **religious commandment** <note>original: "mitzvah." The mandatory obligation of the Passover sacrifice.</note>?

->3<-

**Rabbi Akiva responded:** 
The act of **sprinkling** <note>original: "haza’ah." The ritual sprinkling of purification water on a person who is ritually impure.</note> will prove the point, for it is a religious commandment and is forbidden only as a secondary prohibition,

<summary>This page concludes the logistics of the Passover sacrifice groups and begins a legal debate on which sacrificial tasks may be performed when Passover falls on the Sabbath. <keywords>Sabbath laws, Passover sacrifice, Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Joshua, Rabbi Akiva, primary labor (melacha), secondary prohibitions (shevut), Temple Mount, purification</keywords>

...does not override the Sabbath; 
and you should not be surprised by these other cases, 
for even though they are a **commandment** <note>original: "mitzvah."</note> and are restricted only by a **rabbinic safeguard** <note>original: "shevut." A category of activities forbidden by the Sages on the Sabbath to prevent one from accidentally performing a biblically forbidden labor.</note>, 
they still do not override the Sabbath.

### 4

**Rabbi Eliezer said to him:**
I am drawing a logical inference from the act of slaughtering itself:
If **slaughtering**, which is forbidden as a **primary labor** <note>original: "melacha." One of the 39 categories of work forbidden by the Torah on the Sabbath.</note>,
overrides the Sabbath,
shouldn't **sprinkling** <note>original: "hazayah." Referring here to the sprinkling of purification water (ashes of the Red Heifer) on someone ritually impure so they can offer the sacrifice.</note>, which is only a **rabbinic safeguard**,
override the Sabbath?
**Rabbi Akiva said to him:**
It is the reverse!
If **sprinkling**, which is a **rabbinic safeguard**,
does not override the Sabbath,
perhaps even **slaughtering**, which is a **primary labor**,
should not override the Sabbath either?

### 5

**Rabbi Eliezer said to him:**
"Akiva!
You have uprooted that which is written in the Torah: (Numbers 9:3)
'between the evenings... **at its appointed time**,'
implying it must be offered whether it is a weekday or the Sabbath."
**[Akiva] said to him:**
"Bring me proof of an 'appointed time' for these secondary tasks like the 'appointed time' that exists for the slaughtering!" <note>Rabbi Akiva argues that while the slaughtering must happen on the 14th of Nisan, the purification of the person could have happened earlier.</note>

### 6

**Rabbi Akiva stated a general rule:**
Any **labor** that can be performed before the eve of the Sabbath
does not override the Sabbath.
**Slaughtering**,
which cannot be performed before the eve of the Sabbath, <insert>which is impossible</insert> <note>The Passover sacrifice has a specific window of time on the afternoon of the 14th of Nisan; it cannot be done a day early.</note>
overrides the Sabbath.

->Tractate Pesachim Chapter 6 Mishnah 3<-

### 7

**When do they bring a festival-offering along with [the Passover sacrifice]?** <note>original: "chagigah." A voluntary peace offering brought so that the participants would eat the Passover lamb while already satiated.</note>
When the sacrifice is brought on a weekday, in a state of ritual purity, and in a small quantity <note>Meaning the group sharing the lamb is small and requires additional meat to feel full.</note>.
But when it is brought on the Sabbath, in a large quantity, or in a state of ritual impurity, [the festival-offering is not brought].

## One does not bring a Festival offering with it [on the Sabbath].

## Tractate Pesachim Chapter 6 Mishnah 4

8
The **Festival offering** <note>original: "Chagigah." This was a peace offering brought by pilgrims to the Temple. Unlike the Passover lamb, it was not considered mandatory to offer it specifically on the Sabbath if the 14th of Nisan fell on that day, as it could be brought later.</note> was brought from the cattle or from the flock, from the lambs or from the goats, from the males or from the females; and it is eaten for two days [and the intervening night].

## Tractate Pesachim Chapter 6 Mishnah 5

9
If one slaughtered the **Passover sacrifice** <note>original: "Pesach."</note> on the Sabbath not for its own sake <note>meaning, they performed the ritual with the stated intention that it was a different type of sacrifice, such as a peace offering.</note>, he is liable to bring a **sin offering** <note>original: "Chatat." An offering required for the unintentional violation of a Torah prohibition, in this case, performing the labor of slaughtering on the Sabbath for a purpose that does not override the Sabbath.</note> for it.
And regarding all other sacrifices that one slaughtered for the sake of the Passover sacrifice:
If they are not fit <note>for example, if they were types of animals that could never serve as a Passover lamb.</note>, he is liable;
but if they are fit, **Rabbi Eliezer** deems him liable for a sin offering,
and **Rabbi Yehoshua** exempts him.

10
**Rabbi Eliezer said:**
"If the Passover sacrifice—which is permitted to be slaughtered for its own sake—makes one liable when he changes its 'name' <note>its designated purpose.</note>, 
then other sacrifices—which are forbidden to be slaughtered for their own sake on the Sabbath—should it not stand to reason that one is liable when he changes their 'name' [to a Passover sacrifice]?"
**Rabbi Yehoshua said to him:**
"No. If you say this regarding the Passover sacrifice, it is because he changed it to something **forbidden** <note>slaughtering other sacrifices is forbidden on the Sabbath.</note>; but will you say the same for other sacrifices, which he changed to something **permitted** <note>slaughtering a Passover sacrifice is permitted on the Sabbath.</note>?"
**Rabbi Eliezer said to him:**
"The **communal offerings** <note>original: "Emurei Tzibur." Here referring to mandatory public sacrifices like the Daily Offering (Tamid) which override the Sabbath.</note> shall prove the point:
for they are permitted to be slaughtered for their own sake, yet one who slaughters other animals for their sake is liable."
**Rabbi Yehoshua said to him:**
"No. If you say this regarding communal offerings, it is because they have a **fixed limit** <note>original: "kitzvah." Only a specific number of communal offerings are required each day; therefore, an error is less excusable.</note>; but will you say this of the Passover sacrifice, which has no fixed limit <note>because any number of households may bring their own individual lambs.</note>?"
**Rabbi Meir says:**
Even one who slaughters for the sake of communal offerings is exempt from a sin offering.

## Tractate Pesachim Chapter 6 Mishnah 6

### 11
If one slaughtered the Passover lamb for those who cannot eat it <note>such as the sick or the elderly who are unable to consume a portion the size of an olive</note>, or for those who were not registered for it <note>individuals must be pre-registered to a specific group for a specific lamb before it is slaughtered</note>,
or for the **uncircumcised**, or for the **ritually impure**,
he is **liable** <note>original: "chayav." In this context, it means he has violated the Sabbath because the slaughter was not halakhically valid and thus did not override the Sabbath restrictions.</note>.
But if he slaughtered it for both those who can eat it and those who cannot,
or for those registered for it and those not registered,
or for both the circumcised and the **uncircumcised**,
or for both the **ritually impure** and the **ritually pure**,
he is **exempt** <note>original: "patur." Since the sacrifice is valid for at least some of the participants, the act of slaughtering on the Sabbath is permitted after the fact.</note>.
If he slaughtered it and it was found to have a visible **blemish** <note>original: "ba'al mum." A physical defect that disqualifies an animal for sacrifice.</note>,
he is **liable**.
If he slaughtered it and it was found to have a **hidden internal defect** <note>original: "terefah baseter." A fatal physiological defect that was not visible from the outside.</note>,
he is **exempt**.
If he slaughtered it and it was later discovered that the registered owners had withdrawn their hands <note>meaning they opted out of that specific lamb's group before the slaughter</note>,
or that they had died, or that they had become ritually impure,
he is **exempt**, because he slaughtered it with **permission** <note>he acted under the valid assumption that the owners were still eligible at the moment of slaughter.</note>.

A **limb**, part of which **went outside** <note>referring to meat that passed beyond the boundaries of Jerusalem or the house where the group was eating, which renders that portion invalid.</note>,
one cuts the meat until reaching the **bone**,
and peels the meat until reaching the **joint**, and then cuts [the joint to remove the invalid portion].
But with other **consecrated offerings** <note>original: "kodashim." These are other types of sacrifices that do not carry the specific prohibition against breaking bones.</note>, one may chop with a **cleaver**,
because there is no concern regarding the **breaking of a bone**.
From the **doorframe** and inward is considered **inside**;
from the **doorframe** and outward is considered **outside**.
The **windows** and the **thickness of the wall** are considered **inside**.

### Tractate Pesachim Chapter 7 Mishnah 13
->13<-

**Two groups** <note>original: "chaburot." The Passover lamb was eaten by pre-registered groups of people.</note> that were eating in **one house**,
these turn their faces this way and eat,
and those turn their faces that way and eat,
and the **water-heater** <note>used for diluting the wine.</note> is in the middle.
And when the **servant** <note>original: "shammash." The person attending to the groups.</note> stands to **pour the wine**,
he closes his mouth <note>to avoid any suspicion that he is eating from a group he is not registered with.</note> and turns his face away,
until he returns to his own **group** and eats.
And the **bride** turns her face away and eats <note>This is done out of modesty, as a bride may be shy about eating in front of others during her first year of marriage.</note>.

### Tractate Pesachim Chapter 8 Mishnah 5
->5<-
A **man with a discharge** <term>Zav<note>original: "Zav." A man who has experienced a specific type of genital discharge that renders him ritually impure (Tamei).</note></term> who has seen **two emissions**,
we **slaughter** the sacrifice for him on the **seventh day** of his purification. <note>If he immerses in a ritual bath on the seventh day, he will be pure enough to eat the meat by evening.</note>
If he saw **three emissions**,

we **slaughter** for her on the **eighth day**.

### Tractate Pesachim Chapter 8 Mishnah 6
->7<-
A **mourner** <term>Onen<note>original: "Onen." and likewise one who was **promised to be released from prison**,
the **sick** and the **elderly** who are physically **able to eat an olive-bulk**,
we **slaughter** the sacrifice for them.
However, for all of these,
we **do not slaughter for them alone**, <note>They must be part of a larger group that includes at least one person who is definitely able to eat.</note>
so that they do not **bring the sacrifice to a state of disqualification**. <note>Because their status is uncertain—the prisoner might not be released, the seeker might find a body, or the sick person might take a turn for the worse—they might end up unable to eat the meat, which would result in the sacrifice being wasted.</note>

they are **exempt from performing the Second Passover** <note>A "make-up" holiday held a month later for those who were impure or away during the first Passover.</note>,
**except** for the one **digging through the rubble** <note>Because he was potentially impure at the very moment of slaughter if there was a body under the debris, he must observe the Second Passover to be certain.</note>.

## Tractate Pesachim Chapter 8 Mishnah 8

If so, **why was it stated** in the Torah:
"**ritually impure or on a distant journey**"?
Because **these** [the impure and the traveler] are **exempt from excision** <term>excision<note>original: "Karet." A severe divine punishment where the soul is "cut off" from its people.</note></term>,
while **those** [who intentionally skipped the first] are **liable to excision** <note>Even though an intentional sinner can "make up" the sacrifice on the second date, they still bear the spiritual penalty for their initial willful neglect, unlike those who were physically unable to attend.</note>.

### Tractate Pesachim Chapter 9 Mishnah 2
#### 2

And **what is** considered a **"distant journey"**? <note>The Torah (Numbers 9:10) excuses someone on a "distant journey" from the first Passover, allowing them to observe the Second Passover instead.</note>
From **Modi'in** <note>original: "Ha-Modi'it." An ancient village about 15-20 miles from Jerusalem, famous as the home of the Maccabees.</note> **and beyond**,
and a **similar distance** in **every direction**.
These are the **words of Rabbi Akiba**.
**Rabbi Eliezer says**:
It is measured from the **threshold of the Temple courtyard and beyond** <note>Rabbi Eliezer takes a very literal view: if you are not inside the Temple gates at the time of slaughter, you are "distant."</note>.
**Rabbi Yose said**:
Therefore, there is a **dot over the letter *He*** <note>In the Hebrew Bible (Numbers 9:10), the word "distant" (רחוקה) has a scribal dot over the final letter. This is an ancient technique to suggest an alternative interpretation.</note>, to say:

**but** rather anyone who is **from the threshold of the Temple courtyard and beyond** is excluded.

### Tractate Pesachim Chapter 9 Mishnah 3
#### 3

**What is the difference between the first** [Passover] **and the second** [Passover]?
Regarding the **first**, it is **forbidden** for leaven to **be seen or be found** <term>be seen or be found<note>original: "Bal yera'eh u-val yimatze." The biblical prohibitions against owning or seeing leaven during the seven days of Passover.</note></term>;
Regarding the **second**, a person may have **leavened bread and unleavened bread with him in the house** <note>On the Second Passover, one only needs to eat the sacrifice with matzah and bitter herbs, but there is no requirement to remove all leaven from the home.</note>.
The **first requires** the chanting of **Hallel** <term>Hallel<note>original: "Hallel." Psalms 113–118, sung as songs of praise and thanksgiving.</note></term> **while it is being eaten**,
but the **second does not require Hallel while it is being eaten**.
Both **this and that** [the first and second] **require Hallel during their preparation** <note>The Hallel was sung by the Levites in the Temple while the lambs were being sacrificed.</note>,
they are **eaten roasted with unleavened bread and bitter herbs**,
and they **override the** [restrictions of the] **Shabbat**.

### Tractate Pesachim Chapter 9 Mishnah 4
#### 4

A **Passover sacrifice that is offered in a state of impurity** <note>If the majority of the community is ritually impure, the sacrifice is offered anyway, but certain rules change.</note>,
**men and women with discharges**, **menstruating women**, and **women after childbirth may not eat from it**;
yet **if they did eat, they are exempt** from the penalty of spiritual excision <note>original: "karet." Usually, an impure person eating sacred meat is a severe sin, but because this sacrifice was already offered in a state of impurity, the usual severe penalty does not apply.</note>.
**Rabbi Eliezer exempts** them **even for entering the Sanctuary** in that state.

### Tractate Pesachim Chapter 9 Mishnah 5
#### 5

**What is the difference between the Passover of Egypt and the Passover of** later **generations**?
The **Passover of Egypt** required its **acquisition on the tenth** of the month,
and it **required the sprinkling** of blood with a **bundle of hyssop**
**upon the lintel and upon the two doorposts**,
and it was **eaten in haste during one night**.
But the **Passover of** later **generations is observed for all seven days** <note>In Egypt, the "Passover" was specifically the night of the sacrifice and the departure; later, it became a seven-day festival of Matzot.</note>.

# Tractate Pesachim Chapter 9 Mishnah 6

-> 6 <-

**Rabbi Joshua said**: 
I have **heard** that the **substitution of the Passover sacrifice** <term>substitution<note>original: "Temurah." According to biblical law (Leviticus 27:10), if a person tries to swap an animal already consecrated for a sacrifice with another, both animals become holy. This creates a legal dilemma for the Passover lamb, which has very specific rules.</note></term> **is sacrificed**, 
and that the **substitution of the Passover sacrifice is not sacrificed**, 
and **I cannot explain** the distinction between these two traditions. 
**Rabbi Akiba said**: 
**I will explain it**: 
A **Passover lamb that was found before the slaughtering** of the [replacement] Passover sacrifice must be allowed to **graze until it develops a blemish** <note>Once a sanctified animal has a physical defect, it can no longer be sacrificed, but its holiness is "transferred" to its monetary value.</note>, then it is **sold**, 
and he should **bring a peace-offering with its proceeds**, and **likewise for its substitute**; 
If it was found **after the Passover** sacrifice was already offered, he should **bring it as a peace-offering**, and **likewise for its substitute** <note>A Passover lamb not used for its intended purpose usually defaults to the status of a "Shelamim" (peace-offering), which is a more general category of sacrifice.</note>.

# Tractate Pesachim Chapter 9 Mishnah 7

One who **designates a female** animal for his Passover sacrifice,

# Tractate Shekalim

## Chapter 1

### Tractate Shekalim Chapter 1 Mishnah 1

1
On the first of Adar <note>The last month of the Hebrew calendar year, occurring in late winter/early spring.</note>,
announcements are made regarding the half-shekel coins <note>The annual tax paid by every adult male to fund the daily public offerings in the Temple.</note> and regarding forbidden mixtures of seeds <term>Kilayim<note>original: "Kilayim." The biblical prohibition against sowing two different types of seeds in the same field.</note></term>.
And on the fifteenth of that month [Adar],
the Scroll of Esther <term>Megillah<note>original: "Megillah." The book of Esther, read on the holiday of Purim.</note></term> is read in walled cities.
They also repair the roads and the public squares,
and the ritual immersion pools <term>Mikvaot<note>original: "Mikvaot." Pools used for ritual purification.</note></term>.
They perform all necessary public needs,
they mark the locations of graves <note>Using white lime to warn passersby of ritual impurity.</note>,
and [the court's messengers] also go out to inspect the fields for forbidden mixtures of seeds.

# Tractate Shekalim Chapter 1 Mishnah 3
## 3
On the fifteenth day of that month [Adar],
money-changing tables were set up in the provinces <note>The outlying towns outside of Jerusalem.</note>.
On the twenty-fifth, they sat in the Temple;
once they sat in the Temple, they began to seize <term>Collateral<note>original: "Memashkenin." If a person had not yet paid the required half-shekel tax, the authorities would take a personal item from them as security to ensure payment.</note></term>.
And from whom do they seize collateral?
From Levites and Israelites,
converts and freed slaves,
but not from women, [unfreed] slaves, or minors.
And for any minor whose father [once] began to pay the shekel on his behalf,
the father may not stop paying in subsequent years.
And they do not seize collateral from the priests,
for the sake of peace <note>To avoid public conflict and maintain the dignity of the priests who performed the Temple service.</note>.

# Tractate Shekalim Chapter 1 Mishnah 4
## 4
Rabbi Yehuda said:
Ben Kochri testified in <term>Yavne<note>The center of Jewish leadership and scholarship after the destruction of the Second Temple.</note></term>,
that any priest who pays the shekel tax is not committing a sin.
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai said to him:
Not so!
Rather, any priest who does *not* pay the tax is a sinner.
However, the priests interpret this verse to their own advantage:
<margin>(Leviticus 6:16)</margin>
"And every grain offering of a priest shall be entirely burned; it shall not be eaten."
[The priests argued:] Since the <term>Omer<note>The first-fruits offering of barley brought on the second day of Passover.</note></term>, the <term>Two Loaves<note>Offered on the holiday of Shavuot.</note></term>, and the <term>Bread of the Presence<note>The twelve loaves of "Showbread" displayed weekly in the Temple.</note></term> are provided by us <note>Funded by the communal shekel tax which they would be contributing to.</note>,
how could they be eaten by us? <note>The priests' logic was that if they contributed to the communal fund, the communal grain offerings would technically be "priestly offerings." According to the Law in Leviticus, a priest's offering must be totally consumed by fire and never eaten. Since priests must eat the Showbread and other offerings, they argued they must be exempt from the tax so the food remains "non-priestly" and permitted for consumption.</note>

---

# Tractate Shekalim Chapter 1 Mishnah 5
## 5
Even though the Sages said:
We do not seize collateral from women, slaves, and minors,
nevertheless, if they choose to pay the tax, we accept it from them.
But from a Gentile or a <term>Samaritan<note>original: "Kuti." Historically, a group that lived in the northern Kingdom of Israel who observed their own version of the Torah; the Sages restricted their participation in communal Temple offerings.</note></term> who attempts to pay, we do not accept it from them.

### Tractate Shekalim Chapter 2 Mishnah 4

### Tractate Shekalim Chapter 2 Mishnah 5

ו
The surplus of **Shekel** funds is non-sacred.
The surplus of the **Tenth-Ephah** <note>original: "asirit ha-ephah." The daily meal offering brought by the High Priest.</note>,

Anything that comes because of a **sin** or because of **guilt**,
its surplus goes toward **freewill offerings**.

ז
The surplus of a **Burnt-offering** is for a **Burnt-offering**.
The surplus of a **Meal-offering** is for a **Meal-offering**.
The surplus of **Peace-offerings** is for **Peace-offerings**.
The surplus of the **Passover-offering** is for **Peace-offerings**. <note>If money was set aside for a Passover lamb but the lamb was not needed, the money is used for a different category of "peace" sacrifice.</note>
The surplus of funds for **Nazarites** <note>Plural; referring to a general fund collected for multiple people.</note> is for other **Nazarites**.
The surplus of a specific **Nazarite** <note>Singular; the leftover money from an individual's specific animal fund.</note> is for **freewill offerings**.

They withdraw the contribution from the chamber [into three large baskets],

nor with shoes, nor with sandals,

For a person must be as blameless in the eyes of other people

as it is said:

and it says:
> "So shall you find favor and good favor in the sight of God and man" (Proverbs 3:4).

### Tractate Shekalim Chapter 3 Mishnah 4

He withdrew the first basket and covered it with leather mats <note>original: "kitbaliyot." Large leather covers or sacks used to prevent new coins from falling into the baskets already filled.</note>;

And why did he not cover it?
Lest he forget and accidentally withdraw funds from a basket that had already been withdrawn <note>The third basket remained uncovered as a visual reminder that the process was complete.</note>.
He withdrew the first basket on behalf of the Land of Israel,
the second on behalf of the cities surrounding it,

## Tractate Shekalim Chapter 4 Mishnah 
## 5

**The surplus incense—what did they do with it?**
They would set aside the wages of the craftsmen <note>original: "umanim." Specifically, the families like the House of Avtinas who were experts in the secret recipe and manufacture of the sacred incense.</note> from it,
and they would **deconsecrate** <note>Transfer the status of holiness from the physical incense to the money.</note> the incense upon the money intended for the craftsmen's wages,
and they would give the incense to the craftsmen as their wages,
and then they would buy it back using the **new contribution** <note>original: "terumah chadashah." The law required that sacrifices for the new year (starting in the month of Nisan) be purchased with funds from the new year's collection. This complex transaction was a legal workaround to "renew" the status of the leftover incense.</note>.
If the new month <note>The month of Nisan, the start of the Temple's new fiscal year.</note> arrived in its proper time,
they would buy it back using the **new contribution**;
but if not, they would use the **old** fund.

## Tractate Shekalim Chapter 4 Mishnah 
## 6

That is not the correct procedure.
Rather, they should set aside the wages of the craftsmen from them,
and **deconsecrate** them upon the money intended for the craftsmen’s wages,
and give that money to the craftsmen as their wages,
and then buy the items back using the **new contribution**.

# Chapter 5

## Tractate Shekalim, Chapter 5, Mishna 1

### 1
And these are the **appointed officials** <note>original: "memunnim." These were the department heads responsible for various aspects of Temple life.</note> who were in the Sanctuary:
**Yochanan ben Pinchas** was over the **seals** <note>original: "chotamot." These were tokens or receipts purchased by people bringing offerings to prove they had paid for the necessary accompaniments like flour or wine.</note>,
**Achiyah** was over the **libations** <note>The wine and water offerings poured on the Altar.</note>,
**Matya ben Shmuel** was over the **lots** <note>original: "pyasot." The system used to fairly distribute daily tasks among the priests.</note>,
**Petachyah** was over the **bird-nests** <note>original: "kinnim." Referring to the turtle-doves or pigeons brought as offerings, specifically by those who could not afford more expensive animals.</note>;
this Petachyah is the same as **Mordechai** <note>The hero of the Purim story, according to tradition.</note>.
And why was his name called Petachyah?
Because he would **open** <note>The name Petachyah relates to the Hebrew word "petach," meaning opening.</note> matters and expound upon them,
and he was knowledgeable in **seventy languages** <note>A traditional way of saying he was a master of all the world's spoken languages.</note>.

### 2
**Ben Achiyah** was over the **bowel sickness** <gloss>sickness</gloss> <note>Priests often suffered from intestinal issues because they walked barefoot on the cold marble floors and ate significant amounts of sacrificial meat.</note>,
**Nechunyah** was the digger of **cisterns** <note>Providing water for the pilgrims coming to Jerusalem.</note>,
**Gevini** was the **herald** <note>The person who woke the priests and the city with a loud cry to begin the Temple service.</note>,
**Ben Gever** was over the **closing of the gates**,
**Ben Bevai** was over the **wick** <note>original: "peki'ah." This likely refers to the maintenance of the lamp wicks or, according to some, a whip used to wake sleeping guards.</note>,
**Ben Arza** was over the **cymbal** <note>Marking the beginning of the Levites' song.</note>,
**Hugras ben Levi** was over the **song**,
The **House of Garmo** was over the making of the **Showbread** <note>original: "lechem ha-panim." Twelve loaves kept on a golden table inside the Sanctuary.</note>,
The **House of Avtinas** was over the making of the **incense**,
**Eleazar** was over the **curtains** <note>The massive veils that separated different areas of the Temple.</note>,
and **Pinchas** was over the **clothing** <gloss>the dresser</gloss> <note>The vestments worn by the priests during their service.</note>.

### Tractate Shekalim, Chapter 5, Mishna 3
4

There were four **seals** <note>original: "chotamot." These functioned like tokens or receipts.</note> in the Sanctuary, and written upon them were these words:
**Calf**, **Ram** <note>original: "zachar," literally "male."</note>, **Kid**, and **Sinner**.
**Ben Azzai** says: There were five, and they were written in **Aramaic** <note>The common spoken language of the Jewish people during the Second Temple period, rather than the sacred Hebrew.</note>:
**Calf**, **Ram**, **Kid**, **Poor Sinner**, and **Rich Sinner**.

The **Calf** [seal] served for the **libations** <note>original: "nesachim." These were the supplementary offerings of flour, oil, and wine that accompanied an animal sacrifice.</note> of cattle, whether large or small, male or female.
The **Kid** [seal] served for the libations of the flock <note>Sheep or goats.</note>, whether large or small, male or female, except for those of **rams**.
The **Ram** [seal] served for the libations of rams alone.
The **Sinner** [seal] served for the libations of the three animals offered by a **purifying leper** <note>original: "metzora." A person who had recovered from a specific ritual skin affliction and was required to bring three animal sacrifices to complete their purification process.</note>.

### Tractate Shekalim, Chapter 5, Mishna 4
5

One who requires **libations** goes to **Yochanan**, who is appointed over the **seals**;
he gives him money and receives a **seal** from him.
He then goes to **Achiyah**, who is appointed over the **libations**,
gives him the **seal**, and receives the libations from him.
In the evening, they <note>Yochanan and Achiyah</note> come together,
and Achiyah produces the seals [he collected] and receives the corresponding money against them.
If there was a surplus [in the money box], the surplus goes to the **Sanctuary funds**;
but if there was a deficit, Yochanan must pay from his own house,
for **the Sanctuary’s hand is uppermost** <note>original: "ha-yad hekdesh la-elyonah." As noted previously, this legal principle ensures the Temple’s treasury is protected against loss.</note>.

### Tractate Shekalim, Chapter 5, Mishna 5
6

One who lost his **seal**—they wait for him until the evening.
If they found [in the audit] a surplus for him equal to the value of his seal, they give [the libations] to him;
<note>If the money in Yochanan's box exceeded the number of seals returned by Achiyah, it proved the person had paid but lost their token.</note>

before his soul departed <note>original: "yatzeta nishmato." This is a poetic idiom for sudden death. The implication is that Heaven prevented him from revealing the secret location of the Ark.</note>,
and they knew for certain that the Ark was hidden there.

## Tractate Shekalim, Chapter 6, Mishna 3

->ג<-

And where were these thirteen prostrations <note>original: "hishtachavuyot." This refers to a full act of bowing where the person lies flat on the ground with arms and legs outstretched.</note> performed?
Four in the North, and four in the South,
three in the East, and two in the West,
corresponding to the gates.
The Southern gates near the West:
the Upper Gate, the Fuel Gate <note>original: "Sha'ar HaDelek." This gate was used for bringing in the wood used for the Altar fire.</note>,
the Firstborn Gate, and the Water Gate.
And why was its name called the Water Gate?
Because through it, they would bring in the flask of water for the Water Libation on the Festival <note>original: "he-Chag." This refers to the holiday of Sukkot (Tabernacles). A unique ceremony involved pouring water on the Altar alongside the daily wine offering.</note>.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says: <insert>for the designation</insert>
through it, the water trickles <note>original: "mepakim" — meaning to bubble or flow out slowly.</note> and in the future will flow out 
from under the threshold of the House <note>This is a reference to a prophecy in Ezekiel (47:1-2), which describes a miraculous river flowing from the future Temple to heal the Dead Sea.</note>.

->ד<-

Opposite them in the North, near the West:
the Jeconiah Gate, the Offering Gate,
the Women's Gate, and the Song Gate.
And why was its name called the Jeconiah Gate?
Because through it, Jeconiah went out into his exile <insert>and his exile</insert> <note>Jeconiah (also known as Jehoiachin) was a king of Judah who was taken captive to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar about 11 years before the First Temple was destroyed.</note>.
And in the East was the Nicanor Gate <note>Famous for its massive bronze doors, which were said to have been miraculously saved from a storm at sea.</note>,
and it had two small side-doors,
one on its right and one on its left.
And there were two in the West that had no name.

one of marble and one of silver.
On the marble one, they would place the limbs [of the sacrifices],
and on the silver one, they would place the service vessels;

And two tables were in the Entrance Hall <note>original: "Ulam." The large vestibule leading into the main Sanctuary building.</note> on the inside, by the doorway of the House:
one made of marble and one made of gold.
On the marble table, they would place the Showbread <note>original: "Lechem HaPanim," literally "Bread of the Faces" or "Bread of the Presence." Twelve loaves of bread were displayed in the Sanctuary at all times.</note> upon its entry to the Sanctuary,
and on the gold table, they would place it upon its exit.
This is because the rule is: we rise in matters of holiness and do not descend <note>original: "ma'alin bakodesh v'lo moridin." This is a fundamental principle in Jewish law; once an object or person has achieved a level of sanctity, they should move to a higher level rather than a lower one. Since gold is more precious than marble, the bread "ascends" to the gold table after serving its holy purpose inside.</note>;
And there was one additional table of gold inside the Sanctuary itself,
upon which the Showbread rested continually.

## Tractate Shekalim, Chapter 6, Mishna 6

->ו<-

Thirteen shofars <note>original: "shofarot." While the word usually means a ram's horn, here it refers to thirteen collection chests shaped like horns—narrow at the top and wide at the base—to prevent people from reaching in and stealing the money.</note> were in the Temple,
and inscribed upon them were these labels:
"New Shekels" and "Old Shekels,"
"Bird-pair Offerings" and "Chicks for Burnt Offerings,"
"Wood" and "Frankincense,"
"Gold for the Mercy-Seat" <note>original: "Kapporet." While this usually refers to the Ark's cover, in this context it refers to funds donated for the gold plating and vessels of the Holy of Holies.</note>,
and six chests labeled "For Free-will Offerings."
"New Shekels" refers to the tax for each current year,
and "Old Shekels" refers to those who did not pay their tax last year <note>original: "ashtakad," an Aramaic term for the previous year.</note>, 
who must pay it in the coming year;

->ז<-

"Bird-pair Offerings" <note>original: "kinim."</note> refer to turtledoves;
and "Chicks for Burnt Offerings" refer to young pigeons,
all of which are offered as burnt offerings.
These are the words of Rabbi Yehuda.
But the Sages say:
In the chest for "Bird-pair Offerings," one bird is a sin offering and one is a burnt offering <note>The Sages clarify that these funds were used for the specific pairs required by law for purification, whereas Rabbi Yehuda believes this specific chest was only for voluntary burnt offerings.</note>,
but for "Chicks for Burnt Offerings," they are all indeed burnt offerings.

One who says:

he must not give less than a handful <note>original: "kometz." The amount held in the palm by the three middle fingers.</note>;
If he says: "I take upon myself to give gold,"
he must not give less than a gold dinar.
Six chests were for "Free-will Offerings."
What was done with the "Free-will Offering" funds?

What would they do with it <note>Referring to the surplus funds collected in the chests for "Gold for the Mercy-Seat" or general donations.</note>?
They would purchase Burnt Offerings with it;
the meat is for God <note>original: "la-Shem." Literally "for the Name," a common substitution for the Tetragrammaton to avoid speaking the Divine Name.</note> and the hides belong to the priests.
This is an interpretation <note>original: "Midrash." A method of biblical exegesis used to derive legal or ethical principles from the scriptural text.</note> that Jehoiada the High Priest taught:
"It is a guilt offering; he has certainly trespassed against the LORD" <gloss>(Leviticus 5:19)</gloss>.
This is the general rule:
Anything that comes because of a sin or because of guilt,
Burnt Offerings shall be purchased with it;
the meat is for God, and the hides are for the priests.
Thus, two scriptural verses are found to be upheld:
"A guilt offering for the LORD" and "A guilt offering for the priest."
And it says: <gloss>(2 Kings 12:17)</gloss>
"The money of guilt offerings and the money of sin offerings was not brought into the house of the LORD;
it belonged to the priests." <note>This verse explains that while the animals themselves are sacrificed, certain monetary equivalents or surpluses remained the property of the priestly class to maintain their service.</note>

# Chapter 7
## Tractate Shekalim, Chapter 7, Mishna 1

**1**
Money that was found between the chest for "Shekels" and the chest for "Voluntary Offerings":
If it is closer to the Shekels, it shall fall to the Shekels;
If it is closer to the Voluntary Offerings, it shall fall to the Voluntary Offerings;
If it is exactly halfway between them, it shall fall to the Voluntary Offerings.
Between the Wood and the Frankincense:
If it is closer to the Wood, it shall fall to the Wood;
If it is closer to the Frankincense, it shall fall to the Frankincense;
If it is exactly halfway between them, it shall fall to the Frankincense.
Between the Bird-pairs <term>Kinnim: Pairs of doves or pigeons brought as offerings, usually one as a sin offering and one as a burnt offering.</term> and the Chicks for Burnt Offerings:
If it is closer to the Bird-pairs, it shall fall to the Bird-pairs;
If it is closer to the Chicks for Burnt Offerings, it shall fall to the Chicks for Burnt Offerings;
If it is exactly halfway between them, it shall fall to the Chicks for Burnt Offerings.
Between Non-sacred <term>Chullin: Ordinary property or money that has not been consecrated for Temple use and has no special sanctity.</term> money and Second Tithe <term>Ma’aser Sheni: A tenth of one’s produce that the owner must bring to Jerusalem and spend on food to be eaten there in a state of ritual purity.</term>:
If it is closer to the Non-sacred money, it shall fall to the Non-sacred money;
If it is closer to the Second Tithe, it shall fall to the Second Tithe;
If it is exactly halfway between them, it shall fall to the Second Tithe.
This is the general rule:
We follow the closest proximity;
but if it is exactly halfway between them, we follow the more stringent law <note>In cases of doubt where the distance is equal, the money is assigned to the category with higher sanctity or stricter usage rules to ensure the law is not accidentally violated.</note>.

### Tractate Shekalim Chapter 7 Mishna 2

->2<-

Money that was found in front of livestock traders,
is always considered Second Tithe <note>original: "Ma'aser." Specifically, the "Second Tithe" which had to be spent on food and consumed within the walls of Jerusalem. Since livestock traders sold animals for these feasts, money dropped near them was presumed to be Tithe money.</note>.
But if found on the Temple Mount, it is non-consecrated <term>Chullin: Secular or common funds that have no sacred status and may be used for any purpose</term>.
And if found in the rest of Jerusalem,
during the rest of the days of the year, it is non-consecrated;
but during the time of the Pilgrimage Festivals, it is all considered Second Tithe <note>During the three festivals (Passover, Shavuot, and Sukkot), the city was crowded with pilgrims spending their Tithe money, so any lost coin was assumed to be from those funds.</note>.

### Tractate Shekalim Chapter 7 Mishna 3

->3<-

Meat that was found in the Temple Courtyard <note>original: "Azarah." The inner sanctum of the Temple where sacrifices were performed.</note>:
If found as whole limbs, they are presumed to be Burnt Offerings <term>Olot: Sacrifices that are entirely consumed by fire on the altar</term>;
if found as sliced pieces, they are Sin Offerings <term>Chattaot: Sacrifices brought for atonement, where the meat is eaten by the priests</term>.
And if found in the city of Jerusalem, it is presumed to be Peace Offerings <term>Shelamim: Sacrifices whose meat was shared between the altar, the priests, and the person who brought the offering</term>.
In both this case and that case,
its appearance shall be allowed to disfigure <note>The meat is left overnight until it reaches a state of "notar" (leftover beyond its permitted time), which renders it legally invalid.</note> and then it shall go out to the place of burning.

->4<-

If meat was found in the provinces <note>original: "Gevulim." Areas outside of the central sanctuary/Jerusalem.</note>:
If found as whole limbs, they are considered carcasses <note>original: "Nevelot." Meat from an animal that was not slaughtered according to ritual law; it is unkosher and prohibited for consumption.</note>;
if found as sliced pieces, they are permitted <note>It is assumed they were prepared by a butcher for local consumption.</note>.
But during the time of the Pilgrimage Festivals, when meat is abundant,
even whole limbs are permitted.

### Tractate Shekalim Chapter 7 Mishna 4

->5<-

An animal that was found between Jerusalem and Migdal Eder <term>Migdal Eder: Literally "Tower of the Flock," a location mentioned in Genesis 35:21, used here to define the radius around the city</term>,
and at a similar distance in every direction:
If they are males, they are considered Burnt Offerings; and if they are females, they are Peace Offerings.
Rabbi Judah says: <gloss>Judah</gloss> <note>The gloss "Yoda" reflects a phonetic variant of the name Yehuda/Judah common in certain manuscript traditions.</note>
Even that which is suitable for a Passover offering is considered a Passover offering,
provided it is found within thirty days before the festival.

### Tractate Shekalim Chapter 7 Mishna 5

->6<-

Originally, they would seize a person who found such an animal as a pledge,
until he would also bring the accompanying drink offerings <term>Nesachim: The wine libations and grain offerings that must accompany animal sacrifices</term>.
As a result, people began to leave the animal and run away.
Therefore, the Court <term>Beit Din: The central Jewish legal authority</term> ordained
that the drink offerings for such found animals should come from public funds.

### Tractate Shekalim Chapter 7 Mishna 6

->7<-

Rabbi Shimeon said:
The Court established seven regulations,
and this is one of them.
A Gentile <note>original: "Goy." A non-Jew who wishes to honor the God of Israel with a sacrifice.</note> who sent his Burnt Offering from a land across the sea,
if he sent libations <term>Nesakhim: The wine and flour offerings that must accompany an animal sacrifice</term> with it, they are offered from his own funds;
but if not, they are offered from the public funds.
And similarly, a proselyte <note>original: "Ger." A convert to Judaism.</note> who died and left animal sacrifices behind,
if he has libations, they are offered from his own funds;
but if not, they are offered from the public funds.
And it is a regulation of the Court regarding a High Priest who died <note>Specifically, the time between his death and the appointment of a successor.</note>,
that his daily meal offering shall be offered from the public funds.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
It is offered from the funds of the heirs.
And in either case, it was offered as a whole <note>The High Priest's meal offering was normally offered in two halves (morning and evening), but in this interim period, the entire portion was offered at once.</note>.

### Tractate Shekalim Chapter 7 Mishna 7

->8<-

[There were regulations] regarding the salt and regarding the wood,
that the priests may benefit from them <note>The Court allowed priests to use the Temple's salt and wood to season and cook their own portions of the sacrificial meat, not just for the altar itself.</note>.
And regarding the Red Heifer,
that the laws of misappropriation <insert>misappropriation</insert> <term>Me'ilah: The sin of using sacred property for personal benefit</term> should not apply to its ashes <note>The ashes of the Red Heifer were used for ritual purification; this rule prevented people from accidentally committing a sacrilege when handling them.</note>.
Regarding bird-offerings that become disqualified,
that they shall be replaced from the public funds;
Rabbi Yose says:
The one who supplies the bird-offerings
must supply the replacements for the disqualified ones.

## Chapter 1

### Tractate Yoma Chapter 1 Mishnah 1

**1**

Seven days before the Day of Atonement,
they separate the High Priest <term>Kohen Gadol: The highest-ranking priest in the Temple</term> from his home to the Palhedrin Chamber <note>original: "Lishkat Palhedrin." A special room in the Temple complex where the High Priest lived during his week of preparation</note>,

as it is said in the Torah: (Leviticus 16:6)

The Sages said to him:
If so, there would be no end to the matter <note>The Sages argued that if we worry about the death of one wife, we would have to worry about the death of the second, and so on, which is impractical</note>.

## Tractate Yoma Chapter 1 Mishnah 3
### 3

The elders from the elders of the Court <term>Beit Din: The high council of Jewish law</term> handed him over to others, and they would read before him from the "Order of the Day" <note>the specific biblical and traditional instructions for the Yom Kippur ritual</note>. They would say to him: "My master, High Priest, read it yourself with your own mouth, for perhaps you have forgotten or perhaps you have not learned this." On the eve of the Day of Atonement in the morning, they would stand him at the Eastern Gate and pass bulls, rams, and lambs before him, so that he would become familiar with and accustomed to the sacrificial service.

## Tractate Yoma Chapter 1 Mishnah 4
### 4

Throughout all seven days of his isolation, they did not withhold food or drink from him. However, on the eve of the Day of Atonement toward nightfall <note>just before the fast begins</note>, they would not let him eat much, because food brings on sleep <note>and the goal was to keep him awake and alert to prevent accidental ritual impurity</note>.

## Tractate Yoma Chapter 1 Mishnah 5
### 5

The elders of the Court then handed him over to the elders of the Priesthood, and they led him to the upper chamber of the House of Abtinas <term>Beit Abtinas: The family responsible for the secret formula of the Temple incense</term>. They adjured him <note>made him take a formal oath</note>, took their leave, and went on their way. 

And they said to him: "My master, High Priest, we are the emissaries of the Court, and you are our emissary and the emissary of the Court. We adjure you by Him who caused His Name to dwell in this House, that you shall not change a single thing from all that we have told you." 

He would turn away and weep <note>at the insult of being suspected of sectarianism</note>, and they would turn away and weep <note>at the necessity of suspecting a fellow Jew and their leader</note>.

### Tractate Yoma Chapter 3 Mishnah 1
1
The appointed official said to them:
> "Go out and see if the time for slaughtering has arrived."
> If it has arrived, the observer says:
