Matya ben Shmuel says:
> [The official asks:] "Has it lit up the face of the entire east as far as Hebron?" <note>Hebron is mentioned to invoke the merit of the Patriarchs buried there at the start of the day's service</note>
And he [the observer] says:
> "Yes."

### Tractate Yoma Chapter 3 Mishnah 2
2
And why did they require this?
Because once, the light of the moon rose,
and they imagined that the east had lit up.
They slaughtered the daily offering <term>Tamid: the morning sacrifice</term>,
and [subsequently] had to take it out to the place of burning <note>The sacrifice was invalid because it was slaughtered before dawn</note>.
And they [then] brought the High Priest down to the place of immersion.
This was the rule in the Temple:
Anyone who "covers his feet" <note>original: hamesach et raglav; a modest euphemism for defecating</note> requires immersion,
and anyone who urinates requires the sanctification of hands and feet <term>Kiddush Yadayim ve-Raglav: the ritual washing from the Temple's bronze basin</term>.

In the morning, he wore garments of Pelusium linen <note>original: pilosin; a high-quality, expensive flax from Pelusium in Egypt</note> valued at thirty <note>original: sheloshim; some versions read twelve or eighteen</note>—thirteen *maneh*.

->but today, he scoops with one holding three *kabs*,<-
->and with it, he would enter.<-

->Every day, the incense was finely ground,<-

From where does he begin <note>the application of blood to the corners of the Golden Altar</note>?
From the North-east corner,
then the North-west,
then the South-west,
and finally the South-east.
The place where he begins for a standard sin-offering on the Outer Altar <note>which is the South-east corner</note>, 
is the place where he concludes on the Inner Altar.
**Rabbi Eliezer says:**
He would stand in his place and apply the blood <note>original: *mechatte*; applying blood to cleanse the altar</note> to the corners.
On all of them, he applies the blood from bottom to top,
except for the one that was directly in front of him <note>the corner he reached first</note>,
where he would apply the blood from top to bottom.

### Tractate Yoma Chapter 5 Mishnah 6

->8<-

He sprinkled upon the "cleansed surface" of the altar <term>toharo: the clear, gold-plated top surface of the Golden Altar</term> seven times.
The residual blood <note>from the inner service in the Holy of Holies and Sanctuary</note> he would pour 
at the western base of the Outer Altar.
As for the blood of the Outer Altar service <note>sacrifices offered year-round</note>, he would pour it at the southern base.
These and those <note>the blood from both the inner and outer services</note> would mix in the drainage channel <term>amah: a water conduit in the Temple court</term> and flow out to the Kidron Valley.
The remains were then sold to gardeners for fertilizer,
and they were subject to the laws of misappropriation <term>me'ilah: the prohibition against personal use of consecrated property</term>.

### Tractate Yoma Chapter 5 Mishnah 7

->9<-

All the acts of the Day of Atonement mentioned must be done in order.
If he performed one act before its fellow,
he has done nothing <note>the service is invalid and must be repeated correctly</note>.
If he applied the blood of the goat before the blood of the bull,
he must return and sprinkle from the blood of the goat after the blood of the bull.
If the blood was spilled before he finished the applications inside <note>in the Holy of Holies</note>,
he must bring other blood and repeat the sprinkling from the beginning inside.
And so too in the Sanctuary <term>Heichal</term>, and so too at the Golden Altar,
because each of these areas is an independent atonement.
**Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon say:**
From the place where he stopped, from there he begins again <note>they argue that he does not need to restart the entire sequence for that specific area, only complete what was missed</note>.

### Tractate Yoma Chapter 6 Mishnah 1

->**1**<-

The two goats of the Day of Atonement:
The commandment regarding them is that they should be identical
in appearance, in height, and in price, and their purchase should be at the same time.
Nonetheless, even if they are not identical, they are valid.
If he purchased one today and the other tomorrow, they are valid.
If one of them died:
If it died before he had cast the lots <note>The High Priest would draw lots to determine which goat would be sacrificed to God and which would be sent to the wilderness</note>,
he should purchase a partner for the remaining one.
But if it died after he had cast the lots,
he must bring a new pair and cast lots over them from the beginning.

->**2**<-

And he shall say <note>at the casting of the second set of lots</note>,
if the one designated **"For the Lord"** died:
"This one upon which the lot **'For the Lord'** has fallen shall stand in its place";
and if the one designated **"For Azazel"** <term>Azazel: the name of the rugged cliff in the wilderness to which the goat was sent</term> died:
"This one upon which the lot **'For Azazel'** has fallen shall stand in its place."
The second goat <note>the leftover goat from the first pair</note> shall graze until it develops a blemish <term>yistayev: becomes ritually unfit for sacrifice due to a physical defect</term> and is then sold,
and its value shall fall into the fund for voluntary offerings,
as a communal sin-offering is not left to die.
**Rabbi Yehuda says:**
It is left to die.
And **Rabbi Yehuda** further said:
If the blood <note>of the goat sacrificed to the Lord</note> was spilled, the goat to be sent away <note>the scapegoat</note> is left to die;
if the goat to be sent away died, the blood <note>of the sacrificed goat</note> shall be poured out.

---

### Tractate Yoma Chapter 6 Mishnah 2

->**3**<-

He <note>the High Priest</note> comes over to the goat that is to be sent away <term>Se’ir HaMishtaleach: the scapegoat</term>
and leans his two hands upon it and confesses <term>Vidui: the act of verbal confession of sins</term>.
And this is what he would say:
> "Please, **O Name** <note>original: *HaShem*; a substitute used to avoid pronouncing the Tetragrammaton</note>,
> Your people, the House of Israel, have committed iniquity, have transgressed, and have sinned before You.
> Please, **O Name**..." <note>The High Priest would continue by asking for atonement for these sins</note>

However, the High Priests <note>Refers to the priestly families of the Second Temple period who sought to keep the ritual strictly within their control</note> made it a fixed practice, and they would not allow a common Israelite to lead the goat.
**Rabbi Yosei** said: 
Once it happened that **Sheila of Tzippori** <note>Sepphoris, a prominent city in the Galilee</note> <note>original: "kakh" - a scribal mark indicating the spelling is as intended</note> led the goat, and he was a common Israelite.

## Tractate Yoma Chapter 6 Mishnah 4
->5<-

And they would construct a **ramp** for the goat because of the **Babylonians** <term>Babylonians: Historically, this may refer to Jews from Alexandria who were nicknamed "Babylonians"; they were known for their exuberant and sometimes rowdy behavior during the festival</term>, who would pluck at the goat's hair and say to the one leading it:
> "Take [our sins] and go, take and go!" <note>original: "tol ve-tze, tol ve-tze"</note>

The distinguished people of **Jerusalem** would accompany him until the **first booth**. There were **ten booths** along the path from Jerusalem to the **Cliff** <term>Cliff: Heb. "Tzok," the jagged mountain from which the goat was cast</term>. The distance was **ninety *ris*** <term>ris: an ancient unit of distance, approximately 175-200 meters</term>, which is **seven and a half** *ris* for every **mil** <term>mil: a Talmudic mile, roughly 1 kilometer</term>.

## Tractate Yoma Chapter 6 Mishnah 5
->6<-

At every single booth, they would say to the man leading the goat:
> "Here is food and here is water."

And they would accompany him from one booth to the next, except for the person at the final booth. That person would not reach the **Cliff** with him, but would instead stand at a distance and watch his actions. <note>Though food and water were offered to fulfill the law of hospitality, the man never actually ate, as he was fasting for the Day of Atonement</note>

## Tractate Yoma Chapter 6 Mishnah 6
->7<-

And what did he do at the Cliff?
He divided a **tongue-shaped strip of crimson wool** <term>lashon shel zehorit: a piece of wool dyed with the pigment of a mountain worm; traditionally, it was believed this strip would miraculously turn white as a sign of God's forgiveness</term>. Half of it he tied to the rock, and half of it he tied between the goat's horns.
He then pushed the goat backward; it would roll and descend, and it would not even reach halfway down the mountain before it was torn limb from limb.
The man then came and sat under the last booth until it grew dark <note>He remained there until the fast ended, as he could not return to Jerusalem immediately after his task</note>.
And from what point do those involved in the ritual **contract impurity** in their garments?
From the moment the man exits the **wall of Jerusalem**.
**Rabbi Shimon** says:
Only from the moment of the goat’s pushing at the **Cliff**.

### Tractate Yoma Chapter 6 Mishnah 7

->8<-
He <note>The High Priest</note> comes to the **Bull** and to the **Goat** that are to be burned <note>These are the sin-offerings whose blood was previously sprinkled in the Holy of Holies and the Sanctuary; unlike other sacrifices, their remains were burned outside the city</note>.
He tore them open and removed their **sacrificial portions** <term>sacrificial portions: Heb. "emurim," the specific internal fats and organs, such as the kidneys and liver lobe, designated for the altar</term>,
placed them in a **large bowl** <term>large bowl: Heb. "mages," a ceremonial basin</term> and burned them upon the **Altar**.

### Tractate Yoma Chapter 6 Mishnah 8

->9<-

and they would thus know that the goat had reached the wilderness.

->10<-

And was there not a great sign for them?
From **Jerusalem** to **Beit Hidudo** <note>The edge of the wilderness, often identified as a site about 3 miles from the city</note> was **three miles**;
they could walk a mile, return a mile, and wait the duration of a mile,
and they would then know that the goat had reached the wilderness.

### Tractate Yoma Chapter 7 Mishnah 1

The **High Priest** stands and receives [the Torah scroll] and reads while standing.
He reads the portion **"After the death"** <note>Leviticus 16, which details the Yom Kippur service</note> and the portion **"But on the tenth"** <note>Leviticus 23:26-32, regarding the laws of the fast</note>.
He then rolls the Torah scroll and places it in his lap,
and says:
"More than what I have read before you is written here."
Then, the portion **"And on the tenth"** <note>Numbers 29:7-11</note> which is in the **Book of Numbers** <term>Book of Numbers: Heb. "Chumash HaPekudim," literally "The Five-Books of the Countings"</term>,
he recites by heart <note>He recites this from memory rather than rolling the scroll to the different book, so as not to keep the congregation waiting in silence</note>.
And he recites **eight blessings** over it:
For the **Torah**,
and for the **Temple Service**,
and for the **Thanksgiving**,
and for the **Forgiveness of Sin**,
and for the **Sanctuary**,
and for **Israel**,
and for the **Priests**,
and for the **rest of the prayer**.
->(Tractate Yoma Chapter 7 Mishnah 1)<-
<note>The transcription labels this as Mishnah 2, but standard editions identify the preceding text as Mishnah 1.</note>
One who sees the **High Priest** as he is reading
does not see the **Bull** and **Goat** being burned;
and one who sees the **Bull** and **Goat** being burned
does not see the **High Priest** as he is reading.
This is not because one is not permitted [to see both],
but because the distance was great,
and both actions were performed at the same time.

### Tractate Yoma Chapter 7 Mishnah 2

->**2**<-

descended and **immersed** <note>in a Mikvah, or ritual bath</note>, came up and dried himself.

### (Tractate Yoma Chapter 7 Mishnah 3)

He <note>The High Priest</note> **sanctified his hands and feet** <term>Sanctification: Heb. "Kiddush," the ritual washing of hands and feet from a golden basin before and after changing garments</term> and **undressed**,
and he **descended and immersed** <note>In the ritual bath, or Mikveh</note> and **ascended and dried himself**.
They **brought him the white garments** and he **dressed**,
and he **sanctified his hands and feet**.

### 4

He **entered** <note>The Holy of Holies, for the final time</note> **to remove the ladle and the coal pan** <note>These had been left inside the inner sanctum since the morning incense service</note>.
He **sanctified his hands and feet and undressed**,
**descended and immersed, ascended and dried himself**.
They **brought him the golden garments** <note>The "Golden Garments" were the elaborate vestments worn for the daily service, as opposed to the simple white linen worn for the atonement rituals</note> and he **dressed**,
and he **sanctified his hands and feet**.

### 5

He **entered to burn the evening incense**
**and to tend the lamps** <note>The Menorah</note>.
He **sanctified his hands and feet and undressed**.
They **brought him his own garments** <note>His everyday, non-priestly clothes</note> and he **dressed**.
They **escort him to his home**.
He **makes a feast for all his loved ones**
**because he emerged in peace** <note>There was a great fear that the High Priest might die while performing the service in the Holy of Holies; his safe exit was a cause for national celebration</note>.

## Tractate Yoma Chapter 7 Mishnah 5

### 6

The **High Priest serves in eight garments**,
and the **ordinary priest in four**:
In a **tunic** and **breeches**, a **turban** and a **sash**.
The **High Priest adds** to these:
a **breastplate**, and an **ephod** <note>original: "ephod," a decorative apron-like vestment</note>, and a **robe**, and a **frontlet** <note>original: "tzitz," a gold plate worn on the forehead inscribed "Holy to the Lord"</note>.
In **these** <note>The eight garments, specifically the breastplate</note>, **inquiry is made of the Urim and Thummim** <term>Urim and Thummim: Sacred elements of the breastplate used to seek divine guidance</term>.
And **inquiry is not made of them for an ordinary person**,
**but only for the king, and for the court** <note>The Sanhedrin</note>,
**and for one whom the community requires**.

# Tractate Sukkah Chapter 1 Mishnah 5

->6<-

Bundles of straw, bundles of wood, and bundles of brushwood <note>original: זרדים (zeradim), referring to thin or moist twigs used for fuel or fodder.</note>—one may not use them for roofing <term>Skhakh: The "covering" of the sukkah, which must be made of organic material disconnected from the ground.</term>. If one untied them, they are **valid**. And all of these materials are valid for the walls <note>The restrictions on roofing materials are stricter than those for the walls, which can be made of almost anything.</note>.

---

# Tractate Sukkah Chapter 1 Mishnah 6

->7<-

One may roof with planks <note>original: נסרים (nesarim), referring to flat wooden boards.</note>; these are the words of **Rabbi Yehuda**. **Rabbi Meir** forbids it <note>Rabbi Meir is concerned that using wide planks makes the sukkah look too much like a permanent house roof, which might lead people to sit in their homes instead of the ritual booth.</note>. If one placed a plank that is four handbreadths wide <term>Tefachim: Heb. טפחים, a unit of measurement roughly the width of a fist, about 3-4 inches.</term> upon it, the sukkah is **valid**, provided that one does not sleep beneath that specific plank.

---

# Tractate Sukkah Chapter 1 Mishnah 7

->8<-

Regarding a ceiling that has no plaster coating <term>Ma’azivah: Heb. מעזיבה, a layer of clay, lime, or plaster used to level and seal a permanent roof.</term>, **Rabbi Yehuda** says in the name of **the School of Hillel**: One must either loosen the boards <note>original: מפקפק (mefakpek), meaning to physically shake or lift the boards to negate their status as a permanent, fixed ceiling.</note> or remove one board from between the others and replace it with valid roofing. **The School of Shammai** say: One must both loosen the boards *and* remove one from between them. **Rabbi Meir** says: One removes one from between them and there is no need to loosen the rest.

---

# Tractate Sukkah Chapter 1 Mishnah 8

->9<-

One who roofs his *sukkah* with metal spits or with the long side-frames of a bed—if there is a space between them equal to their own width <note>This space must then be filled with valid organic material like bamboo or evergreen branches.</note>, it is **valid**. One who hollows out a haystack to make himself a *sukkah*—this is **not a sukkah** <note>The law requires the roof to be "made" (placed over a space) rather than "found" (by digging into an existing pile). This is known as the principle of *Ta'aseh v'lo min ha-asui*.</note>.

---

# Tractate Sukkah Chapter 1 Mishnah 9

->10<-

One who lowers the walls from the top down—if the wall is higher than three handbreadths from the ground, it is **invalid** <note>A wall that "floats" too far above the ground is not considered a legal barrier.</note>. If one builds from the bottom up—if the wall is ten handbreadths high...

...is **valid**.
**Rabbi Yose** says: Just as from the bottom up [a wall must be] ten handbreadths <term>Tefachim: A unit of measurement roughly the width of a fist, approximately 3–4 inches.</term> high, so too from the top down [a wall hanging from the ceiling] must be ten handbreadths [to be valid]. If one distanced the roofing <term>Skhakh: The ritual covering of the sukkah, which must be made of natural materials.</term> three handbreadths away from the walls, it is **invalid** <note>A gap of three handbreadths or more is considered a significant breach that separates the roof from the wall, making the structure legally "roofless."</note>.

### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 1 Mishnah 10

11
A house that was breached <note>Referring to a permanent house where the center of the roof collapsed or was removed.</note> and one placed ritual roofing over the gap: if there are four cubits <term>Amot: A cubit, roughly the length of a forearm, approx. 18–24 inches.</term> of [permanent ceiling] between the wall and the ritual roofing, it is **invalid** <note>This refers to the rule of "the curved wall" (Dofen Akumah), which allows a small amount of permanent ceiling to be viewed as an extension of the wall, but not if it exceeds four cubits.</note>. Similarly, this applies to a courtyard surrounded by a portico <note>original: אַכְסַדְרָה (akhsadra), a covered colonnade or gallery surrounding an open space.</note>. Regarding a large sukkah that was surrounded with material that is unfit for roofing: if there are four cubits [of that material] beneath it, it is **invalid**.

### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 1 Mishnah 11

12
One who makes his sukkah like a cone-shaped hut <note>original: צְרִיף (tzrif), a structure where the walls slant inward to meet at a point rather than having a flat roof.</note>, or one who leans the roofing against a wall: **Rabbi Eliezer** declares it **invalid** because it has no roof; but **the Sages** declare it **valid**.
A reed mat: [If it is] a large mat and one made it for the purpose of lying upon, it is susceptible to ritual impurity <term>Tum'ah: Ritual impurity. Law dictates that anything designed to be sat or slept upon can become "impure," and such objects are disqualified from being used as sukkah roofing.</term> and one may not roof with it. But if it was made for the purpose of roofing, one may roof with it, and it is not susceptible to ritual impurity.

13
**Rabbi Eliezer** says: Whether it is a large one or a small one—if one made it for the purpose of lying upon, it is susceptible to ritual impurity and one may not roof with it; but if it was made for the purpose of roofing, one may roof with it and it is not susceptible to ritual impurity.

### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 2 Mishnah 1

#### 1

One who sleeps under a bed inside a Sukkah has not fulfilled his obligation <note>Because the bed acts as a second "roof" or tent within the Sukkah, separating the person from the ritual covering (Skhakh).</note>.
**Rabbi Yehuda** said:
We used to have the custom of sleeping under the beds in the presence of the elders.
**Rabbi Shimon** said:
There was an incident involving **Tabi**, the slave of **Rabban Gamliel** <note>Rabban Gamliel was a leading first-century sage. Tabi was his personal servant, renowned for his piety and knowledge of Jewish law.</note>, who used to sleep under the bed.
**Rabban Gamliel** said to the elders:
"Have you seen my slave Tabi? He is a scholar <term>Talmid Chacham: Literally "a student of the wise," a person well-versed in Torah law.</term>, and he knows that slaves are exempt from the commandment of the Sukkah; therefore, he sleeps under the bed" <note>By sleeping under the bed, Tabi showed he knew he was not fulfilling the commandment, thereby demonstrating his knowledge of the law.</note>.
Through our ordinary conversation, we learned that one who sleeps under a bed has not fulfilled his obligation.

### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 2 Mishnah 2

#### 2

If one leans his Sukkah against the legs of a bed, it is **valid**.
**Rabbi Yehuda** says:
If it cannot stand on its own <note>meaning, if the Sukkah would collapse if the bed were moved</note>, it is **invalid**.

#### 3

A "disordered" Sukkah <note>original: הַמְדֻבְלֶלֶת (ha-meduvlelet); referring to a roof where the branches are thin, detached, or hanging unevenly.</note>, if its shade is still greater than its sunlight, it is **valid**.
One that is thick like a house <note>where the roofing material is very dense</note>, even though the stars cannot be seen from within it, is **valid**.

### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 2 Mishnah 3

#### 4

One who makes his Sukkah on top of a wagon or on top of a boat: it is **valid**, and one may go up into it on a Festival <term>Yom Tov: A "Good Day" or Jewish holiday on which work is restricted, similar to the Sabbath.</term>.
If he makes it on top of a tree or on the back of a camel, it is **valid**, but one may not go up into it on a Festival <note>While the Sukkah itself is structurally sound, Rabbinic law prohibits climbing trees or riding animals on a holiday to prevent accidental breaking of branches or other violations.</note>.
If two walls were made by human hands and one was a tree, or two were formed by the tree and one by human hands, it is **valid**, but one may not go up into it on a Festival.

One who makes his Sukkah between trees, such that the trees serve as its walls, it is **valid**.

## Tractate Sukkah Chapter 2 Mishnah 5
->6<-

There was an incident where they brought a dish to **Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai** <note>A primary Jewish sage in the era of the Second Temple's destruction.</note> to taste, and to **Rabban Gamliel** they brought two dates and a bucket of water. 
They said: 
> "Bring them up to the Sukkah!" <note>Even though these were minor snacks, these leaders chose to be extra-stringent and only eat them inside the Sukkah.</note>
But when they gave **Rabbi Tzadok** food less than the volume of an egg <term>Kebetzah: A standard Talmudic unit of measurement, roughly the size of a modern large egg.</term>, he took it with a cloth <note>He used a napkin to avoid the need for ritual hand-washing required for bread.</note> and ate it outside the Sukkah, and he did not recite the blessing after it.

## Tractate Sukkah Chapter 2 Mishnah 6
->7<-

**Rabbi Eliezer** says: 
A person is obligated to eat fourteen meals in the Sukkah—one by day and one by night <note>Referring to the seven days of the festival of Sukkot.</note>. 
But the **Sages** say: 
There is no fixed requirement for this, except for the first night of the Festival alone. 
And **Rabbi Eliezer** said further: 
Whoever did not eat [the required meal] on the first night of the Festival should make it up <note>original: "yashlim" (יַשְׁלִים); to complete or compensate.</note> on the last night of the Festival. 
But the **Sages** say: 
There is no "making up" for this matter; concerning this, it was said: (Ecclesiastes 1:15) 
> "That which is crooked cannot be made straight, <insert>and that which is wanting cannot be numbered.</insert>"

"...and a deficiency that cannot be numbered." <note>original: "v’chesron lo yukhal l’himanot" (וְחֶסְרוֹן לֹא יוּכַל לְהִמָּנוֹת); a quote from Ecclesiastes 1:15. In this legal context, it refers to a religious duty that was missed and can no longer be rectified once the time for it has passed.</note>

### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 2 Mishnah 7

->8<-

One whose head and the majority of his body were inside the Sukkah, but his table was inside the house:
The **House of Shammai** <note>One of the two major schools of early Jewish law, known for a more stringent approach.</note> declare it **invalid**,
and the **House of Hillel** <note>The second major school of law, generally known for a more lenient or pragmatic approach.</note> declare it **valid**.
The House of Hillel said to the House of Shammai:
"There was an incident where the elders of the House of Shammai and the elders of the House of Hillel went to visit **Yochanan the Choronite**, and they found him with his head and the majority of his body in the Sukkah, while his table was inside the house."
The House of Shammai said to them:
"Is that where you find proof? They actually said to him:
'If this is how you have been acting, you have never in your life fulfilled the commandment of the Sukkah!'"

### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 2 Mishnah 8

->9<-

Women, slaves, and minors are exempt from the [obligation of] Sukkah.
However, any minor who no longer needs his mother <note>This usually refers to a child around 5 or 6 years old who no longer wakes up in the night calling for his mother.</note> is obligated in the Sukkah.
There was an incident where the daughter-in-law of **Shammai the Elder** gave birth, and he broke away the plaster of the roof and placed Sukkah-covering <term>Skhakh: The organic material, such as branches or reeds, that forms the roof of the Sukkah.</term> over the bed for the sake of the newborn child.

### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 2 Mishnah 9

->10<-

All seven days [of the festival], a person should make his Sukkah a permanent residence and his house a temporary residence.
If it rains, from what point is it permitted to vacate [the Sukkah]?
From the time the porridge spoils. <note>original: "mikpah" (מִקְפָּה); a thick soup or stew. If it rains hard enough to ruin the food, one is no longer required to stay.</note>
They illustrated this with a parable:
To what is the matter comparable?
To a slave who comes to pour a cup for his master, and the master pours the pitcher <term>Kiton: A water jug or pitcher.</term> back in his face. <note>In this analogy, the slave is the Jewish person trying to perform the commandment, and the rain is seen as a sign from Heaven that the service is not currently desired.</note>

### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 3 Mishnah 1
->1<-

A **stolen** or **dry** lulav <note>The closed, green frond of a date palm; one of the Four Species used during the Sukkot festival.</note> is **invalid** <term>pasul: a legal term meaning the object does not meet the requirements to fulfill a religious duty</term>.
One coming from an **Asherah** <note>A tree worshipped as part of pagan rites, which Jewish law forbids for any benefit.</note> or from a **condemned city** <note>A city whose residents turned to idolatry and whose property must be destroyed according to Deuteronomy 13.</note> is **invalid**.
If its **tip was cut off**, or its **leaves were split**, it is **invalid**.
If its leaves were merely spread apart, it is **valid** <term>kasher: fit for ritual use</term>;
**Rabbi Yehuda** says:
He should **tie it together** at the top.
The palms of the **Iron Mountain** <note>A specific geographical location, likely near the Judean desert or the Dead Sea, known for having very short or rough palm leaves.</note> are **valid**.
Any lulav that is **three handbreadths** <note>A handbreadth (tefach) is approximately 3 to 4 inches; the lulav must be long enough to have a "spine" that extends above the other species.</note> in length, so that it is long enough to be waved,
is **valid**.

### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 3 Mishnah 2
->2<-

A **stolen** or **dry** myrtle branch <note>Original Hebrew: Hadass. The second of the Four Species.</note> is **invalid**.
One coming from an **Asherah** or from a **condemned city** is **invalid**.
If its **tip was cut off**, or if its **leaves were split**,
or if its **berries were more numerous** than its leaves, it is **invalid**;
however, if he **diminished** their number <note>By removing the excess berries.</note>, it becomes **valid**.
But one may **not diminish** them on the Festival day itself <note>Because picking fruit or trimming a plant is a prohibited labor on the holiday.</note>.

### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 3 Mishnah 3
->3<-

A **stolen** or **dry** willow branch <note>Original Hebrew: Aravah. The third of the Four Species.</note> is **invalid**.
One coming from an **Asherah** or from a **condemned city** is **invalid**.
If its **tip was cut off**, or its **leaves were split**,
or if it is a **poplar** <note>Original Hebrew: Tsaf-tsafa. A tree that looks like a willow but is biologically distinct and therefore unfit for the ritual.</note>, it is **invalid**.
One that is **withered**, or that has **lost some of its leaves**, or a **mountain-willow** <note>Original Hebrew: Baal. A willow that grows in dry soil sustained by rain rather than by a river.</note>,
is **valid**.

### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 3 Mishnah 4
->4<-

**Rabbi Ishmael** says:
Three myrtle branches, two willow branches,
one lulav, and one citron <note>Original Hebrew: Etrog. The fourth species, a fragrant citrus fruit.</note> are required;
even if **two** of the myrtles have their tips **cut off** and only one is not cut.
**Rabbi Tarfon** says:
Even if **all three** of them are cut, they are valid.
**Rabbi Akiva** says:
Just as there is only **one** lulav and **one** citron...

## Tractate Sukkah Chapter 3 Mishnah 5
### 5
A **stolen** or **dry citron** <note>Original Hebrew: *etrog*; the citrus fruit that serves as the fourth of the species used on the festival.</note> is **invalid** <term>pasul: a legal term meaning the object does not meet the requirements to fulfill a religious duty</term>.
One coming from an **Asherah** <note>A tree worshipped as part of pagan rites.</note> or from a **condemned city** <note>A city whose residents turned to idolatry; its property is forbidden for use.</note> is **invalid**.
And one of ***orlah*** <note>The fruit of a tree during its first three years of growth, which is forbidden by biblical law for any use.</note> is **invalid**.
And one of **impure *terumah*** <note>A portion of the crop set aside for the priests; if it becomes ritually impure, it cannot be eaten and must be burned, thus it cannot be used for the commandment.</note> is **invalid**.
Regarding one of **pure** [priestly tithe], he should not take it <note>This is a precaution to prevent the fruit from becoming impure through contact with the hands.</note>,
but if he did take it, it is **valid** <term>kasher: fit for ritual use</term>.
Regarding one of ***demai*** <note>Produce purchased from a commoner where it is uncertain if the required tithes were separated.</note>, the **School of Shammai** disqualifies it,
and the **School of Hillel** validates it.
Regarding one of the **second tithe** in Jerusalem <note>A portion of the harvest that must be eaten by the owner within the city of Jerusalem; since it is in its proper place, it is available for use.</note>, he should not take it,
but if he did take it, it is **valid**.

## Tractate Sukkah Chapter 3 Mishnah 6
### 6
If a **scab-like growth** <note>Original Hebrew: *chazazit*; likely a lichen, rust, or fungus that creates a raised blemish on the fruit's skin.</note> spread over **most of it**,
if its ***pitama*** <note>The "nipple" or style at the top of the citron; if it naturally lacks one, it is valid, but its removal through damage is a defect.</note> was removed,
if it was **punctured**, **peeled**, or **split**,
or if it was **missing** any amount, it is **invalid**.
If the **scab-like growth** spread over a **minority of it**,
if its **stem** was removed,
or if it was **punctured** but no part of it was **missing**, it is **valid**.
A **"Cushite"** citron <note>A dark or black citron, possibly referring to a variety from Ethiopia/Sudan or simply one that grew in deep shade.</note> is **invalid**.
And one that is **green like a leek**,
**Rabbi Meir** validates it,
and **Rabbi Yehuda** disqualifies it <note>Yehuda considers it unripe and therefore not a "beautiful" fruit as required by the Torah.</note>.

## Tractate Sukkah Chapter 3 Mishnah 7
### 7
The **minimum size** of a citron:
**Rabbi Meir** says:
Like a **walnut**;
and **Rabbi Yehuda** says:
Like an **egg**.
And for the **maximum size**,
so that he can **hold two** in his **one hand** <note>Referring to holding the citron in one hand and the bundle of the other three species in the other, as per Rabbi Yehuda's specific view on the ritual handling.</note>.
These are the words of **Rabbi Yehuda**.
**Rabbi Yose** says:
**Even if [it requires] both his hands**.

<meta>This page continues the laws concerning the "Four Species" used during the festival of Sukkot. ### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 3 Mishnah 8

#### 8

One may only bind the **palm branch** <note>Original Hebrew: *lulav*.</note> with its own kind <note>Meaning fibers from a palm tree, to ensure the bundle remains a "single unit" of the species.</note>.
These are the words of **Rabbi Yehuda**.
**Rabbi Meir** says:
One may bind it even with **twine**.
**Rabbi Meir** said:
There was an incident involving the **people of Jerusalem**,
who used to bind their palm branches 
with **bands of gold**. <note>Rabbi Meir uses this historical precedent to argue that the binding is merely for convenience or beauty, not a legal requirement of the species itself.</note>

### (Tractate Sukkah Chapter 3 Mishnah 9)

And where [at which points in the prayer] did they shake the branches?
At "**Give thanks to the Lord**" <note>Hebrew: *Hodu la-Adonai*; the opening of Psalm 118.</note> at the beginning and the end,
and also at "**Please, Lord, deliver us**" <note>Hebrew: *Ana Adonai hoshia na* (Psalm 118:25).</note>.
These are the words of the **School of Hillel**.
The **School of Shammai** says:
Also at "**Please, Lord, grant us success**" <note>Hebrew: *Ana Adonai hatzlicha na* (the second half of Psalm 118:25).</note>.
**Rabbi Akiva** said:
I was watching **Rabban Gamliel** and **Rabbi Joshua**,
and while all the people were agitating their palm branches vigorously <note>The Hebrew *metarfim* suggests a shaking so energetic it was perhaps distracting or disorganized.</note>,
they only shook them at "**Please, Lord, deliver us**" alone.

#### 9

One who was **traveling on a journey** and did not have a palm branch in his hand,
when he enters his home, he should take it up at his table <note>Even if he has already begun his meal, he must stop to perform the commandment.</note>.
And if he did not take it in the **morning**, he should take it in the **afternoon**,
for the **entire day** is valid for the commandment of the palm branch.

### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 3 Mishnah 10

#### 10

If a **slave**, a **woman**, or a **minor** <note>Groups who, in the social structure of the time, were not legally obligated to perform this specific time-bound commandment.</note> reads the Hallel <term>Hallel: a prayer service consisting of Psalms 113–118 recited on festivals</term> to a man [who is illiterate],
he must repeat after them whatever they say,
but **may a curse come upon him** <note>This "curse" is a expression of social shame; it was considered a disgrace for a grown man to have neglected his education to the point that he needed those not obligated in the rite to lead him in prayer.</note>.
If an **adult male** reads it to him,
he only answers "**Hallelujah**" <note>Translating the Hebrew "Praise the Lord"; in this case, the listener fulfills his obligation by answering "Hallelujah" at the appropriate breaks rather than repeating every word.</note>.

### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 3 Mishnah 11

#### 11

In a place where it is the **custom to double** the verses [of Hallel], one should double them;
where the custom is to **read them simply** [once], one should read them simply;

...d perform the blessing afterward, he should perform the blessing.
**Everything follows the local custom.**
One who purchases a **palm branch** <note>Hebrew: *lulav*.</note> from another person during the **Sabbatical Year** <note>Hebrew: *Sheviit*; the seventh year of the agricultural cycle in which the land of Israel must lie fallow and commerce of produce is restricted.</note>, 
the seller gives him the **citron** <note>Hebrew: *etrog*.</note> as a **gift**, 
because he is not permitted to purchase it during the Sabbatical Year. <note>Since the citron is a fruit, it is subject to the sanctity of the Sabbatical Year and cannot be sold in a typical commercial transaction; the palm branch, not being a fruit, does not have the same restriction.</note>

### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 3 Mishnah 12

#### 12
Originally, the **palm branch** was taken in the **Temple** <note>Hebrew: *Beit HaMikdash*.</note> for **seven days**, 
but in the **provinces** <note>Hebrew: *medinah*; referring to anywhere outside the Jerusalem Temple.</note> for only **one day**. 
After the **Temple was destroyed**, **Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai** ordained 
that the palm branch should be taken in the provinces for **seven days**, 
in **remembrance of the Temple**; 
and he also ordained that the entire **Day of Waving** <note>Hebrew: *Yom Henef*; the 16th of Nisan, when the "Omer" of the new harvest was waved in the Temple. Before the destruction, new grain could be eaten as soon as the waving was done; afterward, it was forbidden for the entire day to ensure no one ate it prematurely.</note> shall be forbidden for eating new grain.

### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 3 Mishnah 13

#### 13
When the **first festival day** of the holiday falls on the **Sabbath**, 
all the people bring their palm branches to the **synagogue**. 
Each and every person identifies their own and takes it, 
because the Sages said: 
A person does not fulfill his obligation 
on the **first festival day** of the holiday 
with the **palm branch of his fellow**, <note>Based on the biblical verse "And you shall take for yourselves," which the Sages interpreted to mean that the species must be one's own legal property on the first day.</note>
but on all the **rest of the days** of the holiday, 
a person does fulfill his obligation with the palm branch of his fellow.

### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 3 Mishnah 14

#### 14
**Rabbi Yose** says: 
On the **first festival day** of the holiday that falls on the **Sabbath**, 
if one forgot and carried the palm branch out into the **public domain**, he is **exempt** <note>Hebrew: *patur*; meaning he is not liable for a sin offering normally required for desecrating the Sabbath.</note>, 
because he carried it out with permission. <note>Meaning he was preoccupied with the performance of a commandment (mitzvah), which provides a degree of legal leniency for the error.</note>
<insert>(Tractate Sukkah Chapter 3 Mishnah 15)</insert>
A **woman** may receive the branch from the hand of her son or from the hand of her husband 
and **return it to the water** on the **Sabbath**. 
**Rabbi Yehuda** says: 
On the **Sabbath** one may return it, 
on the **Festival** one may add water, 
and during the **Intermediate Days** <note>Hebrew: *Moed* or *Chol HaMoed*; the days between the start and end of the pilgrimage festivals.</note> one may change the water entirely. 
And any **minor** who has the knowledge to shake the branch is **obligated** in the palm branch. <note>This refers to the educational obligation to train children in the performance of commandments.</note>

# Chapter 4

## Tractate Sukkah Chapter 4 Mishnah 1

->**1**<-
->The **palm branch** <note>Hebrew: *lulav*.</note> and the **willow branch** <note>Hebrew: *aravah*.</note> are taken for **six or seven days**;<-
->the **Hallel** <note>A collection of Psalms (113–118) recited on festive occasions.</note> and the **Rejoicing** <note>Hebrew: *Simchah*; the obligation to eat peace-offering sacrifices during the festival.</note> are for **eight days**;<-
->the **Sukkah** and the **Water Libation** <note>The special ceremony of pouring water on the Temple Altar during Sukkot.</note> are for **seven days**;<-
->and the **Flute** <note>Referring to the musical accompaniment (wind instruments) for the "Celebration of the House of the Water Drawing."</note> is for **five or six days**.<-

## (Tractate Sukkah Chapter 4 Mishnah 2)

->The **palm branch** for **seven days**, how so?<-
->If the **first festival day** of the holiday falls on the **Sabbath**,<-
->the palm branch is for **seven days**;<-
->and in all other years, it is for **six days**.<-

## Tractate Sukkah Chapter 4 Mishnah 3

->**2**<-
->The **willow branch** for **seven days**, how so?<-
->If the **seventh day** of the willow ceremony <note>The final day of Sukkot, known as Hoshana Rabbah.</note> falls on the **Sabbath**,<-
->the willow branch is for **seven days**;<-
->and in all other years, it is for **six days**.<-

## Tractate Sukkah Chapter 4 Mishnah 4

->**3**<-
->The commandment of the **palm branch**, how was it performed?<-
->All the people would bring their palm branches to the **Temple Mount**,<-
->and the **attendants** <note>Hebrew: *hazzanim*; in this context, Temple officials or sextons, not prayer leaders.</note> would receive them from their hands,<-
->and arrange them on the roof of the **portico** <note>Hebrew: *itztaba*; a covered colonnade or walkway in the Temple complex.</note>,<-
->while the **elders** would place theirs in the **chamber**.<-
->And they would teach the people to say:<-
->"Whosoever receives my palm branch in his hand,<-
->let it be a **gift** to him." <note>Because the law requires the palm branch to belong to the person who performs the ritual on the first day, this declaration ensured that whoever picked it up the next morning would own it legally.</note><-
->And the next day they would rise early and come,<-
->and the attendants would throw the branches before them,<-
->and the people would snatch them and even **strike one another**.<-
->And when the **Court** <note>Hebrew: *Beit Din*; the religious legal authority.</note> saw that they were coming to a point of danger,<-
->they ordained that each and every person should take the palm branch in **his own home**.<-

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Temple rituals for the festival of Sukkot from the previous page. Having described the palm branch (lulav) ceremony, the text now details the willow branch (aravah) ceremony, the circumambulation of the Altar, and the conclusion of the festival rituals for children.</meta>

### The commandment of the willow, how was it performed?
There was a place below Jerusalem called **Motza**. 
They would go down there and gather large **willow shoots**, 
and they would come and stand them up along the sides of the **Altar**, 
with their tops leaning over the top of the Altar. 
They sounded a long blast, a wavering blast, and a long blast <note>Hebrew: *Tekiah, Teruah, and Tekiah*—the traditional sequence of Shofar sounds.</note>. 
Every day they would circle the Altar one time, 
and they would say: 
> "Please, O Lord, save us now! 
> Please, O Lord, save us now!" <note>original: "Ana Adonai hoshia na." These verses are from Psalm 118:25.</note>

Rabbi Yehuda says they would say: 
> "**I and He**, save us now! 
> **I and He**, save us now!" <note>original: "Ani Ve-hu hoshia na." This is a cryptic phrase. It may be a numerical substitution for the Name of God, or a reference to God sharing in Israel's suffering.</note>

On that day <note>The seventh day of the festival, known today as Hoshana Rabbah.</note>, they would circle the Altar seven times.

(At the time of their departure <note>Missing in the Kaufmann Manuscript</note>, 
what would they say? 
> "Beauty to you, O Altar! 
> Beauty to you, O Altar!"

Rabbi Eliezer says: 
> "To **Jah** and to you, O Altar! 
> To **Jah** and to you, O Altar!" <note>original: "Le-Yah u-le-kha." "Yah" is a shortened form of the Divine Name.</note>)

# Tractate Sukkah Chapter 4 Mishnah 6
**5**
Just as it was performed on a weekday, so was it performed on the **Sabbath**, 
except they would gather the willow branches on the eve of the Sabbath, 
and place them in golden basins so they would not wilt. 
Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka says: 
They would gather **palm fronds** <note>The hard central ribs of the palm branches.</note> 
and strike them against the ground at the sides of the Altar. 
That day was called the "**Day of the Striking of the Palm Fronds**."

## (Tractate Sukkah Chapter 4 Mishnah 7)
Immediately after this, the children would drop their palm branches <note>Hebrew: *lulavim*.</note> 
and eat their **citrons** <note>Hebrew: *etrogim*. This indicates that the commandment to hold the etrog only applied for the duration of the ritual on the final day.</note>.

# Tractate Sukkah Chapter 4 Mishnah 8
**6**
The **Hallel** and the **Rejoicing** are for **eight days**, how so?

### Tractate Sukkah Chapter 4 Mishnah 9

**7**
The **Water Libation** <note>The ritual pouring of water on the Altar, unique to this festival</note> was for seven days. How so? 
A golden flask that held three **log** <note>original: "lugin"—a liquid measure approximately equal to the volume of six eggs</note> would be filled from the **Siloam** <note>original: "Shiloah"—a pool of fresh water in Jerusalem</note>.

one was thick and one was thin, 
so that both [the water and the wine] would finish pouring at the same time <note>Because wine is thicker than water, its hole was wider to ensure the libations, poured simultaneously, ended together</note>.

**8**
The western basin was for the water, 
and the eastern one for the wine. 
If he poured the water into the wine basin, 
or the wine into the water basin, he has fulfilled the obligation.

He would perform the libation with a **log** measure for all eight days.

"**Raise your hand!**"

# Tractate Beitzah

## Chapter 1

### Tractate Beitzah, Chapter 1, Mishnah 1

**1**
**An egg that was laid on a festival day,** <note>original: "Yom Tov." While work is generally forbidden on festivals, the Torah permits labor necessary for food preparation. This Mishnah debates whether an egg formed on the holiday is permitted.</note>
**Beit Shammai say:**
**It may be eaten.**
**And Beit Hillel say:**
**It may not be eaten.** <note>Beit Hillel's school generally rules that an object not designated for use before the holiday begins is "set aside" (Muktzeh) and cannot be handled or consumed.</note>
**Beit Shammai say:**
**[The minimum volume of] <term>leaven</term> is the size of an olive, and <term>leavened bread</term> is the size of a date.** <note>original: "Se'or" (leaven/sourdough starter) and "Chametz" (leavened bread). This refers to the prohibition of owning leaven during Passover.</note>
**And Beit Hillel say:**
**Both this and that are the size of an olive.**

**2**

**He may dig with a <term>spade</term> and cover [the blood].** <gloss><deleted: with a palm branch></gloss> <note>original: "Deker." Beit Shammai permits the labor of digging to fulfill the commandment of covering the blood.</note>

**He may not slaughter,**
**unless he had loose earth prepared [from before the holiday].**
**But they agree,**

**because the ash from the stove is [considered] prepared.** <note>Ash that was already in the stove before the holiday is considered ready for use and does not involve the forbidden labor of "creating" a tool or digging.</note>

### Tractate Beitzah, Chapter 1, Mishnah 10

11

## Chapter 2

### Tractate Beitzah, Chapter 2, Mishnah 1

1
When a **Festival** falls on the eve of the **Sabbath** <note>Friday</note>,
one may not begin cooking on the Festival for the Sabbath,
but he may cook for the Festival [itself],
and if he has leftovers, they are left for the Sabbath.
And one may prepare a cooked dish on the eve of the Festival <note>Thursday</note>,
and rely upon it [to continue cooking] for the Sabbath. <note>This is the legal mechanism called "Eruv Tavshilin." By starting the Sabbath food preparation before the holiday begins, any subsequent cooking done on the holiday is viewed as a continuation of that earlier act rather than a new labor.</note>
**Beit Shammai** say:
[One must prepare] **two cooked dishes**.
And **Beit Hillel** say:
**One cooked dish**.
They agree regarding **fish and the egg** cooked upon it,
that they are [considered] two dishes.
If he ate [the dish] or if it was lost,
he may not cook based on it from the start.
But if even a small amount of it remains,
he may rely upon it for the Sabbath.

# Tractate Beitzah, Chapter 2, Mishnah 5
## **5**
**The House of Shammai say:**
**A person may not heat water for his feet**
**unless it is also suitable for drinking.** <note>On a holiday, labor is permitted only for the necessity of "soul-sustenance" (eating). Shammai argues that heating water specifically for washing feet is a luxury, not a necessity of food preparation.</note>
**But the House of Hillel permit it.**
**One may make a fire and warm himself by it.**

# Tractate Beitzah, Chapter 2, Mishnah 6
## **6**
**In three matters**
**Rabban Gamliel** <note>The head of the Sanhedrin/High Court.</note> **rules strictly, in accordance with the House of Shammai:**
**One may not insulate hot food on a Festival for the Sabbath;**
**one may not assemble a lampstand on a Festival;** <note>original: "zokfin." This refers to putting together a sectional candlestick, which resembles building.</note>
**and one may not bake thick loaves, but only thin wafers.** <note>original: "gritzot... rakikim." Thick bread required more effort and time to prepare.</note>
**Rabban Gamliel said:**
**"In all the days of my father’s house,**
**they never baked thick loaves, but only thin wafers."**
**They [the other Sages] said to him:**
**"What shall we do for your father's house?**
**For they were stringent upon themselves, but lenient for all of Israel"** <note>Meaning: his family's personal piety is commendable, but it does not set the legal standard for the general public, who are permitted to bake thick bread on a holiday.</note>

but one may <term>scrape</term> <note>original: "mekartzipim." A gentler grooming.</note> it. <gloss>scraping with a wooden comb</gloss>
**And the Sages say:**

### Tractate Beitzah, Chapter 2, Mishnah 9

#### 9

A pepper mill is susceptible to <term>impurity</term> <note>original: "temeah." Ritual impurity (Tum’ah) that makes a vessel unfit for use with sacred food.</note> on account of being three types of vessels:
on account of being a "receptacle" <note>the lower part that catches the spice</note>,
on account of being a "metal vessel" <note>the grinding mechanism</note>,

### (Tractate Beitzah, Chapter 2, Mishnah 10)

A child's wagon is susceptible to <term>pressure-impurity</term> <note>original: "midras." A high level of impurity contracted when a person with a specific ritual discharge sits or leans on an object.</note>,
and it may be moved on the **Sabbath**,
but it may not be dragged [on the ground] except over [other] vessels <note>The Sages were concerned that dragging the heavy wagon on soft earth would create a furrow (trench), which is a form of prohibited plowing.</note>.
**Rabbi Judah says:**
No vessels may be dragged [on the ground],
except for the wagon,
because it merely presses down [the earth rather than digging it up].

# Chapter 3

## Tractate Beitzah Chapter 3, Mishnah 1

1
One may not trap fish from **vivaria** <note>original: "bibarin." These are enclosed hunting preserves or ponds where animals or fish are kept.</note> on a **Festival**,
and one may not place food before them <note>The Sages generally forbade feeding animals that are not entirely dependent on human care on a Festival, as it may appear as though one is tending to a commercial stock.</note>.

and one may place food before them.
**Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:**
Not all vivaria are equal.
**This is the general rule:**
Anything that <term>lacks trapping</term> <note>original: "mechussar tzeidah." This refers to an animal that is not yet fully under human control and would require significant effort or specialized tools to catch.</note> is **forbidden** to be caught on a Festival,
but anything that does not lack trapping is **permitted**.

## Tractate Beitzah Chapter 3, Mishnah 2

2
Traps for wild animals, birds, or fish

unless it is known that they were caught <term>before sunset</term> <note>original: "mib'od yom." Literally "while it was still day," meaning before the holiday officially began.</note>.
A story is told of a certain **non-Jew**
who brought fish to **Rabban Gamliel**, and he [Gamliel] said:
"They are **permitted** <note>meaning they were likely caught before the holiday or in a permitted manner.</note>,
but I have no desire to accept them from him."

Even an olive-bulk of raw meat from the place of the <term>slaughter-cut</term> <note>original: "beit tevichatah." This refers to the neck area where the ritual slaughter is performed, which is available immediately.</note> is sufficient.
If one slaughtered it in the field, he should not bring it [back to the home] on a pole or a stretcher <note>because this looks like a weekday commercial activity.</note>;
but he may bring it in his hands, limb by limb.

### Tractate Beitzah Chapter 4, Mishnah 7

7

## Chapter 5

### Tractate Beitzah Chapter 5, Mishnah 1

1
**They may lower fruit through a skylight on a Festival,** <note>To prevent the fruit from rotting or being damaged if a roof is leaking, provided it is done in a way that does not constitute heavy labor.</note>
**but not on the Sabbath.**
**And they may cover fruit with vessels because of a drip [of rain],**
**and similarly wine jars and oil jars.**
**And they may place a vessel under a drip on the Sabbath.** <note>Collecting rainwater in a bowl to prevent it from making a mess is permitted, but one cannot move the fruit themselves on the Sabbath as it involves more significant labor than moving a single vessel.</note>

### Tractate Beitzah Chapter 5, Mishnah 2

2
**Everything for which one is liable on account of Rabbinic "Rest,"** <term>shvut: a category of activities forbidden by the Rabbis to safeguard the biblical prohibition against work.</term>
**or on account of optional acts, or on account of religious duties on the Sabbath,**
**one is likewise liable for on a Festival.**
**And these are those [forbidden] on account of Rabbinic "Rest":**
**They do not climb a tree,**
**and they do not ride upon the back of an animal,**
**and they do not float upon the water,** <note>This refers to swimming, which was restricted lest one come to build a life-preserver or a boat.</note>
**and they do not clap [thighs],**
**and they do not clap [hands],**
**and they do not dance.** <note>These rhythmic activities were restricted to prevent the fixing of musical instruments.</note>
**And these are those [forbidden] on account of optional acts:**
**They do not judge,** <note>Holding court was considered a weekday activity that might lead to writing.</note>

...and they may not consecrate <note>original: "מקדשים" — dedicating an item to the Temple.</note>, nor perform the shoe-removal ceremony <term>chalitzah: a ritual to release a childless widow from the obligation of levirate marriage</term>, nor perform levirate marriage <term>yibbum: marrying the widow of a childless brother to carry on his name</term>. And these are [forbidden] by way of a religious duty: they may not consecrate, nor declare items devoted to the Temple <note>original: "מחרימים" — *cherem*, a specific type of dedication that usually goes to the Priests.</note>, nor make a valuation <note>original: "מעריכים" — pledging the fixed biblical value of a person or item to the Temple.</note>, nor set aside the "heave-offering" <term>terumah: the portion of crops given to the Priests</term> and tithes. All these are forbidden on a Festival, and it goes without saying they are forbidden on the Sabbath. There is no difference between a Festival and the Sabbath except regarding the preparation of food alone <term>ochel nefesh: literally "sustenance for the soul," referring to the permission to cook and prepare meals on a Festival, which remains forbidden on the Sabbath.</term>.

## Tractate Beitzah Chapter 5, Mishnah 3

### 3

Livestock and vessels follow the "feet of the owner" <note>This refers to the *Techum*, the 2,000-cubit travel limit from a person's location at the start of the holy day. An object's "travel rights" are tied to its owner.</note>. If one hands over his animal to his son or to a shepherd, they are still restricted by the owner's feet <note>The animal’s travel limit is determined by the owner's location, not the shepherd's.</note>. Vessels specifically designated for one of the brothers in a household follow his feet; but those that are not specifically designated follow the place where all of them may go <note>If brothers share ownership, the vessel can only be moved within the area that is common to all of their individual travel limits.</note>.

## Tractate Beitzah Chapter 5, Mishnah 4

### 4

One who borrows vessels from a friend before the start of the Festival — they follow the feet of the borrower; [if borrowed] on the Festival itself, they follow the feet of the lender. If a woman borrowed spices from her friend for her pot, or water and salt for her dough — these follow the feet of both of them <note>Because the spices or water are now part of the food, the dish cannot be carried further than the travel limits of either woman allow.</note>. Rabbi Yehuda exempts water and salt, because they have no [tangible] substance <note>They dissolve into the dough and are considered to have lost their independent identity.</note>.

## Tractate Beitzah Chapter 5, Mishnah 5

### 5

A coal follows the feet of the owners, but a flame [may go] anywhere <note>A flame is considered a "non-substantial" entity; unlike a physical coal, it is not restricted to the owner's travel boundary.</note>. Regarding a coal belonging to the Temple property: one who uses it commits sacrilege <term>me'ilah: the transgression of misappropriating sacred property for personal use</term>; but for a flame, one neither benefits [in a way that requires atonement] nor commits sacrilege. (One who carries out a coal to the public domain [on the Sabbath] is liable, but for a flame, he is exempt.)

### Tractate Rosh Hashanah Chapter 1 Mishnah 2

**ג**
At **four seasonal intervals** the world is judged:
On **Passover** <note>original: "Pesach"</note> regarding the **grain**;
On **Shavuot** <note>original: "Atzeret" — the Festival of Weeks</note> regarding the **fruit of the tree**;
And on **Rosh Hashanah**,
**all who enter the world** pass before Him like **young sheep** <note>original: "kivnei maron" — This evocative phrase suggests individuals passing one-by-one through a narrow gate, like sheep being counted or soldiers being reviewed.</note>,

> He who understands all their deeds";
And on the **Festival** <note>Sukkot, the Feast of Tabernacles</note> they are judged regarding **water** <note>Meaning the rainfall for the upcoming year.</note>.

### Tractate Rosh Hashanah Chapter 1 Mishnah 3

**ד**
On account of **six months** messengers go out <note>In the era before a fixed mathematical calendar, the central court in Jerusalem sent messengers to distant communities to announce when a new month had been declared based on the sighting of the moon.</note>:
For **Nisan**, because of **Passover**;
For **Av**, because of the **fast** <note>The 9th of Av, a day of mourning for the destruction of the Temples.</note>;
For **Elul**, because of **Rosh Hashanah**;
For **Tishrei**, because of the **fixing of the festivals** <note>To ensure people knew the correct dates for Yom Kippur and Sukkot.</note>;
For **Kislev**, because of **Hanukkah**;
For **Adar**, because of **Purim**.
And when the **Temple** stood,
they would also go out for **Iyar**, because of the **Minor Passover** <note>original: "Pesach Katan" — also known as "Second Passover," a makeup date for those unable to bring the sacrifice in Nisan.</note>.

**Representations of the shapes of the moon**

and the next day her belly is still between her teeth?" <note>This is a vivid folk idiom. ## Tractate Rosh Hashanah Chapter 3 Mishnah 7

## Tractate Rosh Hashanah Chapter 4 Mishnah 1
### 1
When the festival day of Rosh Hashanah 
fell on the Sabbath, 
they would blow the shofar in the Temple, 
but not in the provinces <term>The provinces: "Medina" in Hebrew, referring to any location outside of the Holy Temple in Jerusalem</term>. 
After the Temple was destroyed, 
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai <note>A leading sage who helped preserve Jewish tradition and law after the Roman destruction of Jerusalem</note> ordained 
that they should blow the shofar in every place where there is a Beth Din <term>Beth Din: A Jewish religious court of law</term>.

Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai ordained that they should blow 
only in Yavne <note>The city where the primary religious leadership relocated after the fall of Jerusalem</note> alone.

The rule applies both to Yavne and to any place where there is a Beth Din.

**Originally,**

**The order of the soundings** <note>original: "סֵדֶר תְּקִיעוֹת" (Seder Tekiot) — the sequence of blasts on the ram's horn.</note> **is three [sets] of three [blasts] each.** <note>This refers to the three themes of the Musaf prayer: Sovereignty, Remembrance, and Shofars, each accompanied by a set of shofar blasts.</note>
**The duration of a *tekiah*** <term>Tekiah: A long, continuous blast of the shofar.</term> **is equal to three *teruahs***. <term>Teruah: A series of short, staccato or sobbing sounds.</term>

**[repeating this sequence] three times.**

**The prayer leader fulfills the obligation on behalf of the many.** <note>Rabban Gamliel believes the communal leader's recitation exempts those in the congregation from praying individually if they are unable to do so themselves.</note>

**to wear sandals, and to have marital relations.** <note>These are "minor" fasts where only eating and drinking are prohibited during the day.</note>

# Tractate Ta'anit Chapter 2, Mishnah 5

## 11

It happened in the days of Rabbi Halafta and in the days of Rabbi Hanina ben Teradion <note>Two prominent scholars of the 2nd century CE. Hanina ben Teradion was one of the ten martyrs killed by the Romans.</note> that a certain prayer leader went before the Ark <note>original: "תֵּבָה" (teivah) — Referring to the portable chest containing the Torah scrolls, which served as the prayer leader's lectern on fast days.</note> and finished the entire blessing, and the people responded after him:
> "Amen! Blast the horns, O Priests, blast!"
> "He who answered Abraham our Father on Mount Moriah,
> may He answer you and hear the sound of your cry this day."
> "Sound the alarm, O sons of Aaron, sound the alarm!" <note>original: "הָרִיעוּ" (hari’u) — To sound a series of short, staccato blasts on the trumpets or shofar, signaling alarm or intense prayer.</note>
> "He who answered your ancestors at the Reed Sea,
> may He answer you and hear the sound of your cry this day."

But when the matter came before the Sages, they said:
"We did not follow this custom except at the Eastern Gate." <note>This refers to the gate of the Temple in Jerusalem. The Sages are clarifying that the specific ritual of shouting "Blast!" or "Sound the alarm!" after the blessings was a unique Temple practice and not meant to be performed in local synagogues.</note>

---

# Tractate Ta'anit Chapter 2, Mishnah 6

## 12

During the first three communal fasts, the men of the Watch <term>Watch: (Hebrew: Mishmar) One of the twenty-four groups of priests who rotated weekly service in the Temple.</term> would fast but not complete the day <note>They would break their fast before sunset so they would have strength to perform the Temple service.</note>, while the men of the Father's House <term>Father's House: (Hebrew: Beit Av) A sub-division of the Watch that was responsible for the Temple service on a specific day of that week.</term> did not fast at all.

During the second three fasts, the men of the Watch would fast and complete the full day, while the men of the Father's House would fast but not complete the day.

During the final seven fasts <note>The most severe fasts, held if the rains still had not fallen.</note>, both these and those—the men of the Watch and the men of the Father's House—would fast and complete the full day.
These are the words of Rabbi Joshua.

However, the Sages say:
During the first three fasts, both these and those did not fast at all.
During the second three fasts, the men of the Watch would fast but not complete the day, while the men of the Father's House did not fast at all.
And during the final seven fasts, the men of the Watch would fast and complete the full day, while the men of the Father's House would fast but not complete the day.

## Tractate Ta'anit Chapter 2, Mishnah 8
14
Everything written in the **Scroll of Fasting** <note>original: "Megillat Ta'anit" — an early Rabbinic document listing joyful dates when fasting and/or eulogizing were prohibited.</note> as a day "not to eulogize," 
the day before it is also forbidden to fast, but the day after it is permitted.

Where it is written "not to fast,"

## Tractate Ta'anit Chapter 2, Mishnah 9
15
A communal fast is not decreed to begin on a Thursday,
so as not to **drive up market prices**; <note>original: "le-hafki'a ha-shearim" — If a fast begins on Thursday and the Sabbath follows on Friday evening, people would buy large quantities of food for both the pre-fast meal and the Sabbath at the same time, leading merchants to raise prices.</note>
rather, the first three fasts are held on
Monday, Thursday, and Monday.
And the second three fasts are held on
Thursday, Monday, and Thursday.
Rabbi Yose says: 
Just as the first fasts do not begin on a Thursday,
so too neither the second set nor the final set.

## Tractate Ta'anit Chapter 2, Mishnah 10
16
A communal fast is not decreed on the **New Moons**,
on **Hanukkah**, or on **Purim**. 
If they had already begun their series of fasts and one of these days occurs, they do not interrupt them; 
these are the words of Rabban Gamliel. 
Rabbi Meir said: 
Even though Rabban Gamliel said "they do not interrupt," 
he would agree that they do not **complete the fast** <note>Meaning, they would eat something before sunset rather than fasting until nightfall, to honor the festive nature of the day.</note>. 
And the same applies to the **Ninth of Av** <note>The major fast day mourning the destruction of the Temple.</note> when it falls on a Friday.

Chapter 3

## Tractate Ta'anit Chapter 3, Mishnah 1

### 1
The order of these fasts <note>referring to the progressive series of fasts mentioned in the previous chapters</note> was stated in relation to the **first rainfall**. <term>First rainfall: (Hebrew: Revi'ah Rishonah) The early rains in the Land of Israel, usually occurring in late autumn, which are crucial for the agricultural cycle.</term>
But regarding **plants** <note>original: "tzmachim" — emerging crops or sprouts</note> that have withered, they sound the alarm for them immediately.
And likewise, if the rains have ceased,
such as if there were **forty days** between one rain and the next,
they sound the alarm for them immediately,
because it is a **plague of drought**. <term>Plague of drought: (Hebrew: Makat Batzoret) A severe lack of rain that threatens the entire season's yield, rather than just a delay in the first rains.</term>

## Tractate Ta'anit Chapter 3, Mishnah 2

### 2
If rains fell for the **plants**
but not for the **trees**,
or for the trees but not for the plants;
or if they fell for both of these,
but not for the **cisterns, ditches, and caves**; <note>referring to the essential water storage systems for drinking water and irrigation</note>
they sound the alarm for them immediately.

## Tractate Ta'anit Chapter 3, Mishnah 3

### 3
And likewise, a city upon which rain did not fall,
as it is written: (Amos 4:7)
> “And I caused it to rain upon one city,
> and upon another city I caused it not to rain;
> one portion was rained upon,
> and the portion whereupon it rained not withered.” <note>original: "ve-himtarti al ir achat..." — The Mishnah cites this verse to show that localized drought is a sign of Divine displeasure.</note>
That city fasts and **sounds the alarm**, <term>Sounds the alarm: (Hebrew: Matri'at) This involves blowing the Shofar (ram's horn) and adding special cries and prayers to the service.</term>
and all its surrounding areas fast but do not sound the alarm.
**Rabbi Akiva** <note>a leading 1st-2nd century sage and one of the most influential figures in Rabbinic Judaism</note> says:
They sound the alarm but do not fast.

## Tractate Ta'anit Chapter 3, Mishnah 4

### 4
And likewise, a city in which there is a **plague** <note>original: "dever" — an outbreak of infectious disease</note> or **collapse**, <note>original: "mapolet" — referring to buildings or walls falling down, usually due to structural instability or natural disaster</note>
that city fasts and sounds the alarm,
and all its surrounding areas fast but do not sound the alarm.
Rabbi Akiva says:
They sound the alarm but do not fast.

## 8

Which is considered a **large town**?
Any town that has ten **men of leisure** <term>original: "batlanim" — ten men of the community who are supported by public funds to be constantly available for prayer services and communal needs</term>. <insert>All</insert>
Less than this is considered a **village**.
Regarding these [Purim dates], the Sages said:
They may move them earlier, but they may not move them later.
But the time for the **priests' wood-offering**, and the fast of the **Ninth of Av**, and the **Festival Offering** <term>original: "Chagigah" — the sacrifice brought by pilgrims during the three festivals</term>, and the **Assembly** <term>original: "Hakhel" — the once-in-seven-years gathering where the King read the Torah to the entire nation</term>,
they move them later and do not move them earlier <note>If these dates fall on a Sabbath, they are postponed until Sunday, unlike Purim which is moved earlier</note>.
Even though they said that they move [Purim] earlier and not later,
it is permitted [on those earlier reading days] to deliver a eulogy or to fast, but **gifts to the poor** <note>Hebrew: matanot la-evyonim</note> must be distributed.

When is this the case?
In a place where people enter [the town from the countryside] on **Monday and Thursday**;

### Tractate Megillah Chapter 1 Mishnah 4

י
If they read the **Scroll** <note>The Scroll of Esther</note> in the **First Adar** <note>original: "Adar Rishon." The Jewish calendar occasionally adds a leap month to stay aligned with the solar year, resulting in two months of Adar</note>, and then the year was **intercalated** <note>The court officially declared it a leap year after the reading had already occurred</note>, they must read it again in the **Second Adar**. 
There is no difference between the **First Adar** and the **Second Adar** except for the reading of the **Scroll** and the giving of **gifts to the poor** <note>These specific Purim obligations are only mandatory in the second Adar during a leap year</note>.

### Tractate Megillah Chapter 1 Mishnah 5

יא
There is no difference between a **Festival Day** <note>Yom Tov</note> and the **Sabbath** except for the **preparation of food** <term>original: "okhel nefesh" — activities like cooking or baking which are permitted on Festivals but strictly forbidden on the Sabbath</term> alone. 
There is no difference between the **Sabbath** and the **Day of Atonement** <note>Yom Kippur</note> except that the willful violation of this [the Sabbath] is punished by **human hands** <note>By an earthly court</note>, and the willful violation of that [the Day of Atonement] is punished by **excision** <term>original: "karet" — a spiritual punishment of being "cut off" from the people, handled by Heaven rather than a human court</term>.

### Tractate Megillah Chapter 1 Mishnah 6

יב
There is no difference between one who is forbidden by a **vow** from deriving **benefit** from his fellow and one who is forbidden by a vow from his fellow's **food**, except for the **right of passage** and the use of **vessels** in which food is not prepared <note>One forbidden from "benefit" cannot even walk on the other's land, while one forbidden only from "food" may still use the other's property for non-culinary purposes</note>.
There is no difference between **vows** <note>A personal obligation to bring an offering</note> and **freewill offerings** <note>An offering of a specific animal</note>, except that for **vows**, one is **responsible for their replacement** <note>If the animal dies or is lost, the person must bring another</note>, but for **freewill offerings**, one is not responsible for their replacement.

### Tractate Megillah Chapter 1 Mishnah 7

יג
There is no difference between a **Zav** <term>original: "zav" — a man experiencing a specific type of ritual impurity due to a physical discharge</term> who experiences **two sightings** and one who experiences **three**, except for the requirement of a **sacrifice** <note>Both are ritually impure, but the third sighting triggers the obligation to bring an offering at the Temple</note>.
There is no difference between a **confined leper** and a **certified leper** <term>original: "metzora" — one afflicted with "tzara'at," a spiritual skin condition often translated as leprosy</term>, except for the **loosening of hair** and the **rending of clothes** <note>The certified leper must let their hair grow wild and tear their clothes as a sign of mourning/warning; the confined leper awaiting a final diagnosis does not</note>.
There is no difference between one declared **pure after confinement** and one declared **pure after certification**, except for the **shaving of hair** and the offering of **birds**.

### Tractate Megillah Chapter 1 Mishnah 8

יד
There is no difference between **Scrolls** <note>Torah, Prophets, and Writings</note> and **Tefillin** <term>original: "tefillin" — phylacteries, small black leather boxes containing parchment scrolls of Torah verses</term> or **Mezuzot** <term>original: "mezuzot" — parchment scrolls affixed to doorposts</term>, except that **Scrolls** may be written in **any language**, but **Tefillin** and **Mezuzot** may only be written in **Assyrian script** <term>original: "Ashurit" — the square Hebrew character still used in Torah scrolls today</term>.
**Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel** says: Even with **Scrolls**, they only permitted them to be written in **Greek**.
