## Tractate Yevamot Chapter 4, Mishnah 9
### 9

In the case of a **widow waiting for a levir** <note>original: "shomeret yavam"—a widow whose husband died childless and is bound to his brother</note> whose brother-in-law <note>a different brother</note> betrothed her sister:
In the name of **Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira**, they said:
We say to him:
"Wait until your **eldest brother** performs an act!" <note>The eldest brother must first resolve the status of the widow through marriage or release before the younger brother can marry her sister.</note>
If the brothers performed the **shoe-removal ceremony** or married the widow,
then he may marry his betrothed wife.
If the widow **dies**, he may marry his wife.
If the **potential levir** dies, he must release his betrothed wife with a **bill of divorce** <term>Get: A formal Jewish divorce document.</term>
and release his brother’s widow with the **shoe-removal ceremony** (Halizah).

## Tractate Yevamot Chapter 4, Mishnah 10
### 10

A widow must not perform the **shoe-removal ceremony** (Halizah) nor enter **Levirate marriage** (Yibbum)
until **three months** have passed <note>after her husband's death</note>.
Similarly, **all other women**
should not marry and should not become **betrothed** <term>Erusin: The legal first stage of marriage which creates a binding tie but does not yet allow the couple to live together.</term>
until three months have passed for them,
whether they are **virgins** or **non-virgins**, **widows** or **divorcees**,
whether they were previously only **betrothed** or fully **married**.
**Rabbi Yehuda** says:
Those who were **married** may be betrothed, and those who were **betrothed** may be married <note>within the three months</note>,
except for a betrothed woman in **Judea**,
because the groom there is **intimate** <note>original: "libo gas bah"—referring to a Judean custom allowing betrothed couples private time, which created a concern regarding paternity.</note> with her.
**Rabbi Yose** says:
**All women** may be betrothed <note>immediately</note>,
except for a **widow**, due to the period of **mourning**.

## Tractate Yevamot Chapter 4, Mishnah 11
### 11

If **four brothers** were married to **four women** and the brothers died childless,
if the **eldest** of the surviving brothers wishes to perform **Levirate marriage** with all of them,
the **permission is in his hand**.

<meta>This page continues the legal discussions of Tractate Yevamot, Chapter 4. Following the previous page's discussion on betrothing the sister of a woman awaiting a levir, this text concludes the rules regarding multiple wives and moves into a foundational debate regarding "mamzerut"—the status of children born from forbidden unions. If a man was married to two women and died childless,
the **intercourse** <term>Yibbum: The act of marrying a deceased brother's widow to continue his line.</term> or the **shoe-removal ceremony** <term>Halizah: A ritual release that frees a widow to marry someone else.</term> of one of them exempts her **rival wife** <term>Tzarah: A co-wife. In levirate law, if one wife is released or married by the brother-in-law, the other co-wives are also released.</term>.
If one wife was **fit** <note>legally permitted to marry a priest or of unblemished status</note> and the other was **disqualified** <note>such as a woman of illegitimate birth</note>,
if he performs the **shoe-removal ceremony**, he should perform it for the **disqualified** one;

# Tractate Yevamot Chapter 4, Mishnah 12

**12**
One who **takes back his divorcee** <note>after she had been married to and then divorced or widowed from another man, which is forbidden in Deuteronomy 24:4</note>,
one who **marries the woman he released through shoe-removal**,
or one who **marries the relative of the woman he released**,
must **divorce** her, and the **offspring is a mamzer** <term>Mamzer: Often translated as "illegitimate," this refers to a child born from a forbidden, incestuous, or adulterous union who faces restrictions in marriage.</term>.
These are the words of **Rabbi Akiva**.
But the **Sages** say:
The offspring is **not a mamzer**.
However, they **agree** in the case of one who marries the **relative of the woman he released**,
that the offspring is a **mamzer**.

# Tractate Yevamot Chapter 4, Mishnah 13

**13**
**Who is considered a mamzer?**
Anyone born from a **forbidden relative** <note>original: "shear basar"—literally "kin of the flesh"</note> for whom there is a prohibition against **entering the congregation** <note>original: "bal yavo"—referring to the biblical law that such individuals may not marry into the community</note>.
These are the words of **Rabbi Akiva**.
**Shimon of Timna** says:
Anyone born from a union for which the parents are liable for **divine excision** <term>Karet: A spiritual penalty of being "cut off" from the people, reserved for the most serious biblical transgressions.</term>.
And the **ruling** follows his words.
**Rabbi Yehoshua** says:
Anyone born from a union for which the parents are liable for **execution by the court**.

If he **divorced her** and then she died, he is **permitted to marry her sister**.
If his **sister-in-law** <note>the widow of his childless brother</note> **dies**, he is **permitted to marry her sister**.
If he performed the **shoe-removal ceremony** for her and then she died, he is **permitted to marry her sister**.

# Chapter 5

## Tractate Yevamot Chapter 5 Mishnah 1
### 1
->Rabban Gamliel says:<-
->There is no **bill of divorce** after another **bill of divorce**,<-
->nor a **formal betrothal** after another **formal betrothal**,<-
->nor **intercourse** after **intercourse**,<-
->nor a **shoe-removal ceremony** after a **shoe-removal ceremony**.<-
->But the Sages say:<-
->There is a **bill of divorce** after another **bill of divorce**, and after a **formal betrothal**,<-
->but after **intercourse** or the **shoe-removal ceremony**, nothing has effect.<-

<note>Rabban Gamliel argues that the first legal act performed on a widow completely "fills" that category of action; once a man gives a woman a divorce document (Gett), a second one is redundant. The Sages argue that some acts only partially change her status, allowing subsequent acts to create further legal complications.</note>

## Tractate Yevamot Chapter 5 Mishnah 2
### 2
->How so?<-
->If he performed **formal betrothal** <term>Ma'amar: A rabbinic requirement where the brother-in-law gives money or a document to betroth the widow before the final marriage.</term> with his **widowed sister-in-law** <term>Yevamah: The childless widow awaiting levirate marriage.</term> and then gave her a **bill of divorce**,<-
->she still requires from him the **shoe-removal ceremony**.<-
->If he performed **formal betrothal** with her and then performed **shoe-removal**,<-
->she still requires from him a **bill of divorce**.<-
->If he performed **formal betrothal** with her and then had **intercourse**,<-
->this is in accordance with the commandment.<-

<note>The "commandment" refers to the biblical duty of Yibbum (levirate marriage). Since the betrothal and intercourse were both done by the same man to the same woman, the marriage is successfully completed.</note>

## Tractate Yevamot Chapter 5 Mishnah 3
### 3
->If he gave a **bill of divorce** and then performed **formal betrothal**,<-
->she requires both a **bill of divorce** and the **shoe-removal ceremony**.<-
->If he gave a **bill of divorce** and then had **intercourse**,<-
->she requires both a **bill of divorce** and the **shoe-removal ceremony**.<-
->If he gave a **bill of divorce** and then performed **shoe-removal**,<-
->nothing follows the **shoe-removal**.<-

<note>Once a divorce document is given, the "holy" connection of the levirate bond is damaged. Therefore, even if he follows it with intercourse, it cannot be a perfect fulfillment of the commandment, and they must separate.</note>

### 4
->If he performed **shoe-removal** and then performed **formal betrothal**, gave a **bill of divorce**, or had **intercourse**—<-
->or if he had **intercourse** and then performed **formal betrothal**, gave a **bill of divorce**, or performed **shoe-removal**—<-
->nothing has any effect after the **shoe-removal ceremony**.<-
->This applies whether to **one widow** or to **two widows**.<-

<note>The shoe-removal ceremony (Halizah) is the ultimate legal "seal." Once it is performed, the widow is completely released from the levirate bond, and no subsequent levirate-specific acts (like Ma'amar) have any legal standing.</note>

<summary>This page discusses the legal validity of sequential acts—divorce, betrothal, intercourse, and shoe-removal—performed on a widow awaiting levirate marriage. It highlights the debate between Rabban Gamliel and the Sages over whether a second act carries legal weight after a first one has been performed.</summary>

<keywords>levirate marriage, Yibbum, Halizah, Ma'amar, Gett, sequence of acts, Rabban Gamliel, Sages, legal status, divorce</keywords>

<header>Tractate Yevamot Chapter 7 Mishnah 5</header>

->6<-

One who coerces <note>original: "ha-ones," referring to a rapist</note>, or one who seduces, or one who is mentally incompetent, neither disqualifies a woman [from eating priestly tithes] nor enables her to eat them. But if they are among those who are unfit to enter into the assembly of Israel <note>i.e., people with whom marriage is biblically forbidden, such as certain non-Jewish groups or those of specific prohibited lineages</note>, behold, these disqualify her.

How so?
If an Israelite <note>a non-priestly Jew</note> had relations with a priest’s daughter, she may [continue to] eat of the <term>Terumah: the portion of crops given to the priests, which may only be eaten by those in a state of ritual purity who belong to a priestly household</term>;
If he impregnated her, she may not eat of the priestly tithe;
If the fetus was terminated <note>lit. "cut"</note> in her womb, she may eat.

If a priest had relations with an Israelite’s daughter, she may not eat of the priestly tithe;
If he impregnated her, she may not eat;
Once she has given birth, she may eat.
Thus, it is found that the power of the son is greater than the power of the father <note>The father's act alone did not grant the mother the right to eat his priestly food, but the birth of his son does.</note>.

->7<-

A slave disqualifies a woman [from eating priestly tithe] by means of intercourse, but he does not disqualify her by means of offspring.

How so?
[If] an Israelite’s daughter married a priest, or a priest’s daughter married an Israelite,
and she bore a son from him,
and the son went and had relations with a female slave, and she bore a son from him,
behold, this [grandson] is a slave.

If the father’s mother was an Israelite’s daughter married to a priest,
she may no longer eat of the priestly tithe <note>Because her son is dead and her only descendant is a slave, who does not legally count as "offspring" to maintain her priestly status.</note>;
If she was a priest’s daughter married to an Israelite, she may [return to her father's house and] eat of the priestly tithe.

->8<-

A <term>Mamzer: A person born from certain forbidden unions, such as adultery or incest</term> disqualifies and enables eating.

How so?
[If] an Israelite’s daughter married a priest, or a priest’s daughter married an Israelite,
and she bore a daughter from him,
and the daughter went and married a slave,
or married a gentile, and bore a son from him,
behold, this [grandson] is a mamzer.

If his mother’s mother was an Israelite’s daughter married to a priest,
she may [continue to] eat of the priestly tithe <note>In this specific legal context, the mamzer grandson is considered a valid descendant who maintains his grandmother's right to eat her husband's priestly food.</note>;
But if she was a priest’s daughter married to an Israelite,
she may not eat of the priestly tithe.

# Tractate Yevamot Chapter 7 Mishnah 6

### 9

A **High Priest** <note>original: "Kohen Gadol"</note>, there are times when he **disqualifies** [his relative from eating priestly food].
How so?
The daughter of a priest <note>who was born into a priestly family and has the right to eat sacred food</note> married an **Israelite** <note>original: "Yisrael," referring here to a Jewish man who is not a priest</note>,
and she bore a daughter from him,
and that daughter went and married a priest,
and she bore a son from him.
Behold, this son is worthy to become a **High Priest**,
standing and serving upon the **altar**,
and he enables his mother <note>the daughter of the Israelite</note> to eat [priestly food, because she is the mother of a priest's son],
but he **disqualifies** his maternal grandmother <note>the original priest's daughter. Because she has a living descendant from her marriage to a non-priest, she cannot return to eating her father's priestly food after her husband's death</note>.
This woman [the grandmother] says:
"Let my grandson not be like a High Priest,
for he disqualifies me from the **Terumah** <term>Terumah: the "heave-offering" or sacred gift of produce given to priests, which may only be eaten by priests and their eligible household members</term>."

# Tractate Yevamot Chapter 8 Mishnah 1

The **uncircumcised** and all those who are **ritually impure**

Their wives and their slaves may eat.

they and their slaves may eat,
but their wives may not eat <note>These men are biblically forbidden from entering the "assembly of the Lord" in marriage. Therefore, their marriage is not legally recognized in a way that would grant the wife the right to eat the husband's priestly food</note>.

behold, these [wives] may eat.

## Tractate Yevamot Chapter 8 Mishnah 3
### 3

An **Ammonite** and a **Moabite** [male convert] are **forbidden** [from marrying into the assembly],
and their prohibition is an **eternal prohibition**,
but their **females** are **permitted immediately**. <note>The tradition interprets the biblical prohibition as applying only to the men of these nations, as they failed to greet the Israelites with bread and water.</note>
An **Egyptian** and an **Edomite**
are only forbidden until the **third generation**,
whether they are **males** or **females**.
[**Rabbi Shimon** permits the females immediately.]
**Rabbi Shimon** said:
This is a matter of **logical inference** <note>original: "Kal Vachomer," a "light and heavy" logical argument</note>:
If in a case where the law forbade the **males** with an **eternal prohibition** [Ammon and Moab],
it nevertheless permitted the **females immediately**,
then in a case where it did not forbid the **males**
except until the **third generation** [Egypt and Edom],
is it not logical that we should permit the **females immediately**?
They said to him:
> "If this is a received **law** <term>Halakhah: a binding legal tradition passed down through generations</term>, we shall accept it,
> but if it is based on **logical deduction**, there is a rebuttal."
He said to them:
> "Not so; rather, I am stating a **received law**!"
**Bastards** <term>Mamzerin: children born from forbidden, incestuous, or adulterous unions</term> and **Netinim** <term>Netinim: descendants of the Gibeonites who served as temple laborers</term> are **forbidden**,
and their prohibition is an **eternal prohibition**,
applying to both **males** and **females**.

## Tractate Yevamot Chapter 8 Mishnah 4
### 4

**Rabbi Joshua** said:
I heard a tradition that the **saris** <term>Saris: a man who is sterile or has been castrated; a eunuch</term> performs **chalitzah** <term>Chalitzah: the "removal of the shoe" ceremony that releases a childless widow from the obligation of marrying her deceased husband's brother</term>, and others perform **chalitzah** for his wife,
and [conversely] that the **saris** does not perform **chalitzah**, and others do not perform **chalitzah** for his wife,
but I have no way to **explain** [the difference between these two contradictory traditions].
**Rabbi Akiva** said:
I will **explain** them:
A **saris by human action** <note>one who was castrated by man or through illness after birth</note> performs **chalitzah**, and others perform **chalitzah** [for his wife],
because he once had a **time of fitness** <note>meaning he was born fertile and later became sterile</note>.
A **saris by nature** <note>original: "saris chama," literally "a eunuch of the sun," meaning one who was born sterile</note> does not perform **chalitzah**, and others do not perform **chalitzah** for his wife [because he was never fit to procreate].

...because he never had a **moment of fitness** <note>original: "she'at kosher"—a time when he was physically capable of fulfilling the obligation of fathering children</note>.
**Rabbi Eliezer** says:
Not so; 
rather, a **sun-eunuch** <term>Saris hammah: a man who is born sterile, as though the sun "saw" him in this state from birth</term> performs the **shoe-removal ceremony** <term>Halitzah: a ceremony that releases a widow from the obligation to marry her deceased husband's brother</term>, and they perform the ceremony for his wife,
because he has a **cure** <note>Rabbi Eliezer refers to historical or theoretical medical treatments for congenital conditions</note>.
A **man-made eunuch** <term>Saris adam: a man who became sterile through human intervention or injury</term> neither performs the shoe-removal ceremony, nor do they perform it for his wife,

<meta>This page continues the discussion of a woman's status and rights within the Jewish social hierarchy—specifically concerning the Priests, Levites, and common Israelites—and how marriage and offspring determine her right to eat sacred tithes.</meta>

**7**
A **daughter of an Israelite** <note>a woman born to a commoner family, not of the priestly or Levite lines</note> who married a **priest**,
she may eat of the **Terumah** <term>Terumah: the "heave-offering," a portion of the harvest given to priests that may only be eaten by them and their households in a state of ritual purity</term>;
If he died, and she has a **son from him**,
she may still eat of the **Terumah** <note>The presence of a priestly son preserves her status as a member of a priestly household</note>.
If she then married a **Levite**,
she may eat of the **Ma'aser** <term>Ma'aser: the first tithe of the harvest, which is the designated portion for the tribe of Levi</term>;
If he died, and she has a **son from him**,
she may still eat of the **Ma'aser**.
If she then married an **Israelite** <note>a commoner</note>,
she may eat neither of the **Terumah** nor of the **Ma'aser**.

**8**
If **her son from the Israelite died**,
she may eat of the **Ma'aser** <note>By the death of the son who tied her to the commoner class, she "returns" to the status of her surviving son from the Levite</note>.
If her son **from the Levite** died,
she may eat of the **Terumah** <note>With the Levite son gone, she "returns" to the status afforded by her surviving son from the priest</note>.
If **her son from the priest died**,
she may eat neither of the **Terumah** nor of the **Ma'aser** <note>Having lost all sons who gave her status, and being a commoner by birth, she no longer has any claim to sacred tithes</note>.

### Tractate Yevamot Chapter 9 Mishnah 6

**9**
A **daughter of a priest** <note>a woman born into a priestly family</note> who married an **Israelite**,
she may **not eat of the Terumah** <note>Marriage to a commoner disqualifies a priest's daughter from eating the sacred offerings of her father's house</note>;
If he died, and she has a **son from him**,
she may **not eat of the Terumah**.
If she then married a **Levite**,
she may eat of the **Ma'aser**;
If he died, and she has a **son from him**,
she may still eat of the **Ma'aser**.
If she then married a **priest**,
she may eat of the **Terumah**;
If he died, and she has a **son from him**,
she may eat of the **Terumah**.
If **her son from the priest died**,
she may **not eat of the Terumah** <note>Her remaining son from the Levite or Israelite prevents her from regaining her full priestly status</note>.
If her son **from the Levite** died,
she may **not eat of the Ma'aser**.
If **her son from the Israelite died**,
she **returns to her father’s house**. Of her it is said: <note>original: Leviticus 22:13</note>
> "And she returns to her father’s house as in her youth, [she may eat of her father’s bread]."

# Chapter 10

## Tractate Yevamot Chapter 10 Mishnah 1

**1**
In the case of **a woman whose husband went to a province across the sea** <note>original: "מדינת הים" (Medinat HaYam); a term used in the Mishnah for any distant land or overseas territory</note>,
and people **came and told her: "Your husband is dead,"**
**and she remarried**,
**and afterward her [first] husband returned**;
**she must leave this one** <note>the first husband</note> **and that one** <note>the second husband</note>,
**and she requires a bill of divorce** <term>Gett: a formal Jewish document of divorce</term> **from this one and from that one**.
**She has no claim to a marriage contract** <term>Ketubah: the financial settlement a husband owes a wife upon death or divorce</term>, **nor to the usufruct** <note>the right to profits from her property</note>,
**nor to maintenance** <note>alimony/support</note>, **nor to worn-out items** <note>the remains of the goods she brought into the marriage</note> **from this one or from that one**.
**If she had already taken [these payments] from this one or from that one, she must return them**.
**And the child [born of the second marriage] is a mamzer** <term>Mamzer: a child born from a forbidden relationship, such as adultery, who faces significant restrictions in Jewish marriage law</term> **from this one and from that one** <note>the child is legally stigmatized regardless of which husband's lineage is considered</note>.
**Neither this one nor that one may become ritually impure for her** <note>if they are Priests, they are forbidden from tending to her burial</note>.
**And neither this one nor that one is entitled to what she finds**,
**nor to the work of her hands, nor to the annulment of her vows**.
If **she was the daughter of an Israelite** <note>a commoner</note>, **she is disqualified from the Priesthood** <note>she can no longer marry a Priest</note>;
**if she was the daughter of a Levite, she is disqualified from the tithe** <term>Ma'aser: the portion given to Levites</term>;
**and if she was the daughter of a Priest, she is disqualified from the Terumah** <term>Terumah: the sacred "heave-offering" given to Priests</term>.
**The heirs of this one and the heirs of that one do not inherit her marriage contract**.
**If the brothers of this one or the brothers of that one die**,
**they perform the chalitzah ceremony** <term>Chalitzah: the "removal of the shoe" ceremony that releases a childless widow from the obligation of marrying her brother-in-law</term> **and they do not perform levirate marriage** <term>Yibbum: the practice of a man marrying his deceased brother's childless widow</term>.

**2**
**Rabbi Yose says:**
**Her marriage contract is [still a lien] upon the property of her first husband**.
**Rabbi Elazar says:**
**The first husband is entitled to what she finds and to the work of her hands**,
**and to the annulment of her vows**.
**Rabbi Shimon says:**
**Intercourse or the chalitzah ceremony [performed] by the brothers of the first husband exempts her co-wife** <note>if the first husband had other wives, the actions taken regarding this woman affect their status as well</note>,
**and the child from him** <note>the second husband</note> **is not a mamzer**.
**And if she remarried without permission** <note>meaning she remarried based on her own testimony or without a formal court decree</note>,
**she is permitted to return to him** <note>to the first husband, according to Rabbi Shimon's lenient view in specific circumstances</note>.

# Tractate Yevamot Chapter 10 Mishnah 2
## 3
If she **remarried based on the ruling of a court** <term>Beit Din: a rabbinical court of three or more judges</term>,
**she must leave** <note>she must divorce both the first and second husband</note>, **but she is exempt from bringing a sacrifice** <note>original: "קרבן" (Korban); specifically the sin-offering usually required for unintentional adultery, because she acted on the court's legal authority</note>.
**But if** she remarried **not based on the ruling of a court**,
**she must leave, and she is liable to bring a sacrifice**.
**The power of the court is considered "beautiful"** <note>meaning "effective" or "great"</note>,
**as she is exempt from the sacrifice** due to their ruling.
If **the court instructed her to remarry,**
**and she went and acted corruptly** <note>original: "וקלקלה" (v'kilkelah); this refers to engaging in a forbidden sexual relationship or promiscuity rather than a formal marriage</note>,
**she is liable to bring a sacrifice,**
**because they only permitted her to remarry** <note>their legal protection only applies to the specific act of marriage they authorized based on the evidence</note>.

# Tractate Yevamot Chapter 10 Mishnah 3
## 4
In the case of **a woman whose husband and son went to a province across the sea,**
and people **came and told her:**
> **"Your husband died, and afterward your son died,"** <note>in this order, the woman is free to marry anyone, as her husband had a living heir at the moment of his death</note>
**and she remarried,**
**and afterward they told her:**
> **"The matters were reversed,"** <note>meaning the son died first, then the husband, which would mean the husband died childless and she was actually bound to her brother-in-law in a Levirate marriage</note>
**she must leave, and the child [born] first or last is a mamzer** <term>Mamzer: a child born from a forbidden relationship, such as adultery or certain cases of incest, who faces marriage restrictions</term>.

## 5
If **they said to her:**
> **"Your son died and afterward your husband died,"**
**and she performed a Levirate marriage** <term>Yibbum: the Torah's requirement for a man to marry his deceased brother’s childless widow to continue the brother's line</term>,
**and afterward they told her:**
> **"The matters were reversed,"** <note>the husband died while the son was still alive, meaning no Levirate obligation ever existed and she was forbidden to her brother-in-law as "a brother's wife"</note>
**she must leave, and the child [born] first or last is a mamzer.**

## 6
If **they said to her:**
> **"Your husband died,"**
**and she remarried,**
**and afterward they told her:**
> **"He was alive at the time** of your remarriage, **but then he died,"**
**she must leave. The child born first is a mamzer,**
**but the child born last is not a mamzer** <note>The child conceived while the first husband was still alive is a product of adultery. However, the child conceived after he died—though the mother is still forbidden to the second husband by rabbinic decree—is not legally a mamzer because she was technically a widow at the time of conception</note>.

They said to her:
'**Your husband died**,'
and **she became betrothed** <term>Kiddushin: the formal first stage of Jewish marriage which requires a legal divorce to break, even if the marriage was not consummated</term>,
and **afterward her husband arrived**,
**she is permitted to return to him**.
**Even though the second man gave her a bill of divorce** <note>original: "גט" (Get)</note>,
**he did not disqualify her from the priesthood** <note>According to biblical law (Leviticus 21:7), a Kohen (priest) may not marry a divorcee. However, since her betrothal to the second man was invalid (as her first husband was alive), the divorce is legally redundant and does not grant her the status of a "divorcee" that would forbid her to her priest-husband</note>.
**This is the exposition that Rabbi Eleazar ben Matya expounded:** (Leviticus 21:7)
"**And a woman divorced from her husband**" <note>original: "ואשה גרושה מאישה"</note> —
**and not a woman divorced from a man who is not her husband** <note>Rabbi Eleazar uses a close reading of the text to prove that a divorce only carries legal weight and consequences if it is from a valid, legal husband</note>.

### Tractate Yevamot Chapter 13 Mishnah 4
#### 4

->One who performs <term>refusal</term> <note>original: "מְמָאֶנֶת" (mema'enet); the act of mi'un, where a minor girl annuls her marriage.</note> against a man,<-
->he is permitted to marry her relatives, and she is permitted to marry his relatives,<-
->and the act does not disqualify her from the <term>priesthood</term> <note>original: "כְּהֻנָּה" (Kehunah). According to Jewish law, a woman who has been divorced may not marry a Kohen (a member of the priestly class). However, "refusal" is an annulment rather than a divorce, so this restriction does not apply.</note>.<-
->But if he gave her a bill of divorce <note>original: "גֵּט" (get)</note>,<-
->he is forbidden from marrying her relatives and she is forbidden from marrying his relatives,<-
->and the divorce disqualifies her from the priesthood.<-
->If he gave her a bill of divorce and then took her back as a wife,<-
->and she then performed refusal against him and married another man,<-
->and was subsequently widowed or divorced from that second man,<-
->she is permitted to return to her first husband.<-
->However, if she performed refusal against him and he then took her back,<-
->and then he gave her a bill of divorce and she married another man,<-
->and was subsequently widowed or divorced,<-
->she is forbidden to return to him.<-
->This is the general rule:<-
->If a bill of divorce follows refusal, she is forbidden to return to him.<-
->If refusal follows a bill of divorce, she is permitted to return to him.<- <note>The law treats the "last" act as the defining status of their separation. A formal divorce (get) creates a permanent barrier that prevents remarriage if she marries someone else in between, whereas refusal (mi'un) essentially "erases" the previous marriage.</note>

->Any husband from whom she departed with a bill of divorce, she is forbidden to return to him;<-
->But any husband she departed from through refusal, she is permitted to return to him.<-

### Tractate Yevamot Chapter 13 Mishnah 7

If two brothers are married to two minor orphan sisters, 
and the husband of one of them dies, 
she is released from any obligation to her brother-in-law because she is the **sister of his wife** <note>In Jewish law, a man is forbidden from marrying his wife's sister while his wife is alive. Since the surviving brother is already married to the widow's sister, the levirate bond cannot be realized.</note>.

And likewise, if two deaf-mute sisters <note>original: "חֵרְשׁוֹת" (chershot); in this historical legal context, deaf-mutes were considered to have a different level of legal competence regarding contracts like marriage.</note>, one an adult and one a minor, were married to two brothers:

**Rabbi Eliezer** says: 
We instruct the minor to perform <term>refusal</term> <note>original: "תְּמָאֶנֶת" (tema'enet); an annulment of marriage by a minor girl.</note> against him <note>the surviving husband</note>, so that she is no longer his wife, and he can then perform levirate marriage with the widow.

**Rabban Gamliel** says: 
If she performs refusal, she has refused; 
but if not, she must wait until she reaches adulthood, 
and then the widow is released from him because she is the sister of his wife.

**Rabbi Joshua** says: 
Woe to him for his wife, 
and woe to him for the wife of his brother! <note>A phrase expressing a legal dilemma where the husband may lose both relationships.</note>
He must release his wife with a **bill of divorce** <note>original: "גֵּט" (get)</note>, 
and his brother's wife with the **ritual of shoe-removal** <note>original: "חֲלִיצָה" (chalitzah); the ceremony that releases a widow from the requirement of levirate marriage.</note>.

### Tractate Yevamot Chapter 13 Mishnah 8

8
If a man was married to two minor orphan sisters and then died, 
the sexual act <note>original: "בִּיאָתָהּ" (bi'atah); the consummation of the levirate marriage.</note> or the ritual of shoe-removal performed by one of them exempts her <term>co-wife</term> <note>original: "צָרָתָהּ" (tzaratah); the term for a fellow wife in a polygamous marriage.</note> from further obligation. 
The same applies to two deaf-mutes.

However, if one was a minor and the other a deaf-mute, 
the act of one of them does **not** exempt her co-wife <note>Because their legal statuses are derived from different rabbinic decrees, the act of one does not satisfy the requirements for the other.</note>.

9
If one wife was of sound senses and the other was a deaf-mute, 
the act of the one with sound senses exempts the deaf-mute, 
but the act of the deaf-mute does **not** exempt the one with sound senses.

10
If one wife was an adult and the other was a minor, 
the act of the adult exempts the minor, 
but the act of the minor does **not** exempt the adult.

### Tractate Yevamot Chapter 13 Mishnah 9

->**11**<-

**One who was married to two minor orphans, and died,** <note>original: "שְׁתֵּי יְתוֹמוֹת קְטַנּוֹת" (shetei yetomot ketannot). These are girls under the age of twelve whose fathers have died. Their mother or brothers married them off, making their marriage valid by Rabbinic decree but not by full Scriptural law.</note>
**and the levir <term>performed levirate marriage</term> with the first,** <note>original: "בָּא הַיָּבָם" (ba ha-yabbam), literally "the levir came upon," a euphemism for the act of cohabitation that consummates the levirate marriage.</note>
**and subsequently performed levirate marriage with the second,**
**or his brother performed levirate marriage with the second,**
**he did not disqualify the first.** <note>Because both marriages are of equal legal weight (both are Rabbinic), the second act does not invalidate the first marriage to her sister.</note>
**And likewise, the same applies to two deaf-mutes.** <note>original: "חֵרְשׁוֹת" (chershot); like minors, their marriages are recognized by Rabbinic law rather than Scriptural law.</note>
**In a case involving a minor and a deaf-mute:**
**If the levir performed levirate marriage with the minor,**
**and subsequently performed levirate marriage with the deaf-mute,**
**or if his brother performed levirate marriage with the deaf-mute,**
**he did not disqualify the minor.**
**But if the levir performed levirate marriage with the deaf-mute,**
**and subsequently performed levirate marriage with the minor,**
**or if his brother performed levirate marriage with the minor,**
**he disqualified the deaf-mute.** <note>This suggests that in the hierarchy of Rabbinic status, the marriage of a minor is considered slightly "stronger" than that of a deaf-mute, or at least creates a legal conflict that affects the first woman's status.</note>

### Tractate Yevamot Chapter 13 Mishnah 10

->**12**<-

**In a case involving a competent woman and a deaf-mute:** <note>original: "פִּקַּחַת" (pikkachat); literally one who is "open-eyed" or "hearing," referring to a woman with full legal capacity whose marriage is recognized by Scriptural law.</note>

**and subsequently performed levirate marriage with the deaf-mute,**
**or if his brother performed levirate marriage with the deaf-mute,**
**he did not disqualify the competent woman.**
**But if the levir performed levirate marriage with the deaf-mute,**
**and subsequently performed levirate marriage with the competent woman,**
**or if his brother performed levirate marriage with the competent woman,**
**he disqualified the deaf-mute.** <note>The Scriptural marriage of the competent woman is so much stronger than the Rabbinic marriage of the deaf-mute that the act with the competent woman effectively overrides and cancels the bond with the deaf-mute sister.</note>

### Tractate Yevamot Chapter 13 Mishnah 12

->**14**<-

**A minor <term>levir</term>** <note>A boy under the age of thirteen who is obligated to perform the levirate marriage for his deceased brother's wife.</note> **who performed levirate marriage with a minor levirate widow,**
**they shall grow up together.** <note>The marriage is valid by Rabbinic law, and they live together until they reach adulthood, at which point the marriage gains full legal standing.</note>
**If he performed levirate marriage with an adult levirate widow, she shall raise him.**
**A levirate widow who said within thirty days: "I have not had intercourse,"**
**we compel him to perform <term>chalitzah</term> for her;** <note>original: "חֲלִיצָה" (chalitzah). This is the "removal of the shoe" ceremony that releases a widow from the levirate obligation, allowing her to marry someone else.</note>
**after thirty days,**
**we request from him that he perform chalitzah for her.** <note>The court uses persuasion rather than force, as the delay in her claim creates a doubt as to her honesty.</note>

**even after twelve months,**
**we compel him to perform chalitzah for her.**

### Tractate Yevamot Chapter 13 Mishnah 13

->**15**<-

**One who vows against deriving benefit from her levir,** <note>A woman who makes a religious vow to avoid any contact or benefit from her brother-in-law, perhaps to avoid being forced into a levirate marriage.</note>
**if [the vow was made] while her husband was alive, we compel him to perform <term>chalitzah</term> for her;**
**after her husband’s death, we request from him that he perform chalitzah for her.**
**If she intended this [vow specifically to avoid the levirate marriage],**

### Tractate Yevamot Chapter 14 Mishnah 1

->**1**<-

**A <term>deaf-mute</term>** <note>original: "חֵרֵשׁ" (cheresh). In Rabbinic law, this term usually refers to someone who can neither hear nor speak.</note> **who married a woman with sound senses, or a man with sound senses who married a deaf-mute:**
**if he wishes, he may divorce her, and if he wishes, he may maintain [the marriage].**
**Just as he marries through gestures, so he may divorce through gestures.** <note>Since a deaf-mute was traditionally considered to lack full legal "competence," the Sages instituted a form of marriage for them conducted through sign language or gestures, which can likewise be dissolved through gestures.</note>
**But a man with sound senses who married a woman with sound senses, and she [subsequently] became a deaf-mute:**
**if he wishes, he may divorce her, and if he wishes, he may maintain [the marriage].**
**If she became insane, he may not divorce her.** <note>To protect a woman who has lost her mental faculties from being cast out without protection, the Sages prohibited a man from divorcing her in this state.</note>
**If he became a deaf-mute or became insane,**
**he may never divorce her.** <note>Divorce requires the conscious will and "sound mind" of the husband. If he loses his legal capacity, he can no longer execute a valid bill of divorce.</note>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page's discussion of levirate marriage (yibum) law involving deaf-mutes and minors. The previous page ended with Tractate Yevamot Chapter 13 Mishnah 12 and the rules for a minor levir. **Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri said:**
Why is it that if a wife becomes deaf, her husband may divorce her,
yet if a husband becomes deaf, he cannot divorce his wife?
They replied to him:
The case of a husband who divorces is not the same as that of a wife who is divorced —
for a wife is sent away whether she wishes to be or not,
but a husband can only divorce of his own free will. <insert>of his own will</insert>

<note>This exchange highlights a fundamental asymmetry in classical Jewish divorce law: a divorce (get) must be issued by the husband and cannot be compelled without his willing participation. A wife has no equivalent power to initiate divorce unilaterally. When a husband becomes deaf, he loses the legal capacity to willingly issue a divorce, and so the marriage is legally frozen. When a wife becomes deaf, however, the husband retains full legal capacity and may still issue a divorce.</note>

### Tractate Yevamot, Chapter 14, Mishnah 2

**3**

**Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgeda testified**
**concerning a deaf-mute woman who had been given in marriage by her father,**
**that she may leave the marriage by means of a bill of divorce.**
<note>original: "גֵט" (get) — the formal written document of divorce in Jewish law.</note>
They said to him:
This case too is subject to the same rule. <note>That is, the sages agreed that her case follows the same principle as the one just discussed — even though she is a deaf-mute, because her father gave her in marriage with full legal authority, her husband must issue her a proper get to dissolve the marriage.</note>

### Tractate Yevamot, Chapter 14, Mishnah 3

**4**

**Two deaf-mute brothers married to two deaf-mute sisters,**
**or to two hearing sisters,**
**or to two sisters, one deaf-mute and one hearing;**
**and likewise two deaf-mute sisters married to two hearing brothers,**
**or to two deaf-mute brothers,**
**or to two brothers, one deaf-mute and one hearing —**
**all of these women are exempt from both <term>chalitzah</term> and <term>levirate marriage</term>.** <note>original: "חֲלִיצָה" (chalitzah) — the shoe-removal ceremony releasing a widow from the levirate bond; "יִבּוּם" (yibum) — levirate marriage, the obligation for a surviving brother to marry his deceased brother's childless widow. They are exempt here because in every scenario, the surviving brother's wife is a sister of the widow, and one may not perform levirate marriage with one's wife's sister — a prohibition that applies regardless of whether the parties are deaf-mute or hearing.</note> <insert>they are exempt</insert>
**But if they were strangers** <note>That is, if the wives were not sisters of one another.</note> **— they may enter into levirate marriage,**
**and if they wish to divorce, they may divorce.**

### Tractate Yevamot, Chapter 14, Mishnah 4

**5**

**Two brothers,**
**one deaf-mute and one hearing,**
**married to two hearing sisters.**
**The deaf-mute brother, husband of the hearing woman, died —**
**what shall the hearing brother, husband of the hearing woman, do?**
**She** <note>the widow of the deaf-mute man</note> **must be released on account of her being his wife's sister.** <note>The surviving hearing brother cannot perform levirate marriage with his deceased deaf-mute brother's widow, because she is the sister of his own living wife. This would constitute marrying one's wife's sister, which is forbidden.</note>
**The hearing brother, husband of the hearing woman, died —**
**what shall the deaf-mute brother, husband of the hearing woman, do?**
**He divorces his own wife by means of a bill of divorce,**
**and his brother's wife is forbidden to him forever.** <note>The deaf-mute surviving brother faces an impossible situation: he is obligated in principle to perform levirate marriage with his deceased hearing brother's widow, but he cannot do so properly because his own wife — whom he cannot fully divorce, since a deaf-mute's get is only Rabbinic in force — is her sister. He must issue his wife a Rabbinic-level divorce, but the widow remains permanently forbidden to him, since his marriage to her sister, even at the Rabbinic level, creates an enduring barrier.</note>

### Tractate Yevamot, Chapter 14, Mishnah 5

**6**

Two hearing brothers, <note>original: "פִּקְחִין" (pikchin) — literally "open-eyed" or "seeing," used here to mean those with full hearing and speech who possess full legal capacity.</note>
married to two sisters,
one a deaf-mute <note>original: "חֵרֶשֶׁת" (chereshet) — a woman who cannot hear or speak, who in this legal context has limited legal agency.</note> and one a hearing woman;
The hearing brother who was the husband of the deaf-mute died:
What should the hearing brother, the husband of the hearing woman, do?
She <insert>the widow</insert> is released from the obligation <note>Released from both Levirate marriage (yibum) and the shoe-removal ceremony (chalitzah).</note> because she is his **wife’s sister**. <note>Biblical law prohibits a man from marrying his wife's sister while his wife is alive. Since the widow is the sister of his current wife, the obligation of levirate marriage cannot apply.</note>

If the hearing brother who was the husband of the hearing woman died:
What should the hearing brother, the husband of the deaf-mute, do?
He releases his own wife with a **bill of divorce**, <note>original: "גֵט" (get).</note>
and his brother’s wife <insert>is released</insert> through the **ceremony of shoe-removal**. <note>original: "חֲלִיצָה" (chalitzah). This complex ruling occurs because the legal bond with the hearing widow is considered "stronger" than the marriage to the deaf-mute wife. To resolve the conflict of interest, he must end both relationships.</note>

### Tractate Yevamot, Chapter 14, Mishnah 6

**7**

Two brothers,
one a deaf-mute and one a hearing man,
married to two sisters,
one a deaf-mute and one a hearing woman;
If the deaf-mute brother died:
What should the hearing brother, the husband of the hearing woman, do?
She is released because she is his **wife’s sister**.

If the hearing brother who was the husband of the hearing woman died:
What should the deaf-mute brother, the husband of the deaf-mute woman, do?
He releases his own wife with a **bill of divorce**,
and his brother’s wife <insert>the hearing woman</insert> is **forbidden to him forever**. <note>Because he is a deaf-mute, he lacks the legal capacity to perform the chalitzah ceremony (which requires reciting specific verses), and he cannot perform yibum because she is his wife's sister. Thus, she can never be permitted to him.</note>

### Tractate Yevamot, Chapter 14, Mishnah 7

**8**

Two brothers,
one a deaf-mute and one a hearing man,
married to two unrelated women <note>original: "נָכְרִיּוֹת" (nochriyot) — here meaning "strangers" to one another, i.e., not sisters.</note> who are both hearing;
If the deaf-mute brother, the husband of the hearing woman, died:
What should the hearing brother, the husband of the hearing woman, do?
He either **performs the ceremony of shoe-removal** or **marries her** <insert>through levirate marriage</insert>.

If the hearing brother, the husband of the hearing woman, died:
What should the deaf-mute brother, the husband of the hearing woman, do?
He **marries her**, but he may **never divorce her**. <note>Since a deaf-mute man's marriage is legally recognized but his capacity to issue a divorce is restricted, once he enters this levirate union, the law ensures the woman is protected by not allowing him to cast her out, as he cannot provide a standard divorce.</note>

We have only heard [this ruling] regarding a woman who comes back from the **harvest** <note>original: "קָּצִיר" (katzir). the Sages only spoke of the "harvest" as a common example of what usually happens.
The House of Hillel then changed their position to rule according to the words of the House of Shammai.

[If she said:] 'He [God] gave me a son in a distant land' <note>original: "בִּמְדִינַת הַיָּם" (bimdinat hayam). This refers to any location far across the sea, usually outside the borders of the Land of Israel.</note>,

she is not believed <note>In this case, she is not believed because her testimony would free her from the obligation of the brother-in-law, and the court suspects she might be lying to avoid him.</note>.
[However], we are concerned by her words <note>The court does not ignore her testimony entirely but treats it as a case of legal doubt.</note>,
[therefore] she performs the ritual of **removing the shoe** <term>Chalitzah — a ceremony where the widow removes her brother-in-law’s shoe to release them both from the obligation to marry</term> but she does not enter into **Levirate marriage** <term>Yibbum — the marriage of a man to his deceased brother's childless widow</term>.

## Tractate Yevamot Chapter 15 Mishnah 10

### 13

[If she said:] 'He [God] gave me a brother-in-law in a distant land',
she [then] said:
'My husband died, and afterward my brother-in-law died,'
[or] 'My brother-in-law [died], and afterward my husband died,'
she is believed <note>Since it was not previously known that a brother-in-law existed, her word is accepted when she says he is no longer a factor.</note>.
If she, her husband, and her brother-in-law went to a distant land,
[and] she said:
'My husband died, and afterward my brother-in-law died,'
[or] 'My brother-in-law [died], and afterward my husband died,'
she is not believed,
for a woman is not believed when she says, 'My brother-in-law died,'
so that she might [be free to] remarry,
nor [is she believed to say] 'My sister died,'
so that she might enter into her [sister's] house <note>Meaning, so she can marry her sister’s husband, which is forbidden while the sister is alive.</note>.
And a man is not believed when he says, 'My brother died,'
so that he might enter into Levirate marriage with his [brother’s] wife,
nor [is he believed to say] 'My wife died,'
so that he might marry her sister.

There was an incident involving a man who fell into a large pit <note>original: *bor ha-gadol*</note> and emerged after three days <note>A miraculous survival that cautions judges not to assume death too quickly in certain accidents.</note>.

# Tractate Yevamot Chapter 16 Mishnah 7

### 7

Rabbi Akiva said:
When I went down to Nehardea <note>original: *Neharde’a*; a major center of Jewish life and scholarship in Babylonia.</note> to intercalate the year <note>The process of adding an extra month to the lunar calendar to ensure the festivals remain in their proper seasons.</note>,
Nehemiah of Beit Deli found me,
and he said to me:
"I have heard that in the Land of Israel, they do not permit a woman to remarry
based on the testimony of a single witness,
except for the ruling of Judah ben Baba."
I told him: "That is indeed the case."
He said to me:
"Go and tell them in my name:
You know that this country <note>Referring to Babylonia/Mesopotamia.</note> is disturbed by roving troops <note>original: *gyasot*; mercenary bands or military units that made travel and communication dangerous.</note>;
yet I have received a tradition from Rabban Gamliel the Elder <note>The head of the Sanhedrin in the mid-1st century CE, known for his leadership and legal leniencies.</note>,
that they permit a woman to remarry based on the testimony of a single witness."
And when I came and presented these matters before Rabban Gamliel <note>This refers to Rabban Gamliel II of Yavne, the grandson of the Elder.</note>,
he rejoiced at my words and said:
"We have found a companion for Judah ben Baba <note>Meaning, another authority who supports the lenient view that one witness is enough.</note>."

---

### 8

During these discussions, Rabban Gamliel remembered 
that certain people had been killed at Tel Arza <note>A location whose exact identification is debated, likely in the Judean hills.</note>,
and Rabban Gamliel the Elder had permitted their wives to remarry 
based on the testimony of a single witness.
And it was thus established as a legal precedent <note>original: *huchzequ*; it became a settled practice.</note> that they may permit remarriage based on hearsay <note>literally "a witness from the mouth of a witness."</note>,
on the word of a woman, on the word of one woman reporting what she heard from another woman,
and even on the word of a male or female servant <note>In standard ancient Jewish legal proceedings, slaves and women were generally not qualified to give formal testimony; this exception highlights the high priority given to freeing a woman from her status as an agunah.</note>.

---

### 9

Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Joshua say:
They do not permit a woman to remarry based on the testimony of a single witness.
Rabbi Akiva says:
Not based on the testimony of a woman, and not based on the testimony of relatives.

# Tractate Ketubot

## Chapter 1

Tractate Ketubot Chapter 1 Mishnah 1
### 1
A virgin is married on the fourth day <note>Wednesday</note>, 
and a widow on the fifth day <note>Thursday</note>, 
because twice in the week the courts sit in the towns—on the second day <note>Monday</note> and on the fifth day <note>Thursday</note>. 
The reason for this timing is so that if the groom had a "claim regarding virginity" <note>A legal dispute regarding whether the bride was indeed a virgin as expected.</note>, 
he could go early to the court the next morning.

Tractate Ketubot Chapter 1 Mishnah 2
### 2
A virgin’s <term>Ketubah: The marriage contract establishing the financial settlement the husband must pay the wife in the event of divorce or his death.</term> is two hundred <note>denarii</note>, 
and a widow’s is one *maneh* <note>One hundred denarii.</note>. 
A woman who is technically a virgin but is also a widow, a divorcee, or a woman released from a levirate bond <note>original: *chalutza*; a woman who underwent the "shoe-removal" ceremony to release her from marrying her late husband's brother.</note> from the stage of betrothal only <note>That is, the previous marriage or bond was never consummated.</note>—
their marriage contract is two hundred, and they are subject to a claim regarding virginity. 
A female convert, a captive, or a maidservant, 
who were ransomed, converted, or freed 
when they were less than three years and one day old—
their marriage contract is two hundred, and they are subject to a claim regarding virginity.

Tractate Ketubot Chapter 1 Mishnah 3
### 3
An adult <note>A male aged thirteen or older.</note> who has relations with a minor <note>A female under the age of three years and one day.</note>...

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 1 Mishnah 4

->4<-

A "virgin widow" <note>A woman whose first husband died after the legal betrothal but before the marriage was consummated.</note>, a divorcee, or a woman who underwent **halitzah** <term>Halitzah: The biblical ceremony (involving the removal of a shoe) that releases a childless widow from the obligation to marry her deceased husband's brother.</term> following a marriage—

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 1 Mishnah 5

->5<-

One who eats at the home of his father-in-law in Judea without witnesses <note>In ancient Judea, it was customary for the betrothed couple to spend time alone together before the final wedding ceremony.</note>,
cannot later lodge a claim regarding virginity,
because he was already secluded with her.
Whether they are widows of Israelites or widows of priests,
their **Ketubah** is one *maneh*.
The Court of the Priests, however,
used to collect four hundred *zuz* <note>A zuz is equivalent to one denarius; this was double the standard amount.</note> for a virgin,
and the Sages did not stop them <note>The Sages allowed the priestly families to maintain their own stricter and more prestigious traditions regarding marriage settlements.</note>.

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 1 Mishnah 6

->6<-

If a man marries a woman and does not find [evidence of] her virginity,
she says:
"After you betrothed me, I was raped, and it is your field that has been devastated." <note>original: "nis-tahafah sadekha." This is a legal metaphor: since the betrothal had already occurred, the woman argued that the "damage" happened while she was already legally tied to him, and thus it is his misfortune, not a breach of contract.</note>
But he says:
"Not so; rather, it happened before I betrothed you, and my purchase was a 'purchase made in error.'" <note>A legal term meaning the contract is void because it was based on false pretenses.</note>
Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer say:
She is believed. <note>They accept her word because of a legal principle that favors a person's status of bodily integrity.</note>
But Rabbi Joshua says:
She is not believed! We do not live by her mouth <note>We do not rely solely on her testimony.</note>!
Rather, she is presumed to have had relations before she was betrothed—
and she has deceived him—
until she can bring proof for her words.

## Tractate Ketubot Chapter 2 Mishnah 5

### 5
A woman who said:
‘I was a married woman, and now I am divorced,’
is believed, for ‘the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted’ <note>original: "ha-peh she-asar hu ha-peh she-hittir." This is a fundamental legal principle: since the person volunteered the information that made them forbidden, they are also trusted when they provide the information that makes them permitted.</note>.
But if there are witnesses that she was a married woman, and she says:
‘I am divorced,’
she is not believed <note>Because the "prohibition" is now established by external witnesses, her own word is no longer the sole source of the status.</note>.

## Tractate Ketubot, Chapter 4, Mishnah 3

### 5

A **convert** <term>convert<note>Hebrew: *Giyoret*. A woman who converted to Judaism. The laws of adultery and their penalties apply to her differently depending on when she converted relative to her birth and her daughter's birth.</note></term> whose daughter converted along with her, and that daughter committed **adultery** —
she is punished by **strangulation** <note>The standard biblical punishment for a married woman who commits adultery, as distinct from the more severe punishment described below. Strangulation was considered the "default" capital punishment in rabbinic law.</note>.
She does not have the **doorway of her father's house** <note>Hebrew: *Petach beit av*. A reference to Deuteronomy 22:21, which prescribes that a bride accused of not being a virgin is brought to the entrance of her father's house and stoned there. This provision applies only to a daughter of Israel who was raised in her father's household — not to a convert who has no such status.</note>, nor the **one hundred selah** fine <note>The fine of one hundred *selah* (silver coins) paid to the father of a falsely accused bride, described in Deuteronomy 22:19. If her **conception** was outside of holiness <note>That is, before her mother's conversion to Judaism.</note> but her **birth** was within holiness <note>That is, after the conversion was completed.</note> —
she is treated like a **daughter of Israel** and is punished by **stoning** <note>A more severe penalty than strangulation, applied here because she was born into the Jewish covenant. Though her conception preceded the conversion, her birth into the community gives her full status.</note>.
She does not have the doorway of her father's house, nor the one hundred selah fine.
If both her **conception and her birth** were within holiness —
she is treated like a **daughter of Israel in every respect**.
If she has a father but **no** doorway of a father's house <note>Meaning: she has a living father, but the household does not qualify legally as the requisite "father's house" for the biblical procedure — for example, if she no longer lives there.</note>;
if she has a doorway of a father's house but **no** father —
she is punished by **stoning** <note>The rabbinic ruling is that even when only one of the two conditions is present — a father, or his household threshold — the more severe punishment of stoning applies. The full procedure of Deuteronomy 22:21 need not be carried out in all its details.</note>.
The verse <gloss>(Deuteronomy 22:21)</gloss> <note>original: "פֶּתַח בֵּית אָבִיהָ" — "the doorway of her father's house"</note> "the doorway of her father's house" was stated only as a **prescribed ideal** <note>Hebrew: *Mitzvah*. The Mishnah teaches that bringing the accused to her father's doorway is the preferred, commanded manner of carrying out the penalty, but it is not an absolute prerequisite. Where it cannot be done, the sentence is still carried out.</note>.

## Tractate Ketubot, Chapter 4, Mishnah 4

### 6

A **father** has the following rights over his daughter:
her **betrothal** — whether by money, by document, or by consummation <note>These are the three valid modes of betrothal (*kiddushin*) in Jewish law: transfer of money or an object of value, a written betrothal document, or cohabitation with intent to betroth.</note>;
he is entitled to her **found property** and to her **handiwork**;
he may **annul her vows** <note>A father has the biblical authority to nullify the vows of his minor daughter (Numbers 30:4–6). This power ends when she marries, at which point it transfers jointly to her husband.</note>;
he receives her **bill of divorce** <note>If the betrothed daughter is divorced before the marriage is consummated, the father receives the get (bill of divorce) on her behalf.</note>;
but he **does not consume the produce** <note>Hebrew: *Ochel peirot*. The husband's right to benefit from the income and yield of his wife's property during the marriage. The father does not have this right — he cannot profit from the earnings of his daughter's property while she is alive, since she remains a legal person in her own right.</note> of her property during her lifetime.
Once she **marries**,
the husband surpasses him <note>The husband takes on greater rights — and greater responsibilities — than the father ever had.</note>
in that the husband **consumes the produce** of her property during her lifetime,
and he is **obligated** for her **sustenance**, her **ransom** <note>If she is taken captive, the husband is legally required to pay for her release.</note>, and her **burial**.
**Rabbi Yehudah says:**
Even the **poorest man in Israel** <note>Rabbi Yehudah begins a statement that continues on the next page, likely regarding the minimum standard of burial arrangements that even a poor husband must provide for his wife.</note>

->**The father is not legally obligated to provide for his daughter's sustenance.**<-

->**before the Sages in the "Vineyard of Yavne":**<- <note>The "Vineyard of Yavne" was the poetic name for the great academy of scholars who gathered after the destruction of the Second Temple.</note>
->**"The sons shall inherit and the daughters shall be supported,"**<-
->**just as the sons only inherit after the death of their father,**<-
->**so too the daughters are only supported [from the estate] after the death of their father.**<- <note>Rabbi Eleazar argues that while there is a moral duty to support daughters while alive, the legal obligation mentioned in the marriage contract refers specifically to support from the father's estate after his passing.</note>

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 6 Mishnah 1

1

That which is **his** is given to him immediately,
And that which is **hers** is used to **purchase land**,
And he **enjoys the fruits** of that land.

## Tractate Ketubot Chapter 6 Mishnah 5
### 5
One who marries off his daughter **without specifying** <note>original: "stam". This means without a prior agreement regarding the amount of the dowry.</note> a dowry,
shall not give her less than **fifty zuz** <term>zuz<note>An ancient silver coin. Fifty zuz was a modest but standard amount intended to provide a basic trousseau of clothing and household items.</note></term>.
If he stipulated that he would bring her in **naked** <note>A legal idiom meaning "without any dowry or clothing provided by the father."</note>,
the husband may not say:
"When she comes to my house, I will cover her with my own clothing,"
rather, he must provide her with clothing while she is **still in her father’s house**.
And so too, those who marry off an **orphan girl** <note>Usually referring to a girl whose father has passed away; the community or a charity fund acts in his place.</note>,
they shall not give her less than fifty zuz.
And if there is enough in the **communal fund** <note>original: "bakis". Literally "in the pocket," referring to the charity treasury.</note>,
they support her according to her **social standing**.

## Tractate Ketubot Chapter 6 Mishnah 6

An **orphan girl** whose mother and brothers married her off <note>When a father is deceased, the mother and brothers may arrange a marriage for a daughter who is a minor, but this has different legal weight than a father’s arrangement.</note>,
and they wrote for her a dowry of **one hundred or fifty zuz**,
she is able, once she **reaches majority** <note>original: "mishetagdil". When she becomes an adult at age twelve and a half.</note>,
to **extract from them** what was appropriate to be given to her <note>She can sue for her fair share of her father's estate if they gave her less than she deserved.</note>.
**Rabbi Judah** says:
If they married off the first daughter,
the second should be given in the **same manner** that he gave to the first.
But the **Sages** say:
Sometimes a person is poor and then becomes rich,
or rich and then becomes poor;
rather, one **appraises the property** and gives her her share <note>The Sages suggest giving her a fixed percentage—typically one-tenth—of the current value of the father's estate, regardless of what the previous sisters received.</note>.

## Tractate Ketubot Chapter 6 Mishnah 7
### 7
One who **places money with a trustee** for his daughter, and she says:
"My husband is **trustworthy** to me" <note>She is asking the trustee to hand the money directly to her husband instead of holding it for her or buying land with it.</note>,
the trustee should nonetheless **do what was entrusted to him**.
These are the words of **Rabbi Meir**.
**Rabbi Yose** said:
Is it not just like a field? If she wanted to sell it, would it not be sold from this moment on? <note>Rabbi Yose argues that if she is an adult, she has the legal right to give her property to whomever she wishes, including her husband.</note>
In what case does this apply? To an **adult woman**.
But for a **minor**, the actions of a minor are of **no consequence**.

It also debates whether a trustee must follow a father's instructions or a daughter's wishes regarding her wedding funds.</summary>

# Chapter 7

## Tractate Ketubot Chapter 7 Mishnah 1
### 1
One who **vows** to forbid his wife from deriving **benefit** from him <note>original: "Hamaddir." This refers to a husband who makes a formal vow (neder) that restricts his wife's access to his property or financial support.</note>,
for up to **thirty days**, he must appoint a **provider** <term>parnas<note>A third party or trustee who provides the wife with her necessities so the husband does not violate his vow while still fulfilling his obligation to support her.</note></term>.
If the vow lasts longer than that, he must **divorce her** and pay the **marriage contract** <term>ketubah<note>The financial settlement guaranteed to a woman upon divorce or the death of her husband.</note></term>.
**Rabbi Yehuda** says:
For an **Israelite** <note>A commoner, as opposed to a member of the priestly class.</note>,
if the vow is for **one month**, he may maintain the marriage; if for **two**, he must divorce her and pay the marriage contract.
But for those of the **priesthood** <note>original: "kehannot." Families of the Kohanim (priests).</note>,
if for **two months**, he may maintain the marriage; if for **three**, he must divorce her and pay the marriage contract <note>Kohanim were given longer periods because it was harder for them to remarry their wives if they divorced, due to stricter priestly marriage laws.</note>.

## Tractate Ketubot Chapter 7 Mishnah 2
### 2
One who **vows** to forbid his wife from **tasting** any kind of fruit,
he must divorce her and pay the marriage contract.
**Rabbi Yehuda** says:
For an **Israelite**,
if the vow is for **one day**, he may maintain the marriage; if for **two**, he must divorce her and pay the marriage contract.
But for those of the **priesthood**,
if for **two days**, he may maintain the marriage; if for **three**, he must divorce her and pay the marriage contract.

## Tractate Ketubot Chapter 7 Mishnah 3
### 3
One who **vows** to forbid his wife from **adorning** herself with any kind of cosmetic or jewelry,
he must divorce her and pay the marriage contract.
**Rabbi Yose** says:
For **poor women**, this applies if he did not set a **time limit**;
but for **wealthy women**, the limit is **thirty days** <note>Since wealthy women rely more on social standing and elaborate grooming, a vow of 30 days is considered the maximum tolerable limit before the marriage must end.</note>.

## Tractate Ketubot Chapter 7 Mishnah 4
### 4
One who **vows** to forbid his wife from going to her **father’s house**,
if they live with her **in the same city**,
if the vow is for **one month**, he may maintain the marriage; if for **two**, he must divorce her and pay the marriage contract.
If they live in **another city**,
if the vow is for **one pilgrimage festival** <term>regel<note>The three major festivals (Passover, Shavuot, Sukkot) when families traditionally gathered.</note></term>, he may maintain the marriage; if for **two**, he must divorce her and pay the marriage contract.

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 7 Mishnah 5

-> 5 <-

One who **vows** to restrict his wife so **that she may not go** to a **house of mourning**
or to a **house of feasting** <note>These were the primary social outlets in the ancient world. Attending a funeral was a duty of kindness, and attending a wedding was a duty of joy; preventing her from going isolated her from her community.</note>,
he must **divorce her and pay the marriage contract** <term>ketubah</term>, because he **locks the door before her** <note>meaning he causes her to be socially isolated and prevents her from reciprocating social kindnesses, which will result in no one coming to her own future times of grief or joy.</note>.
If he claimed he did so **"because of another matter"** <note>A euphemism for a concern regarding immodesty or a specific person at these gatherings who might be a bad influence.</note>,
he is **permitted** to do so.
If he said to her:
**"On the condition that you tell so-and-so what you said to me,"**
or **"what I said to you,"** <note>forcing her to reveal private or intimate conversations.</note>
or that she should **fill [a jug] and pour it out into the refuse**, <insert>to the trash-heaps</insert> <note>forcing her to perform degrading and pointless labor.</note>
he must **divorce her and pay the marriage contract**.

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 7 Mishnah 6

-> 6 <-

And **these** are the women who are **divorced without a marriage contract** <term>ketubah</term>:
One who **violates the Law of Moses or Jewish Law**.
And what is the **Law of Moses**? <note>original: "Dat Moshe." This refers to biblical commandments.</note>
If she **feeds him** food that has **not been tithed**, <term>ma'aser<note>Biblical law requires a portion of produce to be given to the Priests and Levites; eating untithed food is a serious transgression.</note></term>
or has **sexual relations with him** while she is a **menstruant**, <term>niddah</term>
or does **not separate the dough-offering**, <term>challah<note>The requirement to set aside a portion of dough for the Priest.</note></term>
or she **makes a vow but does not fulfill it**. <note>The Sages believed that the sin of unfulfilled vows could result in the death of one's children, thus endangering the household.</note>
And what is **Jewish Law**? <note>original: "Dat Yehudit." This refers to the standards of modesty and custom practiced by Jewish women at the time.</note>
If she **goes out with her head uncovered**,
or **spins thread in the marketplace** <note>considered a public display that invited unwanted attention.</note>,
or **speaks with every man**. <note>engaging in overly familiar or flirtatious conversation with strangers.</note>
**Abba Shaul** says:
Also one who **curses his parents** in his presence.
**Rabbi Tarfon** says:
Also a **loud-voiced woman**.
And who is a **loud-voiced woman**?
Any woman who **speaks inside her house**
and her **neighbors can hear her voice** <note>referring specifically to speaking about intimate matters so loudly that they are overheard outside.</note>.

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 7 Mishnah 7

-> 7 <-

One who **betroths a woman** on the **condition** that she is **not under any vows**,
and **vows were found** upon her,
she is **not betrothed**. <note>The marriage is considered a transaction based on a false premise and is void.</note>
If he **married her without specifying**, and **vows were found** upon her,
she is **divorced without a marriage contract**.

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the dissolution of marriage. [If he betrothed a woman] **on the condition that she has no blemishes**,
and **blemishes were found in her**,
she **is not betrothed** <note>Because the marriage was based on a false premise, the legal act of betrothal is considered void from the outset.</note>.

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 7 Mishnah 8
### 8
If **she had blemishes while she was still in her father’s house**,
the **father must bring proof**
**that these blemishes arose after she was betrothed**,
and [therefore] **his field was overwhelmed** <note>original: "nistahafah sadehu". A legal idiom meaning the husband has had "bad luck" with his acquisition. Once betrothed, she legally belongs to the husband, so if a defect develops then, it is his misfortune, not the father's fault.</note>.
If **she had entered the husband’s domain**,
the **husband must bring proof**
**that these blemishes were born in her before she was betrothed**,
and [therefore] **his purchase was a mistaken purchase** <term>mikach ta'ut</term> <note>A legal term for a transaction made under false pretenses which can be nullified.</note>.
These are the **words of Rabbi Meir**.
But the **Sages say**:
**Regarding what matters are these words said?**
Regarding **hidden blemishes**;
**but regarding visible blemishes, he cannot make a claim** <note>The husband is assumed to have seen them before the marriage and accepted them.</note>.
If there is a **bathhouse in that city**,
**even regarding hidden blemishes he cannot make a claim**,
**because he checks her by way of his [female] relatives.**

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 7 Mishnah 9
### 9
A **man who developed blemishes**,
**they do not compel him to divorce** <note>The law is more lenient toward men's defects, as the wife is assumed to accept the husband as he is to avoid being alone.</note>.
**Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said**:
**Regarding what matters are these words said?**
Regarding **minor blemishes**, but regarding **major blemishes**,
**they do compel him to divorce.**

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 7 Mishnah 10

One **afflicted with boils** <note>original: "mukke shehin". A severe and painful skin condition.</note>, and **one who has a polyp** <note>original: "ba'al polypus". Interpreted as a foul odor emanating from the nose or mouth, often due to a medical growth.</note>,

# Chapter 8

## Tractate Ketubot Chapter 8 Mishnah 1

->1<-

A woman to whom property fell [as an inheritance] before she was betrothed, 
the School of Shammai <term>Bet Shammai</term> and the School of Hillel <term>Bet Hillel</term> agree 
that she may sell it or give it away, and the act is valid. 
If the property fell to her after she was betrothed, 
the School of Shammai say: 
She may sell it. 
And the School of Hillel say: 
She may not sell it. 
Yet both of these schools agree 
that if she has already sold or given it away, the act is valid. 
Rabbi Yehuda said: 
They [the students] said before Rabban Gamliel: 
"Since the husband has acquired the woman [through betrothal], has he not also acquired the property?" 
He said to them: 
> "We are ashamed [troubled] by the new property rights, 
> and yet you wish to roll the old ones upon us!" <note>original: "ba'chadashim anu boshim...". This is a famous legal idiom. Rabban Gamliel argues that the husband's rights to property acquired *after* marriage are already difficult to justify; he refuses to extend those rights further to property she acquired *before* the marriage was even finalized.</note>

->2<-

If property fell to her <note>Inherited by the wife.</note> after she was married, 
both these and those <note>The House of Shammai and the House of Hillel, who usually disagree on the prior case of betrothal, are in agreement here.</note> agree 
that if she sold it or gave it away, 
the husband may seize it from the hands of the purchasers. 
If property fell to her before she was married, and then she was married, 
Rabban Gamliel says: 
If she sold it or gave it away, the transaction stands. <note>Rabban Gamliel protects the woman's right to dispose of property she owned prior to the marriage, even if she didn't sell it until after the wedding.</note>

They argued before Rabban Gamliel: 
Since he has acquired the woman <note>Through the marriage covenant.</note>, shall he not also acquire the property? 
He said to them: 
We are already embarrassed by our rulings regarding the new property,

He feels the law already grants the husband too much power over property inherited *during* marriage ("new"), and he refuses to extend that power to property she brought *into* the marriage ("old").</note>

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 8 Mishnah 2

->3<-

Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between types of property: 
Property that is known to the husband <note>original: "nechasim ha-yeduim". Typically land or assets that are public knowledge.</note>, she may not sell, 
and if she sold or gave it away, the act is void; 
but property that is not known to the husband <note>original: "she-einan yeduim". Such as a surprise inheritance from a distant relative overseas that the husband is unaware of.</note>, she may not sell, 
but if she sold or gave it away, the transaction stands.

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 8 Mishnah 3

->4<-

If money <note>original: "kesafim". Cash or silver coins.</note> fell to her, 
land should be purchased with it, and he <note>The husband.</note> consumes the fruit <term>usufruct: the right to enjoy the profit or harvest of a property without owning the underlying asset.</term>. 
Produce that is detached from the ground <note>Already harvested crops.</note>, 
land should be purchased with it, and he consumes the fruit. 
Regarding produce that is still attached to the ground: 
Rabbi Meir says: 
They appraise them for how much the land is worth with the produce, 
and how much it is worth without the produce, 
and with the difference <note>original: "ha-motar". The value of the growth.</note>, land is purchased for her, and he consumes the fruit. 
But the Sages say: 
Produce attached to the ground belongs to him <note>As part of his right to the "fruits" of her property.</note>, 
and produce detached from the ground belongs to her <note>As part of her principal capital.</note>, 
and land should be purchased with it, and he consumes the fruit.

Where his power is strengthened at her entry <note>When she enters the marriage.</note>, 
his power is weakened at her exit <note>Upon divorce or his death.</note>;

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 8 Mishnah 5

->6<-

If slaves and maidservants fell to her <note>As an inheritance.</note>, 
the elderly among them should be sold, 
and land should be purchased with the proceeds, and he <note>the husband</note> consumes the produce <note><term>usufruct: the right to enjoy the fruits or profits of property owned by another.</term></note>. 
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: 
She should not sell them, because they are the "honor of her father’s house" <note>Maintaining the family's prestige and sentimental connection to long-serving servants.</note>.

the old ones should be sold for wood, 
and land should be purchased with the proceeds, and he consumes the produce. 
Rabbi Yehuda says: 
She should not sell them, because they are the "glory of her father’s house" <note>original: "shevach beit aviha". Even if they are no longer productive, the physical presence of the orchard maintains the family's standing.</note>.
