If a man incurs expenses on his wife’s property— 
if he spent a large amount and consumed only a little <note>of the produce</note>, 
or if he spent a little and consumed a great deal— 
what he spent, he has spent, and what he consumed, he has consumed <note>The law assumes a mutual trade-off; he cannot claim reimbursement for his labor or costs if he enjoyed any of the benefits.</note>. 
But if he spent money and consumed nothing at all, 
he must swear an oath as to how much he spent and then he may take <note>reimbursement</note>.

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 8 Mishnah 6

A woman waiting for a levirate marriage <note><term>Shomeret Yavam: a widow whose husband died childless, awaiting either marriage to her deceased husband's brother (yibbum) or a formal release (halizah).</term></note> to whom property fell— 
the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel agree 
that she may sell it or give it away, and the transaction is valid. 
If she dies, 
what should be done with her marriage contract <note>the Ketubot</note> and with the property that enters and exits with her? <note>This refers to <term>Niksei Melog</term> (usufruct property) and <term>Niksei Tzon Barzel</term> (assets for which the husband takes financial responsibility but enjoys the use).</note> 
The House of Shammai say: 
The heirs of the husband and the heirs of the father <note>the woman's own family</note> shall divide it. 
And the House of Hillel say: 
The property remains in its status of possession <note>original: "ke-chezkatan". It stays with whoever currently holds it or follows the established legal presumption of ownership.</note>.

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 8 Mishnah 7

If his brothers <note>The brothers of the deceased husband</note> left money, land should be purchased with it, and he <note>The *Yavam*, the surviving brother who is obligated to perform the levirate marriage</note> consumes the produce <note><term>usufruct: the legal right to use and enjoy the profits from property that belongs to another.</term></note>. ### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 8 Mishnah 11

->11<-

He <note>the brother-in-law</note> may not say to her: 
"Behold, your marriage settlement is set aside on the table" <note>Meaning, he cannot simply set aside a specific pile of money for her and then use the rest of the estate freely</note>, 
rather, all of his property is collateral for her marriage settlement. 
And likewise, a man <note>in a standard marriage</note> may not say to his wife: 
"Behold, your marriage settlement is set aside on the table," 
but rather he must say, "All my property is collateral for your marriage settlement." 
If he divorces her, she is entitled only to her marriage settlement. 
If he remarries her, she is like all other women, and she is entitled only to her marriage settlement <note>original: "ketubatah". Meaning, she does not receive a second, additional settlement upon remarriage to the same man.</note>.

# Tractate Ketubot Chapter 9 Mishnah 1

## 1

One who writes to his wife:
"I have no legal standing or claim over your property,"
he nevertheless consumes the fruit <note>The produce or profits, known as usufruct</note> during her lifetime,
and if she dies, he inherits her.
If so, why did he write to her:
"I have no legal standing or claim over your property"?
So that if she sold it or gave it away, the transaction is valid <note>Usually, a wife cannot sell her property without her husband's consent because he has a right to the profits; this waiver removes that restriction.</note>.

If he wrote to her:
"I have no legal standing or claim over your property or its fruit <note>The profits/produce</note>,"
he does not consume the fruit during her lifetime,
but if she dies, he inherits her.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
He always consumes the fruit unless he writes to her:
"I have no legal standing or claim over your property, its fruit, or the fruit of its fruit, forever." <note>Rabbi Yehuda argues that a general waiver of "fruit" doesn't cover the reinvested profits of those profits.</note>

If he wrote to her:
"I have no legal standing or claim over your property, its fruit, or the fruit of its fruit, during your life and upon your death,"
he does not consume the fruit during her lifetime,
and if she dies, he does not inherit her.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
Even if he wrote this, if she dies, he should inherit her,
because he has made a condition that contradicts what is written in the Torah <note>The laws of inheritance are seen as divine decrees that cannot be overridden by private contract.</note>;
and anyone who makes a condition that contradicts what is written in the Torah,
his condition is void.

---

# Tractate Ketubot Chapter 9 Mishnah 2

## 2

One who died and left a wife, creditors, and heirs,
and he had a deposit <note>An object or money left for safekeeping</note> or a loan in the hands of others,
Rabbi Tarfon says:
They should be given to the weakest among them <note>original: "hakoshel" — referring to the party who is at the greatest disadvantage or whose claim is most vulnerable, often interpreted as the creditor.</note>.
But Rabbi Akiva says:
There is no mercy in justice <note>Meaning legal procedures must be followed strictly without regard for pity or the financial status of the parties.</note>; rather, they should be given to the heirs;
for all of the others <note>The wife and the creditors</note> must take an oath before they can collect,
but the heirs do not need to take an oath to receive their inheritance.

# Chapter 10

## Tractate Ketubot Chapter 10 Mishnah 1

-> 1 <-

A man who was married to two women and died, <gloss><note>original: "Nesu’ei" — the plural/construct form for "married."</note> Married. And so for all of them.</gloss>
the first wife takes precedence over the second, 
and the heirs of the first wife take precedence over the heirs of the second. 
If he married the first and she died, 
and then he married the second and he himself died, 
the second wife and her heirs take precedence over the heirs of the first <note>In Jewish law, the surviving wife is paid her settlement before the children of a previous wife can inherit their mother's specific marriage settlement portion (a provision known as "Ketubat Benin Dikhrin").</note>.

## Tractate Ketubot Chapter 10 Mishnah 2

-> 2 <-

A man who was married to two women, and they both died, 
and afterwards he died, 
and the orphans seek the marriage settlement of their respective mothers, 
but there is only enough there for the two marriage settlements, <gloss>but this was added by a proofreader <note>original: "Magiah"</note></gloss>
they divide the estate equally. 
If there was an extra denar <term>Denar: a standard Roman silver coin used as currency in the Mishnaic period</term> there, 
these heirs take their mother's marriage settlement, 
and those heirs take their mother's marriage settlement. 
And if the orphans said: 
"We will value our father’s property at one denar more," <gloss>more</gloss>
so that they may take their mother's marriage settlement, 
they are not listened to; 
rather, the court appraises the property.

## Tractate Ketubot Chapter 10 Mishnah 3

-> 3 <-

If there were prospective assets <term>Ra'ui: property that a person is legally entitled to inherit or receive, but which has not yet come into their actual possession</term>, <gloss>properties that they do not have as prospective assets</gloss>
they are not treated as property already in possession <term>Muhzak: assets currently and physically held by the deceased at the time of death</term>. 
Rabbi Shimon says: 
Even if there are unsecured properties <note>original: "Nekhasim she-ein lahem aharayut" — literally "property for which there is no responsibility," referring to movable goods as opposed to real estate.</note> there, 
they count for nothing, 
until there are secured properties <note>original: "Nekhasim she-yesh lahem aharayut" — real estate or land, which serves as a legal guarantee for the collection of debts or marriage settlements.</note> there.

## Tractate Ketubot Chapter 10 Mishnah 4

-> 4 <-

A man who was married to three women, and died,
the marriage settlement <term>Ketubah: the legal contract detailing a husband's financial obligations to his wife, payable upon his death or divorce</term> of this one was a maneh <term>Maneh: a weight of silver equivalent to 100 silver denarii</term>, and of that one was two hundred [denarii],
and of that one was three hundred [denarii],
and there is only a maneh in the estate,
they divide it equally <note>Since the estate cannot even cover the smallest claim, all wives are treated as equal creditors for the existing sum.</note>.
If there were two hundred [denarii] there,
the one with the maneh-settlement takes fifty,
and the one with the two hundred and the one with the three hundred
each take three gold coins <term>Gold Denar: a coin worth 25 silver denarii. Three gold coins equal 75 silver denarii.</term>.
If there were three hundred [denarii] there,
the one with the maneh-settlement takes fifty,
and the one with the two hundred takes a maneh <note>100 silver denarii.</note>,
and the one with the three hundred takes six gold coins <note>6 gold denarii = 150 silver denarii. This specific mathematical distribution has been studied by modern mathematicians and economists as an early example of game theory and "contested garment" logic.</note>.
And so, three people who placed money into a common purse <note>A shared investment or business partnership.</note>,
and they gained or lost—this is how they divide the proceeds.

## Tractate Ketubot Chapter 10 Mishnah 5

-> 5 <-

A man who was married to four women, and died,
the first wife takes precedence over the second,
and the second over the third,
and the third over the fourth <note>In this legal system, the date on the contract creates a "lien" on the husband's property. The earliest date has the first right to collect from the assets.</note>.
The first wife must swear an oath to the second <note>She must swear that she has not already collected her settlement from her husband during his lifetime and that she has not waived her rights.</note>,
and the second to the third,
and the third to the fourth,
but the fourth is paid without an oath.
Ben Nanas <note>A scholar known for his sharp legal mind in civil and financial matters.</note> said:
How so? And is she to be rewarded simply because she is the last?
She too should not be paid except through an oath.
If all their contracts were issued on the same day,
any wife who preceded her fellow even by a single hour, she has won the right.
This is how they used to write the hours in Jerusalem <note>Scribes in Jerusalem were known for their precision, recording the specific hour of the day on legal documents to establish clear chronological priority.</note>.
And if they were all issued at the same hour,
and there is only a maneh there, they divide it equally.

A man who was married to two women,
and sold his field,
and the first wife wrote to the buyer:
"I have no legal claim or dealings with you" <note>This is a formal waiver of her lien on the property. Ordinarily, a wife's marriage settlement acts as a mortgage on her husband's real estate.</note>,
the second wife may seize the field from the buyer <note>Because she did not sign a waiver, and her claim is still active.</note>,

and they continue to go around in a circle,

# Chapter 11

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 11 Mishnah 1

-> 1 <-

A widow is sustained from the property of the orphans <note>The late husband's estate.</note>,
and the products of her labor belong to them.
But they <note>The orphans/heirs.</note> are not obligated to pay for her burial.
Rather, her heirs—those who inherit her marriage settlement—
are obligated to pay for her burial <note>The principle is that the party receiving the financial benefit of her estate (the Ketubah payment) also bears the responsibility for her final expenses.</note>.

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 11 Mishnah 2

-> 2 <-

A widow, whether from betrothal <term>Erussin: the first stage of the marriage process which is legally binding but does not yet involve living together</term> or from marriage <term>Nissu'in: the completion of the marriage process when the woman enters her husband's home</term>,
may sell [the husband's property] without the authorization of a court <term>Beit Din: a Jewish rabbinic court</term> <note>She can sell land to collect her settlement or for her sustenance without waiting for a formal court proceeding, to ensure she does not go hungry.</note>.
Rabbi Shimon says:
A widow from marriage may sell without a court's authorization,
but a widow from betrothal may not sell except through a court,
because she is not entitled to sustenance payments <note>Since a betrothed woman does not yet live with her husband, she was not entitled to daily food from his estate, only the lump sum of her settlement; therefore, the urgency of selling property is reduced.</note>,
and anyone who is not entitled to sustenance payments
may not sell property except through a court.

or mortgaged it, or part of it,
or gave it to another as a gift, or part of it,
she may no longer sell the remainder except through a court.

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 11 Mishnah 4

A widow whose marriage settlement <note>original: "Ketubah"</note> was two hundred *zuz* <term>Zuz: An ancient silver coin. Two hundred zuz was the standard marriage settlement for a woman's first marriage.</term>,
and she sold property worth a *maneh* <term>Maneh: A unit of currency equal to 100 zuz (dinars).</term> for two hundred,

#### 5

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
In truth, her sale remains valid,
unless there is [an amount of land] there such that she would leave

or, according to the words of Rabbi Akiva, an area of a quarter-*kab*.
If her marriage settlement was four hundred *zuz*,

and to the last person [she sold property] worth a *maneh* and a *dinar* for the price of a *maneh*,
the sale to the last person is void, but the sales to all the others remain valid.

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 11 Mishnah 5

#### 6

An assessment by judges <note>A court-ordered valuation and sale of property to pay debts.</note> that undervalued by a sixth or overvalued by a sixth,
their sale is void.

If so, what is the benefit of the power of the court? <note>If a court's sale can be overturned as easily as a private sale, the court loses its legal authority and stability.</note>
Rather, if they issued a "document of inspection" <term>Iggeret Bikoret: A public notice or proclamation of an upcoming court-ordered auction, allowing the public to inspect the property and bid, ensuring a fair market price.</term>,
even if they sold property worth a *maneh* for two hundred,
or property worth two hundred for a *maneh*,
their sale remains valid.

## Tractate Ketubot Chapter 12 Mishnah 1

->1<-

->One who marries a woman,<-

->and agreed with him as well that he would support her daughter for five years,<-

# Chapter 13

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 13 Mishnah 1

**1**
There were two judges of civil law <term>Dayyanei Gezelot: Literally "judges of robberies," these were civil magistrates in Jerusalem during the Second Temple period who adjudicated property and monetary disputes.</term> in Jerusalem:
Admon, and Chanan ben Avishalom.
Chanan says two things <note>Referring to two specific legal rulings attributed to him.</note>,
and Admon says seven.
If someone went overseas <term>Medinat HaYam: Literally "the province of the sea," referring to any foreign land across the sea, often implying a distance that makes communication difficult.</term>,
and his wife claims maintenance <note>Sustenance and living expenses (Mezonot) provided from her husband's estate while he is away.</note>,
Chanan says:
Let her take an oath at the end, but let her not take an oath at the beginning. <note>Chanan argues she should receive support immediately and only swear an oath that she hasn't misappropriated funds later, when she eventually claims her final marriage settlement.</note>
But the sons of High Priests <note>original: "bnei kohanim gedolim"; a specific judicial group or council of elite priestly families in Jerusalem.</note> disagreed with him, and said:
Let her take an oath at the beginning and at the end.
Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas spoke in accordance with their words.
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai <note>One of the most important Jewish leaders at the end of the Second Temple period.</note> said:
Chanan spoke well;
she should only take an oath at the end.

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 13 Mishnah 2

**2**
If someone went overseas,
and another person stood up and provided maintenance for his wife <note>Meaning a stranger or acquaintance voluntarily paid for her food and needs without being asked by the husband.</note>,
Chanan says:
He has lost his money. <note>The benefactor cannot demand reimbursement from the husband, as it is viewed as a voluntary gift.</note>
But the sons of High Priests disagreed with him, and said:
Let him swear how much he spent and then collect [the payment].
Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas spoke in accordance with their words.
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai said:
Chanan spoke well;
he has placed his money on the horn of a deer. <note>original: "keren ha-tzvi"; a famous Talmudic idiom meaning the money is irretrievably lost, as if one placed it on the antler of a wild deer that has now run away.</note>

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 13 Mishnah 3

**3**
Admon says seven [things]:
If someone died and left behind both sons and daughters,
at a time when the assets are abundant,
the sons inherit the estate and the daughters must be maintained <note>The daughters receive food and support from the estate until they reach maturity or marry, but the sons receive the bulk of the inheritance.</note>.
If the assets are meager,
the daughters shall be maintained,
and the sons shall go begging at the doors. <note>In cases of a small estate, the legal priority is to ensure the daughters are supported so they do not become destitute; the sons are expected to find their own way.</note>

He has lost his right [to the claim].
If he designated it [the field] as a boundary marker for another [person’s deed], he has lost his right.

### Tractate Ketubot Chapter 13 Mishnah 11

## Chapter 1

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 1 Mishnah 1
### 1

All substitutes for vows <term>Nedarim: Formal promises to prohibit an object or benefit to oneself, often using the language of a sacrifice.</term> are like vows,
and [substitutes for] bans <term>Charamim: A form of vow that dedicates property to the Temple or the Priests.</term> are like bans,
and [substitutes for] oaths <term>Shevuot: Oaths taken in God's name to do or not do an action.</term> are like oaths,
and [substitutes for] Nazirite vows <term>Nezirut: A vow to abstain from wine, hair-cutting, and contact with the dead.</term> are like Nazirite vows.
One who says to his fellow:
"I am forbidden [by vow] from you,"
"I am separated from you,"
"I am removed from you,"
"That I will not eat of yours," <note>The Mishnah is establishing that even if a person does not use the formal, biblical language of a vow, but uses euphemisms or "substitutes" (*kinnuyim*), the vow is still legally binding.</note>

"[If one says:] 'That I will not taste of yours,' [or] 'The second,' <note>original: שֵׁנִי - The meaning of "the second" in this context is debated by the sages; it likely refers to a shorthand for a secondary vow or a specific forbidden state.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the end of the first chapter of Tractate Nedarim regarding the specific language used to create a binding vow. "[If one says:] 'A burnt offering, a meal offering, a sin offering, a thanksgiving offering, or a peace offering, [so that] I shall not eat of yours,'"
it is **forbidden**; <note>By comparing his neighbor's food to these specific types of Temple sacrifices, the speaker makes the food as forbidden to himself as a holy offering.</note>
Rabbi Yehuda **permits** it. <note>Rabbi Yehuda holds that unless the speaker uses the general term "Offering" (Korban), the vow is not legally binding.</note>
"The offering," "as the offering," or "an offering [is what] I shall eat of yours,"
it is **forbidden**.
"Not an offering, I shall not eat of yours,"
Rabbi Meir **forbids** it. <note>Even though the speaker used a double negative ("not... shall not"), Rabbi Meir interprets the intent as a binding vow.</note>
One who says to his fellow:
"**Konam** <term>Konam: A substitute word for 'Korban' (Offering), used to avoid misusing sacred terminology in everyday speech.</term> [upon] my mouth speaking with you,
or my hand working with you,
or my foot walking for you,"
it is **forbidden**.

...it is **forbidden**. <note>original: "Asur." This concludes the previous section regarding vows made using the language of Temple gifts or items that are intrinsically forbidden, such as meat from a "torn" animal.</note>

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 2 Mishnah 2
**2**
"[If one says:] 'An offering [is what] I shall not eat of yours,'"
or "An offering [is] what I shall eat of yours,"
[or] "Not an offering, I shall not eat of yours,"
it is **permitted**. <note>In these specific phrasing combinations, the Sages rule that the language is too ambiguous or contradictory to create a binding legal vow. It is seen as casual speech rather than a formal commitment.</note>
"[If one says:] An oath! I shall not eat of yours,"
"An oath! [is] what I shall eat of yours,"
[or] "Not an oath! I shall not eat of yours,"
it is **forbidden**. <note>The laws of Oaths (Shevuot) are more sensitive to these types of declarations than the laws of Vows (Nedarim). Even slightly irregular phrasing can trigger a binding oath.</note>
This is a stringency of **oaths** over **vows**.
And [as for] a stringency of **vows** over **oaths**,
how so?
[If] one said:
"**Konam** <term>Konam: A substitute word for 'Offering' (Korban), used to avoid misusing sacred terminology while still creating a binding vow.</term> [be] the Sukkah <term>Sukkah: A temporary hut constructed for the week-long festival of Sukkot; dwelling in it is a biblical commandment.</term> that I would make," <gloss>second</gloss> <note>The gloss "second" likely refers to a scribal notation of a repeated or secondary phrase.</note>
"the Lulav <term>Lulav: A palm branch used in ritual observance during the holiday of Sukkot.</term> that I would take," <gloss>second</gloss>
"the Tefillin <term>Tefillin: Phylacteries; small leather boxes containing Torah verses worn on the head and arm during prayer.</term> that I would don,"
in the case of **vows**, it is **forbidden**, but in the case of **oaths**, it is **permitted**,
for one cannot take an oath to transgress the commandments. <note>A vow works by forbidding an *object* to a person (e.g., "this Sukkah is forbidden to me"), whereas an oath is a commitment by the *person* to act or not act. Since every person is already "sworn" from Mount Sinai to perform the commandments, a new oath cannot override that existing obligation. However, a vow can effectively make the object of a commandment "off-limits" to the person.</note>

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 2 Mishnah 3
**3**
There is a **vow within a vow**,
but there is no **oath within an oath**.
How so?
[If] one said:
"I am hereby a **Nazirite** <term>Nazirite: One who vows to abstain from grape products, cutting hair, and contact with the dead for a set period, usually 30 days.</term> if I eat [this],"
"I am hereby a Nazirite if I eat [this],"
"I am hereby a Nazirite if I eat [this]," and he ate [it],
he is liable for **each and every one**. <note>Vows can accumulate. In this case, the person would have to observe three consecutive 30-day periods of Naziritehood.</note>
"[If he says:] An oath that I shall not eat,"
"An oath that I shall not eat,"
"An oath that I shall not eat," and he ate,
he is only liable for **one**. <note>Once an oath is made, the person is already forbidden from the act. Subsequent oaths on the same matter are considered redundant and have no additional legal weight.</note>

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 2 Mishnah 4
**4**
Unspecified vows are [interpreted] to be **stringent**, but their explanations [can be interpreted] to be **lenient**.
How so?

[If one] said:
> “Behold, this is to me like salted meat, or like libation wine,” <note>original: "kibsar maluach, u-k'yein nesekh." Referring to meat used in sacrifices or wine poured on an altar.</note>

If he intended a vow for Heaven, it is **forbidden**.
If he intended it for idolatry, it is **permitted**,
And if it was unspecified, it is **forbidden**.
> “Behold, this is to me like a devoted thing,” <term>Devoted thing (Cherem): Property or items legally "banned" from common use and dedicated to the Temple or Priests.</term>

If he intended a vow like a thing devoted to Heaven, it is **forbidden**,
But if he intended it like a thing devoted to the Priests, it is **permitted**,
And if it was unspecified, it is **forbidden**.
> “Behold, this is to me like a tithe,”

If he intended a vow like an animal tithe, it is **forbidden**, <insert><like a tithe></insert>
But if he intended it like a grain tithe, it is **permitted**, <note>A vow must be "anchored" to something consecrated by a human act, like an animal tithe. Grain tithes are considered "standard" obligations and do not usually serve as a valid anchor for a new vow.</note>
And if it was unspecified, it is **forbidden**.
> “Behold, this is to me like a heave-offering,” <term>Heave-offering (Terumah): A portion of the harvest given to the Priests.</term>

If he intended a vow like the heave-offering of the Temple Chamber, it is **forbidden**,
But if he intended it like the heave-offering of the threshing floor, it is **permitted**,
And if it was unspecified, it is **forbidden**.
These are the words of Rabbi Meir.
But the Sages say:
An unspecified heave-offering in **Judea** is **forbidden**, but in the **Galilee**, it is **permitted**,
because the people of the Galilee are not familiar with the heave-offering of the Temple Chamber.
Unspecified "devoted things" in **Judea** are **permitted**, but in the **Galilee**, they are **forbidden**,
because the people of the Galilee are not familiar with things devoted to the Priests. <note>This highlights how local vernacular and common practice determined the legal weight of a person's words.</note>

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 2 Mishnah 5

[If] one made a vow using the word "devoted thing" (*Cherem*), and said:
> “I did not vow except regarding a net of the sea,” <note>original: "cheremo shel yam." The word *Cherem* can mean both a consecrated object and a fishing net.</note>

[Or if] he made a vow using the word "offering" (*Korban*), and said:
> “I did not vow except regarding the 'offerings of kings',” <note>Refers to secular gifts or taxes paid to royalty, rather than a sacrifice to God.</note>
> “Behold, my very self is an offering,” and then said:
> “I did not vow except regarding a bone (*Etzem*) that I set aside for myself to vow by,” <note>A play on words; the Hebrew word for 'self' (*Atzmi*) and 'bone' (*Atzmi*) share the same root.</note>
> “*Konam*! My wife shall not benefit from me,” and then said:
> “I did not vow except regarding my first wife, whom I have already divorced,”

Regarding all of these cases: They are not "asked" about them. <note>In Jewish law, a person usually "asks" a Sage to annul a vow. Here, the person claims the vow was never valid because they meant something else entirely.</note>
But if they were asked,
we punish them and act stringently toward them.
These are the words of Rabbi Meir.
But the Sages say:
We open a "door" for them from another place, <note>A legal opening or justification to annul the vow.</note>
and we instruct them [so they do not treat vows lightly].

# Chapter 3

## Tractate Nedarim Chapter 3 Mishnah 1

### 1

Four [types of] vows the Sages permitted [to be broken without formal annulment]:
Vows of incitement, vows of exaggeration,
vows of error, and vows of compulsion.
**Vows of incitement:**
[For example], if one was selling an object and said:
"It is *Konam* <term>Konam: A common substitute word for "Korban" (offering), used to create a vow of prohibition without using a Divine name.</term> that I shall not reduce [the price] for you below a *sela*," <term>Sela: A silver coin worth four denars.</term>
and the other [the buyer] says:
"It is *Konam* that I shall not add [to the price] for you above a *shekel*," <term>Shekel: In the context of the Mishnah, this usually refers to a half-sela, or two denars.</term>
[yet] both of them [actually] agree upon three denars. <note>original: "shlosha dinarin." Since the vows were made merely to "incite" or pressure the other party during haggling, they are not considered a serious commitment.</note>
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says:
Even one who wishes to compel his friend by vow to eat with him, and said:
"Any vow that I am destined to vow in the future shall be void,
provided that he remembers [this disclaimer] at the time of the vow." <note>This refers to a "pre-emptive" cancellation of vows, a concept that allows for social pressure without spiritual consequence.</note>

## Tractate Nedarim Chapter 3 Mishnah 2

### 2

**Vows of exaggeration:** [For example, if] he said:
"May this be forbidden to me if I did not see on this road [a crowd] like those who went up from Egypt!" <note>Referring to the 600,000 men who left Egypt in the Exodus; a figure of speech for an immense crowd.</note>
"Or if I did not see a snake like the beam of an olive press!" <note>Ancient olive press beams were massive; this is recognized as hyperbolic language rather than a literal oath.</note>
**Vows of error:**
[For example, if] he said:
"[May this be forbidden] if I have eaten and drunk,"
and he then remembered that he [actually] had eaten and drunk.
[Or if he said]: "That I shall not eat and that I shall not drink,"
and he forgot, and ate and drank.
[Or if] he said:
"It is *Konam* that my wife should benefit from me,
because she stole my purse," or "because she struck my son,"
and it became known that she had not struck him, and it became known that she had not stolen.
[If] he saw people eating figs and said to them:
"Behold, they are to you like an offering," <term>Offering (Korban): Dedicating something to the Temple, which makes it "holy" and forbidden for common use.</term>
and they turned out to be his father or his brothers, and there were others with them—
The School of Shammai says: <note>The text concludes here as the debate between the School of Shammai and the School of Hillel regarding partial vs. total annulment of such a vow begins.</note>

[Beit Shammai] permit [the exaggerated part of the vow], but that which is associated with them remains forbidden. <note>original: "hen mattirin, u-mah she-immahen asurin." This refers to a case where a person vows against a group based on an exaggerated observation. Both these and those are permitted. <note>Beit Hillel views the entire vow as a single, invalid statement based on an error.</note>

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 3 Mishnah 3
### 3

**Vows of compulsion:**
If a friend pressured someone by a vow to eat with him,
and that person became ill, or his son became ill, or a river blocked his path [preventing him from coming],
behold, these are "vows of compulsion" <note>original: "nedrei anasin." These are vows that could not be fulfilled due to circumstances beyond the person's control, and are therefore naturally void.</note>.

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 3 Mishnah 4
### 4

One may vow to murderers, to robbers, and to tax collectors <note>original: "mochesim." In this context, these are considered illegal or unauthorized collectors who seize property by force.</note> that [the property] is *Terumah* <term>Terumah: A sacred portion of the harvest given to the Priests. Because it is holy, it is forbidden for non-priests to consume or take it; the vower lies to protect his goods from being stolen.</term>,
even though it is not *Terumah*;
[or] that they belong to the royal house,
even though they do not belong to them. <insert>that it is not [theirs]</insert>
Beit Shammai say:
One may vow with any [language], except for an oath. <note>Beit Shammai is stricter, allowing a "vow" (neder) but forbidding the use of God's name in a formal "oath" (shevuah), even to save property.</note>
And Beit Hillel say:
Even with an oath.
Beit Shammai say:
He should not initiate the vow himself [but wait to be asked].
And Beit Hillel say:
He may even initiate [the vow].
Beit Shammai say:
[He is only permitted to vow] that which the other compels him to vow.
And Beit Hillel say:
Even that which the other does not compel him to vow.

### 5

How so?
If they said to him:
"Say:
'It is *Konam* <term>Konam: A substitute word for a Temple offering (Korban), used to prohibit something to oneself or others.</term> that my wife should benefit from me!'"
And he said:
"It is *Konam* that my wife and my children should benefit from me,"
Beit Shammai say:
His wife is permitted [to benefit], but his children are forbidden. <note>Because he was only pressured to mention his wife; adding the children was his own choice and thus binding according to Beit Shammai.</note>
And Beit Hillel say:
Both these and those are permitted.

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 3 Mishnah 5
#### 6

"Behold, these saplings are a sacrifice <note>original: "korban." A term used to dedicate an object to the Temple treasury, rendering it forbidden for personal use.</note> if they are not cut down,"
and "This cloak is a sacrifice if it is not burned,"
they have a [possibility of] redemption <term>Redemption: The process of "buying back" a consecrated item from the Temple treasury by transferring its holiness to money. Once redeemed, the item can be used normally again.</term>.
"Behold, these saplings are a sacrifice *until* they are cut down," <gloss>that they are cut down</gloss>
and "This cloak is a sacrifice *until* it is burned,"
they have no redemption. <note>In the first case, the vow is a conditional penalty; if the condition (cutting/burning) is met, the vow might never take effect. In the second case, the object becomes holy immediately and remains so for its entire existence, leaving no room for the holiness to be transferred elsewhere.</note>

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 3 Mishnah 6
#### 7

One who vows [to abstain] from **those who go down to the sea**, is permitted [to benefit] from **those who dwell on land**;
but [one who vows to abstain] from **those who dwell on land**, is forbidden [from benefiting] from **those who go down to the sea**,
because those who go down to the sea are included in [the category of] those who dwell on land;
[the term "those who go down to the sea" refers] not to those who merely travel from Akko to Jaffa <note>Akko and Jaffa are coastal cities in Israel; this refers to a short coastal voyage rather than a deep-sea journey.</note>,
but rather to one whose way is to set sail [on long journeys].

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 3 Mishnah 7
#### 8

One who vows [to abstain] from **those who see the sun**,
is forbidden even [from benefiting] from the blind,
for this person intended [to refer to] anyone whom the sun "sees" <note>meaning anyone upon whom the sun shines, regardless of whether they have the faculty of sight themselves.</note>.

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 3 Mishnah 8
#### 9

One who vows [to abstain] from **those with dark heads** <note>original: "shechorei harosh." In the common language of the time, this referred to the black hair of youth and prime adulthood.</note>,
is forbidden [from benefiting] from the bald and from those with gray hair,
but is permitted [to benefit] from women and children,
for only [adult] men are called "those with dark heads."

Rabbi Meir permits even [benefit] from **those already born**. <gloss>from the born ones</gloss>
And the Sages say:
This person intended [to refer to] anyone whose nature it is to be born <note>The Sages argue that "noladim" is a general term for the human race, including those already living and those who will be born in the future.</note>.

# 1

->There is no difference between one who is forbidden by a vow from deriving **benefit** from his fellow and one who is forbidden by a vow from **food** from him,<-
->except for the **right of passage**,<- <note>original: "derisat ha-regel." This refers to the permission to walk across someone else's land. A person forbidden from "food" may still walk on the other's property, as walking is not a form of consuming food.</note>
->and vessels that are not used for **preparing food**.<- <note>original: "okhel nefesh." This term refers to items used for basic life-sustaining needs, specifically food preparation.</note>
->One who is forbidden by a vow from **food** from his fellow,<-
->[the fellow] may not lend him a sifter, a sieve, a millstone, or an oven.<- <note>These are forbidden because they are directly used to create food.</note>
->But he may lend him a tunic, a cloak, earrings, or rings,<-
->and anything that is not used for **preparing food**.<-
->In a place where it is customary to rent out such items, it is forbidden.<- <note>If people usually pay to use these items, providing them for free constitutes a financial benefit, which would violate a vow against deriving "benefit."</note>

## Tractate Nedarim Chapter 4 Mishnah 2

# 2

->One who is forbidden by a vow from deriving **benefit** from his fellow:<-
->[The fellow] may still pay his half-shekel tax, pay off his debt,<-
->and return his lost object to him.<- <note>These actions are permitted because they are considered "restoring" what the person already has or fulfilling a religious duty (mitzvah), rather than giving a new gift or benefit.</note>
->In a place where a fee is normally taken for [returning a lost object],<-
->the value of that benefit should go to the **Temple treasury**.<- <note>original: "hekdesh." To avoid the person under the vow from gaining a "free" service that usually costs money, the equivalent of the finder's fee is donated to the Temple.</note>

## Tractate Nedarim Chapter 4 Mishnah 3

# 3

->And he may set aside his **priest’s share** and his **tithes** with his [the owner's] consent.<- <note>original: "terumato u-ma'asrotav." These are portions of produce given to Priests and Levites. The person making the vow is performing a religious duty for the other, which is permitted.</note>
->And he may offer on his behalf the **bird-offerings** for those with discharges, bird-offerings for women after childbirth,<- <note>original: "kinnei zavim ve-kinnei zavot, kinnei yoledot." These are specific ritual offerings required for purification.</note>
->**sin-offerings**, and **guilt-offerings**.<- <note>original: "chatta'ot ve-ashamot."</note>
->And he may teach him scriptural interpretation, laws, and homiletic stories.<- <note>original: "midrash, halachot, ve-aggadot." These forms of oral tradition were traditionally taught for free.</note>
->He may not teach him **Scripture**,<- <note>original: "mikra." This refers to the Written Torah. In this era, teachers were often paid for teaching the Written Torah (specifically for the "supervision" of the children), so doing it for free would be a prohibited benefit.</note>
->but he may teach his children **Scripture**.<-
->And he may provide food for his wife and his children,<-
->even though he [the forbidden person] is obligated to support them. <gloss>their sustenance</gloss><-
->He may not feed his animal, whether it is an **impure** or a **pure** animal.<-
->Rabbi Eliezer says:<-
->He may feed the **impure** animal, but he may not feed the **pure** animal.<-
->They said to him:<-
->What is the difference between an **impure** and a **pure** animal?<-
->He said to them:<-
->Regarding the **pure** animal, its soul belongs to Heaven but its body belongs to him,<- <note>Because a "pure" (kosher) animal can be eaten or sold for meat, the owner gains a direct physical benefit if it is fed and kept alive.</note>
->whereas regarding the **impure** animal, its soul and its body belong to Heaven.<- <note>Since it cannot be eaten, Rabbi Eliezer argues the owner doesn't "own" its physical substance in the same way; he only benefits from its labor.</note>
->They said to him:<-
->Even regarding the **impure** animal, its soul belongs to Heaven but its body belongs to him,<-
->for if he wishes, he can sell it to the gentiles,<-
->or feed it to the dogs.<- <note>The Sages argue that even non-kosher animals have market value; therefore, feeding them provides a financial benefit to the owner.</note>

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 4 Mishnah 4

->4<-

One who is forbidden by a vow from deriving **benefit** from his fellow and enters to visit him <note>This refers to the religious duty of visiting the sick (bikur cholim).</note>: 
He may **stand**, but he may **not sit**. 
And he may **heal** him with medical healing, 
but not with **monetary healing**. <note>original: "refuat nefesh" (healing of the soul/body) and "refuat mamon" (healing of wealth). A doctor may treat the person's body because it is a religious obligation, but he cannot treat the person's livestock or property, as that is a purely financial benefit.</note>
And he may **bathe** with him in a large bath, 
but not in a **small one**. <note>In a small bath, one person's body heat or displacement of water directly affects the other, providing a forbidden benefit. In a large public bath, this effect is negligible.</note>
And he may **sleep** with him in a bed. 
Rabbi Judah says: 
During the **summer months**, but not during the **rainy months**, 
because [in the winter] he provides him with **warmth**. <note>Body heat shared in a bed during cold weather is considered a tangible benefit.</note>
And he may **recline** with him on a couch, 
and **eat** with him at the table, 
but not from the same **serving dish**. 
But he may eat from a **serving dish that is returned**. <note>original: "tamchui ha-chozer." This refers to a large communal dish that is passed around or returned to the kitchen, where the two individuals are not sharing the exact same portion simultaneously.</note>

---

->5<-

He may **not eat** with him from the trough that is placed before the laborers. 
And he may **not work** with him in a furrow. <note>original: "oman." This refers to the line or row of a field being plowed or harvested.</note>
These are the words of **Rabbi Meir**. 
But the **Sages** say: 
He may work at a **distance** from him.

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 4 Mishnah 5

->6<-

One who is forbidden by a vow from deriving **benefit** from his fellow before the **Sabbatical year** <note>original: "Shevi'it." According to the Torah, every seventh year the land in Israel must lie fallow and its produce is free for all to take.</note>: 
He may **not enter** into his field, <gloss>he may enter</gloss> <note>The gloss "he may enter" reflects a variant tradition or a clarification that entering might be permitted if no benefit is derived.</note>
and he may **not eat** from the branches that hang over; 
But during the **Sabbatical year**, he may **not enter** into his field, 
but he **may eat** from the branches that hang over. <note>In the Sabbatical year, the fruit is ownerless, so eating it is not a benefit from the owner. However, walking on the land itself (the right of passage) is still a benefit derived from the owner's property.</note>
If he vowed against **food** from him before the Sabbatical year: 
He may **enter** into his field, but he may **not eat** from the fruit. 
And during the **Sabbatical year**, he may **enter and eat**.

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 4 Mishnah 6

->7<-

One who is forbidden by a vow from deriving **benefit** from his fellow: 
[The fellow] may **not lend** to him, and he may **not borrow** from him; 
He may **not lend** [money] to him, and he may **not borrow** from him; <gloss>may he borrow</gloss>
And he may **not sell** to him, and he may **not buy** from him. <note>All commercial interactions, even at fair market value, are forbidden because they involve a level of mutual cooperation and benefit.</note>

He said to him:
> "Lend me your cow,"
He [the owner] said to him:
> "It is not available."
He [the first man] said:
> "**Konam** <note>original: *Konam*. A substitute word for a vow, effectively declaring an object 'consecrated' or forbidden for use as if it were a temple sacrifice.</note> be my field, such that I shall **never plow** in it [with your cow],"
If it was his habit to plow [his own field himself],
**he** is forbidden [from using that cow], and **all other people** are permitted;
If it is not his habit to plow in it [meaning he usually hires others to plow his field],
**he** and **all other people** are forbidden. <note>In this case, the vow was interpreted as being against the field itself being plowed by that specific cow. Therefore, even if he hires someone else to do the work, the vow is violated because the forbidden cow is still working the field.</note>

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 4 Mishnah 7

->8<-

One who is **forbidden by a vow from deriving benefit** from his fellow and he has **nothing to eat**,
[The fellow] goes to the **shopkeeper**, and says:
> "A certain man is forbidden by a vow from deriving benefit from me,
> and I do not know what I shall do."
The shopkeeper gives [food] to him [the person under the vow], and then comes and takes payment from this one [the fellow]. <note>This is a legal "workaround." Since the fellow does not give the food directly to the person he vowed not to benefit, and doesn't even explicitly tell the shopkeeper to give it on his behalf, the benefit is considered indirect and therefore permitted.</note>

->9<-

If he had his **house to build**, his **wall to fence**, or his **field to harvest**,
[The fellow] goes to the **laborers**, and says:
> "A certain man is forbidden by a vow from deriving benefit from me,
> and I do not know what I shall do."
And they perform the work with him, and then they come and take their wages from this one.

->10<-

If they were **traveling on the road** and he [the person under the vow] has **nothing to eat**,
[The fellow] gives [food] to another person as a **gift**,
and the other [the person under the vow] is **permitted** to it.
If there is no other person with them,
he places it on a **rock** or on a **fence**,
and says:

and the other takes and eats.
**Rabbi Yose** forbids this. <note>Rabbi Yose is stricter; he believes that "renouncing" something specifically so a certain person can take it is a legal fiction that still violates the spirit of the vow.</note>

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Chapter 5 of Tractate Nedarim. While the previous chapter focused on how one might provide food or services to someone they are forbidden to benefit through indirect "workarounds," this chapter shifts focus to the laws of joint ownership. It explores what happens when partners in a property—such as a shared courtyard—vow not to benefit from one another, and whether the right to walk through one's own property overrides the vow against benefiting from a partner's share.</meta>

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 5 Mishnah 1
1
**Partners** who vowed [not to derive] **benefit** from one another,
they are **forbidden** from entering the [shared] **courtyard**.
**Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov** says:
This one enters into his own [space], and that one enters into his own. <note>Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds a legal view that when partners use a shared space, they are essentially using their own portion, rather than benefiting from the other's share.</note>
Both of them are **forbidden** from setting up **millstones** or an **oven**,
or from **raising chickens**. <note>Even according to the more lenient view, these activities are forbidden because they take up permanent space and interfere with the other partner’s use of the land, which constitutes a direct benefit.</note>
If only **one** of them was forbidden by a vow from deriving benefit from his fellow,
he may **not enter** the courtyard.
**Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov** says:
He is able to say to him:
> "I am entering **into my own** [property],
> and I am not entering into yours."

The court **compels** the one who made the vow to **sell his share** [to the other partner]. <note>Since the vow makes it impossible for the two to share the property effectively, the person who caused the restriction is forced to liquidate his interest in the partnership.</note>

---

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 5 Mishnah 2
2
If **someone from the public** <note>original: *echad min ha-shuk* — literally "one from the marketplace," meaning an outsider who is not a partner.</note> was forbidden by a vow from deriving benefit from **one of the partners**,
he may **not enter** the courtyard.
**Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov** says:
He is able to say to him [the partner who forbade him]:
> "I am entering into **the portion of your partner**,
> and I am not entering into yours."

---

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 5 Mishnah 3
3
One who is **forbidden from deriving benefit** from his fellow,
and that fellow has a **bathhouse** or an **olive press** rented out in the city:
If the fellow has a **financial stake** <note>original: *tefisat yad* — literally "a grasp of the hand," meaning he retains a share of the profits or a right to use the facility personally.</note> in them, it is **forbidden**;
If he has **no financial stake** in them, it is **permitted**.
One who says to his fellow:
> "**Konam** <note>original: *Konam*. A substitute word used in vows to declare an object forbidden as if it were a temple sacrifice.</note> be **your house** such that I shall not enter it," or "**your field** such that I shall not buy it,"

If the owner **died** or **sold them** to another person, it becomes **permitted**. <note>Because the vow was specifically tied to the person's ownership ("your house"), once the ownership changes, the vow no longer applies.</note>
[However, if he said:]
> "Konam be **this house** such that I shall not enter it,"
> or "**this field** such that I shall not buy it,"

Even if the owner **died** or **sold them** to another person, it remains **forbidden**. <note>In this case, the vow was directed at the physical object itself ("this house") rather than the owner's relationship to it.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter 5, Mishnah 4. Having established that partners who vow against one another are forbidden from shared private property, the text now explores the status of public and communal property. It distinguishes between property owned by the entire nation (the "Ascenders from Babylon") and property owned by a specific municipality.</meta>

"**Behold, I am *cherem* to you**," <note>original: *cherem*. A "cherem" is a severe form of a vow that renders an object or person prohibited, often associated with things dedicated to the Temple or excluded from common use.</note> the one barred by the vow is **forbidden** [from benefiting from the speaker].
"**Behold, you are *cherem* to me**," the one who made the vow is **forbidden** [from benefiting from the other].
"**Behold, I am [forbidden] to you and you are [forbidden] to me**," **both of them are forbidden**.
And both of them are **permitted** to use a thing belonging to the **Ascenders from Babylon**, <note>original: *Olei Bavel*. This refers to the Jewish people who returned from the Babylonian exile. Legally, it signifies property owned collectively by the entire nation, such as the Temple or major roads, which cannot be restricted by a private vow.</note>
but they are **forbidden** from using a thing belonging to **that city**. <note>Municipal property—like a local bathhouse—is owned by the citizens. Since each citizen has a share, the partners are benefiting from each other's share, which the vow prohibits.</note>

## Tractate Nedarim Chapter 5 Mishnah 5

### 5

And what is a thing belonging to the **Ascenders from Babylon**?
For example: the **Temple Mount**, the **Temple Courtyards**, and the **cistern** situated in the middle of the road.
And what is a thing belonging to **that city**?
For example: the **town square**, the **bathhouse**, the **synagogue**, the **Ark** <note>The chest used to house Torah scrolls.</note>, and the **Books** <note>Torah scrolls and other sacred scriptures owned by the community.</note>.
And [the solution for one who wishes to use these is] the one who **writes over his share** to the **Nasi**. <note>original: *Nasi*. The "Prince" or head of the High Court. By legally gifting his share of communal property to the Nasi, a person no longer "owns" it, allowing his fellow—who is forbidden from his property—to use it without violating the vow.</note>

### 6

**Rabbi Yehuda** says:
It is the same whether one writes over his share to the **Nasi** or one writes it to a **commoner**;
what is the difference between writing to the Nasi and writing to a commoner?
Only that the one who writes to the **Nasi** does not need to formally **grant possession**, <note>original: *lezakot*. A legal procedure to finalize a transfer. Rabbi Yehuda argues the Nasi "acquires" it automatically through his status.</note>
while the one who writes to a **commoner** must formally grant possession.
But the **Sages** say:
Both this one and that one **must grant possession**;
they only mentioned the Nasi because that was the **common practice**. <note>original: *ba-hoveh* (or *ba-havai* as noted in the transcription). This means the law mentions the Nasi only because he was the most frequent recipient of such transfers, not because the law is unique to him.</note>
**Rabbi Yehuda** says:
The people of the **Galilee** do not need to write [these documents],
for their **ancestors** <note>original: *avoteihem* / *avotam*</note> have already **written on their behalf**.

## Tractate Nedarim Chapter 5 Mishnah 6

### [7]

One who is **forbidden** by a vow from deriving **benefit** from his fellow and has **nothing to eat**,
[the fellow] may **give [food] to another** as a gift, and the forbidden person is then **permitted** to use it. <note>This is a legal "workaround." Since the food now belongs to a third party, the person bound by the vow is not benefiting from the original owner.</note>
A **story** occurred in **Beit Horon** <note>A town located on the border of the territories of Ephraim and Benjamin.</note>
involving one whose **father** was forbidden by a vow from deriving benefit from him,
and he [the son] was **marrying off his daughter**.
He said to his friend:
"Behold, the **courtyard** and the **feast** are given to you as a **gift**;
they are only before you <note>Meaning: "I am giving them to you only for the purpose of..."</note> so that **Father may come and eat** with us at the feast."
[The friend] said to him:
"If they are truly mine, they are hereby **sanctified to Heaven**!" <note>original: *muqdashin la-shamayim*. The friend realized the gift was a legal fiction (a sham) meant only to circumvent a vow. To test the son's sincerity, he "donated" the gift to the Temple. If the gift were real, the son would have no right to complain.</note>

<summary>This page defines the boundaries between national property and municipal property regarding vows, and discusses the legality of "gift-giving" as a means to circumvent a vow, illustrated by the cautionary tale of Beit Horon.</summary>
<keywords>cherem, Olei Bavel, communal property, Nasi, legal possession, Beit Horon, fictitious gifts, Temple sanctification</keywords>

--- Page 541 ---
<meta>This page concludes the final ruling of Chapter 5 regarding the "Man of Beth Horon" incident—a legal case where a person tried to use a third party to circumvent a vow—and then transitions into Chapter 6, which analyzes the specific definitions of food categories in vows.</meta>

He <note>The father or the donor in the legal story from the previous page.</note> said to him:
"I did not give you what is mine except so that you would sanctify them to **Heaven**!" <note>original: *la-Shamayim*. In this context, it refers to dedicating property to the Temple to ensure the father could not benefit from it, as the son's vow intended.</note>
He <note>The third party (the friend) who received the "gift."</note> replied to him:
"You did not give me what is yours for that purpose, but rather so that **you and your father could eat and drink**,
and be reconciled with one another,
and the **sin** <note>The spiritual liability for facilitating the violation of a vow.</note> would be **hanging over my head**."
The **Sages** said:
**Any gift** that is not given such that if the recipient **sanctified it**, it would be legally **sanctified**, **is not considered a gift**. <note>This is a major legal principle: a gift must be absolute. If the donor places so many conditions on it that the recipient doesn't truly "own" it (like being unable to donate it to the Temple), the transfer of ownership is legally void.</note>

One who **vows [to abstain] from vegetables** is **permitted [to have] gourds** <term>diluim: specifically refers here to various types of pumpkins or bottle gourds</term>. 
**But Rabbi Akiva forbids [them]**. 
**They said to Rabbi Akiva**: 
"Does a man not say to his messenger: 
> 'Buy us vegetables,' 
and [the messenger] returns and says: 
> 'I found nothing but gourds'?" 
<note>The Sages argue that because the messenger distinguishes between "vegetables" and "gourds," they must be different categories.</note>
**He said to them**: 
"That is exactly the point! Does he perhaps say to him: 
> 'I found nothing but legumes' <term>kitnit: seeds like beans, lentils, or peas</term>?

[One who vows against vegetables] is **prohibited from fresh Egyptian beans** <term>pol hamitzri: likely the cowpea or a variety of fava bean</term>, 
but is **permitted to have them when they are dry**.

**"Konam! Whatever you produce is forbidden to me,"** <term>Konam: a substitute word for "offering" (korban); by using this word, a person declares an object to be as forbidden for use as a sacrifice in the Temple.</term>

## Tractate Nedarim Chapter 7 Mishnah 8

->9<-
**"[That] which you produce and I shall not eat until Passover,"**
**"[That] which you produce and I shall not cover [myself with] until Passover,"**
if **she produced [the item] before Passover,**
it is **permitted to eat it or cover [with it] after Passover.** <note>In this phrasing, the time limit "until Passover" refers to the duration of the prohibition itself. Once Passover arrives, the vow expires.</note>

->10<-
**"[That] which you produce until Passover and I shall not eat,"**
**"And [that] which you produce until Passover and I shall not cover [myself with],"**
if **she produced [it] before Passover,**
it is **forbidden to eat it or cover [with it] even after Passover.** <note>In this case, the time limit "until Passover" defines *which* items are forbidden (anything made before the deadline). Those items remain forbidden forever.</note>

# Tractate Nedarim Chapter 8 Mishnah 1

## 1
**"Konam [as an offering] wine that I shall not taste today,"** <term>Konam: a substitute word for "offering" (korban); it renders the item forbidden as if it were a sacrifice.</term>
**he is only forbidden until it gets dark;** <note>In the Jewish calendar, the day ends at nightfall.</note>
**"this week,"** <note>The Hebrew word "Shabbat" here refers to the seven-day week cycle ending with the Sabbath.</note>
**he is forbidden for the whole week, including the Sabbath that passed;** <insert>Correction: and the past Sabbath</insert>
**"this month,"**
**he is forbidden for the whole month, including the upcoming New Moon;** <note>The "New Moon" (Rosh Chodesh) marks the beginning of the next month.</note>
**"this year,"**
**he is forbidden for the whole year, including the upcoming New Year;**
**"this sabbatical cycle,"** <term>Sabbatical cycle: a "Shavu'a" or "week of years," referring to the seven-year agricultural cycle in Israel.</term>
**he is forbidden for the whole cycle, including the previous Seventh Year.** <insert>Correction: and the past Seventh Year</insert> <note>The Seventh Year (Shemitah) is the final year of the cycle.</note>

## 2
**And if he said:**
**"one day," "one week," "one month,"**
**"one year," "one sabbatical cycle,"**
**he is forbidden from day to day.** <note>Unlike "this year," which ends at the calendar New Year, "one year" means a full 365-day period (or 24-hour period for a day) starting from the moment the vow was spoken.</note>

## 3

**"Until it shall be [Passover]," he is forbidden until it departs.** <note>Original: "ad she-ye'hei." This phrasing implies the duration remains as long as the state of "Passover" exists, meaning until the holiday ends.</note>
**"Until before Passover,"**
**Rabbi Meir says:**
**he is forbidden until it arrives.**
**Rabbi Yose says:**
**he is forbidden until it departs.**

## Tractate Nedarim Chapter 8 Mishnah 4

->5<-

**"Until the summer,"** or **"Until it shall be the summer,"**
**is until the people begin to bring [figs] in baskets.** <note>The Hebrew "Kayitz" (summer) specifically refers to the fig harvest season. The vow ends when it becomes common practice to gather the ripened fruit into harvesting baskets.</note>
**"Until the summer passes,"**
**is until the scraping-knives are folded away.** <note>The "makzo'ot" were tools used to scrape or prepare figs for drying. Folding them away signaled the end of the processing season.</note>
**"Until the harvest,"**
**is until the people begin to reap the wheat harvest, but not the barley harvest.** <note>In the land of Israel, the barley harvest occurs earlier (around Passover), while the "harvest" usually refers to the primary wheat harvest (around Shavuot).</note>
**Everything depends on the place of his vow:**
**If he was in the mountains, [it follows the harvest] in the mountains;**
**and if he was in the valley, [it follows the harvest] in the valley.** <note>Crops ripen at different times depending on the local climate and elevation.</note>

## Tractate Nedarim Chapter 8 Mishnah 5

->6<-

**"Until the rains,"** or **"Until there shall be rains,"**
**is until the second rainfall descends.** <term>Second rainfall: "Revi'ah Shniyah," the second of the three major periods of the early rainy season in Israel, usually occurring in the Hebrew month of Marcheshvan.</term>
**Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:**
**Until the time for the second rainfall arrives.** <note>He argues the vow depends on the calendar date the rain is expected, even if the rain is delayed.</note>
**"Until the rains cease,"**
**is until Nissan ends.** <note>Nissan is the month of Passover, marking the end of the rainy season.</note>
**These are the words of Rabbi Meir.**
**And Rabbi Yehuda says:**
**Until Passover passes.**

->7<-

**"Konam [as an offering] wine that I shall not taste this year,"**
**if the year was intercalated, he is forbidden during the year and its intercalation.** <term>Intercalated: "Nit'abrah ha-shanah," a leap year in the Hebrew calendar where an extra month (Adar II) is added to align the lunar year with the solar seasons.</term>
**"Until the start of Adar,"**
**is until the start of the first Adar;**
**"Until the end of Adar,"**
**is until the end of the first Adar.** <note>In a leap year, if the speaker does not specify "Adar II," the law assumes the earliest occurrence of the month.</note>

->8<-

**Rabbi Yehuda says:**
**"Konam wine that I shall not taste until it shall be Passover,"**
**he is only forbidden until the nights of Passover,**
**for this person only intended [the vow to last] until the hour when it is the custom of people to drink wine.** <note>Since there is a religious obligation to drink four cups of wine at the Passover Seder, the law assumes the person did not intend to forbid themselves from a required religious act.</note>

## Tractate Nedarim Chapter 8 Mishnah 7

**One who says to his fellow:**

**this person can annul his own vow without [recourse to] a sage;**

If the friend insists that refusing the gift is more honorable, the condition is considered met or waived.</note>

# Chapter 9

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 9 Mishnah 1
## 1
Rabbi Eliezer says:
They may "open" for a person [an avenue for regret] by invoking the honor of his father and mother. <term>Opening [Petach]: A legal mechanism where a Sage finds a detail the vower didn't consider, allowing the vower to say, "Had I known this, I wouldn't have vowed," which permits the Sage to annul it.</term>
But the Sages forbid this.
Rabbi Tzadok said:
Rather than opening for him by the honor of his father and mother,
let them open for him by the honor of the Omnipresent! <note>original: "Makom" (The Place). Rabbi Tzadok argues that if we use "honor" as a reason to regret, the honor of God is the ultimate reason. However, if that were allowed, every vow would be immediately voided.</note>
If so, there would be no vows!
The Sages agree with Rabbi Eliezer
in a matter that is directly between him and his father and mother,
that they may open for him by the honor of his father and mother.

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 9 Mishnah 2
## 2
And Rabbi Eliezer also said:
They may open by a "newly born" [unforeseen] event. <term>Nolad: A circumstance that did not exist and could not have been easily anticipated at the time the vow was made.</term>
But the Sages forbid it.
How so?
If he said:
> "Forbidden by vow [Konam] is any benefit I might have from so-and-so,"
and that person became a scribe <note>original: "Sofer." A professional writer of holy scrolls and legal documents whose services might be essential.</note>,
or was marrying off his son,
and he [the vower] said:
> "Had I known that he would become a scribe, [I would not have vowed...]"

...or if he [the person the vower was avoiding] was soon marrying off his son <note>The vower realizes he will miss a major family celebration because of his vow</note>, [and he said:] 
"Had I known this, I would not have vowed." 

[Similarly, if one said:] 
"Forbidden by vow [<term>Konam: A word used to give an object the status of a holy sacrifice, making it forbidden for personal use.</term>] to this house that I shall not enter," 
and it was subsequently converted into a synagogue, 
and he said: 
"Had I known that it would become a synagogue, I would not have vowed," 
**Rabbi Eliezer permits** the annulment <note>original: "mattir." He believes a change in the status of the object is a valid reason for regret.</note>, 
**but the Sages forbid it.** <note>The Sages generally do not allow a vow to be annulled based on "new developments" (nolad) that did not exist at the time the vow was made.</note>

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 9 Mishnah 3
## 3
> **Rabbi Meir says:** 
> There are things that are like "new developments" and yet are not [legally considered] "new developments"; 
> and the Sages agree with him. 
> How so? 
> [If] he said: 
> "Forbidden by vow [Konam] that I shall not marry so-and-so, for her father is a wicked man!" 
> and they said to him, "He has died!" or "He has repented!"; 
> [or if he said:] "Forbidden [Konam] to this house that I shall not enter, for there is a vicious dog inside," or "because there is a snake inside," 
> and they said to him, "The dog has died," or "The snake was killed," 
> these are like "new developments" and yet are not "new developments" <note>Meir argues these aren't truly new circumstances because the vow was explicitly based on a condition (the dog or the father's character). Once that condition is gone, the vow is fundamentally altered.</note>. 
> And the Sages agree with him.

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 9 Mishnah 4
## 4
> **And Rabbi Meir also said:** 
> They may "open" for him <note>Finding a legal loophole for regret.</note> by citing what is written in the Torah, and they say to him: 
> <margin>(Leviticus 19:17-18)</margin> "Had you known that you were violating the commandments: 
> 'Do not take revenge' and 'Do not bear a grudge,' 
> and 'Do not hate your brother in your heart,' 
> and 'Love your neighbor as yourself,' 
> <margin>(Leviticus 25:36)</margin> and 'Let your brother live with you'— 
> [for] perhaps he will become poor and you will be unable to support him <note>Because the vow forbids you from benefiting him.</note>?" 
> [If] he said: 
> "Had I known it was so, I would not have vowed," 
> he is permitted [to have the vow annulled].

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 9 Mishnah 5
## 5

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion of "openings" for the annulment of vows. In the previous section, the Sages debated whether unforeseen "new developments"—circumstances that did not exist at the time of the vow—could serve as a valid basis for regret and subsequent annulment by a sage.</meta>

One may open [a way to annulment] for a man by pointing to his wife’s **marriage contract** <note>original: "ketubbat ishto." The Ketubbah is a legal document outlining a husband's financial obligations to his wife, particularly the amount he must pay her in the event of divorce or his death.</note>.

It once happened that a certain man vowed to deny his wife any benefit from him. 
Her marriage contract was valued at **four hundred zuz** <note>Zuz was a silver coin; 400 zuz was a significant sum, double the standard minimum for a virgin bride.</note>.
She came before **Rabbi Akiva** <note>One of the greatest foundational scholars of the Mishnah, active in the late 1st and early 2nd centuries CE.</note>, 
and he ruled that the man was obligated to pay her the marriage contract [since his vow effectively ended the marriage].

The man said to him: 
"Rabbi! My father left eight hundred dinars <note>A dinar is equivalent to a zuz.</note> as an inheritance. 
My brother took four hundred, and I took four hundred. 
Is it not enough that she should take two hundred and I keep two hundred?"

Rabbi Akiva said to him: 
"Even if you must **sell the hair on your head**, 
you must pay her marriage contract."

The man replied: 
"Had I known it was so [that I would be forced to pay the full amount immediately], I would not have vowed!" 
And so, Rabbi Akiva permitted the annulment of his vow.

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 9 Mishnah 6

## 6
One may open [a way to annulment] by citing the **Festivals** and the **Sabbaths**. 
At first, the Sages used to say: 
On those specific [holy] days, the vow is permitted <note>Because one has a religious obligation to enjoy the Sabbath and Festivals, the vow cannot apply to them.</note>, 
but on all other days, the vow remains forbidden. 

This was the rule until **Rabbi Akiva** came and taught: 
A vow that has been annulled in part is annulled in its entirety <insert>as a consequence of its general nature</insert> <note>original: "miklaló." This is a major legal principle: if a "hole" is poked in the validity of a vow for one scenario, the entire legal structure of that vow collapses.</note>.

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 9 Mishnah 7

## 7
How so? 
If a man said: 
"**Forbidden** <note>original: "Konam," a formula used to prohibit an object to oneself like a holy sacrifice.</note> be any benefit I have from all of you!" 
If the vow is permitted regarding one of them, it is permitted for all of them. 

[However, if he said:] 
"That I shall not benefit from **this** one, and from **this** one, and from **this** one!" 
If the first person mentioned is permitted [annulled], 
then all of them are permitted. 
But if the last one is permitted, 
only the last one is permitted, while all the others remain forbidden. 
If the middle one is permitted, 
then from that person and "downward" <note>Meaning those mentioned after him in the list.</note> is permitted, but from that person and "upward" <note>Those mentioned before him.</note> remains forbidden. 

[If he said:] 
"That I shall not benefit from this one, for it is a **sacrifice**; and from this one, for it is a **sacrifice**; and from this one, for it is a **sacrifice**," 
then they require a separate "opening" for the annulment of each and every one.

<term>Tractate Nedarim: A volume of the Mishnah dealing with the laws of vows and their annulment.</term>
<term>Mishnah: The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions and legal rulings, compiled around 200 CE.</term>
<term>Rabbi Akiva: A primary figure in the Mishnah known for his creative and influential legal interpretations.</term>
<term>Opening for a vow: A technique where a Sage finds a detail the vower overlooked, causing the vower to regret the vow and allowing for its cancellation.</term>
<term>Ketubbah: A marriage contract that provides financial protection for the wife.</term>
<term>A vow annulled in part is annulled in its entirety: The principle that a single vow covering multiple items is indivisible.</term>

# Chapter 10

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 10 Mishnah 1
**1**
**A betrothed young woman,** <term>Na'arah Me'orasah: A girl between the ages of twelve and twelve and a half who has undergone the first stage of marriage (betrothal/erusin) but does not yet live with her husband.</term>
**her father and her husband [together] annul her vows.**
If the father annulled the vow but the husband did not,
or if the husband annulled it but the father did not,
it is not annulled.
It goes without saying that it is not annulled if one of them upheld the vow <note>If one of the two authorities explicitly confirms the vow, the other's attempt to cancel it is completely void.</note>.

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 10 Mishnah 2
**2**
**If the father died,**
**the authority does not pass to the husband.** <note>The husband cannot unilaterally annul the vows of his betrothed wife if her father is no longer alive to join him in the action.</note>
**If the husband died,**
**the authority passes [back] to the father.**
In this regard, the power of the father is greater than the power of the husband.
Alternatively,
the power of the husband is greater than the power of the father,
because the husband may annul the vows of a woman in her adulthood, <term>Bagrut: The stage of full legal adulthood (usually twelve and a half years old), when a father's legal authority over his daughter normally ceases entirely.</term>

# Tractate Nedarim Chapter 10 Mishnah 3
## 3
If she made a vow while she was **betrothed**, <term>arusah: a woman who has completed the first stage of marriage (erusin) but does not yet live with her husband</term>
and she was divorced on that same day,
and betrothed again on that same day—
even to a hundred [different men]—
her father and her **last husband** together annul her vows.
This is the general rule:
In any case where she has not left for her own independent authority <note>meaning she has not become a legal adult (bogeret) or fully married (nissu'in)</note> for even a single hour,
her father and her last husband annul her vows.

# Tractate Nedarim Chapter 10 Mishnah 4
## 4
It is the **way of the scholars** <note>a phrase describing ethical or proactive behavior practiced by the wise</note>
that before a man’s daughter leaves his house <note>to move into her husband's home for the final marriage ceremony</note>,
he says to her:
"All the vows that you vowed while in my house,
they are hereby annulled."
And likewise, the husband,
before she enters into his authority,
says to her:
"All the vows that you vowed before you entered my authority, <note>original: "tikanesi lirshuti"</note>
they are hereby annulled."
For once she enters into his authority, he can no longer annul [her previous vows]. <note>original: "lirshuti" — once the marriage is finalized, the husband can only annul vows she makes from that point forward, not those she made as a single or betrothed woman</note>

# Tractate Nedarim Chapter 10 Mishnah 5
## 5
A **mature woman** <term>bogeret: a girl who has reached the age of twelve and a half years plus one day, at which point she is no longer under her father's legal domain</term> who waited twelve months [after betrothal for her husband to finalize the marriage],
and a widow who waited thirty days [after betrothal];
**Rabbi Eliezer** says:
Since her husband is now obligated to provide her sustenance, he may annul [her vows alone].
But the **Sages** say:
The husband cannot annul her vows until she enters into his authority <note>meaning the marriage ceremony must be fully completed first</note>.

whether she is waiting for one brother-in-law or for two brothers-in-law <note>if the deceased husband had multiple brothers</note>;
**Rabbi Eliezer** says:

<meta>This page continues the legal debate from the previous page regarding whether a husband can annul his wife's vows in advance, before she even makes them. The previous page ended with a husband saying to his wife that any vows she makes until his return are void.</meta>

May he not annul vows that have not yet reached the status of a prohibition?
**They said to him:** (Numbers 30:15)
**"Her husband may confirm it, and her husband may annul it,"** <note>original: "ishah yeqimenu ve-ishah yeferenu"</note>
**[this means] that which has come to the stage of being confirmed, comes to the stage of being annulled;**
**that which has not come to the stage of being confirmed, does not come to the stage of being annulled.** <note>This establishes a legal principle: a husband can only annul a vow that already exists and is therefore eligible to be "confirmed." He cannot preemptively annul a vow that hasn't been spoken yet.</note>

---

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 10 Mishnah 8

->8<-

**[A husband] may annul vows all day.** <note>The "day" here refers to the specific Jewish calendar day—from sunrise to sunset—on which the husband first hears about the vow, rather than a 24-hour period from the moment of hearing.</note>
**And there is a lenient and a stringent aspect to this matter.**
**How so?**
**If she vowed on Friday night,** <note>the start of the Sabbath</note>
**he may annul it on Friday night,**
**and throughout the day of the Sabbath until it grows dark.** <note>In this case, he has nearly 24 hours.</note>
**If she vowed as it was growing dark** <note>at the end of the Sabbath</note>,
**he may annul it only until it grows dark,**
**for if he did not annul it and it grew dark,**
**he is no longer able to annul it.** <note>In this case, he might have only a few minutes to act before the "day" ends and his authority to annul that specific vow expires.</note>

### Tractate Nedarim Chapter 11 Mishnah 1

**These are the vows that he may annul:**

**"If I should adorn myself," and "If I should not adorn myself."** <note>These refer to vows where the woman forbids herself from bathing or using cosmetics, which were considered essential for well-being and the marital relationship.</note>

**These are not considered vows of "affliction of the soul."**

**If she said:**

**[If she said,] "The fruits of this province are forbidden to me,"**
**he may bring her [fruits] from another province.**
**[If she said,] "The fruits of this shopkeeper are forbidden to me,"** <note>The Mishnah continues on the next page regarding whether this is considered "affliction" if he can buy from someone else.</note>
