## Tractate Nedarim Chapter 11 Mishnah 3

->3<-

"**Konam** <note>original: "Konam" — a substitute word used for making a vow, acting as a legal shorthand for declaring something forbidden like a Temple sacrifice.</note> **that I shall not benefit from any people**," <gloss>second</gloss> <note>This gloss likely refers to this being the second category of vows discussed in this section.</note> 
he is unable to annul, 
but she is able to benefit from **gleanings**, **forgotten sheaves**, the **corner of the field**, and **ownerless property**. <note>The Hebrew terms *Leket*, *Shikhah*, and *Peah* refer to parts of the harvest that the Torah requires farmers to leave for the poor. Since these belong to the poor by divine decree, and not by the "gift" of any specific person, her vow to not benefit from "people" does not apply to them.</note>
"**Konam, if priests or Levites benefit from me**," 
they may take [their dues] against his will. 
"**These specific priests or these specific Levites benefit from me**," 
others may take [those dues]. <note>The law distinguishes between a general vow against a whole class (which is invalid because the husband is obligated to give them their tithes) and a vow against specific individuals.</note>

## Tractate Nedarim Chapter 11 Mishnah 4

->4<-

"**Konam, that I will not work** <gloss>working</gloss> **according to the instructions of my father**," 
or "**according to your father**," or "**according to my brother**," or "**according to your brother**," 
he is unable to annul. 
"**That I will not work** <gloss>working</gloss> **according to your instructions**," <note>Referring to her husband.</note>
he does not need to annul. <note>Because a wife was legally obligated to perform certain labors for her husband, a vow cannot override an existing prior obligation.</note>
**Rabbi Akiva says:** 
He should annul it, lest she produce more for him than what is properly due to him. <note>Rabbi Akiva is concerned that if she works extra hard, that "surplus" might become forbidden by the vow.</note>
**Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says:** 
He should annul it, lest he divorce her and she will then be forbidden from returning to him. <note>If they divorce and later wish to remarry, the vow (which would have been active while she was single) might create a legal barrier to their reconciliation.</note>

# Tractate Nazir Chapter 1 Mishnah 2

->2<-

"[If one says:] I am [to abstain] **from the grape seeds**," or "**from the grape skins**," <gloss>the grape skins</gloss>
or "**from shaving**," or "**from ritual impurity**,"
this person is a **Nazirite** <note>term: *Nazir* — a person who takes a vow of asceticism, traditionally involving three prohibitions: consuming grape products, cutting their hair, and coming into contact with a corpse.</note>, and all the **finer regulations** <note>original: *dikdukei nezirot* — the specific legal stringencies and requirements</note> of Naziriteship are upon him. <gloss>The word "upon him" [Hebrew: *alav*] is pointed as *ali* and the letter *vav* is erased in the manuscript.</gloss>
"I am a Nazirite **like Samson**," "**like the son of Manoah**,"
"**like the husband of Delilah**," "**like he who uprooted the gates of Gaza**,"
"**like he whose eyes the Philistines gouged out**,"
this person is a **Samson Nazirite** <note>A unique legal category. Unlike a standard Nazirite, a "Samson Nazirite" can never cut his hair even if it becomes heavy, but he is not required to bring a sacrifice if he is accidentally defiled by a corpse.</note>.
What is the difference between a **perpetual Nazirite** <note>term: *Nazir Olam* — one who vows to be a Nazirite for their entire life.</note> and a **Samson Nazirite**?
A perpetual Nazirite:
[If] his hair becomes **heavy** <note>burdensome due to its weight or length</note>, he may **thin it with a razor** <note>trimming his hair periodically</note>,
and he must bring **three animal sacrifices**.
And if he becomes **ritually impure**, he does **not** bring a sacrifice for impurity <note>The text here follows a specific opinion; usually, a standard Nazirite who becomes impure must restart their count and bring a sacrifice, but the rules for lifelong vows differ.</note>.
A Samson Nazirite:
[If] his hair becomes heavy, he does **not** thin it,
and if he becomes ritually impure, he does **not** bring a sacrifice for impurity.

# Tractate Nazir Chapter 1 Mishnah 3

->3<-

An **unspecified** <note>original: *stam* — a vow made without a specified timeframe</note> Nazirite vow lasts **thirty days**.
If one said:
"I am a Nazirite for **one big [period]**,"
"I am a Nazirite for **one small [period]**,"
or even "**from now until the end of the world**,"
he is a Nazirite for **thirty days** <note>Hyperbolic language does not extend the legal minimum of the vow unless specific numbers are used.</note>.
"I am [a Nazirite for] **one day**,"
"I am a Nazirite for **one hour**,"
"I am a Nazirite for **one and a half [periods]**,"
this person is a Nazirite for **two [periods]** <note>Because the law does not recognize a Nazirite term shorter than 30 days, any fraction or shorter time is rounded up to a full term or added as a second full term.</note>.
"I am [a Nazirite for] **thirty days and one hour**,"
he is a Nazirite for **thirty-one days**,
because one does not vow Naziriteship in terms of **hours**.

**Rabbi** <note>When mentioned without a name in the Mishnah, "Rabbi" refers to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of this text.</note> says:

### Tractate Nazir Chapter 1 Mishnah 5

### Tractate Nazir Chapter 1 Mishnah 6
6
"[If one says:] Behold, I am a Nazirite **from here until such-and-such a place**,"
one **estimates** how many days it takes to travel from here to that place.
If it is **less than thirty days**, he is a Nazirite for **thirty days**;
and if not <note>meaning, if the journey is longer than thirty days</note>, he is a Nazirite for the **actual number of days** it takes to travel.

### Tractate Nazir Chapter 1 Mishnah 7
7

he counts his Naziriteship according to the **number of days in the year** <note>This would be 354 days for a lunar year or 365 for a solar year.</note>.
**Rabbi Judah** said:
There was once an **incident** [of a man who made such a vow], and as soon as he completed it, **he died**.

### Tractate Nazir Chapter 2 Mishnah 9
#### 9
> If one says: "Behold, I am a Nazirite, and also a Nazirite when I have a son,"
> and he began counting his own term, and afterward a son was born to him:
> He completes his own term, and afterward counts the term for his son.
> But if he says: "Behold, I am a Nazirite when I have a son, and also a Nazirite,"
> and he began counting his own term, and afterward a son was born to him:
> He sets aside his own term, and counts the term for his son,
> and afterward he completes his own term. <note>This illustrates a principle in Jewish law where the order of words in a vow dictates the priority of fulfillment.</note>

### Tractate Nazir Chapter 2 Mishnah 10
#### 10
> If one says: "Behold, I am a Nazirite when I have a son, and also a Nazirite for one hundred days,"
> and a son was born to him before seventy days had passed, he has lost nothing <note>He can finish the 30-day term for his son and still have enough time to complete the remaining 30 days of his own 100-day term.</note>;
> but if the son was born after seventy days, it invalidates the seventy days he already counted,
> because there can be no <term>shaving</term> <note>term: *Tiglahat*. The ritual cutting of the hair and the offering of sacrifices that concludes a Nazirite term.</note> in less than thirty days. <note>The law requires at least a 30-day interval of hair growth between two ritual shavings. If he shaves for his son's birth on day 71, he only has 29 days left of his 100, which is not enough for a valid second term.</note>

# Chapter 3

### Tractate Nazir Chapter 3 Mishnah 1
#### 1
> One who said, "Behold, I am a Nazirite,"
> performs the ritual shaving on the thirty-first day.
> But if he shaved on the thirtieth day, he has fulfilled his obligation <note>Since the default Nazirite term is thirty days, the 30th day can technically count as both the end of the term and the day of the ceremony.</note>.
> If he said, "Behold, I am a Nazirite for thirty days,"
> and he shaved on the thirtieth day, he has not fulfilled his obligation. <note>By specifying "thirty days," he implies thirty full days are required before the shaving can occur on the 31st.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the end of Chapter 2 and transitions into Chapter 3 of Tractate Nazir. One shaves <note>The ritual shaving of the head, or tonsure, performed at the Temple to mark the completion of a Nazirite term.</note> for the first term on the thirty-first day, 
and for the second term on the sixty-first day. 
If he shaved for the first term on the thirtieth day, 
he shaves for the second on the sixtieth day. 
And if he shaved on the sixtieth day minus one <note>The 59th day.</note>, he has fulfilled his obligation <note>original: "yatsa" — literally "he has gone out," meaning he has satisfied the legal requirement.</note>. 
This is the testimony testified by **Rabbi Papias** 
concerning one who vowed two <term>Nazirite terms</term><note>A Nazirite vow (Nazirut) typically lasts 30 days unless specified otherwise. During this time, the person abstains from wine, cutting their hair, and contact with the dead.</note>: 
that if he shaved for the first on the thirtieth day, 
he shaves for the second on the sixtieth day, 
and if he shaved on the sixtieth day minus one, he has fulfilled his obligation, 
for the thirtieth day counts toward the total <note>This follows the principle of "part of the day is like the whole day." If the first term is ended early on day 30, that same day can serve as day 1 of the second term.</note>.

### Tractate Nazir Chapter 3 Mishnah 6

6
One who vowed a long <term>Nazirite term</term><note>Hebrew: "Nazirut." A person who takes this vow (a Nazirite) abstains from grape products, hair cutting, and contact with the dead.</note>, 
completed his Nazirite term, and afterward arrived in the Land <note>The Land of Israel. The Sages decreed that the atmosphere of the land of the Gentiles is ritually impure; therefore, a vow served outside the Land was often required to be partially or fully repeated upon arrival in the pure Land of Israel.</note>,

**The House of Hillel** say: 
He is a Nazirite as from the beginning <note>Meaning he must repeat the entire long term he originally vowed.</note>. 
An incident occurred with **Queen Helene** <note>Helene of Adiabene, a first-century queen who converted to Judaism and was famous for her generosity and piety.</note>, 
whose son went to war, and she said: 
"If my son returns from the war in peace, 
I shall be a Nazirite for seven years." <meta>Original: "I shall be"</meta> 
And her son returned from the war, 
and she was a Nazirite for seven years. 
And at the end of seven years, she went up to the Land [of Israel], 
and the **House of Hillel** instructed her, 
that she must be a Nazirite for another seven years. 
And at the end of those other seven years, she became ritually impure. 
Thus, she was found to have been a Nazirite for twenty-one years. 
**Rabbi Yehuda** said: 
She was a Nazirite for only fourteen years. <meta>Original: "Twenty"</meta> <note>Rabbi Yehuda likely holds that the final impurity only required her to observe an additional thirty days, rather than repeating the entire seven-year cycle a third time.</note>

### Tractate Nazir Chapter 3 Mishnah 7

7
One about whom two groups of witnesses were testifying, 
these testify that he vowed two terms, 
and those testify that he vowed five, 
**The House of Shammai** say: 
The testimony is divided; there is no Nazirite vow here <note>Because the two groups do not agree on the facts, Shammai views the testimony as entirely void.</note>. 
**The House of Hillel** say: 
Included within five are two; 
therefore, let him be a Nazirite for two terms <note>Hillel applies a principle of logic where the lesser amount is contained within the greater; since both groups agree he vowed at least two terms, he must fulfill at least those two.</note>.

# Tractate Nazir Chapter 4 Mishnah 1

## 1

One who said, "**I am hereby a Nazirite**,"
and his friend heard and said,
"Me," "And me,"
they are all <term>Nazirites</term><note>Hebrew: "Nezirim." Individuals who have taken a vow of abstinence including no grape products, no hair cutting, and no contact with the dead.</note>.
If the first person was released <note>A vow can be "released" or "undone" by a sage if the person regrets it based on certain legal grounds.</note>, they are all released;
but if the last one was released, only the last one is released, and all the others remain bound by their vows.
If one said, "**I am hereby a Nazirite**,"
and his friend heard and said,
"My mouth is like his mouth, and my hair is like his hair," <insert>and my hair is like his hair</insert>
he is a Nazirite.
If a man said, "**I am hereby a Nazirite**,"
and his wife heard and said, "**And me**,"
he may annul <note>According to biblical law in Numbers 30, a husband has the authority to annul his wife's vows on the day he hears them.</note> hers, but his own remains standing.
If a woman said, "**I am hereby a Nazirite**,"
and her husband heard and said, "**And me**,"
he can no longer annul her vow <note>By saying "And me," he has effectively ratified her vow, and a husband cannot annul a vow after he has expressed his acceptance of it.</note>.

### Tractate Nazir Chapter 4 Mishnah 4
#### 4
A woman who vowed to be a **Nazirite** <note>A Nazirite is a person who takes a vow of asceticism, abstaining from wine, hair cutting, and contact with the dead.</note>,
and set aside her animal for the required sacrifice,
and afterward her husband annulled her vow:
If the animal was his,
it shall go out and graze in the herd <note>Since the vow was annulled, the animal returns to its secular status as his property.</note>.
But if the animal was hers,
the <term>Sin Offering</term> <note>Hebrew: "Hattat." A specific animal sacrifice brought at the conclusion of a Nazirite term.</note> shall be left to die, and the <term>Burnt Offering</term> <note>Hebrew: "Olah." An offering entirely consumed on the altar.</note> shall be offered as a burnt offering,
and the <term>Peace Offerings</term> <note>Hebrew: "Shelamim." An offering shared between the altar, the priests, and the owners.</note> shall be offered as peace offerings,
and they are eaten for one day and do not require bread <note>A standard Nazirite peace offering required accompanying loaves of bread and was eaten for a specific time; here, because the vow is void, the animal is treated as a generic voluntary offering which has different rules.</note>.
If she had unallocated money <note>Money set aside for the sacrifices but not yet designated for a specific animal.</note>, it shall fall to voluntary offerings; <gloss>to him</gloss>
If she had allocated money:
The money for a <term>Sin Offering</term>
shall go to the Salt Sea <note>The Dead Sea. This is a method of disposal for money that has become sacred but cannot be used for a sacrifice whose owner no longer requires it.</note>; one may not benefit from it, but the laws of sacrilege do not apply;
The money for a <term>Burnt Offering</term>
shall be used for a burnt offering, and the laws of sacrilege apply to it;
The money for a <term>Peace Offering</term>
shall be used for a peace offering, and it is eaten for one day and does not require bread.

### Tractate Nazir Chapter 4 Mishnah 5
#### 5
Once the blood of one of the sacrifices has been sprinkled on the altar for her,
he can no longer annul the vow.
**Rabbi Akiva** says:
Even if only one of any of the animals has been slaughtered for her,
he can no longer annul.
To what circumstances do these words apply?
To the **shaving of purity** <note>The ritual hair cutting performed at the successful completion of a Nazirite term.</note>;
but regarding the **shaving of impurity** <note>The ritual hair cutting performed if a Nazirite becomes ritually impure during their term, requiring them to start over.</note>, he may still annul,
because he can say:
> "I do not want a repulsive wife" <note>The husband can claim that the process of becoming impure and having to shave and restart the vow makes the wife unappealing to him.</note>.
**Rabbi** <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, the editor of the Mishnah.</note> says:
Even regarding the **shaving of purity**, he may annul,
because he can say:
> "I do not want a shaven wife."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of legal authority within a family regarding Nazirite vows. While the previous page focused on a husband's power to annul his wife's vow, this page explores a father's unique legal right to initiate a vow for his minor son and the rules for inheriting sacrificial funds when a father dies before completing his own term.</meta>

A man may impose a **Nazirite vow** <note>A Nazirite is a person who takes a vow of holiness, abstaining from wine, cutting their hair, and contact with the dead.</note> upon his son, but a woman may not impose a Nazirite vow upon her son. 

How does this work? 
If the son cut his hair, or if relatives cut it for him; if he objected, or if relatives objected on his behalf: 
If there was an animal already designated for his sacrifice, the <term>Sin Offering</term> <note>Hebrew: "Hattat." A required sacrifice for the Nazirite that, if the vow is invalidated, cannot be used for any other purpose and must be left to die.</note> shall be left to die. 
The <term>Burnt Offering</term> <note>Hebrew: "Olah." An offering entirely consumed by fire on the altar.</note> shall be offered as a voluntary burnt offering, 
and the <term>Peace Offerings</term> <note>Hebrew: "Shelamim." An offering shared between the altar, the priests, and the owner.</note> shall be offered as peace offerings; these are eaten for one day and do not require the accompanying loaves of bread <note>Usually, a Nazirite's peace offering requires special bread, but because the vow was invalidated, the animal is treated as a standard voluntary sacrifice which has simpler rules.</note>.

If he had unallocated money <note>Money set aside for the sacrifices but not yet designated for a specific animal (e.g., "this coin is for the Sin Offering").</note>, it shall fall to the fund for voluntary communal gifts <note>Used to buy burnt offerings for the altar during "down-time" when no individual sacrifices were being offered.</note>. 
If the money was allocated: 
Money designated for a **Sin Offering** shall be cast into the Dead Sea <note>Meaning it must be destroyed and made unusable, as a Sin Offering whose owner is no longer obligated cannot be used.</note>; it is forbidden to benefit from it, but if one does so, they are not liable for sacrilege <note>Hebrew: "Me'ilah." A legal category for the accidental secular use of holy property.</note>. 
Money designated for a **Burnt Offering** shall be used to bring a burnt offering, and the laws of sacrilege apply to it. 
Money designated for **Peace Offerings** shall be used to bring peace offerings, which are eaten for one day and do not require bread.

### Tractate Nazir Chapter 4 Mishnah 7

->7<-

A man may "shave" <note>This refers to the completion of the Nazirite term, which involves cutting the hair and bringing three animal sacrifices.</note> using the sacrifices designated for his father's Nazirite vow, but a woman may not "shave" using her father's Nazirite sacrifices. 

How so? 
Consider a man whose father was a Nazirite, and the father had set aside unallocated money for his Nazirite offerings and then died. 
If the son said: 
> "I hereby become a Nazirite on the condition that I may complete my term using my father's money," 
Rabbi Yose says: 
This money must instead fall to the fund for voluntary communal gifts; such a person is not considered to be "shaving" on his father's vow. 

Who then is the one who "shaves" on his father's Nazirite vow? 
It is one who was already a Nazirite at the same time as his father, and his father had set aside unallocated money for his own vow and then died—this son may use his father's designated money to complete his own requirements.

<meta>This page continues the debate between the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel regarding "erroneous consecrations." The previous page established that Shammai holds a verbal vow as binding even if based on a mistake, while Hillel argues that the intent must match the reality. This page provides the concluding arguments of that debate before moving into practical cases involving Nazirite vows and the destruction of the Temple.</meta>

**The House of Hillel said to the House of Shammai:**
"Do you not agree in this case <note>Referring to the previous examples of the wrong animal or coin being produced.</note> that because it is an erroneous consecration, the animal should go out and graze in the flock?" <note>Meaning it should remain mundane property and not be considered holy.</note>
**The House of Shammai said to them:**
"Do you not agree in the case of one who erred [while tithing his flock], and called the ninth animal the 'tenth,' and the tenth animal the 'ninth,' and the eleventh animal the 'tenth,' that the animal is nevertheless consecrated?" <note>This refers to the <term>Animal Tithe</term> (Maaser Behemah), where the Torah specifies that even if a mistake is made in the counting process, the animals designated as the tenth remain holy.</note>
**The House of Hillel said to them:**
"It was not the staff that sanctified it! <note>During tithing, the owner would count animals as they passed under a staff. Hillel argues that the Animal Tithe is a unique scriptural exception.</note> For what if he had erred and placed the staff upon the eighth or the twelfth animal? Would he have accomplished anything? Certainly not. Rather, it is because the Scripture explicitly sanctified the tenth that it also sanctified the ninth and the eleventh [in cases of error]." <note>Hillel argues that the rules of tithing are a "decree of the King" and cannot be used as a logical proof for other types of vows.</note>

### Tractate Nazir, Chapter 5, Mishnah 4

->5<-

One who vowed to be a <term>Nazirite</term> <note>A person who takes a vow of abstinence, including not cutting hair or drinking wine, ending with a sacrifice at the Temple.</note> and went to bring his animal [for the concluding sacrifice] and found that it had been stolen:
If he vowed before the animal was stolen, he remains a Nazirite.
If he vowed after the animal was stolen [but he was unaware of the theft], he is not a Nazirite.
This was an error made by **Nahum the Mede**:
When Nazirites ascended from the Exile <note>Referring to the Jewish community in Babylon returning to Jerusalem.</note> and found the **Holy Temple** destroyed,
Nahum the Mede said to them:

> "If you had known that the Temple was destined to be destroyed,
> would you have become Nazirites?"
> They said to him, "No!"

And Nahum the Mede released them from their vows.
But when the matter came before the Sages, they said:
Anyone who vowed before the Temple was destroyed is a Nazirite.
Anyone who vowed after the Temple was destroyed is not a Nazirite. <gloss>since it was destroyed</gloss> <note>The Sages disagreed with Nahum. They held that a vow can only be annulled based on a fact that existed at the time of the vow, not a "new development" like the destruction of the Temple, unless the vow was made after the destruction occurred in ignorance of the fact.</note>

# Tractate Nazir Chapter 6 Mishnah 5

**Three categories** [of things] are forbidden to a Nazirite:

There is a **greater stringency** regarding impurity and haircutting than regarding that which comes from the vine,

There is a **greater stringency** regarding that which comes from the vine than regarding impurity and haircutting:
for that which comes from the vine was never permitted by an exception to its general rule, <insert>~~for that which comes from the vine was not permitted within the general category of that which comes from the vine~~</insert> <note>This struck-through text represents a scribal correction in the manuscript, likely removing a redundant phrase.</note>
<insert><impurity and haircutting were permitted></insert>
and impurity and haircutting **were** permitted by exceptions to their general rules
in the case of an **obligatory shaving** <note>Hebrew: *tiglatzet mitzvah* – such as the shaving required for a person healed from leprosy (tzara'at).</note> and a **neglected corpse** <note>Hebrew: *met mitzvah* – a corpse found with no one to bury it; even a Nazirite or High Priest must become impure to ensure its burial.</note>.

There is a **greater stringency** regarding impurity than regarding haircutting,
for impurity invalidates the **entire** [previous count],

How is the **shaving for ritual impurity** <note>The procedure a Nazirite must follow if they become ritually impure (e.g., by touching a corpse) during their term.</note> performed?

# Chapter 9

## Tractate Nazir Chapter 9 Mishnah 1

->1<-

**Gentiles** <note>Non-Jews</note> cannot become **Nazirites**.
**Women** and **slaves** can become **Nazirites**.
The law is more **stringent** regarding **women** than **slaves**,
for a master can **compel** his **slave** <note>to violate the vow by forcing him to drink wine or work in a cemetery</note>,
but a husband cannot **compel** his **wife** <note>he may only nullify the vow itself through a specific legal process.</note>.
The law is more **stringent** regarding **slaves** than **women**,
for a husband may **nullify** the **vows** of his **wife** <note>erasing the vow entirely</note>,
but a master may not **nullify** the **vows** of his **slave**.
If a husband **nullified** his wife's vow,
it is **nullified** for her **forever**.
If a master **compelled** his **slave** <note>original: "hefer," though here meaning he forced the slave to break it rather than legally annulling the vow's existence</note>,
and the slave then **went out to freedom**, he must **complete** his **Nazirite** vow.
If the slave **passed out of the master's presence** <note>meaning he moved away or escaped, but remained legally a slave</note>,
**Rabbi Meir** says:
He **shall not drink** wine.
And **Rabbi Yose** says:
He **may drink**.

### Tractate Nazir Chapter 9 Mishnah 2

->2<-

A **Nazirite** who shaved [at the completion of his vow] and then it became known that he had been **impure**, 
if it was a **known impurity**, he voids [his previous days and must restart his term], 
but if it was an **impurity of the abyss** <note>original: "tumat ha-tehom." This refers to a hidden corpse whose presence was unknown to anyone at the time.</note>, he does not void [his term]. 
If [he found out] before he had shaved, 
in either case, he voids [his term]. 
How so? 
If he went down to immerse in a cave, 
and a corpse was found floating at the mouth of the cave, he is **impure**. 
If it was found sunken into the floor of the cave: 
If he had gone down [only] to cool himself, he is **pure**; 
if he went down specifically to **purify** himself from **corpse-impurity**, he is **impure**. 
For the **legal presumption** of one who is **impure** is that he remains **impure**, 
and the **legal presumption** of one who is **pure** is that he remains **pure**, 
for there are **grounds for the matter** <note>A legal principle meaning the circumstantial evidence supports the ruling.</note>.
<gloss>The law of "The one who finds" and after it "Every doubt" and after it</gloss> <note>This is a scribe's navigational note indicating the order of the following laws.</note>

### Tractate Nazir Chapter 9 Mishnah 3 (found later in the manuscript)

->4<-

One who finds a **corpse** for the first time, lying in its usual way, 
may remove it and its **surrounding earth** <term>tivusato: the soil immediately around the body that might contain decomposed remains</term>. 
If he found two, he may remove them and their **surrounding earth**. 
If he found three: 
if there are between four and eight **cubits** <term>amah: an ancient unit of measurement, approximately 18–22 inches</term> between one and the other—
about the space of a bier and its bearers—
then this is considered a **burial ground**. 
He must then check from that point onward for twenty **cubits**. 
If he found one [corpse] at the end of twenty cubits, 
he must check from there for another twenty cubits, 
for there are **grounds for the matter**; 
for had he found it alone at the beginning, 
he would have removed it and its **surrounding earth**.

<margin>As it is stated: (Numbers 12:15)</margin>

Joseph merited to bury his father,
and there was none among his brothers greater than he,

Who is greater to us than Joseph, <insert>The word "from Joseph" is erased and replaced with "from Moses"</insert>

And Moses merited [to attend to] the bones of Joseph,
and there was none among Israel greater than he,
<margin>As it is stated: (Exodus 13:19)</margin>
> "And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him."

And who is greater to us than Moses,
for whom no one but the Omnipresent <note>Hebrew: "HaMakom," literally "The Place," a rabbinic title for God.</note>, blessed be He, attended to [his burial]?
<margin>As it is stated: (Deuteronomy 34:6)</margin>

And they did not say this regarding Moses alone,

<margin>As it is stated: (Isaiah 58:8)</margin>

## 5

He may not write [the text] on a tablet,
nor on papyrus <note>Original: "niyar." Early paper-like material made from reeds.</note>, nor on unprocessed hide <note>Original: "diphthera." A Greek loanword for skin that has been treated with salt and flour but not with gall-nuts for longevity.</note>,
but only on a scroll <note>Meaning parchment made from the skin of a clean (kosher) animal.</note>, as it is said (Numbers 5:23) "in a book."
And he may not write with gum-resin <note>Original: "kumos." Used to make ink thick and permanent.</note>, nor with copperas <note>Original: "kalkantos." Vitriol or sulfate of copper, which makes ink bite into the parchment.</note>,
nor with anything that leaves a permanent mark,
but only with ink <note>Original: "dyo." A simple ink, usually made of soot or lampblack, which sits on the surface of the parchment.</note>, as it is said "And he shall blot out"—
writing that is capable of being completely blotted out <note>The ritual requires the physical ink of the divine name and the curses to be dissolved into the water the woman drinks.</note>.

->Tractate Sotah Chapter 2 Mishnah 5<-

## 6

And why does she say "Amen, Amen"?
"Amen" to the curse,
"Amen" to the oath,
"Amen" that I did not stray with this man,
"Amen" that I did not stray with any other man,
"Amen" that I have not been defiled, and if I have been defiled, let [the waters] enter me.
"Amen" that I did not stray while betrothed or while married, <insert>as a wayward woman</insert>
or while waiting for a levirate marriage <term>Shomeret Yavam: A widow waiting to marry her deceased husband's brother to continue the family line.</term>, or after being taken in such a marriage.
Rabbi Meir says:
"Amen" that I have not been defiled in the past,
and "Amen" that I shall not be defiled in the future.

### Tractate Sotah Chapter 2 Mishnah 6

All agree <note>Referring to the various Rabbinic authorities</note> that he cannot make a condition with her <note>A condition that the "bitter waters" should test her conduct</note> regarding the time before she was betrothed, nor for the time after she was betrothed <insert>one who was betrothed</insert> <note>Meaning the husband's warning and the subsequent ordeal only apply to the period when they were fully bound in a marriage relationship.</note>.

This is the general rule:
For any [act of] sexual intercourse which, if it occurred, would not make her forbidden to him <note>The husband</note>, he could not make a condition with her.

[The water] is poured out and her meal-offering is scattered upon the ashes <note>This occurs if the woman refuses to drink before the holy name of God is blotted into the water</note>. ### Tractate Sotah Chapter 3 Mishnah 4

->4<-

She does not finish drinking before her face turns yellow and her eyes bulge, and she becomes full of [swollen] veins. And they <note>the priests and witnesses</note> say: "Remove her, remove her!" so that she does not defile the Courtyard <note>The sacred Temple precinct must be kept free of the impurity of death; they hurry to remove her before she dies</note>. 

If she possesses merit <note>original: *zekhut*; referring to previous good deeds or study</note>, it would suspend the punishment for her. There is merit that suspends the punishment for one year, there is merit that suspends it for two years, and there is merit that suspends it for three years. 

From here, Ben Azzai said: A person is obligated to teach his daughter Torah, so that if she [ever] has to drink, she will know that her merit suspends the punishment for her. 

Rabbi Eliezer says: Anyone who teaches his daughter Torah is [effectively] teaching her frivolity <note>original: *tiflut*. This term carries connotations of both foolishness and sexual impropriety; Rabbi Eliezer argues that a woman might use her knowledge of the Law to manipulate the system or hide her sins</note>. 

Rabbi Joshua says: A woman prefers one measure <term>kav: a unit of volume, about 1.2 liters</term> [of food] and frivolity over nine measures and abstinence. 

He <note>Rabbi Joshua</note> used to say: A foolish pious person, a cunning wicked person, an abstinent woman <note>one who makes a public show of piety</note>, and the "plagues of the Pharisees" <note>referring to those who perform religious acts for outward show rather than sincerity</note>—these are the destroyers of the world.

### Tractate Sotah Chapter 3 Mishnah 5

->5<-

Rabbi Shimon says: Merit does not suspend the effect of the bitter waters <note>original: *mayim ha-me’arerim*</note>. For if you say that merit suspends the effect of the bitter waters, you discredit the waters in the eyes of all the women who drink them [in the future], and you bring a bad name upon the pure women who drank [and were fine], for people will say: "They were actually defiled, but their merit suspended the punishment <insert>for them</insert>."

->6<-

Rabbi <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, the primary editor of the Mishnah</note> says: Merit [does] suspend the effect of the bitter waters.

### Tractate Sotah Chapter 3 Mishnah 6

->7<-

If her meal-offering became impure before it was sanctified in a [sacred] vessel, it is like all other meal-offerings and may be redeemed <note>Meaning it can be sold and the money used to buy a new offering, as it has not yet attained a high level of sanctity</note>. But once it has been sanctified in a vessel, it is like all other [disqualified] meal-offerings and must be burned.

### Tractate Sotah Chapter 3 Mishnah 7

->8<-

The daughter of an Israelite <term>Israel: a non-priestly Jew</term> who is married to a Priest, her meal-offering is burned <note>According to the law in Leviticus 6:16, a Priest’s meal-offering must be entirely burned and not eaten; since she is married to him, her offering takes on his status</note>. But a woman of priestly descent who is married to an Israelite, her meal-offering is eaten. 

What is the difference between a male Priest and a woman of priestly descent? 
The meal-offering of a woman of priestly descent is eaten, but the meal-offering of a male Priest is not eaten. 
A woman of priestly descent can be "profaned" <note>original: "mit-chal-lelet"; she loses her priestly status and the right to eat sacred food if she has forbidden sexual relations</note>, but a male Priest is not profaned. 
A woman of priestly descent may contract impurity from the dead <note>male priests are forbidden from contact with corpses, with few exceptions</note>, but a male Priest may not contract impurity from the dead. 
A male Priest eats of the "Most Holy" offerings, but a woman of priestly descent does not eat of the "Most Holy" offerings.

### Tractate Sotah Chapter 3 Mishnah 8

->9<-

What is the difference between a man and a woman? 
A man [who is a leper] must let his hair grow wild and rend his clothes <note>Leviticus 13:45</note>, but a woman does not let her hair grow wild or rend her clothes. 
A man can vow his son to be a Nazirite <term>Nazir: one who takes a vow of asceticism, abstaining from wine and hair-cutting</term>, but a woman cannot vow her son to be a Nazirite.

<meta>This page concludes the list of legal distinctions between men and women from Chapter 3 and begins Chapter 4, which identifies specific women who are exempt from the ritual of the bitter waters because their marital status or the nature of their union does not meet the strict biblical criteria.</meta>

And a woman does not vow her son as a Nazirite <term>Nazirite: one who takes a vow of abstinence from wine, hair-cutting, and contact with the dead</term>. 
A man may shave his head using the offerings of his father’s Nazirite vow <note>If a father dies before completing his term, the son can sometimes utilize the set-aside sacrifices</note>, but a woman may not shave her head using the offerings of her father’s Nazirite vow.
A man may betroth his daughter <note>while she is a minor</note>, but a woman may not betroth her daughter.
A man may sell his daughter <term>Hebrew Maidservant: a minor daughter sold due to extreme poverty</term>, but a woman may not sell her daughter.
A man who is sentenced to death is stoned while naked, but a woman is not stoned while naked <note>This was a rabbinic provision to preserve the dignity and modesty of the woman even during execution</note>.
A man who is stoned is afterwards hanged <note>displayed briefly on a post as a deterrent</note>, but a woman is not hanged.
A man who cannot repay what he stole may be sold as a slave for his theft, but a woman is not sold for her theft.

# Chapter 4

## Tractate Sotah Chapter 4 Mishnah 1

1
A betrothed woman <note>original: "arusah"; a woman who has undergone the first stage of marriage but does not yet live with her husband</note> and a widow waiting for her brother-in-law <term>Shomeret Yavam: a childless widow awaiting Levirate marriage or release</term>, 
<margin>Numbers 5:29</margin> neither drink the bitter water nor receive their marriage settlement <term>Ketubah: the financial contract a husband owes his wife upon divorce or death</term>, as it is said: 
"When a woman goes astray under her husband" <note>Numbers 5:19</note>, 
which excludes a betrothed woman and a widow waiting for her brother-in-law <note>because they are not yet fully living "under" or with a husband</note>.

2
A widow married to a High Priest, 
a divorcee or a woman who has undergone the ritual of release <term>Khalutzah: a widow released from the obligation of Levirate marriage</term> married to an ordinary Priest, 
an illegitimate woman <term>Mamzeret: a woman born from a forbidden union</term> or a descendant of the Temple servants <term>Netinah: a descendant of the Gibeonites</term> married to an Israelite, 
or the daughter of an Israelite married to an illegitimate man or a Temple servant; 
none of these drink the water, nor do they receive their marriage settlement <note>Because these marriages are legally forbidden, the water ritual—which is meant to restore a valid marriage—is not applied</note>.

## Tractate Sotah Chapter 4 Mishnah 2

3
The following women neither drink the water nor receive their marriage settlement: 
She who says, "I am impure to you" <note>meaning she confesses to adultery</note>, 
and she against whom witnesses arrived to testify that she is impure, 
and she who says, "I will not drink." 
However, if her husband says, "I will not make her drink," 
or if her husband had sexual relations with her on the way to the Temple, 
she receives her marriage settlement and does not drink.

# Tractate Sotah Chapter 4 Mishnah 3
## 4

A woman pregnant by another man <note>original: "meuberet chavero"; referring to a woman who was pregnant from a previous husband before marrying her current one</note> or nursing the child of another man,
She does not drink and she does not receive her marriage settlement.
These are the words of **Rabbi Meir**.
But **the Sages** say:
He [the husband] may separate from her [temporarily] and then take her back after the allotted time <note>Once the pregnancy or nursing period is over, the marriage is considered fully valid for the purposes of the Sotah law</note>.
A woman who is physically incapable of bearing children <term>Ailonit: a woman who has reached maturity without showing signs of puberty and is naturally infertile</term>, or an elderly woman, or one who is otherwise unable to give birth,
She does not drink and she does not receive her marriage settlement.
**Rabbi Eliezer** says:
[She should drink, for] he is able to marry another woman and "be fruitful and multiply" <note>Genesis 1:28</note> through her.
But all other women [not excluded by these conditions],
Either they drink, or they do not receive their marriage settlement <note>meaning if they refuse to drink, they forfeit the financial payment</note>.

# Tractate Sotah Chapter 4 Mishnah 4
## 5

The wife of a priest drinks <note>though usually a priest’s wife is forbidden to him if she has been secluded with another man, the ritual still applies here</note> and, if proven innocent, is permitted to remain with her husband.
The wife of a eunuch <note>original: "saris"; a man who is physically unable to father children</note> drinks.
One may issue a legal warning <note>original: "mekanim"; the formal warning a husband gives his wife regarding a specific man</note> regarding any of the forbidden sexual relations,
Except for a minor and for one who is not a man <note>such as an animal, as these do not constitute a legal act of adultery that the ritual is designed to test</note>.

# Tractate Sotah Chapter 4 Mishnah 5
## 6

And these are the ones for whom the court issues a legal warning [in place of the husband]:
One whose husband has become deaf, or has become mentally unstable <note>original: "nishtah"</note>,
Or if he was held captive in a prison.
They [the Sages] did not say this was done so that she should eventually drink,
But rather to disqualify her from receiving her marriage settlement <note>By issuing the warning, the court protects the husband's estate; if she then secludes herself with the forbidden man, she loses her financial claim</note>.
**Rabbi Yose** says:
It is even so that she may drink:
When her husband is released from prison, he shall make her drink.

# Tractate Sotah Chapter 5

### Tractate Sotah Chapter 5 Mishnah 1

**1**
Just as the [bitter] waters test her, 
so they test him <note>The "him" refers to the paramour—the man with whom she is suspected of committing adultery</note>, as it is said: <gloss>(Numbers 5:22; 27)</gloss>
"And [the water] shall enter," and "they shall enter" <note>original: "u-vau", "ve-yavo'u". The plural phrasing in the biblical text is interpreted by the Sages to mean the water affects both the woman and the adulterer simultaneously</note>.
Just as she is forbidden to her husband [if found guilty], 
so is she forbidden to the paramour, as it is said: <gloss>(Numbers 5:27; 29)</gloss>
"If she has been defiled," and "she is defiled" <note>The repetition of the word for defilement (tuma) implies she is now doubly prohibited: she cannot stay with her husband, nor can she marry the man she cheated with</note>.
These are the words of **Rabbi Akiva**.
**Rabbi Joshua** said:
Thus did **Zechariah ben HaKatzav** <note>Zechariah "the son of the Butcher," a priest and scholar of the late Second Temple period</note> used to expound.
**Rabbi** <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, the editor of the Mishnah</note> says:
The two times "defiled" is mentioned in the Torah portion <gloss>Numbers 5</gloss>:
"If she has been defiled," and "she is defiled,"
one refers to her being forbidden to the husband and one to the paramour.

### Tractate Sotah Chapter 5 Mishnah 2

**2**
On that day <note>This refers to a famous day in the Academy at Yavne when the leadership changed and many previously unsettled legal questions were decided</note>, **Rabbi Akiva** expounded: <gloss>(Leviticus 11:33)</gloss>
"And every earthen vessel into which any of them falls, 
whatever is inside it shall be unclean." 
It does not say "is unclean" [tamei], but "shall make unclean" [yitma] <note>Akiva is sensitive to a grammatical nuance where the word can be read as an active verb, meaning the object inside doesn't just *become* impure, but *conveys* impurity to something else</note>, 
to make others unclean;
this teaches that a loaf of bread of the "second degree" of impurity makes a "third degree" loaf unclean <term>Degrees of Impurity: A system where ritual uncleanness weakens as it is passed from one object to another. A "third degree" is the furthest reach of impurity for common food</term>.

**3**
**Rabbi Joshua** said:
Who will remove the dust from your eyes, **Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai**! <note>A respectful exclamation used when a student discovers something their deceased teacher had wondered about</note>
For you used to say:
In the future, another generation will rule that the "third degree" loaf is ritually pure, 
because there is no explicit verse for it in the Torah.
But look, **Akiva** your disciple has brought a verse from the Torah <insert>to me</insert> 
stating that it is indeed unclean, as it is said: <gloss>(Leviticus 11:33)</gloss>
"whatever is inside it shall be unclean."

On that same day, **Rabbi Akiva** expounded:
> "And you shall measure from outside the city on the east side, two thousand cubits," <gloss>Numbers 35:5</gloss>

And another verse says:
> "From the wall of the city and outward, a thousand cubits round about." <gloss>Numbers 35:4</gloss>

It is impossible to say "one thousand cubits," <gloss>In the margins, the corrector adds: "and if..."</gloss> since it has already been said "two thousand cubits."
And it is impossible to say "two thousand cubits," since it has already been said "one thousand cubits"!
Why then was it said "one thousand cubits," and why was it said "two thousand cubits"?
Rather, "one thousand cubits" refers to the <term>Migrash</term> <note>The "Migrash" was an open, uncultivated area surrounding the city walls intended for the city's beauty and for livestock, where building and planting were forbidden</note>, and "two thousand" refers to the <term>Shabbat Boundary</term> <note>The "Tehum Shabbat" is the maximum distance a person is permitted to walk outside their city limits on the Sabbath</note>.
**Rabbi Eliezer the son of Rabbi Yose the Galilean** says:
> "One thousand cubits" is for the <term>Migrash</term>, and "two thousand" is for fields and vineyards.

### Tractate Sotah Chapter 5 Mishnah 4

<page-num>5</page-num>

On that same day, **Rabbi Akiva** expounded:
> "Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song to the Lord, and they spoke, saying..." <gloss>Exodus 15:1</gloss>

The text did not need to include the word "saying" <note>original: "lemor." In biblical Hebrew, this often functions as a technical marker for how a text was recited</note>. Why then was "saying" stated?
It teaches that the Israelites would respond after Moses for every single word, like those who recite the <term>Hallel</term> <note>The Hallel (Psalms 113–118) was recited in a call-and-response format where the leader says a line and the congregation responds with a refrain or repeats the line</note>.
> "I will sing to the Lord, for He is highly exalted," <gloss>Exodus 15:1</gloss> for this reason it says "saying."

**Rabbi Nehemiah** says: They were reciting it together like those who recite the <term>Shema</term> <note>The "Shema" is the central declaration of Jewish faith, traditionally recited by the entire congregation in unison, rather than call-and-response</note>, and not like those who recite the <term>Hallel</term>.

The matter is still balanced: <gloss>Still</gloss> <note>The glossator notes "Adayin," meaning "yet" or "still," highlighting the linguistic ambiguity in the Hebrew text</note> do I hope "in Him" <note>original: "Lo" (לוֹ)</note>, or do I "not" <note>original: "Lo" (לֹא)</note> hope? <note>In the original Hebrew, the word "Lo" can be spelled two ways: with a *Vav* (לוֹ) meaning "to Him," or with an *Aleph* (לֹא) meaning "not." <meta>This page continues the legal analysis of testimony in the case of a Sotah (a woman suspected of adultery). It follows the previous page's introduction of witnesses and the ritual of the bitter waters, specifically addressing why the legal requirements for "first testimony" (the warning) differ from the "final testimony" (the act of adultery).</meta>

For this was the logical argument:
If for the first testimony <note>Referring to the *kinui* (the husband's warning) and *setirah* (the wife's subsequent seclusion with the man), which starts the legal process.</note>,
which does not prohibit her [to her husband] as a permanent prohibition,
it cannot be established by fewer than two witnesses,
then for the final testimony <note>The testimony regarding the actual act of adultery.</note>,
which prohibits her [to her husband] as a permanent prohibition,
is it not logical that it should not be established by fewer than two witnesses?
But the Scripture says: <gloss>(Numbers 5:13)</gloss>
"And there is no witness against her," [implying] any [witness] that there is against her <note>The Rabbis interpret the singular "witness" in this verse to mean that even one witness is sufficient to establish the "defilement" and prevent her from drinking the bitter waters.</note>.

### 4

Now, let us apply an *a fortiori* <term>Kal Vachomer</term> <note>A traditional Jewish logical tool where a rule from a "lenient" case is applied to a "stringent" case, or vice versa.</note> argument to the first testimony: <gloss><voice></gloss>
If for the final testimony,
which prohibits her as a permanent prohibition,
it is indeed established by a single witness,
then for the first testimony,
which does not prohibit her as a permanent prohibition,
is it not logical that it should be established by a single witness?
But the Scripture says: <gloss>(Deuteronomy 24:1)</gloss>
"Because he found some unseemly matter in her,"
and elsewhere it says: <gloss>(Deuteronomy 19:15)</gloss>
"By the mouth of two witnesses, <gloss><</gloss> By the mouth of two witnesses or by the mouth of three witnesses" <gloss>(Deuteronomy 17:6)</gloss>
"or by the mouth of three witnesses shall a matter be established."
Just as the "matter" mentioned there must be established by the mouth of two witnesses,
so too the "matter" mentioned here <note>The "matter" of the initial warning and seclusion.</note> must be established by the mouth of two witnesses.

## Tractate Sotah Chapter 6 Mishnah 4

### 5

[If] one witness says, "She was defiled,"
and another witness says, "She was not defiled,"
[or if] a woman says, "She was defiled,"
and another woman says, "She was not defiled,"
she would drink <note>The ritual of the "bitter waters" is performed when there is a deadlock of testimony, as the doubt remains unresolved.</note>.
[If] one witness says, "She was defiled,"
and two witnesses say, "She was not defiled,"
she would not drink <note>Because two witnesses carry more legal weight than one, her innocence is considered established and the ritual is unnecessary.</note>.
[If] two witnesses say, "She was defiled,"
and one witness says, "She was not defiled,"
she would not drink <note>In this case, the testimony of two witnesses establishes her guilt; therefore, she is forbidden to her husband and does not undergo the ritual test.</note>.

It also outlines how conflicting testimonies determine whether the ritual of the bitter waters is performed.</summary>

### Chapter 8

### Tractate Sotah Chapter 8 Mishnah 1

**1**
The Priest Anointed for War <term>Meshua Milchamah; a priest specifically designated to accompany the army and address the troops before battle</term>, at the time when he speaks to the people, <margin>(Deuteronomy 20:2-3)</margin> he would speak in the Holy Tongue <note>original: "Lashon HaKodesh"; i.e., Hebrew</note>, as it is said:
> "And it shall be, when you draw near to the battle, that the priest shall approach,"
this refers to the Priest Anointed for War.
"And he shall speak to the people," in the Holy Tongue.
"And he shall say to them:
'Hear, O Israel,
you are approaching today the battle against your enemies.'"
"Against your enemies," and not against your brothers—not Judah against Simeon, nor Simeon against Benjamin, who, if you were to fall into their hands, would have mercy on you.

**2**
<margin>(2 Chronicles 28:15)</margin>
Just as it is said elsewhere <note>regarding the civil war between the Northern Kingdom of Israel and the Southern Kingdom of Judah</note>:
> "And the men who were designated by name rose up
> and took the captives, and with the spoil they clothed all that were naked among them;
> they clothed them and gave them sandals, and gave them to eat and to drink, and anointed them,
> and carried all the feeble of them upon donkeys,
> and brought them to Jericho, the city of palm trees, near to their brothers;
> then they returned to Samaria."
[But here], you are going against your enemies—who, if you fall into their hands, will not have mercy on you.

**3**
<margin>(Deuteronomy 20:3)</margin>
"Let not your heart be faint; do not fear, and do not tremble, and do not be terrified because of them."
"Let not your heart be faint"—

...because of the neighing of horses and the flashing of swords.
"Fear not,"
because of the clashing of shields and the multitude of soldiers <term>Kalgassim; originally from the Latin *caligatus*, referring to Roman legionaries in heavy boots</term>.
"Do not hurry," because of the sound of the trumpets.
"Do not be terrified," because of the sound of the shouting.
> <margin>(Deuteronomy 20:4)</margin> "For the Lord your God is the one who goes before you,"

They come with the victory of flesh and blood,
but you come with the victory of the Omnipresent <term>HaMakom; literally 'the Place', a traditional rabbinic title for God indicating His presence everywhere</term>;
The Philistines came with the victory of Goliath;
and what was his end?
In the end, he fell by the sword, and they fell with him.
The Ammonites came with the victory of Shobach <note>The commander of the army of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, mentioned in 2 Samuel 10</note>;
and what was his end?
In the end, he fell by the sword, and they fell with him.
But you, you are not like that; rather:
> "For the Lord your God is the one who goes with you
> to fight for you against your enemies, to save you,"

this is the camp of the Ark of the Covenant <note>original: "Machaneh HaAdon"; literally 'The camp of the Lord', referring to the presence of the Ark on the battlefield</note>.

## Tractate Sotah Chapter 8 Mishnah 2

### 4
> <margin>(Deuteronomy 20:5)</margin> "And the officers shall speak to the people, saying:
> 'What man is there who has built a new house and has not dedicated it?
> Let him go and return to his house,
> lest he die in the battle and another man dedicate it.'"

This includes one who builds a straw-shed,
a cattle-shed, a wood-shed, or a storehouse.
Whether he is the one who built it, or one who purchased it, or one who inherited it,
or one to whom it was given as a gift.

### 5
> <margin>(Deuteronomy 20:6)</margin> "And what man is there who has planted a vineyard and has not redeemed its fruit <note>original: "v'lo chillelo"; referring to the fourth-year fruit that must be redeemed or eaten in Jerusalem</note>,
> let him go and return to his house,"

This includes one who plants a vineyard,
and one who plants five fruit-bearing trees,
even if they are of five different species.
Whether he is the one who plants it, or one who layers a vine <note>a method of propagation where a branch is bent into the soil to take root</note>, or one who grafts a branch,
or one who purchased it, or one who inherited it,
or one to whom it was given as a gift.

<margin>(Deuteronomy 20:7)</margin> "And what man is there who has betrothed a woman and has not taken her?
Let him go and return to his house,"
this applies equally to one who betroths a virgin,
and one who betroths a widow,
or even a woman awaiting levirate marriage <term>Shomeret Yavam; a childless widow waiting to marry her deceased husband's brother</term>.
And even if he heard that his brother died in the war <note>original: "met ahiv ba-milhamah"; if the brother dies childless, the survivor must perform the levirate marriage, thus granting him an exemption</note>, he turns back and comes home.
All of these men hear the words of the priest regarding the protocols of war and return,
but they must provide water and food for the army and repair the roads.

## Tractate Sotah Chapter 8 Mishnah 3
->7<-
And these are the ones who do *not* return:
One who builds a gatehouse, a veranda <term>Akhsadrah; a covered portico or colonnade</term>, or a balcony.
One who plants only four fruit trees,
or five non-fruit-bearing trees.
One who takes back his own divorcee <note>While permitted for a common Israelite, this is not considered a "new" marriage worthy of exemption</note>,
or a High Priest who marries a widow,
or an ordinary priest who marries a divorcee or a woman who has undergone the "removal of the shoe" ceremony <term>Halutzah; a widow who has performed the ritual to decline a levirate marriage</term>,
or an Israelite who marries a woman of illegitimate birth <term>Mamzeret; a woman born from an adulterous or incestuous union</term> or a Temple servant <term>Netinah; a descendant of the Gibeonites</term>,
or a daughter of an Israelite who marries a man of illegitimate birth or a Temple servant;
such a man would not return from the front.
Rabbi Yehudah says:
Even one who rebuilds a house on its old foundation would not return.
Rabbi Elazar says:
Even one who builds a brick house in the Sharon <note>A coastal region in Israel where the soil was sandy and bricks were notoriously unstable, making the house temporary rather than a permanent home</note> would not return.

## Tractate Sotah Chapter 8 Mishnah 4
->8<-
These are the ones who do not even move from their place <note>Unlike those mentioned before, these men do not even travel to the border to hear the priest's speech or perform support duties</note>:
One who built a house and dedicated it,
one who planted a vineyard and redeemed its fruit <term>Hillalo; the process of making the fourth-year fruit permissible for consumption</term>,
and one who marries his betrothed,
or one who marries his deceased brother's widow, as it is said: <margin>(Deuteronomy 24:5)</margin>
"He shall be free for his house [for one year]."
"For his house," this refers to his house.
"He shall be," this refers to his vineyard.
"And shall cheer his wife," this refers to his wife.
"Whom he has taken," this serves to include the deceased brother's widow.
These men do not provide water and food,
and they do not repair the roads.

# Tractate Sotah Chapter 8 Mishnah 5
->9<-
<margin>(Deuteronomy 20:8)</margin> "And the officers shall speak further to the people, and they shall say:
'What man is there who is fearful and soft-hearted? Let him go and return to his house.'"
**Rabbi Akiva** says:
"Fearful and soft-hearted" is to be understood literally—
meaning he is unable to stand in the battle lines
or to see a drawn sword.
**Rabbi Yose the Galilean** says:
"Fearful and soft-hearted"
refers to one who is afraid because of the transgressions he has committed <note>Rabbi Yose suggests that the previous exemptions for a new house or vineyard were provided by the Torah as "covers." If a man leaves the front because of his sins, he can pretend he is leaving for his house or vineyard to avoid public embarrassment.</note>.
Therefore, the Torah associated his return with all of those other reasons,
so that he may return because of them.
**Rabbi Yose** says:
If a High Priest married a widow,
or an ordinary priest married a divorcee or a woman who performed the "removal of the shoe" ceremony <term>Halutzah; a widow who has performed the ritual to decline a levirate marriage</term>,
or an Israelite married a woman of illegitimate birth <term>Mamzeret</term> or a Temple servant <term>Netinah</term>,
or the daughter of an Israelite married a man of illegitimate birth or a Temple servant—
this is the man who is "fearful and soft-hearted" <note>Rabbi Yose (ben Halafta) identifies the "sins" mentioned by the Galilean specifically as being in a marriage that violates biblical law.</note>.

# Tractate Sotah Chapter 8 Mishnah 6
->10<-
<margin>(Deuteronomy 20:9)</margin> "And it shall be, when the officers have finished speaking to the people,
that they shall appoint captains of the armies at the head of the people,"
and at the rear of the people.
They station sentries in front of them, and others behind them,
with iron axes <note>original: "khashilim shel barzel"</note> in their hands.
And for anyone who seeks to turn back,
the sentry has the authority to strike his legs <note>The rear guard was tasked with preventing a retreat that could turn into a panicked stampede.</note>,
for the beginning of a retreat is the start of a defeat, as it is said: <margin>(1 Samuel 4:17)</margin>
"Israel has fled before the Philistines,
and there has also been a great slaughter among the people."
And elsewhere it says: <margin>(1 Samuel 31:1)</margin>
"And the men of Israel fled from before the Philistines,
and fell down slain on Mount Gilboa."

# Tractate Sotah Chapter 8 Mishnah 7
In what case do these things apply? In a discretionary war <term>Milhemet Ha-Reshut; a war of expansion or choice initiated by the king and the Sanhedrin</term>.
But in an obligatory war <term>Milhemet Mitzvah; a mandatory war, such as defending against an attack or the original conquest of Canaan</term>, everyone goes out—
even a groom from his chamber and a bride from her wedding canopy.
**Rabbi Yehuda** says:
In what case do these things apply? In an obligatory war <note>Rabbi Yehuda disagrees on the terminology; he views the "commandment" war as the standard for these exemptions, whereas a "mandatory" war (defense) allows for no exemptions at all.</note>.

<summary>This section discusses the exemption for soldiers who are "fearful," debated as either a literal fear of battle or a spiritual fear of one's sins, and outlines the strict protocols for preventing retreat during battle. It concludes by distinguishing between discretionary wars, where exemptions apply, and obligatory wars, where they do not.</summary>

> "If a slain person is found

->and since a **court** <term>Bet Din</term> cannot consist of an even number <note>Jewish law requires an odd number of judges so that a majority decision is always possible.</note>,
->they add one more to their number, totaling five.<-

## Tractate Sotah Chapter 9 Mishnah 2

->2<-

> "**Lying**"—this excludes a body hanging from a tree.

->They would only measure the distance to a city that possesses a court.<-
->If the body was found exactly between two cities,<-
->both cities must bring two separate heifers.<-
->These are the words of **Rabbi Eliezer**.<-

And the place where its neck was broken is forbidden to be sown or worked [for agriculture]. 
But it is permitted to comb flax there or to clear stones from there.

### Tractate Sotah Chapter 9 Mishnah 6

But would it ever enter our minds

Rather, [the meaning is]: He did not come into our hands and we dismissed him [without food],

## Tractate Sotah Chapter 9 Mishnah 7

### 8

<margin>The heifer</margin>
->If the killer is found before the heifer’s neck is broken,<-
->it [the heifer] shall go out and graze among the herd.<-
->But if it was found after the neck was broken, it must be buried in its place;<-
->for since it was brought originally because of a doubt,<-
->it has atoned for that doubt and gone its way.<-
->If the heifer’s neck was broken and only afterward the killer was found,<-
->behold, he must be executed. <note>The ritual atonement for the community does not exempt the individual murderer from legal punishment if they are eventually caught.</note><-

## Tractate Sotah Chapter 9 Mishnah 8

### 9

->If one witness says, "I saw the killer,"<-
->and another witness says, "You did not see him,"<-
->or if one woman says, "I saw him,"<-
->and another woman says, "You did not see him,"<-
->they would still break the heifer's neck.<-
->If one witness says, "I saw him,"<-
->and two witnesses say, "You did not see him,"<-
->they would break the neck.<-
->If two witnesses say, "We saw him,"<-
->and one witness says to them, "You did not see him,"<-
->they would not break the neck. <note>The ritual is only performed when there is no legal testimony identifying the murderer. Two witnesses constitute a valid legal testimony in Jewish law, thereby removing the "unknown" status of the crime.</note><-

## Tractate Sotah Chapter 9 Mishnah 9

### 10

->When murderers increased in number,<-
->the ritual of the broken-necked heifer was abolished.<-
->This occurred from the time of Eleazar ben Dinai and Techina ben Perisha,<-
->who was originally called "ben Perisha"<-
->but they returned to calling him "son of the murderer." <note>Eleazar ben Dinai was a notorious leader of rebel/bandit groups during the late Second Temple period; the increase in public violence made the communal atonement ritual for "unknown" victims irrelevant.</note><-

### 11

->When adulterers increased in number,<-
->the use of the bitter waters ceased. <note>original: "Mayim HaMararim"; the ordeal of the "Sotah" used to test a woman suspected of infidelity by her husband.</note><-

<note>The vocabulary list below clarifies the technical terms used in the text.</note>
<term>Sotah: A woman suspected of adultery.</term>
<term>Egla Arufa: The heifer whose neck is broken to atone for an unsolved murder.</term>
<term>Murderers: Violent bandits or sicarii during the Roman period.</term>
<term>Eleazar ben Dinai and Techina ben Perisha: Historical figures associated with the rise of lawlessness.</term>
<term>Adulterers: Those committing marital infidelity.</term>
<term>Bitter Waters: The ritual potion described in Numbers 5 used to test a wife's faithfulness.</term>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the spiritual and social decline in Israel, moving from the suspension of the "Heifer whose neck is broken" ritual to a broader list of ancient traditions and divine blessings that ceased following the deaths of great leaders and the destruction of the Temple.</meta>

Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai <note>A leading sage during the late Second Temple period who helped ensure the survival of Judaism after the Temple's destruction in 70 CE.</note> stopped them <note>Referring to the ritual of the "bitter waters" for a suspected adulteress (*Sotah*), because the practice of adultery had become so widespread that the ritual no longer functioned.</note>, as it is said: <margin>(Hosea 4:14)</margin>
> "I will not punish your daughters when they play the harlot,
> nor your daughters-in-law when they commit adultery."

### 12
From the time Jose ben Joezer of Zeredah
and Jose ben Yohanan of Jerusalem <note>These two were the first of the "Pairs" (*Zugot*), the successive duos of spiritual leaders who headed the Sanhedrin.</note> died,
the <term>Eshkolot</term> <note>Literally "clusters." This is a title for early sages who were "clusters of Torah," meaning they possessed comprehensive knowledge of all laws and traditions without dispute.</note> ceased, as it is said: <margin>(Micah 7:1)</margin>
> "There is no cluster to eat; my soul desires the first-ripe fruit."

## Tractate Sotah Chapter 9 Mishnah 10
### 13
Yohanan the High Priest <note>Usually identified as John Hyrcanus I, a Hasmonean ruler and High Priest (r. 134–104 BCE).</note> abolished the confession of the tithe <note>The declaration made every three years regarding the proper distribution of tithes (Deuteronomy 26).</note>.
He also abolished the "awakeners" and the "strikers" <note>The "awakeners" were Levites who sang "Awake, why do You sleep, O Lord?" (Psalm 44:24), and the "strikers" were those who would wound the sacrificial animal in a way he deemed inappropriate.</note>.
Until his days, the hammer would strike in Jerusalem <note>referring to work on the intermediate days of festivals</note>,
and in his days, no person needed to ask about <term>Demai</term> <note>Produce purchased from a common person where it was uncertain if the tithes had been removed. Hyrcanus established a system to handle this doubt uniformly.</note>.

## Tractate Sotah Chapter 9 Mishnah 11
### 14
From the time the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>The supreme judicial and legislative council of ancient Israel.</note> ceased,
song ceased from the drinking houses, as it is said: <margin>(Isaiah 24:9)</margin>
> "With a song they shall not drink wine; strong drink shall be bitter to those who drink it."

## Tractate Sotah Chapter 9 Mishnah 12
### 15
From the time the early prophets died,
the <term>Urim and Thummim</term> <note>The sacred objects used by the High Priest to inquire of the Divine will.</note> ceased.
From the time the Temple was destroyed,
the <term>Shamir</term> <note>A legendary worm or substance used to cut the stones for the Temple without the use of iron tools.</note> and the "honey of the combs" <note>original: "Nofet Tzufim"; referring to a specific high-quality honey or a metaphor for spiritual sweetness</note> ceased,
and men of faith perished, as it is said: <margin>(Psalm 12:2)</margin>
> "Save, O Lord, for the godly man ceases;
> for the faithful fail from among the children of men."

### 16
Rabban Simeon ben Gamliel says in the name of Rabbi Joshua:
From the day the Temple was destroyed,
there is no day that does not contain a curse,
the dew has not descended for a blessing,
and the flavor has been taken from the fruits.
Rabbi Yose says:
Even the fatness <note>The richness or nutritional quality</note> of the fruits was taken away.

->During the war of Vespasian,<-

### Tractate Gittin Chapter 1 Mishnah 1

->1<-

**One who brings a bill of divorce** <note>term: "Get," the formal document used in Jewish law to effect a divorce</note> **from lands across the sea** <note>term: "Medinat Ha-Yam," referring to any location outside the halakhic boundaries of the Land of Israel</note>,
**must say:**
> **"In my presence it was written, and in my presence it was signed."**
**Rabban Gamliel says:**
**Even one who brings it from Rekem or from Cheger** <note>border towns on the eastern and southern edges of Israel</note>.
**Rabbi Eliezer says:**
**Even from Kephar Ludim to Lod.**
**And the Sages say:**
**He does not need to say:**
**"In my presence it was written, and in my presence it was signed,"**
**except for one who brings it from lands across the sea, or one who delivers it there.**
**And one who brings it from one province to another province within the lands across the sea,** <note>The letter "Bet" is erased in the original manuscript</note>
**must say:**
> **"In my presence it was written, and in my presence it was signed."**
**Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:**
**Even from one governorship** <note>term: "Hegemony," referring to a Roman administrative district or province</note> **to another governorship.**

### Tractate Gittin Chapter 1 Mishnah 2

->2<-

**Rabbi Yehuda says:**
**From Rekem to the east, and Rekem is like the east** <note>meaning Rekem is considered outside the Land of Israel</note>,
**from Ashkelon to the south, and Ashkelon is like the south,**
**from Akko to the north, and Akko is like the north.**
**Rabbi Meir says:**
**Akko is like the Land of Israel regarding bills of divorce.**

### Tractate Gittin Chapter 1 Mishnah 3

->3<-

**One who brings a bill of divorce from within the Land of Israel,**
**does not need to say:**
> **"In my presence it was written, and in my presence it was signed."**
**If there are challengers against it,**
**it should be validated by its signatures.**
**And one who brings a bill of divorce from lands across the sea,**
**and is unable to say:**
> **"In my presence it was written, and in my presence it was signed,"**
**if there are witnesses to the document,**
**it should be validated by its signatures.**

<summary>This page introduces the laws of Gittin (divorce documents), specifically the requirement for a messenger bringing a document from abroad to testify to its authentic writing and signing. It includes a geographical debate on the exact halakhic borders of the Land of Israel for these legal purposes.</summary>

->This is one of the ways<-

# Tractate Gittin Chapter 1 Mishnah 5
## 5

->Any bill of divorce that has a Samaritan witness on it is invalid,<- <note>term: "Kuti," a member of the Samaritan community. In the Mishnaic period, their status as reliable observers of Jewish law was a subject of significant legal debate.</note>
->except for bills of divorce for women and deeds of manumission for slaves.<-
->It happened that they brought before Rabban Gamliel at Kephar Othnai a bill of divorce for a woman,<-
->and its witnesses were Samaritan witnesses, and he declared it valid.<-
->All legal documents that are processed in Gentile courts,<- <note>term: "Arka'ot," from the Greek word *archai*, referring to secular or Roman administrative and judicial offices.</note>
->even though those who sign them are Gentiles, are valid,<-
->except for bills of divorce for women and deeds of manumission for slaves.<-
->Rabbi Shimon says:<-
->They are all valid;<-
->they were only mentioned [as invalid] when they were drawn up by laypeople.<- <note>Rabbi Shimon argues that documents from official Gentile courts are trustworthy; the concern only applies to private documents drafted by non-experts.</note>

# Tractate Gittin Chapter 1 Mishnah 6
## 6

->One who says:<-
->"Give this bill of divorce to my wife and this deed of manumission to my slave,"<-
->if he wants to retract either of them, he may retract.<-
->These are the words of Rabbi Meir.<-
->But the Sages say:<-
->He may retract regarding bills of divorce for women, but not regarding deeds of manumission for slaves,<-
->because one may act for a person's benefit in their absence,<- <note>term: "Zakin," the legal principle that an agent can perform an action that benefits someone even without that person's knowledge.</note>
->but one may only act to a person's disadvantage in their presence.<- <note>term: "Chavin," the principle that you cannot legally impose a disadvantage or change of status on someone without their direct involvement. The Sages view freedom as an absolute benefit for a slave, but view divorce as a disadvantage for a wife due to the loss of her husband's financial support.</note>
->For if he wishes not to feed his slave, he is permitted [to stop doing so],<- <note>A master could theoretically stop supporting a slave, though there are social and religious expectations otherwise.</note>
->but if he wishes not to feed his wife, he is not permitted.<- <note>A husband has a strict legal obligation to provide food and sustenance to his wife.</note>
->He [Rabbi Meir] said to them:<-
->But surely he disqualifies his slave from eating the Priestly Offering,<- <note>term: "Terumah," the holy portion of produce given to the Priests. If a master is a Priest, his slaves may eat this holy food; once freed, the slave loses this privilege, which Rabbi Meir considers a disadvantage.</note>
->just as he disqualifies his wife?<- <note>A Priest's wife may eat Terumah, but loses that right upon divorce.</note>
->They said to him:<-
->Because he [the slave] is his property.<- <note>The slave's right to eat the Priestly food is merely a byproduct of being the master's "possession," not a personal right of his own.</note>
->One who says:<-
->"Give this bill of divorce to my wife, <insert>give</insert><-
->and this deed of manumission to my slave"<-

## Chapter 2

### Tractate Gittin Chapter 2 Mishnah 1

1
**One who brings** a bill of divorce <note>term: "Get," the formal Jewish legal document used to effect a divorce.</note> from overseas <note>original: "Medinat Ha-yam," literally "the province of the sea," referring to any location outside the Land of Israel.</note> and says:
"In my presence it was written, but not in my presence it was signed";
"In my presence it was signed, but not in my presence it was written";
"In my presence it was written entirely and in my presence it was signed halfway";
"In my presence it was written halfway and in my presence it was signed entirely,"
it is invalid. <note>term: "Pasul," meaning legally disqualified or unfit for use.</note>
If one person says "In my presence it was written,"
and another says "In my presence it was signed,"
it is invalid.
If two people say "In our presence it was written,"
and one says "In my presence it was signed,"
it is invalid.
And Rabbi Judah declares it valid. <note>term: "Kasher," meaning legally fit or effective.</note>
If one says "In my presence it was written,"
and two say "In our presence it was signed,"
it is valid.

### Tractate Gittin Chapter 2 Mishnah 2

2
If it was written during the day and signed during the day,
or written at night and signed at night,
or written at night and signed during the day,
it is valid.
If it was written during the day and signed at night,
it is invalid.
Rabbi Shimon declares it valid,
for Rabbi Shimon used to say:
All bills <note>Rabbi Shimon refers to legal documents in general, such as loan contracts.</note> that were written during the day and signed at night
are invalid, except for bills of divorce for women. <note>Rabbi Shimon's leniency for divorce documents is intended to prevent a woman from being "chained" to a marriage (agunah) if her paperwork has a technical timing flaw that does not affect the actual intent of the divorce.</note>

<summary>This page addresses the specific verbal declarations required to validate a bill of divorce brought from abroad and the legal requirements for when the document must be written and signed. It highlights disputes between the Sages, Rabbi Judah, and Rabbi Shimon regarding the validity of testimony and timing.</summary>
