# Tractate Gittin Chapter 2 Mishnah 3
## 3
**One may write with anything:**
with ink <note>original: "deyo"</note>, with red paint <note>original: "sikra," likely minium or cinnabar used as a pigment</note>, with gum <note>original: "komos," a resin often used as a binder</note>, and with vitriol <note>original: "kalkanthos," a mineral-based sulfate used to make black ink</note>,
and with anything that leaves a permanent mark.
**But one may not write** with liquids,
nor with fruit juice,
nor with anything that is not lasting.
**One may write upon anything:**
upon an olive leaf,
provided that he gives her the olive <note>Meaning, if the leaf is still attached to the fruit, he must hand over the entire unit to fulfill the requirement of "giving" the document.</note>.
And upon the horn of a cow,
provided that he gives her the cow.
And upon the hand of a slave,
provided that he gives her the slave.
**Rabbi Yose the Galilean says:**
One may not write upon any living thing,
nor upon food. <note>Rabbi Yose derives this from the biblical text, arguing that the "scroll" mentioned must be an inanimate, non-edible object like parchment.</note>

# Tractate Gittin Chapter 2 Mishnah 4
## 4
**One may not write** on something attached to the ground. <note>The bill of divorce must be a "scroll," implying something already detached and mobile.</note>
If he wrote it on something attached, then detached it, signed it, and gave it to her,
it is valid <note>term: "Kasher," legally fit according to Jewish law.</note>.
**Rabbi Yehuda declares it invalid** <note>term: "Pasul," legally disqualified.</note>
unless its writing and its signing both take place while it is detached.
**Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says:**
One may not write upon erased paper <note>Paper from which writing has been scraped off, making it easier to forge or alter.</note>
nor upon unfinished hide <note>original: "diftera," a skin that has been treated with salt and flour but not with gallnuts; it remains susceptible to being erased and rewritten without detection.</note>,
because it can be easily forged.
**But the Sages declare these valid.**

# Tractate Gittin Chapter 2 Mishnah 5
## 5
**Everyone is fit to write the bill of divorce,**
even a deaf-mute, a person of unsound mind, or a minor. <note>These individuals are usually excluded from legal actions requiring intent, but because the scribe is merely a technical agent and the document's validity rests on the witnesses, they may perform the writing.</note>
**The woman may write her own bill of divorce,**
and the man may write his own receipt <note>original: "shovar," a document acknowledging that he has paid the marriage settlement (Ketubah) or other debts.</note>,
for the confirmation of the bill of divorce is established only by its signers.
**Everyone is fit to bring the bill of divorce,**

### Tractate Gittin Chapter 3 Mishnah 7

#### 7

One who lends money to a **Priest**, a **Levite**, or a **poor person** on the condition that he may set aside their portions <note>The tithes or gifts that the lender would normally be required to give to people of these statuses.</note> against the debt, he may continue to set aside those portions under the **legal presumption that they remain in their status** <note>original: "be-chezkat she-hen kayamin"; meaning the lender assumes they are still alive and, in the case of the poor person, still poor.</note>. He need not worry that perhaps the Priest or Levite has died, or that the poor person has become wealthy <note>which would make them ineligible for the gifts.</note>. 

If they died, the lender must obtain permission from the heirs <note>to continue the arrangement of keeping the tithes to pay off the debt</note>; but if he lent the money to them in the presence of a **Rabbinic Court** <term>Beit Din: a Jewish court of law</term>, he does not need to obtain permission from the heirs.

### Tractate Gittin Chapter 3 Mishnah 8

#### 8

If one designated produce to be used for the separation of **Priestly Gifts** <term>Terumah: the sacred portion of the harvest given to the Priests</term> and **Tithes** <term>Ma’aserot: the ten-percent portion given to Levites or the poor</term>, or if he designated money for the redemption of the **Second Tithe** <term>Ma’aser Sheni: a portion of the crop to be eaten by the owner in Jerusalem, or redeemed for money to buy food there</term>, he may continue to separate tithes relying on them under the legal presumption that they still exist. 

However, if they were found to be lost or spoiled, he must be concerned <note>regarding the ritual status of the produce he thought he had tithed</note> for the preceding **twenty-four hour period** <note>original: "me-et le-et," literally 'from time to time'; a standard Rabbinic window of retrospective doubt.</note>; these are the words of Rabbi Elazar. 

Rabbi Judah says: At **three times** during the year the wine must be checked <note>to ensure it has not turned to vinegar, as one cannot separate vinegar as a tithe for wine</note>: when the east wind blows at the conclusion of the **Festival** <note>Sukkot, the Feast of Tabernacles</note>, when the **grape blossoms** <note>original: "smadar"</note> emerge, and at the time when water enters the **unripe grapes** <note>original: "boser"</note>.

### Tractate Gittin Chapter 4 Mishnah 5

->5<-

One who is half-slave and half-free <note>This occurs, for example, if an enslaved person was owned by two partners and only one partner granted them freedom</note>,
serves his master one day,
and serves himself one day.
These are the words of **the House of Hillel** <term>Beit Hillel: a school of Jewish law known for generally more lenient or practical rulings</term>.
**The House of Shammai** <term>Beit Shammai: a school of Jewish law often known for stricter or more theoretical rulings</term> say:
You have repaired the master's situation, but you have not repaired his own.
To marry a maidservant is impossible, as he is half-free. To marry a free woman is impossible, as he is half-slave.
Shall he remain idle [and never marry]?
But was the world not created for anything other than **procreation** <term>Peru u’Revu: the first commandment in the Torah to 'be fruitful and multiply'</term>,
as it is said: (Isaiah 45:18)
"He did not create it to be a waste, He formed it to be inhabited"!
Rather, for the **repair of the world** <term>Tikkun HaOlam: a legal principle used by the Sages to enact social reforms for the public interest</term>,
we compel his master to make him a free man,
and the [former] slave writes a promissory note for half of his value.
The House of Hillel retracted their opinion and ruled according to the words of the House of Shammai.

### Tractate Gittin Chapter 4 Mishnah 6

One who sells his slave to **non-Jews** <note>original: "Goyim"</note> or to a location outside the Land [of Israel],
the slave goes free <note>The Sages penalized the master for selling a slave into a situation where they could no longer observe Jewish commandments</note>.
We do not ransom captives for more than their [market] value,
for the repair of the world <note>This was to prevent kidnappers from targeting the Jewish community for exorbitant profits</note>.
And we do not help captives escape,
for the repair of the world.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
[This is] for the benefit of the captives <note>To ensure they are not treated more harshly or chained more tightly by their captors out of fear of escapes</note>.
We do not purchase **Torah scrolls, Tefillin** <term>Phylacteries: small leather boxes containing scrolls worn during prayer</term>, **and Mezuzot** <term>Doorpost scrolls: ritual scrolls placed on the doorposts of a Jewish home</term> from non-Jews for more than their value,
for the repair of the world.

## Tractate Gittin Chapter 5 Mishnah 2
### 2

## Tractate Gittin Chapter 5 Mishnah 4

The matters are reversed <note>Meaning Abba Shaul believes the court-appointed guardian must swear, while the father-appointed one does not</note>.

...and regarding a **minor daughter of an Israelite** who was married to a **priest** <note>In this context, a "minor" refers to a girl under the age of twelve and a day whose father has died, and she was married off by her mother or brothers</note>, she may eat **priestly tithes** <term>Terumah: the portion of produce given to priests, which may only be eaten by the priest and his household in a state of ritual purity</term>, and if she dies, her husband inherits from her.

### Tractate Gittin Chapter 5 Mishnah 6

->6<-

The law of the **Sikrikon** <term>Sikrikon: a term likely derived from the Latin "sicarius," referring to Roman occupiers or extortionists who seized Jewish-owned land by force or threat of death</term> was not in effect in **Judea** among those killed in the war. From the time of those killed in the war and onward, the law of the **Sikrikon** is in effect. 

How does this work? 
If one purchased land from a **Sikrikon** and then returned and purchased it from the **original owner**, the purchase is **void** <note>Because it is assumed the original owner only agreed to the sale out of fear of the confiscator</note>. 
If one purchased from the **original owner** and then returned and purchased it from the **Sikrikon**, the purchase is **valid**. 

If a man purchased land from the **husband** and then returned and purchased it from the **wife**, the purchase is **void** <note>Regarding her properties, it is assumed she only agreed to please her husband</note>. 
If one purchased from the **wife** and then returned and purchased it from the **husband**, the purchase is **valid**. 

This was the **First Mishnah** <note>The earlier version of the law</note>. 
But the **court that followed them** said: 
One who purchases land from the **Sikrikon** must give the original owner **one quarter** [of the value or the land itself].

->7<-

When is this the case? 
At a time when the original owners **do not have the means to buy it back** themselves. But if they **do have the means to buy it back**, they take precedence over any other person. 

**Rabbi** <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, the editor of the Mishnah</note> convened a court, and they voted: 
That if the land remained in the possession of the **Sikrikon** for **twelve months**, anyone who is first to come and purchase it may do so, provided they give the original owner **one quarter**.

### Tractate Gittin Chapter 5 Mishnah 8

### 8

These matters were stated for the sake of the **Ways of Peace** <term>Darkhei Shalom: legal ordinances enacted to prevent social strife and promote harmony among different social and religious groups</term>:
A **Priest** <term>Kohen: a member of the hereditary clergy</term> reads [from the Torah] first, and after him a **Levite**, and after him an **Israelite**, for the sake of the **Ways of Peace** <note>This established a fixed order for synagogue honors to prevent arguments over who is most distinguished</note>.
We establish an **Eruv** <term>Eruv Chatzerot: a legal mechanism that allows residents of different homes to carry items in a shared courtyard on the Sabbath</term> in an **old house** <note>meaning the Eruv is kept in the same house where it was traditionally placed to avoid confusing the neighbors or causing jealousy</note>, for the sake of the **Ways of Peace**.
A **cistern** that is closest to the **aqueduct** is filled first, for the sake of the **Ways of Peace**.
The **finds** <note>lost objects found in the street</note> of a **deaf-mute**, an **insane person**, or a **minor** are subject to the laws of **theft** [if taken from them by others], for the sake of the **Ways of Peace** <note>While these individuals legally cannot "own" property under strict biblical law, the Rabbis protected their findings to prevent them from being exploited</note>.
**Rabbi Yose** <note>Rabbi Yose ben Halafta, a prominent 2nd-century scholar</note> says:
It is **actual theft** <note>original: "gezel gamur"; Rabbi Yose argues this is a full legal violation, not just a social etiquette</note>.
**Traps** for wild animals, birds, or fish [belonging to others] are subject to the laws of **theft**, for the sake of the **Ways of Peace**.
**Rabbi Yose** says:
It is **actual theft**.
Regarding a **poor person** who shakes the **top of an olive tree**, what falls **beneath him** is considered **stolen** [if another takes it], for the sake of the **Ways of Peace**.
**Rabbi Yose** says:
It is **actual theft**.
We do not prevent the **non-Jewish poor** from gathering **Gleanings**, **Forgotten Sheaves**, and the **Corner of the Field** <term>Leket, Shikhah, and Pe'ah: agricultural gifts mandated by the Torah to be left for the poor</term>, for the sake of the **Ways of Peace** <note>This encourages positive relations and ensures the survival of all poor people in the community, regardless of their background</note>.

### Tractate Gittin Chapter 5 Mishnah 9

### 9

A woman may **lend** to her friend who is **suspected** [of not observing the laws] of the **Sabbatical Year** <term>Shvi'it: the seventh year of the agricultural cycle in which the land must lie fallow and the produce is holy</term> a **sieve**, a **strainer**, a **hand-mill**, or an **oven**, but she may not **sift** or **grind** with her <note>To provide the tools is permitted for social harmony, but performing the labor would be direct participation in a sin</note>.
The **wife of a Fellow** <term>Haver: a person who is meticulously observant of tithes and ritual purity laws</term> may lend to the **wife of a commoner** <term>Am Ha'aretz: one who is not trained in or strictly observant of complex purity and tithing laws</term> a **sieve** or a **strainer**, and she may **sort**, **grind**, and **sift** with her.
However, from the moment she **pours water** [into the flour], she may **not touch anything** near her, for one does not **strengthen the hands of transgressors** <note>In Jewish law, moisture makes food susceptible to ritual impurity; a Haver cannot help prepare food that will be made impure</note>.
And all these [lenicencies] were stated only for the sake of the **Ways of Peace**.
And we **strengthen the hands of non-Jews** <note>by greeting them or offering verbal encouragement in their work</note> in the **Sabbatical Year**,

# Chapter 6

## Tractate Gittin Chapter 6 Mishnah 1

1
One who says [to a messenger]:
> "Receive this **bill of divorce** <term>Get: a formal Jewish legal document that effects a divorce</term> for my wife,"
or:
> "Deliver <note>original: "holekh"; literally "go" or "take"</note> this bill of divorce to my wife,"
if he wishes to retract [the divorce before it reaches her], he may retract.
A woman who said [to a messenger]:
> "Receive my bill of divorce for me,"
if [the husband] wishes to retract, he may not retract <note>Because the woman has legally designated the messenger as her personal representative (agent for receipt), as soon as the messenger receives the document from the husband, she is legally divorced and it is too late for the husband to change his mind</note>.
Therefore, if the husband said to [her messenger]:
> "I do not wish for you to **receive** it for her, 
> but rather, **deliver** it and give it to her,"
if he wishes to retract, he may retract <note>By using the word "deliver" instead of "receive," the husband overrides the woman's agency and makes the messenger his own agent instead</note>.
**Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel** <note>A leading 2nd-century sage and head of the Sanhedrin</note> says:
Even a woman who says:
> "**Take** <note>original: "tol"</note> my bill of divorce for me,"
if [the husband] wishes to retract, he may not retract <note>He argues that the word "take" is equivalent to "receive," making the messenger her agent immediately</note>.

## Tractate Gittin Chapter 6 Mishnah 2

2
A woman who said:
> "Receive my bill of divorce for me,"
needs two sets of witnesses:
two who say "In our presence she spoke [and appointed the agent],"
and two who say "In our presence [the agent] received and tore [the document]" <note>Tearing the document was a common practice after the divorce was finalized to ensure it could not be used again</note>,
even if the first witnesses are the same as the last,
or one from the first set and one from the last set,
and another joins with them <note>This explains that different combinations of witnesses are valid as long as the legal requirements for testimony are met at each stage</note>.
An **engaged young woman** <term>Na'arah Me'orasah: a girl between the ages of twelve and twelve-and-a-half who has undergone the first stage of marriage (betrothal) but does not yet live with her husband</term>,
she or her father may receive her bill of divorce.
**Rabbi Yehuda** says:
Two hands cannot acquire as one <note>Rabbi Yehuda argues that legal authority cannot be shared; either the father has the sole right to receive it for her, or she does, but not both simultaneously</note>.

### Tractate Gittin Chapter 6 Mishnah 3

3
A **minor** <term>Ketannah: a girl under the age of twelve years and one day</term> who said:
> "Go and **receive** <note>original: "hitkabel"; this implies appointing an agent for receipt, who legally becomes "her hand"</note> my bill of divorce for me,"
it is not a valid divorce until the bill of divorce reaches her own hand.
Therefore, if the husband wished to retract the divorce [before she personally receives it], he may retract,
because a minor does not have the legal capacity to appoint a messenger.
But if her father said to [a messenger]:
> "Go and receive my daughter's bill of divorce for her,"
if [the husband] wished to retract, he may not retract <note>Because a father has the legal authority to act on behalf of his minor daughter, his appointment of a messenger is legally binding immediately upon the messenger's receipt of the document</note>.

4
One who says [to a messenger]:
> "Give this bill of divorce to my wife in such-and-such a place,"
and [the messenger] gave it to her in a different place, it is **invalid** <note>original: "passul"; the husband's specific instruction was treated as a limiting condition</note>.
[But if he said:] "Behold, she is in such-and-such a place,"
and he gave it to her in a different place, it is **valid** <note>original: "kasher"; here, the husband's mention of the location is seen as helpful advice on where to find her, rather than a strict condition of the divorce</note>.

5
A woman who said:
> "Receive my bill of divorce for me from such-and-such a place,"
and he received it for her from a different place, it is invalid.
**Rabbi Eleazar** <note>A prominent scholar of the late 1st/early 2nd century CE</note> declares it valid.
[But if she said:] "Bring me my bill of divorce from such-and-such a place,"
and they brought it to her from a different place, it is valid.

### Tractate Gittin Chapter 6 Mishnah 4

6
[A woman who says to a messenger:]
> "Bring me my bill of divorce,"
may continue to eat **terumah** <term>Terumah: the "heave-offering" or priestly tithe, which only priests and their wives may eat</term> until the bill of divorce reaches her hand <note>Since the messenger is acting for the husband to "bring" it, she is not divorced until she personally receives it</note>.
[If she says:] "Receive my bill of divorce for me,"
she is forbidden from eating **terumah** <insert>with the priestly portions</insert> immediately <note>Because the messenger becomes her legal representative; she is divorced the moment he receives the document, which could happen at any time, so she must stop eating the sacred food immediately out of caution</note>.
[If she says:] "Receive my bill of divorce for me in such-and-such a place,"
she may eat **terumah** until the bill of divorce reaches that specific place.
Rabbi Eleazar forbids her from eating it immediately.

## Tractate Gittin Chapter 6 Mishnah 6
### 8
One who was cast into a pit and said:
"Let anyone who hears my voice write a bill of divorce for my wife,"
behold, these should write and give it <note>This applies even if the listeners cannot see the man's face, as the distress of the situation verifies his intent</note>.
[In the case of] a healthy person who said:
"Write a bill of divorce and give it to my wife,"
and his intention was to tease her <note>He spoke in a moment of anger or jest without true legal intent</note>.
It once happened that a healthy person said:
"Write a bill of divorce and give it to my wife,"
and then he went up to the roof, fell, and died.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said:
The Sages said:
If he fell of his own accord, it is a valid **bill of divorce**;
If the wind pushed him, it is not a valid bill of divorce <note>If he jumped, it is assumed his instruction was made in contemplation of his immediate death, giving it legal weight. If he was pushed, his death was an accident, and his previous instruction is treated as the non-binding words of a healthy man who might have changed his mind</note>.

"Write a **bill of divorce** <term>Get: the formal document required by Jewish law to effect a divorce</term> and give it to my wife,"

# Chapter 7

## Tractate Gittin Chapter 7 Mishnah 1

### 1

One who was seized by **kordyakos** <note>original: "kordyakos," likely derived from the Greek "kardiakos," referring to a state of delirium, temporary insanity, or a seizure that impairs cognitive function</note>, and said:
"Write a bill of divorce for my wife,"
he has said nothing <note>A legal act requires a "sound mind"; because he is currently incapacitated, his instructions carry no weight</note>.
If he said:
"Write a bill of divorce for my wife,"
and then he was seized by **kordyakos**,
and subsequently [in his delirium] said:
"Do not write it,"
his later words are nothing <note>Once a healthy person gives a valid instruction, a subsequent instruction given while they are not of sound mind cannot cancel the first one</note>.

### Tractate Gittin Chapter 7 Mishnah 3
3
[If a man says:] "Behold, this is your bill of divorce if I die,"
"This is your bill of divorce [if I die] from this illness,"
or "This is your bill of divorce after my death,"
he has said nothing <note>A divorce cannot take effect after death because the marriage bond is already severed by the husband's passing, leaving no marriage to "divorce"</note>.
[But if he says:] "From today if I die,"
or "From now if I die,"
behold, this is a valid bill of divorce.
[If he says:] "From today and after my death,"

4

and he then got up and walked in the marketplace, but later fell ill again and died—
they must assess <gloss>evaluate</gloss> him:
If he died as a result of the first illness,
behold, this is a valid bill of divorce,
but if not, it is not a valid bill of divorce.

"If I do not return from now until twelve months have passed, write a **bill of divorce** <term>Get: the formal document of Jewish divorce</term> and give it to my wife!"
If they wrote it within the twelve months and gave it within the twelve months, it is not a valid **bill of divorce**. <note>The husband's instructions implied that the writing and giving should only happen after the twelve-month condition was met.</note>
"Write and give a **bill of divorce** to my wife, if I do not return from now until twelve months have passed."
If they wrote it within the twelve months and gave it after the twelve months, it is not a valid **bill of divorce**.
**Rabbi Yose** says:
In such a case, it is a valid **bill of divorce**. <note>Rabbi Yose argues that the command to "write" was meant to be carried out immediately, even if the "giving" was conditional on his absence.</note>
If they wrote it after twelve months and gave it after twelve months, and then the husband died:
If the delivery of the **bill of divorce** preceded his death, behold, it is a valid **bill of divorce**.
But if his death preceded the delivery of the **bill of divorce**, it is not a **bill of divorce**. <note>A divorce cannot take effect after a husband's death because the marriage is already dissolved by death; the document must be received while he is still alive.</note>
And if it is not known which occurred first, this is the case of which they said:
She is **divorced and not divorced**. <note>This is a state of legal doubt. She must follow the restrictions of both a divorcee and a widow—for example, she cannot marry a Priest (who may not marry a divorcee) but she also requires a formal release (Chalitzah) from her late husband's brother if they were childless.</note>

# Chapter 8

## Tractate Gittin Chapter 8 Mishnah 1

### 1
If a man throws a **bill of divorce** to his wife, and she is inside her house or inside her courtyard, behold, she is divorced. <note>In Jewish law, a person's property can act as their "hand" to acquire objects. If she owns the space where the document lands, it is as if she caught it.</note>
If he threw it to her inside his house or inside his courtyard, even if he is with her in bed, she is not divorced. <note>Since the house belongs to him, the document is still technically in his "hand" or domain, and the transfer of ownership to her has not occurred.</note>
If he threw it into her lap or into her basket, behold, she is divorced. <note>A woman's personal containers or clothing are considered her private domain, even when she is standing on her husband's property.</note>

## (Tractate Gittin Chapter 8 Mishnah 2)

If he said to her:
"Collect this **promissory note**," <note>original: *Shtar Chov*</note>
or if she found it behind him <note>Meaning she found the document behind his back without a formal act of giving</note>,

...reading it, and behold, it is her **bill of divorce**, <note>original: *gitah*</note> <קוֹרֵא>
it is not a valid **bill of divorce** <term>Get: the formal document of Jewish divorce</term> until he explicitly says to her: "Behold, this is your **bill of divorce**."

### Tractate Gittin Chapter 8 Mishnah 3
#### 2
And the same rules apply to the matter of **betrothal** <term>Kiddushin: the first stage of the Jewish marriage process</term> and to the matter of a debt.
If a creditor said to a borrower: "Throw me the money I am owed!"
and he threw it to him:
if it landed closer to the lender, the borrower has fulfilled the obligation; <note>The lender now legally "owns" the money once it enters his proximity.</note>
if it landed closer to the borrower, the borrower is still liable;
if it landed exactly half-and-half, they must divide the disputed amount.
If she was standing on top of a roof and he threw the document to her:
as soon as the document enters the "airspace" of the roof,
behold, she is divorced. <note>In Jewish law, the airspace above a person's property is considered part of that property.</note>
If he was above and she was below and he threw it to her:
as soon as it has left the domain of the roof,
even if the document was subsequently erased or burned before reaching her,
behold, she is divorced.

### Tractate Gittin Chapter 8 Mishnah 4
#### 4
The **House of Shammai** <note>One of the two major schools of early Rabbinic thought, often known for stricter interpretations.</note> say:
A man may release his wife with an "old" **bill of divorce**.
But the **House of Hillel** <note>The school of thought usually followed in Jewish law, often more focused on practical application.</note> forbid this.
And what constitutes an "old" **bill of divorce**?
Any document where the husband secluded himself with her after he had already written it for her. <note>The concern is that if they were alone together, they might have reconciled and engaged in intimacy, which would conceptually cancel the intent of the previously written document.</note>

## Chapter 9

### Tractate Gittin, Chapter 9, Mishnah 1
# 1
One who divorces his wife and says to her:
"Behold, you are permitted to marry any man except for so-and-so,"
Rabbi Eliezer permits this divorce,
and the Sages forbid it. <note>The Sages believe a divorce must be a "total severance"; if she is still forbidden to even one man because of her previous marriage, she is not fully "divorced."</note>
What should he do to correct this?
He should take the document back from her and then give it back to her again, and say to her:
"Behold, you are permitted to any man."
If he wrote the restriction inside the document itself,
even though he later went back and erased it, the document is invalid. <note>The document must be valid from the moment it is written; a fundamental flaw in the text cannot be fixed by erasure.</note>

### Tractate Gittin, Chapter 9, Mishnah 2
# 2
If he said, "Behold, you are permitted to any man,
except for my father and your father," "my brother and your brother,"
or to a slave or a gentile,
or to anyone with whom she could not legally contract a marriage anyway,
the document is **valid**. <note>Since she is biblically forbidden from marrying these people regardless of her divorce status, his restriction is considered meaningless and does not hinder her general freedom to remarry.</note>
But if he said, "Behold, you are permitted to any man, except..."
[to a man where the marriage would make her] a widow married to a High Priest,
a divorcee or a *chalutzah* married to an ordinary priest,
a *mamzeret* or a *Netinah* married to an Israelite,
or an Israelite woman married to a *mamzer* or a *Natin*,
or to anyone with whom she can contract a marriage even if it involves a transgression,
the document is **invalid**. <note>Because these marriages—while sinful—are legally binding if they occur, excluding them constitutes a significant restriction on her freedom.</note>

<note>Original terms: "Chalutzah" refers to a woman released from levirate marriage; "Mamzer" refers to a person born of an adulterous or incestuous union; "Natin" refers to a descendant of the Gibeonites.</note>

### Tractate Gittin, Chapter 9, Mishnah 3
# 3

# Tractate Kiddushin

## Chapter 1

<vocab>Mishnah, Masekhet Gittin, Masekhet Kiddushin, Halakhah, Divorce, Get, Marriage, Beth Shammai, Beth Hillel, Rabbi Akiva, Deuteronomy</vocab>

<summary>This page concludes Tractate Gittin by defining the valid grounds for divorce according to the competing schools of Shammai and Hillel, and addresses how public rumors of marriage or divorce affect legal status. It marks the transition into Tractate Kiddushin, which deals with the laws of betrothal.</summary>
<keywords>grounds for divorce, forced Get, public rumor, Matla, House of Shammai, House of Hillel, Rabbi Akiva, betrothal, Jewish law, Deuteronomy 24:1</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the end of Tractate Gittin (laws of divorce) to the beginning of Tractate Kiddushin (laws of betrothal). This page begins the systematic legal definitions of how marriage, servitude, and property are initiated and dissolved.</meta>

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 1 Mishnah 1
### 1
A woman is acquired <note>Hebrew: *nikneit*. In this legal context, "acquisition" refers to the formal process of betrothal (*kiddushin*), where a woman becomes legally sanctified/exclusive to her husband, rather than literal property ownership.</note> in three ways, and she acquires herself <note>meaning, she regains her legal independence</note> in two ways:
She is acquired through money, through a contract <term>Shtar: a legal document of betrothal</term>, or through sexual intercourse.
Regarding money, the House of Shammai say:
With a dinar, or the value of a dinar.
And the House of Hillel say:
With a *perutah* <note>the smallest copper coin used in the Mishnaic period</note>, or the value of a *perutah*.
And how much is a *perutah*?
One eighth of an Italian *issar* <note>a Roman copper coin</note>.
And she acquires herself through a bill of divorce <note>original: *get*</note> and through the death of the husband.
The childless widow <term>Yevamah: a widow whose husband died without children, who is legally bound to her brother-in-law</term> is acquired through intercourse,
and she acquires herself through the ceremony of "removal" <term>Chalitzah: a ritual shoe-removal ceremony that releases the widow from her obligation to her brother-in-law</term>, and through the death of the brother-in-law.

---

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 1 Mishnah 2
### 2
A Hebrew slave is acquired through money and through a contract,
and he acquires himself through years <note>the completion of six years of service</note>, through the Jubilee year, and by the deduction of money <note>repaying a prorated portion of the purchase price to the master</note>.
The Hebrew maidservant has an advantage over him,
in that she acquires herself through physical signs <note>original: *simanim*, referring to the onset of puberty</note>.
The "pierced" slave <note>original: *nirtza*; a slave who chose to remain with his master after six years and had his ear pierced against a doorpost</note> is acquired through the act of piercing,
and he acquires himself through the Jubilee year and through the death of the master.

---

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 1 Mishnah 3
### 3
A Canaanite slave <note>a general term for a non-Jewish slave</note> is acquired through money, through a contract, and through a demonstration of ownership <term>Chazakah: taking possession through a physical act of labor or service</term>.
And he acquires himself through money provided by others,
or through a contract received by himself.
These are the words of Rabbi Meir.
But the Sages say:
With money provided by himself,
and through a contract received by others,
provided that the money belongs to the others <note>since a slave’s assets usually belong to the master, the funds for his manumission must technically come from a third party to be legally effective</note>.

---

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 1 Mishnah 4
### 4
Large livestock <note>such as cattle or camels</note> are acquired through "delivery" <term>Mesirah: the act of the seller handing over the reins or the animal itself to the buyer</term>,
and small livestock <note>such as sheep or goats</note> are acquired through "lifting" <term>Hagbahah: physically raising the object to demonstrate ownership</term>.
These are the words of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eleazar.
But the Sages say:

Small livestock <note>original: *behemah dakkah*; specifically referring to sheep and goats</note> are acquired through pulling <term>Meshikhah: a legal act of acquisition where the buyer physically pulls the object into their own space or domain</term>.

## Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 1 Mishnah 5

->5<-

Property that has security <note>original: *achrayut*; this refers to real estate (land), which is "secure" because it cannot be moved or hidden and can serve as a guarantee for debts</note>
is acquired through money, through a contract, and through taking possession <term>Chazakah: demonstrating ownership through a physical act of improvement or use of the land</term>,
and property that does not have security <note>movable goods and personal property</note> is acquired only through pulling.
Property that does not have security
is acquired along with property that has security
through money, through a contract, and through taking possession.
And property that does not have security "binds" <note>this refers to the legal concept of *gilgul shevuah*, where a person required to swear an oath regarding movable property can also be forced to swear regarding land in the same claim</note>
the property that has security,
requiring an oath to be taken regarding them.

## Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 1 Mishnah 6

->6<-

Anything that is used as value <note>as a medium of exchange or barter</note> for another item,
once this party gains possession of the first item, the other party becomes liable for the exchange <note>this describes *Kinyan Chalipin*, a barter-style acquisition where the transfer of one object immediately effects the transfer of the other</note>.
How so?
If one exchanged an ox for a cow, or a donkey for an ox,
once this party gains possession, the other becomes liable for the exchange.
The domain of the High <note>the Temple or sacred property</note> is acquired through money,
whereas the domain of an ordinary person is through possession.
One's word to the High is like one's delivery to an ordinary person <note>a verbal commitment to donate to the Temple is legally binding the moment it is spoken, unlike private transactions which require physical acts</note>.

## Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 1 Mishnah 7

->7<-

Regarding all commandments of the father upon the son <note>duties a father owes to his son, such as circumcision or teaching him a trade</note>,
men are obligated and women are exempt.
Regarding all commandments of the son upon the father <note>duties a child owes to a parent, such as honor and reverence</note>,
both men and women are obligated.
Every positive commandment that is time-bound <note>original: *she-hazman geramah*; commandments performed only at specific times, like sitting in a Sukkah or hearing the Shofar</note>,
men are obligated and women are exempt.
And every positive commandment that is not time-bound,
both men and women are obligated.
And regarding every negative commandment <note>prohibitions</note>,
whether it is time-bound or not time-bound,
both men and women are obligated,
except for "do not round" <note>rounding the corners of the head/hairline</note>,
and "do not destroy" <note>marring the corners of the beard</note>,
and "do not become impure for the dead" <note>a prohibition specifically for Priests/Kohanim</note>.

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 1 Mishnah 8

#### 8

->The laying on of hands <term>Semichah: a sacrificial rite where the owner leans their weight on the animal's head before it is slaughtered</term>, the waving of offerings, and the bringing near <note>original: *Haggashah*; the act of bringing a grain offering to the corner of the altar</note>,<-
->The taking of the handful <term>Kemitzah: the method of "slaughtering" a grain offering by scooping a three-finger handful of flour</term>, the burning of fats or incense, and the pinching of a bird's neck <note>original: *Melikah*; the ritual slaughter of a bird offering using a fingernail</note>,<-
->The receiving of the sacrificial blood, and the sprinkling of the blood,<-
->Are practiced by men but are not practiced by women,<-
->Except for the grain offering of a *Sotah* <note>original: *Sotah*; a woman suspected by her husband of infidelity who undergoes a specific ordeal/ritual</note> and a female Nazirite,<-
->For they wave their own offerings.<-

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 1 Mishnah 9

#### 9

->Every commandment that is not dependent on the Land <note>this refers to personal obligations, such as wearing ritual fringes or observing the Sabbath, which are not tied to the soil of Israel</note>,<-
->Is practiced both in the Land of Israel and outside the Land,<-
->And every commandment that is dependent on the Land <note>agricultural laws such as tithing or leaving corners of the field for the poor</note>,<-
->Is practiced only in the Land of Israel,<-
->Except for the laws of *Orlah* <term>Orlah: the prohibition against eating fruit from a tree during its first three years of growth</term> and *Kilayim* <term>Kilayim: the prohibition against cross-breeding animals, planting mixed seeds, or wearing wool and linen together</term>.<-
->Rabbi Eliezer says:<-
->Also the law of New Grain <note>original: *Chadash*; the prohibition against eating from the new harvest before the Omer offering is brought on Passover; Rabbi Eliezer argues this applies everywhere in the world</note>.<-

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 1 Mishnah 10

#### 10

->Anyone who performs even a single commandment, they <note>Heaven or the Divine Court</note> do good for him,<-
->And his days are lengthened,<-
->And he inherits the Land.<-
->But anyone who does not perform even a single commandment,<-
->They do not do good for him,<-
->And his days are not lengthened,<-
->And he does not inherit the Land.<-
->And anyone who is not involved in Scripture,<-
->Nor in the Mishnah, nor in the way of the world <term>Derech Eretz: a term encompassing both civil behavior, etiquette, and having an honest profession</term>,<-
->Is not considered part of civilized society.<-
->But one who holds fast to all three,<-
->Of him the verse says: <gloss>(Ecclesiastes 4:12)</gloss><-
->"And the threefold cord is not quickly broken."<-

It concludes with a moral teaching on the importance of balancing Torah study, tradition, and civil conduct for the stability of a person's life and society.</summary>

# 1

A man betrothes <note>original: *mekaddesh*; the first stage of the Jewish marriage process, creating a legal bond that requires a divorce to dissolve</note> a woman either by himself or through his agent,
And a woman may be betrothed either by herself or through her agent.
A man may betroth his daughter when she is a young girl <term>Na'arah: a girl between the ages of twelve and twelve and a half</term>
Either by himself or through his agent.
If a man says to a woman:
"Be betrothed to me with this date,"
"Be betrothed to me with this one,"
"Be betrothed to me with this one,"
If any one of them is worth a *perutah* <term>Prutah: the smallest copper coin of the era, the minimum value required for a legal transaction</term>, she is betrothed;
But if not, she is not betrothed.
If he said, "[Be betrothed] with this one, and this one, and this one,"
If the total value of all of them is worth a *perutah*, she is betrothed;
But if not, she is not betrothed.
If she was eating them one by one as he gave them to her,
She is not betrothed,
Unless at least one of them was worth a *perutah*. <note>Once she eats the item, it is considered a consumed gift or a debt rather than a transfer of value for betrothal, unless a single remaining item meets the minimum value on its own.</note>

---

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 2 Mishnah 2

# 2

If he says: "Be betrothed to me with this cup of wine,"
And it is found to be honey;
Or "with this cup of honey," and it is found to be wine;
"With this silver denarius," and it is found to be gold;
"With this gold one," and it is found to be silver;
"On condition that I am a poor man," and he is found to be a rich man; <insert>second</insert> <note>the word "second" likely refers to a scribal numbering or a textual variant</note>
"On condition that I am a rich man," and he is found to be a poor man,
She is not betrothed. <note>The law views this as a "mistaken transaction"; because the reality did not match the stated condition, there was no true consent.</note>
Rabbi Shimon says:
If he deceived her for the better <note>original: *hit’ah lishvach*; for example, promising silver but giving gold</note>,
Then she is betrothed.

---

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 2 Mishnah 3

# 3

"On condition that I am a priest," and he is found to be a Levite; <insert>second</insert>
"On condition that I am a Levite," and he is found to be a priest;
"On condition that I am a *Natin*," <term>Natin: a descendant of the Gibeonites, a specific social class in ancient Israel with certain marriage restrictions</term> and he is found to be a *Mamzer*; <term>Mamzer: a person born from an illicit union, such as adultery or incest, who is restricted from marrying into the general community</term>
"On condition that I am a *Mamzer*," and he is found to be a *Natin*;
"On condition that I am a town-dweller," and he is found to be a city-dweller;
"On condition that I am a city-dweller," and he is found to be a town-dweller;
"On condition that my house is near the bathhouse," and it is found to be far away;

<note>This list of vocabulary refers to: Tractate Kiddushin, Mishnah, Betrothal, His Agent, Small Coin, Deceived for the Better, Priest, Levite.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter 2 of Tractate Kiddushin regarding conditional betrothals. "[On condition that my house is] far," and it is found to be near;
"On condition that I have a daughter or a grown maidservant," and he does not have one;
"On condition that I do not have [them]," and he does have them;
"On condition that I have sons," and he does not;
"On condition that he does not have [them]," and he does;
And regarding all of these cases, even if the woman said:
"In my heart, I intended to be betrothed to him regardless [of the error],"
She is not betrothed. <note>In Jewish law, for a betrothal to be valid, the conditions set at the time of the transaction must be factually accurate. A "change of heart" cannot retroactively validate a legally flawed contract.</note>
And the same rule applies if she deceived him.

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 2 Mishnah 4

->4<-

One who says to his agent:
"Go and betroth for me a certain woman in a certain place,"
And the agent went and betroth her in a different place,
She is not betrothed. <note>In this case, the location was specified as a condition of the agent's authority. By changing the location, the agent exceeded his power.</note>
[But if he said,] "She is currently in a certain place,"
And the agent went and betrothed her in a different place,
She is betrothed. <note>Here, the location was merely descriptive, intended to help the agent find the woman, rather than a strict legal condition.</note>

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 2 Mishnah 5

->5<-

One who betrothes a woman on the condition that she has no vows <term>Nedarim: religious or personal commitments to abstain from certain things, which could create a burden in a marriage</term> upon her,
And she is found to have vows, <insert>and it was found</insert>
She is not betrothed.
If he married her without specifying conditions, and she is found to have vows,
She must leave without her marriage settlement <term>Ketubah: the financial contract that a husband provides to his wife, payable upon divorce or his death</term>.
[If he betrothed her] on the condition that she has no physical defects <term>Mumim: blemishes or health conditions that were considered significant in the ancient world</term>,
And she is found to have defects,
She is not betrothed.
If he married her without specifying conditions, and she is found to have defects,
She must leave without her marriage settlement,
For all the physical defects that disqualify Priests <note>original: Kohanim; refers to the physical requirements for those serving in the Temple as described in the Bible</note> from service,
Also disqualify women [in the context of these marriage laws].

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 2 Mishnah 6

->6<-

One who betrothes two women with the shared value of a single *perutah* <term>Prutah: the smallest copper coin of the Roman era, the minimum legal value required to effect a betrothal</term>,
Or one woman with less than the value of a *perutah*,
Even if he sent gifts <term>Sivlonot: customary presents sent by a groom to his bride's house during the engagement period</term> afterward,
She is not betrothed,

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 2 Mishnah 7
->7<-

One who betrothes a woman and her daughter,
or a woman and her sister as one <note>meaning simultaneously, in a single declaration</note>,
they are not betrothed. <note>Biblical law prohibits a man from being married to two sisters at once, or a woman and her daughter. Since the act was performed simultaneously and the law cannot distinguish which one should take precedence, the entire act is void.</note>
It once happened that there were five women,
and among them were two sisters,
and a man gathered a basket of figs,
which belonged to the women, and it was the Sabbatical year <term>Shvi'it: the seventh year of the agricultural cycle in which land must lie fallow and crops are considered ownerless and free for all to take</term>,
and he said to them:
> "Behold, you are all betrothed to me with this basket [of figs],"
and one of them accepted it on behalf of all of them,
and the Sages said:
The sisters are not betrothed. <note>However, the other three women in the group who were not related to one another were successfully betrothed.</note>

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 2 Mishnah 8
->8<-

One who betrothes [a woman] with his portion of the Most Holy offerings <term>Kodshei Kodashim: the highest level of Temple sacrifices, such as the sin offering, which may only be eaten by priests within the Temple courtyard</term>, or with Lesser Holy offerings <term>Kodashim Kalim: sacrifices such as the peace offering, which may be eaten by the owners or priests throughout Jerusalem</term>,
she is not betrothed. <note>Even though the priest receives a portion of the meat, it is considered "from the table of the Most High" rather than his private property, and therefore cannot be used as a marriage payment.</note>
[If he betrothes] with Second Tithe <term>Ma'aser Sheni: a portion of the crop that must be brought to Jerusalem and eaten there in a state of ritual purity</term>,
whether it was done unintentionally or intentionally, he has not betrothed her.
These are the words of Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
If it was intentional, he has betrothed her; if it was unintentional, he has not betrothed her.
And with Consecrated property <term>Hekdesh: property donated to the Temple treasury</term>,
if it was intentional, he has betrothed her; if it was unintentional, he has not betrothed her.
These are the words of Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
If it was unintentional, he has betrothed her; and if it was intentional, he has not betrothed her. <note>The debate centers on "Meilah" (misappropriation of sacred property). Rabbi Yehuda argues that when one unintentionally uses Temple property for a personal transaction, the object becomes "profane" (secularized) and the betrothal takes effect, whereas an intentional act is a different legal category.</note>

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 2 Mishnah 9
->9<-

One who betrothes with *Orlah* <term>the fruit of a tree during its first three years of growth, which is forbidden for any use</term>,
with Mixed Seeds of the vineyard <term>Kilayim: the forbidden planting of grain or vegetables in a vineyard</term>,
with an ox condemned to stoning <term>an ox that killed a person and was sentenced by a court; it may not be eaten or used for benefit</term>,
with the heifer whose neck is broken <term>Eglah Arufah: a calf killed as part of an atonement ritual for an unsolved murder</term>,
with the birds of a leper <term>birds used in the purification ritual for one healed of "tzara'at," a biblical skin disease</term>,
or with the hair of a Nazirite <term>the hair of one who has taken a vow of abstinence, which must be burned at the end of their term</term>,
[she is not betrothed]. <note>All these items are "forbidden for benefit." Because they have no legal value for trade or use, they cannot serve as the "perutah" (minimum value) required for a marriage contract.</note>

...and with the firstborn of a donkey <note>original: "פֶטֶר חֲמוֹר" — A donkey's firstborn must be redeemed with a lamb or killed; until redeemed, it is forbidden for use or benefit.</note>,
and with meat [cooked] in milk <note>original: "בָּשָׂר בְּחָלָב" — According to Jewish law, meat and milk cooked together may not be eaten, nor may any benefit be derived from them (such as selling them).</note>,
and with non-sacred animals that were slaughtered in the Temple courtyard <note>original: "חֻלִּין שֶׁנִּשְׁחֲטוּ בָעֲזָרָה" — It is a violation to slaughter ordinary animals inside the sacred Temple space; such animals are forbidden for any use.</note>,

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 2 Mishnah 10
->10<-
One who betroths a woman with priestly portions <term>Terumah: the portion of the harvest given to the Priests, which is sacred</term>, or with tithes <term>Ma'aserot: the various portions separated from produce for the Levites or the poor</term>, or with the priestly gifts <note>original: "מַתָּנוֹת" — refers to the foreleg, cheeks, and stomach given to Priests from slaughtered non-sacred animals.</note>,
or with the water of purification <note>original: "מֵי חַטָּאת" — water mixed with the ashes of the Red Heifer used to purify those who had come into contact with the dead.</note>, or with the ashes of purification,
behold, she is betrothed,
even if [the man who gave them] is a common Israelite <note>Even though a non-priest cannot eat these items, they have a "value of benefit" because he can give them to a specific Priest of his choosing, a right that has monetary worth.</note>.

# Chapter 3

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 3 Mishnah 1
->1<-
One who says to his fellow:
"Go and betroth for me such-and-such a woman,"
and the agent went and betrothed her for himself,
she is betrothed [to the agent]. <note>Though this is considered a deceitful and morally wrong act, the legal transaction between the agent and the woman is valid.</note>
And likewise, one who says to a woman:
"Behold, you are betrothed to me after thirty days,"
and another man came and betrothed her within those thirty days,
she is betrothed to the second man.
If she was the daughter of a common Israelite betrothing a Priest, <unclear>the words after 'daughter' were erased and cannot be read</unclear>
she may eat of the priestly portion <term>Terumah</term>. <note>This refers to a case where the betrothal is valid; a woman betrothed to a priest gains the right to eat sacred food.</note>
If he said, "Behold, you are betrothed to me from now and after thirty days,"
and another man came and betrothed her within the thirty days,
she is "betrothed and not betrothed." <note>original: "מְקֻדֶּשֶׁת וְאֵינָהּ מְקֻדֶּשֶׁת" — This is a legal stalemate. It is unclear if the first man's "from now" takes precedence or his "after thirty days" takes precedence. Therefore, she is in a state of doubtful marriage to both.</note>
If she was the daughter of a Priest betrothed to a common Israelite,
she may no longer eat of the priestly portion. <note>Due to the doubt, she loses her priestly privileges but does not gain the rights of a commoner's wife yet.</note>

> then they shall receive a possession among you in the land of Canaan." 
<note>Rabbi Meir derives from here the rule of the "Double Condition": for a condition to be legally binding, one must explicitly state both the positive outcome if the condition is met and the negative outcome if it is not.</note>

[If a father says,] "I betrothed my daughter,

"I am the one who betrothed her," he is believed <note>original: "נֶאֱמָן" (ne'eman) — Legally trusted. In Jewish law, a father has the authority to accept betrothal on behalf of his daughter while she is still a minor or a young maiden.</note>.
If this one says, "I am the one who betrothed her,"

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 3, Mishnah 8

[If a father says,] "I betrothed my daughter while she was a minor,
and I betrothed her and divorced her while she was a minor,"
and she is still currently a minor, he is believed.
[But if he says,] "I betrothed her and divorced her while she was a minor,"
and she is now an adult <note>original: "גְּדוֹלָה" (gedolah) — Meaning she has reached the age of majority/physical maturity, at which point the father's absolute legal control over her marriage ends.</note>, he is not believed.
[If he says,] "She was taken captive and I redeemed her,"
whether she is a minor or she is an adult,
he is not believed <note>Captivity often implies a suspicion of sexual assault, which would legally disqualify the daughter of a Priest from certain marriages. Because this testimony would damage her reputation and future marriage prospects, the father is not given the same legal trust as he is for betrothal.</note>.
One who is dying and said at the time of his death:
"I have sons," he is believed.
"I have brothers," he is not believed <note>These statements affect "Yibbum" (Levirate marriage). If a man has sons, his widow is free to marry anyone. If he has only brothers, she is bound to them. He is believed when his words release her from a restriction, but not when they impose one.</note>.
One who betroths his daughter without specifying which one,
the mature daughters are not included <term>Mature daughters: "Bogrot," daughters who have reached full physical maturity, usually six months after becoming a "Gedolah." At this stage, they are legally independent and the father cannot betroth them without their consent.</term>.

# Chapter 4

## Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 4 Mishnah 1
### 1
Ten lineages ascended from Babylon <note>This refers to the return of the Jewish people from the Babylonian exile during the time of Ezra the Scribe</note>:
Priests, Levites, Israelites,
*Challalim* <term>Challalim: Individuals disqualified from the priesthood because they were born from a marriage forbidden to a priest</term>, converts, freed slaves,
*Mamzerim* <term>Mamzerim: Individuals born from forbidden incestuous or adulterous unions</term> and *Netinim* <term>Netinim: Descendants of the Gibeonites who were assigned as Temple servants</term>,
*Shetuki* <term>Shetuki: Literally "the silenced one"; a person who knows their mother but not their father</term> and *Asufi* <term>Asufi: A foundling gathered from the street whose parentage is entirely unknown</term>.
Priests, Levites, and Israelites are permitted to marry one another.
Levites, Israelites, *Challalim*, converts, and freed slaves are permitted to marry one another.
Converts, freed slaves, *Mamzerim*, *Netinim*, *Shetuki*, and *Asufi* are permitted to marry one another.

---

## Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 4 Mishnah 2
### 2
And who is a *Shetuki*?
Anyone who recognizes their mother, but does not recognize their father.
And who is an *Asufi*?
Anyone who was gathered from the market and recognizes neither their father nor their mother.
Abba Shaul used to call the *Shetuki* a *Beduki* <note>original: "בְּדוּקֵי" (beduki) — meaning "one who is examined." This implies that the mother is questioned to determine if the child was conceived from a permitted union</note>.

---

## Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 4 Mishnah 3
### 3
All those who are forbidden from entering the congregation <note>Meaning those with lineage flaws that restrict them from marrying into the general Jewish population</note> are permitted to marry one another.
Rabbi Yehuda forbids this.
Rabbi Eliezer says: Those of certain status [marrying] those of certain status is permitted.
But those of certain status with those of doubtful status, those of doubtful status with those of certain status, and those of doubtful status with those of doubtful status—these are forbidden.
And who are those of "doubtful status"?
The *Shetuki*, the *Asufi*, and the *Kuti* <term>Kuti: A Samaritan; in this context, their lineage was considered questionable due to uncertainties regarding their observance of divorce and conversion laws</term>.

---

### Tractate Kiddushin Chapter 4 Mishnah 9
->9<-

One who gave permission to his agent to betroth <note>Hebrew: *kiddushin*. In ancient Jewish law, this is the first formal stage of marriage, which can only be dissolved by a formal divorce.</note> his daughter to someone,

If his own betrothal came first, his betrothal is valid; 
and if the agent’s betrothal came first, the agent's betrothal is valid. 
If it is not known which occurred first, both men must give her a bill of divorce <note>original: "גֵּט" (*get*)</note>. 
If they wish, one gives a bill of divorce and the other enters into marriage <note>original: "כּוֹנֵס" (*kones*), refers to completing the marriage process through *nissu'in*</note>.

->10<-

And similarly, a woman who gave permission to her agent to betroth her to someone, 
and then she herself went and betrothed herself: 
If her own betrothal came first, her betrothal is valid; 
and if the agent’s came first, his betrothal is valid. 
If it is not known which occurred first, both men must give her a bill of divorce. 
If they wish, one gives a bill of divorce and the other enters into marriage.

# Order of Damages 
<term>Order of Damages: "Seder Nezikin" — the division of the Mishnah and Talmud focusing on civil law, property rights, torts, and the judicial system.</term>

## Tractate Bava Kamma 
<term>Bava Kamma: "The First Gate" — the first of three volumes originally comprising one large book on civil law. This section focuses on physical and property damages.</term>

## Tractate Bava Kamma, Chapter 2, Mishnah 1

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on "Tooth" (damage caused by eating) and "Foot" (damage caused by walking). If [an animal] **ate clothing or vessels,**
**[the owner] pays half-damages.** <note>Eating non-food items like clothing is considered unusual behavior for most livestock, falling under the category of 'Goring' (Keren), which results in half-damages for a first-time offender.</note>
**In what case does this apply?**
**In the property of the injured party.**
**But in the public domain, [the owner] is exempt.** <note>Since it is natural for animals to eat as they walk, the law expects people to protect their belongings in public spaces. However, the owner is still liable for the actual benefit gained.</note>
**But if it derived benefit, [the owner] pays for the amount of benefit derived.** <note>For example, if the animal ate a cake, the owner pays the value of cheap animal fodder, as they saved money on a meal for their animal.</note>

### 4

**How does one pay for the "amount of benefit derived"?**
**If it ate from the middle of the plaza, he pays for the benefit derived;**
**If [it ate] from the sides of the plaza, he pays for the damage caused.** <note>The 'sides' of the plaza are treated more like private property where merchants display wares, so the liability is higher.</note>
**From the entrance of a shop, he pays for the benefit derived;**
**From inside the shop, he pays for the damage caused.**

**[the owner] pays full damages, because they are <term>mu'adin</term>.** <note>original: 'mu'adin'—habitual or forewarned. Jumping is considered a natural behavior for dogs and goats, so the owner is expected to prevent it.</note>
**A dog that took a cake <note>specifically a 'chararah,' a cake baked directly on hot coals.</note> and went to a haystack,**
**ate the cake and set the haystack on fire [with a coal stuck to the cake],**
**for the cake, [the owner] pays full damages,**
**but for the haystack, he pays half-damages.** <note>Full damages are paid for the eating (Tooth) because that is natural, but only half for the fire (Aish) because it happened in an unusual way involving the coal.</note>

->### 8<-

->**Rabbi Tarfon said to them:**<-
->**How is this so?**<-
->**If in a case where the law was lenient regarding "Tooth" and "Foot" in the public domain—**<-
->**where the owner is exempt—**<- <note>Animals are expected to walk and eat in public; therefore, owners aren't liable for these natural acts in public spaces.</note>

->**requiring the payment of full damages?**<-
->**They said to him:**<-
->**"It is enough for a law derived from logical inference to be as strict as the case it was derived from."** <term>Dayo</term><note>original: "Dayo la-ba min ha-din lihyot ka-niddon." This is a fundamental principle of Talmudic logic: a conclusion reached through an "all the more so" argument cannot be more restrictive than the original premise. In this case, since the premise for "Goring" is half-damages, the conclusion cannot exceed half-damages.</note><-
->**Just as in the public domain it is half-damages,**<-
->**so too in the property of the injured party, it is half-damages.**<-

->**in the public domain,**<-
->**yet it was strict regarding "Goring" [in that same public domain];**<-
->**then in a place where it was already strict regarding them [Tooth and Foot] in the property of the injured party [requiring full damages],**<-
->**is it not logical that we should be even stricter regarding "Goring"?**<-
->**They said to him:**<-
->**It is enough for a law derived from logical inference to be as strict as the case it was derived from:**<-
->**Just as in the public domain it is half-damages,**<-
->**so too in the property of the injured party, it is half-damages.**<-

### Tractate Bava Kamma, Chapter 2, Mishnah 6

->,<-
->**A person is always <term>mu'ad</term> [legally forewarned and liable],**<- <note>original: "Adam mu'ad le'olam." Unlike an animal, which might be considered "innocent" for its first three offenses, a human is considered fully aware and responsible for their actions at all times.</note>
->**whether [acting] accidentally or intentionally,**<-
->**whether awake or asleep.**<- <note>This establishes the principle of absolute liability in Jewish tort law; even if a person causes damage while sleeping, they are generally held responsible for the costs.</note>
->**If he blinded the eye of his fellow**<-
->**or broke vessels,**<-
->**he pays full damages.**<-

# Chapter 3

## The First Gate, Chapter 3, Oral Teaching 1
<note>original: "Massekhet Bava Kama, Perek 3, Mishnah 1"</note>

### 1
->**One who places a jug in the public domain,**<-
->**and another person comes and trips over it and breaks it,**<-
->**the passerby is exempt.**<- <note>The passerby does not have to pay for the broken jug because the owner had no right to place an obstacle in a public thoroughfare; people are not expected to constantly look down at their feet while walking.</note>
->**But if the passerby was injured by it,**<-
->**the owner of the barrel is liable for the passerby's damages.**<-

### 2
->**If his jug broke in the public domain,**<-
->**and another person slipped on the water,**<-
->**or was cut by its shards,**<-
->**the owner is liable.**<-
->**Rabbi Yehuda says:**<-
->**If he intended to claim the broken pieces, he is liable;**<-
->**but if he did not intend to keep them, he is exempt.**<- <note>Rabbi Yehuda argues that if a person abandons the property after the accident, it becomes "ownerless" and they are no longer responsible for it as a hazard, whereas the majority view holds them responsible for the hazard they created initially.</note>

<note>original: "Massekhet Bava Kama, Perek 3, Mishnah 2"</note>

->**is liable for their damages.**<-

->**or one who builds his fence with thorns [that protrude],**<-
->**or a wall that fell into the public domain—**<-
->**and another person was injured by them—**<-
->**the owner is liable for their damages.**<-

**Damages** <term>Nezikin</term>: The general category of law covering torts and injuries.

they pay half-damages from the difference. <note>original: "ba-motar." This refers to an offset. If Ox A caused 100 in damage and Ox B caused 40, they calculate the difference (60) and the owner of the more damaging ox pays half of that difference.</note>

An ox worth two hundred <term>zuz</term> <note>A silver coin of the era; the text uses "two hundred" as a standard unit of value.</note> that gored an ox worth two hundred,
and the carcass is worth nothing,
Rabbi Meir said:
Concerning this it is said: (Exodus 21:35)
"Then they shall sell the live ox and divide its money."
Rabbi Yehuda said to him:
And such is the law <note>original: "halakha"</note>.
You have fulfilled the verse "And they shall sell the live ox and divide its money,"
but you have not fulfilled "And also the dead one they shall divide."
And which case is that?
This is an ox worth two hundred that gored an ox worth two hundred,
and the carcass is worth fifty <term>zuz</term>.
In this case, this one takes half the live animal and half the dead animal,
and that one takes half the live animal and half the dead animal. <note>Rabbi Yehuda argues that the Bible’s instruction to "divide the dead one" means both the owner of the goring ox and the owner of the victim share the value of the remains, ensuring that the loss is split exactly in half.</note>

### The First Gate, Chapter 3, Oral Teaching 10
<note>original: "Massekhet Bava Kamma, Perek 3, Mishnah 10"</note>

->יג<-

There are cases where one is liable for the actions of his ox but exempt for his own actions,
and cases where one is liable for his own actions but exempt for the actions of his ox.
If his ox caused shame to someone, he is exempt,
but if he himself caused shame, he is liable. <note>Human liability for "shame" or humiliation requires intent, which an animal is not considered to possess.</note>
If his ox blinded the eye of his own slave or knocked out his tooth, the owner is exempt <note>from paying the slave</note>,
but if he himself blinded the eye of his slave or knocked out his tooth, he is liable. <note>Under Biblical law, a master who permanently maims a slave must set that slave free as compensation.</note>
If his ox injured the owner's father or mother, the owner is liable <note>to pay for the medical costs and damages</note>,
but if he himself injured his father or mother, he is exempt <note>from payment</note>. <note>This is a legal principle called "kim lei b'drabba minei"—if an act carries a capital or corporal punishment (like striking a parent), the court does not also impose a monetary fine for the same act.</note>
If his ox set fire to a grain heap on the Sabbath, the owner is liable,
but if he himself set fire to the grain heap on the Sabbath, he is exempt <note>from payment</note>,
because he is judged with his life. <note>Violating the Sabbath by fire was a capital offense; as with the previous note, the more severe punishment cancels the lesser monetary fine.</note>

### The First Gate, Chapter 3, Oral Teaching 11
<note>original: "Massekhet Bava Kamma, Perek 3, Mishnah 11"</note>

->יד<-

If an ox was chasing after another ox, and that ox was injured—
this owner says, "Your ox caused the injury,"
and the other says, "No, it was not so; rather, it was injured by a rock"—
the burden of proof lies upon the claimant. <note>original: "Hamotzi me-chavero alav ha-reayah." This is a fundamental principle of Jewish civil law: one who wishes to take money from another must provide the evidence.</note>

->יה<-

If two oxen were chasing after one ox—
this one says, "Your ox caused the injury,"
and that one says, "Your ox caused the injury"—
both are exempt. <note>Because it cannot be proven which ox caused the damage, neither owner can be legally compelled to pay.</note>

If both [damaging animals] belonged to one man, both are liable. <note>This concludes a previous discussion: if it is unclear which of two animals caused damage, but both belong to the same person, the owner cannot avoid payment because he is responsible for both.</note>

### 10

If there was one large [ox] and one small [ox], and the victim says, "The large one caused the damage," but the owner of the damaging animals says, "Not so; rather, the small one caused the damage"; or if one was <term>innocent</term> <note>Hebrew: "Tam." An animal with no history of violence. The owner is only liable for half-damages, paid exclusively from the value of the ox itself.</note> and one was <term>forewarned</term> <note>Hebrew: "Mu'ad." An animal that has gored three times; the owner is liable for full damages paid from his best property.</note>, and the victim says, "The forewarned one caused the damage," while the owner says, "Not so; rather, the innocent one caused the damage"—the rule is: **The burden of proof lies with the claimant.** <note>original: "Ha-motzi me-havero alav ha-re'ayah." A foundational legal principle: if you want to take money from someone else, you must provide the evidence.</note>

### 11

If there were two victims, one large and one small, and two damaging animals, one large and one small, and the victim says:
"The large [attacker] damaged the large [victim], and the small [attacker] damaged the small [victim],"
and the owner of the damaging animals says:
"Not so; rather, the small one damaged the large one, and the large one damaged the small one";
or if one [attacker] was innocent and one was forewarned, and the victim says:
"The forewarned one damaged the large one, and the innocent one damaged the small one,"
and the owner says:
"Not so; rather, the innocent one damaged the large one, and the forewarned one damaged the small one"—
**the burden of proof lies with the claimant.**

### 1

An ox that gored four or five oxen one after another: [the owner] shall pay the last of them. <note>In the case of an "innocent" ox, the damage is a lien on the animal's body. If it gores again, the new victim essentially "seizes" the animal, pushing the previous claimants back in line.</note>

These are the words of Rabbi Meir.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of liability for damages caused by oxen, moving from general property damage into the legal status of owners who lack legal competency (minors or those with mental disabilities), the status of oxen used in public spectacles, and the specific penalties for oxen that kill human beings.</meta>

An ox belonging to a person of sound mind that gored an ox belonging to a **deaf-mute, a person of unsound mind, or a minor**, 
is liable <note>The owner of sound mind is fully responsible for the damage caused to the property of those who cannot protect themselves.</note>. 
But an ox belonging to a **deaf-mute, a person of unsound mind, or a minor** that gored an ox belonging to a person of sound mind, 
is exempt <note>Under Jewish law, individuals in these categories are generally not held legally responsible for damages caused by their property because they lack the "da'at" (legal intent or cognitive capacity) to supervise them.</note>. 
If the oxen of a deaf-mute, a person of unsound mind, or a minor gored, 
the court appoints **guardians** <term>epitropin</term> <note>From the Greek "epitropos," meaning a legal guardian or trustee appointed to manage the affairs of those unable to do so themselves.</note> for them, 
and witnesses testify against the animals in the presence of the guardians. 
If the deaf-mute gained his hearing, the person of unsound mind recovered, or the minor grew up—<gloss>recovered</gloss> <note>The Hebrew gloss "shapa" clarifies the recovery of mental faculties.</note>— 
the animal returns to its status as **"innocent"** <note>Hebrew: "Tam." An animal that has not yet established a pattern of goring. This means even if it was declared "forewarned" (Mu'ad) while under a guardian's care, the new legally competent owner is given a fresh start to supervise it.</note>. 
These are the words of **Rabbi Meir**. 
**Rabbi Yose** says: 
The animal remains in its established status <note>Rabbi Yose argues that the animal's behavioral history (its "chazakah") doesn't change just because the owner's legal status changed.</note>. 
An **arena ox** <note>Hebrew: "Shor ha-istadin." This refers to oxen used in Roman-style stadium games or bullfights.</note> is not liable to the death penalty, as it is said: (Exodus 21:28)
> "If an ox **gores**," <note>original: "Ki yigach"</note> meaning of its own volition, and not that people incite it to gore.

An ox that gored a person and they died: 
one that is **forewarned** pays the **ransom** <term>kofer</term> <note>A "kofer" is a compensatory payment made by the owner to the heirs of the deceased as an atonement for the life lost.</note>, 
but an **innocent** ox is exempt from the ransom; 
however, both are liable to death <note>Regardless of the owner's prior knowledge, any ox that kills a human is executed by stoning, and its meat may not be eaten.</note>. 
And the same applies if it killed a son or a daughter. 
If it gored a **male slave** or a **female slave**, 
the owner gives **thirty shekels** <term>sela</term> <note>A fixed biblical penalty (Exodus 21:32). A sela is equivalent to a shekel.</note>, 
whether the slave was worth a hundred <term>maneh</term> <note>A maneh is 100 silver denarii. Some slaves were highly skilled and worth much more than the statutory fine.</note>, 
or whether he was worth only a single **gold denarius** <note>A gold coin worth 25 silver denarii. Even if the slave's market value was very low, the owner must pay the full thirty-shekel fine.</note>.

A **desert ox** <note>original: "Shor HaMidbar"; an ownerless ox roaming in the wild.</note>, 
a **consecrated ox** <note>An ox dedicated to the Temple treasury.</note>, 
and the **ox of a convert who died and has no heirs** <note>Under Jewish law, if a convert to Judaism dies without Jewish heirs, his property becomes ownerless (hefker) and can be claimed by anyone.</note>, 
are all liable to the death penalty <note>If they kill a human being, they are stoned as per Exodus 21:28.</note>. 
**Rabbi Yehuda** says: <gloss>Yehuda</gloss> 
A **desert ox**, 
a **consecrated ox**, 
and the **ox of a convert who died and has no heirs**, 
are exempt from the death penalty, 
because they have no owners <note>Rabbi Yehuda interprets the biblical requirement of "warning the owner" literally; if there is no owner to warn, the penalty cannot be applied to the animal.</note>.

# Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 4, Mishnah 8
->9<-

An ox that is being led out to be **stoned**, and its owner **consecrated** it <note>Dedicated it to the Temple.</note>, 
it is not considered consecrated. 
And if they **slaughtered** it, its meat is forbidden to be eaten or used. 
But if the owner consecrated it **before its verdict was finalized**, 
it is consecrated. 
And if they slaughtered it, its meat is permitted.

# Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 4, Mishnah 9
->10<-

If one handed the ox over to an **unpaid bailee** or to a **borrower**, 
to a **paid bailee** or to a **renter**, 
these individuals have **stepped into the place of the owners**. 
If the ox then got out and caused damage, 
a **forewarned** ox <term>Mu'ad</term> <note>An animal that has gored three times and whose owner has been officially warned.</note> pays for the **full damage**, 
and an **innocent** ox <term>Tam</term> <note>An animal with no prior history of goring; the owner only pays for half the damage caused.</note> pays for **half the damage**. 
If the owner tied it with a **lead-rope**, 
and locked the door before it **properly**, 
but it still got out and caused damage, 
the owner is liable. 
**Rabbi Yehuda** says: 
An **innocent** ox is liable, but a **forewarned** ox is exempt, as it is said: (Exodus 21:36) 
> "And its owner has **not guarded it**," but this one was indeed guarded <note>Rabbi Yehuda argues that for a "forewarned" ox, the Torah only requires a standard level of guarding. If the owner provided that and the ox still escaped, he has fulfilled his duty.</note>. 
**Rabbi Eliezer** says: 
There is no "guarding" for such an animal except for the **knife** <note>Rabbi Eliezer holds the strictest view: once an animal is known to be dangerous, the owner's only responsible course of action is to slaughter it.</note>.

[the owner of the ox] pays **half-damage** <term>Chatzi Nezek: the standard penalty for a first-time damaging animal, which pays half the value of the loss</term> for the cow, and a **quarter-damage** for the offspring <note>Because of the uncertainty, the court applies a compromise: the defendant pays half of the disputed half-damage.</note>.

### **Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 5, Mishnah 4**
->**6**<-

An **ox that intended [to strike] its fellow**, 
but **struck a woman** and her **children departed** <note>A common Rabbinic euphemism for a miscarriage caused by trauma.</note>, 
[the owner] is **exempt from paying the value of the offspring** <note>Torah law (Exodus 21:22) stipulates that the fine for causing a miscarriage applies only to human-on-human violence, not damage caused by an animal.</note>. 
A **person who intended [to strike] his fellow**,
