**pays the value of the offspring**. 
**How** does he pay the value of the offspring? 
We **assess the woman**: 
**how much she was worth** <note>Literally "how beautiful/valuable she was" in the labor market (as a slave)</note> before she gave birth, 
and **how much she is worth** after she has given birth. 
**Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said**: 
If so, once a woman gives birth, **she improves in value**! <note>He argues that a woman's market value often increases after the physical burden and danger of pregnancy are over, which would mean the damager pays nothing.</note> 
Rather, we **assess the offspring** to see how much they would be worth [if sold as slaves], 
and give that to the **husband**; 
and if she has no husband <note>For example, if he died after the injury occurred but before the payment.</note>, they give it to **his heirs**. 
If she was a **slave who was emancipated**, or a **convert** <note>These individuals are considered legally "rootless" in terms of inheritance; if they have no husband or recognized heirs, there is no claimant for the damages.</note>, 
he is **exempt**.

<meta>This page continues the legal discussions in Tractate Bava Kamma. The previous page ended mid-sentence during a discussion on assessing the value of a woman in a personal injury case. This page transitions to defining the legal parameters of a "pit" (a category of damages) and the specific liabilities of those who dig them or leave them uncovered.</meta>

Rather, just as "the pit" <note>The legal archetype of a pit as described in Exodus 21:33.</note> must be deep enough to cause death, which is **ten handbreadths** <term>Tefachim: a Talmudic unit of measure based on the width of a palm, approximately 3.2 to 3.8 inches</term>, so too any object or hazard must be deep enough to cause death—at least ten handbreadths. If the hazard was **less than ten handbreadths** deep and an ox or a donkey fell into it and died, the owner of the pit is **exempt** <note>original: "patur" (exempt) — under the logic that a shallower pit is not inherently lethal, so the death is considered an unavoidable accident.</note>. But if the animal was **injured** by it, the owner is **liable** <note>original: "hayyav" (liable/obligated to pay)</note>.

## 8

One who **digs a pit on private property** and opens its mouth toward the **public domain** <term>Reshut HaRabim: a public thoroughfare where many people and animals pass</term>, or digs it in the public domain and opens it toward **another person’s private property**, is **liable** for any resulting damages.

### Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 5, Mishnah 6

## 9

Regarding a **pit belonging to two partners**: if the **first partner passed by** it and did not cover it, and then the **second partner passed by** it and did not cover it, the **second partner is liable** <note>Because the second partner had the final opportunity to prevent the hazard, the responsibility shifts to him.</note>. If the **first partner covered it**, and the **second partner arrived and found it uncovered** but did not cover it, the **second partner is liable**. 

If he **covered it properly** and an ox or a donkey fell into it and died, he is **exempt**. If he **did not cover it properly** and an ox or a donkey fell into it and died, he is **liable**. 

If an animal fell **forward** due to the **sound of the digging** <note>i.e., the noise of the person actually digging the pit startled the animal into falling</note>, the digger is **liable**. If it fell **backward** due to the sound of the digging, he is **exempt**. 

If an **ox and its gear** <note>The vessels, packs, or tools being carried by the animal</note> fell into it and the gear was broken, or a **donkey and its gear** fell into it and the gear was torn, he is **liable for the animal** but **exempt for the gear** <note>Rabbinic law derives from the biblical text that liability for a "pit" applies only to living creatures (animals) and not to inanimate objects like vessels.</note>. 

If a **deaf-mute ox, a deranged ox, or a young ox** <note>These represent animals that lack the typical instinct to avoid hazards</note> fell into it, the owner of the pit is **liable**. But if a human **son or daughter, a male slave or a female slave** falls into it [and dies], he is **exempt** <note>The specific tort of "The Pit" applies to property damage; human injury or death is handled under different legal categories where the principle is that a walking human is responsible for watching their own path.</note>.

## Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 6, Mishnah 1
->1<-
->One who brings sheep into a pen and locked the gate before them properly,<-
->but the animal nonetheless went out and caused damage,<-
->is exempt from payment.<- <note>original: "patur" — since the owner took standard precautions, the escape is viewed as an unavoidable accident.</note>
->If he did not lock the gate before them properly,<-
->and the animal went out and caused damage,<-
->he is liable.<- <note>original: "hayyav" — the owner is responsible due to negligence.</note>

->and the animal went out and caused damage,<-
->he is exempt.<-
->If the bandits themselves brought the animal out,<-
->the bandits are liable for any damages.<- <term>Listim: bandits or outlaws; in this case, they assume legal responsibility for the animal as if they were its owners.</term>

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the assessment of damages in a field. The previous page established that the standard method for appraising damage caused by an animal grazing in a field is "appraising by the area of sixty," meaning the damage is assessed based on how much the value of a large plot of land decreased, rather than the price of the individual stalks of grain. This page begins with the conclusion of that discussion and moves into the laws regarding grain storage and damages caused by fire.</meta>

[The court assesses the field by asking:] "How much was it worth [before the damage] and how much is it worth [now]?" <note>This "global" assessment usually resulted in a lower payment than if each stalk were sold individually at market price, reflecting a more lenient rule for accidental grazing.</note>
**Rabbi Shimon says:**
If the animal ate fully ripened fruit, 
the owner pays for fully ripened fruit [at market value];
if it ate a *se'ah*, he pays a *se'ah*, and if it ate two *se'ah*, he pays two *se'ah*. <note>original: "se'ah" — an ancient Judean unit of volume, roughly 7 to 13 liters depending on the historical period.</note>

## Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 6, Mishnah 3

### 3

One who stacks grain in the field of another without permission, 
and the animal of the field owner ate the grain, 
the owner is exempt. <note>original: "patur" — because the owner of the grain had no right to place it there, the field owner is not responsible for guarding his animal against it.</note>
And if the animal was harmed by the grain, 
the owner of the grain stack is liable. 
But if he stacked the grain with permission, 
the field owner is liable [if his animal eats it].

## Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 6, Mishnah 4

### 4

One who sends out a fire via a person who is a deaf-mute, mentally incompetent, or a minor, 
is exempt from the laws of man, but liable according to the laws of Heaven. <note>In Jewish law, those who lack full legal capacity cannot act as legal "agents." Therefore, the sender is not technically the one who set the fire in a court of law, but he remains morally responsible for the outcome.</note>
If he sent it via a person of sound mind, 
the person of sound mind is liable. 
If one person brought the flame, and another person brought the wood, 
the one who brought the wood is liable. <note>This refers to a case where the wood was placed in a way that the existing flame could now spread.</note>
If one person brought the wood, and another person brought the flame, 
the one who brought the flame is liable. 
If another person then came and fanned the flame, 
the one who fanned the flame is liable. 
If the wind fanned it, 
then all of them are exempt.

---

### 5

One who sends out a fire, 
and it consumes wood, stones, or soil, 
is liable, as it is stated: (Exodus 22:5)
> "When a fire breaks out and spreads to thorns,
> so that a stack of grain or standing grain or the field itself is consumed,
> the one who started the fire must make full restitution." 
If the fire crossed a fence that was four cubits high, 
or a public road, or a river, 
the sender is exempt. <note>At these distances (four cubits is approximately 6 feet or 2 meters), the spread of the fire is considered an unforeseeable accident rather than negligence.</note>

### 6

If one kindles a fire within his own property, how far must it spread [before he is no longer liable for the damage it causes]? <note>This discussion establishes the "safety zone" a person must maintain when burning something on their own land to avoid being held responsible if sparks fly onto a neighbor's property.</note>
**Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah says:**
We view the area as if it were in the middle of a *beit kor*. <note>original: "beit kor" — an area of land required to sow a *kor* of seed, roughly 5-6 acres. This is a very large distance.</note>
**Rabbi Eliezer says:**
Sixteen cubits, which is the width of a public road. <note>original: "amah" — a cubit, the length of a forearm, roughly 18 inches or 45-50 centimeters.</note>
**Rabbi Akiva says:**
Fifty cubits.
<margin>(Exodus 22:5)</margin> <note>The marginal note refers to the biblical source: "If fire breaks out and spreads into thorn bushes so that it consumes stacked grain... the one who started the fire must make restitution."</note>
**And Rabbi Shimon says:**
"The one who kindled the fire shall surely pay," —
it is all according to the nature of the fire. <note>Rabbi Shimon argues that there is no fixed distance; a small candle and a massive bonfire require different precautions.</note>

### Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 6, Mishnah 5
### 7

If one sets fire to a stack of grain and there were vessels <note>or "tools/items"</note> inside it,
**Rabbi Yehuda says:**
He must pay for everything that was inside it.
**But the Sages say:**
He only pays for a stack of wheat or a stack of barley. <note>The Sages hold the principle of *tamun* ("hidden"): one is not usually liable for destroying items hidden from view in a fire, as they could not have anticipated the value of what was being burned.</note>
If a goat was tied to the stack, and a slave was standing nearby, and they were burned with it, 
he is **liable** [to pay for the goat].
If a slave was tied to the stack and a goat was nearby, and they were burned with it, 
he is **exempt** [from paying for the goat]. <note>This is a complex legal principle: because the arsonist is technically guilty of a capital crime for killing the tied-up slave, the law "exempts" him from the lesser monetary fine for the goat. If the slave was free to move but didn't, the arsonist isn't legally responsible for the slave's death, and thus must pay for the goat.</note>
**And the Sages agree with Rabbi Yehuda** regarding one who sets fire to a mansion, 
that he must pay for everything inside it; 
for such is the way of people, to keep their belongings inside houses.

---

### Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 6, Mishnah 6
### 8

If a spark flies out from under a hammer and causes damage,
[the worker] is **liable**.
If a camel is loaded with flax and is passing through a public domain,
and its flax enters into a shop and catches fire from the shopkeeper's lamp, 
subsequently setting fire to the mansion, 
the owner of the camel is **liable**.
But if the shopkeeper placed his lamp outside [the shop], 
the shopkeeper is **liable**.
**Rabbi Yehuda says:**
In the case of a Hanukkah lamp, he is **exempt**. <note>Rabbi Yehuda argues that because there is a religious requirement to place the Hanukkah lamp outside to publicize the miracle, the shopkeeper is not penalized for a fire caused by a lamp placed there for a *mitzvah* (commandment).</note>

# Chapter 7

## Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 7, Mishnah 1

->1<-
->The scope of the rule for double payment is greater<-
->than the scope of the rule for four-fold and five-fold payment, <insert>In every place: four [and] five</insert><-
->for the rule for double payment applies to things that have a spirit of life,<-
->and to things that do not have a spirit of life,<- <note>original: "ruach chayim" — this means that if one steals an inanimate object like a garment or a tool, they must pay back double the value.</note>
->while the rule for four-fold and five-fold payment<-
->applies only to an ox and a sheep alone, as it is stated: (Exodus 21:37)<-
> ->"If a man steals an ox or a sheep and slaughters it or sells it,<-
> ->he shall pay five cattle in place of the ox and four sheep in place of the sheep."<-
->One who steals from a thief does not pay double payment,<- <note>The penalty is only paid by the original thief to the rightful owner; a secondary thief is not subject to the same punitive fine.</note>
->nor does one who slaughters or sells after [stealing from] a thief<-
->pay the four-fold and five-fold payment.<-

## Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 7, Mishnah 2

->2<-
->If one stole based on the testimony of two witnesses,<-
->and he slaughtered or sold based on their testimony, or based on the testimony of two other witnesses,<-
->he pays the four-fold or five-fold payment.<-
->If he stole and sold on the Sabbath,<- <note>Even though performing a transaction or slaughtering on the Sabbath is a religious violation, he is still liable for the civil penalty.</note>
->[or] if he stole and sold for the purpose of idol worship,<-
->[or] if he stole, slaughtered, and sold on Yom Kippur,<- <note>The Day of Atonement.</note>
->[or] if he stole from his father and slaughtered and sold, and afterward his father died,<- <note>At the time of the theft, the property belonged to his father, so the penalty applies even if he later inherits the estate.</note>
->[or] if he stole, slaughtered, and sold, and afterward consecrated the animal to the Temple,<-
->he pays the four-fold or five-fold payment.<-
->If he stole, slaughtered, and sold for medicinal use or for dogs,<- <note>Meaning the meat was not intended for human consumption.</note>
->[or] if he slaughters and the animal is found to be fatally defective,<- <term>treifah: an animal with a physical injury or defect that would cause it to die within a year, making it non-kosher</term>
->[or] if he slaughters non-sacred animals in the Temple Courtyard,<- <note>A violation of sacrificial law.</note>
->he pays the four-fold or five-fold payment.<-
->Rabbi Shimon exempts the thief in these last two cases.<- <note>Rabbi Shimon argues that "slaughtering" in the law of theft refers only to a slaughtering that makes the meat permitted for eating.</note>

## Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 7, Mishnah 3

->3<-

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the laws of theft (Gneiva) from Chapter 7, moving from the basic definitions of double and four-fold/five-fold payments into complex legal scenarios involving witnesses, self-incrimination, and the status of the stolen property.</meta>

If he stole based on the testimony of two witnesses,
and he slaughtered or sold based on the testimony of two other witnesses,
and both sets of witnesses were found to be **conspiring witnesses**,
the first set pays **double payment**,
and the second set pays **three-fold payment**. <note>The "three-fold" payment refers to the difference between the double payment for theft and the five-fold payment for an ox. If the animal was a sheep, they would pay a two-fold difference to reach the four-fold total.</note>
If the second set of witnesses were found to be **conspiring witnesses**,
the thief pays **double payment**,
and they (the witnesses) pay **three-fold payment**.
If one of the second set of witnesses is found to be a **conspirator**,
the second testimony is void.
If one of the first set of witnesses is found to be a **conspirator**,
the entire testimony is void,
for if there is no theft, there is no slaughter and there is no sale. <note>original: "Im ein gneiva, ein tvicha v'ein mechira." This is a logical legal principle: one cannot be liable for "slaughtering a stolen animal" if the legal proof for the original theft has collapsed.</note>

### Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 7, Mishnah 4

->4<-

If he stole based on the testimony of two witnesses,
but slaughtered or sold based on the testimony of only one witness,
or based on his own confession,
he pays **double payment**,
but he does not pay the **four-fold and five-fold payment**. <note>Under Jewish law, a person who confesses to a crime that carries a punitive fine (knas) is exempt from that fine. Since the 4/5 payment is a penalty beyond the value of the object, self-incrimination waives it.</note>

->5<-

If he stole and slaughtered on the Sabbath,
or if he stole and slaughtered or sold for the sake of **idolatry**, <note>original: "avodah zarah" — literally "foreign worship."</note>
or if he stole from his father, and then his father died, and afterwards he slaughtered or sold it, <note>Because he inherited a portion of the animal upon his father's death, the subsequent slaughter is no longer entirely a "slaughter of a stolen animal."</note>
or if he stole and **consecrated** it, and afterwards slaughtered or sold it, <note>original: "hikdish" — to designate an object as sacred property for the Temple.</note>
he pays **double payment**,
but he does not pay **four-fold and five-fold payment**.
Rabbi Shimon says:
For **sacrificial animals** for which he is financially responsible, <note>original: "kodashim she'hu chayav b'achrayutan" — animals he vowed to bring; if they die or are lost, he must replace them. Because he is responsible for them, they are considered "his" enough to trigger the penalty.</note>
he pays **four-fold and five-fold payment**,
but for those for which he is not financially responsible,
he is exempt.

# 7

If he stole within the owner’s domain, and slaughtered and sold outside their domain;
or if he stole outside their domain, and slaughtered and sold within their domain;

## Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 7, Mishnah 6

# 8

If he was pulling the animal to take it out, and it died while still within the owner’s domain,
he is **exempt**. <note>The act of "pulling" (meshikha) is a legal method of acquisition, but it is not completed until the object is moved into a space controlled by the thief or into a public area.</note>
If he lifted it up, <note>Lifting an object (hagbahah) is considered an immediate and total form of legal acquisition, regardless of where it takes place.</note>
or if he led it outside the owner’s domain and then it died,
he is **liable**.

# 9

If he gave the stolen animal to a priest for the **redemption of his firstborn son**, <gloss>to the firstborns</gloss> <note>A Jewish father is traditionally required to "redeem" his firstborn son from a priest (Kohen) for five silver shekels; here, he uses the stolen animal as value.</note>
or to his **creditor**,
or to an **unpaid bailee**, or to a **borrower**,
to a **paid bailee**, or to a **renter**,
and the person was pulling it to take it out, and it died while still in the owner's domain,
he is **exempt**.
If he lifted it up,
or if he led it outside the owner's domain and it died,
he is **liable**.

## Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 7, Mishnah 7

# 10

One may not raise **small livestock** <note>original: "behemah dakkah." This refers to sheep and goats, which are difficult to contain and prone to grazing on others' crops.</note> in the settled areas of the **Land of Israel**,
but one may raise them in **Syria** <note>A region with a lower level of agricultural sanctity/restriction than the heart of Israel.</note> and in the wildernesses of the **Land of Israel**.
One may not raise **chickens** in **Jerusalem**,
on account of the **holy offerings**, <note>original: "kodashim." Chickens scratch in the dirt and might uncover small carcasses or impurities that could contaminate the sacrificial meat being eaten in the city.</note>
nor may **priests** raise them throughout the **Land of Israel**,
on account of **purity laws**. <note>original: "teharot." Priests must maintain a higher level of ritual purity to eat their tithes; a chicken uncovering a source of impurity (like a dead reptile) could disqualify their food.</note>
An **Israelite** may not raise **pigs** in any place.
And a person should not raise a **dog**,
unless it is kept tied with a chain.

## Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 8, Mishnah 1

->1<-

# Chapter 9

## Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 9 Mishnah 1

->1<-

One who steals wood and fashions it into vessels,
or wool and fashions it into garments, <note>In the manuscript, the Hebrew plural suffix "im" is erased.</note>
pays according to the value at the time of the theft.
If he stole a pregnant cow and she gave birth,
or a laden ewe <note>A female sheep with a heavy coat of wool.</note> and he sheared her,
he pays the value of a pregnant cow about to give birth,
or the value of a laden ewe about to be shorn.
If he stole a cow and she became pregnant while in his possession and gave birth,
or a ewe and she grew wool while in his possession and he sheared her,
he pays according to the value at the time of the theft.
This is the general principle:
All robbers pay according to the value at the time of the theft. <note>This principle, known as *Kinyan Shinui* (acquisition through change), suggests that if a thief significantly alters a stolen object, they "acquire" the physical object but owe the original owner its monetary value at the moment it was first taken.</note>

## Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 9 Mishnah 2

### Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 9 Mishnah 5

One who robs his fellow of the value of a *perutah* <term>perutah; the smallest denomination of copper coin in the Roman-era economy</term> and swears falsely to him <note>regarding the theft, denying he took it</note>, 
he must bring it after him even as far as Medea <note>original: "Madai" — a distant land in the Persian Empire. This emphasizes that the thief must bear any burden or expense to return the stolen item to the victim personally</note>. 
He may not give it to the victim’s son or to his messenger <note>the thief's obligation to restore the object is not fulfilled until it reaches the victim's hand</note>, 
but he may give it to a messenger of the court <term>shaliach beit din; an official agent appointed by the Rabbinical court</term>. 
And if the victim died, he must return it to his heirs.

### Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 8 Mishnah 6

**8**
If he gave him the principal <term>keren; the original value of the stolen item</term>, 
but did not give him the fifth <note>original: "chomesh" — an additional 25% penalty added to the principal when a thief confesses after swearing falsely. In Jewish law, this "fifth" is calculated so that it constitutes one-fifth of the new, total amount</note>; 
or if the victim forgave him for the principal, 
but did not forgive him for the fifth; 
or if he forgave him for both this and that, 
except for less than the value of a *perutah* of the principal 
he does not need to go after him <note>because a value less than a *perutah* is not legally considered "money" for the purpose of the obligation to travel to return it</note>.

**9**
If he gave him the fifth, 
but did not give him the principal; 
or if the victim forgave him for the fifth, 
but did not forgive him for the principal; 
or if he forgave him for both this and that, 
except for the value of a *perutah* of the principal, 
he must go after him <note>to return the remaining amount, regardless of the distance</note>.

### Tractate Bava Kamma Chapter 8 Mishnah 7

**10**
If he gave him the principal, 
and then swore falsely to him regarding the fifth <note>denying he owed the penalty</note>, 
he must pay a fifth upon the fifth <note>an additional penalty on top of the first penalty</note>, 
until the principal of the penalty is reduced to less than a *perutah*. 
And so it is with a deposit <term>pikadon; an item left with someone for safekeeping</term>, as it is said: [Leviticus 5:21-22] 
"Regarding a deposit <gloss>original: "b'pikadon"</gloss>, or a pledge <gloss>original: "teshumet yad"</gloss>, or a robbery, 
or if he has oppressed his fellow, 
or if he has found a lost item and lied about it, 
and swore falsely," 
he must pay the principal, the fifth, and a guilt offering <term>asham; a specific sacrifice brought to the Temple as part of the atonement process</term>.

# Tractate Bava Metzia

## Chapter 1

->Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 1 Mishnah 1<-
->1<-

->Two are holding onto a garment <term>tallit; a cloak or rectangular outer garment</term>,<-
->this one says, "I found it,"<-
->and that one says, "I found it";<-
->this one says, "It is all mine,"<-
->and that one says, "It is all mine,"<-
->this one shall swear that he has no less than half of it,<-
->and that one shall swear that he has no less than half of it,<-
->and they shall divide it.<- <note>The court requires an oath to discourage false claims. They do not swear "It is mine" (which might be a total lie), but rather "I have a right to at least half," acknowledging the physical reality of the dispute.</note>
->[If] this one says, "It is all mine,"<-
->and that one says, "Half of it is mine,"<-
->the one who says "It is all mine" shall swear<-
->that he has no less than three-quarters,<-
->and the one who says "Half of it is mine" shall swear<-
->that he has no less than one-quarter,<-
->this one takes three-quarters and that one takes one-quarter.<- <note>This follows the principle that we only litigate the portion that is actually in dispute. Since both agree that one person owns at least half, they only argue over the remaining half.</note>

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 1 Mishnah 3

-> 3 <-

[If] one was riding on the back of an animal, <gloss>rider</gloss>
and saw a lost object, and said to his companion: <gloss>said</gloss>
"Give it to me!"
And [the companion] took it and said:
"I have acquired it for myself,"
he has acquired it. <note>Under Jewish law, merely seeing an object doesn't grant ownership. The companion performed the physical act of "taking" (lifting the object), which is the legal mechanism of acquisition (Kinyan). Even though he was asked to help, he is not legally bound to act as an agent for the rider until he agrees to do so.</note>
If after he gave it to [the rider], he said:
"I acquired it for myself first,"
he has said nothing. <note>original: "lo amar klum"</note>

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 1 Mishnah 4

-> 4 <-

[If] he saw a lost object and fell upon it,
and another person came and took hold of it,
the one who took hold of it has acquired it. <note>Falling on an object is not considered a formal act of acquisition (Kinyan); the physical grasping or lifting by the second person is what legally transfers ownership.</note>
[If] he saw them running after a lost object,
after a broken-limbed deer,
or after chicks that cannot yet fly, and he said:
"My field has acquired it for me,"
it has acquired it for him. <note>This refers to the concept of "Acquisition by Courtyard" (Kinyan Hatzer). A person's private property can legally acquire an item for them if the item is "protected" within that property and cannot escape.</note>
[If] the deer was running in its usual manner,
or if the chicks were flying, and he said:
"My field has acquired it for me,"
he has said nothing.

## Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 1 Mishnah 6

### 6

[If] one found debt contracts:
If they contain a <term>lien on property</term> <note>original: "ahrayut nekhasim". This is a clause that allows a creditor to seize land that was sold to a third party after the debt was created to satisfy the loan.</note>,
he should not return them.
[If] they do not contain a lien on property,
he should return them, because the court does not collect payment from [encumbered property] based on them.
These are the words of Rabbi Meir.
But the Sages say:
In either case, he should not return them,
because the court [otherwise] collects payment from them. <note>The Sages are concerned that even without an explicit lien clause, the court might still allow the creditor to seize property, potentially causing a loss to an innocent buyer if the document was actually dropped by the debtor after being repaid.</note>

## Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 1 Mishnah 7

### 7

[If] one found <term>bills of divorce</term> <note>original: "gittei nashim".</note>,
or records of the manumission of slaves,
<term>wills</term> <note>original: "diatiki", a loanword from the Greek 'diatheke'.</note>, deeds of gift, or receipts,
he should not return them,
for I say: <gloss>a second thought</gloss>
they were indeed written, but [the one who commissioned them] changed his mind and decided not to give them. <note>In Jewish law, many documents only become legally binding once they are physically delivered. If found in the street, we cannot be sure if they were lost after delivery or dropped by the scribe before the sender made the final decision to proceed.</note>

## Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 1 Mishnah 8

### 8

[If] one found assessment documents <note>Records of a court's valuation of property for debt collection.</note> or documents of maintenance <note>Agreements regarding the provision of food and support for a wife or daughters.</note>,
documents of <term>Halitzah</term> <note>The ceremony that releases a widow from the obligation of levirate marriage.</note> or documents of "refusal" <note>original: "me'unim", where a girl married off as a minor by her mother or brothers annuls the marriage upon reaching maturity.</note>,
documents of arbitration, or any act of the court,
he should return them. <note>Because these are court-issued records of public legal facts, there is no concern that they were "unissued" or that the parties changed their minds.</note>
[If] he found a roll of documents in a leather pouch or in a <term>casket</term> <note>original: "gluskama", from the Greek 'glossokomon', a box for keeping scrolls or even bones.</note>,
or a bundle of documents,
he should return them.
And what constitutes a "bundle" of documents?
Three tied together. <gloss>tied</gloss>
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
[If] one [person] borrowed from three, he should return them to the borrower;
[If] three [people] borrowed from one, he should return them to the lender.
[If] one found a document among his own documents,
and it is not known what its nature is <note>Meaning, he does not know if the debt was paid or why he has it.</note>,
it shall be left until Elijah comes. <note>A traditional phrase meaning the matter is legally unsolvable and must remain in limbo until the arrival of the Prophet Elijah, who will resolve all doubts in the future.</note>

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 2 Mishnah 8
,

If he found **scrolls**,
he should read from them once every thirty days. <note>To ensure the parchment is aired out and does not rot or become infested with insects.</note>
And if he does not know how to read, he should roll them.
But he should not study a subject for the first time from them,
nor should another person read along with him. <note>These restrictions prevent excessive wear and tear on the owner's property while the finder is maintaining it.</note>
If he found a **garment**,
he should shake it out once every thirty days,
and spread it out for its own benefit, but not for his own honor. <note>He may air the clothes to prevent moth damage, but he may not display them to make himself look wealthy or his home look better.</note>
**Silver vessels** and **copper vessels**,
he may use them for their own benefit, but not to wear them out. <gloss>to wear them down.</gloss> <note>Regular use of these metals actually prevents them from tarnishing or rusting, but the finder must not use them so roughly that the metal is diminished.</note>
**Gold vessels** and **glass vessels**,
he should not touch them until **Elijah arrives**. <note>Elijah the Prophet is expected to resolve all legal mysteries in the future. Because gold and glass do not degrade, they should be left alone until the owner is supernaturally identified.</note>
If he found a **sack** or a **basket**, <gloss>sack</gloss>
if it is not his usual way to carry such things,
then he does not have to carry it. <note>The Torah does not require a person of high social standing to perform a task that would be personally humiliating or beneath their dignity (Zaken ve-eino lefi kevodo).</note>

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 2 Mishnah 9
11

**What is considered a lost item?**
If he found a donkey or a cow grazing by the road,
this is not a lost item.
But if he found a donkey with its **gear overturned**,
or a cow running among the **vineyards**,
this is indeed a lost item.
If he returned the animal and it ran away, and he returned it and it ran away—
even four or five times—
he is still obligated to return it, as it is said: <note>(Deuteronomy 22:1)</note>
> "You shall surely return them." <note>The Hebrew original "Hashev Teshivem" uses a double verb, which the Sages interpret as a command to return the item even a hundred times if necessary.</note>
If he lost time from work that would have earned him a **sela** <note>A significant silver coin of the era.</note>,
he should not say to the owner, "Give me a sela,"
but rather the owner gives him his wage as an **idle laborer**. <gloss>idle</gloss> <note>He is compensated at the rate of a worker who would accept less pay for an easier, idle task rather than his usual strenuous labor.</note>
If there is a **court** <note>Beth Din</note> present,
he should make a stipulation before the court; <note>He can legally declare that he will only perform the rescue if he is fully compensated for his lost wages.</note>
if there is no court there, before whom could he make a stipulation?
His own interests come first. <note>If he cannot secure a legal guarantee for his lost wages and the loss is significant, he is not obligated to lose his own money to save another's.</note>

# Chapter 3

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 3 Mishnah 1

->**1**<-

One who deposits <term>Pikadon: an item entrusted to another for safekeeping</term> an animal or vessels with his fellow,
and they were stolen or they were lost,
if he [the guardian] paid and did not want to take an oath—
for they [the Sages] said: "An unpaid guardian <term>Shomer Chinam: a person who watches property for free; they are generally exempt from liability for theft or loss if they take an oath of innocence</term> takes an oath and is released from liability"—
and then the thief was found,
[the thief] pays double payment <note>original: *tashlumei kefel*. Based on Exodus 22:3, a thief caught with stolen goods must pay twice the value to the owner.</note>.
If he slaughtered or sold [the animal],
he pays fourfold or fivefold payments. <gloss>five</gloss> <note>Biblical law requires a thief to pay five times the value for an ox and four times for a sheep if the animal was slaughtered or sold (Exodus 21:37).</note>
To whom does he [the thief] pay?
To the one with whom the deposit was kept <note>Because the guardian chose to pay the owner rather than swearing an oath, he effectively "purchased" the rights to any future fines the thief might owe.</note>.

->**2**<-

If he [the guardian] took an oath and did not want to pay,
and then the thief was found,
[the thief] pays double payment.
If he slaughtered or sold,
he pays fourfold or fivefold payments.
To whom does he [the thief] pay?
To the owner of the deposit.

## 4

## 5

Two people who deposited money with one individual,

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 3 Mishnah 7

->8<-

One who deposits produce <term>Produce: usually referring here to dry grains and seeds</term> with his fellow,
this [guardian] may deduct for him the standard losses:
For wheat and for rice, nine half-*kavs* <term>Kav: a unit of volume, roughly 1.4 liters or 1.5 quarts</term> per *kor* <term>Kor: a large bulk measure equal to 30 *se'ahs* or 180 *kavs*</term>;
For barley and for millet, nine *kavs* per *kor*;
For spelt and for flaxseed, three *se'ahs* <term>Se'ah: a unit of volume equal to 6 *kavs*</term> per *kor*;
All according to the measure, and all according to the time <note>The longer the grain is stored, the more is lost to pests and rot; likewise, the larger the quantity, the more loss is expected. This rule provides a fair baseline for what a guardian can claim has naturally disappeared.</note>.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri said:
And what does it matter to them?
The mice eat the same whether there is much or whether there is little!
He may not deduct for him [these] losses, <insert>shall deduct</insert>
except for a single *kor* only <note>Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri argues that the loss from pests is a fixed amount based on the hunger of the rodents, not a percentage of the total pile.</note>.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
If it was a very large measure [of produce],
he may not deduct for him losses, <insert>shall deduct</insert>
because they [large quantities] produce a surplus <note>Rabbi Yehuda believes that in very large piles, the grain at the bottom is compressed or perhaps "increases" in bulk through some natural process that offsets the loss from pests.</note>.

And the House of Hillel say:

If he tilted a barrel [belonging to someone else],

he must pay for the whole thing. <note>The Law of Lifting: In Jewish law, lifting an object is a primary way to take legal possession. ## Chapter 4

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 4 Mishnah 1

->1<-

Silver acquires gold,
but gold does not acquire silver. <note>In the ancient economy described here, silver was the "standard" currency. Therefore, silver is treated as "money" and gold is treated as a "commodity." In a transaction, the physical movement of the commodity (gold) completes the legal sale, not the handing over of the money (silver).</note>
Copper acquires silver, <insert>acquires</insert>
but silver does not acquire copper.
Bad coins <note>Worn or damaged coins that are still legal tender but less desirable.</note> acquire good coins,
but good coins do not acquire bad coins.
An unminted token <term>Unminted token: Hebrew *asimon*. Metal that has the shape or weight of a coin but lacks the official government stamp.</term> acquires a minted coin,
but a minted coin does not acquire an unminted token.
Movable goods acquire a minted coin,
but a minted coin does not acquire movable goods.
This is the general rule:
All movable goods can acquire one another [through exchange].

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 4 Mishnah 2

->2<-

How so?
If he pulled produce from [the seller] <note>Original: *mashakh*. "Pulling" or *Meshikhah* is a formal act of acquisition where the buyer moves the object toward themselves.</note> but did not yet give him money,
he cannot retract the sale.
If he gave him money but did not yet pull the produce from him,
he can retract the sale.
But [the Sages] said:
He who punished the generation of the Flood
and the generation of the Division <note>The "Generation of the Division" refers to the builders of the Tower of Babel.</note>,
will in the future punish him who does not stand by his word. <note>This is a formal judicial curse known as the *Mi She-Para*. While the sale isn't legally "final" until the item is moved, it is considered morally reprehensible to back out after money has been exchanged.</note>
Rabbi Shimon says:
Whoever has the money in his hand has the upper hand.

<summary>This page establishes that physical possession, rather than the exchange of money, is the primary legal mechanism for finalizing a sale of movable goods. It also introduces the "Mi She-Para" curse, a moral sanction against those who break verbal agreements after payment has been made.</summary>

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 4 Mishnah 3

->3<-

> The law of overreaching <note>Original: *ona'ah*. This refers to price fraud or a significant disparity between the sale price and the market value.</note>
> applies when the discrepancy is four silver coins <note>A *ma'ah*, the smallest silver coin.</note> out of twenty-four silver coins that make up a Sela;
> this is one-sixth of the purchase price.
> Until when is the buyer permitted to return the item and cancel the sale?
> Long enough for him to show the item to a merchant or to his relative.
> Rabbi Tarfon gave a ruling in the city of Lod:
> The overreaching threshold is eight silver coins to the Sela,
> which is one-third of the purchase price.
> And the merchants of Lod rejoiced <note>They rejoiced because this allowed for a much higher profit margin before a sale could be legally contested.</note>.
> He then said to them:
> [In exchange for this higher limit,] the buyer is permitted to return the item all day long.
> They said:
> "Let Rabbi Tarfon leave us in our original place" <note>A Hebrew idiom meaning: we prefer the original ruling of the Sages.</note>.
> And they returned to following the words of the Sages. <note>The merchants realized that while a 1/6th threshold was stricter, the short window of time to cancel the sale provided more business stability than a 1/3rd threshold that lasted all day.</note>

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 4 Mishnah 4

->4<-

> Both the buyer and the seller
> are subject to the laws of overreaching.
> Just as the law of overreaching applies to a commoner, so too does overreaching apply to a merchant. <note>A professional trader cannot claim that because they are experts, they are immune to being defrauded, nor are they exempt from the rules when they sell.</note>
> Rabbi Yehuda says:
> A merchant is not subject to the laws of overreaching <note>Rabbi Yehuda argues that a professional merchant is an expert who is presumed to know the value; if they overpay or undersell, it is assumed they did so intentionally and waived their rights.</note>.
> The one who was defrauded has the "upper hand" <note>Original: *yado al ha-elyona*. A legal term meaning the injured party has the power to choose the remedy.</note>,
> for he may say to the other, "Give me back my money" [cancel the sale entirely],
> or, "Give me back the amount by which you defrauded me." <insert>he said</insert> <note>original: *am'*, an abbreviation likely indicating "they said" or "he said," marking the conclusion of the legal claim.</note>

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 4 Mishnah 5

->5<-

> And how much may a Sela coin be missing [from its weight due to wear] and still not be subject to the law of overreaching? <note>In antiquity, coins were valued by the weight of their precious metal. As coins circulated, they lost weight. This Mishnah discusses at what point a worn coin loses its status as legal tender at face value.</note>
> Rabbi Meir says:
> Four Issars <note>A small copper coin.</note>, at a rate of one Issar per Denar. <note>A Sela is worth 4 Denars. Since there are 24 Issars in a Denar, R. Meir allows a loss of 1/24th of the weight.</note>
> Rabbi Yehuda says:
> Four Pundions <note>A copper coin worth two Issars.</note>, at a rate of one Pundion per Denar. <note>This equals a loss of 1/12th of the coin's weight.</note>
> Rabbi Shimon says:
> Eight Pundions, at a rate of two Pundions per Denar. <note>This equals 1/6th of the weight, aligning the laws of currency wear with the general 1/6th rule for overreaching in goods.</note>

Until when is one permitted to return [a worn silver coin]?
In the cities, long enough to show it to a money-changer <note>Original: *shulchani*. In ancient commercial centers, money-changers were the experts who could determine if a coin's weight had decreased beyond the legal limit for circulation.</note>.

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 4 Mishnah 7

->7<-

The amount that constitutes overreaching <note>Original: *ona'ah*. This refers to price fraud or a significant disparity between the sale price and market value.</note> is four silver coins <note>A *ma'ah*, the smallest silver coin, worth 1/6th of a *Sela*.</note>.
A legal claim <note>Original: *ta’anah*. The minimum value of a claim in court to require the defendant to take an oath.</note> must be at least two silver coins.
And the admission of a debt <note>Original: *hoda’ah*. A partial admission of a claim that triggers a biblical oath.</note> must be worth at least a *perutah* <note>The smallest copper coin in circulation during the Mishnaic period.</note>.
There are five legal matters that involve the value of a *perutah*:
1. The admission of a debt must be worth at least a *perutah*.
2. A woman is betrothed <note>Original: *mitkadeshet*.</note> by receiving the value of a *perutah*.
3. One who derives benefit from consecrated property <note>Original: *hekdesh*. Property dedicated to the Temple.</note> worth a *perutah* has committed sacrilege <note>Original: *ma’al*. A legal term for the unintentional misappropriation of holy items.</note>.
4. One who finds a lost object worth a *perutah* is obligated to announce it.
5. One who robs his fellow of the value of a *perutah* and swears [falsely] to him,
must bring the repayment after him even as far as Media <note>A distant region in the Persian Empire; this teaches that a thief must personally ensure the return of even a tiny amount to the victim, regardless of the distance or effort required.</note>.

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 4 Mishnah 8

->8<-

There are five "fifths" <note>Original: *chumashim*. In many cases of misappropriating holy items or theft followed by a false oath, the Torah requires the offender to pay back the principal plus an additional "fifth." In Rabbinic math, this is an "external fifth," meaning one-quarter of the principal is added so that the addition constitutes one-fifth of the new total (e.g., if the item is worth 4, you pay back 5).</note>:
1. One who [accidentally] eats *terumah* <note>The portion of the crop designated for the Priests.</note>.
2. One who eats the "tithe of the tithe" <note>The portion a Levite gives to the Priest.</note>.
3. One who eats the "tithe of the tithe" of *demai* <note>Produce bought from a commoner where it is uncertain if the proper tithes were separated.</note>.
4. One who eats the *challah* <note>The portion of dough set aside for the Priest.</note>.
5. One who eats the first fruits <note>Original: *bikkurim*.</note>.
In all these cases, they must add a fifth to the principal.
One who redeems his own "fourth-year" sapling <note>Original: *neta revai*. Fruit from a tree's fourth year of growth, which must be eaten in Jerusalem or redeemed for money.</note> or his own Second Tithe
must add a fifth.
One who redeems his own consecrated property
must add a fifth.
One who derives benefit from consecrated property worth a *perutah*
must add a fifth.
And one who robs his fellow of the value of a *perutah* and swears [falsely] to him
must add a fifth.

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 5 Mishnah 1

->1<-

**What is "biting" [interest] and what is "increase"?** <note>The Torah uses two terms for interest: *Neshech* (biting) and *Tarbit* (increase). The Rabbis here distinguish between them for legal clarity.</note>
**What is "biting"?**

How so?
[If] one purchased wheat from another at the rate of a golden denar <note>original: *dinar zahav*. A gold coin worth 25 silver denars.</note> per *kor* <note>A unit of volume; approximately 220 to 390 liters.</note>,

### 2

> "If you pay me now,
> it is yours for one thousand *zuz* <note>A silver coin, equivalent to a denar.</note>,
> but if you pay at the harvest time, it is twelve *maneh* <note>One *maneh* equals 100 *zuz*. Therefore, 12 *maneh* is 1,200 *zuz*.</note>,"
this is forbidden <note>Because in a sale, the debt is created the moment the field is transferred. Adding 200 *zuz* for the "wait" until harvest is clearly interest for the extension of credit.</note>.

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 5 Mishnah 4
-> 5 <-

**One may not set up a shopkeeper for a half-profit arrangement,** <note>A partnership where one provides the capital and the other the labor, and they split the profits. Without a wage for the labor, the work is seen as "payment" for the loan, which is forbidden interest.</note>
**nor may one give him money to purchase produce for half the profit;**
**unless one pays him a wage as an idle laborer.** <term>idle laborer: *poel batel*. A nominal fee representing what someone would accept to sit idle rather than doing this specific work. This payment ensures the labor is not a "bonus" for the loan.</term>
**One may not set up chickens for half [the profit/loss],**
**and one may not value calves or foals for half [the profit/loss],** <note>This refers to an "iron sheep" contract where the person raising the animal guarantees the investor the principal value plus half the growth.</note>
**unless one pays him a wage for his toil and his food.**
**But one may accept calves and foals for half [the profit]**
**and raise them until they are "tripled" [three years old].**
**And a donkey, until it can carry a load.**

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 5 Mishnah 5
-> 6 <-

**One may value a cow or a donkey,**
**and anything that works for its food.** <note>Because the animal's labor pays for its own upkeep, the investment does not look like a loan with interest.</note>
**In a place where it is the custom to divide the offspring immediately,**
**they divide them,**
**and in a place where it is the custom to raise them, they shall raise them.**
**Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:**
**One may value a calf along with its mother, and a foal along with its mother.**
**And one may offer a higher price for his field [to a tenant],** <note>original: *mafriz*. For example, a landlord may charge more in rent if the tenant pays in produce at the end of the season rather than cash up front.</note>
**and he need not fear the prohibition of interest.**

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 5 Mishnah 6
-> 7 <-

**One may not accept "iron sheep" from an Israelite,**
**because it constitutes interest.** <term>iron sheep: *tzon barzel*. A contract where the recipient takes animals but guarantees the owner their full value even if they die. Because the owner risks nothing but gains profit, it is legally treated as a loan with interest.</term>
**However, one may accept "iron sheep" from Gentiles,**
**and one may borrow from them and lend to them with interest;**
**and the same applies to a resident alien.** <note>original: *ger toshav*. A non-Jew who has accepted the basic Noahide laws and lives among the Jewish community.</note>
**An Israelite may lend out the money belonging to a Gentile with the Gentile's consent,**
**but not with the consent of an Israelite.** <note>The transaction must be directly between the Gentile and the borrower, not mediated in a way that makes the Israelite the primary creditor.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the laws of interest (ribit) from the previous section. **One may not fix a price for produce until the market price has been established.** <note>original: "Ein poskin". This law prevents "hidden interest." If a buyer pays early for a lower price before the market price is known, the discount looks like interest on the buyer's money-loan.</note>
**Once the market price is established, one may fix a price;**
**even if this seller does not have the goods, another seller has them.**
**If the seller was among the first of the harvesters,**
**he may fix the price with him for the grain-stack,**
**and for the vat of grapes,**
**and for the vat of olives,**
**and for the clay lumps of a potter,**
**and for the lime once it has been sunk into the kiln.** <note>These are exceptions: if the goods are already in a semi-processed state, the transaction is considered a sale of existing goods rather than a loan, even if the price is low.</note>
**And one may fix a price for manure for all the days of the year.**
**Rabbi Yose says:**
**One may not fix a price for manure,**
**until he has the manure already in the dung-heap.**
**But the Sages permit it.**
**One may fix a price at the "highest market price."** <note>A clause where the seller agrees to give the buyer the lowest price found in the market at the time of delivery.</note>
**Rabbi Yehuda says:**
**Even if he did not explicitly fix the price with him,**
**[the buyer] can say to him:**
> **"Give me [produce] like this, or give me back my money."**

## Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 5 Mishnah 8

-> 9 <-

**A man may lend to his sharecroppers wheat in exchange for wheat,** <term>sharecropper: *aris*. A tenant farmer who pays the landowner a percentage of the crop.</term>
**for the purpose of sowing, but not for the purpose of eating.** <gloss>for eating</gloss> <note>Lending grain for food is a standard loan; if the price rises, returning the same amount of grain is forbidden interest. Lending for seed is viewed as an investment in the farm they both profit from.</note>
**For Rabban Gamliel used to lend to his sharecroppers**
**wheat when it was expensive and it later became cheap,**
**or when it was cheap and it later became expensive,**
**and he would take back from them at the cheaper price.**
**Not because the law is so,**
**but because he wished to be strict with himself.** <note>Rabban Gamliel went beyond the letter of the law to ensure there was no possible appearance of taking interest.</note>

## Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 5 Mishnah 9

**A man may not say to his fellow:**
> **"Lend me a *kor* of wheat, and I will give it back to you at the threshing floor."** <note>A *kor* is a large dry measure (about 390 liters). This is forbidden because if the price of wheat rises by harvest time, the borrower is returning something worth more than what they received.</note>
**Rather, he says to him:**
> **"Lend it to me until my son comes,"**
> **or "until I find the key."** <note>These phrases imply that the borrower already owns the wheat and just needs a temporary supply. This makes the transaction a "loan of convenience" rather than a financial loan.</note>
**Hillel forbids [even this].**
**And thus Hillel used to say:**
**A woman should not lend a loaf of bread to her neighbor**
**until she establishes its value in money,**
**lest the price of wheat rises,** <note>and she ends up returning a loaf that is more valuable than the one she borrowed, which technically constitutes interest.</note>

## Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 5 Mishnah 10

->**11**<-

A man may say to his fellow:
"Weed with me [today], and I will weed with you [tomorrow],"
"Dig with me [today], and I will dig with you [tomorrow]."
But he may not say to him:
"Weed with me [today], and I will dig with you [tomorrow],"
"Dig with me [today], and I will weed with you [tomorrow]." <note>Reciprocal labor is permitted only if the tasks are of equal difficulty. Digging is harder than weeding; therefore, doing a harder task in exchange for an easier one is considered a form of "interest" paid in labor.</note>
All the days of the dry season are considered equal, and all the days of the rainy season are considered equal. <note>original: "garir" (dry/dragging season) and "revi'ah" (rainy/saturation season).</note>
He may not say to him:
"Plow with me in the dry season, and I will plow with you in the rainy season." <note>Plowing is much more difficult when the ground is dry and hard than when it is softened by rain; an exchange across seasons would be unequal.</note>

->**12**<-

Rabban Gamliel says:
There is **early interest**, and there is **late interest**.
How so?
If one set his eyes on borrowing from another,
and he sent him a gift,
and said, "This is so that you will lend to me,"
this is **early interest**.
If he borrowed from him and returned his money,
and then he sent him a gift,
and said, "This is because of your money, which was idle while in my possession,"
this is **late interest**.
Rabbi Shimon says:
There is **interest of words**: <note>Even non-monetary favors can be considered interest.</note>
One should not say to his lender:
"Tell me if such-and-such a man has arrived from such-and-such a place." <note>The borrower is providing a service—acting as an informant—which he would not have done if not for the loan.</note>

# Chapter 6

## Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 6 Mishnah 1
**1**
One who hires craftsmen, 
and they misled one another, <note>This refers to cases where an agent (an intermediary) told workers the pay was higher than what the employer offered, or told the employer the workers accepted less than they actually did.</note>
neither party has anything against the other but a **grievance**. <note>original: "tar'omet"; a term for a moral complaint or resentment that cannot be settled in a court of law, as no financial damage was proven, but the trust was broken.</note>
If he hired a donkey-driver or a potter <note>Hiring for specific transport or production tasks.</note> 
to bring musicians for a bride or for the deceased, <note>original: "chalilim" (flutes). Flutes were played at both weddings and funerals in the ancient world.</note>
or workers to remove his flax from the steeping-pool, <note>original: "mishrah." Flax was soaked in water to separate the fibers; if left too long, it would rot and be destroyed.</note>
or any matter that involves an **irreparable loss**, <note>original: "davar ha-aved"; a legal category for time-sensitive tasks where a delay causes a total loss of property.</note>
and the workers backed out—
in a place where there is no one else to hire, he may hire others at their expense or mislead them. <note>In an emergency where property will be lost, the employer can legally trick the workers into staying or hire replacements at a much higher wage and deduct that cost from the original workers' pay.</note>

## Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 6 Mishnah 2
**2**
One who hires craftsmen and they back out,
their hand is at the bottom. <note>original: "yadan la-tachtona"; a legal idiom meaning they are at a financial disadvantage. If the market price for labor rose, they only get the lower original rate; if it fell, their pay is docked to cover the cost of hiring new workers.</note>
And if the employer backs out,
his hand is at the bottom.
Anyone who changes the terms of the agreement, his hand is at the bottom,
and anyone who backs out of the agreement, his hand is at the bottom.

## Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 6 Mishnah 3
**3**
One who hires a donkey to lead it on the mountain, <insert><to lead it></insert>
but led it in the valley;
or in the valley, but led it on the mountain;
even if both routes are ten miles long, and the animal died,
the hirer is liable. <note>Since he deviated from the specific instructions of the owner, he assumes full responsibility for the "accident" of the animal's death.</note>
If he hired a donkey and it went blind in one eye, <note>original: "hivrikah," literally "flashed" or "sparkled," referring to a cataract or a specific type of eye disease.</note>
or if it was seized for **royal service**, <note><term>angaria</term>: derived from the Greek *angareia*, referring to the Roman practice of state officials or soldiers forcibly requisitioning animals or people for government transport.</note>
he may say to the hirer: "Here is yours before you!" <note>The hirer must accept the animal as it is and cannot demand a replacement if it is still capable of doing the work, even if it is now slower or has been temporarily seized.</note>
But if it died or its leg was broken,
the owner is obligated to provide him with another donkey.

--- Page 720 ---
<meta>This page continues the laws of labor and hiring from Chapter 6. While the previous page discussed the initial hiring process and "grievances" when workers or employers back out, this page focuses on specific liability when a person deviates from the agreed-upon conditions of the rental (such as the route taken or the type of load carried).</meta>

One who hires a donkey to lead it on a mountain, 
and he led it in a valley: 
if she slipped, he is exempt <note>Since a valley is generally less slippery than a mountain path, the renter is not held responsible for an accident that was even less likely to happen in the valley than on the agreed-upon mountain route.</note>, 
but if she overheated, he is liable <note>original: "huchama." The air in valleys is often more humid and stagnant than on mountains, making heatstroke or exhaustion more likely.</note>. 
If he hired her for a valley, and he led her on a mountain: 
if she slipped, he is liable, 
and if she overheated, he is exempt. 
But if she overheated due to the ascent, he is liable. <note>The general principle here is that if a renter deviates from the agreement and the animal is damaged by a risk typical of the new environment, they must pay for the loss.</note>

## Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 6 Mishnah 4

<meta>5</meta>

One who hires a cow to plow on a mountain, 
and he plowed in a valley, and the plowshare was broken, 
he is exempt. <note>original: "kankan." This refers to the wooden or iron part of the plow that cuts into the earth. Plowing in a valley is generally easier on the equipment than plowing rocky mountain soil.</note>
If he hired it for a valley, and he plowed on a mountain, and the plowshare was broken, 
he is liable. 
If he hired it to thresh legumes, and he threshed grain, 
he is exempt. 
If he hired it for grain, and he threshed legumes, 
he is liable, because legumes are slippery. <note>original: "kitnit machleket." Legumes like lentils or beans release a slick residue when crushed, making it much easier for an animal to slip and injure itself compared to dry stalks of grain.</note>

## Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 6 Mishnah 5

<meta>6</meta>

One who hires a donkey to bring wheat, 
and he instead brought barley, 
or grain, and he brought straw, 
he is liable, because the volume is as difficult to bear as the weight. <insert>because the volume</insert> <note>Even if the weight is the same or less, a bulkier load (like straw or barley) shifts more, catches the wind, and places different kinds of strain on the animal's back and balance.</note>
If he hired it to bring a *letech* of wheat, and he brought a *letech* of barley, <note>term: "letech" (a biblical measure of volume equal to fifteen se'ahs, or about 130-150 liters).</note>
he is exempt, 
but if he added to its load, 
he is liable. 
And how much may he add to its load and still be liable? 
Sumchos says in the name of Rabbi Meir: 
A *se'ah* for a camel, <note>term: "se'ah" (a unit of volume; roughly 8 to 13 liters).</note>
and three *kavs* for a donkey. <note>term: "kav" (a smaller unit; six kavs make one se'ah). A donkey is smaller and more sensitive to overloads than a camel.</note>

## Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 6 Mishnah 6

<meta>7</meta>

All craftsmen are considered paid bailees. <note>term: "shomrei sachar" (paid guardians). In Jewish law, a person who is paid to look after an object—or in this case, a craftsman who is paid to work on an object—has a high level of responsibility. They are liable for theft or loss, not just for negligence.</note>
And all of them, if they said, "Bring the money and take what is yours!" <note>This marks the beginning of a discussion on when the craftsman's high level of liability ends and reverts to a lower level, such as once the work is done and they are simply waiting for the owner to pick up the item.</note>

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 6 Mishnah 7

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 6 Mishnah 8
## 8
One who moves a barrel from one place to another and broke it,
whether he is an unpaid guardian or a paid guardian,
he must take an oath <note>This refers to a "guardians' oath" used in court to prove that the damage was an unavoidable accident rather than negligence.</note>.

Both this one and that one take an oath; 
but I wonder if both [the unpaid and paid guardian] are truly able to take an oath <note>Rabbi Eliezer is questioning the fairness of the rule; normally, a paid guardian is liable for theft or loss, so swearing it was an accident might not always exempt them from payment.</note>.

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 7 Mishnah 1
## 1
One who hires laborers,
and told them to start early or to stay late—
in a place where the custom was not to start early and not to stay late,
he cannot compel them [to do so].
In a place where the custom was to provide food, he must provide food;
[where the custom is] to provide sweets, he must provide them;
everything follows the custom of the province <note>original: "minhag ha-medina." This is a fundamental principle in Jewish labor law: in the absence of a specific contract, local community standards and traditions dictate the working conditions and benefits.</note>.
There was an incident involving Rabbi Yohanan ben Matya, who said to his son:
> "Go out and hire laborers for us!"
And the son agreed to provide them with food.

but for the sake of returning lost property to the owners <note>original: "hashev avedah la-ba'alim." In this context, "lost property" refers to the employer's time. The workers may eat while walking from one furrow to the next <note>original: "me-uman le-uman." An *uman* refers to a row or a specific area of professional work.</note>,
and on their return from the winepress;
and a donkey [may eat] until it is unloaded.

A worker may eat a cucumber, even if it is worth a denarius <term>denarius: (Hebrew: *dinar*) a silver coin that often constituted a full day's wage.</term>,

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 7 Mishnah 6

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 8 Mishnah 1

One who borrows a cow, and borrows its owners with it <note>The "owner present" rule (Hebrew: *Be'alav Imo*). he is liable, as it is said:
<margin>(Exodus 22:13)</margin>
"If its owner is not with him, he shall surely pay."

he is liable <note>In this case of uncertainty, because the borrower has a definite obligation to return a borrowed animal (high liability) and cannot definitively claim it was the rented one (lower liability) that died, the court rules in favor of the lender.</note>.

**and he has a right to the beams of a sycamore tree.** <gloss>regarding the beam</gloss> <note>In a longer lease, the tenant has time to restore the land's nutrients after flax, and the growth of the trees is considered part of his long-term investment.</note>

### Tractate Bava Metzia Chapter 10 Mishnah 2

->2<-

**[In the case of] a house and an upper story belonging to two people,**

**Rather, the owner of the upper story builds both the house and the upper story,**

### 5

**One whose wall was adjacent to his neighbor’s garden and it fell,**
**and [the garden owner] said to him: "Clear away your stones!"**
**and [the wall owner] replied to him: "They are yours!"** <note>original: "הגיעוך" — literally "they have reached you." This is a legal formula where the owner of the debris attempts to relinquish ownership to avoid the cost or effort of clearing the mess, essentially telling the neighbor to keep the stones as compensation.</note>
**They do not listen to him** <note>The law does not allow the owner of the debris to force the neighbor to accept the stones; he is still obligated to clear them.</note>
**Once [the garden owner] has accepted [the stones] upon himself, [if the wall owner] then said:**
**"Here is [reimbursement for] your expenses, and I will take what is mine,"**
**they do not listen to him.** <note>Once the agreement is made and the neighbor takes ownership, the original owner cannot change his mind if he later realizes the stones are worth more than the clearing costs.</note>

### 6

**One who hires a worker to work with him in [moving or processing] straw and stubble,**
**and [the worker] said to him: "Give me my wages!"**
**and [the employer] said to him: "Take what you have worked with as your wages!"**
**They do not listen to him.**
**Once [the worker] has accepted [the material] upon himself, [if the employer] then said to him:**
**"Here are your wages [in cash], and I will take what is mine,"**
**they do not listen to him.**

### 7

**One who brings out manure to the public domain:** <note>Manure was often placed in the street to be trampled into fertilizer before being moved to fields.</note>
**as the bringer brings it out, the one who fertilizes must use it.** <note>The waste must be cleared or used promptly to prevent it from becoming a permanent public nuisance.</note>
**One may not soak clay in the public domain,**
**and one may not mold bricks [there].**
**One may knead mortar in the public domain,**
**but not for bricks.** <gloss>The proofreader added: for bricks.</gloss> <note>original: "המגיה הוסיף ל, ללבנים" — refers to a marginal or interlinear correction in the manuscript clarifying that while mortar for immediate building is permitted, long-term brick-making is not.</note>
**One who builds in the public domain:**
**as the bringer brings stones, the builder must build [them into the wall].**
**And if he caused damage, he must pay for what he damaged.**
**Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:**
**He may even prepare his work thirty days in advance.** <note>Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel offers a more lenient view, allowing for the staging of materials for up to a month before construction begins.</note>

# Tractate Bava Batra

## Chapter 1

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 1 Mishnah 1

### 1

Partners who wished to make a partition <note>original: "מחיצה" — mechitzah. Here it refers specifically to a wall that provides "visual privacy," which the Sages deemed a legal necessity.</note> in a courtyard,
they build the wall in the middle.
In a place where it is customary to build with unhewn stones, hewn stones, half-bricks, or bricks,
they must build. Everything follows the custom of the land. <note>original: "מנהג המדינה" — minhag hamedinah. This is a crucial legal principle where local standard practices override general law in civil matters.</note>
With **unhewn stones** <note>original: "גויל" — gvil; rough, uncut stones</note>,
this one gives three handbreadths <note>A "tefach" or handbreadth is approximately 3 to 4 inches.</note> and that one gives three handbreadths.
With **hewn stones** <note>original: "גזית" — gazit; squared and smoothed stones</note>,
this one gives two and a half handbreadths and that one gives two and a half handbreadths.
With **half-bricks** <note>original: "כפיסים" — kefisim; smaller stones or wooden beams</note>,
this one gives two handbreadths, [and that one gives two handbreadths].
And with **bricks** <note>original: "לבנים" — levenim</note>,
this one gives one and a half handbreadths and that one gives one and a half handbreadths.
Therefore, if the wall falls,
the space and the stones belong to both of them. <note>Because they contributed equally to the thickness and the land, they remain equal partners in the debris.</note>

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 1 Mishnah 2

### 2

And so too in a garden:

<meta>This page continues the laws of property boundaries from the first chapter of Tractate Bava Batra. In a place where it is customary to build a fence, **they may compel him** <note>original: "מְחַיְּבִין אוֹתוֹ" — an individual can be legally forced by their neighbor to contribute to a boundary wall if it is the local norm.</note> to do so.
However, in a valley <note>original: "בִּקְעָה" — biq'ah. This refers to wide, open agricultural fields where fences were not usually necessary to protect privacy.</note>,
in a place where it is customary not to fence, they cannot compel him.
Rather, if one neighbor wishes to build a fence,
he must move the wall into his own territory and make a **mark** <note>original: "חָזִית" — chazit. A distinctive strip of plaster or a specific stone layout on the outer side of the wall to prove he is the sole owner.</note> on the outside.
Therefore, if the wall falls,
the place where it stood and the stones belong to him.

## 3

And if they built the wall by the mutual consent of both parties,
they build the wall in the middle,
and they make a mark on both sides.
Therefore, if the wall falls,
the place and the stones belong to both of them.

->Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 1 Mishnah 3<-

## 4

One who surrounds his neighbor on three sides <note>This refers to a situation where a landowner builds walls around three sides of a neighbor's field, effectively providing security but without the neighbor's request.</note>
and fenced the first, second, and third sides,
the neighbor cannot be compelled to pay for the cost.
**Rabbi Yose says:**
If the neighbor then stands up and fences the fourth side himself,
**they roll the entire cost upon him** <note>original: "מְגַלְגְּלִין עָלָיו אֶת הַכֹּל" — m'galgelin. A legal principle where once the neighbor demonstrates that he benefits from the entire enclosure (by closing the fourth side), he becomes retroactively liable for his share of all four walls.</note>.

->Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 1 Mishnah 4<-

## 5

If a courtyard wall falls,
they compel each neighbor to rebuild it up to a height of four cubits <note>Approximately 6 feet (1.8 meters), the standard height required to ensure "visual privacy" for people standing in their yards.</note>.
The neighbor is **under the legal presumption of having paid** <gloss>that it fell</gloss>,
until the claimant brings proof that he did not pay. <gloss>fell</gloss> <note>Because a person is expected to pay for essential structures immediately, the law assumes he has done so unless proven otherwise.</note>
If the wall is built higher than four cubits,
the neighbor cannot be compelled to contribute to the extra height.
However, if the neighbor built another wall near it <note>Specifically, if he builds a structure that relies on the shared wall's height.</note>,
even if he has not yet placed a roof upon it,
they roll the entire cost upon him,
under the legal presumption that he has **not** paid,
until he brings proof that he did pay.

->Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 1 Mishnah 5<-

## 6

They may compel a resident of a shared courtyard to contribute to the building of a **gatehouse** <note>original: "בֵּית שַׁעַר" — beit sha'ar. A small structure for a watchman at the entrance to a courtyard to prevent passersby from looking in.</note> and a door for the courtyard.

**Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:**
Not all courtyards are suitable for a gatehouse <note>original: "בֵּית שַׁעַר" — a small structure at the entrance of a courtyard where a porter sits. Shimon ben Gamliel argues that only certain types of large or public-facing courtyards require such an addition.</note>.
They may compel a resident to contribute to building a wall, doors, and a bolt for the city.
**Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:**

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 1 Mishnah 6
->7<-

They do not divide a shared courtyard,
until there will be four cubits <term>cubit: "amah" — a standard unit of length, approximately the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger (about 18 inches).</term> for this partner and four cubits for that partner <note>If the courtyard is smaller than eight cubits total, one partner cannot force the other to divide it, as the resulting spaces would be too small to be useful.</note>.
Nor do they divide a field,
until there will be nine *kavs* <term>kav: a measure of volume; in land management, this refers to a "beit kav," the area required to sow one kav of seed.</term> for this one and nine *kavs* for that one.
**Rabbi Yehuda says:**
Nine half-*kavs* for this one and nine half-*kavs* for that one.
Nor do they divide a garden,
until there will be half a *kav* for this one and half a *kav* for that one.
And according to the words of **Rabbi Akiva**, a quarter-measure <note>original: "בֵּית רֹבַע" — *beit rova*, the area needed to sow a quarter of a *kav*.</note>.
They do not divide a dining hall <note>original: "טְרַקְלִין" — *triclinium*, a formal Roman-style room for entertaining.</note>, nor a tower <note>original: "מוֹרָן" — possibly a watchtower or a specialized storage room.</note>, nor a dovecote,
nor a garment <note>original: "טַלִּית" — while often meaning a prayer shawl today, in this context it refers to any large expensive cloak or piece of fabric.</note>, nor a bathhouse, nor an olive press,
until there will be enough remaining for this one and enough for that one <note>The principle is that the division must not destroy the utility of the item. If dividing a garment makes it unwearable, it cannot be forcibly partitioned.</note>.
(This is the general rule:
Anything that, when divided, retains its name, they may divide,
and if not, they do not divide.) <note>Note: "אינו בכתב היד" — this sentence is not found in the original manuscript but is common in other versions of the Mishnah.</note>
When does this apply?
At a time when both partners do not agree to the division <note>Meaning, one partner is trying to force the division against the other's will.</note>,
but when both of them agree,
even if the resulting portions are less than these measurements, they may divide.
But with **Holy Scriptures** <note>original: "וְכִתְבֵי הַקֹּדֶשׁ" — sacred scrolls containing the Bible.</note>,
even though both of them agree,
they may not divide them <note>Because cutting a sacred scroll into pieces to share the parchment would be a desecration and render the text unreadable.</note>.
