<meta>This page transitions from the first chapter of Tractate Bava Batra, which focused on shared property and partitions, into the second chapter. The focus now shifts to "zoning laws"—the legal distances one must maintain when building or performing activities on one's own property to avoid causing damage or a nuisance to a neighbor's property.</meta>

## Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 2 Mishnah 1

A person may not dig a pit near the pit of his fellow,
nor a ditch, nor a cave, nor a water channel,
nor a laundry pool <note>original: "נִבְרֶכֶת שֶׁלְּכֹבְסִים" — a large stone-lined tank used for soaking and washing clothes.</note>,
unless he distances it from the wall of his fellow by three handbreadths <term>handbreadth: "tefach" — a unit of measurement based on the width of a palm, roughly 3.2 to 3.5 inches.</term>,
and plasters it with lime <note>original: "סָד בַּסִּיד" — sealing the surface with lime plaster prevents water from seeping through the earth and undermining the neighbor's wall.</note>.

One must distance olive-refuse, dung,
salt, lime, and flint-stones,
from the wall of his fellow by three handbreadths,
and plaster it with lime.

One must distance seeds,
the path of a plow, and urine,
from a wall by three handbreadths.

One must distance a hand-mill <note>The vibrations from a heavy grinding stone could weaken nearby structures.</note> three handbreadths from the lower stone <note>original: "שֶׁכֶב" — the stationary bottom stone of a mill.</note>,
which results in four handbreadths from the upper stone <note>original: "רֶכֶב" — the moving top stone, which is wider than the base.</note>,
and an oven <note>original: "תַּנּוּר" — typically a clay oven that radiates significant heat.</note> three handbreadths from its base <note>original: "כִּלְיָא" — the foundation or belly of the oven.</note>,
which results in four handbreadths from its upper rim.

## Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 2 Mishnah 2

**2**

A person may not set up an oven inside a house,
unless there is a height of four cubits <term>cubit: "amah" — a standard unit of length, approximately 18 inches.</term> above it <note>This height was required to ensure the heat from the oven would not set the ceiling or roof on fire.</note>.
If he was setting it up in an upper story <note>original: "עֲלִיָּה" — a room on the second floor.</note>,
there must be a layer of stone and mortar <note>original: "מַעֲזִיבָה" — a thick flooring made of plaster and stones to insulate the heat from the wooden beams below.</note> three handbreadths thick beneath it,
and for a small stove <note>original: "כִּירָה"</note>, one handbreadth is sufficient.
Even so, if the fire caused damage, he must pay for what he damaged.
**Rabbi Shimon says:**
All of these measurements were stated only so that if he followed them and still caused damage, he would be exempt from paying <note>Rabbi Shimon argues that these regulations serve as a legal "safe harbor"; if you follow the building code, you are not liable for accidental damage.</note>.

## Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 2 Mishnah 3

**3**

A person may not open a bakery or a dyer's shop
underneath the storehouse of his fellow <note>The heat from a bakery or the fumes/humidity from a dyer's shop could spoil grain or wine stored above.</note>,
nor may he keep a cattle stall there.
In truth, they permitted a wine cellar in such a location, but not a cattle stall.
Regarding a shop located within a shared courtyard,
a neighbor can protest and say to the shopkeeper:
> "I cannot sleep because of the noise of those entering and the noise of those exiting!"

However, a resident may make tools <note>original: "עוֹשֶׂה כֵלִים" — practicing a craft or trade privately.</note> in his home,
and go out and sell them in the market;
the neighbor cannot protest against him and say:
> "I cannot sleep because of the sound of the hammer, or the sound of the millstones, or the sound of the children <note>This refers to the sound of students in a home-based school; the rabbis prioritized the noise of education over a neighbor's desire for quiet.</note>."

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 2 Mishnah 4
4

If a person had a wall already built near the wall of his neighbor,
he may not build another wall next to it,
unless he distances it from the original wall by four cubits <term>cubit: "amma" — an ancient unit of measurement based on the length of the forearm, approximately 18 inches or 45-50 centimeters.</term>.
And regarding windows,
one must distance a wall four cubits from above, from below, and from across <note>original: "מִלְמַעְלָן וּמִלְּמַטָּן וּמִכְּנֶגְדָּן" — this spacing ensures that the neighbor's light is not blocked and that their privacy is protected.</note>.

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 2 Mishnah 5
5

One must distance a ladder from a dovecote <note>original: "שּׁוֹבָךְ" — a structure, often a tower, built to house pigeons or doves for their meat and fertilizer.</note> by four cubits,
so that a marten <note>original: "נְמִיָּה" — likely a mongoose or a large weasel. If a ladder is too close, the predator could use it to jump into the dovecote and kill the birds.</note> cannot jump in.
One must distance a wall from a neighbor's roof-gutter by four cubits,
so that the neighbor has enough room to set up a ladder <note>Maintenance of gutters and roofs required space to safely stand and angle a ladder.</note>.
One must distance a dovecote from a city by fifty cubits.
A person should not build a dovecote within his own property,
unless he has fifty cubits of space in every direction.
**Rabbi Yehuda says:**
The distance should be enough to sow four *kor* of seed <term>kor: a large measure of volume; a "beit kor" refers to the area of land required to sow that much seed, roughly 5-6 acres.</term>,
which is the full range of a dove’s flight.
But if he purchased the dovecote as it is, even if it is on a plot only a quarter of a *kab* in size,
it remains in his possession <note>original: "בְּחֶזְקָתוֹ" — a legal status (chazakah) where a pre-existing condition is allowed to continue because it is assumed to have been established legally in the past.</note>.

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 2 Mishnah 6
6

A fledgling bird <note>original: "נִיפּוֹל" — a young bird that has fallen from the nest but cannot yet fly.</note> that is found within fifty cubits of a dovecote
belongs to the owner of the dovecote.
If it is found beyond fifty cubits,
it belongs to the one who finds it.
If it is found between two dovecotes,
if it is closer to this one, it belongs to him; and if closer to that one, it belongs to him.
If it is exactly half-way between them, the two owners shall divide its value.

One must distance a tree from a city by twenty-five cubits;
but for a carob tree or a sycamore tree, the distance must be fifty cubits.
<note>These trees were larger and had more extensive root systems and foliage, which could interfere with the city's open space or walls.</note>

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 2 Mishnah 9

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 2 Mishnah 11

whether the tree is positioned above the level of the cistern or to the side.
If the cistern was there first, the owner of the tree cuts it down and the owner of the cistern pays him for the wood;
but if the tree was there first, he does not have to cut it down.
If there is a doubt as to which was there first, he does not have to cut it down.

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 2 Mishnah 12

->12<-

A person should not plant a tree near his neighbor’s field, unless he distances it at least **four cubits** <note>approx. 6–8 feet. This distance provides enough space for a farmer to turn his plow without being obstructed by the neighbor’s tree.</note> from the boundary. This rule applies whether the plants are **vines** or any other type of **tree**.

If there was a **fence** between the two properties, each person may plant right up to the fence on either side.

If **roots** from a tree were spreading into a neighbor's field, the neighbor may dig down to a depth of **three handbreadths** <note>approx. 9–12 inches. This is deep enough to ensure the roots do not catch on a plow.</note> and cut them away, so that they do not hinder the plow. If the neighbor was digging a **pit, a trench, or a cave** <term>pit, trench, or cave: "bor, shiach, u-me'arah" — the three standard types of excavations: round pits for water, long narrow trenches, and square vaulted chambers</term>, he may cut the roots as he digs down, and the wood from those roots belongs to him.

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 2 Mishnah 13

->13<-

If a tree’s branches lean over into a neighbor's field, the neighbor may trim them up to the height of the **full length of a plow-goad** <term>plow-goad: "mardea" — a long stick used to guide oxen, serving here as a standard unit of height</term> above the path of the plow.

However, in the case of a **carob tree** or a **sycamore tree** <note>These trees have particularly dense foliage and heavy branches, which cast deep shade and interfere more significantly with the neighbor's crops.</note>, he must trim the branches back until they are exactly aligned with the **plumb line** <term>plumb line: "mishkolet" — a vertical line marking the exact property boundary</term>.

In an **irrigated field** <term>irrigated field: "beit ha-shlachin" — a field that requires intensive watering and is thus more sensitive to the shade and water-theft of a neighbor's tree</term> or a field specifically for **orchard trees**, any overhanging branches must be trimmed back to the plumb line.

**Abba Shaul** says: In the case of any **non-fruit-bearing tree** <note>original: "ilan srak" — trees grown for wood or shade rather than food.</note>, the branches must be trimmed back to the plumb line.

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 2 Mishnah 14

->14<-

If a tree leans over into the **public domain** <note>original: "reshut ha-rabim" — public streets or thoroughfares.</note>, its branches must be trimmed high enough so that a **camel** may pass through with its **rider** safely.

**Rabbi Yehuda** says: The height must accommodate a camel carrying a load of **flax** or a load of **vine-branches** <note>These loads are typically bulky and sit high on the animal's back, requiring even more clearance than just a rider.</note>.

**Rabbi Simeon** says: For any tree in the public domain, the branches must be trimmed back to the **plumb line**, because of the concern for **ritual impurity** <term>ritual impurity: "tum'ah" — laws regarding the transfer of spiritual impurity. A tree might act as a "tent" or canopy, inadvertently spreading impurity from a source (like a leper or a bone) to a passerby underneath.</term>.

And for anything that produces fruit constantly, its **presumptive ownership** <term>presumptive ownership: "Hazakah" — a legal status where occupying land for a set period (usually three years) without protest from the owner serves as evidence of ownership</term> is established after **three years**, calculated exactly from "day to day" <note>meaning three full calendar years from the start of possession</note>. A **rain-watered field** <term>rain-watered field: "sedeh ha-baal" — a field dependent on rainfall rather than manual irrigation</term>, its presumptive ownership is established after **three years**, but it is not calculated "day to day" <note>because the three-year period is measured by the agricultural seasons rather than specific calendar dates</note>.

->2<-

**Rabbi Ishmael** says:
Three months in the first year,
and three months in the final year,
and twelve months in the middle—
totaling **eighteen months**.
**Rabbi Akiva** says:
One month in the first year,
and one month in the final year,
and twelve months in the middle—
totaling **fourteen months**.
**Rabbi Ishmael** said:
Regarding what were these words spoken? Regarding a **grain field** <term>grain field: "sedeh ha-lavan" — literally a "white field," so named because the grain turns the field pale when it ripens</term>.
But in a **tree-field** <note>an orchard or grove</note>,
if the possessor gathered his grain, and harvested his olives, and gathered his summer fruit—
these count as **three years** <note>meaning that harvesting three distinct seasonal crops is equivalent to three years of possession, even if less than 36 months have passed</note>.

->Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 3 Mishnah 2<-

->3<-

There are **three lands** regarding the laws of presumptive ownership:
**Judea, Transjordan, and Galilee**.
If the owner was in **Judea** and the possessor held the land in **Galilee**,
or if the owner was in **Galilee** and the possessor held the land in **Judea**,
it is **not a valid presumptive ownership**, until the owner is with the possessor in the same province.
**Rabbi Judah** said:
The Sages only mentioned a period of **three years**
so that even if the owner were as far away as **Spain** <note>original: "Aspanya" — referring to Roman Hispania, used here to represent the furthest edges of the known world</note>,
the possessor would hold the land for a year,
messengers would travel and inform the owner for a year,
and the owner could return or send a protest in the third year.

->Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 3 Mishnah 3<-

->4<-

Any **presumptive ownership** that is not accompanied by a **legal claim** is not a valid presumptive ownership.
For example, if the original owner said to the possessor:
"What are you doing in my property?" <note>If the possessor cannot claim a specific reason for being there—such as "I bought it from you"—his long-term presence alone does not grant him ownership.</note>

"[The claim that] no person ever said a word to me [challenging my presence]"
is not a valid **presumptive ownership** <term>Hazakah: a legal status where occupying land for a set period serves as evidence of ownership</term>.
[However, the claims] "You sold it to me," or "You gave it to me as a gift,"
constitute a valid **presumptive ownership**.
And one who comes [to claim the land] by right of **inheritance** <term>original: "yerushah"</term> does not need to provide a specific claim <note>meaning they do not need to explain how the original owner acquired the property, only that they inherited it from them</note>.

### 5

**Partners**, **sharecroppers** <term>original: "arisim" — tenant farmers who pay a portion of their crop as rent</term>, and **guardians** <term>original: "apotropim" — legal administrators of property, such as those appointed for orphans</term>

A man has no **presumptive ownership** over his wife’s property,
nor does a wife have **presumptive ownership** over her husband’s property,
nor a father over the property of his son,
nor a son over the property of his father.
To what circumstances do these words apply? To one attempting to establish ownership through **possession** <term>original: "mahazik"</term>,
but in the case of one giving a **gift**,
or **brothers who divided** an estate,
or one who takes possession of the **property of a proselyte** <note>referring to a convert to Judaism who dies without Jewish heirs, leaving their property legally ownerless and available to the first person to claim it</note>,
if he locked a gate, built a fence, or breached a wall even slightly,
this constitutes a valid **presumptive ownership**.

### Tractate Bava Batra, Chapter 3, Mishnah 4

### 6

If two witnesses testify for a person that he enjoyed the produce of the land for three years,
and they are found to be **conspiring witnesses** <term>original: "zomemim" — witnesses proven to have been elsewhere at the time of the alleged event, thus disqualifying their testimony</term>,
they must pay the claimant the full value [of the land].
If two witnesses testify about the first year, and two about the second, and two about the third,
they **divide the payment into thirds** among themselves.
If **three brothers** and one other person join together [to testify for different years],
these constitute three separate testimonies,
yet they are considered as **one testimony** <note>for the purpose of legal disqualification; if one part of the chain is proven false, the entire claim of three-year possession fails</note>.

### Tractate Bava Batra, Chapter 3, Mishnah 7

A person may not open **windows** facing a **shared courtyard** <term>original: "chatzar shutafin"</term> <note>to protect the privacy of the other residents</note>.

and then build the **upper story** on top of their house,
opening it into their own house <note>thereby ensuring that the new residents of the upper story enter through the private home rather than increasing the foot traffic in the shared courtyard</note>.

A person may not open a **doorway** facing another's **doorway** in a shared courtyard,

# Chapter 4

## Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 4 Mishnah 1
->1<-

One who **sells a house** has not sold the **annex** <term>original: "yatzia" — a side-structure or loft attached to the main building</term>, even if it is **open to the inside** of the house; nor has he sold the **inner room** located behind it, nor the **roof**, provided that it has a **parapet** <term>original: "ma'akeh" — a safety railing</term> that is **ten handbreadths** high <note>Approximately 30-40 inches; a height that legally defines the roof as a separate, functional domain</note>. Rabbi Yehuda says: If it has the **form of a doorway** <note>Meaning it has two side-posts and a lintel</note>, even if it is not ten handbreadths high, it is **not sold**.

## Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 4 Mishnah 2
->2<-

[The sale likewise does] not [include] the **cistern**, nor the **vault** <term>original: "dut" — a stone-lined cellar or storage pit</term>, even though the seller wrote to the buyer in the contract, "I am selling you its **depth and its height**" <note>The seller must specifically name the cistern or vault to include them in the sale, as they are considered distinct from the "house" itself</note>. The seller [retains ownership of these and] must **purchase a path** [from the buyer] to reach them. [These are] the **words of Rabbi Akiva**.

## Chapter 5

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 5 Mishnah 1

1
**One who sells a ship**,
**has sold the mast, the sail** <note>original: "nes" — literally a banner, but in maritime context, the main sail</note>, **and the anchors**,
**and all the things that lead it** <note>The steering gear or customary equipment used to navigate the vessel.</note>.
**But he has not sold neither the slaves** <note>Slaves who worked as rowers or sailors were considered separate property from the vessel itself.</note>,
**nor the packing bags** <note>original: "martsafim" — large sacks or leather coverings for cargo</note>,
**nor the cargo-vessels** <term>original: "antiki" — likely from the Greek "anteke," referring to large storage jars or the ship's hold/cargo area</term>.
**At a time when he says** to the buyer, "**It and everything within it**,"
**behold, all of them are sold**.

2
[If] he **sold the wagon**, he **has not sold the mules**;
[if] he **sold the mules**, he **has not sold the wagon**.
[if] he **sold the yoke**, he **has not sold the oxen**;
[if] he **sold the oxen**, he **has <insert>sold</insert> not the yoke** <note>The scribe inserted the word "sold" here to correct the sentence flow.</note>.
**Rabbi Yehuda says**:
**The price informs** <term>original: "ha-damim modi'in" — the principle that the amount of money paid can be used to clarify the scope of a sale</term>.
**How so?**
[If] he **said to him**:
"**Sell me your yoke for two hundred Zuz**,"
**it is a known thing that a yoke is not [worth] two hundred Zuz** <note>A yoke is a simple wooden beam; paying a high price suggests the buyer clearly intended to include the valuable team of oxen in the purchase.</note>.
**And the Sages say**:
**The price is no proof** <gloss>for the price</gloss> <note>The Sages maintain that the definition of the sale depends on the words used, not the price paid, which could simply be a bad deal or an error.</note>.

3
**One who sells a donkey, has not sold its equipment**.
**Nahum the Mede says**:

## Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 5 Mishnah 3

**4**
**One who sells a donkey, has not sold the pack-saddle** <note>original: "sakka" — a specific wooden or padded saddle for carrying heavy loads</note>.
[If] he **sold a cow, he has not sold its calf**.
[If] he **sold a dung heap, he has sold the manure** within it.
[If] he **sold a cistern, he has sold its water**.
[If] he **sold a dovecote, he has sold the pigeons**.
[If] he **sold a beehive, he has sold the bees**.
**One who purchases the offspring of a dovecote**, must **allow the first brood to fly away** <note>To ensure the parent birds do not abandon the dovecote and that the population remains sustainable for the seller.</note>.
[One who purchases] the **offspring of a beehive, takes three swarms and then castrates** <term>castrates: "mesares" — a method of preventing further swarming, often by disrupting the reproduction of the queen or removing specific cells, to focus the bees on honey production</term>.
[One who takes] **honeycombs, must leave two combs** <note>This ensures the bees have enough food to survive the winter.</note>.
[One who buys] **olive trees for wood** <note>Meaning he intends to cut them down for timber.</note>, **must leave two shoots** <note>original: "grofiyot" — the buyer cannot uproot the tree entirely; he must leave enough of the stump so that the tree can eventually grow back for the landowner.</note>.

## Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 5 Mishnah 4

**5**
**One who buys two trees within the property of another**, <gloss>two</gloss>
**behold, he has not acquired the land**.
**Rabbi Meir says**:
**He has acquired the land**.
[If the trees] **grew large, he may not trim** <note>The buyer cannot cut the overhanging branches because he does not own the airspace or the ground beneath; doing so might interfere with the landowner's ability to plow.</note>.
**That which grows from the trunk belongs to him** <note>The owner of the trees.</note>;
**and [that which grows] from the roots, belongs to the owner of the land**.
**And if they died, he has no land**. <note>If the trees die, the buyer's rights end; he cannot plant new ones in their place.</note>

**6**
[If] he **bought three [trees], he has acquired the land**.
[If they] **grew large, he may trim**.
**And that which grows from the trunk and from the roots, belongs to him**.
**And if they died, he has [the rights to] the land**. <note>In Jewish law, three trees are considered a "grove." Buying a grove automatically includes the land around and between them, giving the buyer permanent real estate rights.</note>

While the previous page discussed the sale of working animals and their equipment, this page narrows the focus to the sale of specific animal parts, the legal consequences of quality mismatches in goods like grain and wine, and the formal acts of "pulling" (meshikha) required to finalize a sale of produce or flax.</meta>

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 5 Mishnah 5

[7]

**One who sells the head of a large animal** <note>Large livestock refers to cattle, such as oxen or cows.</note>,
**has not sold the feet**;
[If] he **sold the feet, he has not sold the head**.
[If] he **sold the trachea** <note>original: "kaneh" — literally "the reed," referring here to the windpipe and the respiratory organs attached to it</note>, **he has not sold the liver**;
[If] he **sold the liver, he has not sold the trachea**.
**But regarding a small animal** <note>Small livestock refers to sheep or goats.</note>:
[If] he **sold the head, he has sold the feet**;
[If] he **sold the feet, he has not sold the head**;
[If] he **sold the trachea, he has sold the liver**;
[If] he **sold the liver, he has not sold the trachea**. <note>The Mishnah distinguishes between large and small animals because in large animals, these parts are substantial enough to be sold as independent units, whereas in small animals, the lower-value parts are often bundled together by custom.</note>

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 5 Mishnah 6

8

**There are four standards among sellers**:
[If] he **sold him high-quality wheat, and it turned out to be of poor quality**,
**the purchaser may retract** [the deal];
[If it was] **poor quality, and it turned out to be high-quality**,
**the seller may retract**; <note>In Jewish law, if the person who was "wronged" by the change in quality gains an advantage, the other party has the right to cancel the transaction because the item delivered was not what was agreed upon.</note>
[If it was] **poor, and turned out to be poor**,
[or] **high-quality, and turned out to be high-quality**,
**neither of them may retract**.
[If he sold] **dark wheat** <note>original: "shhamtit" — a dark-colored or reddish grain</note>, **and it turned out to be white**, <insert>sandy-colored wheat</insert> <note>original: "shmatit" — a variant reading referring to a different variety of grain</note>
**white, and it turned out to be dark**, <insert>sandy-colored wheat</insert>
**olive wood, and it turned out to be sycamore**,
**sycamore, and it turned out to be olive**,
**wine, and it turned out to be vinegar**,
**vinegar, and it turned out to be wine**,
**both of them may retract**. <note>In these cases, the error is not merely about quality but about the "essence" or "type" of the object. Because the buyer received a different species or category than requested, the transaction is considered fundamentally voidable by either side.</note>

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 5 Mishnah 7

9

**One who sells produce to his fellow**,
[if the buyer] **pulled** <term>pulled: "mashakh" — the act of "meshikha," a formal legal procedure where the buyer physically moves the item to finalize ownership</term> **and did not measure, he has acquired it**;
[if the seller] **measured and [the buyer] did not pull, he has not acquired it**.
**If [the buyer] was clever, he rents the place** [where the produce is located]. <insert>rents</insert> <note>By renting the floor space where the produce sits, the buyer's "domain" (property) performs the acquisition for him as soon as the produce is measured into it.</note>
**One who purchases flax from his fellow**,
**behold, he has not acquired it**,
**until he moves it from place to place**,
**and if it was still attached to the ground...**

# Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 5 Mishnah 8
## 10

->One who sells wine or oil to his fellow,<-
->and they rose in price or decreased in price,<-
->if the measure was not yet filled,<-
->[the gain or loss belongs] to the seller;<-
->and once the measure is filled,<-
->[it belongs] to the purchaser.<- <note>The completion of filling the measure marks the point where ownership—and thus the risk of price fluctuation—transfers to the buyer.</note>
->If there was a broker between them,<- <note>A middleman or agent who handles the goods.</note>
->and the jug broke,<-
->it broke to the broker's loss.<-
->He [the seller] is obligated to let three drops drip for him [the buyer].<- <note>After pouring, the seller must wait for these last drops to ensure the buyer receives the full measure.</note>
->If he tilted the vessel and drained it,<-
->this [excess] belongs to the purchaser.<-
->And the shopkeeper is obligated to let three drops drip for him.<-
->Rabbi Yehuda says:<-
->On Friday evenings at dusk,<-
->he is exempt.<- <note>original: "erev Shabbat" — The rush to finish business before the Sabbath begins waives the requirement for the time-consuming "three drops."</note>

# Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 5 Mishnah 9
## 11

->One who sends his son to the shopkeeper,<-
->and he [the shopkeeper] measured out an <term>issar</term> of oil for him, and gave him the <term>issar</term>;<- <note>An *issar* was a common Roman copper coin; here it refers to a small quantity of oil worth that coin.</note>
->if [the son] broke the flask and lost the <term>issar</term>,<-
->the shopkeeper is liable.<- <note>Because the shopkeeper gave the oil and change to a minor who is not legally responsible, the shopkeeper remains liable for the loss.</note>
->Rabbi Yehuda exempts [the shopkeeper],<-
->for it was on this condition [accepting the risk] that he [the father] sent him.<-
->But the Sages agree with Rabbi Yehuda:<-
->When the flask is in the child’s hand,<-
->and the shopkeeper measured into it,<-
->the shopkeeper is exempt.<- <note>In this case, the shopkeeper did not provide the vessel, so he is not responsible for its breaking.</note>

## Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 5 Mishnah 11

->13<-

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel <note>A leading 2nd-century sage and head of the Sanhedrin.</note> said:
In what case do these words apply? Regarding liquid [measures],
but regarding dry [measures], he does not need to [clean them as frequently].
He is obligated to tilt the balance for him [the buyer] by a <term>handbreadth</term>. <note>Hebrew: *tefach*. In weighing, the seller must allow the scale to dip visibly in the buyer's favor rather than keeping it perfectly level.</note>
If he was weighing for him exactly "eye to eye" <note>meaning the scale was perfectly level</note>,
he must give him <term>additions</term> <note>Hebrew: *gerumim*—extra amounts to ensure the buyer is not cheated by the weight of the container or loss of product.</note>,
one [part] in ten for liquids,
and one [part] in twenty for dry goods.

->14<-

In a place where they are accustomed to measure with a small measure,
one may not measure with a large measure; <gloss><with a large [measure]></gloss> <note>original: "be-gassa"—the gloss provides an alternate spelling/Aramaic variant.</note>
with a large measure, one may not measure with a small measure.
In a place where it is customary to level [the measure], one may not heap it;
where it is customary to heap it, one may not level it. <note>These laws emphasize that local commercial custom defines the legality of a transaction; any deviation is considered a form of deception.</note>

# Chapter 6

## Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 6 Mishnah 1

->1<-

One who sells produce to his fellow and they did not sprout—
even if they were flax seeds—
he is not liable for their warranty. <note>The assumption is that the buyer bought them for food or oil, not for planting. Therefore, the seller is not responsible if they fail to grow.</note>
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
For garden seeds that are not edible,
he is liable for their warranty. <note>Since these seeds cannot be eaten, it is obvious they were purchased for planting; if they do not sprout, the "product" is considered fundamentally defective.</note>

## Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 6 Mishnah 2

->2<-

One who sells produce to his fellow,
the buyer must accept upon himself [a standard amount of] a quarter-measure of refuse per <term>se'ah</term>; <note>A *se'ah* is an ancient volume measure (approx. 7–8 liters). It was standard for bulk produce to contain a small amount of pebbles or chaff.</note>
For figs, he accepts upon himself ten wormy ones per hundred;
For a wine cellar, he accepts upon himself ten [jars of] souring wine per hundred;
For jars in the Sharon [region], he accepts upon himself ten <term>damaged jars</term> per hundred. <note>Hebrew: *potsot*. These were jars from the Sharon coastal plain, known for being poorly fired or thin-walled and thus prone to cracking.</note>

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 6 Mishnah 3

ג
One who sells wine to another, and it turned sour,
he is not liable for its replacement. <note>Under normal circumstances, once the wine is delivered, the buyer assumes the risk that it might spoil. Ancient wine was prone to turning into vinegar if not handled correctly.</note>
But if it was known that his wine <note>referring to the seller's stock in general</note> habitually turns sour,
then it is a <term>transaction in error</term> <note>Hebrew: *mikach ta'ut*. This is a legal grounds for voiding a sale if the product had a hidden defect unknown to the buyer at the time of purchase.</note>.
If the seller said to him:
"I am selling you fragrant wine,"
he is liable to ensure it remains good until the <term>Festival of Assembly</term> <note>Hebrew: *Atzeret*, referring here to the holiday of Shavuot. This occurs in late spring/early summer; if the wine survives the initial seasonal heat until Shavuot, the seller has fulfilled his word.</note>.
If he sells "old" wine, it must be from the previous year;
if "aged" wine, it must be from three years ago.

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 6 Mishnah 4

ד
One who sells a space to another for him to build a house,
and likewise, one who accepts a contract from another to build a wedding house for his son,

he must build it four <term>cubits</term> by six. <note>A cubit (amah) is approximately 18 inches or 45-50 centimeters. This 4x6 proportion was considered the minimum functional living space.</note>

Rabbi Ishmael says:
That is merely a cattle stall!
One who wants to make a cattle stall,
builds it four cubits by six.
A "small house" is six by eight.
A "large house" is eight by ten.
A <term>parlor</term> <note>Hebrew: *Traklin*, from the Greek *triclinium*, a formal reception or dining room.</note> is ten by ten.
Its height must be equal to half its length and half its width combined. <note>For example, if a room is 10x10, the total is 20, so the height should be 10.</note>
As proof of this standard,
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
It should be according to the proportions of the <term>Sanctuary</term> <note>Hebrew: *Heikhal*, the main hall of the Holy Temple in Jerusalem.</note>.

# Chapter 7

## Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 7 Mishnah 1
### 1

**One who says to his fellow:**
**"I am selling you a <term>beit kor</term> of soil,"** <note>A *beit kor* is an area of land requiring one *kor* (approx. 390 liters) of seed for sowing; roughly 75,000 square cubits or 3.7 acres.</note>
**if there were crevices ten <term>handbreadths</term> deep,** <note>Hebrew: *tefachim*. A handbreadth is the width of a fist, about 3-4 inches (8-10 cm).</note>
**or rocks ten handbreadths high,**
**they are not measured with it.** <note>Because these features are too deep or high for normal plowing, they are not counted toward the total area of the "soil" sold.</note>
**If they are less than this, they are measured with it.**
**And if he said to him:**
**"Approximately a *beit kor*,"**
**even if there were crevices deeper than ten handbreadths,**
**or rocks higher than ten handbreadths,**
**behold, these are measured with it.**

> **"Measure by the rope,"** <note>A legal phrase indicating the buyer expects an exact measurement.</note>

<header>Chapter 8</header>

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 8 Mishnah 1

->1<-

There are those who **inherit** <note>Hebrew: *nochalim* – receiving an estate from a deceased relative.</note> and **bequeath** <note>Hebrew: *manchilim* – passing an estate to heirs upon one's own death.</note>,
those who **inherit** but do not **bequeath**,
those who **bequeath** but do not **inherit**,
and those who neither **inherit** nor **bequeath**.
These **inherit** and **bequeath**:
A father from his sons,
and sons from their father,
and brothers from the same father **inherit** from one another and **bequeath** to one another.
A man inherits from his mother,
a man inherits from his wife,
and the sons of sisters inherit from their mother's brothers—these **inherit** but do not **bequeath**. <note>The Mishnah explains that while a man inherits his mother or wife, the law does not allow the mother or wife to inherit from him. Similarly, nephews inherit from their maternal uncles, but the uncles do not inherit from the nephews.</note>
A woman to her son,
a woman to her husband,
and the brothers of one's mother to their sister's sons—these **bequeath** but do not **inherit**.
And brothers from the same mother neither **inherit** from one another nor **bequeath** to one another. <note>Biblical inheritance law is based on the paternal line; therefore, maternal half-siblings are not legally considered heirs to one another.</note>

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 8 Mishnah 2

->2<-

**The order of inheritance is as follows:** (Numbers 27:8)
> "If a man dies and has no son, 
> then you shall transfer his inheritance to his daughter."
The son takes precedence over the daughter,
and all descendants of the son take precedence over the daughter.
The daughter takes precedence over the brothers [of the deceased],
and all descendants of the daughter take precedence over the brothers.
The brothers take precedence over the brothers of the father [uncles],
and all descendants of the brothers take precedence over the brothers of the father.
This is the general rule:
Whoever takes precedence in the order of inheritance, their descendants also take precedence.
The father takes precedence over all his descendants. <note>If the deceased has no children or grandchildren, the estate goes "upward" to the father before it goes "sideways" to the brothers.</note>

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 8 Mishnah 3

->3<-

The **daughters of Zelophehad** <note>A landmark biblical case from the Book of Numbers, where five sisters petitioned for their deceased father's land portion since he had no sons. Their plea established the law that daughters inherit when there are no male heirs.</note> took three portions in the inheritance:

It outlines the specific biblical order of succession, prioritizing sons and their descendants before daughters, and daughters before brothers.</summary>

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 8 Mishnah 4

## 4

->4<-

Both the **son** and the **daughter** are equal regarding the right to an **inheritance** <term>nachala: a hereditary estate</term>, except that the [firstborn] son takes a **double portion** <note>Hebrew: *pi shenayim*</note> in the property of the father, but he does not take a double portion in the property of the mother.
And daughters are **sustained** <note>provided with food, clothing, and shelter</note> from the property of the father, but they are not sustained from the property of the mother.

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 8 Mishnah 5

## 5

->5<-

One who says:
"My son, so-and-so, who is a **firstborn**, shall not take a double portion,"
or "My son, so-and-so, shall not inherit with his brothers,"
has said **nothing** <note>Meaning: his words have no legal standing.</note>,
for he has stipulated against that which is written in the **Torah** <note>Torah law defines the firstborn's right as absolute; a father cannot simply "veto" it through the laws of inheritance.</note>.
If one divides his property by his own word,
increasing for one and decreasing for another,
or equating the **firstborn** to the others,
his words **stand**.
But if he said this "by way of **inheritance**,"
he has said nothing.
If he wrote—whether at the beginning, middle, or end—
"by way of a **gift**,"
his words **stand**. <note>A person cannot change the *laws* of inheritance, but they can distribute their wealth as *gifts* while they are alive.</note>

## 6

->6<-

One who says:
"So-and-so shall inherit from me" in a place where there is a **daughter**,
or "My daughter shall inherit from me" in a place where there is a **son**,
has said **nothing**,
for he has stipulated against that which is written in the **Torah**.
**Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka** says:
If he said this regarding someone who is **eligible** to inherit from him <note>For example, choosing one son over another among several sons.</note>,
his words **stand**;
but regarding someone who is **not eligible** to inherit from him,
his words do not stand.

<summary>This page outlines the legal distinction between "inheritance" and "gifts," establishing that while Torah-mandated inheritance (like the firstborn's double portion) cannot be verbally canceled, a person may redistribute their estate if they frame the transfer as a gift.</summary>

If the father sold it, it is sold only **until he dies** <note>The buyer only purchases the father's temporary right to use the land.</note>.
If the son sold it, the buyer has **nothing** in it until the father dies.

## Chapter 9

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 9 Mishnah 1

->1<-

One who died and left sons and daughters: 
When the property is **plentiful**, the sons inherit and the daughters are sustained <note>The daughters receive their maintenance (food, clothing, shelter) from the estate until they come of age, while the sons take the remainder as inheritance.</note>. 
When the property is **meager**, the daughters are sustained, and the sons shall **beg at the doors** <note>This is a radical social safety net: the law prioritizes the daughters' survival and dignity, even if it leaves the sons with nothing, to prevent the daughters from being forced into a state of total vulnerability.</note>. 
**Admon** <note>A famous judge in Jerusalem during the late Second Temple period.</note> says: 
"Because I am male, have I lost out?" <note>Admon argues against this ruling, questioning why the son should be penalized simply because the estate is small.</note>

<summary>This page outlines the laws of inheritance and maintenance for adult and minor children, establishing that while heirs generally share equally, daughters' basic sustenance takes legal priority over sons' inheritance in cases of poverty.</summary>

## Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 9 Mishnah 2

If a person died and left behind sons, daughters, and a **tumtum**, <term>tumtum: a person whose biological sex is not discernible at birth</term>
In a case where the estate is large, 
the males "push" him toward the females. <note>In a large estate, sons inherit while daughters receive only maintenance. Because the tumtum's status as a male is uncertain, he cannot claim a son's share of the inheritance; instead, he is treated like a daughter and receives only basic maintenance.</note>
In a case where the estate is small, 
the females "push" him toward the males. <note>In a small estate, the law prioritizes the maintenance of daughters, sometimes leaving nothing for the sons' inheritance. Here, because the tumtum's status as a female is uncertain, he cannot claim the daughter's priority right to maintenance and is left with the sons who receive nothing.</note>
If a person says:
> "If my wife bears a **male**, he shall take a **maneh**," <term>maneh: a unit of currency worth 100 silver zuz</term>
If she bears a male, he takes a *maneh*.
> "And if she bears a **female**, she shall take **two hundred**,"
If she bears a female, she takes two hundred. 
> "If a **male**, a **maneh**; if a **female**, **two hundred**,"
If she bears both a male and a female, 
the male takes a *maneh* and the female takes two hundred.

**3**
If she bears a *tumtum*, he takes nothing. 
But if the father had said:
> "Whatever my wife shall bear shall take [a portion]," 
then this child [the *tumtum*] shall take a portion. 
If there is no other heir but him, 
he inherits everything.

### Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 9 Mishnah 4

these are not collectible in court,
because they are acts of loving-kindness.

intended to eventually come with her to her husband’s house,

## Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 10 Mishnah 1

1
A **simple document** <term>simple document: "get pashut," a standard flat deed where the text and signatures are on the same side</term> has its witnesses signed within it <note>original: "mitokho," meaning on the face of the document below the text</note>.
A **folded document** <term>folded document: "get mekushar," a more complex deed where each line of text is folded and stitched, with signatures on the back of each fold to prevent forgery</term> has its witnesses signed on its back.
If a simple document was written with its witnesses on its back,
or a folded document was written with its witnesses within it,
both are **invalid.**
Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel says:
A folded document that was written with its witnesses within it is **valid**, because the holder could simply choose to treat it as a simple document <note>by not folding or stitching it</note>.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
Everything follows the **local custom.** <note>The validity of the document's format depends on the established practice of that specific region.</note>

---

## Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 10 Mishnah 2

2
A simple document requires **two witnesses**,
while a folded document requires **three witnesses**.
A simple document that has only [one witness,
or a folded document that has only] two witnesses <gloss>its witnesses</gloss>,
both are **invalid.**
If it was written in the document:
"One hundred Zuz, which are twenty Selas," <gloss>Selas</gloss> <note>A "Sela" is worth 4 "Zuz." Therefore, 20 Selas equal only 80 Zuz. There is a contradiction in the amount.</note>
the claimant is entitled to only **twenty Selas.** <note>The rule is that the smaller amount is always enforced in cases of discrepancy to protect the person who owes the money.</note>
"One hundred Zuz, which are thirty Selas," <gloss>Selas</gloss> <note>30 Selas equal 120 Zuz. Again, a contradiction.</note>
the claimant is entitled to only [one Maneh.] <note>A "Maneh" is 100 Zuz. Since the document mentioned 100 Zuz first, and 30 Selas (120 Zuz) second, the smaller amount (100) is taken.</note>
"Silver Zuz that they are..." and the rest was erased,
the claim is for **no less than two** Zuz. <note>Because the plural "Zuzin" (Zuz units) implies at least two.</note>
"Silver Selas that they are..." <gloss>silver</gloss> and the rest was erased,
the claim is for **no less than two** Selas.
"Darics <term>Daric: "darkon," a Persian gold coin</term> that they are..." and the rest was erased,
the claim is for **no less than two** Darics.

3
If it was written at the top "one Maneh" <note>100 Zuz</note> and at the bottom "two hundred,"
or at the top "two hundred" and at the bottom "one Maneh,"
**everything follows the text at the bottom.**
If so, why do we bother writing the text at the top?
So that if a single letter is erased from the bottom text,
one may learn the correct reading from the top text.

**Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel** <note>A leading 2nd-century sage and head of the Sanhedrin.</note> says:
If the borrower has assets,
in either case, the lender may not collect from the guarantor. <note>RSbG argues that the guarantor is only a backup; as long as the primary debtor has the means to pay, the lender must pursue them first.</note>

### 15
Similarly, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said:
Even one who is a guarantor for a woman regarding her **marriage contract** <term>marriage contract: "Ketubah," the document outlining a husband's financial obligations to his wife in the event of death or divorce</term>,
and her husband was divorcing her,
[the guarantor] must make [the husband] vow against any benefit [from her], <note>The husband must take a "Neder" (vow). This prevents the couple from colluding to divorce, having the guarantor pay the Ketubah, and then the couple remarrying and sharing the money.</note>
lest they perform a **conspiracy** <term>conspiracy: "Knunyah," a fraudulent plot to extract money</term> against this person's assets,
and then the husband takes back his wife.

## Tractate Bava Batra Chapter 10 Mishnah 8

### 16
One who lends to his fellow by means of a **formal deed** <term>formal deed: "Shtar," a document signed by witnesses which creates a public lien on the debtor's property</term>,
may collect from **encumbered properties** <term>encumbered properties: "Nekhasim Meshubadim," assets that the debtor sold to others after the debt was contracted, which can still be seized because the public deed serves as a warning to buyers</term>.
[One who lends] by means of [oral] witnesses,
may collect only from **free properties** <term>free properties: "Nekhasim Bnei Chorin," assets currently owned by the debtor and not sold to others</term>.
If he produced [the debtor's] own **handwriting** <term>handwriting: "K'tav Yado," a note of debt written by the borrower but lacking formal witness signatures</term> stating that he owes him,
he may collect only from free properties.
And a guarantor who appears after the signing of the deeds, <note>The text breaks off here; it refers to a guarantor who signs their name after the witnesses have already finalized the document.</note>

he may collect from **unencumbered property**. <term>unencumbered property: "nechasim bnei chorin," assets still owned by the debtor which are not "locked" by other legal liens</term>
An incident came before Rabbi Ishmael, and he said:
He may collect from unencumbered property.

Ben Nanas said to him:
He may collect neither from **liened property** <term>liened property: "nechasim meshubadim," assets the debtor sold to a third party after the debt was created</term>,
nor from unencumbered property.
He [Rabbi Ishmael] said to him:

He [Ben Nanas] said to him:
Consider the case of one who is choking another in the marketplace [demanding payment],
and a bystander says to him: "Leave him alone and I will give [the money] to you!"
The bystander is exempt from paying, because it was not upon the bystander's **trustworthiness** <note>original: "אֱמוּנָתוֹ" (emunato)</note> that the creditor lent the money. <gloss>The corrector wrote "his craft/profession" <note>original: "אוֹמָנוּתוֹ" (omanuto)</note> over an erased spot. And who is the guarantor that is indeed liable to pay?
If one says to the lender: "Lend to him and I will give [it] to you,"
he is liable, for it was on that condition that he lent it to him.
Rabbi Ishmael said:
One who wishes to become wise should occupy himself with **monetary laws**, <term>monetary laws: "dinei mamonot," civil and commercial jurisprudence</term>
for there is no discipline in the Torah greater than them,
as they are like a flowing spring.
And one who wishes to occupy himself with monetary laws
should serve [as a student of] Shimon ben Nanas.

but they may declare one or two.

# Chapter 2
## Tractate Sanhedrin Chapter 2, Mishnah 1

->1<-

The **High Priest** <term>High Priest: "Kohen Gadol," the supreme religious official in the Temple</term> **judges** others, and others **judge him**;
He **testifies**, and others **testify against him**;
He performs **Chalitzah** <term>Chalitzah: the "removal of the shoe" ceremony that releases a widow from the obligation of marrying her deceased husband’s brother</term>, and others perform **Chalitzah for his wife**;
Others may perform **Levirate marriage** <term>Levirate marriage: "yibbum," the practice of marrying the widow of a childless brother</term> **with his wife**,
But **he does not perform Levirate marriage**,
Because he is **forbidden from marrying a widow** <note>according to Leviticus 21:14, the High Priest may only marry a virgin</note>.
If a **death** occurs in his family,
He **does not go out behind the bier** <note>he does not follow the coffin in the funeral procession to maintain his ritual purity</note>.

## Chapter 3

### Tractate Sanhedrin Chapter 3 Mishnah 1

**1**
**Monetary cases** <term>Monetary cases: *Dinei Mamonot*; civil litigations involving money, property, or damages, as opposed to capital cases</term> are decided by **three judges**.
This party chooses one judge for himself, and that party chooses one for himself,
and both of them together choose another one.
These are the words of **Rabbi Meir** <note>Rabbi Meir was a famous scholar of the 2nd century known for his sharp logic</note>.
But the **Sages** say:
The two judges themselves choose the third one for them.

**2**
This party may **disqualify** the judge chosen by that one, and that party may disqualify the judge chosen by this one <insert>his judge</insert>.
These are the words of **Rabbi Meir**.
But the **Sages** say:
When is this so?
Only when he brings **proof** against them that they are relatives or are otherwise **disqualified** <note>legal disqualification could be due to past criminal behavior, such as gambling or usury, or a blood relationship to the litigants</note>.
But if the judges were **upright** or were **experts** <note>original: *mumchin*; recognized legal authorities</note> authorized by the court,
he cannot disqualify them.

<summary>This page concludes the laws of the king's conduct and introduces the procedures for appointing judges in civil monetary cases, highlighting the "Zabla" method of selection.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Tractate Sanhedrin Chapter 3, regarding the selection of judges and the disqualification of witnesses. The previous page established that in civil cases, each party selects a judge, and together they select a third.</meta>

### 3

This party may **disqualify** <term>Disqualify: *Posel*; to declare a witness or judge unfit for service based on legal grounds</term> the witnesses of that party, and that party may disqualify the witnesses of this party. 
These are the words of **Rabbi Meir**. 
But the **Sages** say: 
When is this the case? 
Only when he brings **proof** regarding them that they are relatives or otherwise disqualified. 
But if they were **fit** <note>original: *kesherim*; meaning they meet the legal and moral requirements to testify</note>, he cannot disqualify them.

## Tractate Sanhedrin Chapter 3 Mishnah 2

### 4

If one said to another: 
"I accept **my father** as a judge for me," 
or "I accept **your father**," 
or "I accept **three cattle herders** <note>Cattle herders were often uneducated and lived away from society, making them generally undesirable as judges in a formal court</note> as judges for me,"
**Rabbi Meir** says: 
He is able to **retract** his agreement. 
But the **Sages** say: 
He is not able to retract his agreement.

### 5

If one owed his fellow an **oath** in court, 
and the fellow said to him: 
"Vow to me by the **life of your head**" <note>This refers to an informal oath rather than the standard legal oath using a sacred object or God's name</note>,
**Rabbi Meir** says: 
He is able to retract his agreement. 
But the **Sages** say: 
He is not able to retract his agreement.

# Tractate Sanhedrin Chapter 4 Mishnah 1

## 1
Both **civil law cases** <note>original: *dinei mamonot*; literally "laws of money," referring to lawsuits regarding property, debt, or damages.</note> and **capital law cases** <note>original: *dinei nefashot*; literally "laws of souls," referring to criminal cases where the defendant’s life is at stake.</note> require **inquiry and examination** <note>original: *drishah u’chakirah*; a rigorous cross-examination of witnesses to ensure their testimony is consistent and accurate.</note>, as it is stated in the Torah: <gloss>(Leviticus 24:22)</gloss>
"You shall have one manner of law." <note>This verse is interpreted to mean that the strict standards of evidence required for the death penalty should also be applied to monetary disputes to ensure justice.</note>
What are the differences between civil law cases and capital law cases?
Civil law cases are decided by **three** judges,
while capital law cases are decided by **twenty-three** judges.
In civil law cases,
the court may begin the deliberation with an argument either for **acquittal** <note>original: *zechut*; merit or innocence.</note> or for **conviction** <note>original: *chovah*; liability or guilt.</note>,
but in capital law cases,
the court must begin with an argument for **acquittal** and may not begin with an argument for **conviction**. <note>The court is required to search for a defense first to protect the life of the accused.</note>

## 2
In civil law cases, the judges reach a decision by a majority of **one**, <gloss>The proofreader added the word "even" <note>original: *ad*</note> above the line before "one," and did the same below.</gloss>
whether for acquittal or for conviction;
but in capital law cases, they reach a decision by a majority of one for **acquittal**,
yet they require a majority of **two** for **conviction**. <note>A 12-to-11 split can free a man, but it takes a 13-to-10 split to sentence him to death.</note>

## 3
In civil law cases,
the court may reverse a ruling either for acquittal or for conviction. <note>If new evidence or a legal error is found, the verdict can be changed regardless of who it helps.</note>
But in capital law cases,
the court may reverse a ruling for **acquittal**, but they may **not** reverse a ruling for **conviction**. <note>Once a person is found innocent in a capital trial, the case is closed to protect them from "double jeopardy."</note>

## 4
In civil law cases,
**everyone** may argue for either acquittal or conviction. <note>Even the students of the sages who are watching the proceedings may offer their opinions.</note>
But in capital law cases,
**everyone** may argue for acquittal,
but not everyone may argue for conviction. <note>In capital cases, students may speak up to save the accused, but only the ordained judges may argue to convict.</note>

## 5
In civil law cases,
one who argued for conviction may later argue for acquittal,
and one who argued for acquittal may later argue for conviction.
But in capital law cases,
one who argued for conviction may later argue for acquittal,
however, one who argued for acquittal
**cannot** turn back and argue for conviction. <note>This rule ensures that the judges lean toward mercy; once a judge sees a reason for innocence, they are not permitted to change their mind to favor death.</note>

<term>Civil law cases (Dinei Mamonot)</term>: Legal disputes regarding money or property.
<term>Capital law cases (Dinei Nefashot)</term>: Criminal trials where the punishment can be the death penalty.
<term>Acquittal (Zechut)</term>: A judgment that the defendant is innocent or not liable.
<term>Conviction (Chovah)</term>: A judgment that the defendant is guilty or liable for payment.
<term>Sanhedrin</term>: The rabbinic judicial assembly.
<term>Inquiry and Examination (Drishah u’Chakirah)</term>: The process of questioning witnesses about the specific time, place, and circumstances of an event.

<summary>This page outlines the fundamental differences in judicial procedure between civil and capital cases, highlighting the many safeguards placed on capital trials to favor the defendant's acquittal. It establishes that while both require rigorous cross-examination, capital cases require more judges, a larger majority for conviction, and stricter rules against reversing an innocent verdict.</summary>
<keywords>Sanhedrin, civil law, capital punishment, acquittal, conviction, judicial procedure, cross-examination, majority rule, Jewish law, Mishnah</keywords>

--- Page 782 ---
<meta>This page continues the comparison between civil and capital legal procedures from the previous page, focusing on the timing of verdicts, the order of judicial deliberation, and the physical layout of the courtroom.</meta>

6
In **civil law cases**, they may judge during the day and finish the proceedings at night. <note>In property or money disputes, the law is more flexible regarding time to ensure a swift resolution.</note>
But in **capital law cases**, they must judge during the day and finish the proceedings only during the day. <note>Cases involving life and death require the clarity of daylight to prevent errors that might occur in the exhaustion or darkness of night.</note>

7
In **civil law cases**, they may conclude the trial on that same day, whether for **acquittal** <note>original: *zechut*; a ruling in favor of the defendant.</note> or for **conviction** <note>original: *chovah*; a ruling against the defendant.</note>.
But in **capital law cases**, they may conclude the trial on that same day for **acquittal**,
but only on the following day for **conviction**. <insert><the following day></insert> <note>original: *she-l’acharyo*; this requirement for a "cooling-off" period ensures the judges have slept and reflected before deciding to end a human life.</note>
Therefore, the court does not sit to judge capital cases on the **Eve of the Sabbath** or on the **Eve of a Festival**. <note>Because if the defendant were to be convicted, the verdict would have to be delayed until after the holy day, causing unnecessary emotional distress (affliction of the soul) to the prisoner.</note>

### Tractate Sanhedrin Chapter 4 Mishnah 2

8
In **civil law cases** and cases of **ritual purity and impurity**, <note>original: *teharot* and *temeot*; laws regarding the spiritual status of objects and people.</note>
they begin the deliberation with the **greatest** judge. <note>The most senior or learned judge speaks first to set the tone for the discussion.</note>
But in **capital law cases**, they begin from the **side**. <note>original: *min ha-tzad*; meaning they start with the most junior judges. This prevents the younger judges from being intimidated or simply agreeing with the Chief Justice’s opinion without thinking for themselves.</note>
Everyone is eligible to judge **civil law cases**,
but not everyone is eligible to judge **capital law cases**—
only **Priests**, **Levites**, and **Israelites** who are of sufficient lineage to marry into the Priesthood. <note>Judges in capital cases had to come from families with impeccable records of conduct and ancestry to ensure the gravity of the office was maintained.</note>

### Tractate Sanhedrin Chapter 4 Mishnah 3

9
The **Sanhedrin** <note>The High Court of twenty-three or seventy-one judges.</note> was arranged in the shape of a **half-circular threshing floor**,
so that they could all see one another.
And two **scribes of the judges** stood before them,
one on the right and one on the left,
and they would write down the arguments of those who favored **conviction** and the arguments of those who favored **acquittal**.
**Rabbi Judah** says:
There were three scribes:
one to write the arguments for **conviction**,
one to write the arguments for **acquittal**,
and the third to write both the arguments for **conviction** and for **acquittal**. <note>The third scribe served as a backup to verify the records of the first two and resolve any discrepancies.</note>

## Tractate Sanhedrin Chapter 5 Mishnah 2

->2<-

Whoever increases the <term>examinations</term> <note>original: *bedikot*; supplementary questions about circumstantial details, such as the color of clothing or the type of tree at a crime scene.</note> is considered praiseworthy. <gloss>is praised</gloss>
There was a case where Ben Zakkai <note>Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, a leading sage in the late Second Temple period.</note> examined witnesses even regarding the stalks of figs <note>original: *oktzei te'enim*. This story illustrates the extreme detail of his questioning to test the witnesses' consistency.</note>.
And what is the difference between <term>investigations</term> <note>original: *hakirot*; the seven mandatory questions concerning the time and place of the event.</note> and examinations?
Regarding investigations, if one witness says "I do not know," or if two witnesses say "we do not know," their testimony is voided. <note>Since time and place are essential for the defense to potentially provide an alibi, ignorance of these details invalidates the case.</note>
But regarding examinations, if one says "I do not know," or even if two say "we do not know," their testimony remains valid.
However, whether it be investigations or examinations, at any time that the witnesses contradict one another, their testimony is voided.

## Tractate Sanhedrin Chapter 5 Mishnah 3

->3<-

If one witness says, "it happened on the second of the month,"
and the other says, "it happened on the third,"
their testimony remains valid,
because one might have known of the <term>fullness of the month</term> <note>original: *iburo shel chodesh*; the Jewish calendar alternates between 29 and 30 days. If a witness didn't know the previous month was "full" (30 days), they would be off by one day.</note> and the other did not.
If one says, "it happened on the third,"
and the other says, "on the fifth,"
their testimony is voided.
If one says, "it was at the second hour," <note>Roughly 8:00 AM.</note>
and the other says, "it was at the third," <note>Roughly 9:00 AM.</note>
their testimony remains valid. <note>Small discrepancies in time are attributed to human error in estimating the sun's position.</note>
If one says, "it was at the third hour,"
and the other says, "it was at the fifth,"
their testimony is voided.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
It remains valid.
But if one says, "it was at the fifth hour,"
and the other says, "it was at the seventh," <note>11:00 AM vs 1:00 PM. This spans the noon hour when the sun moves from east to west, making such an error unlikely.</note>

Their testimony is voided, [for example, if one says] that at the fifth hour the sun was in the east, and [the other says] at the seventh hour the sun was in the west. <note>In the ancient world, the "fifth hour" is roughly 11:00 AM and the "seventh hour" is roughly 1:00 PM. Since the sun cannot move from the eastern sky to the western sky in just two hours, such a contradiction proves the witnesses are unreliable.</note>

## Tractate Sanhedrin Chapter 5 Mishnah 5
### 5
If they found grounds for <term>merit</term> for him, they released him. And if not, they delay his judgment until the next day. <note>In capital cases, a conviction could not be reached on the same day as the trial to prevent impulsive rulings; the judges had to sleep on the decision.</note>
And they would pair up in groups, and they would reduce their food, and they would not drink wine all day, and they would discuss the matter all night. And on the next day, they would rise early and come to the court.
The one who <term>acquits</term> <note>original: *mazkeh*</note> says:
> "I am one who acquits, and I remain acquitting in my place."
And the one who <term>convicts</term> <note>original: *mechayev*</note> says:
> "I am one who convicts, and I remain convicting in my place."
One who taught <term>liability</term> <note>original: *chovah*</note> may now teach <term>merit</term>, but one who taught <term>merit</term> cannot go back and teach <term>liability</term>. <note>This rule demonstrates the strong legal bias toward saving a life: a judge could change his mind from 'Guilty' to 'Innocent' after a night of reflection, but he was not permitted to change from 'Innocent' to 'Guilty'.</note>
And if they erred in the matter, <insert>wandered/erred</insert> <note>original: *ta'u*; the text provides a spelling variant in brackets.</note>

### Chapter 8

#### Tractate Sanhedrin Chapter 8 Mishnah 1
->1<-

**A wayward and rebellious son**,
from what time does he become liable as a wayward and rebellious son?
From the time he produces two [pubic] hairs, until his beard is fully grown.
This refers to the "lower" beard, not the "upper" [facial] beard,
but the Sages spoke in refined language <note>The Sages used the word "beard" as a euphemism for pubic hair to maintain modesty in the text.</note>,
as it is said (Deuteronomy 21:18) "**If a man has a son**,"
meaning a "son," but not a daughter;
a "son," but not yet a man <note>An adult male is no longer under the specific jurisdiction of this law, which applies only to the transitional period of early puberty.</note>.
A minor is exempt, as he has not yet reached the age of accountability for the commandments.

#### Tractate Sanhedrin Chapter 8 Mishnah 2
->2<-

From what point is he liable?
From the time he eats a **tartemar** <term>tartemar: an ancient weight roughly equal to half a pound (a half-litra)</term> of meat,
and drinks a half-**log** <term>log: a liquid measure roughly equal to the volume of six eggs</term> of Italian wine.
Rabbi Yosei says:
A maneh <note>a larger weight, roughly 100 dinars or 500 grams</note> of meat and a full log of wine.
If he ate at a feast for the sanctification of the New Moon,
if he ate the Second Tithe in Jerusalem <note>Second Tithe (Ma'aser Sheni) had to be eaten in Jerusalem in a state of purity; eating it did not count toward the "gluttony" of a rebellious son because it was a religious duty.</note>,
if he ate carcasses of animals not properly slaughtered, torn animals, swarming creatures, or crawling things,
if he ate something that was a religious duty <note>original: mitzvah</note> or something that was a specific transgression <note>original: averah; i.e., he ate non-kosher food</note>;
if he ate any other food but did not eat meat,
or if he drank any other drink but did not drink wine,
he does not become a wayward and rebellious son,
until he eats meat and drinks wine, as it is said: (Deuteronomy 21:20)
"**a glutton and a drunkard**."
Even though there is no absolute proof for these specific amounts, there is a scriptural allusion to it: (Proverbs 23:20)
"**Do not be among those who drink wine to excess, or among those who gorge themselves on meat.**"

## Tractate Sanhedrin Chapter 8 Mishnah 5

->7<-

A **wayward and rebellious son** <note>original: *ben sorer u-moreh*</note> is judged according to his ultimate end.
Let him die while he is still innocent <note>meaning, before he has committed a capital crime like murder</note> and let him not die when he is truly guilty.
For the death of the wicked is a benefit to them and a benefit to the world,
but for the righteous, it is a hardship for them and a hardship for the world.
Wine and sleep for the wicked is a benefit to them and a benefit to the world <note>As they are prevented from sinning while asleep or incapacitated</note>,
but for the righteous, it is a hardship for them and a hardship for the world.
The dispersion of the wicked is a benefit to them and a benefit to the world,
but for the righteous, it is a hardship for them and a hardship for the world.
The gathering of the wicked is a hardship for them and a hardship for the world,
but for the righteous, it is a benefit to them and a benefit to the world.
Tranquility for the wicked is a hardship for them and a hardship for the world,
but for the righteous, it is a benefit to them and a benefit to the world.

## Tractate Sanhedrin Chapter 8 Mishnah 6

->8<-

One who **breaks into a house** <note>original: *ha-ba ba-machtaret*, literally "one who comes through a tunnel/breach."</note> is judged according to his ultimate end <note>The law presumes that a burglar is prepared to kill the homeowner if resisted; therefore, the homeowner may kill the burglar in self-defense.</note>.
If he was breaking in and shattered a jug [belonging to the homeowner]:
if he "has blood," <note>original: *yesh lo damim*. This is a legal idiom meaning the burglar's life is still protected—for example, if it is known he would not kill, such as a father breaking into a son's home—and thus killing him would be considered murder.</note> he is liable [to pay for the jug].
if he "has no blood," <note>original: *ein lo damim*. This means his life is legally forfeit in that moment; the homeowner can kill him with impunity.</note> he is exempt [from paying for the jug]. <note>This follows the principle that a person is not punished twice (financially and with death) for a single act.</note>

## Tractate Sanhedrin Chapter 8 Mishnah 7

->9<-

These are the ones who are **saved at the cost of their lives** <note>This refers to the "Law of the Pursuer" (*rodef*). It means a bystander must stop these individuals from committing their crime, even if it requires killing them.</note>:
One who pursues his fellow to kill him,
and one who pursues a male [for sexual assault], and one who pursues a betrothed maiden [to rape her].
But one who pursues an animal [to commit bestiality],
or one who desecrates the Sabbath,
or one who worships idols—
one does not "save" them at the cost of their lives <note>Because these sins, while grave, do not involve the immediate, irreversible physical violation or death of another person that would justify a bystander taking the law into their own hands. These individuals must be judged in a formal court.</note>.

And included in the general category of **"a woman and her daughter"** <note>This refers to the biblical prohibition in Leviticus 18:17. In the Mishnaic legal system, these specific forbidden relationships are punished by burning.</note> are:
His daughter, his granddaughter through his daughter, and his granddaughter through his son;

A murderer and the inhabitants of a **subverted city** <note>original: *ir ha-nidachat*. This refers to an Israelite city that has been led astray into idolatry, as described in Deuteronomy 13.</note>.

### 2

A **murderer** <note>original: *rotzeach*</note> is one who strikes his fellow with either a stone or an object of iron,
or one who holds another person down in the water or in a fire,
so that he is unable to climb out of there, and he dies:
he is **liable** <note>original: *chayav*, meaning legally responsible and subject to the death penalty.</note>.
If he pushed him into the water or into the fire,
but the victim was capable of climbing out of there, yet he died:
the attacker is **exempt** <note>original: *patur*. In this context, it means he is not liable for capital punishment by the court, though the act is still forbidden.</note>.
If he incited a dog against him,
or incited a snake against him:
he is **exempt**.
If he caused the snake to bite him <note>By pressing the snake's fangs into the victim's flesh.</note>:
Rabbi Yehuda deems him **liable**,
but the Sages deem him **exempt**.

### 3

If one strikes his fellow, whether with a stone or with a fist,
and they **assessed** <note>original: *amaduho*. A medical/legal evaluation performed by the court to see if the blow was lethal.</note> that he would die from the blow,
but then the victim’s condition improved from what it was,
and afterward it worsened and he died:
the attacker is **liable**.
Rabbi Nehemiah deems him **exempt**, for **there is a basis for the matter** <note>original: *raglayim la-davar*. This idiom suggests that because the victim’s condition improved, there is a "footing" or logical reason to assume that a secondary cause—not the original blow—led to the eventual death.</note>.

->Tractate Sanhedrin Chapter 9 Mishnah 2<-

### 4

If he **intended** to kill an animal but killed a person instead,
or intended to kill a non-Jew but killed an Israelite,
or intended to kill a non-viable newborn <note>original: *nefalim*, infants born prematurely who cannot survive.</note> but killed a viable infant:
he is **exempt**.

### 5

If he intended to strike him on his waist,
and the blow was not sufficient to kill him if it landed on his waist,
but the blow landed instead upon his heart <note>A more vulnerable area where the same amount of force would be lethal.</note>, and he died:
[the attacker is exempt].

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion from the previous page regarding the "assessment" of a lethal blow. ...And the blow had enough force to kill if it struck the heart,
and he died.
If he aimed for the heart,
and there was enough force in the blow to kill if it struck the heart,
but the blow struck him on his waist,
and there was not enough force in it to kill if it struck the waist,
yet he died:
If he aimed to strike a large person,
and there was not enough force in the blow to kill a large person,
but the blow struck a small person instead,
and there was enough force to kill the small person,
and he died:
If he aimed to strike a small person,
and there was enough force in the blow to kill a small person,
but the blow struck a large person instead,
and there was not enough force in it to kill a large person,
yet he died:
he is **exempt** <note>original: *patur*. In Jewish law, for a person to be executed for murder, there must be a perfect alignment of intent, the potential of the weapon, and the specific result. If the physics of the blow did not match the intent, the court cannot impose the death penalty.</note>.

ו

If he aimed to strike him on his waist,
and there was enough force in the blow to kill if it struck the waist,
but the blow struck him on his heart instead,
and he died:
If he aimed to strike a large person,
and there was enough force in the blow to kill a large person,
but the blow struck a small person instead,
and he died:
he is **liable** <note>original: *chayav*. Here, because the blow was already deemed "lethal" for the intended target, the fact that it struck a more vulnerable person or a more vulnerable part of the body does not excuse the killer.</note>.
**Rabbi Simeon says:**
Even if he intended to kill one specific person but killed another person instead,
he is **exempt**.

## Tractate Sanhedrin, Chapter 9, Mishnah 3

A murderer who was mixed among others <note>meaning a group of people where one is a known murderer, but he can no longer be identified</note>, they are all **exempt**.

We place him in the **cell** <note>original: *kippah*. This was a small, vaulted room or cell. When a murderer could not be legally executed due to a technicality, they were sometimes placed in this cell and fed a meager diet of bread and water until their health failed, effectively a life sentence.</note>.
And all those liable for different types of death penalties who became mixed with one another,
they are judged by the **lighter** penalty <note>The four types of capital punishment—stoning, burning, decapitation, and strangulation—were ranked by severity. If the court knows a person deserves death but isn't sure which kind, they apply the most lenient one.</note>.
For example: those liable to be **stoned** who were mixed with those liable to be **burned**.
**Rabbi Simeon says:**
They are judged by **stoning**, because **burning** is more severe. <note>original: *serefah chamura*. There is a famous debate in the Talmud about which death penalty is the most painful or shameful; Rabbi Simeon considers burning to be the most severe of all.</note>

**Rabbi Akiva says:**
**[He is punished] by strangulation.**
**And the Sages say:**
**[He is punished] by the hands of Heaven <note>meaning he is not executed by a human court, but faces divine retribution</note>.**

# Chapter 11

## Tractate Sanhedrin Chapter 11 Mishnah 1

->1<-
->These are those who are executed by strangulation:<- <note>Strangulation (chenek) was one of the four types of capital punishment in Jewish law, traditionally considered the least severe of the four.</note>
->One who strikes his father or his mother,<-
->one who kidnaps a person <note>literally: "steals a soul"</note> from Israel,<-
->a rebellious elder who defies the ruling of the High Court,<- <term>Zaken Mamre: a qualified judge who rules against the final decision of the Great Sanhedrin in Jerusalem.</term>
->a false prophet,<-
->one who prophesies in the name of an idol,<-
->one who has forbidden relations with a married woman,<-
->and conspiring witnesses who testified against a priest's daughter and her lover.<- <note>Normally, a priest's daughter who commits adultery is executed by burning, but her lover and those who conspired to frame her are executed by strangulation.</note>

->2<-
->One who strikes his father or his mother<-
->is not liable for the death penalty unless he causes them a physical wound.<-
->In this regard, the law is more stringent for one who curses a parent than for one who strikes a parent,<-
->for one who curses a parent after their death is still liable,<-
->whereas one who strikes a parent after their death is exempt.<-
->One who kidnaps a person from Israel<-
->is not liable until he brings the victim into his own domain.<-
->Rabbi Judah says:<-
->He is not liable until he brings him into his domain and makes use of him as a servant,<-
->as it is said (Deuteronomy 24:7): "and treats him as a slave and sells him."<-
->Regarding one who kidnaps his own son:<-
->Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka holds him liable,<-
->but the Sages exempt him from the death penalty.<-
->If one kidnapped a person who is half-slave and half-free,<-
->Rabbi Judah holds him liable,<-
->but the Sages exempt him.<-
