### 4
If he <note>the Rebellious Elder</note> returned to his city,
and repeated and taught in the manner he was accustomed to teaching,
he is exempt,

he is not liable until he instructs them to act.
A student who instructed others to act is exempt;
thus, his stringency is his leniency. <note>Because a student has not reached the level of a formal judge, his unauthorized rulings are not considered legally impactful enough to warrant the death penalty of a 'Rebellious Elder,' even though his arrogance is a 'stringent' or serious matter.</note> <gloss>his leniency</gloss>

### 5
There is greater stringency in the words of the Scribes than in the words of the Torah.
One who says "There is no requirement for Tefillin," <term>Tefillin: Phylacteries; leather boxes containing Torah verses worn during prayer.</term>
thereby seeking to bypass the words of the Torah, he is exempt;
but if he says "There must be five compartments," <note>original: "חָמֵשׁ טוֹטָפוֹת"</note>
thereby adding to the words of the Scribes, he is liable. <note>The Torah requires four compartments in the head-tefillin. The Sages (Scribes) defined exactly how they are made. A judge who defies the Sages' specific definitions is punished more severely than one who simply denies the biblical root, because the Sages' authority is the final protection for the Law's application.</note>

# Tractate Makkot

## Chapter 1

### Tractate Makkot Chapter 1 Mishnah 1

**1**
**How do witnesses become "conspiring witnesses"?** <note>original: "עדים זוממים" (Edim Zomemim). These are witnesses who are proven false not by evidence regarding the crime itself, but by "alibi" evidence proving the witnesses were in a different location at the time of the alleged event.</note>
**"We testify against man so-and-so, that he is the son of a divorcee,"**
**or "the son of a woman who underwent *chalitzah*,"** <term>Chalitzah: A ritual that releases a widow from the requirement of marrying her deceased husband's brother. The son of such a woman or a divorcee is disqualified from serving as a Priest (Kohen).</term>
We do not say,
"Let this witness be made the son of a divorcee or the son of a woman who underwent *chalitzah* in his place" <note>This refers to the biblical principle of "You shall do to him as he conspired to do to his fellow" (Deut 19:19). Since priesthood status cannot be transferred to someone not born into it, the literal punishment is impossible.</note>,
rather, he receives forty lashes. <note>In practice, the court administered thirty-nine lashes.</note>
**"We testify against man so-and-so, that he is liable to go into exile,"** <note>Exile to a City of Refuge was the penalty for accidental manslaughter.</note>
We do not say, "Let this witness go into exile in his place,"
rather, he receives forty lashes.
**"We testify against man so-and-so,**
**that he divorced his wife and did not give her the settlement of her marriage contract";** <term>Ketubbah: The marriage contract providing a financial settlement for a woman in the event of divorce or the husband's death.</term>
But surely, whether today or tomorrow,
he will eventually have to give her the marriage settlement! <note>The witnesses are not trying to create a new debt, but rather to force the husband to pay immediately instead of at an undetermined future date.</note>
They estimate how much a person would be willing to pay for the rights to this woman’s marriage settlement,
considering that if she becomes a widow or is divorced [the buyer would receive the money],
but if she dies [before her husband], her husband will inherit her [and the buyer would receive nothing].

**2**
**"We testify against man so-and-so,**
**that he owes his fellow one thousand *zuz*,** <note>A *zuz* is a silver coin equivalent to a Roman denarius.</note>
**on the condition that he pays them from now until thirty days,"**
and the defendant says:
**"from now until ten years,"**
they estimate how much a person would be willing <insert>to give</insert> to have one thousand *zuz* in his hand,
the difference between paying them from now until thirty days,
and paying them from now until ten years.

### Tractate Makkot Chapter 1 Mishnah 2

### 3

"We testify against man so-and-so,
that he owes his fellow two hundred *zuz*," <note>A *zuz* was a silver coin, roughly a day's wage.</note>
and they were found to be conspiring witnesses,
they receive lashes and they pay [the money],
for the legal category that brings them to lashes is not the same as that which brings them to payment. <note>Rabbi Meir argues that the prohibition against bearing false witness is a separate violation from the attempted financial harm.</note>
These are the words of Rabbi Meir.
But the Sages say:
Anyone who pays does not receive lashes. <note>The Sages hold by the principle that a person is not punished twice for a single act; the more severe or specific penalty (usually the payment in civil cases) cancels out the other.</note>

->Tractate Makkot Chapter 1 Mishnah 3<-

### 4

"We testify against man so-and-so,
that he is liable for forty lashes,"
and they were found to be conspiring witnesses,
they receive eighty lashes: [forty] from there <gloss>(Exodus 20:13)</gloss>
"You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor,"
and [forty] from there <gloss>(Deuteronomy 19:19)</gloss>
"Then you shall do to him as he conspired to do to his brother,"
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
But the Sages say:
They receive only forty lashes.

### 5

Financial [penalties] are divided into three, but lashes are not divided into three. <note>Meaning, shared among the group of witnesses.</note>
How so?
If they testified against him that he owes his fellow two hundred *zuz*,
and they were found to be conspiring witnesses,
they divide [the payment] among themselves.
If they testified against him that he is liable for forty lashes,
and they were found to be conspiring witnesses,
each and every one [of the witnesses] receives forty lashes. <note>While a debt is a single sum to be repaid collectively, corporal punishment is an individual obligation of the body that cannot be mathematically split between people.</note>

->Tractate Makkot Chapter 1 Mishnah 4<-

### 6

Witnesses do not become conspiring witnesses
until they themselves are conspired against. <note>This is a technical requirement: to be "conspiring witnesses," a second set of witnesses must testify against the *people* rather than just contradicting the *facts*. They must say: "You could not have seen this, because you were with us in a different city at that time."</note>
How so?
If they said:
"We testify against man so-and-so,
that he killed a person."

If [other witnesses] said to them:
"How can you testify?
For this victim or this killer
was with us on that day in such-and-such a place,"
they are not **conspiring witnesses.** <note>This is a case of simple contradiction (*hakhashah*). Because the second set of witnesses only disputes the facts of the crime, we do not know which pair is lying, and no one is punished.</note>

This is seen as a direct assault on the witnesses' persons rather than just their story.</note>

If a tree stands inside the boundary but its foliage <note>original: "nofo" — the branches and leaves of the tree</note> hangs outside the boundary, or if it stands outside the boundary and its foliage hangs inside the boundary—everything follows the foliage <note>For the purposes of legal boundaries, the location of the branches determines whether the killer is considered "inside" the protected area or "outside" and vulnerable to the blood redeemer.</note>.
If he killed someone within that same city <note>meaning, a person who was already in exile in a City of Refuge committed another accidental killing there</note>, he must exile from one neighborhood to another neighborhood within the city.
A **Levite** <note>original: "Ben Levi" — a member of the tribe of Levi; they were the residents and owners of the Cities of Refuge</note> who kills accidentally must exile from one city to another city.

## Tractate Makkot Chapter 2 Mishnah 8

14
Similarly, if a **manslayer** <note>original: "rotzeach" — one who kills accidentally</note> arrived at his City of Refuge and the people of the city wished to honor him <note>perhaps because of his previous social status or scholarly standing</note>, he must say to them: "I am a killer."
If they replied to him: "Even so, we wish to honor you," he may accept the honor from them, as it is stated: "And this is the matter <note>original: "dvar" — can also mean "word" or "speech"</note> of the killer" (Deuteronomy 19:4) <note>The Sages interpret "the word" to mean the killer must speak and declare his status.</note>.

15
The cities provided to the **Levites** <note>original: "Leviyim"</note> were for a fee <note>the killer paid rent for his dwelling</note>. These are the words of **Rabbi Judah**.
**Rabbi Meir** says: They did not pay a fee to them.
And he returns to the **position of authority** <note>original: "serarah" — such as a communal leadership role or public office</note> that he previously held. <gloss>to the position of authority</gloss> These are the words of Rabbi Meir.
But Rabbi Judah says: He did not return to the position of authority that he previously held <note>Rabbi Judah believes that although the exile atones for the sin, the stigma remains enough to disqualify him from leadership.</note>. <gloss>to the position of authority</gloss>

## Tractate Makkot Chapter 3 Mishnah 12

->14<-

**How do they flog him?**
One **binds his two hands to a column** on this side and on that side.
The **court officer** <note>original: "hazan haknesset" — here referring to the executive officer of the court who carries out the sentence</note> **takes hold of his garments**;
if they tear, they tear; and if they come apart at the seams, they come apart,
**until he uncovers his chest.** <note>the Hebrew "libo" literally means "his heart," referring to the chest area</note>
And a **stone is placed behind him** <note>the offender</note>,
the **court officer stands upon it**,
and a **calf-hide strap** is in his hand,
**doubled** from one into two, and from two into **four**,
and two additional straps rise and fall within it. <note>these smaller thongs were attached to the main strap to increase the effect of the lash</note>

## Tractate Makkot Chapter 3 Mishnah 13

->15<-

Its **handle is a handbreadth** <note>original: "tefach" — a standard unit of measure based on the width of a fist, roughly 3–4 inches</note> and its **width is a handbreadth**,
and its **tip reaches the pit of his stomach.**
And he **strikes him one-third in the front** <note>on the chest</note>
and **two-thirds in the back** <note>divided between the two shoulders</note>.
And he **does not strike him while he is standing or sitting**,
but rather **leaning**, as it is said: (Deuteronomy 25:2)
> **"And the judge shall cause him to fall."** <note>the Hebrew "v'hipilo" implies a stooped or prostrate position</note>
And the one who strikes, **strikes with one of his hands with all his strength.**

> **all the words of this Law** <note>original: "Torah"</note>

the officer is **exempt** <note>from legal liability, as he was performing a court-mandated duty</note>.

# Tractate Shevuot
<note>Shevuot translates to "Oaths." While the title refers to verbal promises, the tractate also covers the laws of ritual impurity and the specific sacrifices required for various transgressions.</note>

## Chapter 1

### Tractate Shevuot Chapter 1 Mishnah 1
**1**
**Oaths** are **two**, which are [actually] **four**.
**Awareness of impurity** <note>original: "yedi'ot ha-tum'ah" — knowing that one is ritually impure or that they have entered the Sanctuary while impure</note> is **two**, which are [actually] **four**.
**Exits of the Sabbath** <note>referring to the prohibition of carrying objects from a private domain to a public one</note> are **two**, which are [actually] **four**.
**Appearances of plagues** <note>original: "negayim" — skin afflictions described in Leviticus, often translated as leprosy</note> are **two**, which are [actually] **four**.
<note>The "two that are four" formula refers to the two primary categories mentioned explicitly in the Torah and the two secondary categories derived from them by the Sages.</note>

### Tractate Shevuot Chapter 1 Mishnah 2
**2**
**In any case where there is awareness at the beginning and awareness at the end, but a lapse of awareness in between,**
**behold, this is [atoned for] by a sliding-scale sacrifice.**
<note>original: "oleh ve-yored" — literally "rising and falling." This is a sacrifice where the type of offering depends on the person's wealth: a lamb for the rich, two birds for those of modest means, or fine flour for the poor.</note>
**If there is awareness at the beginning but no awareness at the end,**
**the goat offered inside** <note>one of the two goats used in the Yom Kippur service in the Temple</note> **and the Day of Atonement suspend [the punishment]**
**until it becomes known to him, and then he brings a sliding-scale sacrifice.**

## Tractate Shevuot Chapter 2 Mishnah 1

->1<-
->The [types of] awareness of ritual impurity are two that are four:<-
->He became impure and knew it,<-
->but the impurity was forgotten by him, while he remained mindful of the holy food;<-
->[or] the holy food was forgotten by him, while he remained mindful of the impurity;<-
->[or] both this and that were forgotten by him,<-
->and he ate the holy food without knowing [of the violation at the time],<-
->he is liable for a "rising and falling" sacrifice. <note>original: "oleh ve-yored" — a sliding-scale offering where the cost is adjusted based on the person's financial means, ranging from a lamb to birds or fine flour.</note>

->2<-
->He became impure and knew it,<-
->but the impurity was forgotten by him, while he remained mindful of the Sanctuary;<-
->[or] the Sanctuary was forgotten by him, while he remained mindful of the impurity;<-
->[or] both this and that were forgotten by him,<-
->and he entered the Sanctuary without knowing, and once he exited he knew [of the violation],<-
->he is liable for a "rising and falling" sacrifice.

<meta>This page continues the legal debate regarding the validity of oaths, specifically contrasting "optional" oaths with those made concerning religious commandments. It transitions into defining the legal categories of "oaths of expression" and "vain oaths."</meta>

They said to him:
No!
If you spoke regarding an **optional oath** <note>original: "shevuat ha-reshut" — an oath regarding mundane, voluntary activities like eating or sleeping.</note>,
where the Torah treated a negative oath like a positive one <note>Meaning, both a promise to do something and a promise *not* to do something are equally binding.</note>,
would you say the same regarding an **oath of a commandment**,
where the Torah did not treat the negative like the positive? <note>This refers to the principle that one cannot "swear away" a biblical obligation; an oath *not* to perform a commandment is legally void from the start.</note>

## Tractate Shevuot Chapter 3 Mishnah 7

### 8

> "I swear that I will not eat this loaf,"
> [and then again,] "I swear that I will not eat it,"
> and he ate it,
> he is only liable for one [violation].
> This is an **oath of expression** <note>original: "Shevuat Bitui" — a standard oath regarding one's own future or past actions.</note>,
> for which intentional violation incurs **lashes**,
> and for unintentional violation, one must bring an **ascending and descending offering** <note>original: "korban oleh ve-yored" — a variable sacrifice where the cost is adjusted based on the person's financial means (wealthy bring a lamb, poor bring birds, the very poor bring flour).</note>.

### 9

> A **vain oath** <note>original: "Shevuat Shav" — an oath taken in vain, such as swearing to something obviously false or impossible.</note>,
> for its intentional violation, one is liable for **lashes**,
> but for its unintentional violation, one is **exempt** <note>Meaning, unlike the "oath of expression," there is no requirement for a sacrifice if the vain oath was made by mistake.</note>.

->(Tractate Shevuot Chapter 3 Mishnah 8)<-

> What is a **vain oath**?
> Swearing to change that which is known to man:
> [For example,] he said of a stone pillar that it is of gold,
> or of a man that he is a woman,
> or of a woman that she is a man.
> [Or swearing] about a thing that is impossible for him:
> "If I did not see a camel flying in the air,"
> or "If I did not see a snake as large as the beam of an olive press" <note>An ancient hyperbole for an impossibly thick or straight creature.</note>.
> [Or if] he said to witnesses, "Come and testify for me!"
> and they replied, "We swear that we will not testify for you!" <note>This is a vain oath because they are already commanded by the Torah to testify; an oath cannot cancel that duty.</note>
> Swearing to cancel a **commandment** <note>original: "mitzvah" — a divine decree.</note>:
> such as not to build a <term>Sukkah</term> <note>A temporary hut used during the festival of Sukkot.</note>,
> or not to take a <term>Lulav</term> <note>The palm branch used in Sukkot rituals.</note>,
> or not to don <term>Tefillin</term> <note>Phylacteries; small leather boxes containing scrolls of Torah used during prayer.</note>,
> this is a **vain oath**,
> for which intentional violation incurs **lashes**,
> and for unintentional violation, one is **exempt**.

## Tractate Shevuot Chapter 3 Mishnah 9

<summary>This page defines the legal distinctions between an 'oath of expression' (regarding personal actions) and a 'vain oath' (regarding impossible or forbidden acts), detailing the different punishments and sacrificial requirements for each.</summary>
<keywords>oaths, Shevuat Bitui, Shevuat Shav, lashes, sacrifice, mitzvah, Sukkot, Tefillin, legal liability</keywords>

--- Page 834 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical classification of oaths, specifically differentiating between the "oath of expression" (a standard promise regarding one's actions) and the "vain oath" (swearing to something contradictory or impossible). It also introduces the "oath of testimony," which deals with witnesses in a legal setting.</meta>

"I swear that I ate this loaf,"
"I swear that I will not eat it,"
the first is an **oath of expression** <note>original: "shevuat bitui" — an oath regarding one’s past or future actions, such as "I ate" or "I will eat."</note>,
and the second is a **vain oath** <note>original: "shevuat shav" — an oath that is inherently false or contradictory. Here, since he already swore that he ate it, swearing he will not eat it is a "vain" use of God's name because it contradicts his own established testimony.</note>.
If he ate it, he has violated the **vain oath**.
If he did not eat it, he has violated the **oath of expression**. <note>Because his first statement—that he had already eaten it—turned out to be false.</note>

## Tractate Shevuot Chapter 3 Mishnah 10

->**11**<-
An **oath of expression** applies to men, to women,
to those unrelated [to the case], to relatives,
to those legally fit [to testify], to those legally unfit,
in the presence of a **court of law** <note>original: "Beit Din"</note>, and not in the presence of a court of law,
[when made] from one's own mouth.
And one is liable for its intentional violation with **lashes** <note>original: "makkot" — judicial corporal punishment.</note>,
and for its unintentional violation, an **ascending and descending offering** <note>original: "korban oleh ve-yored" — a sliding-scale sacrifice where the cost depends on the person's financial means.</note>.

## Tractate Shevuot Chapter 3 Mishnah 11

->**12**<-
A **vain oath** applies to men, to women,
to those unrelated, to relatives,
to those legally fit, to those legally unfit,
in the presence of a court of law, and not in the presence of a court of law,
[when made] from one's own mouth.
And one is liable for its intentional violation with **lashes**,
but for its unintentional violation, one is **exempt** <note>Unlike the oath of expression, there is no sacrifice brought for accidentally taking a vain oath.</note>.
Both regarding this [the oath of expression] and regarding that [the vain oath],
one who is put under oath by the words of others is liable.
[For example, if someone else says:] "I adjure you that you did not eat today,"
or "I adjure you that you did not put on **phylacteries** <term>tefillin: ritual leather boxes containing scrolls of the Torah, worn during prayer</term> today,"
and he replied "**Amen**," he is liable. <note>In Jewish law, answering "Amen" to another person's adjuration is the legal equivalent of uttering the oath oneself.</note>

How does the **oath of testimony** <term>original: "Shevuat Ha-Edut" — an oath taken by potential witnesses claiming they have no evidence to offer in a financial case.</term> work?

Because [after the first denial in court] they are unable to retract and confess <note>In Rabbi Shimon's view, once the witnesses deny testimony in court, their legal status is "set." ### Tractate Shevuot Chapter 6 Mishnah 1

### 1

**The Oath of the Judges** <term>Shevuat HaDayanin: An oath imposed by the court on a defendant who admits to part of a monetary claim but denies the rest.</term>
[is required when] the claim is at least **two silver coins**, and the admission is worth at least a **perutah**. <term>perutah: the smallest copper coin of the era</term> <note>original: *shetei kesef*. --"I have nothing of yours in my possession,"
he is **exempt** [from the biblical oath]. <note>This is a "total denial." A biblical oath is only triggered by a partial admission.</note>
"I have **two silver coins and a perutah** in your possession,"
--"I have nothing of yours in my possession,"
he is **exempt**.
"I have **two silver coins and a perutah** in your possession,"
--"I have nothing of yours except for a **perutah**,"
he is **liable** [to take the oath]. <note>Since he admitted to a portion (the perutah) and denied the rest (the two silver coins), the requirements for a court-imposed oath are met.</note>
"I have a **maneh** in your possession," <term>maneh: a sum of 100 silver zuz (denarii)</term>

But can we not learn this from the scroll of her ketubah,
for he [the husband] writes for her:
"If you should marry another,
you shall take what is written for you."
The House of Hillel retracted to concede to the words of the House of Shammai.

## Tractate Eduyot Chapter 1 Mishnah 13

## Tractate Eduyot Chapter 1 Mishnah 14
->16<-

An earthenware vessel protects everything [inside it from impurity],
according to the words of the House of Hillel <note>This refers to "corpse-impurity" in a tent. If a sealed earthenware jar is in a room with a body, the items inside normally remain pure because impurity cannot penetrate the outer walls of earthenware.</note>.
The House of Shammai say:
It only protects food, liquids,
and other earthenware vessels.
The House of Hillel said to them:
For what reason?
The House of Shammai said to them:
Because the vessel itself is [considered] ritually impure according to the standards of the <term>common folk <note>original: *am ha-aretz*. In this period, those who were not scrupulous about purity laws were assumed to be ritually impure. Shammai argues that an impure vessel cannot act as a barrier to protect other items from further impurity.</note></term>,
and an impure vessel cannot act as a screen [against impurity].
The House of Hillel said to them:
But did you not [just] declare the food and liquids within it to be pure?
The House of Shammai said to them:
When we declared the food and liquids within it pure,
we did so only for the common person's own needs;
but if you declare the [metal or wooden] vessel pure,
you have declared it pure for both yourself <note>The scholar/priest who maintains high purity standards.</note> and for him.
And the House of Hillel retracted their opinion to rule according to the words of the House of Shammai.

# Chapter 2

## Tractate Eduyot Chapter 2 Mishnah 1

**1**
Rabbi Hananiah, the Deputy High Priest <note>original: *Segan ha-Kohanim*. He was the second-in-command to the High Priest during the Second Temple period.</note>, testified about four things:
In all the days of the priests,
they never refrained from burning meat that had been defiled by a <term>secondary source of impurity <note>original: *velad ha-tum'ah*, literally "offspring of impurity." In the laws of ritual purity, this is an object that became unclean by touching a primary source.</note></term>
together with meat that had been defiled by a <term>primary source of impurity <note>original: *av ha-tum'ah*, literally "father of impurity." This is a source of uncleanness, such as a carcass, that transmits a higher level of ritual impurity.</note></term>,
even though they are thereby adding impurity to its existing impurity <note>Usually, one is forbidden to cause a sacred item to become more impure. However, since the meat was already destined for burning, the priests were not concerned about increasing its level of defilement.</note>.

**2**
Rabbi Akiva added to this:
In all the days of the priests,
they never refrained from lighting oil that had been disqualified by a <term>one who had immersed that day <note>original: *tevul yom*. This refers to a person or object that has gone to the ritual bath (mikvah) but must wait until sunset to be fully pure. In this state, they can still invalidate sacred food like oil.</note></term>
in a lamp that had been defiled by <term>corpse-impurity <note>original: *tamei met*. This refers to an object that has become a primary source of impurity through contact with a human body.</note></term>,
even though they are thereby adding impurity to its existing impurity.

## Tractate Eduyot Chapter 2 Mishnah 2

**3**
Hananiah, the Deputy High Priest, said:
In all my days, I never saw a hide go out to the place of burning <note>Meaning he never saw the hide of an animal designated for sacrifice being destroyed, even if the animal itself was found to be unfit for the altar.</note>.
Rabbi Akiva said:
From his words we have learned
that one who skins a <term>firstborn animal <note>original: *bechor*. The firstborn of a "clean" animal belongs to the priest.</note></term> and it is found to be <term>unfit <note>original: *treifah*. A term for an animal with a life-threatening physical defect that makes it forbidden to eat.</note></term>,
the priests may still derive benefit from its hide.
But the Sages say:
"We have not seen" is not a proof <note>This is a legal principle: the fact that someone did not witness an event does not prove that the event never happens or is forbidden.</note>, <insert>they are</insert>
rather, the hide must go out to the place of burning.

## Tractate Eduyot Chapter 2 Mishnah 4

### 5

Rabbi Ishmael said three things
before the Sages in the "Vineyard at Yavneh"<note>The "Vineyard" was a poetic name for the Sanhedrin (supreme court) at Yavneh, because the scholars sat in rows like vines in a vineyard.</note>:

it belongs to the homeowner;
otherwise, it belongs to the poor<note>This refers to the law of *Leket* (Gleanings), which mandates that stalks dropped during the harvest must be left for the poor. If the stalk is still effectively part of the unharvested crop, the owner may keep it.</note>.

it may be sown [with other seeds],

he is exempt;
but if it is for medicinal use,
he is liable.

<meta>This page continues Tractate Eduyot, moving into the third chapter. The previous page concluded the teachings of Rabbi Akiva regarding the duration of divine judgments. This section shifts focus to the legal disputes of Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas, a scholar of the late Second Temple and early Yavne periods, primarily concerning the laws of ritual impurity and agricultural tithes.</meta>

## 1

**And in the case of a corpse,**
**one who touches <term>half an olive’s bulk<note>original: *ke-chatzi zayit*. The standard minimum measure of a corpse’s flesh that conveys ritual impurity is the size of an olive (*zayit*).</note></term>, and <term>overshadows<note>original: *ma’ahil*. The law of "tents" (Ohel) states that if a person or object is under the same roof or overhang as a piece of a corpse, they become ritually impure.</note></term> half an olive’s bulk;**
**or touches half an olive’s bulk,**
**and half an olive’s bulk overshadows him;**
**or overshadows two half-olive bulks;**
**or overshadows half an olive’s bulk,**
**and half an olive’s bulk overshadows him;**
**Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas <term>declares him pure<note>original: *metaher*. Rabbi Dosa believes these different methods of contracting impurity—touching and overshadowing—do not combine to reach the required full "olive's bulk."</note></term>,**
**and the Sages <term>declare him impure<note>original: *metamein*. The majority view is that since the impurity comes from the same source (a corpse), the measures combine regardless of the method of contact.</note></term>.**

## 2

**But one who touches half an olive’s bulk,**
**and another object overshadows him and half an olive’s bulk;**
**or [if] he overshadows half an olive’s bulk,**
**and another object overshadows him and half an olive’s bulk,**
**he is pure.**
**Rabbi Meir said:**
**Even in this case, Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas declares him pure,**
**and the Sages declare him impure.**
**Everything is impure, except for [the combination of] contact**
**and carrying with a "tent" <note>Referring to the "overshadowing" mentioned previously.</note>.**
**This is the general rule:**
**Anything that comes from <term>one name<note>original: *mishem echad*. This refers to a single category or mode of transmitting impurity.</note></term> is impure;**
**from <term>two names<note>original: *mishnei shemot*. This refers to two different modes, such as touching versus carrying.</note></term>, it is pure.**

### Tractate Eduyot Chapter 3 Mishnah 2

## 3

**Separate food items do not combine [to reach the minimum measure of impurity].**
**These are the words of Rabbi Dosa.**
**And the Sages say:**
**They do combine.**
**One may <term>redeem<note>original: *mechalelin*. Second Tithe (Ma'aser Sheni) was produce that had to be eaten in Jerusalem. If one lived far away, they could "transfer" its sanctity onto a coin and spend that money on food in the city.</note></term> Second Tithe on <term>an unminted coin<note>original: *asimon*. A piece of metal used as a token that lacks an official government stamp or image.</note></term>.**
**These are the words of Rabbi Dosa.**
**And the Sages forbid it.**
**One may <term>immerse the hands<note>original: *matbilin yadayim*. Washing or immersing the hands to reach a high level of ritual purity.</note></term> for the <term>purification water<note>original: *chattat*. Specifically the water mixed with the ashes of the Red Heifer, used to purify those who have come into contact with the dead.</note></term>.**
**These are the words of Rabbi Dosa.**
**And the Sages say:**
**If his hands became impure, his [entire] body became impure.** <note>The Sages hold a more stringent view: in the context of the highly sacred Red Heifer water, there is no "impurity of the hands" alone; if the hands are touched by impurity, the whole person is considered unfit for the task.</note>

There is a captive woman who may eat <term>Terumah<note>original: *terumah*. The portion of the harvest given to the Priests. A Priest’s wife or daughter may eat it, but she is disqualified if she has been violated by a non-Jew. Captivity in wartime often raised this suspicion.</note></term>,
and there is a captive woman who may not eat.
How so?
A woman who says:
"I was taken captive, but I am <term>pure<note>original: *tehorah*. In this context, it means she was not violated during her captivity and thus remains ritually permitted to her husband and to the consumption of sacred food.</note></term>,"

and she says:
"I am pure,"
she may not eat <note>Because witnesses have established the fact of her captivity, her own testimony is no longer sufficient to overcome the legal suspicion of violation.</note>.

### Tractate Eduyot Chapter 3 Mishnah 7
->9<-

Regarding four cases of doubt, Rabbi Yehoshua declares the person or object <term>impure<note>original: *metame*. A state of ritual unfitness where one cannot touch sacred items or enter the Temple.</note></term>,
and the Sages declare them <term>pure<note>original: *mitaherin*.</note></term>.
How so?
When an impure person is standing and a pure person passes by,
or when a pure person is standing and an impure person passes by,
or when there is impurity in a <term>private domain<note>original: *reshut ha-yachid*. Usually an enclosed area. In Jewish law, a doubt regarding impurity in a private domain is generally ruled strictly (impure).</note></term> and a pure object in a <term>public domain<note>original: *reshut ha-rabbim*. A thoroughfare or open space. A doubt regarding impurity here is generally ruled leniently (pure).</note></term>,
or when there is a pure object in a private domain and impurity in a public domain.
Whether it is a doubt if one touched or did not touch,
or a doubt if one <term>overshadowed<note>original: *he’ehil*. The transmission of impurity (especially from a corpse) by being under the same roof or by one object being directly over another.</note></term> or did not overshadow,
or a doubt if one <term>moved<note>original: *hissit*. Impurity conveyed by causing an object to move, even without direct physical contact.</note></term> an object or did not move it—
Rabbi Yehoshua declares it impure,
and the Sages declare it pure.

## Chapter 4

### Tractate Eduyot Chapter 4 Mishnah 1
א
These are the matters among the leniencies of the **House of Shammai** and the stringencies of the **House of Hillel**:
An egg that was laid on a Festival,
the **House of Shammai** says:
It may be eaten;
and the **House of Hillel** says:
It may not be eaten.
The **House of Shammai** says:
The minimum volume of <term>leaven<note>original: *se’or*. A sourdough starter or fermenting agent.</note></term> for which one is liable on Passover is an <term>olive-bulk<note>original: *kezayit*. The standard Rabbinic unit of volume, approximately the size of a large olive.</note></term>, and for <term>leavened bread<note>original: *chametz*.</note></term> it is a <term>date-bulk<note>original: *kekotevet*. A volume slightly larger than an olive.</note></term>;
but the **House of Hillel** says:
For both this and that, the measure is an **olive-bulk**.

### Tractate Eduyot Chapter 4 Mishnah 2
ב
One who slaughters a wild beast or a bird on a Festival,
the **House of Shammai** says:
He may dig with a <term>spade<note>original: *deker*. A pointed tool or crowbar used for digging.</note></term> and cover the blood;
but the **House of Hillel** says:
He should not slaughter at all,
unless he already had loose earth ready for use.
However, they agree that if he has already slaughtered,
he may dig with a spade and cover the blood;
for the ashes of the stove are considered already prepared.

and the poor may redeem the fruit for themselves;
but the **House of Hillel** says:

### Tractate Eduyot Chapter 4 Mishnah 7

### ז

A woman is <term>betrothed<note>original: *mitkadeshet*. The first legal stage of a Jewish marriage, where the woman becomes "set apart" for her husband.</note></term> with a <term>denarius<note>original: *dinar*. A silver coin of significant value.</note></term> or the value of a denarius,
according to the words of the **House of Shammai**;
But the **House of Hillel** say:
With a <term>perutah<note>original: *perutah*. The smallest denomination of copper coin in the Second Temple period.</note></term> or the value of a perutah.
And how much is a **perutah**?
One-eighth of an **Italian issar** <note>The *issar* was a Roman copper coin (*as*). Rabbinic law defines the minimum value of marriage based on these historical currencies.</note>.

The **House of Shammai** say:
A man may release his wife with an <term>old bill of divorce<note>original: *get yashan*. A divorce document that was written, but then the couple was alone together before it was actually delivered.</note></term>;
But the **House of Hillel** prohibit it <note>The House of Hillel is concerned that if they were alone together after the document was written, they may have reconciled, making the previous document void.</note>.
And what is an **old bill of divorce**?
Any document where he stayed alone with her after he wrote it for her.

One who divorces his wife and then stays with her in an <term>inn<note>original: *pundaki*. A public lodging house.</note></term>:
The **House of Shammai** say:
She does not require a second **bill of divorce** from him;
But the **House of Hillel** say:
She requires a second **bill of divorce** from him <note>Hillel's school assumes that if a divorced couple stays in an inn together, they may have acted as a married couple, thus necessitating a new divorce to end the potential "new" marriage.</note>.
When does this apply?
In a case where she was divorced after **marriage**;
But they agree in a case where she was divorced after <term>engagement<note>original: *erusin*. The period after the legal betrothal but before the couple lives together in a shared home.</note></term>,
that she does not require a second **bill of divorce** from him,
because he is not yet <term>intimate with her<note>original: *libo gas bah*. Literally "his heart is familiar with her." Since they never lived together as a married couple, there is no legal assumption that they would have been intimate at the inn.</note></term>.

# [8]

The **House of Shammai** permit <term>rival wives<note>original: *tzarot*. In the context of levirate marriage (*yibbum*), if a man died childless, his brother was to marry his widow. If the man had multiple wives, and one was forbidden to the brother (e.g., she was his own daughter), the other wives were called 'rivals.' Shammai permitted the brother to marry these 'rival' wives, while Hillel forbade it.</note></term> to marry the surviving brothers,
but the **House of Hillel** forbid them.
(If they performed the <term>ceremony of release<note>original: *chalitzah*. A ritual involving the removal of a shoe that releases a widow and her brother-in-law from the obligation of levirate marriage.</note></term>, the **House of Shammai** disqualify them from marrying into the **priesthood**;
and the **House of Hillel** qualify them.
If they entered into <term>levirate marriage<note>original: *yibbum*. The act of a man marrying the childless widow of his deceased brother to continue the brother's line.</note></term>, the **House of Shammai** qualify them;
and the **House of Hillel** disqualify them.
And even though these disqualify and these qualify,
the **House of Shammai** did not refrain from marrying women from the **House of Hillel**,
nor did the **House of Hillel** refrain from marrying women from the **House of Shammai**.
And regarding all matters of **purity and impurity** that these would declare pure and those would declare impure,
they did not refrain from preparing <term>pure foods<note>original: *teharot*. Foods or vessels kept in a state of ritual readiness for consumption, often involving complex laws of contact.</note></term> using one another’s [vessels or food]. )
->(Tractate Eduyot Chapter 4 Mishnah 9)<-

Three brothers,
two of whom are married to two sisters,
and one is <term>unattached<note>original: *mufneh*. A brother who is currently single and available for levirate marriage obligations.</note></term>;
if one of the husbands of the sisters died,
and the unattached brother made a <term>formal proposal<note>original: *ma'amar*. A legal declaration or minor act of betrothal that reinforces the bond between a levir (surviving brother) and the widow.</note></term> to her,
and afterward his second brother died,
The **House of Shammai** say:
His [betrothed] wife remains with him,
and the other [sister] must depart because she is his **wife’s sister**.
But the **House of Hillel** say:
He must release his wife with a **bill of divorce** and the *ceremony of release*,
and his brother’s wife with the *ceremony of release*.
This is what they meant when they said:
"Woe to him because of his wife,
and woe to him because of his brother’s wife!"

If there is [an egg] similar to it sold in the market <note>This refers to an egg found inside a bird that was slaughtered and then discovered to be "treifah"—mortally wounded and thus unkosher.</note>,
it is **permitted**,
and if not, it is **prohibited**,
according to the words of the **House of Shammai**.
But the **House of Hillel** prohibit it [regardless],
though they agree regarding the egg of a <term>terefah<note>original: *treifah*. An animal with a physical defect or injury that makes it forbidden to eat.</note></term> <insert>moribund animal</insert> that it is **prohibited**,
because it grew in a state of prohibition.

The **blood of a Gentile woman** and the **blood of purity of a woman with a skin affliction** <term>tzara'at<note>original: *meczora'at*. A biblically described skin condition that requires ritual purification.</note></term>,
the **House of Shammai** declare them **ritually pure**,
and the **House of Hillel** say:
[Their status is] like **her saliva or her urine** <note>Meaning they are "secondary" liquids that convey impurity only through contact, unlike menstrual blood which is a "primary" source of impurity.</note>.

One may **eat the fruits of the Sabbatical year** <term>shvi'it<note>original: *shevi'it*. The seventh year of the agricultural cycle where the land in Israel lies fallow and produce is free for all.</note></term> whether as a **favor** or **not as a favor** <note>This refers to whether one expresses gratitude to the owner of the field, which might look like a commercial transaction.</note>,
according to the words of the **House of Shammai**.
But the **House of Hillel** say:
One may **not eat** them whether as a favor or not as a favor.

Regarding a **leather water-skin** <note>original: *hachemet*. A skin used for holding liquids.</note>,
the **House of Shammai** say:
[It is susceptible to ritual impurity only if it is] **tied up and stands** [on its own].
And the **House of Hillel** say:
**Even if it is not tied up**.

### Tractate Eduyot Chapter 5 Mishnah 2

#### 2

**Rabbi Yose** says:
There are **six matters** which are among the **lenient rulings of the House of Shammai** and the **stringent rulings of the House of Hillel**:

1. **Poultry** may be **placed on the table** with **cheese**, though it may not be eaten [together],
according to the words of the **House of Shammai**.
But the **House of Hillel** say:
It may **neither be placed** [on the table] **nor eaten**.

2. One may **separate tithes** <note>original: *tormin*. The act of setting aside the 'terumah' or priestly portion.</note> from **olives** to cover the obligation of **oil**,
or from **grapes** to cover the obligation of **wine**,
according to the words of the **House of Shammai**.
But the **House of Hillel** say:
One **may not separate tithes** [in this manner] <note>Usually, one must tithe processed goods from other processed goods, not from the raw fruit.</note>.

3. One who **sows** [crops] within the **four cubits of a vineyard** <note>This refers to 'kilayim', the prohibition against mixing species in a vineyard.</note>,
the **House of Shammai** say:
He has **sanctified** <note>In this context, 'sanctified' means the crop is forbidden for use and must be burned.</note> **one row**.
But the **House of Hillel** say:
He has **sanctified two rows**.

4. Regarding **dough-paste** <note>original: *me'isah*. A thick dish made by pouring boiling water over flour.</note>,
the **House of Shammai** **exempt** [it from the dough-offering] and the **House of Hillel** **obligate** [it].

<summary>This page concludes several disputes between Shammai and Hillel regarding purity and the Sabbatical year, before beginning a specific list where Shammai's school is surprisingly more lenient than Hillel's.</summary>
<keywords>Mishnah, Eduyot, Beit Shammai, Beit Hillel, Rabbi Yose, Sabbatical Year, Ritual Purity, Tithes, Poultry and Dairy, Kilayim</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the transition from the end of Chapter 4 into Chapter 5 of Tractate Eduyot. It concludes the discussion on Sabbatical year ethics and moves into specific instances where the House of Shammai is surprisingly more lenient than the House of Hillel, focusing on ritual purity and the status of sacred texts.</meta>

...the words of the **House of Shammai**.
One may **immerse** for ritual purification in a **rain torrent** <term>hardalit<note>original: *hardalit*. A swift flow of rainwater down a slope or hillside.</note></term>,
according to the words of the **House of Shammai**.
But the **House of Hillel** say:
One may **not immerse** [in it] <note>The House of Hillel requires the water for a ritual bath (mikvah) to be stationary rather than a flowing stream of rainwater.</note>.
A **convert** who converted on the **Eve of Passover**,
the **House of Shammai** say:
He **immerses and eats his Passover sacrifice** in the evening.
But the **House of Hillel** say:
One who **separates from the foreskin** <note>Referring to a newly circumcised convert.</note>
is like **one who separates from a grave** <note>The House of Hillel argues that the impurity of the "uncircumcised state" is severe; once removed, the convert must wait seven days of purification before eating the sacrifice, just as if they had been contaminated by a corpse.</note>.

## Tractate Eduyot Chapter 5 Mishnah 3
->3<-

**Rabbi Simeon** says:
There are **three things** that are among the **leniencies of the House of Shammai** and the **stringencies of the House of Hillel**:
The Scroll of **Ecclesiastes** <term>Kohelet<note>original: *Kohelet*. One of the books of the Hebrew Bible, traditionally attributed to King Solomon.</note></term> **does not render the hands impure**,
according to the words of the **House of Shammai** <note>In Rabbinic law, sacred scrolls "render the hands impure" to ensure they are handled with ritual care. Shammai's school held that Ecclesiastes was a work of human wisdom rather than divine inspiration, so it did not carry this status.</note>.
And the **House of Hillel** say:
It **renders the hands impure**.
**Purification waters** <term>mei chattat<note>original: *mei chattat*. Water mixed with the ashes of the Red Heifer, used to purify those who have come into contact with the dead.</note></term> that have **fulfilled their purpose** <note>Water that has already been sprinkled for purification.</note>,
the **House of Shammai** declare them **ritually pure**,
and the **House of Hillel** declare them **impure**.
**Black cumin** <term>ketzach<note>original: *ketzach*. Nigella sativa, a plant with small black seeds used for seasoning.</note></term>,
the **House of Shammai** declare it **pure**,
and the **House of Hillel** declare it **impure** <note>The dispute is whether these seeds are considered a "food" that can contract ritual impurity. Shammai considers them a spice/medicine, while Hillel considers them food.</note>.
And the **same** rule applies to **tithes** <note>Regarding whether black cumin is subject to the requirement of setting aside a portion for the priesthood.</note>.

---

## Tractate Eduyot Chapter 5 Mishnah 4
->4<-

**Rabbi Eleazar** says:
There are **two things** that are among the **leniencies of the House of Shammai** and the **stringencies of the House of Hillel**:
The **blood of a woman after childbirth** who has **not yet immersed**,
the **House of Shammai** say:
[Its status is] like **her saliva or her urine** <note>Meaning it is a "liquid" that only conveys impurity through direct contact while wet, rather than having the severe impurity of menstrual blood.</note>.
And the **House of Hillel** say:
It **conveys impurity** whether **wet or dry**.
But they **agree** regarding a **woman after childbirth who also has an irregular discharge** <term>zavah<note>original: *zova*. A woman experiencing blood flow outside her normal cycle, which carries a more severe ritual status.</note></term>,
that it **conveys impurity** whether **wet or dry**.

---
